topics.name: A Fib
topics.clinical_significance: An abnormal heart rhythm in which the heart's upper chambers (atria) beat chaotically instead of contracting in an organized way. The heartbeat is often irregular and may be fast, but some people have no symptoms. Blood may pool in the atria and form clots, increasing the risk of stroke.

topics.name: Abdominal Aortic Branch Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: A blockage in a branch of the abdominal aorta cuts blood flow to the organ or tissue it supplies. It may happen suddenly because of a blood clot or a tear in the artery wall, or develop slowly from narrowed arteries or pressure from a nearby mass. The effects depend on which artery is blocked and may include damage to the intestines, kidneys, liver, spleen, or legs.

topics.name: Abdominal Pain, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Recent abdominal pain can have many causes, from minor problems to emergencies such as a blocked bowel, a hole in the stomach or intestine, poor blood flow to the bowel, or a burst bulge in the main artery in the abdomen. Severe pain, a very tender or rigid abdomen, or signs of shock can occur with serious causes.

topics.name: Abdominal Pain, Chronic and Recurrent
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic abdominal pain lasts more than 3 months, either all the time or off and on. Recurrent abdominal pain means at least 3 episodes over 3 months that interfere with usual activities. Causes include diseases of abdominal organs and gut-brain disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome.

topics.name: Abdominal Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Abdominal injuries can follow a blow or a wound that enters the body. They may damage the abdominal wall, organs, or blood vessels. Serious injuries can cause internal bleeding or let stomach or bowel contents leak into the abdomen, causing severe inflammation. Some problems, such as infection or bowel blockage, may appear later.

topics.name: Abdominal Trauma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A blow, crash, or wound that enters the body can injure the abdominal wall, organs, or blood vessels. Serious injuries can cause internal bleeding or let stomach, bowel, or bladder contents leak into the abdomen, causing inflammation. Infection, bowel blockage, or pressure that harms organ function may develop later. Injuries to other parts of the body can occur at the same time.

topics.name: Ablation for Cardiac Arrhythmia
topics.clinical_significance: Ablation treats some abnormal heart rhythms by destroying or isolating a small area of heart tissue that triggers the rhythm. It is often done by passing a thin tube (catheter) into the heart and using heat, freezing, or electrical pulses. Possible serious complications include stroke, blood-vessel damage, or a hole in the heart.

topics.name: Abnormal Cervical Mucus
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical mucus is fluid made by the cervix. If it stays thick around ovulation, sperm may not pass through; infection or, rarely, antibodies may damage sperm. This problem rarely reduces fertility, except when long-term cervix inflammation or narrowing is present.

topics.name: Abnormal Liver Test Results, Asymptomatic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal liver blood tests can be found in people who feel well. Changes in liver enzymes, bile-related tests, or bilirubin may point to liver-cell injury, poor bile flow, or another problem. Causes include liver disease, alcohol, medicines, and some other conditions. Mild changes may go away, while lasting or large changes may need further evaluation.

topics.name: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: In people of reproductive age, uterine bleeding is abnormal when periods are heavier, longer, more frequent, irregular, or occur between periods. Causes include hormone or ovulation problems, fibroids, polyps, bleeding disorders, medicines, and rarely cancer. Heavy or prolonged bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia.

topics.name: Abortion, Spontaneous
topics.clinical_significance: A spontaneous abortion, also called a miscarriage, is the loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks. It often causes vaginal bleeding and cramps. Early losses are often linked to chromosome problems, although the cause is frequently unknown. Tissue left in the uterus can cause continued bleeding or infection.

topics.name: Abrasions
topics.clinical_significance: An abrasion is a scrape that removes the outer layer of skin and may reach deeper layers. It may cause pain or bleeding. Dirt or small objects can become trapped in deeper scrapes and raise the risk of infection.

topics.name: Abscesses
topics.clinical_significance: An abscess is a pocket of pus trapped in tissue, usually from a bacterial infection. A skin abscess is often painful, warm, red, and swollen; a deeper abscess may cause fever or affect an organ, and the infection can spread.

topics.name: Abuse of Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Mistreatment of older adults includes physical or emotional harm, sexual abuse, neglect, or improper use of their money or property. It may be intentional or unintentional and can cause injury, poor health, emotional distress, financial loss, or early death.

topics.name: AC Joint Sprain
topics.clinical_significance: An AC joint sprain injures the ligaments joining the collarbone to the top of the shoulder blade, usually after a fall onto the shoulder. It causes pain and tenderness; severe injuries can tear the ligaments and separate the bones, a problem often called shoulder separation.

topics.name: Acalculous Biliary Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Acalculous biliary pain is pain like gallstone pain even though routine scans do not find gallstones. It may be caused by tiny particles missed on scans or by poor emptying or other problems with the gallbladder or bile ducts. The pain is usually in the upper middle or right abdomen and may come with nausea or vomiting.

topics.name: Accelerated Interstitial Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute interstitial pneumonia, also called accelerated interstitial pneumonia, is a rare, rapidly worsening lung disease with no known cause. It causes fever, cough, and shortness of breath that can quickly progress to severe low blood oxygen and breathing failure. It is often fatal.

topics.name: Acetaminophen Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: An overdose of acetaminophen (paracetamol) may cause few or no early symptoms, then damage the liver over the next 1 to 3 days. Severe poisoning can lead to liver failure, kidney injury, and death.

topics.name: Achalasia
topics.clinical_significance: Achalasia is a disorder in which the tube carrying food to the stomach loses its normal squeezing movement and the valve at its lower end does not relax. Food and drink then pass slowly, causing trouble swallowing both solids and liquids and bringing up undigested food. The tube may widen, and food can enter the lungs, especially during sleep.

topics.name: Achilles Tendinopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Achilles tendinopathy is a problem caused by repeated strain to the tendon connecting the calf muscles to the heel. It causes pain and tenderness at the back of the heel, often worse during activity, and can make walking or running difficult. In some cases, the tendon can tear.

topics.name: Achilles Tendon Bursitis, Anterior
topics.clinical_significance: Anterior Achilles tendon bursitis is swelling and irritation of the small fluid-filled sac between the Achilles tendon and heel bone. It causes pain, warmth, and swelling at the back of the heel, which can make walking or wearing shoes difficult. It may follow rubbing or injury, or occur with gout or rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.name: Achilles Tendon Bursitis, Posterior
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior Achilles tendon bursitis is swelling of a small fluid-filled sac between the skin and Achilles tendon where the back of a shoe presses on the heel. It causes pain, warmth, and redness and may form a tender bump. Ongoing rubbing can wear down the skin.

topics.name: Achilles Tendon Enthesopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Achilles tendon enthesopathy is pain where the Achilles tendon attaches to the heel bone. It is often linked to repeated pulling on the tendon, tight calf muscles, or overuse, and can also occur with some types of inflammatory arthritis. Pain is usually at the back of the heel and worse when walking; a bone spur may form.

topics.name: Achilles Tendon Tears
topics.clinical_significance: An Achilles tendon tear is a partial or complete break in the tendon connecting the calf muscles to the heel, often during running or jumping. It causes sudden pain in the lower calf or ankle, with possible swelling and bruising. A complete tear makes walking and pushing off with the foot difficult.

topics.name: Acid Secretion, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cells in the upper part of the stomach make acid, which helps digestive enzymes break down food. Mucus and bicarbonate protect the stomach lining from this acid. Damage to these defenses, including from H. pylori infection or some pain medicines, can lead to stomach inflammation or ulcers.

topics.name: Acid-Base Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Acid-base disorders occur when changes in body acids, bicarbonate, or carbon dioxide disturb the blood’s balance. They may make the blood too acidic or too alkaline and are grouped as metabolic or breathing-related disorders. Mild cases may cause no symptoms, but severe cases can affect the heart, breathing, and brain.

topics.name: Acid-Base Regulation
topics.clinical_significance: Normal metabolism continually makes acids. Buffers, lungs, and kidneys work together to keep blood pH within a narrow range. The lungs adjust carbon dioxide through breathing; the kidneys remove acid and control bicarbonate, a base. Poor regulation can disrupt cell function and the body’s fluid and salt balance.

topics.name: Acid-Base Regulation and Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: The body keeps blood pH steady using chemical buffers, breathing, and the kidneys. If these controls fail, the blood can become too acidic or too alkaline. Severe imbalance can interfere with the work of the heart, lungs, and brain.

topics.name: Acinetobacter Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Acinetobacter bacteria can live on skin or surfaces without causing illness, but they can cause infections, most often in the lungs or wounds of hospitalized or critically ill people. Some strains resist many antibiotics, making serious infections difficult to treat.

topics.name: Acne
topics.clinical_significance: Acne is a common, long-lasting skin condition caused by blocked and inflamed hair follicles and oil glands, usually on the face, chest, or back. It causes blackheads, whiteheads, pimples, and sometimes deep, painful lumps. Severe acne can leave scars and cause emotional distress.

topics.name: Acne and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Acne and related skin conditions cause pimples or other acne-like changes, often on the face. Acne can cause blackheads, whiteheads, and inflamed bumps; severe cases may scar and cause emotional distress. Rosacea and perioral dermatitis can look similar but have different patterns, so telling them apart helps guide care.

topics.name: Acne Rosacea
topics.clinical_significance: Rosacea, sometimes called acne rosacea, is a long-lasting skin condition that usually affects the central face. It can cause flushing, lasting redness, visible small blood vessels, and acne-like bumps, but it does not cause acne blackheads or whiteheads. Some people develop eye irritation; in a smaller number, the skin thickens, often on the nose.

topics.name: Acne Vulgaris
topics.clinical_significance: Acne vulgaris is a long-lasting inflammation of hair follicles and oil glands, usually on the face, chest, or back. It causes blackheads, whiteheads, pimples, and sometimes deep, painful lumps. Severe or deep acne can leave scars or dark spots and cause emotional distress.

topics.name: Acoustic Neurinoma
topics.clinical_significance: An acoustic neurinoma (vestibular schwannoma) is usually a slow-growing, noncancerous tumor of the nerve that carries hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the brain. It often causes gradual hearing loss in one ear and may cause ringing in the ear, dizziness, or unsteadiness. A larger tumor can press on nearby nerves or the brainstem.

topics.name: Acoustic Neuroma
topics.clinical_significance: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) is usually a slow-growing, noncancerous tumor of the nerve that carries hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the brain. It often causes gradual hearing loss in one ear and may cause ringing in the ear, dizziness, or unsteadiness. A larger tumor can press on nearby nerves or the brainstem.

topics.name: Acquired Angioedema
topics.clinical_significance: Acquired angioedema is repeated swelling caused by low or poorly working C1 inhibitor, a blood protein. It usually begins in adulthood and may be linked to a blood cancer or an autoimmune disease. Swelling can affect the face, lips, tongue, gut, or airway and usually occurs without hives or itching. Throat swelling can block breathing and be life-threatening.

topics.name: Acquired Platelet Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Platelets help stop bleeding by sticking together and forming a plug. In acquired platelet dysfunction, they do not work normally, often because of medicines such as aspirin or ibuprofen, kidney failure, or other illnesses. The platelet count may be normal, but bleeding can last longer than usual, especially after an injury or procedure.

topics.name: Acquired Renal Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Acquired kidney cysts are fluid-filled sacs that develop later in life, often in people with chronic kidney disease or many years of dialysis. Most cause no symptoms and are found by chance on imaging. Some can bleed, become infected, or cause side pain. People with many acquired cysts have a higher risk of kidney cancer, although it is unclear whether the cysts themselves can become cancerous.

topics.name: Acrochordons
topics.clinical_significance: Acrochordons (skin tags) are common, soft, small growths that usually appear on the neck, armpits, or groin. They are usually harmless and cause no symptoms, but rubbing can irritate them. Having many skin tags may be linked with insulin resistance.

topics.name: Acrocyanosis
topics.clinical_significance: Acrocyanosis causes ongoing, usually painless bluish color and coldness in both hands or feet, often worse in cold weather. It results from narrowing of small blood vessels in the skin; larger artery pulses and blood oxygen are usually normal, and skin ulcers do not occur. Temporary blue hands and feet are common and usually normal in newborns.

topics.name: Acromioclavicular Joint Sprains
topics.clinical_significance: An acromioclavicular (AC) joint sprain injures the ligaments connecting the collarbone to the top of the shoulder blade, usually after a fall onto the shoulder. It causes pain and tenderness. Severe sprains can tear several ligaments and shift the collarbone out of place, a problem often called shoulder separation.

topics.name: Actinic Keratoses
topics.clinical_significance: Actinic keratoses are rough, scaly spots on skin exposed to years of sunlight. They are precancerous: some can develop into squamous cell skin cancer, although most do not. They often occur on the face, scalp, and arms, and may stay, return, or go away.

topics.name: Actinomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Actinomycosis is a slow-growing infection caused by bacteria that normally live in the mouth and other parts of the body. It often affects the jaw and face, but can also involve the lungs, abdomen, or pelvis. It can form hard lumps, pus-filled pockets, and draining channels through the skin, and may resemble cancer or tuberculosis. Treatment usually needs a long course of antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

topics.name: Acupuncture
topics.clinical_significance: Acupuncture uses thin needles to stimulate specific points on the body. It may help some forms of long-term pain and nausea or vomiting after surgery, but its effects vary by condition. Side effects are usually mild, though fainting, infection, or tissue injury can occur.

topics.name: Acute Abdomen and Surgical Gastroenterology
topics.clinical_significance: An acute abdomen is severe abdominal pain or other signs that raise concern for a problem needing urgent surgery. Causes include a hole in the stomach or bowel, intestinal blockage, appendicitis, or loss of blood flow to the bowel. Some causes can quickly lead to serious harm, so rapid diagnosis is important.

topics.name: Acute Abdominal Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Acute abdominal pain can have minor causes, but sudden or severe pain may signal a life-threatening problem such as a hole in the gut, intestinal blockage, appendicitis, loss of blood flow to the bowel, or a ruptured aneurysm. Some causes can worsen within hours, so severe pain needs rapid medical assessment.

topics.name: Acute Altitude Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Acute altitude illness occurs when the body gets too little oxygen after a rapid climb to high elevation. Mild illness can cause headache, tiredness, nausea, or dizziness. Severe forms can cause brain swelling with confusion or poor balance, or fluid in the lungs with severe shortness of breath; either can be fatal without prompt descent and treatment.

topics.name: Acute and Posttraumatic Stress Disorders (ASD and PTSD) in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: After trauma, children may have distressing memories or nightmares, avoid reminders, feel persistently fearful or numb, or become unusually alert. Acute stress disorder lasts from 3 days to 1 month; PTSD lasts longer than 1 month and may begin months after the event. Symptoms can disrupt daily life, but early trauma-focused therapy can help.

topics.name: Acute Anterior Poliomyelitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute anterior poliomyelitis (polio) is a contagious infection caused by poliovirus, usually spread through stool-contaminated food or water. Most infections cause no symptoms or only mild illness, but a small number affect the brain or spinal cord and cause sudden, uneven muscle weakness or paralysis. Paralysis can be permanent and may affect breathing; vaccination is the main way to prevent polio.

topics.name: Acute Bacterial Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis is an infection of the thin lining over the eye and inside the eyelids. It causes redness, irritation, tearing, and pus-like discharge, often starting in one eye and spreading to the other. It spreads easily. Gonococcal conjunctivitis can be severe and damage the cornea, threatening vision; conjunctivitis in newborns needs special treatment.

topics.name: Acute Bacterial Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute bacterial meningitis is a fast-moving infection of the membranes and fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It often causes fever, severe headache, and a stiff neck, but symptoms can differ, especially in infants and older adults. It can quickly cause seizures, brain injury, hearing loss, shock, or death, so it needs immediate treatment with antibiotics.

topics.name: Acute Bronchitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute bronchitis is short-term inflammation of the breathing tubes, usually caused by a virus. It causes a cough, sometimes with mucus or a mild fever, and the cough may last for several weeks. Most people recover with time, and antibiotics usually do not help. A high or lasting fever may point to another illness, such as pneumonia.

topics.name: Acute Calcium Pyrophosphate Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals in a joint can cause sudden pain, swelling, and warmth, often in the knee or wrist. This attack is called acute calcium pyrophosphate arthritis or pseudogout. The condition can also cause long-term joint damage and may resemble gout, osteoarthritis, or rheumatoid arthritis. In an acute attack, joint fluid testing helps identify the crystals and rule out infection.

topics.name: Acute Cholecystitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute cholecystitis is sudden inflammation of the gallbladder, usually when a gallstone blocks its outlet. It causes lasting pain and tenderness in the upper right abdomen, often with nausea, vomiting, or fever. Without treatment, infection, death of gallbladder tissue, or rupture can occur. Hospital care and early gallbladder removal are often needed.

topics.name: Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
topics.clinical_significance: The main acute diabetes emergencies are diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). DKA causes high blood sugar, ketone buildup, acid in the blood, and dehydration; HHS causes extremely high blood sugar and severe dehydration, often with confusion, and usually occurs in type 2 diabetes. Both can lead to coma or death and need urgent hospital treatment.

topics.name: Acute Coronary Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Acute coronary insufficiency, also called unstable angina, occurs when heart muscle suddenly gets too little blood, usually because a coronary artery is partly blocked. Chest discomfort may begin at rest, last longer, or worsen compared with usual angina. There is no clear evidence of heart muscle death, but the risk of a heart attack is higher, so urgent medical evaluation is needed.

topics.name: Acute Coronary Syndromes (ACS), Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Acute coronary syndromes are urgent problems caused by a sudden drop in blood flow to the heart. They include unstable angina and two types of heart attack: NSTEMI and STEMI. Symptoms may include chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea, or sweating. These conditions can cause lasting heart damage or sudden death, so rapid diagnosis and treatment are important.

topics.name: Acute Coronary Syndromes, Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Acute coronary syndromes, especially heart attacks, can cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems, heart block, heart failure, or shock. Other complications include weakening, bulging, or tearing of the heart muscle, blood clots inside the heart, and inflammation around the heart. These problems can be life-threatening and may require close monitoring and urgent treatment.

topics.name: Acute Coronary Syndromes, Revascularization for
topics.clinical_significance: Revascularization restores blood flow to the heart during an acute coronary syndrome to limit damage and improve outcomes. It may open a narrowed or blocked artery with a catheter and balloon, often placing a stent, or route blood around it with bypass surgery. Clot-dissolving medicine is another option for some heart attacks. The method and timing depend on the type of syndrome and the person’s condition; a STEMI usually needs emergency revascularization, most often by catheter.

topics.name: Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare lung illness in which eosinophils build up quickly in lung tissue. It causes sudden fever, cough, and shortness of breath and can quickly progress to dangerously low oxygen and respiratory failure. Prompt steroid treatment usually leads to a good recovery.

topics.name: Acute Febrile Neutrophilic Dermatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (Sweet syndrome) causes sudden fever and painful, tender red or purple raised spots or patches, often on the face, neck, or arms. It can occur with infection, inflammatory disease, certain medicines, or cancer. About 1 in 5 cases are linked to cancer, often a blood cancer, so clinicians may look for an underlying cause. A skin biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis, and corticosteroids usually treat it.

topics.name: Acute Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Acute heart failure is new heart failure or a sudden worsening of existing heart failure. Fluid may build up in the lungs and cause breathlessness, or reduced blood flow may affect vital organs. It can become life-threatening and needs prompt medical assessment and treatment of the cause.

topics.name: Acute Hepatic Infarction
topics.clinical_significance: Acute hepatic infarction (ischemic hepatitis) is sudden liver damage caused by too little blood or oxygen reaching the liver, often during severe low blood pressure, heart or breathing failure, or sepsis. It can cause a sharp rise in liver enzymes and, rarely, liver failure. Prompt treatment of the underlying problem can restore blood flow, and liver function usually recovers.

topics.name: Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure (AHRF), Including Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure means the lungs cannot put enough oxygen into the blood. Causes include pneumonia, fluid in the lungs, and lung bleeding; ARDS is a severe form caused by widespread lung injury. Very low oxygen can damage vital organs and may be fatal, so urgent hospital care with oxygen and sometimes breathing support is needed while the cause is treated.

topics.name: Acute Idiopathic Polyneuritis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute idiopathic polyneuritis (Guillain-Barré syndrome) is an immune-related nerve disorder that can cause rapidly worsening weakness and tingling, often starting in the legs and spreading upward. It may weaken the muscles used for breathing or swallowing and disrupt heart rate or blood pressure. Suspected cases need hospital monitoring and prompt treatment, usually with immune globulin or plasma exchange.

topics.name: Acute Infectious Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute infectious arthritis is a rapidly developing joint infection, usually bacterial, that causes severe pain, swelling, warmth, and difficulty moving the joint. It can damage cartilage within hours or days and may spread into the bloodstream. It is an emergency: joint fluid is tested, and treatment usually requires prompt antibiotics and drainage of the joint.

topics.name: Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy is a common form of Guillain-Barré syndrome. The immune system damages the protective covering of peripheral nerves, causing rapidly worsening weakness, often starting in the legs, and reduced reflexes. Weakness can affect breathing and automatic body functions, so prompt hospital monitoring and treatment with immune globulin or plasma exchange are important.

topics.name: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia (AIP)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute interstitial pneumonia is a rare, sudden, severe lung disease with no known cause. Fever, cough, and shortness of breath can quickly worsen as blood oxygen falls, leading to respiratory failure and a need for a ventilator. More than half of patients die, though some who survive recover lung function.

topics.name: Acute Kidney Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Acute kidney injury is a rapid loss of kidney function over days to weeks; urine output may fall, but it can remain normal. Waste products, fluid, potassium, and acids can build up, causing serious problems such as heart rhythm changes or fluid in the lungs. Promptly finding and treating the cause can help the kidneys recover; severe cases may need dialysis.

topics.name: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a rapid decline in kidney function over days to weeks. Waste products and extra fluid can build up, and potassium and acid levels can become unsafe; urine output may decrease or stay normal. Finding and treating the cause early improves the chance of recovery, while severe cases may need dialysis.

topics.name: Acute Limb Ischemia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute limb ischemia is a sudden loss of blood flow to an arm or leg, usually from a blocked artery. The limb may become very painful, pale, cold, numb, or pulseless, and severe cases can cause weakness or paralysis. It is an emergency: without rapid treatment to restore blood flow, tissue can die and amputation may be needed.

topics.name: Acute Liver Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Acute liver failure is a rapid loss of liver function in someone without known long-term liver disease. It can cause yellow skin or eyes, poor blood clotting, and confusion or reduced alertness; brain swelling and failure of other organs may follow. It is a life-threatening emergency that needs intensive hospital care, and some people need a liver transplant.

topics.name: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing cancer of immature lymphocytes in the blood and bone marrow. It is the most common childhood cancer but can occur at any age. Leukemia cells crowd out normal blood cells, causing fatigue, infections, easy bruising or bleeding, and sometimes bone pain or symptoms from spread to the brain and spinal cord. Prompt diagnosis and cancer treatment are needed.

topics.name: Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute lymphocytic leukemia is another name for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a fast-growing cancer of immature lymphocytes in the bone marrow. It can crowd out normal blood cells, leading to anemia, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. It occurs most often in children but can affect adults, and it needs prompt diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a sudden loss of blood flow to the intestines, often causing severe abdominal pain with few early findings on examination. Without rapid treatment, part of the bowel can die within hours, leading to infection, organ failure, or death. It is a medical emergency that may require urgent restoration of blood flow or removal of damaged bowel.

topics.name: Acute MI
topics.clinical_significance: An acute myocardial infarction (heart attack) is death of heart muscle after its blood supply is sharply reduced. It most often occurs when a clot forms over a ruptured artery plaque, but other causes are possible. It may cause chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea, or sweating, though symptoms can be mild or absent. It is an emergency because it can cause dangerous heart rhythms, heart failure, or shock; prompt treatment can limit heart damage.

topics.name: Acute Myelocytic Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute myelocytic leukemia is another name for acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a fast-growing cancer of immature blood-forming cells, seen mainly in adults. Leukemia cells crowd out normal blood cells, causing fatigue or pallor from anemia, frequent infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. Prompt specialist diagnosis and treatment are needed because the disease can worsen quickly.

topics.name: Acute Myelogenous Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Acute myelogenous leukemia is another name for acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a fast-growing cancer of immature blood-forming cells. It can crowd out healthy blood cells, leading to fatigue and pallor, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. The disease can progress quickly, so prompt diagnosis and specialist treatment are important.

topics.name: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of immature myeloid blood cells, most often affecting adults. The abnormal cells build up in the bone marrow and crowd out healthy cells, which can cause fatigue and pallor, serious infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. AML needs prompt specialist diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Acute Myocardial Infarction (MI)
topics.clinical_significance: An acute myocardial infarction (heart attack) is death of heart muscle from a sudden reduction in blood flow, usually due to a blocked coronary artery. It may cause chest discomfort, shortness of breath, nausea, or sweating, but some heart attacks have mild or no clear symptoms. Dangerous rhythm problems, heart failure, or shock can occur, so it needs emergency assessment and treatment to restore blood flow when indicated.

topics.name: Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (trench mouth) is a rapidly developing, painful gum infection. It causes bleeding gums and punched-out ulcers between the teeth; bad breath, fever, or feeling unwell may also occur. Prompt dental cleaning and careful oral care can control it and help prevent further gum damage. Smoking, stress, poor oral hygiene, and poor nutrition increase risk.

topics.name: Acute Pancreatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas, usually causing severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, often with nausea and vomiting. Gallstones and alcohol are the most common causes. Many cases are mild, but severe disease can damage pancreatic tissue and cause shock or failure of other organs, so prompt medical assessment and supportive care are important.

topics.name: Acute Perforation of the Gastrointestinal Tract
topics.clinical_significance: A gastrointestinal perforation is a hole in the wall of the digestive tract that can let its contents leak into the abdomen, causing peritonitis and shock. It often causes severe abdominal pain, though symptoms may develop gradually when the leak is contained. This is an emergency: prompt treatment usually includes surgery, IV fluids, and antibiotics because delay raises the risk of death.

topics.name: Acute Porphyrias
topics.clinical_significance: Acute porphyrias are inherited disorders of heme production that can cause sudden attacks of severe abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and nerve or mental health symptoms. Certain medicines, alcohol, illness, fasting, or hormonal changes can trigger an attack. Severe attacks may cause muscle weakness, seizures, or breathing failure and need urgent treatment, often with IV heme.

topics.name: Acute Posterior Ganglionitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute posterior ganglionitis (shingles or herpes zoster) occurs when the chickenpox virus reactivates in a sensory nerve ganglion. It causes pain followed by a one-sided band of blisters that usually does not cross the midline. Antiviral treatment works best when started early; persistent nerve pain can last for months, and a rash near the eye can threaten vision.

topics.name: Acute Renal Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Acute renal failure, now usually called acute kidney injury (AKI), is a rapid decline in kidney function over days to weeks. Waste products, fluid, potassium, and acid can build up, even when urine output remains normal. Early treatment of the cause may allow recovery; severe cases can cause dangerous complications and may need dialysis.

topics.name: Acute Severe Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Acute severe hypertension is a hypertensive emergency when very high blood pressure is causing new damage to organs such as the brain, heart, kidneys, eyes, or aorta. It can lead to stroke, heart failure, kidney failure, or death and needs immediate hospital treatment with carefully controlled blood pressure reduction. A high reading without acute organ damage is not by itself a hypertensive emergency.

topics.name: Acute Severe Hypertension in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Acute severe hypertension in a child is a rapid, dangerous rise in blood pressure; what counts as severe depends on the child’s age, sex, and height, and how quickly pressure rose. If it is damaging the brain, heart, kidneys, or eyes, it is an emergency needing urgent hospital care. Blood pressure must be lowered in a controlled way to avoid reducing blood flow to the brain or kidneys.

topics.name: Acute Stress Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Acute stress disorder is significant distress after a traumatic event, with symptoms such as unwanted memories, avoiding reminders, feeling detached, low mood, or being constantly on guard. Symptoms begin after the trauma and last from 3 days to 1 month; if they continue longer, PTSD may be considered. Trauma-focused therapy can help.

topics.name: Acute Transverse Myelitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute transverse myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord that can cause back pain, weakness, numbness, and loss of bladder or bowel control below the affected area. Symptoms may worsen over hours or days; severe cases can cause paralysis and lasting disability. Prompt assessment is important to find a treatable cause and limit further spinal cord injury.

topics.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is injury to kidney tubule cells and a common cause of acute kidney injury. It often follows severe low blood pressure, sepsis, or exposure to kidney-toxic medicines. Kidney function may fall and urine may decrease, though it can stay normal. Treating the cause and stopping harmful medicines can allow recovery; severe cases may need dialysis.

topics.name: Acute Vision Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Acute vision loss is a rapid reduction in sight over seconds to days, affecting one or both eyes or only part of the visual field. It can result from serious problems such as retinal detachment, blocked retinal blood flow, optic nerve damage, or acute glaucoma; some causes are linked to stroke. It needs urgent eye or emergency assessment because prompt treatment may protect vision and health.

topics.name: Addiction
topics.clinical_significance: Addiction, more precisely called a substance use disorder, is a pattern of substance use that is difficult to control and continues despite harm or problems in daily life. It can affect health, relationships, and work, and may lead to intoxication, overdose, or withdrawal. It is a treatable medical condition; care may include counseling, support, and medication, depending on the substance and the person’s needs.

topics.name: Addison's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency: the adrenal glands make too little cortisol and aldosterone. It can cause fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, salt loss, and darkening of the skin. Infection or other major stress can trigger an adrenal crisis, with severe dehydration and shock that can be fatal without urgent treatment. Treatment requires hormone replacement.

topics.name: Adenocarcinoma of the Kidneys
topics.clinical_significance: Renal cell carcinoma is the most common kidney cancer. It often causes no symptoms early and may be found by chance on imaging. Later, it can cause blood in the urine, pain in the side, fever, or weight loss. It can grow into nearby veins or spread to other organs, including the lungs, liver, bones, or brain.

topics.name: Adenoid Hypertrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Enlarged adenoids are common in young children and can block the back of the nose or the openings of the middle ears. They may cause mouth breathing, snoring, disturbed sleep, repeated sinus or ear infections, and hearing loss. Severe blockage can cause obstructive sleep apnea.

topics.name: Adenovirus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Adenoviruses may cause no symptoms or lead to respiratory illness, sore throat, pink eye, or diarrhea. Some infections affect the bladder or lungs. Severe illness is uncommon but is more likely in infants and people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Adherence to a Medication Regimen
topics.clinical_significance: Medication adherence means obtaining and taking medicine as prescribed, including the right dose and schedule. Missing doses or stopping early can make treatment fail or illness worsen; stopping antibiotics or antivirals early may contribute to drug resistance. Cost, side effects, forgetfulness, or unclear instructions can make adherence difficult.

topics.name: Adjustment Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Adjustment disorder is a response to an identifiable stressor that causes significant distress or disrupts daily life. Symptoms may include anxiety, low mood, or changes in behavior. People with this disorder have an increased risk of suicidal behavior, so safety should be assessed.

topics.name: Adnexal Torsion
topics.clinical_significance: Adnexal torsion is twisting of an ovary and/or fallopian tube, which can cut off blood flow. It causes sudden, severe pelvic pain, often with nausea and vomiting. It is a gynecologic emergency: urgent surgery may be needed to restore blood flow and prevent lasting damage or loss of the ovary.

topics.name: Adolescents, Introduction to Problems in
topics.clinical_significance: Adolescence brings rapid physical, emotional, and social changes. Health concerns can include injuries, mental health problems, substance use, sexual and reproductive health, and chronic illness. Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of death and disability in this age group, so prevention, screening, and early support matter.

topics.name: Adolescents, Physical Growth and Sexual Maturation of
topics.clinical_significance: Growth and pubertal timing vary from person to person. Tracking height and the order of pubertal changes can help identify unusually early or delayed development and possible health problems. Very early puberty can close growth plates too soon and limit adult height; many children who mature late eventually catch up.

topics.name: Adolescents, Problems in
topics.clinical_significance: Health concerns in adolescents include injuries, mental health problems, substance use, sexual and reproductive health, and chronic illness. Prevention and screening can help identify problems early. Unintentional injuries are a leading cause of death and disability, and suicide and homicide also cause serious harm.

topics.name: Adrenal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Adrenal disorders occur when the glands make too much or too little hormone. Depending on the hormone, they can affect blood pressure, salt and potassium balance, metabolism, or the body’s response to stress. Adrenal insufficiency can lead to a life-threatening adrenal crisis, especially during illness or injury.

topics.name: Adrenal Function, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The adrenal glands make hormones that help control the body’s stress response, metabolism, blood pressure, and salt and potassium balance. The outer part makes cortisol, aldosterone, and small amounts of sex hormones; the inner part makes adrenaline and related hormones. Too much or too little of these hormones can cause illness.

topics.name: Adrenal Insufficiency, Secondary
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary adrenal insufficiency occurs when the pituitary makes too little ACTH, so the adrenal glands make too little cortisol. It can result from pituitary problems or long-term use or sudden stopping of steroid medicines. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting. Aldosterone and blood potassium are usually less affected than in Addison disease.

topics.name: Adrenal Masses, Nonfunctional
topics.clinical_significance: Nonfunctional adrenal masses are growths that show no clear hormone excess and are often found by chance on imaging. Most are benign, but some release small amounts of cortisol, and some are cancer or tumors that have spread from elsewhere. Hormone tests and imaging help guide whether a mass needs monitoring or removal.

topics.name: Adrenal Virilism
topics.clinical_significance: Adrenal virilism is excess production of male-type hormones (androgens) by the adrenal glands, usually from gland overgrowth or a tumor. It can cause early sexual development in children and, in females, excess facial or body hair, acne, a deeper voice, menstrual changes, or infertility. New or rapid changes need medical assessment to find the cause.

topics.name: Adrenogenital Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Adrenogenital syndrome (adrenal virilism) occurs when the adrenal glands make too much androgen, often because of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and sometimes an adrenal tumor. It can affect genital development before birth, cause early puberty in children, and cause excess body hair, acne, a deeper voice, menstrual changes, or infertility in adults.

topics.name: Adult Chlamydial Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis is an eye infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, usually spread through sexual contact. It often causes long-lasting redness and discharge in one eye and may occur with a genital infection. Treatment requires oral antibiotics, and sex partners also need treatment.

topics.name: Adult Inclusion Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Adult inclusion conjunctivitis is an eye infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, usually spread through sexual contact. It often causes long-lasting redness and discharge in one eye and may occur with a genital infection. Treatment requires oral antibiotics, and sex partners also need treatment.

topics.name: Advance Directives
topics.clinical_significance: Legal documents that let a person state future medical-care wishes and/or name someone to make health care decisions if they become unable to decide or communicate. They help clinicians and loved ones follow the person’s wishes.

topics.name: Adverse Drug Effects
topics.clinical_significance: An unintended, unwanted, or harmful effect of a medicine. Effects range from mild problems such as nausea or rash to serious reactions such as anaphylaxis or liver injury. They can occur even when a medicine is used as directed.

topics.name: Adverse Drug Reactions
topics.clinical_significance: An unintended, unwanted, or harmful effect of a medicine. Reactions can be mild or serious and may be predictable and dose-related or rare and unpredictable. They can occur even when a medicine is used as directed.

topics.name: Adynamic Ileus
topics.clinical_significance: Ileus is a temporary slowing or stoppage of intestinal movement without a physical blockage, most often after abdominal surgery. It can also occur with inflammation, low potassium, or medicines such as opioids. It may cause abdominal swelling, nausea, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or gas. It must be distinguished from a bowel obstruction.

topics.name: Aerotitis Media
topics.clinical_significance: Aerotitis media is ear pain or damage caused by a rapid change in air pressure, often during flying or diving. If pressure cannot equalize across the eardrum, the ear may feel full or painful and hearing may be muffled. Severe cases can damage the eardrum or inner ear; severe vertigo or hearing loss needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: African Eye Worm
topics.clinical_significance: Loiasis is infection with the Loa loa worm, spread by day-biting deerflies in parts of West and Central Africa. Many people have no symptoms; others develop temporary areas of swelling or see a worm move across the eye, usually without lasting eye damage. Heavy infection can cause serious brain complications, especially during treatment, so parasite levels must be checked before treatment.

topics.name: African Sleeping Sickness
topics.clinical_significance: African sleeping sickness is a parasitic infection spread by tsetse-fly bites in sub-Saharan Africa. It can cause fever, headaches, and swollen lymph nodes, then spread to the brain and cause changes in sleep, behavior, balance, or alertness. Without treatment, it can be fatal.

topics.name: African Trypanosomiasis
topics.clinical_significance: African trypanosomiasis is an infection with Trypanosoma brucei parasites spread by tsetse flies. It can cause fever, headaches, and swollen lymph nodes, then spread to the brain and cause sleepiness, confusion, or poor coordination. Without treatment, it can progress to coma and death.

topics.name: Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD or ARMD)
topics.clinical_significance: Age-related damage to the macula causes loss of central vision, which can make reading or recognizing faces difficult. Dry AMD usually worsens slowly; wet AMD can cause rapid vision loss and needs prompt eye care. AMD is a leading cause of permanent central vision loss in older adults.

topics.name: Aging and Quality Of Life
topics.clinical_significance: Quality of life in older adults is personal and includes physical, mental, social, and spiritual well-being, as well as the ability to take part in valued activities. Health decisions should reflect the person’s goals and how tests or treatments may affect daily life.

topics.name: Aging, Physical Changes With
topics.clinical_significance: Body functions gradually change with age, but these changes often have little effect on daily activities. Major loss of function is more often caused by illness than by normal aging alone. Reduced muscle strength, balance, kidney function, vision, or hearing can affect movement, fall risk, medicine levels, and communication; regular activity can help preserve function.

topics.name: Agitation, Confusion, and Neuromuscular Blockade in Critically Ill Patients
topics.clinical_significance: Agitation or confusion in an ICU patient can signal pain, low oxygen, infection, medication effects, withdrawal, or delirium. It can interfere with care and lead patients to remove breathing tubes or IV lines, creating serious danger. Paralytic medicines stop movement but do not relieve pain or distress, so patients still need careful assessment and adequate pain relief and sedation.

topics.name: Agnosia
topics.clinical_significance: Agnosia is inability to recognize familiar objects, sounds, or other things through one or more senses, even when the sense itself is working. It results from damage or degeneration in parts of the brain that interpret sensory information, such as after a stroke, injury, tumor, or dementia. Speech or occupational therapy may help a person adapt.

topics.name: Agoraphobia
topics.clinical_significance: Agoraphobia is intense fear of situations where escape or help may be difficult, such as crowds, public transport, or being outside alone. People may avoid these situations or need a companion, and severe cases can keep them housebound or disrupt daily life. It often occurs with panic disorder; exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy can help.

topics.name: Agoraphobia in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and adolescents, agoraphobia causes persistent fear of places where escape or help may be difficult, such as crowds, public transport, or being outside alone. Avoidance can interfere with school and other daily activities; severe cases may keep a young person housebound. It often occurs with panic attacks, and behavioral therapy can help.

topics.name: Agranulocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: Agranulocytosis is a severe drop in neutrophils, white blood cells that help fight bacterial and fungal infections. It can make infections more likely and more dangerous, while usual signs of inflammation may be weak or absent. Fever may be the only warning and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Air Embolism
topics.clinical_significance: Gas bubbles in arteries can block blood flow and suddenly deprive the brain, heart, spinal cord, or other organs of oxygen. It may follow lung injury when expanding air enters the blood during a dive ascent, or gas entering the circulation during a procedure or injury; symptoms can include sudden confusion, weakness, seizures, or loss of consciousness.

topics.name: Air Pollution–Related Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Air pollution can cause illness or worsen existing disease. It can trigger asthma or COPD flare-ups, reduce lung function, and increase the risk of lung cancer, heart attack, stroke, and coronary artery disease.

topics.name: Air Travel
topics.clinical_significance: Most people tolerate air travel, but lower cabin oxygen can affect people with severe heart or lung disease, and pressure changes can make trapped gas expand and cause pain or tissue injury. Long periods of sitting slightly increase the risk of blood clots; flights can also cause ear or sinus pain, motion sickness, dehydration, and jet lag.

topics.name: Airflow, Lung Volumes, and Flow-Volume Loop
topics.clinical_significance: These lung function tests measure how much air the lungs hold and how quickly a person breathes it in and out. They help distinguish narrowed airways, as in asthma or COPD, from reduced lung expansion, estimate disease severity, and assess response to treatment. Flow-volume loop patterns can also suggest obstruction in the upper airways.

topics.name: Airway and Respiratory Devices
topics.clinical_significance: These devices help keep air moving into the lungs when a person cannot breathe adequately or protect their airway. Bag-mask and supraglottic devices can provide temporary or rescue ventilation; an endotracheal tube can secure the airway, limit aspiration, and allow mechanical ventilation and suctioning.

topics.name: Airway Establishment and Control
topics.clinical_significance: Airway control keeps air moving to the lungs when blockage, unconsciousness, injury, or respiratory failure threatens breathing. Methods range from positioning and clearing an obstruction to using an airway device or creating a surgical airway; assisted ventilation may also be needed to maintain oxygen delivery.

topics.name: Albert Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Albert disease is inflammation of the small fluid-filled sac between the Achilles tendon and heel bone. It causes pain, swelling, and tenderness at the back of the heel, which can make walking or wearing shoes difficult; friction, injury, or inflammatory arthritis may trigger it.

topics.name: Albinism
topics.clinical_significance: Albinism is an inherited reduction in melanin that affects the skin and hair, the eyes, or both. Eye involvement can cause light sensitivity and reduced vision; low skin pigment greatly increases the risk of sunburn and skin cancer. Some rare forms also affect blood clotting or immune function.

topics.name: Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal
topics.clinical_significance: Rapid heavy drinking can suppress breathing, cause vomiting with aspiration, lead to coma, and be fatal. Long-term heavy drinking can damage the liver, heart, nerves, and brain; withdrawal after dependence can cause tremors, seizures, hallucinations, or life-threatening delirium tremens.

topics.name: Alcohol Use Disorder and Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Alcohol use disorder is a pattern of drinking that causes significant problems or loss of control, often with craving, tolerance, or withdrawal. It can harm health, relationships, and work and increase the risk of injury. Counseling, rehabilitation and support programs, and sometimes medication can help reduce drinking or prevent relapse.

topics.name: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term heavy drinking can cause fat buildup and inflammation in the liver, sometimes progressing to scarring (cirrhosis) and liver failure. Cirrhosis can cause fluid buildup, bleeding, or confusion and raises the risk of liver cancer; early fatty liver may cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Alcoholic Liver Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term heavy drinking can cause fat buildup and inflammation in the liver, sometimes progressing to scarring (cirrhosis) and liver failure. Cirrhosis can cause fluid buildup, bleeding, or confusion and raises the risk of liver cancer; early fatty liver may cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Alcohol-Related Liver Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term heavy drinking can cause fat buildup and inflammation in the liver, sometimes progressing to scarring (cirrhosis) and liver failure. Cirrhosis can cause fluid buildup, bleeding, or confusion and raises the risk of liver cancer; early fatty liver may cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Aldosteronism, Secondary
topics.clinical_significance: Another problem, often reduced blood flow to the kidneys, triggers the adrenal glands to make too much aldosterone. The body then retains salt and water and loses potassium, often causing high blood pressure; low potassium can cause weakness, tingling, or rarely temporary paralysis.

topics.name: Allergic and Atopic Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Allergic disorders are harmful immune responses to foreign substances; atopic disorders are the IgE-mediated subset. They commonly affect the nose, eyes, skin, and lungs, causing rhinitis, conjunctivitis, eczema, or asthma. A severe whole-body reaction (anaphylaxis) can cause airway swelling, breathing difficulty, and shock.

topics.name: Allergic, Autoimmune, and Other Hypersensitivity Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders result from immune responses that are too strong or wrongly directed against the body's own tissues. Allergies can affect the skin, eyes, nose, or lungs; autoimmune and other hypersensitivity reactions can inflame or damage organs, and severe allergies can cause life-threatening anaphylaxis.

topics.name: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)
topics.clinical_significance: ABPA is an allergic reaction to Aspergillus fungus present in the airways, usually in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis; the fungus does not invade lung tissue. It can cause repeated asthma flares and thick mucus plugs, and persistent disease can damage and widen the airways (bronchiectasis) or cause lung scarring.

topics.name: Allergic Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Allergic inflammation of the eye’s surface, often caused by airborne allergens, leads to itchy, red, watery eyes and swollen eyelids; it may be seasonal or year-round. Severe forms can scar or ulcerate the cornea and reduce vision.

topics.name: Allergic Granulomatosis and Angiitis
topics.clinical_significance: Now called eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), this rare disease inflames small and medium blood vessels and is linked to adult-onset asthma, allergic rhinitis, and high eosinophil counts. It can damage the lungs, nerves, skin, heart, or kidneys; heart, nerve, or kidney involvement can be especially serious.

topics.name: Allergic Rhinitis
topics.clinical_significance: Allergic rhinitis is swelling of the nasal lining after exposure to pollen or other allergens. It causes an itchy nose, sneezing, and a runny or blocked nose; itchy, watery eyes may also occur. Symptoms may be seasonal or year-round, and the condition often occurs with asthma.

topics.name: Alligator, Crocodile, Iguana, and Venomous Lizard Bites
topics.clinical_significance: These bites can cause wounds and infection. Alligator and crocodile bites may cause severe soft-tissue or bone injury and infection with Aeromonas bacteria. Venomous lizard bites cause intense pain and swelling and may cause whole-body symptoms; cardiovascular collapse is rare. Iguana wounds are usually superficial but can sometimes become infected, often with Salmonella.

topics.name: Alopecia
topics.clinical_significance: Alopecia is hair loss from the scalp or body. Causes include inherited pattern hair loss, immune or hormonal conditions, illness, medicines, infection, poor nutrition, or repeated pulling or tension on the hair. If scarring destroys the hair follicles, the loss may be permanent; nonscarring hair loss may regrow. Hair loss can sometimes be a sign of an underlying illness.

topics.name: Alopecia Areata
topics.clinical_significance: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition that suddenly causes round or patchy, nonscarring hair loss, most often on the scalp or beard. Hair may regrow, but the loss can return or spread to the entire scalp or body.

topics.name: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Low or abnormal alpha-1 antitrypsin leaves lung tissue less protected from damage, which can cause early emphysema, especially in people who smoke. Abnormal protein can also build up in the liver and cause liver disease, including cirrhosis in children or adults.

topics.name: Alport Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited disorder weakens the kidney’s filtering membranes, causing blood and sometimes protein in the urine and, over time, chronic kidney disease or kidney failure. It often also causes hearing loss and can affect the eyes.

topics.name: Alternative Living Arrangements for Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Many older adults rely on close friends, siblings, or unmarried partners rather than a spouse or adult child. Recognizing these relationships helps clinicians respect the person’s wishes and include trusted caregivers in care planning, since partners may be overlooked by health or residential services.

topics.name: Altitude Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Rapid ascent to high altitude can cause illness because less oxygen is available. Mild illness may cause headache, fatigue, nausea, or dizziness; severe forms cause swelling in the brain or lungs and can quickly lead to coma or death.

topics.name: Alzheimer Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia and gradually worsens memory and other thinking skills. Short-term memory loss is often an early sign; judgment, language, recognition, and ability to manage daily activities may later decline. Behavioral changes can also occur.

topics.name: Amblyopia
topics.clinical_significance: Amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye because the brain receives an unclear or misaligned image from it during early visual development. It often has no obvious symptoms, but can cause lasting vision loss if it is not found and treated early in childhood.

topics.name: Ambulatory pH Monitoring
topics.clinical_significance: A small probe or wireless capsule records acid levels in the esophagus, usually for about 24 hours, to measure reflux and see whether symptoms occur with reflux episodes. Combined impedance testing can also detect weakly acidic or nonacid reflux; results can help assess treatment and identify people who may benefit from antireflux procedures.

topics.name: Amebas, Free-Living, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Free-living amebas live independently in soil or water and rarely cause illness in people. Some can infect the eye, skin, or brain; brain infections are usually fatal, while skin or widespread disease mainly affects people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Amebiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Amebiasis is infection with Entamoeba histolytica, usually spread through food or water contaminated with feces. Many people have no symptoms, but infection can cause diarrhea or bloody dysentery; invasive disease can form liver abscesses and rarely spread to the brain or other organs.

topics.name: Amebic Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Amebic keratitis is a rare, potentially sight-threatening infection of the cornea caused by Acanthamoeba. It occurs most often in contact lens users and can cause severe eye pain, redness, sensitivity to light, tearing, and blurred vision. The infection can progressively damage the cornea and reduce vision.

topics.name: Amebic Meningoencephalitis, Primary
topics.clinical_significance: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis is a rare, rapidly progressing brain infection caused by Naegleria fowleri. The ameba can enter the brain when contaminated warm freshwater goes up the nose. The illness causes headache, stiff neck, and changes in mental state, and is usually fatal.

topics.name: Amenorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Amenorrhea is the absence of menstrual periods. Primary amenorrhea means periods have not begun by age 15; secondary amenorrhea means periods stop for 3 months after regular cycles or 6 months after irregular cycles. Pregnancy is a common cause; other causes include hormonal problems, reproductive tract conditions, major changes in nutrition or exercise, and some medicines.

topics.name: American Trypanosomiasis
topics.clinical_significance: American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease) is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, usually when feces from an infected kissing bug enter through a bite wound or the eye. It can also spread through contaminated food, blood, or organs, or from mother to baby. Early illness may be mild or absent; years later, it can damage the heart and sometimes enlarge the esophagus or colon.

topics.name: Amino Acid and Organic Acid Metabolism Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: These are usually inherited disorders that affect how the body processes amino acids or organic acids. They may cause harmful substances to build up, important substances to become too low, or amino acids to be lost in urine. Effects range from no symptoms to severe illness, seizures, developmental problems, or acid buildup in the blood.

topics.name: Aminoglycosides
topics.clinical_significance: Aminoglycosides are antibiotics used mainly for serious infections caused by certain bacteria. They stop bacteria from making proteins. Examples include gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, and streptomycin. They can harm the kidneys and damage hearing or balance, sometimes permanently.

topics.name: Amnesias
topics.clinical_significance: Amnesia is partial or complete memory loss: a person may be unable to recall past events, form new memories, or both. Causes include head injury, seizures, brain disease, some metabolic problems, and severe psychological stress. It may be temporary, permanent, or progressive, depending on the cause.

topics.name: Amniotic Fluid Embolism
topics.clinical_significance: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, life-threatening complication that usually occurs during labor or soon after delivery. It is thought to be a severe reaction to fetal material entering the mother's blood, not a physical blockage by fluid. It can cause sudden breathing problems, low blood pressure, and impaired blood clotting with severe bleeding.

topics.name: Amphetamines
topics.clinical_significance: Amphetamines are stimulant drugs; some are prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or narcolepsy, and some are misused. They increase brain activity and can cause euphoria and alertness. High doses can cause agitation, overheating, seizures, dangerous heart rhythms, or kidney injury; repeated use can lead to psychosis and dependence.

topics.name: Amputation Rehabilitation, Leg
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation after leg amputation helps people regain mobility and daily function. It builds strength and balance, prepares the remaining limb for a prosthesis, and teaches safe walking with a prosthesis or use of a wheelchair. It also helps prevent joint stiffness and address residual-limb pain and skin problems.

topics.name: Amyloidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Amyloidosis is a group of disorders in which misfolded proteins build up as deposits in tissues. Deposits may affect one area or several organs, especially the heart, kidneys, nerves, or digestive tract, and can interfere with how those organs work. The effects and treatment depend on the type of protein involved.

topics.name: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Other Motor Neuron Diseases (MNDs)
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders progressively damage the nerve cells that control voluntary muscles. They can cause worsening muscle weakness, muscle wasting, twitching, or stiffness. In ALS, weakness may also affect speech, swallowing, and eventually breathing.

topics.name: Anabolic Androgenic Steroids
topics.clinical_significance: Anabolic-androgenic steroids are testosterone and related drugs that can increase muscle mass. Some have medical uses, but high-dose or long-term use can disrupt hormone levels and fertility, cause mood and skin changes, and harm the heart, liver, or kidneys.

topics.name: Anaerobic Bacteria
topics.clinical_significance: Anaerobic bacteria can grow without oxygen. Some cannot use oxygen, while others can grow with or without it. Many normally live in the mouth, intestine, and vagina; they can cause infection when tissue barriers are damaged, often forming abscesses in areas with little oxygen.

topics.name: Anaerobic Bacteria, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Anaerobic bacteria normally live on body surfaces such as the mouth, lower intestine, and vagina. If they enter deeper tissues through a break in the body's natural barriers, they can cause infection, often with several bacterial species. These infections commonly form abscesses and may damage tissue or produce gas.

topics.name: Anaerobic Infections, Mixed
topics.clinical_significance: Mixed anaerobic infections involve anaerobic bacteria together with other bacteria. They can develop when normal bacteria enter damaged or poorly supplied tissues, such as after an injury or surgery. These infections often form abscesses, damage tissue, and can become severe; they may affect the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, mouth, or other sites.

topics.name: Anal Atresia
topics.clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the anal opening is absent or closed, sometimes with an abnormal connection between the rectum and the urinary or genital tract. It can block normal stool passage and is often associated with other birth defects, including problems of the spine, heart, kidneys, or limbs.

topics.name: Anal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Anal cancer is most often squamous cell carcinoma and is commonly linked to human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. It may cause bleeding with bowel movements, pain, or a lump, but some people have no symptoms. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes, including those in the groin.

topics.name: Anal Fissure
topics.clinical_significance: An anal fissure is a tear in the lining of the anal canal. It usually causes sharp pain during or after passing stool and sometimes bleeding; hard stools or frequent loose stools can cause it. Chronic or off-center fissures may be linked to another condition, such as Crohn disease, infection, or anal cancer.

topics.name: Anal Ulcer
topics.clinical_significance: An anal ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the anal canal; a chronic anal fissure may appear as an oval ulcer. It can cause severe pain and bleeding, especially during or after passing stool. An ulcer away from the midline may be linked to an underlying condition, such as Crohn disease or infection.

topics.name: Analgesia and Anesthesia for Labor and Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Pain relief during labor and delivery can use epidural or spinal anesthesia, local nerve blocks, or medicines given by injection. Epidural and spinal methods usually provide effective relief while allowing the mother to stay awake. Injected medicines can affect the newborn's breathing, and general anesthesia is usually reserved for emergency cesarean delivery.

topics.name: Analgesic Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Analgesic nephropathy is chronic kidney damage historically linked to very heavy, long-term use of pain medicines, especially combinations containing phenacetin. It can reduce kidney function; advanced damage to kidney tissue may cause blood in the urine or urinary blockage. It is uncertain whether pain medicines without phenacetin cause this condition.

topics.name: Anaphylaxis
topics.clinical_significance: Anaphylaxis is a sudden, severe whole-body allergic reaction that can cause throat swelling, trouble breathing, or a dangerous fall in blood pressure. It can quickly lead to airway blockage or shock and may be fatal. Common triggers include foods, medicines, insect stings, and latex.

topics.name: Ancylostomiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Ancylostomiasis (hookworm infection) is caused by intestinal worms, usually after larvae in contaminated soil enter through the skin. Many infections cause no symptoms, but the worms feed on blood and heavy, long-lasting infection can cause iron-deficiency anemia. In children, severe anemia may lead to heart failure and swelling.

topics.name: Anterior and Posterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse
topics.clinical_significance: Vaginal wall prolapse occurs when the bladder or urethra bulges into the front wall of the vagina, or the small intestine or rectum bulges into the back wall. It may cause pelvic pressure, a vaginal bulge, urine leakage or difficulty urinating, or trouble passing stool. Mild prolapse may cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Anemia, Approach to the Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia is a sign of an underlying problem, not a disease by itself. Evaluation uses the medical history, symptoms, examination, and blood tests to look for causes such as blood loss, reduced red blood cell production, or increased red blood cell destruction. Identifying the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: Anemia, Etiology
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia can result from blood loss, reduced red blood cell production, or red blood cells being destroyed too quickly. Causes include iron or vitamin deficiencies, chronic illness or kidney problems, bone marrow disorders, inherited blood conditions, and immune or mechanical damage to red blood cells.

topics.name: Anemia, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia evaluation aims to find its underlying cause. A blood count, red blood cell size and appearance, and reticulocyte count help distinguish reduced red blood cell production from blood loss or rapid destruction and guide further testing.

topics.name: Anemia in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: A mild fall in hemoglobin can occur normally during pregnancy because plasma volume rises more than red blood cell mass. True anemia is most often due to iron or folate deficiency and is associated with increased risks for the pregnant person and baby, including preterm birth and poor fetal growth. Symptoms may include fatigue, weakness, light-headedness, or shortness of breath.

topics.name: Anemia of Chronic Blood Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Ongoing blood loss can deplete iron and cause anemia, often from bleeding in the digestive tract or heavy menstrual periods. It may cause tiredness, weakness, dizziness, pale skin, and shortness of breath. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia may be the only sign of hidden gastrointestinal bleeding, including cancer.

topics.name: Anemia of Chronic Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia of chronic disease occurs with long-term infection, inflammation, kidney disease, or cancer. It is often mild but can add to tiredness and weakness from the underlying illness. Finding it can point to an ongoing disorder that needs treatment; treating that disorder usually improves the anemia.

topics.name: Anemia of Chronic Inflammation
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia of chronic inflammation can occur with long-term infections, autoimmune diseases, and cancer. It is often mild, and symptoms usually come from the underlying illness. Treating that illness is the main way to improve the anemia.

topics.name: Anemia of Renal Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia of renal disease often develops in chronic kidney disease because the kidneys make too little erythropoietin, a hormone needed to produce red blood cells. It can add to the effects of kidney disease. Treatment may include treating the kidney problem and using erythropoietin or iron when needed.

topics.name: Anemia, Perinatal
topics.clinical_significance: Low red blood cell levels around birth may be part of normal newborn development, especially in preterm infants, but can also result from bleeding, poor red blood cell production, or rapid cell breakdown. Severe or sudden anemia can reduce oxygen delivery and cause fast breathing, a rapid heartbeat, low blood pressure, or shock. Red blood cell breakdown can also cause jaundice.

topics.name: Anemia, Treatment
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia is treated by addressing its cause. If it becomes dangerously severe, causes or risks heart or lung symptoms, or occurs with uncontrolled bleeding or reduced oxygen supply to vital organs, a red blood cell transfusion may be needed to raise the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity temporarily.

topics.name: Anemias Caused by Deficient Erythropoiesis
topics.clinical_significance: These anemias occur when the body makes too few red blood cells. Causes include iron or vitamin deficiencies, kidney disease, chronic inflammation, and bone marrow disorders. Finding the cause matters because treatment differs; a low reticulocyte count can point to reduced red blood cell production.

topics.name: Anemias Caused by Hemolysis
topics.clinical_significance: Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are destroyed faster than the body can replace them. It may cause tiredness, weakness, jaundice, or an enlarged spleen; severe, sudden breakdown can cause shock. Some types also increase the risk of blood clots, and treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Anencephaly
topics.clinical_significance: Anencephaly is a severe birth defect in which much of the brain and skull do not form. It is fatal: affected pregnancies may end in fetal death or stillbirth, and infants born alive usually die within hours or days. Care is palliative.

topics.name: Angina With No Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease [ANOCA]
topics.clinical_significance: This term describes angina even though the large coronary arteries are not blocked. Poor function or tightening of the heart's small vessels can reduce blood flow and cause chest pain. Symptoms may recur for years; the outlook is better than with obstructive coronary artery disease, but the risk of major cardiovascular events is higher than in the general population.

topics.name: Angioedema
topics.clinical_significance: Angioedema causes deep swelling, often of the face, lips, tongue, or intestines. Swelling in the throat can block breathing and is an emergency. Causes include allergic reactions and medicines such as ACE inhibitors; the cause matters because treatment differs.

topics.name: Angiography
topics.clinical_significance: Angiography creates detailed images of blood vessels to find narrowing, blockages, aneurysms, or abnormal connections. Conventional angiography uses a catheter and contrast dye and can guide treatment, such as opening or stenting a vessel. It is invasive and can cause bleeding or contrast-related problems; CT or MRI angiography are often used instead.

topics.name: Angiokeratoma Corporis Diffusum
topics.clinical_significance: This name is associated with Fabry disease, an inherited enzyme disorder that causes fatty material to build up in cells. It can cause small red skin spots and burning pain in the hands and feet, and may lead to kidney or heart failure or stroke.

topics.name: Angiostrongyliasis
topics.clinical_significance: Angiostrongyliasis is a worm infection usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked snails, slugs, or other infected hosts. One species can cause meningitis with severe neurologic complications; another can cause abdominal inflammation that resembles appendicitis. Anti-worm medicines may worsen the illness, so treatment depends on the species and symptoms.

topics.name: Angle-Closure Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: Angle-closure glaucoma occurs when the eye's drainage angle is blocked, raising pressure and damaging the optic nerve. A sudden attack can cause severe eye pain and redness, blurred vision, colored halos, headache, nausea, or vomiting. It is an emergency because vision can be lost quickly and permanently.

topics.name: Anisakiasis
