topics.clinical_significance: Anisakiasis is infection with worm larvae after eating raw or undercooked saltwater fish or squid. It usually causes sudden abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; intestinal infection can appear later and resemble appendicitis. Endoscopy can find and remove the larvae, which cures the infection.

topics.name: Anisocoria
topics.clinical_significance: Unequal pupils are a harmless normal variation in up to 20% of people. New or marked anisocoria can result from eye injury, medicines, or nerve problems such as Horner syndrome or third-nerve palsy. A drooping eyelid, abnormal eye movements, headache, or other neurologic signs may point to a serious cause and need prompt evaluation.

topics.name: Ankle Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Ankle fractures may be stable or unstable, and stability guides treatment: stable fractures often heal with a cast or walking boot, while unstable fractures may need surgery. If the bones do not heal in proper alignment, arthritis or another fracture may develop.

topics.name: Ankle Sprains
topics.clinical_significance: Ankle sprains are ligament injuries that usually cause pain and swelling after the foot turns inward. Most are mild and heal well, but severe or repeated sprains can leave the ankle unstable. Cartilage damage may cause lasting pain, swelling, or early arthritis.

topics.name: Ankle Stirrup Splint
topics.clinical_significance: An ankle stirrup splint holds the joint still after certain sprains, stable fractures, or a dislocation that has been put back in place. It is usually not made for walking or weight-bearing. If it is too tight, it can injure the skin or reduce blood flow.

topics.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis
topics.clinical_significance: Ankylosing spondylitis is a long-term inflammatory disease that mainly affects the spine and joints between the spine and pelvis. It causes back pain and stiffness; over time, vertebrae may fuse and limit movement and chest expansion. It can also cause eye inflammation and, less often, heart or nerve problems.

topics.name: Ankylosis of the Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ)
topics.clinical_significance: TMJ ankylosis is stiffness or fusion of the jaw joint. It causes long-term, often painless difficulty opening the mouth; in children, it can affect jaw growth and cause facial asymmetry. True joint fusion may require surgery, followed by exercises to keep the jaw moving.

topics.name: Anogenital Warts
topics.clinical_significance: Anogenital warts are usually benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), often types 6 and 11, and can recur after treatment. Other HPV types can cause cancers of the cervix, anus, genitals, or throat. HPV vaccination protects against many wart- and cancer-causing types.

topics.name: Anorectal Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: An anorectal abscess is a pocket of pus near the anus or rectum. It can cause pain and swelling; a deeper abscess may cause fever or chills without visible swelling. Prompt drainage is needed, and a fistula may develop afterward. Antibiotics are added for people with fever, diabetes, weakened immunity, or widespread skin infection.

topics.name: Anorectal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Anorectal disorders affect the anus, anal canal, or rectum and include hemorrhoids, fissures, abscesses, infections, incontinence, prolapse, and cancers. They may cause pain, bleeding, swelling, discharge, or loss of bowel control. Because these symptoms have many possible causes, examination may be needed to identify infection or cancer.

topics.name: Anorectal Disorders, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of anorectal symptoms looks for causes such as fissures, hemorrhoids, abscesses, incontinence, and cancer. It uses a careful history and examination, sometimes including a rectal exam, anoscopy, or sigmoidoscopy. Finding the cause guides treatment and helps detect serious disease.

topics.name: Anorectal Fistula
topics.clinical_significance: An anorectal fistula is an abnormal tunnel from the anal canal to the skin near the anus. It often develops after an abscess or with Crohn disease and can cause ongoing discharge and sometimes pain. Treatment often requires surgery.

topics.name: Anorexia Nervosa
topics.clinical_significance: Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder marked by severe food restriction, intense fear of weight gain, and a distorted body image, leading to very low body weight. Malnutrition can harm many organs and cause slow heart rate, low blood pressure, electrolyte problems, bone loss, and sometimes fatal abnormal heart rhythms. Treatment focuses on restoring nutrition and addressing the eating disorder.

topics.name: Anoscopy and Sigmoidoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Anoscopy examines the anal canal and lower rectum; sigmoidoscopy examines the rectum and sigmoid colon. These tests help find causes of rectal bleeding, pain, discharge, or protrusion. Sigmoidoscopy can also take tissue samples or treat some bleeding or blockages.

topics.name: Anosmia
topics.clinical_significance: Anosmia is complete loss of smell and often makes food seem flavorless, even when basic tastes remain. It often follows a viral infection or sinus disease but can also result from head injury, medicines, or neurologic disease; sudden loss or neurologic symptoms need prompt evaluation. It also makes it harder to notice smoke, gas leaks, or spoiled food.

topics.name: Antenatal Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Antenatal complications can increase the risk of illness or death for the pregnant person, fetus, or newborn. They may result from chronic illness, multiple pregnancy, prior complications, or problems that develop during pregnancy. Early risk assessment helps guide monitoring and care.

topics.name: Anterior Achilles Tendon Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the small fluid-filled sac between the Achilles tendon and heel bone causes pain, swelling, and warmth at the back of the heel, making walking or wearing shoes difficult. It may follow friction, injury, gout, or rheumatoid arthritis. Steroid injections must stay in the bursa because injection into the tendon can weaken or tear it.

topics.name: Anterior and Posterior Vaginal Wall Prolapse
topics.clinical_significance: Weak pelvic support can let the bladder or urethra bulge into the front vaginal wall, or the rectum or small intestine bulge into the back wall. This may cause pelvic pressure, a vaginal bulge, urine leakage or retention, or difficulty passing stool; mild prolapse may have no symptoms. Treatment depends on symptoms and may include pelvic floor exercises, a pessary, or surgery.

topics.name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
topics.clinical_significance: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) helps keep the knee stable. A tear can cause pain, swelling, or a feeling that the knee may give way, often after a twist or sudden change in direction. Other knee structures may also be injured. Severe tears may need surgery and rehabilitation.

topics.name: Anthracosis
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term breathing of coal mine dust can cause coal worker pneumoconiosis, also called anthracosis. Early disease may cause no symptoms, but it can progress to lung scarring, shortness of breath, and severe loss of lung function. The disease may worsen even after exposure stops, and coal dust can also cause chronic bronchitis and COPD.

topics.name: Anthrax
topics.clinical_significance: Anthrax is a serious infection caused by bacteria from infected animals or contaminated animal products. It most often affects the skin, but it can also affect the gut or lungs. Inhaled or intestinal anthrax can quickly cause severe illness, shock, and death, so suspected cases need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Antibacterial Drugs, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Antibacterial drugs (antibiotics) treat bacterial infections by killing bacteria or stopping them from growing. The best choice depends on the likely bacteria, test results, infection site, and patient. Unnecessary use can cause side effects, disturb helpful bacteria, and increase antibiotic resistance.

topics.name: Anticardiolipin Antibody Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: This autoimmune syndrome is diagnosed when antiphospholipid antibodies remain present and a person has blood clots or certain pregnancy complications. It can cause clots in veins or arteries, repeated pregnancy loss, and, rarely, sudden clots affecting several organs.

topics.name: Anticholinergic Chemical-Warfare Compounds
topics.clinical_significance: These agents block acetylcholine and can cause anticholinergic poisoning. Exposure may cause dry mouth and skin, dilated pupils, blurred vision, a fast heartbeat, overheating, confusion, and hallucinations. Severe poisoning can cause stupor or coma that may last for hours or days.

topics.name: Antifungal Medications
topics.clinical_significance: Antifungal medicines treat fungal infections, including serious infections that spread through the body. The right medicine depends on the fungus and where the infection is. Some antifungals can harm the liver or kidneys or interact with other medicines, so monitoring may be needed.

topics.name: Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane (Anti-GBM) Disease
topics.clinical_significance: An autoimmune disease in which antibodies damage small blood vessels in the lungs and kidneys. It can cause bleeding into the lungs, sometimes with coughing up blood, and rapidly worsening kidney inflammation or failure. Either organ may be affected alone, and prompt treatment is needed to prevent organ failure.

topics.name: Antineoplastic Therapy, Systemic
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic cancer treatment uses medicines that act throughout the body to treat cancer. It may help cure cancer, lower the chance that it returns, or control cancer that has spread. Treatment may include chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted drugs, or immunotherapy; benefits and side effects depend on the cancer and the medicines used.

topics.name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)
topics.clinical_significance: APS is an autoimmune disorder linked to blood clots in veins or arteries and certain pregnancy problems, such as repeated pregnancy loss. Diagnosis requires a related health problem and antiphospholipid antibodies that remain present on repeat testing; a positive test alone does not mean a person has APS. Rarely, widespread clots can damage several organs.

topics.name: Antipsychotic Medications
topics.clinical_significance: Antipsychotic medicines reduce symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions and are used for schizophrenia and other conditions. Side effects can include sleepiness, movement problems, weight gain, and diabetes risk, so treatment choice and health monitoring matter. These medicines are linked to increased risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

topics.name: Antiretroviral Therapy in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Combination antiretroviral therapy is the standard treatment for children with HIV. It suppresses the virus and lowers the chance of drug resistance. Doses must suit the child's age and weight, and regular checkups and lab tests help detect side effects or treatment failure.

topics.name: Antiretroviral Treatment of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for everyone with HIV. Combination treatment aims to lower the amount of virus in the blood to undetectable levels and restore immune function. Taking treatment consistently helps maintain control and limit drug resistance; side effects and drug interactions require follow-up and monitoring.

topics.name: Antiseizure Medications
topics.clinical_significance: Antiseizure medicines help prevent seizures, but the choice must match the seizure type because some drugs can worsen certain seizures. One medicine controls seizures in many people. Treatment is tailored to reduce seizures while limiting side effects and drug interactions.

topics.name: Antisocial Personality Disorder (ASPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Antisocial personality disorder is a long-term pattern of disregarding other people's rights, often involving deceit, impulsive or aggressive behavior, and little remorse. It can lead to harm and serious problems in relationships or with the law, and often occurs with substance use or other mental health conditions. Diagnosis is made in adults and requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15.

topics.name: Antithrombin Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Antithrombin is a natural protein that helps prevent blood clots. Its deficiency raises the risk of clots in veins, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The deficiency may be inherited or develop with conditions such as liver disease or nephrotic syndrome.

topics.name: Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders can cause persistent, excessive fear or distressing reactions after trauma or stress that interfere with daily life. Symptoms may include avoidance, upsetting memories, low mood, irritability, or sleep problems. Psychotherapy and, in some cases, medication can help.

topics.name: Anxiety Disorders in Children and Adolescents, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: An anxiety disorder may be present when a child's fear or worry is much stronger than expected and causes severe distress or interferes with daily life. Children may avoid school or other situations and have physical symptoms such as stomachaches, headaches, a racing heart, or sleep problems. Behavioral therapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, is the main treatment; medicine may be added for more severe symptoms.

topics.name: Anxiety Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Anxiety disorders involve ongoing, excessive fear or worry that causes major distress or interferes with daily life. Avoidance and physical symptoms, such as a racing heart or nausea, may occur. Assessment should consider medical conditions, medicines, or substances that can cause anxiety. Psychotherapy and sometimes medication can help.

topics.name: Anxiolytics
topics.clinical_significance: Anxiolytics are medicines used to reduce anxiety. Antidepressants are often used for ongoing anxiety, while benzodiazepines may provide faster relief. Benzodiazepines can cause dependence; high doses can dangerously slow breathing, and suddenly stopping after regular use can cause severe withdrawal, including seizures.

topics.name: Aorta and Its Branches, Diseases of
topics.clinical_significance: Diseases of the aorta and its branches include aneurysms, tears in the aortic wall, and blocked arteries. Some cause no symptoms at first, but they can cut off blood flow to organs or rupture, causing severe bleeding, shock, organ damage, or death. Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain may signal an emergency.

topics.name: Aortic Aneurysms, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: An aortic aneurysm is an abnormal widening of a weakened area of the aortic wall. It often causes no symptoms, but can reduce blood flow, form clots, tear, or rupture. Rupture can cause life-threatening internal bleeding. The aneurysm's size, location, and symptoms guide monitoring or repair.

topics.name: Aortic Arch Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Aortic arch syndrome is another name for Takayasu arteritis, an inflammatory disease of the aorta and its major branches. Inflammation usually narrows or blocks arteries, reducing blood flow to the arms, legs, brain, or other organs. Signs may include weak or unequal pulses, different blood pressures in the arms, pain with activity, dizziness, vision changes, or stroke; aneurysms can also occur.

topics.name: Aortic Branch Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: These uncommon bulges in arteries branching from the aorta are often found before symptoms occur. Depending on their location, they may press on nearby structures, reduce blood flow, or rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding. Imaging is used to assess them, and repair depends on size, location, symptoms, and rupture risk; some aneurysms supplying abdominal organs carry higher risk during pregnancy.

topics.name: Aortic Disruption (Traumatic)
topics.clinical_significance: A tear in the aorta after severe chest trauma can cause rapid, life-threatening bleeding. A partial tear may be temporarily contained and have few signs, so a severe crash, fall, or penetrating chest injury may need prompt aortic imaging even if initial findings are unclear. Treatment usually involves a stent graft or surgery.

topics.name: Aortic Dissection
topics.clinical_significance: Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters a tear in the aorta's inner wall and splits its layers. It often causes sudden, severe chest or back pain and can block blood flow to organs, damage the aortic valve, or lead to rupture, shock, and death. It is a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Aortic Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: The aortic valve does not close fully, so blood leaks back into the heart's main pumping chamber. Over time, this can enlarge and weaken the heart and lead to heart failure. Sudden, severe leakage can quickly cause fluid in the lungs and shock.

topics.name: Aortic Regurgitation
topics.clinical_significance: In aortic regurgitation, blood flows backward from the aorta into the left ventricle as the heart relaxes. Chronic disease may cause no symptoms for years, then enlarge and weaken the ventricle and lead to breathlessness, abnormal heart rhythms, or heart failure. Sudden severe regurgitation can cause fluid in the lungs and shock.

topics.name: Aortic Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: A narrowed aortic valve makes it harder for the heart to pump blood to the body and strains the left ventricle. Severe disease can cause fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath during activity. It can progress to heart failure and may cause sudden death.

topics.name: Aortitis
topics.clinical_significance: Aortitis is inflammation of the aorta, the body's main artery. It can narrow or block the aorta or its branches, or weaken the artery wall and cause an aneurysm. It is rare but can be life-threatening; causes include immune diseases and infections.

topics.name: Aortopulmonary Window
topics.clinical_significance: This birth defect creates an opening between the aorta and pulmonary artery, sending too much blood to the lungs. It can cause heart failure and high pressure in the lung arteries, especially in infants. If not repaired, lasting lung blood vessel damage and reversal of blood flow can develop.

topics.name: APAP
topics.clinical_significance: APAP is short for acetaminophen (paracetamol), a common pain and fever medicine. An overdose can cause severe liver damage, liver failure, and death, even when early symptoms are mild. The antidote N-acetylcysteine can prevent or reduce liver injury when given promptly.

topics.name: Aphasia
topics.clinical_significance: Aphasia is a problem with language caused by damage to brain areas that control language. It can affect speaking, understanding, reading, or writing and make communication difficult. Stroke is a common cause; recovery depends on the cause and extent of the brain damage.

topics.name: Apical Block
topics.clinical_significance: An apical block (supraperiosteal infiltration) numbs the nerves serving one tooth by placing local anesthetic near its root tip. It is commonly used for upper teeth in adults and for any tooth in children. Thick bone can make it less reliable, especially for lower teeth.

topics.name: Aplastic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Aplastic anemia occurs when the bone marrow fails to make enough blood cells. Low red cells, white cells, and platelets can cause fatigue, serious infections, and bleeding. Severe disease can be life-threatening, and some cases later develop into a myeloid blood cancer.

topics.name: Apnea of Prematurity
topics.clinical_significance: In premature infants, immature breathing control can cause pauses in breathing that lower oxygen levels and slow the heart rate. Episodes are monitored, and other causes such as infection must be considered. Most infants outgrow this condition by about 40 weeks of postmenstrual age (around their due date).

topics.name: Apoaequorin
topics.clinical_significance: Apoaequorin is a jellyfish protein used in a dietary supplement promoted for age-related memory loss. High-quality studies have not shown that it improves memory or treats disease. Its safety is not well known.

topics.name: Apophysitis of the Calcaneus
topics.clinical_significance: This painful injury affects the growth area at the back of the heel before the heel bone has finished developing. It often occurs in active children and teens when the Achilles tendon pulls on the growth area. Pain worsens with running or standing on tiptoe, but usually resolves as the heel matures; stretching and heel pads can ease symptoms.

topics.name: Appendicitis
topics.clinical_significance: Appendicitis is sudden inflammation of the appendix, often causing abdominal pain that shifts to the lower right side. Without prompt treatment, the appendix can rupture and cause an abscess or widespread abdominal infection, which can be life-threatening. With early treatment, recovery is usually complete.

topics.name: Approach to Parasitic Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Parasites can infect the gut, blood, organs, or skin and cause a wide range of illness. Diagnosis depends on the suspected parasite and exposure history, using tests on samples such as stool, blood, or tissue. Correct identification matters because treatment differs, and some infections can be severe in people with weak immune systems.

topics.name: Approach to Sports Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Sports injuries range from damage caused by repeated strain to sudden injuries such as sprains, strains, fractures, and concussion. The cause and symptoms help determine the injury's severity and whether imaging is needed. Returning to activity before healing can worsen the injury or cause reinjury.

topics.name: Approach to the Cardiac Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment for heart disease starts with a careful history and physical examination. Chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, fainting, and swelling can have heart-related or other causes, so the findings guide which tests are needed to confirm a diagnosis.

topics.name: Approach to the Critically Ill Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Critically ill patients may need intensive monitoring and support for breathing and heart function in an intensive care unit. Care also focuses on pain, nutrition, and preventing complications such as infection, blood clots, and pressure sores.

topics.name: Approach to the Dental Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Dental assessment can find tooth and mouth problems, including signs of oral cancer or disease elsewhere in the body. Dental infections can spread and cause serious illness, while medical conditions and medicines can affect dental care. Oral health can also affect eating and nutrition, especially in older adults.

topics.name: Approach to the Dermatologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Many skin conditions can be recognized by the appearance and pattern of skin changes, together with the patient's history. A skin exam can also reveal possible skin cancer or clues to disease elsewhere in the body. Biopsy or other tests may be needed when the cause is unclear.

topics.name: Approach to the Gastrointestinal Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Digestive symptoms can come from many organs and have many causes. A careful history and physical examination help narrow the cause and guide testing. Warning signs such as blood in the stool, trouble swallowing, ongoing vomiting, fever, anemia, or weight loss may point to more serious disease and need further evaluation.

topics.name: Approach to the Geriatric Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults often have several health conditions and take many medicines, which can complicate diagnosis and raise the risk of side effects. A broad assessment considers daily function, memory, nutrition, mood, and social support as well as physical illness. Early recognition can help prevent loss of independence.

topics.name: Approach to the Gynecologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic care uses a patient's history, symptoms, and risk factors to guide screening and testing across life stages. Pelvic pain, unusual bleeding, or discharge may need focused evaluation. A pelvic exam is based on symptoms and individual needs; it is not required at every routine visit for someone without symptoms.

topics.name: Approach to the Neurologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: A careful history and neurologic examination help locate the problem in the brain, spinal cord, nerves, or muscles and narrow its possible causes. This guides the choice of tests and helps distinguish neurologic disease from conditions that can mimic it.

topics.name: Approach to the Ophthalmologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: A careful eye assessment helps identify the cause of pain, redness, or vision changes and detect problems that may threaten sight. The history and checks of visual sharpness, pupils, visual fields, and eye movements help guide further testing or specialist evaluation.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With a Sleep or Wakefulness Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Sleep problems can affect mood, memory, coordination, and work, and increase the risk of traffic accidents. Insomnia and daytime sleepiness may result from sleep disorders, medical or mental health conditions, medicines, or not getting enough sleep. Finding the cause helps guide the right tests and care.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With a Suspected Inherited Disorder of Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: These rare disorders can cause vague symptoms such as poor feeding, vomiting, weakness, seizures, or delays in growth and development. Some can lead to sudden metabolic crises, lasting brain or organ damage, or death. Early recognition and treatment can prevent serious complications.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With a Thyroid Nodule
topics.clinical_significance: Thyroid nodules are common, and most are benign, but some are cancerous or make too much thyroid hormone. Blood tests and ultrasound help assess the nodule, with biopsy used when needed to check for cancer. Trouble swallowing or breathing, hoarseness, or rapid growth can raise concern.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia means there are too few red blood cells or too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen well. It may cause tiredness, weakness, or shortness of breath, though some people have no symptoms. Anemia is a sign of another problem, such as blood loss or reduced red blood cell production, so tests are needed to find and treat the cause.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Ear Problems
topics.clinical_significance: Ear problems may cause pain, hearing loss, discharge, ringing, or a spinning feeling. Ear pain can come from the ear or from nearby areas, such as the teeth, jaw, or throat. An ear examination and, when needed, hearing or balance tests help identify the cause.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Headache may be a primary disorder, such as migraine or tension-type headache, or a sign of another problem. Sudden severe pain, new neurologic symptoms, or fever with a stiff neck can point to a serious cause and need prompt assessment. The pattern of pain and examination help guide testing.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Joint Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Joint pain, stiffness, or swelling can come from arthritis or from nearby tissues such as tendons or bursae. The pattern of affected joints and other symptoms help identify the cause. A sudden or unexplained swollen joint needs prompt assessment; testing the joint fluid may be needed to check for infection or crystals.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Liver Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Liver disease may cause few symptoms or vague problems such as tiredness, poor appetite, and nausea. Yellow skin or eyes can point to liver or bile duct disease. A careful history, examination, and a combination of tests help find the cause and judge how serious it is.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Nasal and Pharyngeal Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Nasal or throat symptoms, such as congestion, discharge, nosebleeds, pain, trouble swallowing or speaking, or loss of smell, can result from infection, inflammation, injury, or tumors. A nose, throat, and neck examination helps find the cause. A persistent or hard neck lump needs medical assessment.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Psychiatric Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Psychiatric symptoms may come from a mental disorder, a physical illness, medicines, or substance use. New symptoms or a major change in a known condition should prompt a medical assessment, since physical problems can mimic or worsen a psychiatric disorder.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient with Renal Issues
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney disorders may cause few or no symptoms until they are severe. Changes in urine or urine output, swelling, or abnormal blood tests can be clues. Evaluation uses urine tests and blood tests of kidney function, with imaging or other tests when needed to find the cause.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Suspected Immunodeficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Immunodeficiency can cause repeated infections, but repeated infections alone do not prove it. Concern is greater when infections are severe, unusual, affect several body sites, or do not respond to usual treatment. Clinical assessment and immune tests are needed to confirm the cause.

topics.name: Approach to the Patient With Urologic Issues
topics.clinical_significance: Urologic problems can cause painful or frequent urination, blood in the urine, flank pain, or difficulty emptying the bladder. Examination and urine tests help find the cause. Blood in the urine needs a full evaluation because causes include stones and cancer.

topics.name: Approach to the Pregnant Woman and Prenatal Care
topics.clinical_significance: Prenatal care monitors the health of the pregnant person and fetus, screens for health problems, and helps reduce risks through testing, treatment, and counseling. Vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, abdominal pain, headache, or vision changes during pregnancy need medical assessment.

topics.name: Approach to the Pulmonary Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Breathlessness, cough, chest pain, or coughing blood can result from lung disease, but heart and other conditions can cause similar symptoms. A careful history and examination guide tests such as oxygen checks, chest imaging, and lung function tests to find the cause and assess severity.

topics.name: Approach to the Trauma Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Trauma can cause life-threatening airway or breathing problems, severe bleeding, and brain or spinal injuries. A rapid, structured check addresses immediate threats first; a detailed head-to-toe examination and selected imaging follow once the patient is stable.

topics.name: Apraxia
topics.clinical_significance: Apraxia is difficulty carrying out learned, purposeful actions despite being physically able to make the movements. It usually results from brain damage affecting movement planning and can make daily tasks and use of tools difficult or unsafe.

topics.name: Arbovirus, Arenavirus, and Filovirus Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: These viral infections spread in different ways: many arboviruses through insect or tick bites, arenaviruses through contact with infected rodents, and Ebola or Marburg through contact with infected people or body fluids. Illness may be absent or flu-like, but some infections cause bleeding, brain inflammation, or severe lung illness.

topics.name: Arbovirus Infections, Other
topics.clinical_significance: These infections are spread mainly by mosquitoes, biting midges, or ticks and often cause fever, headache, body aches, rash, or joint pain. Some can affect the brain, cause bleeding, or harm a pregnancy. Travel and insect-bite history can help identify the cause of fever or neurologic symptoms.

topics.name: Arboviruses, Arenaviridae, and Filoviridae
topics.clinical_significance: Arboviruses are grouped by how they spread, usually through mosquitoes, ticks, or other biting insects. Arenaviruses usually spread from rodents, while Ebola and Marburg viruses can spread between people. These infections may be mild or cause serious brain inflammation or bleeding.

topics.name: Arginine Vasopressin Resistance
topics.clinical_significance: The kidneys do not respond properly to vasopressin, so they cannot concentrate urine. This causes large amounts of dilute urine and strong thirst; if a person cannot drink enough, severe dehydration and high blood sodium can occur. The condition may be inherited or caused by kidney problems, electrolyte changes, or medicines.

topics.name: Arrhythmias, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Antiarrhythmic drugs can slow the heart rate or help restore a normal rhythm in selected rhythm disorders. The choice depends on the arrhythmia and the person's heart condition because these drugs can also cause or worsen abnormal rhythms and need careful monitoring.

topics.name: Arrhythmias, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: An arrhythmia is a problem with the heart’s electrical signals that changes its rhythm. It may cause no symptoms, palpitations, shortness of breath, chest discomfort, fainting, or cardiac arrest. An ECG, sometimes with longer heart-rhythm monitoring, helps identify the type; treatment depends on its cause, symptoms, and risk.

topics.name: Arrhythmogenic Cardiac Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Some heart muscle and electrical disorders make abnormal heart rhythms more likely, including rhythms that can cause sudden cardiac arrest or death. They may cause palpitations, fainting, or heart failure, but can also have few symptoms. ECG and heart-rhythm monitoring help detect problems; treatment depends on the specific disorder and may include medicines or an implanted defibrillator.

topics.name: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy and Variants
topics.clinical_significance: This usually inherited heart muscle disease mainly affects the right ventricle, where muscle is replaced by scar and fatty tissue. It can cause dangerous ventricular rhythms, fainting, or sudden cardiac death; heart failure may develop as the disease worsens. Variants can affect the left ventricle or both sides. Intense endurance exercise can worsen the disease, and close relatives may need screening.

topics.name: Arterial Gas Embolism
topics.clinical_significance: Gas bubbles in the arteries can block blood flow and deprive the brain or other organs of oxygen. This may cause sudden confusion, weakness, seizures, loss of consciousness, or death, often soon after a diver surfaces. It is a medical emergency: suspected cases need immediate 100% oxygen and urgent recompression treatment; imaging should not delay care.

topics.name: Arteriosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Arteriosclerosis is a general term for thickened, stiff arteries. Its most common and important form, atherosclerosis, involves fatty plaques that can narrow arteries and contribute to heart disease, stroke, or poor blood flow to the legs. Other forms affect small arteries or cause calcium to build up in artery walls.

topics.name: Arteriovenous Fistula
topics.clinical_significance: An abnormal connection between an artery and a vein may be present from birth or result from injury or a procedure. Surgeons also create one to provide access for hemodialysis. The high-pressure blood flow can cause swelling or poor blood flow to nearby tissues and, rarely, strain the heart.

topics.name: Arthritis, Acute Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: A sudden joint infection, usually caused by bacteria, can cause severe pain, swelling, warmth, and limited movement. It can destroy joint cartilage within hours or days and may lead to sepsis. Prompt joint-fluid testing and treatment with antibiotics are needed; the joint often also needs drainage.

topics.name: Arthritis, Chronic Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: A joint infection that persists for weeks is often caused by fungi, mycobacteria, or less aggressive bacteria. It usually affects one joint and may cause gradual swelling and aching, with little redness. It can slowly damage cartilage and bone, and often needs special testing and prolonged treatment.

topics.name: Arthritis of the Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ)
topics.clinical_significance: Arthritis of the jaw joint can cause pain, stiffness, and difficulty opening or moving the mouth. Causes include infection, injury, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis. An infected joint needs rapid diagnosis and treatment to prevent permanent damage; other forms may also limit jaw movement or damage the joint over time.

topics.name: Arthritis, Prosthetic Joint Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: An infection in an artificial joint can cause pain, swelling, and limited movement, and may lead to sepsis. It can occur soon after surgery or later if germs spread through the blood. Diagnosis may be difficult; treatment usually requires prolonged antibiotics and surgery to clean the joint, with the implant sometimes removed or replaced.

topics.name: Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita
topics.clinical_significance: This is a group of rare conditions in which several joints are stiff and bent from birth because movement was limited before birth. It can cause major difficulty with movement, and the underlying cause may affect other parts of the body. Finding the cause helps guide care and family counseling; early stretching, casting, and sometimes surgery can improve function.

topics.name: Arthro-Onychodysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder affecting the fingernails and toenails, kneecaps, elbows, and pelvis. Kidney problems occur in some people and may cause protein or blood in the urine, high blood pressure, or kidney failure; glaucoma can also develop. Recognizing the disorder helps identify and manage these complications.

topics.name: Arthropod Bites, Other
topics.clinical_significance: Bites from non-tick insects and other arthropods can cause itchy or painful skin bumps, swelling, or sores. Mosquitoes can spread serious infections, and bites may also lead to skin infection or, rarely, a severe allergic reaction.

topics.name: Asbestosis
topics.clinical_significance: Asbestosis is progressive lung scarring caused by inhaled asbestos fibers. It can cause worsening breathlessness with activity, dry cough, and fatigue; severe disease may lead to respiratory or right-sided heart failure. Asbestos exposure also raises the risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, especially when combined with smoking for lung cancer.

topics.name: Asbestos-Related Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing asbestos fibers can cause lung scarring, pleural plaques or thickening, and fluid around the lungs. It also raises the risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure. Smoking greatly adds to the lung cancer risk.

topics.name: Asbestos-Related Pleural Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Asbestos can cause calcified pleural plaques, thickening, fluid around the lungs, and mesothelioma. Plaques often cause no symptoms but show past asbestos exposure; widespread thickening can restrict breathing. A pleural effusion needs evaluation to rule out cancer.

topics.name: Ascariasis
topics.clinical_significance: This roundworm infection spreads when a person swallows eggs from fecally contaminated soil, food, or hands. Light infections may cause no symptoms; larvae can cause cough or wheezing as they pass through the lungs. Heavy infections can cause poor nutrition in children or block the intestine or bile and pancreatic ducts.

topics.name: Ascites
topics.clinical_significance: Free fluid in the abdomen is most often due to high pressure in the liver's blood vessels, usually from cirrhosis, but can also result from heart or kidney disease, cancer, or pancreatitis. It can enlarge the abdomen and, when severe, cause breathlessness. New ascites needs evaluation; pain or fever may signal a dangerous infection of the fluid.

topics.name: Ascorbic Acid Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Severe vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) weakens connective tissue and blood vessels. It can cause fatigue, swollen or bleeding gums, easy bruising or internal bleeding, and poor wound healing. In children, bone growth may be impaired. Treatment is vitamin C and a nutritious diet.

topics.name: Ascorbic Acid Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Large doses of vitamin C supplements can cause nausea, diarrhea, and kidney stones. In people with hemochromatosis or thalassemia, high doses may worsen iron overload. Intake below 2 g a day is not toxic for most healthy adults.

topics.name: Aseptic Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord without the bacteria that usually cause acute bacterial meningitis. Viruses are common causes, but medicines, autoimmune disease, fungi, and other infections can also be responsible. Because symptoms can resemble bacterial meningitis, testing is needed to rule out that urgent infection.

topics.name: Aseptic Necrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Death of bone tissue from loss of its blood supply, most often affecting the hip and sometimes the knee or shoulder. It may cause pain and limited movement, and the bone can collapse and lead to arthritis. Causes include injury, corticosteroid use, and heavy alcohol use; early treatment may help preserve the joint.

topics.name: Ashwagandha
topics.clinical_significance: Ashwagandha is an herbal supplement promoted for stress and sleep, but evidence of benefit is limited. It may cause nausea, diarrhea, or sleepiness, and has been linked to liver injury. It can interact with several medicines and should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

topics.name: Aspergillosis
topics.clinical_significance: Aspergillosis includes allergic reactions and fungal infections caused by inhaled Aspergillus spores. It can affect the lungs or sinuses. Invasive infection can spread to other organs, especially in people with weakened immunity; a fungus ball in an old lung cavity may cause bleeding.

topics.name: Aspirin and Other Salicylate Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Too much aspirin or another salicylate can cause vomiting, ringing in the ears, rapid breathing, fever, and confusion. Severe poisoning can lead to seizures, dangerous changes in blood acidity, kidney or respiratory failure, and death. Repeated high doses can cause subtle poisoning, especially in older adults, so suspected overdose needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Assisted Reproductive Technologies
topics.clinical_significance: These fertility treatments handle eggs, sperm, or embryos outside the body to help achieve pregnancy; in vitro fertilization is the main example. Risks include ovarian hyperstimulation and multiple pregnancy, especially if more than one embryo is transferred. Any increase in birth-defect risk is uncertain and may be related to infertility itself.

topics.name: Asthma
topics.clinical_significance: Asthma is a long-term disease in which inflamed, sensitive airways narrow at times, causing wheezing, cough, chest tightness, or shortness of breath. Symptoms may be triggered by allergens, infections, exercise, cold air, smoke, or some medicines. Airway narrowing is often reversible with treatment, but severe attacks can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Asthma and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: This group covers asthma, asthma medicines and flare-ups, and related conditions such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Asthma causes episodes of narrowed airways and breathing symptoms; severe attacks can be life-threatening. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis can inflame and block the airways in people with asthma.

topics.name: Asthma, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Asthma medicines are chosen step by step to control symptoms and prevent attacks. Inhaled corticosteroids are the main long-term treatment; bronchodilators relieve airway narrowing, and combination inhalers or biologic medicines may be added for more severe disease. Long-acting beta agonists should be used with an inhaled corticosteroid, not alone.

topics.name: Asthma Exacerbation, Treatment
topics.clinical_significance: An asthma flare causes worsening airway narrowing and breathing symptoms and can progress to respiratory failure. Treatment aims to quickly open the airways and restore lung function, usually with inhaled bronchodilators and often steroid medicines. Severe flares need urgent care and may require oxygen or hospital treatment.

topics.name: Asthma in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Asthma may improve or worsen during pregnancy. Most pregnant people do not have severe attacks, but poorly controlled asthma raises the risk of poor fetal growth, premature birth, preeclampsia, and serious maternal complications. Keeping asthma controlled with inhaled medicines and limiting triggers helps reduce these risks.

topics.name: Astragalus
topics.clinical_significance: Astragalus is a plant-based supplement used for many claimed health benefits, but high-quality studies have not shown that it treats any condition. It may worsen autoimmune diseases and interact with immune-suppressing drugs, lithium, and diabetes medicines. Animal studies raise concern about use during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

topics.name: Astrocytomas
topics.clinical_significance: Astrocytomas are brain or spinal cord tumors that arise from astrocytes. In children, they range from slow-growing tumors, often in the cerebellum, to aggressive high-grade tumors. They can cause headaches and vomiting from increased pressure in the skull, or symptoms such as seizures, weakness, balance problems, or vision changes, depending on their location. Low-grade tumors often have good outcomes, while high-grade tumors have a poor prognosis.

topics.name: Ataxia-Telangiectasia
topics.clinical_significance: Ataxia-telangiectasia is a rare inherited disorder caused by faulty DNA repair. It leads to worsening problems with balance and movement, small widened blood vessels in the eyes or skin, and weak immune defenses that can cause repeated lung infections. It also raises the risk of cancer, especially leukemia and lymphoma.

topics.name: Atelectasis
topics.clinical_significance: Atelectasis is collapse of part or all of the lung, causing loss of lung volume. Small areas may cause no symptoms, but extensive collapse can lower blood oxygen and cause shortness of breath. It can also lead to pneumonia or, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Common causes include a blocked airway, shallow breathing after surgery, or pressure on the lung.

topics.name: Atherosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Atherosclerosis is buildup of fatty, cholesterol-rich plaques in artery walls. Plaques may slowly narrow an artery or rupture and trigger a blood clot that suddenly blocks blood flow. Depending on which artery is affected, this can cause a heart attack, stroke, or poor circulation in the limbs.

topics.name: Athlete’s Heart
topics.clinical_significance: Athlete’s heart is a normal change in heart size and function caused by long-term intense exercise. It may cause a slow resting heart rate and changes on an electrocardiogram, usually without symptoms. These changes can resemble serious heart disease, so distinguishing athlete’s heart from cardiomyopathy is important.

topics.name: Atlantoaxial Subluxation
topics.clinical_significance: Atlantoaxial subluxation is misalignment or abnormal movement between the first two bones of the neck. It may cause no symptoms, but can cause neck pain or headache and, rarely, compress the spinal cord, which can be life-threatening. It may follow major trauma or occur with conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome.

topics.name: Atopic Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Atopic conjunctivitis is long-lasting allergic inflammation of the eye surface, often triggered by indoor allergens such as dust mites or animal dander. It causes itching, redness, eyelid swelling, and watery or stringy discharge. Severe cases can scar the conjunctiva or cornea and impair vision.

topics.name: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
topics.clinical_significance: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, recurring skin disorder linked to a weak skin barrier and inflammation. It causes intense itching and dry, red, scaly patches; repeated scratching can thicken the skin and increase the risk of skin infections. It often occurs with asthma or allergic rhinitis, but the skin disease itself is not an allergic reaction.

topics.name: Atopic Eczema
topics.clinical_significance: Atopic eczema is another name for atopic dermatitis, a chronic, recurring skin disorder linked to a weak skin barrier and inflammation. It causes intense itching and dry, red, scaly patches; repeated scratching can thicken the skin and increase the risk of skin infections. The skin disease itself is not an allergic reaction.

topics.name: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a long-lasting form of allergic conjunctivitis, often triggered by year-round indoor allergens. It can cause eye itching, redness, eyelid swelling, and watery or stringy discharge. Severe disease may scar the conjunctiva or cornea and reduce vision.

topics.name: Atrial Fibrillation
topics.clinical_significance: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular heart rhythm in which the atria quiver instead of contracting normally. It may cause palpitations or breathlessness, but some people have no symptoms. Blood can pool in the atria and form clots that cause stroke. If the heart rate stays very fast, the heart can weaken and heart failure may develop.

topics.name: Atrial Fibrillation and Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome (WPW Syndrome)
topics.clinical_significance: When atrial fibrillation occurs with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, electrical signals can bypass the heart’s normal rate control and make the lower chambers beat dangerously fast. This can trigger ventricular fibrillation and sudden death, so it is a medical emergency. Digoxin, adenosine, and drugs such as verapamil or diltiazem can be dangerous in this setting.

topics.name: Atrial Flutter
topics.clinical_significance: Atrial flutter is a fast, usually regular heart rhythm caused by a circular electrical signal in the atria. It may cause palpitations, breathlessness, or weakness, but some people have few or no symptoms. Clots can form in the atria and cause stroke. Many people with atrial flutter also have or later develop atrial fibrillation.

topics.name: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
topics.clinical_significance: An atrial septal defect is a hole between the heart’s upper chambers that usually sends extra blood to the right side of the heart and lungs. Small defects may cause no symptoms and can close on their own. Larger defects can strain the right heart, raise pressure in the lung arteries, and cause abnormal heart rhythms or heart failure. Rarely, a clot can cross the opening and cause a stroke.

topics.name: Atrioventricular Block
topics.clinical_significance: Atrioventricular block is slowed or interrupted electrical signaling from the upper to the lower heart chambers. Mild forms may cause no symptoms, while advanced block can cause a very slow heartbeat, dizziness, fainting, or heart failure. Some forms can progress suddenly to complete block and dangerous pauses; a pacemaker is often needed.

topics.name: Atrioventricular Canal Defect
topics.clinical_significance: An atrioventricular canal defect is a birth defect with a hole between the upper heart chambers, sometimes a second hole between the lower chambers, and an abnormal valve between them. Large defects or a leaking valve can send extra blood to the lungs, causing heart failure and poor growth in infancy. This defect is strongly linked with Down syndrome.

topics.name: Atrioventricular Septal Defect
topics.clinical_significance: An atrioventricular septal defect is a birth defect with an opening between the upper heart chambers, sometimes a second opening between the lower chambers, and an abnormal valve between them. Large openings or a leaking valve can send extra blood to the lungs, causing heart failure and poor growth in infancy. Complete defects are strongly linked with Down syndrome.

topics.name: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
topics.clinical_significance: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by ongoing inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity that interferes with daily functioning. It begins in childhood, though difficulties may continue into adulthood. ADHD can affect learning, work, relationships, and daily activities, and may occur with learning, anxiety, or mood disorders.

topics.name: Atypical Fibroxanthoma
topics.clinical_significance: Atypical fibroxanthoma is a rare, low-grade skin sarcoma that usually appears as a fast-growing red or pink lump on sun-exposed skin, especially the head or neck of older adults. It can resemble other skin cancers, so diagnosis requires a biopsy. It rarely spreads, and death from the disease is very unlikely.

topics.name: Atypical Nevi (Moles)
topics.clinical_significance: Atypical nevi are benign moles with uneven color and irregular or unclear borders. They are not melanoma, but having many—especially with a family history of melanoma—increases melanoma risk. Most melanomas arise in normal skin, though some develop in atypical moles. Biopsy may be needed when a mole looks highly unusual or changes.

topics.name: Atypical Nevus
topics.clinical_significance: An atypical nevus is a benign mole with irregular borders and uneven color. It is not melanoma, but having multiple atypical nevi increases melanoma risk. A very unusual or changing mole may need biopsy because atypical nevi can be hard to distinguish from melanoma.

topics.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition involving ongoing differences in social communication and interaction, along with restricted or repetitive behaviors or interests. Features begin in early development, may be recognized later, and can affect daily functioning. Abilities and support needs vary widely; learning difficulties or intellectual disability may also occur.

topics.name: Autoimmune Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune disorders develop when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissues. The attack may involve antibodies or immune cells and can affect one organ or many, causing inflammation and tissue damage. Examples include type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and multiple sclerosis.

topics.name: Autoimmune Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune diseases may improve or worsen during pregnancy, depending on the condition. Some raise the risks of blood clots, pregnancy loss, preeclampsia, poor fetal growth, or preterm birth. In lupus, maternal antibodies can rarely cause fetal heart block or temporary blood-count problems in the newborn. Risks depend on the disease and how active it is.

topics.name: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia occurs when antibodies mistakenly attach to red blood cells and cause their early destruction. This lowers red blood cell levels and may cause fatigue, pale or yellow skin, dark urine, or shortness of breath. It may be linked to medicines or another disease; severe hemolysis can be life-threatening, and blood-clot risk is increased.

topics.name: Autoimmune Metaplastic Atrophic Gastritis
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis occurs when the immune system damages stomach cells that make acid and intrinsic factor, a protein needed to absorb vitamin B12. It can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, and nerve problems. It also increases the risk of stomach cancer and neuroendocrine tumors.

topics.name: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune polyglandular syndromes are disorders in which the immune system damages more than one hormone-producing gland. The affected glands and timing vary, and new hormone deficiencies may appear years apart. Problems can include adrenal insufficiency, thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, or low parathyroid function. Unrecognized adrenal insufficiency can cause a life-threatening crisis.

topics.name: Autoimmune Rheumatic Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic rheumatic diseases are a varied group of inflammatory disorders, many caused by abnormal immune activity, that can affect joints, muscles, blood vessels, connective tissue, and internal organs. They can raise the risk of atherosclerosis. Medicines that suppress the immune system can increase infection risk, and corticosteroids can weaken bones.

topics.name: Autoimmune Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Autoimmune thyroiditis is chronic immune damage to the thyroid, most often Hashimoto thyroiditis. It may cause a painless enlarged thyroid and, over time, low thyroid hormone levels (hypothyroidism); a temporary rise in hormone levels can occur early. It is a common cause of hypothyroidism and may occur with other autoimmune disorders.

topics.name: Autonomic Nervous System
topics.clinical_significance: It controls body functions that happen without conscious effort, such as heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, sweating, pupil changes, bladder function, and sexual function. Problems with it can affect many body systems.

topics.name: Autonomic Nervous System, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The sympathetic division prepares the body for action, while the parasympathetic division supports rest and digestion. Together they regulate automatic functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, sweating, and urination. Autonomic failure can affect many body systems.

topics.name: Autonomic Neuropathies
topics.clinical_significance: These nerve disorders impair automatic control of body functions. They can cause dizziness from low blood pressure on standing, bladder problems, erectile dysfunction, slow stomach emptying, or severe constipation. Diabetes and amyloidosis are common causes.

topics.name: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited condition causes cysts to grow in both kidneys. It can cause high blood pressure, blood in the urine, and pain, and may lead to kidney failure. Cysts can also form in other organs, and the condition raises the risk of brain aneurysms.

topics.name: AV Block
topics.clinical_significance: AV block slows or stops electrical signals from the heart’s upper chambers to its lower chambers. Mild forms may cause no symptoms; more advanced block can cause a slow heartbeat, dizziness, fainting, or heart failure. Mobitz type II and complete block often need a pacemaker unless the cause is reversible.

topics.name: AV Fistula
topics.clinical_significance: An AV fistula is a direct connection between an artery and a vein. Surgeons create one to provide access for hemodialysis; fistulas from birth or injury can reduce blood flow to nearby tissue, cause swelling, or rarely strain the heart enough to cause heart failure.

topics.name: Avascular Necrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) is death of bone tissue after its blood supply is reduced. It most often affects the hip and can also affect the knee or shoulder. It may cause pain, limited movement, collapse of the joint surface, and arthritis. Injury, steroid use, heavy alcohol use, and some diseases can cause it.

topics.name: Avian Influenza
topics.clinical_significance: Avian influenza viruses mostly infect birds, but some can infect people after exposure to infected birds or other animals, such as cattle. Human infections may be mild or cause eye symptoms, flu-like illness, or severe pneumonia and respiratory failure. Spread between people is limited.

topics.name: Avoidant Personality Disorder (AVPD)
topics.clinical_significance: People with AVPD feel inadequate and strongly fear criticism or rejection, so they avoid social and work situations. This can lead to isolation and difficulty functioning; anxiety and depressive disorders often occur alongside it.

topics.name: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)
topics.clinical_significance: People with ARFID eat too little or avoid certain foods because of low interest in food, sensory aversions, or fear of problems such as choking. This is not driven by concern about body weight or shape. It can cause weight loss or poor growth, nutrient deficiencies, need for nutritional support, and social difficulties.

topics.name: Ayurveda
topics.clinical_significance: Ayurveda is a traditional Indian medical system that uses diet, herbs, massage, meditation, movement, and cleansing practices to restore balance. Evidence for its effectiveness is not conclusive, and some herbal products contain toxic amounts of lead, mercury, or arsenic.

topics.name: B Ring
topics.clinical_significance: A Schatzki (B) ring is a thin band of tissue that narrows the lower esophagus near the stomach. It can cause episodes of difficulty swallowing solid food, especially meat or dry bread, and food may get stuck.

topics.name: Babesiosis
topics.clinical_significance: Babesiosis is usually spread by tick bites, but it can also pass through blood transfusion. It may cause no symptoms or a malaria-like illness with fever and anemia from red blood cell breakdown. Severe disease is more likely in people without a spleen, older adults, and people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Bacillary Angiomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: This Bartonella infection usually affects people with weakened immunity. It causes fragile red or purple skin bumps that bleed easily and can spread to organs such as the liver, spleen, bones, or brain. It may resemble Kaposi sarcoma, but antibiotics can treat it.

topics.name: Bacillary Dysentery
topics.clinical_significance: Bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) is a highly contagious infection spread through contaminated hands, food, or objects. It causes diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and often fever; stools may contain blood or mucus. Severe fluid loss can be dangerous, especially for young children and people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Back Pain, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Most back pain comes from mechanical problems, and a single cause may not be clear. Evaluation checks for rare but serious causes and nerve damage. Short-lasting pain usually needs no tests unless warning signs such as fever, unexplained weight loss, weakness, or new bowel or bladder problems are present.

topics.name: Bacopa
topics.clinical_significance: Bacopa is an herbal supplement promoted for memory and focus, but high-quality studies have not confirmed these benefits. It can cause stomach upset and may interact with medicines, including thyroid hormone, warfarin, and some drugs for Alzheimer disease or glaucoma.

topics.name: Bacteremia
topics.clinical_significance: Bacteremia is the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream. It may be brief and cause no symptoms, but bacteria can spread to organs such as the heart valves or lead to sepsis, especially when the infection persists or becomes severe.

topics.name: Bacteria and Antibacterial Medications
topics.clinical_significance: Antibacterial medicines treat bacterial infections, not viral illnesses. The medicine should match the likely bacteria and infection. Unneeded or overly broad use can cause side effects, disrupt helpful bacteria, and promote antibiotic resistance.

topics.name: Bacteria, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Many bacteria normally live on or in the body without causing illness, while some cause infection. Their shape, cell wall staining, and oxygen needs help identify them; antibiotic susceptibility testing helps guide treatment.

topics.name: Bacterial Infections in Infants and Children, Miscellaneous
topics.clinical_significance: This section covers different bacterial infections in infants and children. Symptoms and risks depend on the child’s age and the infection site; serious infections such as meningitis may begin with vague signs and worsen quickly.

topics.name: Bacterial Meningitis in Infants Over 3 Months of Age
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening infection of the tissues around the brain and spinal cord. In infants older than 3 months, it may begin with vague signs such as fever, irritability, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness, then worsen quickly. Prompt diagnosis and antibiotics are vital; survivors may have hearing loss or other lasting problems.

topics.name: Bacterial Nasal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: These infections affect the skin just inside the nostrils, often from Staphylococcus aureus. They can cause crusting, bleeding, pain, or swelling. A nasal boil may spread to the skin of the nose and, rarely, cause a dangerous blood clot near the brain.

topics.name: Bacterial Skin Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial skin infections range from small, superficial sores to deep or rapidly spreading infections that can be life-threatening. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus are common causes; antibiotic-resistant strains such as MRSA can affect treatment choices.

topics.name: Bacterial Tracheitis
topics.clinical_significance: This uncommon infection of the windpipe mainly affects young children, often after a viral respiratory illness. It can cause high fever, harsh cough, noisy or difficult breathing, and rapid airway blockage. It may become life-threatening and require urgent airway support and antibiotics.

topics.name: Bacterial Urinary Tract Infections
topics.clinical_significance: A bacterial UTI may affect the bladder, causing painful or frequent urination, or reach the kidneys, causing fever and side or back pain. Kidney infection can spread to the bloodstream and cause sepsis. Urine tests, sometimes including a culture, help guide antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)
topics.clinical_significance: BV is an imbalance of vaginal bacteria in which usual lactobacilli decrease and other bacteria overgrow. It may cause thin, fishy-smelling discharge, though many people have no symptoms. It is associated with pelvic inflammatory disease and pregnancy complications such as preterm birth.

topics.name: Bad Breath
topics.clinical_significance: Halitosis is persistent unpleasant breath odor. Most cases come from bacteria and food debris on the tongue or between teeth, gum disease, smoking, or certain foods; dry mouth can contribute. Nose, lung, or digestive conditions cause it less often.

topics.name: Baker Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: A Baker cyst is a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee, often related to arthritis or a meniscus injury. It may cause pain or stiffness; if it ruptures, calf swelling can resemble a blood clot.

topics.name: Baker's Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: A Baker cyst is a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee, often related to arthritis or a meniscus injury. It may cause pain or stiffness; if it ruptures, calf swelling can resemble a blood clot.

topics.name: Balancing Treatment Benefits and Adverse Effects
topics.clinical_significance: Clinicians weigh a treatment’s likely benefits against its harms and the patient’s preferences. Absolute risks and estimates of how many people must be treated for one person to benefit or be harmed help make this comparison. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic window need careful dosing.

topics.name: Balanitis, Posthitis, and Balanoposthitis
topics.clinical_significance: Balanitis affects the glans, posthitis the foreskin, and balanoposthitis both. Causes include infection and noninfectious skin irritation; diabetes and a tight foreskin increase risk. Chronic inflammation can lead to scarring, phimosis, or paraphimosis.

topics.name: Baldness
topics.clinical_significance: Baldness usually means loss of scalp hair. The common pattern type is often inherited and linked to androgens, but hair loss can also result from medicines, illness, infection, or scalp disease. Some scarring forms permanently damage hair follicles, and hair loss can signal an underlying disorder.

topics.name: Bancroftian Lymphatic Filariasis and Brugian Lymphatic Filariasis
topics.clinical_significance: These mosquito-borne worm infections affect the lymph vessels. They may cause recurrent fever and inflammation; long-term damage can block lymph flow, leading to severe swelling (elephantiasis) or hydrocele. Some infected people have no symptoms.

topics.name: Barotitis Media
topics.clinical_significance: Barotitis media is middle-ear pain or injury caused by rapid pressure changes, often during flying or diving when the eustachian tube cannot equalize pressure. Severe cases can rupture the eardrum or injure the inner ear, causing hearing loss or vertigo.

topics.name: Barotrauma, Ear and Sinus
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure-related injury to the ear or sinuses can occur when pressure changes faster than these spaces can equalize, often during diving. It can cause ear or sinus pain, hearing loss, dizziness, or congestion; severe cases can rupture the eardrum or damage the inner ear or sinuses.

topics.name: Barotrauma, Gastrointestinal
topics.clinical_significance: During ascent from a dive, swallowed air can expand in the gut and cause temporary fullness, cramps, pain, belching, or gas. Rarely, the gastrointestinal tract can rupture, causing severe abdominal pain and tenderness that needs emergency care.

topics.name: Barotrauma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Barotrauma is tissue injury caused by pressure changes that expand or compress gas in body spaces, often during diving. Effects depend on the area affected and may include ear or sinus pain, hearing loss, dizziness, or abdominal pain; lung or gastrointestinal rupture can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Barrier and Other Pericoital Contraceptives
topics.clinical_significance: These methods are used around the time of sex to lower the chance of pregnancy; how well they work varies and depends on correct use. Condoms also reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections, but diaphragms, caps, sponges, spermicides, and contraceptive gel do not reliably protect against them.

topics.name: Bartholin Gland Cyst and Bartholin Gland Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A blocked Bartholin gland duct can form a cyst beside the vaginal opening. It may be painless, but a large cyst can cause pressure or pain; infection can form a very painful abscess, sometimes with fever. A new or unusual lump, especially after age 40 or menopause, may need assessment to rule out rare gland cancer.

topics.name: Bartonella Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Bartonella are bacteria usually spread to people by insects. Depending on the species, infection may cause swollen lymph nodes, recurring fever, anemia, skin lesions, or heart-valve infection. Widespread disease is more likely in people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Bartonellosis
topics.clinical_significance: Bartonellosis is infection with Bartonella bacteria, usually spread by insect vectors. Depending on the species, it can cause swollen lymph nodes, fever, anemia, skin lesions, or heart-valve infection; widespread disease is more likely in people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Bartter Syndrome and Gitelman Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: These usually inherited kidney disorders cause salt and potassium loss in the urine, low blood potassium, and metabolic alkalosis, often with normal or low blood pressure. They can cause dehydration, muscle weakness or cramps, and poor growth; low magnesium is common in Gitelman syndrome.

topics.name: Bartter's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Bartter syndrome is an inherited kidney tubule disorder that often appears before birth or in early childhood. Salt loss can cause low blood potassium and metabolic alkalosis despite normal or low blood pressure; it may also cause excessive urination, poor growth, and calcium deposits in the kidneys.

topics.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: The most common skin cancer, usually linked to ultraviolet exposure. It often appears as a shiny, slow-growing bump or a sore that repeatedly crusts or bleeds. It rarely spreads to distant organs but can damage nearby tissue. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis; treatment is usually local, often surgery.

topics.name: Basic Calcium Phosphate Crystal Deposition Disease and Calcium Oxalate Crystal Deposition Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Basic calcium phosphate crystals can cause painful inflammation around or within joints and may destroy joints, as in Milwaukee shoulder syndrome. Calcium oxalate crystal deposition is very rare and usually occurs in people with advanced kidney failure on dialysis; crystals can affect joints, skin, and blood vessels.

topics.name: Bath Salts
topics.clinical_significance: “Bath salts” is a street name for synthetic cathinone stimulants, not ordinary bath products. Toxicity can cause severe agitation, rapid heartbeat, high blood pressure, seizures, and dangerous overheating; severe cases may cause abnormal heart rhythms or muscle breakdown.

topics.name: Baylisascariasis
topics.clinical_significance: This rare infection follows accidental ingestion of eggs from the raccoon roundworm, often from contaminated soil or objects. Larvae can migrate through organs; brain infection may cause severe, lasting neurologic damage or death, and eye infection can threaten vision.

topics.name: Becker's Muscular Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Becker muscular dystrophy is an X-linked disorder caused by abnormal or reduced dystrophin, a protein needed for healthy muscle. It causes progressive muscle weakness but usually begins later and is milder than Duchenne muscular dystrophy; the heart can also be affected.

topics.name: Bedbugs
topics.clinical_significance: Bedbugs feed on blood, and their usually painless bites may later cause itchy skin reactions; scratching can lead to infection. Although bedbugs can carry infectious organisms, they are not known to spread them to people. Infestations can also disturb sleep and cause anxiety.

topics.name: Bedsores
topics.clinical_significance: Bedsores (pressure injuries) are skin and deeper tissue damage from prolonged pressure, often over a bone in people with limited mobility. Early injury may leave the skin intact, but damage can deepen into an ulcer and become infected, sometimes affecting bone or the bloodstream.

topics.name: Behavioral and Psychologic Symptoms of Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: Dementia may cause wandering, agitation, sleep changes, depression, or hallucinations, creating safety concerns and caregiver strain. A sudden change in behavior may signal pain, illness, or delirium and needs assessment; supportive environmental measures are preferred, with medicines reserved for selected cases.

topics.name: Behavioral Emergencies
topics.clinical_significance: A behavioral emergency is a severe change in mood, thoughts, or behavior that may threaten the person’s safety, the safety of others, or the person’s ability to care for themself. It needs urgent assessment to identify the cause, which may be a medical problem, substance use, or mental illness, while keeping everyone safe.

topics.name: Behavioral Problems in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Many behavior concerns are part of normal development. They are more concerning when frequent or persistent and interfere with a child’s development, relationships, or daily functioning. Assessment should consider the child’s age, health, and circumstances; early support often includes guidance for caregivers.

topics.name: Behavioral Problems in Children, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A behavior is more concerning when it is frequent or persistent and interferes with a child’s development, relationships, or daily functioning; severe problems may reflect a psychiatric disorder. Concerns vary with age, from eating or sleep issues in young children to activity, defiance, or aggression in older children. Assessment considers development, health, and family or social circumstances.

topics.name: Behçet Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Behçet disease is a relapsing inflammatory disorder that affects mucous membranes and blood vessels. It commonly causes recurrent mouth ulcers, genital ulcers, skin lesions, and eye inflammation. Eye, brain, gut, or blood-vessel involvement can cause serious damage, including vision loss, blood clots, or aneurysms.

topics.name: Behçet's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Behçet’s disease is a relapsing inflammation of mucous membranes and blood vessels. Recurrent mouth ulcers are common, often with genital ulcers, skin lesions, or eye inflammation; severe eye, neurologic, intestinal, or vascular disease can cause blindness, blood clots, or aneurysms.

topics.name: Bejel, Pinta, and Yaws
topics.clinical_significance: These chronic treponemal infections spread through close body contact, often among children. They can cause skin or mouth lesions; bejel and yaws may later damage bone and tissue, while pinta mainly affects the skin and can leave lasting discoloration. They can resemble syphilis, so diagnosis depends on the clinical and exposure history.

topics.name: Bell Palsy
topics.clinical_significance: Bell palsy is sudden weakness or paralysis of one side of the face from peripheral facial-nerve dysfunction, often with no identified cause. The eye may not close fully and can become dry or injured. Prompt assessment is important because other problems, including stroke, can also cause facial weakness.

topics.name: Bell's Palsy
topics.clinical_significance: Bell’s palsy is a common name for sudden, one-sided peripheral facial weakness, often with no clear cause. It can prevent the eye from closing and dry or injure the cornea. Assessment helps distinguish it from stroke and other causes of facial-nerve weakness.

topics.name: Benign Adnexal Masses
topics.clinical_significance: Benign adnexal masses arise in or near the ovaries or fallopian tubes. Many are harmless, temporary ovarian cysts that resolve on their own; most cause no symptoms, though some cause pelvic pain or rarely rupture or twist (torsion). Ultrasound helps assess the mass and check for features that could suggest cancer.

topics.name: Benign Bone Tumors and Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Many benign bone tumors and cysts cause no symptoms, but some cause pain or swelling and weaken bone, increasing the risk of fracture.
