Some can damage nearby bone or recur; giant cell tumors can rarely spread to the lungs despite being benign. Imaging and sometimes biopsy help tell these lesions from cancer.

topics.name: Benign Esophageal Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most benign esophageal tumors are found by chance and cause no symptoms. Larger or growing tumors may cause trouble swallowing, discomfort, bleeding, or weight loss. A few types, including papillomas and granular cell tumors, can rarely become cancerous; evaluation and follow-up help guide whether removal is needed.

topics.name: Benign Familial Hematuria
topics.clinical_significance: This usually inherited condition thins the kidney's filtering membrane and often causes blood in the urine found only on routine testing. Some people have visible blood or mild protein in the urine, but kidney function is usually normal and the long-term outlook is excellent. A few develop worsening kidney function; most people need no treatment.

topics.name: Benign Fibrous Histiocytomas
topics.clinical_significance: These are usually harmless, small, firm skin bumps that cause no symptoms, though some itch or become sore after minor injury. A bump that grows quickly should be checked because a rare soft-tissue cancer can look similar; biopsy may be needed. Removal is usually needed only if symptoms are bothersome.

topics.name: Benign Intracranial Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: This older term refers to idiopathic intracranial hypertension, in which pressure around the brain is high without a mass or hydrocephalus. It often causes frequent headaches and swelling of the optic nerves, sometimes with brief dimming of vision or double vision. Without treatment, it can cause permanent vision loss, so prompt assessment and regular eye checks are important.

topics.name: Benign Laryngeal Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Benign growths in the voice box may cause hoarseness, a breathy voice, trouble swallowing, or breathing problems. Some types, including papillomas and neurofibromas, can become cancerous; white vocal-fold patches may reflect precancerous change. Laryngoscopy, sometimes with imaging or biopsy, helps assess them; removal can protect voice and airway function.

topics.name: Benign Liver Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most benign liver tumors are found by chance and cause no symptoms or need for treatment. Some cause discomfort in the upper right abdomen or, rarely, bleeding. Liver adenomas are important because larger ones can rupture and bleed, and some can become cancerous; imaging and sometimes biopsy help decide whether follow-up or treatment is needed.

topics.name: Benign Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
topics.clinical_significance: This chronic autoimmune disease can scar mucous membranes. When the eyes are involved, redness and irritation may progress to scarring of the conjunctiva and damage to the cornea, with risk of blindness. Mouth sores and scarring are also common. Prompt eye assessment and often treatment that suppresses the immune system help limit damage.

topics.name: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo
topics.clinical_significance: A common inner-ear cause of brief spinning attacks, usually under a minute, triggered by changes in head position. Loose calcium particles in a balance canal cause the attacks, which may come with nausea but not hearing loss. It can impair balance and raise fall risk, especially in older adults; repositioning maneuvers usually help.

topics.name: Benign Positional Vertigo
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV): brief spinning attacks triggered by head movements, such as rolling over or looking up. Displaced calcium particles in an inner-ear balance canal cause the attacks; nausea may occur, but hearing is usually unaffected. Repositioning maneuvers often relieve symptoms.

topics.name: Benign Postural Vertigo
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), a common inner-ear disorder that causes brief spinning when head position changes. Displaced calcium crystals in a balance canal trigger the attacks; nausea may occur, but hearing loss is not typical. Repositioning maneuvers can relieve symptoms.

topics.name: Benign Prostate Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Benign prostate disorders include noncancerous enlargement (benign prostatic hyperplasia) and inflammation (prostatitis). They may cause weak or frequent urination, urgency, incomplete bladder emptying, or pelvic pain; acute bacterial prostatitis can cause fever and rarely sepsis. Similar urinary symptoms can have other causes, including prostate cancer, so medical assessment is needed.

topics.name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
topics.clinical_significance: A noncancerous growth of prostate tissue can narrow the urethra and obstruct urine flow. It may cause a weak or interrupted stream, difficulty starting, urgency, frequent urination at night, dribbling, or incomplete emptying; some people have no symptoms. Severe obstruction can cause urinary retention, infection, bladder stones, or kidney problems. Similar symptoms can have other causes, so medical assessment may be needed.

topics.name: Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a noncancerous enlargement that can block urine flow and cause a weak stream, trouble starting, urgency, nighttime urination, or incomplete emptying. Severe blockage may lead to urinary retention, bladder infection or stones, and kidney problems.

topics.name: Benign Skin Tumors, Growths, and Vascular Lesions
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes skin growths, cysts, and blood-vessel lesions. Many are harmless and need no treatment, but some may become irritated, bleed, or affect nearby function because of their size or location. A fast-changing, bleeding, or unusual growth should be checked because benign lesions can look like skin cancer; biopsy may be needed.

topics.name: Benzodiazepines and Barbiturates
topics.clinical_significance: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates are sedative medicines that can cause drowsiness, poor coordination, and slowed breathing. Overdose, especially when combined with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, can cause coma or death. Regular use can lead to dependence, and suddenly stopping after prolonged use can cause dangerous withdrawal, including seizures; dose reduction should be medically supervised.

topics.name: Berberine
topics.clinical_significance: Berberine is a plant compound found in goldenseal and sold in some supplements. Small studies suggest it may lower blood sugar or cholesterol, but evidence is limited. It can cause nausea or indigestion, interact with many medicines, and alter blood sugar control; goldenseal should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

topics.name: Beriberi
topics.clinical_significance: Beriberi is caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. It can damage peripheral nerves, causing numbness, weakness, or trouble walking, or affect the heart, causing swelling and heart failure. Severe deficiency may also cause Wernicke-Korsakoff brain disease. Prompt thiamine treatment is important because heart failure and brain injury can be life-threatening or lasting.

topics.name: Berylliosis
topics.clinical_significance: Berylliosis is another name for beryllium disease, an immune lung disease caused by breathing beryllium dust or fumes. Chronic disease can cause lung inflammation and granulomas, with cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue, often resembling sarcoidosis. Symptoms may appear years after exposure, and lung damage may progress even after exposure stops.

topics.name: Beryllium Disease
topics.clinical_significance: An occupational lung disease caused by inhaled beryllium. The common chronic form is an immune reaction that causes granulomas in the lungs and chest lymph nodes, with cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and sometimes weight loss. It can resemble sarcoidosis, appear decades after exposure, and progress after exposure ends, so work history and beryllium testing are important.

topics.name: Beta-keto-amphetamine
topics.clinical_significance: Beta-keto-amphetamine (cathinone) is a stimulant found in khat; synthetic cathinones may be sold as "bath salts." Toxicity can cause agitation, rapid heartbeat, high blood pressure, overheating, or seizures, and may progress to dangerous heart rhythms or muscle breakdown. Severe poisoning requires urgent medical care.

topics.name: Beta-Oxidation Cycle Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited disorders prevent the body from using fats well for energy, especially during fasting or illness. They can cause low blood sugar with low ketones and acid buildup, leading to vomiting, severe tiredness, seizures, or coma; some also affect the heart or muscles. Avoiding fasting and prompt glucose treatment during illness help prevent dangerous attacks.

topics.name: Bezoars
topics.clinical_significance: Bezoars are tightly packed masses of swallowed material, usually in the stomach. Many cause no symptoms, but some cause fullness, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. They can block the stomach or intestine and rarely cause bleeding or perforation. Treatment may involve dissolving the mass, removing it endoscopically, or surgery.

topics.name: Bezoars and Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: Bezoars and swallowed or inserted objects can lodge in the digestive tract. Many swallowed objects pass on their own, but an object that gets stuck can block the tract or cause sores, bleeding, fistulas, or perforation. Batteries, sharp objects, multiple magnets, and drug packets can be especially dangerous and may need urgent assessment or removal.

topics.name: Biceps Tendon Tears
topics.clinical_significance: A tear at the shoulder or elbow attachment causes sudden sharp pain, bruising, swelling, and weakness when lifting or pulling; the muscle may bulge in the arm. Tears near the elbow usually need surgery. Some shoulder-end tears can be managed without surgery if the other biceps tendon remains intact, though other shoulder injuries may affect treatment.

topics.name: Bicuspid Aortic Valve
topics.clinical_significance: A congenital aortic valve with two leaflets instead of three. It may cause no symptoms at first, but can become narrowed or leaky and is linked to enlargement or aneurysm of the aorta and infective endocarditis. Ongoing heart and aorta checks are important; because it can run in families, first-degree relatives may need screening echocardiograms.

topics.name: Bilharziasis
topics.clinical_significance: Bilharziasis (schistosomiasis) is a blood-fluke infection acquired when larvae in contaminated freshwater penetrate the skin. It may cause an itchy rash, then fever or abdominal symptoms; chronic infection can cause blood in the stool or urine and damage the intestine, liver, urinary tract, or other organs. Treatment is with praziquantel.

topics.name: Biliary Atresia
topics.clinical_significance: Biliary atresia is progressive scarring and blockage of the bile ducts outside the liver in infants, preventing bile from draining. It causes persistent jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools and can rapidly lead to cirrhosis and liver failure. Urgent diagnosis and early Kasai surgery give the best chance of keeping the child's own liver; many children later need a liver transplant.

topics.name: Biliary Function, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Bile carries bilirubin, cholesterol, and drug waste from the liver for removal and helps digest fats and absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, then releases it after meals. Blocked or slowed bile flow can cause jaundice and poor fat absorption; gallstones or strictures may lead to pain, infection, or liver scarring.

topics.name: Binge-Eating Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: An eating disorder marked by repeated episodes of eating unusually large amounts with a feeling of loss of control and distress, on average at least once a week for 3 months. Unlike bulimia, episodes are not regularly followed by vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise. It is treatable with psychotherapy; body weight alone does not diagnose it.

topics.name: Biofeedback
topics.clinical_significance: Biofeedback uses sensors to show body activity, such as muscle tension or heart rate. With practice, people can learn to change this activity using mental exercises. It may help manage problems such as pain, stress, anxiety, insomnia, headaches, or urinary incontinence.

topics.name: Biological Agents as Weapons
topics.clinical_significance: A deliberate release of germs or toxins can cause an outbreak that may look like a natural one. Unusual diseases, patterns of illness, severe cases, or poor response to usual treatment can raise concern. Early recognition helps guide public health investigation, infection control, and care for people who may have been exposed.

topics.name: Biology of Infectious Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Infection risk and severity depend on the microbe and the body's defenses, including its skin, mucous membranes, immune system, and genes. Normal microbes often help protect the body but can cause disease when defenses are disrupted. Understanding these factors helps clinicians assess infection risk and recognize disease.

topics.name: Biology of the Immune System
topics.clinical_significance: The immune system protects against infections and abnormal cells through fast, general defenses and targeted responses that can remember past exposures. Weak defenses can raise infection risk, while an overactive or misdirected response can damage the body's tissues, as in allergies or autoimmune disease.

topics.name: Biopsy of the Kidneys, Bladder, and Prostate
topics.clinical_significance: A kidney biopsy can help find the cause of unexplained kidney problems; bladder and prostate biopsies can diagnose conditions such as cancer. Risks depend on the site and include bleeding; bladder or prostate biopsy can also cause infection or trouble passing urine.

topics.name: Biotin and Pantothenic Acid
topics.clinical_significance: Biotin and pantothenic acid are B vitamins needed for normal metabolism. Deficiency of either is very rare. Benefits of pantothenic acid supplements for cholesterol, rheumatoid arthritis, or athletic performance have not been proven.

topics.name: Bipolar Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Bipolar disorders cause episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood (mania or hypomania) and depression. Bipolar I includes mania; bipolar II includes hypomania and major depression. Episodes can disrupt daily life and raise suicide risk. Treatment often includes mood-stabilizing medicines and may include psychotherapy.

topics.name: Bipolar Disorders in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and adolescents, bipolar disorder causes episodes of mania or hypomania and often depression. Symptoms can disrupt daily life and lead to unsafe behavior or suicidal thoughts. Careful assessment is needed because medical problems or substance use can cause similar symptoms. Treatment may include medicine and psychotherapy.

topics.name: Bipolar Disorders, Medications for Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines can control mood episodes and help prevent relapse. Choice depends on symptoms, past response, health conditions, and pregnancy plans. Lithium needs blood-level, kidney, and thyroid monitoring; other mood stabilizers and antipsychotics also have serious risks and interactions. Antidepressants are generally not used alone for bipolar depression.

topics.name: Bird Flu
topics.clinical_significance: Avian influenza A viruses mainly infect birds but can spread to people, usually through contact with infected birds, cattle, or their secretions. Human-to-human spread is limited. Illness can range from eye or mild respiratory symptoms to severe pneumonia; suspected cases need RT-PCR testing and public health reporting.

topics.name: Birth Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Birth injuries are physical injuries caused by labor or delivery. Many are minor, but nerve injuries can limit movement and serious bleeding in the scalp or brain can cause shock, seizures, or lasting problems. Breathing trouble, seizures, unusual weakness, or a rapidly growing scalp swelling need prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Bite Wounds of the Hand, Infected
topics.clinical_significance: Even a small hand-bite puncture, especially from a person or cat, can damage a tendon or joint and introduce bacteria. Infection can spread to a tendon sheath, joint, or bone, so prompt medical assessment is important. Treatment may require wound cleaning or surgery and antibiotics.

topics.name: Bites and Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Bites and stings can cause tissue injury, infection, venom poisoning, or a severe allergic reaction. The risks depend on the animal or insect and the exposure. Care may include wound cleaning, tetanus or rabies prevention, antibiotics, or urgent treatment for venom effects or anaphylaxis.

topics.name: Black Cohosh
topics.clinical_significance: Black cohosh is used for menopausal symptoms, but evidence that it helps is mixed. It may cause headache, rash, or stomach upset and has been linked to liver injury. People with liver disease should avoid it.

topics.name: Black Death
topics.clinical_significance: The Black Death was a historic pandemic caused by plague, an infection with Yersinia pestis. Plague still occurs and can cause swollen, painful lymph nodes, severe pneumonia, or sepsis. It can be fatal without prompt antibiotic treatment; pneumonic plague can spread between people and requires respiratory isolation.

topics.name: Black Lung Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Black lung disease results from breathing coal mine dust over time. It may cause few symptoms at first but can progress to lung scarring, shortness of breath, and severe loss of lung function; progression can continue after exposure stops. Reducing further dust exposure and monitoring lung health are important.

topics.name: Bladder Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital bladder problems may affect urine storage or emptying and cause infections, leakage, or backward flow of urine toward the kidneys. Some, especially a high-pressure neurogenic bladder, can damage the kidneys over time. Monitoring bladder and kidney function is important; treatment may include catheterization or surgery.

topics.name: Bladder Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Bladder cancer usually begins in the lining of the bladder. Blood in the urine is common, though frequent or urgent urination can also occur. The cancer may recur or spread, so diagnosis with cystoscopy and biopsy is important; treatment depends on how deeply it has grown.

topics.name: Bladder Catheterization
topics.clinical_significance: A bladder catheter can drain urine, relieve retention, measure urine left after voiding, collect a sample, or deliver medicine or irrigation. Catheters can cause urinary infections or injure the urethra or bladder, so they should be used only when needed, placed with sterile technique, and removed as soon as possible.

topics.name: Bladder Pain Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Bladder pain syndrome is a long-lasting, noninfectious bladder condition that causes pelvic or bladder pain with urinary urgency and frequency. Symptoms often worsen as the bladder fills and ease after urination. Diagnosis requires ruling out infection and other causes; treatment often helps, but cure is uncommon.

topics.name: Bladder Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Bladder trauma can follow a blow or penetrating injury to the lower abdomen or pelvis. Blood in the urine, especially with a pelvic fracture, is an important warning sign. A rupture can let urine leak into the abdomen and cause serious complications, so prompt imaging and treatment are important; some ruptures need surgery.

topics.name: Blastomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Blastomycosis is a fungal infection acquired by inhaling spores from soil, mainly in parts of North America. Lung infection may cause no symptoms, mild illness, or severe or long-lasting pneumonia. The fungus can spread through the blood, most often to the skin, and sometimes to bones or other organs; treatment depends on severity.

topics.name: Bleeding Due to Abnormal Blood Vessels
topics.clinical_significance: Fragile or inflamed blood vessels can cause tiny spots, purple patches, or bruises under the skin, and sometimes bleeding from the nose or other mucous membranes. Most vessel disorders cause little blood loss, but repeated bleeding can lead to iron deficiency, and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia can cause serious bleeding. Evaluation looks for the underlying cause.

topics.name: Bleeding, Excessive
topics.clinical_significance: Unusual or prolonged bleeding, such as frequent nosebleeds, heavy periods, prolonged bleeding after small cuts, or unexplained bruises or spots, may signal a problem with platelets, clotting proteins, or blood vessels. Common causes include blood-thinning medicines, low platelets, and liver disease. Sudden severe bleeding or signs of shock need urgent care; evaluation usually includes blood counts and clotting tests.

topics.name: Blepharitis
topics.clinical_significance: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid edges that can cause itching, burning, redness, crusting, tearing, and dry-eye symptoms. It often recurs; warm compresses and eyelid cleaning are the main treatments, with other medicines chosen for the cause. Persistent one-sided disease, especially with lash loss, needs assessment for other causes such as an eyelid tumor.

topics.name: Blepharospasm
topics.clinical_significance: Blepharospasm is a chronic movement disorder that causes repeated, involuntary blinking or forceful eyelid closure, sometimes making it hard to open the eyes. Its cause is usually unknown; eye irritation or another neurologic disorder can rarely contribute. Botulinum toxin injections often reduce symptoms.

topics.name: Blood Collection
topics.clinical_significance: Blood collection provides donated blood for transfusion. Donor screening helps protect both donors and recipients, and testing checks blood type, antibodies, and signs of infection. Compatibility testing before transfusion helps prevent serious reactions from mismatched blood.

topics.name: Blood Products
topics.clinical_significance: Blood products are chosen for specific needs: red blood cells treat anemia or blood loss; platelets help prevent or control bleeding when platelet numbers or function are low; plasma can replace several clotting factors when their deficiency causes bleeding; and cryoprecipitate provides fibrinogen when it is low and bleeding is present.

topics.name: Blunt Cardiac Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Blunt chest trauma can bruise or tear the heart muscle, valves, or chambers. It may cause abnormal heart rhythms, reduced pumping, heart failure, or fluid around the heart that limits its filling. A blow can also trigger sudden cardiac arrest without structural damage. ECG and blood tests help screen for injury, and some patients need heart monitoring.

topics.name: Blurred Vision
topics.clinical_significance: Blurred vision is reduced clarity of sight. Common causes include an incorrect glasses prescription, cataracts, retinal disease, and problems with the optic nerve. Sudden vision changes, eye pain, or missing areas of vision can signal serious disease and need urgent eye assessment.

topics.name: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)
topics.clinical_significance: Body dysmorphic disorder causes intense worry about a physical feature that other people see as slight or do not notice. Repeated checking, grooming, or hiding the feature can disrupt daily life and relationships. Depression and suicidal thoughts are common, so recognizing the disorder and offering treatment are important. Treatment may include tailored therapy and medicine.

topics.name: Body Packing and Body Stuffing
topics.clinical_significance: Swallowed or concealed drug packets can leak or rupture and cause severe, sometimes fatal poisoning. Packets can also block or injure the bowel. Body stuffing often involves poorly sealed packets, which may rupture more easily. Suspected cases need hospital assessment because serious complications can develop.

topics.name: Body-Focused Repetitive Behavior Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: This disorder involves repeated behaviors such as nail, lip, or cheek biting that a person has trouble stopping despite trying. The behaviors cause significant distress or interfere with daily life, and can lead to bleeding or nail damage. Habit-reversal therapy may help.

topics.name: Bone and Joint Tumors, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Bone tumors may be benign or cancerous; in adults, cancer that has spread to bone is more common than a cancer that starts there. Joint tumors are rare, but some can damage nearby cartilage. Persistent unexplained bone pain, especially at rest or at night, or swelling needs assessment and imaging; a suspected cancer may require biopsy.

topics.name: Bone Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Bone disorders can cause pain, deformity, poor growth, or trouble walking in children. Damage to a growth plate may lead to abnormal bone growth and lasting joint problems. Causes include injury, infection, inherited conditions, and cancer, so assessment is important to guide treatment and protect growth.

topics.name: Bone Tumors and Cysts, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Many benign bone tumors are found by chance and need only follow-up. Others can grow, cause pain, weaken bone, or damage a nearby joint, raising fracture risk. Some, including giant cell tumors, can recur or rarely spread to the lungs despite being benign. Imaging and sometimes biopsy help guide treatment and follow-up.

topics.name: Bone Tumors, Metastatic
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer that spreads to bone can cause pain and weaken the bone, sometimes leading to a fracture. It may be the first sign of cancer or occur after a cancer diagnosis; breast, lung, prostate, kidney, and thyroid cancers are common sources. Early diagnosis can guide treatment to reduce pain, slow bone damage, and stabilize bones at risk of fracture.

topics.name: Bone Tumors, Primary Malignant
topics.clinical_significance: Primary malignant bone tumors are cancers that start in bone. They can cause persistent pain or swelling and may spread, often to the lungs. Imaging and biopsy are used to identify and stage them. Treatment depends on the tumor type and may include surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation.

topics.name: Bones and Joints, Tumors of
topics.clinical_significance: Bone tumors may be benign or cancerous; cancer can start in bone or spread there from another organ. In adults, bone metastases are more common than primary bone cancer, and true joint tumors are rare. Persistent unexplained bone pain, swelling, or a mass needs assessment; imaging and sometimes biopsy help guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Borderline personality disorder can cause intense mood shifts, unstable relationships and self-image, and impulsive behavior. Self-harm and suicidal behavior are common, so checking safety is important. Psychotherapy is the main treatment and can reduce suicidal behavior and improve daily functioning; medicines may help with other mental health conditions.

topics.name: Bornholm Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Bornholm disease is an enterovirus infection that causes sudden, severe, often intermittent chest or upper-abdominal pain with fever. Symptoms usually improve within a few days but may recur. Rare complications include aseptic meningitis, orchitis, or myopericarditis. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms.

topics.name: Botulism
topics.clinical_significance: Botulism is a rare, life-threatening poisoning in which a toxin blocks nerve signals to muscles. It can cause drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble swallowing, and spreading weakness that may lead to breathing failure. It is a medical emergency requiring hospital care and prompt antitoxin; breathing support may be needed.

topics.name: Boutonnière Deformity
topics.clinical_significance: Damage to a finger tendon can make the middle joint bend and the fingertip joint bend backward. Without early treatment, the finger may become stiff in this position and hand use may suffer. Early splinting can help preserve motion; causes include injury and rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.name: Bowen or Bowen's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Bowen disease is an early, noninvasive form of squamous cell skin cancer limited to the outer skin layer. It often appears as a red, scaly patch and can sometimes grow into deeper skin. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis so the lesion can be treated.

topics.name: BPPV
topics.clinical_significance: BPPV causes brief spinning spells triggered by head movements, often with nausea but usually without hearing loss. Loose calcium crystals in an inner-ear balance canal cause the spells. Symptoms can recur and increase fall risk, especially in older adults; repositioning maneuvers usually treat it.

topics.name: Brachial Plexus and Lumbosacral Plexus Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Damage to the brachial or lumbosacral plexus affects the nerve bundle serving an arm or leg and can cause pain, weakness, and altered sensation. Symptoms may not follow a single nerve or spinal root. Injury, compression, tumors, and diabetes are possible causes; nerve tests and imaging help locate the problem and guide treatment.

topics.name: Brain Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A brain abscess is a pocket of pus that can press on and damage brain tissue, causing headache, seizures, confusion, or weakness; fever may be absent. It can follow spread from a nearby infection, a bloodstream infection, or a head wound. Prompt imaging and antibiotics are needed, and the abscess often must be drained.

topics.name: Brain Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: A brain aneurysm is a weak, bulging area in a brain artery. Many cause no symptoms, but rupture can cause life-threatening bleeding around the brain, often with a sudden, severe headache, vomiting, stiff neck, or loss of consciousness. A sudden severe headache needs emergency care. Unruptured aneurysms are monitored or repaired based on their risk of rupture.

topics.name: Brain Death
topics.clinical_significance: Brain death is the permanent loss of all brain function, including the brainstem. The person cannot regain consciousness or breathe independently. A ventilator may keep the heart beating for a time, but brain death means the person has died once confirmed by the required medical tests.

topics.name: Brain Herniation
topics.clinical_significance: Brain herniation occurs when high pressure inside the skull pushes brain tissue through rigid barriers. The shift can compress vital brain structures, including the brainstem, and cause loss of consciousness, neurologic damage, or breathing problems. It is life-threatening and needs immediate treatment to control pressure and address the cause.

topics.name: Brain Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Brain infections can affect brain tissue, its coverings, or nearby spaces and may be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites. They can cause confusion, seizures, weakness, or increased pressure inside the skull and may be life-threatening. Prompt assessment is important because treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Brain Infections, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Infections can affect brain tissue, its coverings, or nearby spaces and may be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, or parasites. They can cause confusion, seizures, weakness, or raised pressure in the skull and may be very serious. Because symptoms overlap, brain imaging is often needed to find the cause and guide treatment.

topics.name: Branched-Chain Amino Acid Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited defects in breaking down branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, and isoleucine) can let harmful substances build up. Some disorders cause severe crises, often during illness, with vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, acidosis, low blood sugar, seizures, or coma; untreated crises can be fatal. Early diagnosis, a condition-specific diet, and emergency care are important.

topics.name: Breakbone Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Breakbone fever is dengue, a virus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It causes sudden fever with severe muscle and joint pain, often with headache or pain behind the eyes. Some cases progress to severe dengue with bleeding, fluid leakage, or shock, so warning signs need urgent medical care.

topics.name: Breast Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Breast cancer may have no symptoms and be found on screening; a new lump or skin or nipple change also needs evaluation. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes and distant organs. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and treatment depends on the cancer’s stage and features, including hormone and HER2 receptors.

topics.name: Breast Cancer Screening and Prevention
topics.clinical_significance: Mammography can find breast cancer before symptoms appear, but false alarms and unnecessary tests can occur. Recommended screening age and frequency vary, so decisions depend on a person’s risk and health. People at high risk may need MRI or preventive medicine or surgery; regular exercise, healthy weight, and limiting alcohol may lower risk.

topics.name: Breast Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Breast lumps, pain, nipple discharge, and skin changes are common and usually have benign causes. Persistent or suspicious changes still need evaluation because breast cancer can resemble a benign problem. Imaging and sometimes biopsy help identify the cause.

topics.name: Breast Disorders, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Most breast symptoms are benign, but breast cancer can look like a harmless disorder. A persistent or fixed lump, skin dimpling or thickening, a newly pulled-in nipple, or spontaneous bloody discharge from one breast needs prompt evaluation. Imaging and sometimes biopsy help find the cause.

topics.name: Breast Lumps
topics.clinical_significance: Most breast lumps are benign, but each new lump needs evaluation because cancer can look similar. Ultrasound can show whether a lump is fluid-filled or solid; solid or suspicious lumps may need mammography and biopsy.

topics.name: Breast Masses
topics.clinical_significance: Breast masses may be painful or painless and may occur with nipple discharge or skin changes. Most are benign, commonly cysts or fibroadenomas, but some are cancer. A hard, irregular, fixed mass or changes in the skin or nipple raise concern. Because benign and cancerous masses can look alike, each mass needs evaluation to rule out cancer.

topics.name: Breastfeeding
topics.clinical_significance: Breast milk provides infant nutrition and immune protection, and breastfeeding is linked to health benefits for both infant and mother. Guidelines recommend exclusive breastfeeding for about the first 6 months when possible, then adding solid foods while breastfeeding continues as desired. Poor milk intake can lead to dehydration, inadequate growth, and jaundice.

topics.name: Breath-Holding Spells
topics.clinical_significance: Breath-holding spells are brief, involuntary episodes in young children after fright, anger, or pain. The child may stop breathing after exhaling, turn blue or pale, and briefly faint; breathing and awareness return on their own. More than half stop having spells by age 4, and almost all stop by age 8. They do not appear to increase epilepsy risk, though brief seizure-like movements can occur.

topics.name: Brief Psychotic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Brief psychotic disorder is a sudden episode of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or markedly disorganized behavior lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, followed by a return to usual functioning. Symptoms must not be better explained by a mood disorder, another psychotic disorder, a medical condition, or a drug effect. Relapse can occur, and some people later develop a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder.

topics.name: Brief, Resolved, Unexplained Events (BRUE)
topics.clinical_significance: A brief, resolved, unexplained event (BRUE) is an episode in an infant under 1 year that lasts less than 1 minute and includes blue or pale color, abnormal breathing, a major change in muscle tone, or reduced responsiveness. The infant returns to normal, and no cause is found after an appropriate history and examination. BRUE is a descriptive diagnosis, not a specific disease, and is distinct from sudden infant death syndrome; if a cause is identified, the event is classified by that cause.

topics.name: Brittle Bone Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is a group of inherited disorders that make bones unusually fragile. Most cases involve gene changes that reduce or alter type I collagen; rarer forms affect other genes. Severity ranges from mild fractures to severe deformity and fractures before birth. Blue sclerae, fragile teeth, loose joints, and hearing loss may also occur.

topics.name: Broken Nose
topics.clinical_significance: A nasal fracture can cause pain, swelling, bruising, nosebleeds, deformity, and blocked nasal breathing. A septal hematoma (blood trapped inside the wall between the nostrils) can damage cartilage and needs urgent treatment. Rarely, an associated skull-base injury causes a cerebrospinal fluid leak, which can lead to meningitis.

topics.name: Bromhidrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Bromhidrosis is unusually strong or unpleasant body odor caused when bacteria and yeasts break down sweat gland secretions and skin debris. Apocrine sweat is odorless when released but develops an odor as it breaks down on the skin. Eccrine sweat usually has little odor, though bacteria can cause odor by breaking down softened skin. Some foods and medicines can also change body odor.

topics.name: Bronchiectasis
topics.clinical_significance: Bronchiectasis is permanent widening and damage of the bronchi, usually from ongoing infection and inflammation. Damaged airways clear mucus poorly, causing a chronic cough with thick, often pus-filled sputum, repeated lung infections, and sometimes breathlessness. Causes include cystic fibrosis, immune or ciliary disorders, past infections, and airway blockage; sometimes no cause is found. Coughing up blood can occur and may be severe.

topics.name: Bronchiectasis and Atelectasis
topics.clinical_significance: Bronchiectasis is permanent widening and damage of the bronchi, which impairs mucus clearance and can cause a chronic productive cough, repeated infections, and sometimes severe coughing of blood. Atelectasis is collapse of part of the lung with loss of volume, often due to airway blockage or shallow breathing. Small areas may cause no symptoms, but extensive collapse can reduce blood oxygen, lead to pneumonia, or cause respiratory failure.

topics.name: Bronchiolitis
topics.clinical_significance: Bronchiolitis is an acute viral infection of the small airways, mainly in children under 2 years; respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most common cause. Swelling and mucus narrow the airways, causing cough, wheezing, fast or labored breathing, and sometimes poor feeding or low blood oxygen. Most children recover, but young or premature infants can develop pauses in breathing or respiratory failure.

topics.name: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung condition of premature infants whose developing lungs are affected by prolonged oxygen or mechanical ventilation. It can cause continued need for oxygen, breathing difficulty, wheezing, and poor growth. Affected infants are more prone to respiratory infections, and severe BPD can lead to high blood pressure in the lungs. Severity varies.

topics.name: Brugada Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Brugada syndrome is an inherited disorder of the heart’s electrical system that can cause dangerous fast heart rhythms, fainting, or sudden death, often during sleep. Many affected people have no symptoms. Fever and some medicines can trigger abnormal rhythms; diagnosis depends on a characteristic ECG pattern and clinical findings.

topics.name: Bruton Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Bruton disease (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) is an inherited immune disorder in which B cells do not mature, so antibody levels are very low or absent. It mainly affects boys and causes recurrent infections, especially of the lungs, sinuses, and skin, often from encapsulated bacteria. Persistent enterovirus infections can involve the brain or spinal cord, and repeated lung infections can lead to bronchiectasis.

topics.name: Bruxism
topics.clinical_significance: Bruxism is clenching or grinding of the teeth while awake or asleep. It may cause no symptoms, but repeated force can wear tooth enamel, loosen or damage teeth and dental crowns, and cause jaw, neck, or headache pain. Sleep problems, stress or anxiety, and alcohol can contribute.

topics.name: Bubonic Plague
topics.clinical_significance: Bubonic plague is a Yersinia pestis infection, usually acquired from the bite of an infected flea. It causes sudden fever and severely tender, swollen lymph nodes called buboes. The bacteria can spread through the blood, causing sepsis, or reach the lungs and cause pneumonic plague. Without prompt treatment, the illness can be fatal.

topics.name: Buckley Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Buckley syndrome (hyper-IgE syndrome) is a rare inherited immune disorder marked by very high IgE, itchy eczema, and repeated infections. Skin abscesses caused by staphylococcal bacteria and infections of the lungs or sinuses are common. Other findings can include delayed loss of baby teeth, unusual facial features, weak bones, and fractures.

topics.name: Budd-Chiari Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Budd-Chiari syndrome is blockage of blood draining from the liver, usually by a clot in the hepatic veins or nearby inferior vena cava. It can cause an enlarged liver, right upper abdominal pain, and fluid buildup in the abdomen (ascites). Long-term blockage may cause portal hypertension, cirrhosis, or liver failure; sudden severe blockage can cause acute liver failure.

topics.name: Buerger Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is inflammation and clotting in small and medium arteries and some superficial veins, usually in the hands and feet. It is strongly linked to tobacco use and reduces blood flow, causing limb pain, coldness, ulcers, or gangrene. Continued tobacco use can drive progression and lead to loss of fingers or toes; stopping tobacco use greatly improves the outlook.

topics.name: Building-Related Illnesses
topics.clinical_significance: Building-related illnesses are health problems linked to exposures in a particular indoor environment. Some are specific diseases, such as asthma, rhinitis, or hypersensitivity pneumonitis; others are nonspecific symptoms such as irritated eyes or throat, cough, headache, or trouble concentrating. Poor ventilation, dampness, mold, dust, chemicals, and other indoor pollutants may contribute. Symptoms may improve when a person is away from the building.

topics.name: Bulimia Nervosa
topics.clinical_significance: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder with repeated episodes of eating unusually large amounts with a sense of loss of control, followed by behaviors to prevent weight gain, such as vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise. Episodes occur at least weekly for 3 months, and body shape or weight strongly affects self-evaluation; body weight is often normal. Purging can damage teeth and the esophagus and cause dangerous fluid or electrolyte disturbances.

topics.name: Bullous Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Bullous diseases are a varied group of conditions that cause large, fluid-filled blisters (bullae, at least 10 mm wide). They may be autoimmune, inherited, infectious, or drug-related; some affect only the skin, while others also involve mucous membranes such as the mouth. Widespread blistering can damage the skin barrier and lead to infection or fluid loss.

topics.name: Bullous Diseases, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Bullae are raised, fluid-filled blisters at least 10 mm across. Bullous diseases are the varied conditions that cause them, including autoimmune disorders, inherited skin-fragility disorders, infections, and some drug reactions. Because the causes and severity differ, bullae are a skin finding rather than one single disease.

topics.name: Bullous Keratopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Bullous keratopathy occurs when the cornea’s inner cell layer fails to remove fluid, causing the cornea to swell and form fluid-filled blisters. It can blur vision and cause glare and sensitivity to light. A blister that ruptures can cause pain and may become infected, leading to a corneal ulcer. Common causes include Fuchs corneal dystrophy and injury during eye surgery.

topics.name: Bullous Myringitis
topics.clinical_significance: Bullous myringitis is inflammation of the eardrum with fluid-filled blisters, often occurring with an acute middle-ear infection. It typically causes sudden, severe ear pain lasting 1 to 2 days; hearing loss and fever may occur, especially when bacteria are involved.

topics.name: Bullous Pemphigoid
topics.clinical_significance: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune skin disease that mainly affects adults over 60. It often begins with itching, followed by firm, tense blisters on normal or red, hive-like skin. Unlike pemphigus, its blisters are less fragile and mouth involvement is rare. The disease is chronic and may require treatment for months or years.

topics.name: Bundle Branch Block and Fascicular Block
topics.clinical_significance: Bundle branch and fascicular blocks are delays or interruptions in the electrical pathways that carry signals through the heart’s ventricles. They often cause no symptoms, but can point to underlying heart disease. Left bundle branch block is more often linked to structural heart disease and higher cardiac risk than isolated right bundle branch block. Blocks in several pathways can signal extensive heart damage, especially after a heart attack.

topics.name: Bunion
topics.clinical_significance: A bunion (hallux valgus) is a bony prominence at the inner base of the big toe, usually with the big toe angling toward the other toes. The joint may become painful, red, and swollen, especially when pressed by tight shoes. Bursitis, arthritis, and reduced toe movement can develop.

topics.name: Buphthalmos
topics.clinical_significance: Buphthalmos is enlargement of an infant’s or young child’s eye due to high pressure inside the eye, most often from congenital glaucoma. The pressure stretches the cornea and outer wall of the eye; the cornea may become enlarged or cloudy, and tearing or light sensitivity may occur. If the pressure is not controlled, the optic nerve can be damaged and vision can be lost.

topics.name: Burkitt Lymphoma
topics.clinical_significance: A very fast-growing cancer of B cells, a type of white blood cell. Endemic disease often forms tumors in the jaw or facial bones, while sporadic disease commonly affects the abdomen; the bone marrow and central nervous system may also be involved. It is linked to a rearrangement of the MYC gene.

topics.name: Burning Mouth Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic burning or tingling pain in the mouth, usually affecting the tongue, with normal-looking oral tissue and no identified cause. Dry mouth or altered taste may also occur. Similar symptoms can result from conditions such as nutritional deficiency, infection, diabetes, or medication effects.

topics.name: Burning Tongue
topics.clinical_significance: Burning, tingling, or numb pain affecting the tongue, often with normal-looking tissue. When persistent and no cause is found, it is a form of burning mouth syndrome; similar symptoms may result from dry mouth, nutritional deficiency, infection, diabetes, allergy, or medicines. Altered taste may also occur.

topics.name: Burns
topics.clinical_significance: Injuries to the skin or other tissues caused by heat, radiation, chemicals, or electricity. Severity depends mainly on burn depth and the area of the body affected. Deep or extensive burns can cause severe fluid loss, shock, infection, scarring, or injury from smoke inhalation.

topics.name: Bursa, Muscle, and Tendon Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Disorders that affect bursae, muscles, or tendons, often after injury or repeated overuse and sometimes because of infection or another disease. They can cause pain, swelling, tenderness, and limited movement.

topics.name: Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of a bursa, a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction where tendons or muscles move near bone or skin. It causes pain and tenderness, sometimes with swelling, and may limit movement. Injury and repeated pressure are common causes; infection and arthritis can also cause it.

topics.name: Buttonhole Deformity
topics.clinical_significance: A deformity of a finger or thumb in which the middle joint bends toward the palm and the fingertip joint bends backward. It usually follows injury to the tendon that straightens the middle joint, but dislocation, fracture, osteoarthritis, or rheumatoid arthritis can also cause it.

topics.name: Byssinosis
topics.clinical_significance: An occupational lung disease caused by inhaling dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp. It causes chest tightness and shortness of breath, usually worst on the first workday after a break and easing over the week. Long-term exposure can cause lasting airflow obstruction with features of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

topics.name: C. diff–Induced Colitis
topics.clinical_significance: Toxins made by Clostridioides difficile bacteria cause diarrhea and inflammation of the colon, often after antibiotics disrupt normal gut bacteria. Illness ranges from mild diarrhea to severe colitis and can recur; severe cases can rarely cause toxic megacolon, bowel perforation, or sepsis. Diagnosis uses stool testing in a person with symptoms.

topics.name: C1–C2 Subluxation
topics.clinical_significance: Misalignment between the first two neck vertebrae, called C1 and C2. It may follow a major injury or occur with conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome. It often causes no symptoms but can cause neck pain or a headache at the back of the head; rarely, it compresses the spinal cord.

topics.name: Cachexia in Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer-related loss of body weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat caused by changes in the body’s metabolism. It is common in advanced cancer and is not explained only by poor appetite or reduced food intake. It can weaken physical function and is linked to a poorer response to cancer treatment and higher mortality.

topics.name: Caisson Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Caisson disease (decompression sickness, or the bends) occurs when a rapid drop in pressure makes gas dissolved in the body form bubbles in blood and tissues. It can follow diving, work in compressed air, or ascent to high altitude. Symptoms range from joint pain and skin changes to breathing or nervous system problems; severe cases can be fatal.

topics.name: Calabar Swellings
topics.clinical_significance: Temporary, localized areas of skin swelling caused by loiasis, an infection with Loa loa worms transmitted by deerflies. The swellings usually affect the arms or legs and last a few days; an adult worm may also migrate across the surface of the eye.

topics.name: Calcaneal Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Breaks in the calcaneus, the heel bone, usually caused by a high-force impact such as landing on the feet after a fall. They cause heel pain and marked swelling and may prevent weight bearing. They can occur with spinal fractures and may lead to compartment syndrome or long-term disability.

topics.name: Calcium Concentration, Disorders of, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Disorders in which blood calcium is too low (hypocalcemia) or too high (hypercalcemia). Calcium supports nerve and muscle function, hormone release, and blood clotting, so abnormal levels can cause cramps, weakness, confusion, seizures, or heart problems. Causes include problems with parathyroid hormone or vitamin D, kidney disease, and cancer.

topics.name: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A condition in which calcium pyrophosphate crystals build up in or around joints. Deposits may cause no symptoms, sudden attacks of painful, swollen joints (acute attacks are called pseudogout), or chronic arthritis that can resemble osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. The knee and wrist are commonly affected.

topics.name: Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of a joint caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. It may cause sudden pain, swelling, and warmth, often in the knee or wrist; these acute attacks are called pseudogout. Chronic disease can resemble osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.name: Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Arthropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Joint disease caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals in or around cartilage. Deposits may cause no symptoms, sudden attacks of painful joint swelling (pseudogout), or chronic, sometimes severe arthritis that can resemble osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.name: Calluses and Corns
topics.clinical_significance: Calluses and corns are thickened areas of skin that form after repeated pressure or friction, usually over bone. Calluses are broad and usually painless; corns are smaller, deeper, and often painful when pressed.

topics.name: Campylobacter Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial infections, often acquired from contaminated food such as undercooked poultry. They usually cause short-term diarrhea, sometimes bloody, with fever and abdominal pain. Rare complications include spread to the blood or other organs, Guillain–Barré syndrome, and reactive arthritis.

topics.name: Canaliculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Infection or inflammation of a small tear-drainage channel near the inner eyelid. It usually causes one-sided tearing, pus-like discharge, redness near the inner corner of the eye, and mild tenderness. Infection is common; a retained tear-duct plug can also cause it.

topics.name: Cancer, Cachexia in
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer cachexia is loss of body weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat caused by cancer-related metabolic changes. It is common in advanced cancer and is not explained only by poor appetite or reduced food intake. It can weaken physical function and is linked to a poorer response to chemotherapy and higher mortality.

topics.name: Cancer, Cellular and Molecular Basis of
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer develops when inherited or acquired genetic changes disrupt the controls that regulate cell growth, division, and DNA repair. Abnormal cells then multiply without control, may evade immune defenses, invade nearby tissues, and spread to distant parts of the body.

topics.name: Cancer Diagnosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer may be suspected from symptoms, examination, or test results, but is usually confirmed by examining a tissue sample (biopsy) under a microscope. Imaging and other tests help identify the cancer and determine whether it has spread. This stage helps guide treatment and estimate prognosis.

topics.name: Cancer in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer during pregnancy requires balancing prompt treatment with risks to the fetus, because some cancer drugs can cause fetal loss or birth defects. The risks and treatment choices depend on the cancer type, its extent, and how far the pregnancy has progressed. Care involves cancer and maternal-fetal medicine specialists.

topics.name: Cancer, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow without normal controls, invade nearby tissues, and may spread to distant sites. Many cancers can be cured, especially when found early; treatment may also prolong life or improve quality of life when cure is not possible.

topics.name: Cancer Screening
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer screening uses tests or examinations in people without symptoms to find certain cancers early, when treatment may be more effective. Recommendations depend on age and risk because screening may reduce cancer deaths but can also cause false alarms, miss cancers, or find slow-growing cancers that would never cause illness. These findings can lead to unnecessary tests or treatment.

topics.name: Cancer, Sequelae
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer may cause pain, weight loss, fatigue, or blockage of internal organs. Spread to distant sites can damage organs, and cancer can also cause blood clots or metabolic and immune problems, such as high blood calcium. Many cancer deaths result from metastases and organ failure.

topics.name: Cancer Surgery
topics.clinical_significance: Surgery removes a cancerous tumor and sometimes nearby tissue or lymph nodes. It may cure some localized solid tumors, treat selected metastases, reduce tumor size when complete removal is not possible, or relieve symptoms. Its role depends on how far the cancer has spread and the patient’s health; it may be combined with other cancer treatments.

topics.name: Cancer, Surgery for
topics.clinical_significance: Surgery removes a cancerous tumor and sometimes nearby tissue or lymph nodes. It may cure some localized solid tumors, treat selected metastases, reduce tumor size when complete removal is not possible, or relieve symptoms. Its role depends on how far the cancer has spread and the patient’s health; it may be combined with other cancer treatments.

topics.name: Cancer Therapy, Management of Adverse Effects
topics.clinical_significance: Management of cancer therapy adverse effects aims to reduce symptoms and preserve quality of life. Common problems include low blood counts, nausea, diarrhea, mouth sores, pain, and anxiety or depression. Some treatments can also cause serious tumor lysis or cytokine release syndromes.

topics.name: Cancer Therapy, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer therapy uses surgery, radiation, systemic medicines (such as chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy), and sometimes stem cell transplantation. Treatments may be combined to cure cancer, lower the risk of recurrence, control growth, or relieve symptoms. Choices depend on the cancer, the patient’s health and preferences, and the likely benefits and harms.

topics.name: Cancer Therapy, Principles of
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer treatment aims to destroy or control cancer cells. It may use surgery, radiation, medicines, or stem cell transplant, alone or in combination. Treatment may be given before or after the main treatment to shrink a tumor or lower the risk of recurrence. When cure is not possible, it may slow cancer and relieve symptoms. The treatment plan weighs likely benefits and harms and considers the cancer, the person’s health, and their preferences.

topics.name: Cancers Affecting the Retina
topics.clinical_significance: Cancers affecting the retina usually begin in the choroid, the blood-rich layer beneath it, and can impair vision by damaging the retina’s support and blood supply. They include melanoma that starts in the eye and cancers that have spread there from elsewhere, often from the breast or lung. Eye melanoma can spread to other parts of the body and may be life-threatening.

topics.name: Cancers Common Among Patients With Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: People with HIV have a higher risk of certain cancers, especially Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and invasive cervical cancer. Anal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and some skin, lung, and liver cancers are also more common. Immune suppression and cancer-causing infections contribute to this risk. Antiretroviral therapy lowers the risk of progression of advanced HIV-related cancers.

topics.name: Cancers of the Skin
topics.clinical_significance: Skin cancers are common and often develop on sun-exposed skin. Basal cell and squamous cell cancers are the most common types and are often curable when found early. Melanoma is less common but causes most skin cancer deaths because it can spread. Long-term exposure to ultraviolet light is an important risk factor.

topics.name: Cancers, Pediatric
topics.clinical_significance: Common childhood cancers include leukemia, brain and spinal cord tumors, and lymphomas; some, such as neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor, occur mainly in children. Many children survive, but cancer treatment can have lasting effects on growth, fertility, heart health, learning, and development. Care by specialists and long-term follow-up help address these effects.

topics.name: Candidal Vaginitis
topics.clinical_significance: A vaginal infection, usually caused by Candida albicans, that commonly causes vulvar or vaginal itching, burning, soreness, and sometimes thick white discharge. Its symptoms can resemble other vaginal infections, so examination and testing may be needed to confirm the cause. Sexual transmission is uncommon, but infections can recur, sometimes because of a less common Candida species or antifungal resistance.

topics.name: Candidiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Candida often lives harmlessly on the skin and in the gut, but it can cause infections such as oral thrush or genital infection. In severely ill or immunocompromised people, it can enter the bloodstream and spread to organs, causing a serious, sometimes fatal illness. Finding Candida in a nonsterile sample alone does not prove invasive infection.

topics.name: Candidiasis (Mucocutaneous)
topics.clinical_significance: A superficial Candida infection of the skin or moist linings of the body, often affecting skin folds, the mouth, genitals, or areas around the nails. It may cause itchy, red, sore, or moist patches, white mouth plaques, or inflamed nail folds. Recurrent infections can be linked to diabetes or weakened immunity; persistent infections may rarely signal an inherited immune disorder. Invasive spread is a separate, serious risk in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Candidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Candidosis, also called candidiasis, is an infection caused by Candida yeast. It can cause localized infections such as oral thrush or genital infection, or spread through the bloodstream to organs in severely ill or immunocompromised people. Invasive infection can cause sepsis and may be fatal. Finding Candida in a nonsterile sample alone does not prove invasive infection.

topics.name: Cannabidiol (CBD)
topics.clinical_significance: Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-intoxicating chemical from the cannabis plant. A prescription form is approved for seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut and Dravet syndromes, while evidence for many other claimed uses is limited. CBD can cause sleepiness, diarrhea, and liver injury, and it can interact with many medicines. Nonprescription products may have inaccurate labels or contain THC.

topics.name: Cannabinoids, Synthetic
topics.clinical_significance: Synthetic cannabinoids are manufactured drugs that act on the same brain receptors as THC, the main intoxicating chemical in cannabis. Their effects are unpredictable and can include severe agitation, hallucinations, psychosis, seizures, a fast heart rate, high blood pressure, heart attack, kidney injury, and muscle breakdown. Routine urine drug screens usually do not detect them.

topics.name: Capacity (Competence) and Incapacity
topics.clinical_significance: Clinical decision-making capacity is a person’s ability to understand a health care choice, its likely benefits and harms, and the alternatives, then make and communicate a decision. It is specific to the decision and can change over time or as a person’s condition changes. If capacity is lacking, clinicians should address reversible causes when possible and involve an authorized surrogate. Legal incapacity is a court determination.

topics.name: Carbapenems
topics.clinical_significance: Carbapenems are very broad-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotics used for serious bacterial infections, including some caused by bacteria resistant to other antibiotics. Resistance to these drugs is increasing, so their use needs to be guided by infection testing and careful antibiotic use. Imipenem can cause seizures, especially in people with kidney problems or brain disorders.

topics.name: Carbohydrate Intolerance
topics.clinical_significance: Carbohydrate intolerance occurs when the small intestine lacks an enzyme needed to digest a sugar, most often lactase, which digests lactose in milk. The undigested sugar draws water into the bowel and is fermented by bacteria, causing watery diarrhea, gas, bloating, and cramps after eating it. It is different from a food allergy, and symptoms are usually managed by limiting the specific sugar.

topics.name: Carbohydrate Metabolism Disorders, Other
topics.clinical_significance: Rare enzyme defects in carbohydrate pathways can disrupt glucose production or energy use. Depending on the enzyme involved, they may cause symptoms like some forms of glycogen storage disease or destruction of red blood cells (hemolytic anemia). Reduced activity of transketolase, an enzyme that needs thiamine (vitamin B1), is linked to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

topics.name: Carbohydrate Metabolism Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Carbohydrate metabolism disorders are usually inherited conditions that prevent the body from properly breaking down or using sugars. The effects depend on the pathway affected and may include low blood sugar, liver or muscle problems, anemia, or brain and developmental problems. Severity and treatment vary by the specific disorder.

topics.name: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing carbon monoxide, a colorless, odorless gas, reduces oxygen delivery and can injure the brain and heart. Symptoms may include headache, nausea, weakness, chest pain, confusion, fainting, seizures, or coma; severe poisoning can be fatal, and brain or mood problems may appear later. Suspected exposure requires immediate fresh air and emergency medical assessment.

topics.name: Carcinoid Tumors, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine tumors that may release hormones or cause no hormone-related symptoms. Some hormone-producing tumors cause flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea; intestinal tumors usually cause this syndrome after they spread to the liver. Long-term hormone release can damage right-sided heart valves. Tumor behavior depends on its site, grade, and spread.

topics.name: Cardiac Arrest
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac arrest is the sudden loss of effective heart pumping and blood flow to vital organs. The person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally or only gasps; without immediate treatment, it leads to death. Call emergency services, start CPR, and use an automated defibrillator if available.

topics.name: Cardiac Arrest and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is the emergency response to cardiac arrest. Chest compressions, with rescue breaths when appropriate, help maintain blood flow; defibrillation can restore a normal rhythm in some cases. Starting CPR quickly and giving an early shock when needed improve the chance of survival. Care also includes treating the cause and supporting the person after circulation returns.

topics.name: Cardiac Auscultation
topics.clinical_significance: Listening to the heart with a stethoscope helps assess its rhythm and identify normal or abnormal heart sounds, murmurs, and friction rubs. These sounds can point to valve disease, abnormal blood flow, or inflammation around the heart and may guide further tests, such as echocardiography.

topics.name: Cardiac Catheterization
topics.clinical_significance: A test or treatment procedure in which a thin catheter is passed through an artery or vein into the heart or its vessels. It can measure pressures and oxygen levels, show the coronary arteries using contrast, take tissue samples, or treat narrowed vessels. Risks include bleeding or vessel injury, abnormal heart rhythms, contrast reactions, kidney injury, and, rarely, heart attack or stroke.

topics.name: Cardiac Contusion
topics.clinical_significance: A bruise to the heart muscle caused by blunt chest trauma. It may cause no symptoms, but can also lead to abnormal heart rhythms or, if severe, reduced heart pumping and heart failure. Blunt chest injuries can also damage heart valves or chambers, so significant chest trauma with a new murmur, fast heartbeat, or low blood pressure needs prompt evaluation and monitoring.

topics.name: Cardiac Imaging Tests
topics.clinical_significance: Heart imaging tests, such as echocardiography, chest X-ray, CT, MRI, and radionuclide scans, show the heart’s structure and function. They help assess problems such as heart failure, valve or congenital disease, and coronary artery disease, and guide diagnosis and treatment. Some tests use radiation or contrast dye, so the choice depends on the clinical question and the person’s health.

topics.name: Cardiac Pacemakers
topics.clinical_significance: A pacemaker senses the heart’s electrical activity and sends impulses when needed to keep the heartbeat from becoming too slow. It is used mainly for symptomatic slow heart rates or serious delay in electrical conduction, such as high-grade heart block. Special pacing devices can improve the timing of heartbeats in some people with heart failure.

topics.name: Cardiac Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of a possible heart problem starts with the person’s symptoms, medical and family history, and a physical examination. This helps identify clues such as chest discomfort, shortness of breath, palpitations, faintness, or swelling. Because these symptoms can also have noncardiac causes, selected tests are used to confirm and clarify the diagnosis.

topics.name: Cardiac Patient, Introduction to Approach
topics.clinical_significance: A careful symptom history, family history, and physical examination are the first steps in evaluating possible heart disease. Symptoms such as chest discomfort, breathlessness, palpitations, or faintness can have cardiac or noncardiac causes, so selected tests are used to confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Cardiac Radionuclide Imaging
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac radionuclide imaging uses an injected radioactive tracer and a camera to assess heart blood flow, muscle viability, or pumping function. SPECT and PET scans can help detect reduced blood flow from coronary artery disease, identify scarred versus living heart muscle, and evaluate some other heart disorders. The test involves exposure to ionizing radiation.

topics.name: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT)
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac resynchronization therapy uses a special pacemaker to coordinate the timing of the heart’s contractions when its electrical signals are delayed or out of sync. It is used for selected people with symptomatic heart failure and reduced pumping function. In suitable patients, it can reduce heart-failure hospitalizations and the risk of death.

topics.name: Cardiac Sarcoidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac sarcoidosis is inflammation that can form granulomas and scar in the heart muscle or its electrical system. It may cause no symptoms, but can lead to heart block, slow or dangerous fast rhythms, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death. It should be considered in people with sarcoidosis and in younger adults with unexplained heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, or cardiomyopathy.

topics.name: Cardiac Stress Testing
topics.clinical_significance: A stress test monitors the heart’s electrical activity and sometimes images the heart while exercise or medicine makes it work harder. It can reveal reduced blood flow from coronary artery disease and help evaluate symptoms, abnormal rhythms, and heart function. A normal result does not rule out a future heart attack.

topics.name: Cardiac Tamponade
topics.clinical_significance: A medical emergency in which blood or other fluid builds up under pressure in the sac around the heart, restricting the heart chambers from filling. This lowers cardiac output and can quickly cause shock, cardiac arrest, or death. Urgent drainage is needed to relieve the pressure.

topics.name: Cardiac Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most tumors found in the heart have spread from another cancer. Tumors that start in the heart are rare, and most are benign. Depending on their location, tumors can block blood flow, cause abnormal heart rhythms, form clots, or lead to fluid around the heart. Treatment depends on the tumor type, location, and whether it has spread.

topics.name: Cardiac Valvular Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Heart valve disorders narrow an opening or let blood leak backward. They can change blood flow and strain the heart, sometimes before symptoms appear. More serious disease may cause shortness of breath, tiredness, or leg swelling and may need valve repair or replacement.

topics.name: Cardiomyopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiomyopathies are disorders of the heart muscle that can make the heart pump or fill poorly. They may cause heart failure, chest pain, fainting, abnormal heart rhythms, or sudden death. Symptoms and risks vary by type, and care depends on the cause and the specific form.

topics.name: Cardiomyopathies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiomyopathies are heart muscle disorders grouped by how they affect the heart’s shape and function. They may impair filling or pumping and cause heart failure, chest pain, fainting, abnormal heart rhythms, or sudden death. The type and cause guide evaluation and care.

topics.name: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) in Adults
topics.clinical_significance: CPR is emergency support for cardiac arrest, when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Chest compressions help keep blood flowing to the brain and heart until circulation returns or advanced care arrives. Starting CPR quickly and using a defibrillator when advised can improve the chance of survival.

topics.name: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac arrest in an infant or child is life-threatening and can lead to death or lasting brain injury. CPR supports breathing and blood flow while the cause is treated. Resuscitation methods, equipment, and medicine doses are adjusted for the child’s age and size, so prompt, age-appropriate care is vital.

topics.name: Cardiovascular Disorders, Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: Chest discomfort, shortness of breath, tiredness, palpitations, fainting, or swelling can be signs of heart or blood vessel disease. These symptoms also have many other causes, and symptoms alone cannot identify the cause. A medical history and examination help decide whether further testing is needed.

topics.name: Cardiovascular Examination
topics.clinical_significance: A cardiovascular examination looks for signs of heart or blood vessel disease and its effects on the body. Checking blood pressure, pulse, veins, heart and lung sounds, and the limbs can reveal clues such as an abnormal rhythm, poor blood flow, or fluid buildup and help guide further testing.

topics.name: Cardiovascular Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiovascular rehabilitation may help people with coronary artery disease or heart failure, or those recovering from a heart attack or bypass surgery, maintain or regain independence. A tailored program gradually increases activity and helps patients return to daily tasks while watching for symptoms of overexertion.

topics.name: Cardiovascular Tests and Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiovascular tests help assess the heart’s structure, pumping, electrical activity, and blood flow to diagnose disease and guide care. Some tests are noninvasive, while catheter-based procedures can both find a problem and treat it, such as by opening a narrowed artery or correcting an abnormal rhythm.

topics.name: Cardiovascular Tests and Procedures, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Noninvasive and invasive tests assess the heart’s structure and function and help diagnose and judge the severity of heart disease. Some invasive tests can also treat a problem during the same procedure, such as opening a narrowed coronary artery or treating an abnormal rhythm.

topics.name: Cardioversion-Defibrillation, Direct Current
topics.clinical_significance: A direct-current shock can stop certain dangerous or troublesome fast heart rhythms and allow the heart’s natural pacemaker to take over. Synchronized cardioversion is used for many fast rhythms; unsynchronized defibrillation is used for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Correct timing matters because a mistimed shock can trigger a dangerous rhythm.

topics.name: Care of Newborns and Infants
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn and infant care supports healthy feeding and growth and helps detect health problems early. Newborn examinations and screening can identify conditions that need prompt attention; ongoing checks of feeding, weight, urine and stools, and sleep help guide care.

topics.name: Care of the Healthy Term Newborn
topics.clinical_significance: Routine care helps a healthy term newborn adjust after birth and supports safe feeding, sleep, and growth. Monitoring weight, feeding, urine and stools, and jaundice can reveal dehydration or other problems early; clean cord care helps lower infection risk, and timely follow-up checks recovery after discharge.

topics.name: Care of the Surgical Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Care before and after surgery helps lower the risk of complications and support recovery. Reviewing a patient’s health problems and medicines guides preparation, while monitoring and treating issues such as breathing problems, bleeding or clots, pain, and wound infection helps recovery proceed safely.

topics.name: Caries
topics.clinical_significance: Caries (tooth decay) occurs when acids made by plaque bacteria damage the teeth. It may cause no symptoms at first, but deeper decay can cause pain, infection, and tooth loss. Early dental checks, fluoride, good oral hygiene, and a healthy diet can prevent or limit damage.

topics.name: Caring for Sick Children and Their Families
topics.clinical_significance: A child’s illness can affect health, development, school, and relationships, while also placing stress on parents and siblings.
