Clear explanations, family involvement, and coordinated care can reduce uncertainty and help meet the child’s medical and developmental needs.

topics.name: Caring for Sick Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Sick or preterm newborns may need intensive care, but family contact, including skin-to-skin contact when safe, can support survival, stability, growth, and development. Keeping parents involved and explaining the infant’s condition helps families cope and prepare to care for the baby after discharge.

topics.name: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure on the median nerve at the wrist causes pain, numbness, or tingling in the hand, usually in the thumb, index, middle, and thumb-side half of the ring finger. Symptoms often occur at night. Long-lasting pressure can weaken the thumb or waste its muscles.

topics.name: Carrión Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Carrión disease is a sand fly–spread infection found in parts of the Andes. Its acute phase can destroy red blood cells, causing severe anemia and sometimes death if untreated. A later phase may cause red-purple skin bumps. Prompt diagnosis and antibiotics are important.

topics.name: Cataract
topics.clinical_significance: A cataract is clouding of the eye’s lens. It usually causes gradual, painless blurred vision, glare, faded colors, or trouble seeing at night. As it worsens, it can interfere with reading, driving, and other daily tasks; surgery can restore vision when needed.

topics.name: Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
topics.clinical_significance: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is an inherited rhythm disorder that can trigger dangerous fast heart rhythms during exercise or strong emotion, even when the resting ECG and heart structure appear normal. It can cause fainting, cardiac arrest, or sudden death, often in young people. Diagnosis, treatment, and screening of close relatives can help reduce risk.

topics.name: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary catheters allow bacteria to enter the bladder, but bacteria in the urine do not always mean there is an infection causing symptoms. When infection occurs, signs may be vague, such as fever or confusion, and it can spread to the kidneys or bloodstream. Avoiding unnecessary catheter use and removing it promptly lower risk.

topics.name: Cathinones
topics.clinical_significance: Cathinones include stimulants from the khat plant and stronger synthetic drugs often sold as “bath salts.” Synthetic cathinone poisoning can cause severe agitation, high blood pressure, a fast heart rate, seizures, and dangerous overheating; severe cases may cause abnormal heart rhythms or muscle breakdown and can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Cat-Scratch Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Bartonella henselae infection is usually spread by a cat scratch, bite, or lick. It often causes a small bump at the injury site and swollen nearby lymph nodes, sometimes with fever; most people recover. Rarely, it affects the eyes, nervous system, liver, spleen, or heart, and severe illness can occur in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Cat-Scratch Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Cat-scratch fever is another name for cat-scratch disease, an infection caused by Bartonella henselae. It usually causes a small bump at the scratch or bite site and swollen nearby lymph nodes; fever may occur, and most people recover. Rarely, the infection affects other organs.

topics.name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cauda equina syndrome is compression or damage to nerves at the bottom of the spine. New leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the buttocks or genitals, or trouble emptying or controlling the bladder or bowel needs emergency assessment. Delay can lead to permanent paralysis or loss of bladder or bowel function.

topics.name: Causes of Hepatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis is liver inflammation that may be short-term or last more than 6 months. Common causes include hepatitis viruses, alcohol, fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems, and medicines; autoimmune and inherited disorders are less common. Finding the cause matters because it guides care, and some cases become chronic.

topics.name: Caustic Ingestion
topics.clinical_significance: Swallowing a strong acid or alkali can burn the esophagus and stomach, even when the mouth looks normal. Severe injury can cause bleeding or a hole in the digestive tract, and scarring may later narrow the esophagus. This can be life-threatening and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Cavernous Lymphangioma
topics.clinical_significance: Cavernous lymphangioma is a benign birth defect in which lymph vessels are abnormally enlarged, forming a soft swelling, often in the head or neck. Many cause no problems and need no treatment, but larger or troublesome lesions can affect nearby structures and may need specialist care.

topics.name: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a rare, life-threatening clot in a vein at the base of the skull, usually caused by a nearby bacterial infection of the sinuses, nose, or teeth. Severe headache or facial pain, fever, swollen or bulging eyes, double vision, or trouble moving the eyes are warning signs. It can cause blindness, stroke, or death and needs urgent hospital treatment.

topics.name: Celiac Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the small intestine and reduces nutrient absorption. It may cause diarrhea or abdominal discomfort, but some people have few digestive symptoms; poor absorption can lead to anemia, weight loss, or weak bones. Blood tests and often a small-bowel biopsy are used to diagnose it while the person is still eating gluten. Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet.

topics.name: Cellophane Maculopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Cellophane maculopathy (epiretinal membrane) is a thin, scar-like layer over the retina that can shrink and wrinkle it. This may blur or distort central vision, making straight lines look wavy. Many people need no treatment; surgery may be considered if vision problems are significant.

topics.name: Cellular and Molecular Basis of Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer develops when changes in genes that control cell growth and DNA repair let abnormal cells multiply without control. These cells can invade nearby tissue, spread to distant parts of the body, and sometimes avoid attack by the immune system. Some gene changes are inherited; others develop during life. Knowing which changes are present can help guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Cellular Components of the Immune System
topics.clinical_significance: Immune cells detect and fight microbes and abnormal cells. B cells make antibodies and memory cells; T cells coordinate immune responses or kill infected cells. Antigen-presenting cells help activate them, while regulatory T cells limit excessive reactions. Problems with these cells can lead to infections, allergies, or autoimmune disease.

topics.name: Cellulitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the skin and tissue beneath it. It usually causes a painful, warm, red, swollen area that may spread; fever can occur. An abscess may form, and rarely the infection can spread into the blood or deeper tissues.

topics.name: Centipede and Millipede Bites
topics.clinical_significance: A bite from a large centipede can cause pain, redness, and swelling, usually lasting less than 48 hours. Millipedes do not bite but release irritating chemicals that can injure the eye if rubbed into it.

topics.name: Central Nervous System Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Central nervous system tumors grow in the brain or spinal cord, or in nearby tissues such as the meninges. They may begin there or spread from cancer elsewhere. By damaging or pressing on nervous tissue, they can cause headaches, seizures, weakness, or other problems that depend on their location. Even noncancerous brain tumors can be dangerous because the skull leaves little room for growth.

topics.name: Central Nervous System Tumors in Children, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Central nervous system tumors are the most common solid cancers in children younger than 15 and the leading cause of cancer-related death in children. They may increase pressure inside the skull, causing headache, vomiting, sleepiness, behavior changes, or balance problems. Seizures and vision loss can occur, depending on the tumor’s location.

topics.name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion and Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: Retinal artery occlusion is an eye stroke that causes sudden, painless loss of part or all of the vision in one eye. Vision loss is often severe and permanent when the central artery is blocked; a branch blockage affects a smaller part of the visual field. The condition may signal vascular disease or giant cell arteritis and is linked to increased risk of stroke.

topics.name: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion and Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: A blood clot blocking a retinal vein causes painless vision loss, usually sudden but sometimes developing over days or weeks. A central blockage affects a wider area of the retina than a branch blockage. Swelling of the macula can reduce central vision, and abnormal new blood vessels may cause bleeding or glaucoma. Older age, high blood pressure, diabetes, and glaucoma increase risk.

topics.name: Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)
topics.clinical_significance: Central sleep apnea causes repeated pauses in breathing during sleep because the brain’s signal to breathe temporarily falls or becomes unstable; the airway is not blocked. It may disrupt sleep and cause daytime sleepiness or waking short of breath. It can be linked to heart failure, opioid use, or disorders affecting the brainstem.

topics.name: Cephalosporins
topics.clinical_significance: Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics that kill susceptible bacteria by disrupting their cell walls. Their activity varies by drug and generation; some cover bacteria such as MRSA or Pseudomonas that most cephalosporins do not. They are used for many bacterial infections and to prevent infection during some surgeries. Important risks include allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile diarrhea.

topics.name: Cerebellar Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Cerebellar disorders affect movement and balance. They often cause ataxia, with an unsteady walk or poorly coordinated movements; slurred speech, abnormal eye movements, and tremor may also occur. Causes include inherited conditions, stroke, alcohol, some medicines or toxins, and structural problems. Some acquired causes can be treated.

topics.name: Cerebral Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: A cerebral aneurysm is a bulge in a brain artery. Many cause no symptoms, but a large or growing aneurysm can press on nearby nerves. If it ruptures, bleeding around or within the brain can cause a sudden, very severe headache, loss of consciousness, seizures, or death. Smoking and high blood pressure increase the risk of rupture.

topics.name: Cerebral Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs)
topics.clinical_significance: A cerebral arteriovenous malformation is a tangle of abnormal blood vessels in which arteries connect directly to veins. It may cause no symptoms, but can lead to bleeding in the brain, seizures, or headache, often in young adults. Bleeding can cause a hemorrhagic stroke.

topics.name: Cerebral Function, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The cerebrum supports conscious movement, sensation, language, memory, emotion, and thought. Different areas have special roles, but most tasks use several areas working together. Brain injury or disease can affect movement, sensation, speech, memory, behavior, or awareness; the problems depend on the areas involved and the extent of damage.

topics.name: Cerebral Hemispheres, Malformed
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital malformations can change the size, shape, or folds of the cerebral hemispheres. The effects vary widely; affected children may have seizures, delays in movement or learning, or intellectual disability. Head size may also be unusually small or large.

topics.name: Cerebral Lobes, Function and Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Different cerebral lobes help control movement, sensation, speech, memory, vision, behavior, and awareness of space. Damage to a lobe can affect the functions it supports, causing problems such as weakness, loss of sensation, language difficulty, memory or behavior changes, or visual loss. The effects depend on which areas and which side are affected.

topics.name: Cerebral Palsy (CP)
topics.clinical_significance: Cerebral palsy is a group of lasting problems with movement, muscle tone, or posture caused by abnormal brain development or injury early in life. The brain injury does not worsen over time, but its effects vary and may include muscle stiffness, poor coordination, or involuntary movements. Seizures, speech, learning, vision, or hearing problems may also occur.

topics.name: Cerebrovascular Examination
topics.clinical_significance: A cerebrovascular examination looks for blood-vessel problems related to stroke and clues to their cause. It includes comparing blood pressure and pulses in both arms, checking heart rhythm, listening over the neck and head arteries, and looking for signs of bleeding or emboli. Unequal arm pressures may suggest aortic dissection; a weak carotid pulse or bruit may suggest severe narrowing.

topics.name: Cervical Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical cancer usually develops after persistent infection with a high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) type. Early cancer often causes no symptoms; abnormal vaginal bleeding, especially after sex, may be the first sign. Larger or advanced cancers can cause unusual vaginal discharge, pelvic or back pain, or leg swelling.

topics.name: Cervical Cancer Screening and Prevention
topics.clinical_significance: HPV vaccination helps prevent infections that cause most cervical cancers. Screening with HPV tests, Pap tests (which check cervical cells), or both can find high-risk HPV or precancerous changes before invasive cancer develops. Screening recommendations vary by age and risk. Vaccination and screening reduce cervical cancer cases and deaths.

topics.name: Cervical Disc Herniation
topics.clinical_significance: A cervical disc herniation occurs when the soft center of a neck disc pushes through its outer layer. It may cause neck pain that spreads into an arm, with tingling, numbness, or weakness from pressure on a nerve root; some herniations cause no symptoms. If it presses on the spinal cord, it can cause serious neurologic problems.

topics.name: Cervical Dystonia
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical dystonia causes involuntary, often painful contractions or spasms of neck muscles that turn or tilt the head. Tremor may also occur. The cause is often unknown, but some cases are linked to brain disorders or medicines.

topics.name: Cervical Fibroids
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical fibroids are benign growths of the cervix’s smooth muscle. They may cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, discharge, or pain during sex. Heavy bleeding can lead to anemia, and large fibroids may block urine flow or cause urinary retention.

topics.name: Cervical Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
topics.clinical_significance: Also called cervical disc herniation, this occurs when the soft center of a neck disc pushes through its outer layer. It may cause neck pain that spreads into an arm, tingling, numbness, or weakness if a nerve root is irritated; many herniations cause no symptoms. Pressure on the spinal cord can cause serious neurologic problems.

topics.name: Cervical Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical insufficiency is painless opening of the cervix during pregnancy without contractions or labor. It may cause pregnancy loss in the second trimester or very early preterm birth. It often has no symptoms until the cervix begins to open.

topics.name: Cervical Leiomyomas
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign tumors of smooth muscle in the cervix. They may cause irregular or heavy bleeding, vaginal discharge, or pain during sex; heavy bleeding can lead to anemia. Large tumors may obstruct urine flow.

topics.name: Cervical Mucus, Abnormal
topics.clinical_significance: Normally, cervical mucus becomes thin and stretchy near ovulation, helping sperm pass into the uterus. Abnormal mucus may remain too thick for sperm to pass or may reduce sperm survival. It rarely affects fertility significantly, except when linked to chronic cervicitis or narrowing of the cervix.

topics.name: Cervical Myomas
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical myomas are benign smooth-muscle tumors in the cervix. They may cause abnormal bleeding, vaginal discharge, or pain during sex; heavy bleeding can lead to anemia. Large tumors may obstruct urine flow.

topics.name: Cervical Polyps
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical polyps are common, usually benign growths of the cervix or its canal. Most cause no symptoms, but some cause bleeding between periods or after sex; infection can cause pus-like discharge. They rarely become cancerous, but unusual-looking polyps may need testing.

topics.name: Cervical Spinal Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal in the neck. It may cause no symptoms, neck pain, or pressure on nerve roots that leads to arm pain, tingling, or weakness. Severe narrowing can press on the spinal cord and affect balance or strength in the arms and legs.

topics.name: Cervical Spondylosis and Spondylotic Cervical Myelopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical spondylosis is osteoarthritis and wear-related change in the neck. Bone spurs and disc changes can narrow the spinal canal or openings for nerve roots. Nerve-root pressure may cause neck or arm pain, tingling, or weakness. Spinal cord pressure (spondylotic myelopathy) can cause numbness, poor balance, and stiffness or weakness in the arms or legs.

topics.name: Cervical Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cervical stenosis is narrowing or closure of the opening between the cervix and uterus. It often causes no symptoms, but in people who menstruate it can block menstrual flow, causing absent or painful periods and a buildup of blood in the uterus. Rarely, it contributes to infertility or allows pus to collect in the uterus.

topics.name: Cervicitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cervicitis is inflammation of the cervix, often caused by an infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhea, though noninfectious causes also occur. It may cause vaginal discharge, bleeding between periods or after sex, or pain during sex, but it often causes no symptoms. Infection can spread upward and cause pelvic inflammatory disease.

topics.name: Cesarean Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Cesarean delivery is birth through incisions in the abdomen and uterus. It is used when it is safer than vaginal birth, such as when the baby is not positioned for vaginal delivery, labor does not progress, the fetal heart rate is concerning, or the placenta blocks the cervix. It is major surgery and can increase risks in later pregnancies.

topics.name: Cestodes (Tapeworms)
topics.clinical_significance: Tapeworms are flat parasitic worms that infect people through food or by swallowing eggs. Adult worms in the intestine often cause few symptoms, though some cause diarrhea, weight loss, or vitamin B12 deficiency. Larvae can form cysts in the brain and other organs and cause severe disease; brain infection may cause seizures.

topics.name: Chagas Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Chagas disease is infection with the parasite \textit{Trypanosoma cruzi}, usually spread when feces from an infected kissing bug enter the bite wound or the eyes or mouth. It can also spread through contaminated food, from mother to baby, or through infected blood or organs. Many people have no early symptoms; years later, some develop heart rhythm problems or heart failure, or enlargement of the esophagus or colon.

topics.name: Chalazion and Hordeolum (Stye)
topics.clinical_significance: A chalazion is a lump caused by blockage of an eyelid oil gland; after early swelling, it usually becomes painless. A hordeolum (stye) is a painful, usually infected swelling at the eyelid edge or within the lid. A large chalazion can press on the cornea and blur vision, and a hordeolum can sometimes spread infection to nearby eyelid tissues.

topics.name: Chamomile
topics.clinical_significance: Chamomile is an herb used in teas, capsules, and skin products. Evidence for health benefits is limited, though it may modestly reduce anxiety or improve sleep. It can cause allergic reactions, sometimes severe, and may increase the effects of blood thinners and sedatives.

topics.name: Chancroid
topics.clinical_significance: Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It causes painful genital sores and tender groin lymph nodes that may fill with pus and form abscesses. The sores can increase the risk of HIV transmission.

topics.name: Charcot Joints
topics.clinical_significance: Charcot joints are damaged by loss of pain and position sense, usually from nerve disease such as diabetes. Repeated injuries may go unnoticed and cause rapid breakdown of bone and joint tissue, swelling, deformity, and instability, often in the foot or ankle. Pain may be mild despite severe damage.

topics.name: Charcot Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Charcot syndrome is another name for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive disease of the nerve cells that control voluntary muscles. It causes worsening muscle weakness and wasting, and may affect speech, swallowing, and breathing. Sensation is usually preserved; respiratory muscle failure is a common cause of death.

topics.name: Charcot's Joints
topics.clinical_significance: Charcot joints (neuropathic arthropathy) result when loss of pain and position sense allows repeated joint injuries to go unnoticed. The joint can rapidly break down, swell, become deformed, and lose stability, often in the foot or ankle. Pain may be mild despite severe damage.

topics.name: Chelation Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Chelation therapy uses a drug to bind a metal so it can be removed from the blood. It is an established treatment for some heavy-metal poisonings, but EDTA chelation is not recommended for heart disease outside research. Risks include kidney damage and dangerously low blood calcium.

topics.name: Chemical Interactions
topics.clinical_significance: Some drugs work through direct chemical reactions or by binding to substances in the body, rather than by acting on cell receptors. Antacids neutralize stomach acid, and cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut.

topics.name: Chemical Pneumonitis and Aspiration Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Chemical pneumonitis is noninfectious lung inflammation after inhaling irritating material, often stomach contents. It can cause sudden cough and breathing difficulty and may lead to severe lung injury. Aspiration pneumonia is a bacterial lung infection after inhaling bacteria-containing material from the mouth or upper digestive tract; aspiration is more likely when swallowing or airway protection is impaired.

topics.name: Chemical Warfare Agents, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Chemical warfare agents are chemicals used as weapons to injure, kill, or temporarily incapacitate people; some are incendiary and cause fires and burns. Toxic agents can damage nerves, lungs, or skin, or block cells from using oxygen. Even agents intended to incapacitate can cause severe injury or death at high doses.

topics.name: Cherry Angiomas
topics.clinical_significance: Cherry angiomas are common small red to purple growths of skin blood vessels that become more numerous with age. They are benign and do not become cancerous, though they may bleed if injured. A sudden appearance of many lesions can be associated with multicentric Castleman disease or blood cancers.

topics.name: Chest Imaging
topics.clinical_significance: Chest imaging uses X-rays, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and nuclear scans to examine the lungs, heart, and other chest structures. A chest X-ray is often the first test; CT gives more detail, and CT angiography can help detect blood clots in the lungs. The method chosen depends on the suspected problem, and some methods use radiation or contrast dye.

topics.name: Chest Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Chest pain or discomfort can come from the heart, lungs, esophagus, chest wall, or other organs. Causes range from muscle or digestive problems to life-threatening conditions such as a heart attack, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, or tension pneumothorax. Shortness of breath, sweating, or fainting may occur with serious causes, but the pain’s character alone cannot reliably show its cause.

topics.name: Chest Physiotherapy
topics.clinical_significance: Chest physiotherapy uses positioning, chest percussion, and vibration to loosen and move mucus from the airways. It is used when coughing does not clear thick or abundant secretions, as may occur with bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, some cases of COPD, neuromuscular disorders, or pneumonia in dependent parts of the lungs. Complications are uncommon but can include low oxygen or aspiration of loosened secretions.

topics.name: Chest Wall Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Chest wall tumors arise in ribs, cartilage, muscle, or other tissues outside the lungs. They may be benign or malignant; many malignant tumors have spread from another site. They may cause a lump, pain, or impaired breathing, and imaging plus biopsy helps identify the tumor type and extent.

topics.name: Chestfeeding
topics.clinical_significance: Chestfeeding (also called breastfeeding) is feeding an infant human milk directly from the chest. Human milk provides nutrition and immune protection. Exclusive chestfeeding is recommended for about 6 months when possible and when there is no contraindication; solid foods are then added while feeding can continue as desired.

topics.name: Chickenpox
topics.clinical_significance: Chickenpox is the highly contagious primary infection with varicella-zoster virus. It spreads through the air or by contact with skin lesions and causes an itchy rash that appears in crops, with spots, blisters, and crusts, often with fever. After recovery, the virus remains inactive in nerve cells and can later reactivate as shingles. Pneumonia and brain inflammation are among the serious complications, which are more likely in adults, newborns, pregnant people, and those with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Chikungunya Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Chikungunya is a viral infection spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It usually causes sudden fever, severe joint pain, and sometimes a rash. Joint pain and arthritis can persist for months or years and may be disabling.

topics.name: Chikungunya Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Chikungunya vaccines can prevent chikungunya disease in people at increased risk of exposure; they do not protect against dengue or Zika. In the United States, a recombinant virus-like-particle vaccine is authorized for people age 12 years and older. The live-attenuated Ixchiq vaccine is no longer licensed there after serious adverse events, including a vaccine-associated death from encephalitis.

topics.name: Child Abuse
topics.clinical_significance: Child abuse is maltreatment by a parent, caregiver, or other person responsible for a child; it includes physical, sexual, or emotional abuse and neglect. It can cause injury, delayed growth and development, and mental health problems, with effects that may persist into adulthood. Medical child abuse occurs when a caregiver fabricates or causes illness, leading to harmful or unnecessary medical care.

topics.name: Child Maltreatment
topics.clinical_significance: Child maltreatment is abuse or neglect of a person younger than 18 by a parent, caregiver, or someone responsible for the child, causing or threatening harm. Forms include physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, neglect, and medical child abuse. It can cause injury, delayed growth and development, mental health problems, and lasting health effects.

topics.name: Child Maltreatment, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Child maltreatment is abuse or neglect of a person younger than 18 by a caregiver or another person responsible for the child, causing or threatening harm. It includes physical, sexual, or emotional abuse, neglect, and medical child abuse. It can cause injury, delayed growth and development, and mental health problems; its effects may last throughout life.

topics.name: Child Neglect
topics.clinical_significance: Child neglect is a caregiver’s failure to meet a child’s basic physical, emotional, educational, or medical needs, causing or risking harm. It can lead to undernutrition, poor hygiene, delayed growth and development, illness, or preventable injury. Poverty alone is not neglect.

topics.name: Childhood Development
topics.clinical_significance: Childhood development is the gradual acquisition of motor, language, thinking, social, and emotional skills. Milestones usually follow a similar sequence, but their timing varies; delays in one or more areas can reflect developmental disorders, illness, or environmental factors and may affect learning and daily functioning.

topics.name: Childhood Vaccination
topics.clinical_significance: Childhood vaccination trains the immune system to protect against specific infections. It greatly reduces the risk of serious illness and death from vaccine-preventable diseases and has made some once-common infections rare in many places. Rare adverse events are monitored.

topics.name: Children and Youth with Special Health Care Needs
topics.clinical_significance: Children and youth with special health care needs have, or are at risk for, chronic physical, emotional, behavioral, or developmental conditions and need more health services than their peers. These conditions can limit activity, affect growth and development, and lead to more medical visits or hospital stays. Coordinated care helps reduce gaps and duplication in services.

topics.name: Chinese Liver Fluke Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Chinese liver fluke infection (clonorchiasis) is usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish; most infections cause no symptoms. Heavy or long-lasting infection can inflame or block the bile ducts and lead to gallstones, pancreatitis, liver scarring, or bile duct cancer.

topics.name: Chinese Medicine, Traditional
topics.clinical_significance: Traditional Chinese medicine is a group of practices, including herbal remedies, acupuncture, diet, massage, and qigong, based on traditional ideas about qi and yin-yang. Evidence of benefit varies by condition. Herbal products may have uncertain ingredients or doses, contamination, or interactions with medicines.

topics.name: Chiropractic
topics.clinical_significance: Chiropractic mainly uses hands-on manipulation of the spine, joints, and soft tissues. Evidence supports its use for low back pain, but evidence for other conditions is limited or does not show benefit. Serious complications are rare but can include nerve or neck artery injury.

topics.name: Chlamydiae
topics.clinical_significance: Chlamydiae are bacteria that live and multiply inside human cells. Three species cause human disease: C. trachomatis causes sexually transmitted and eye infections and can infect newborns; C. pneumoniae can cause pneumonia; and C. psittaci causes bird-associated psittacosis, which can also cause pneumonia.

topics.name: Chlamydiae and Mycoplasmas
topics.clinical_significance: Chlamydiae and mycoplasmas can cause sexually transmitted genital infections and respiratory infections, including pneumonia. Genital chlamydia may cause few symptoms but can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, or infection in newborns. Mycoplasmas lack a cell wall, so penicillin-type antibiotics do not work against them.

topics.name: Chloramphenicol
topics.clinical_significance: Chloramphenicol blocks bacterial protein production and acts against many bacteria. Because it can cause bone marrow suppression, rarely irreversible aplastic anemia, and potentially fatal gray baby syndrome in newborns, it is generally reserved for serious infections when suitable alternatives are unavailable.

topics.name: Chlorosis
topics.clinical_significance: Chlorosis is an obsolete name for iron-deficiency anemia, historically used especially for young women with pallor and weakness. It is not a separate modern diagnosis; iron deficiency can result from blood loss, poor absorption, or increased iron needs.

topics.name: Cholecystitis, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute cholecystitis is sudden inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by a gallstone blocking its outlet. It causes persistent pain and tenderness in the upper right abdomen, often with nausea, vomiting, or fever. Severe cases can lead to infection, tissue death, perforation, or peritonitis.

topics.name: Choledocholithiasis and Cholangitis
topics.clinical_significance: Stones in the common bile duct can block bile flow, causing biliary pain, jaundice, or pancreatitis. If the blocked duct becomes infected (acute cholangitis), abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever or chills may occur; this is a medical emergency and can progress to confusion and low blood pressure.

topics.name: Cholelithiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Cholelithiasis means one or more stones in the gallbladder; most people with gallstones have no symptoms. A stone can cause biliary pain or block a duct, leading to gallbladder inflammation, bile duct infection, or pancreatitis.

topics.name: Cholera
topics.clinical_significance: Cholera is an acute intestinal infection caused by toxin-producing Vibrio cholerae, usually spread through contaminated water or food. It can cause sudden, profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, leading to severe dehydration, kidney injury, shock, and death without timely rehydration.

topics.name: Cholestasis, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal cholestasis is reduced bile flow that causes conjugated jaundice, often with dark urine and pale stools. It is never normal and can result from biliary atresia, infection, or a metabolic or genetic disorder; persistent cholestasis can cause liver damage, poor growth, and vitamin deficiencies.

topics.name: Cholesteatoma
topics.clinical_significance: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal buildup of skin cells and keratin in the middle ear or nearby mastoid. It can cause persistent ear drainage and hearing loss, erode nearby bone, and rarely lead to serious infection in the inner ear or brain.

topics.name: Cholesteryl Ester Storage Disease and Wolman Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Both are rare, inherited lysosomal acid lipase deficiency disorders that cause fats to build up in cells, especially in the liver and spleen. Wolman disease is the severe infantile form and can be fatal in infancy without treatment; later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease can cause an enlarged liver, high LDL cholesterol, and early atherosclerosis. Enzyme replacement treatment is available.

topics.name: Chondrocalcinosis
topics.clinical_significance: Chondrocalcinosis is calcium pyrophosphate crystal buildup in cartilage, often seen on imaging. It becomes more common with age and may cause painful joint inflammation, but deposits can also be present without symptoms and do not by themselves mean active arthritis.

topics.name: Chondroitin Sulfate
topics.clinical_significance: Chondroitin sulfate is a natural component of cartilage and is sold as a supplement for osteoarthritis. Evidence of benefit is mixed: it has not shown clear benefit when used alone, and any benefit with glucosamine may be small. Supplement composition can vary, and chondroitin may increase warfarin’s blood-thinning effect.

topics.name: Chondromalacia Patellae
topics.clinical_significance: Chondromalacia patellae is softening and swelling of the cartilage beneath the kneecap, often related to injury or abnormal kneecap tracking. It commonly causes pain around the front of the knee with stairs, sports, or prolonged sitting, usually without visible swelling.

topics.name: Chorea, Athetosis, and Hemiballismus
topics.clinical_significance: Chorea, athetosis, and hemiballismus are involuntary movement patterns caused by problems in brain motor circuits. Chorea causes irregular, flowing movements; athetosis causes slower, writhing movements; hemiballismus causes forceful flinging movements, usually on one side. Causes include stroke, medications, metabolic or autoimmune disease, and Huntington disease.

topics.name: Chorioamnionitis
topics.clinical_significance: Chorioamnionitis (intraamniotic infection) is infection and inflammation of the fetal membranes, amniotic fluid, placenta, or fetus. It often causes maternal fever and raises the risk of preterm birth, maternal infection, and serious newborn infections such as sepsis or pneumonia.

topics.name: Chromium
topics.clinical_significance: Chromium is a trace mineral that may strengthen insulin’s action. Evidence that chromium supplements improve diabetes, weight, or cholesterol is limited and mixed; supplements may interact with blood sugar medicines or levothyroxine and reduce iron absorption.

topics.name: Chromium Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Chromium deficiency is rare and has mainly been reported in people receiving long-term intravenous nutrition. It may impair glucose tolerance and cause weight loss, confusion, or poor coordination; whether chromium is essential in healthy people remains uncertain.

topics.name: Chromium Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Chromium toxicity depends on its form and route of exposure. High doses of trivalent chromium given by injection can irritate the skin, while lower oral doses are not known to be toxic. Workplace exposure to hexavalent chromium can irritate the skin, lungs, and gut, damage the nasal septum, and may cause lung cancer.

topics.name: Chromoblastomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Chromoblastomycosis is a slowly progressive fungal skin infection, usually acquired when pigmented fungi enter through an injury to an exposed area such as the foot or leg. It causes warty nodules that may ulcerate and spread over years; extensive disease can block lymph drainage and develop secondary bacterial infection.

topics.name: Chromosomal Abnormalities, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Chromosomal abnormalities are changes in the number or structure of chromosomes, such as an extra or missing chromosome or a deleted, duplicated, or rearranged segment. They can cause a range of genetic disorders; effects depend on which genetic material is affected. Different tests may be needed because no single test detects every type.

topics.name: Chromosomal Deletion Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Chromosomal deletion syndromes occur when part of a chromosome is missing, removing genetic material. Effects vary with the size and location of the deletion and may include birth defects and intellectual, developmental, or physical disability. Larger deletions may be seen on karyotyping; smaller ones can require more specialized tests.

topics.name: Chromosome and Gene Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: Chromosome and gene abnormalities are changes in chromosome number or structure or in the DNA sequence of a gene. Depending on the change, they can cause congenital conditions, developmental or intellectual disability, and other health problems; effects range widely.

topics.name: Chronic Abdominal Pain and Recurrent Abdominal Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic abdominal pain lasts more than 3 months; recurrent abdominal pain means at least 3 episodes over 3 months that interfere with normal activities. Most cases are related to gut-brain interaction disorders, but some have a physical cause. Fever, weight loss, blood in vomit or stool, or frequent vomiting can point to a more serious illness.

topics.name: Chronic Acquired Demyelinating Polyneuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic acquired demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an immune-mediated disorder that damages the myelin around peripheral nerves. It causes progressive or relapsing weakness, usually in both near-trunk and far-end limb muscles, often with numbness and reduced reflexes. Progression lasting more than 2 months helps distinguish it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; immune treatments can improve symptoms.

topics.name: Chronic Bilirubin Encephalopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) is lasting brain injury caused by unconjugated bilirubin entering the brain, usually in newborns with very high bilirubin or low albumin. It may cause intellectual disability, a movement disorder called choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and difficulty looking upward; there is no treatment that reverses the brain injury.

topics.name: Chronic Effects of Sunlight
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term sun exposure can cause early skin aging, rough or uneven skin, and actinic keratoses, which are precancerous skin changes. It also raises the risk of basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers and melanoma.

topics.name: Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: This rare lung condition causes eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, to build up in the lungs. It can cause a persistent cough, wheezing, breathlessness, fever, and night sweats; asthma or another allergic condition is common. Steroids usually work quickly, but symptoms often return when treatment is reduced or stopped.

topics.name: Chronic Granulocytic Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic granulocytic leukemia, also called chronic myeloid leukemia, is a blood cancer that causes the bone marrow to make too many white blood cells. It is usually driven by the Philadelphia chromosome, which creates the BCR::ABL1 gene. Without effective treatment, it can advance to an aggressive phase; targeted medicines called tyrosine kinase inhibitors often control it and extend life.

topics.name: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited immune disorder prevents some white blood cells from making the chemicals they need to kill certain bacteria and fungi. It causes repeated infections and abscesses, often beginning in childhood, and can lead to lumps of inflamed tissue that block organs. Aspergillus and other fungal infections can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Chronic Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: A long-term condition in which the heart cannot pump or fill well enough to meet the body’s needs. It can cause shortness of breath, tiredness, and swelling in the legs; symptoms may be stable for a time but can suddenly worsen and require hospital care. Ongoing treatment can ease symptoms and lower the risk of worsening.

topics.name: Chronic Infectious Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: A joint infection that lasts for weeks, often caused by bacteria such as mycobacteria or by fungi. It usually affects one joint and may cause gradual swelling, mild warmth, and aching. Without proper treatment, it can damage the joint; people with weakened immune systems or artificial joints are at higher risk.

topics.name: Chronic Infective Tubulointerstitial Nephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term kidney scarring caused by repeated or ongoing infections, often when urine flows backward toward the kidneys or is blocked. It may cause no clear symptoms, or lead to fever, feeling unwell, or pain in the side. Repeated infections can further damage the kidneys and lead to chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure.

topics.name: Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (CIDP)
topics.clinical_significance: CIDP is an immune system disorder that damages the protective covering of peripheral nerves. It causes weakness, often in both arms and legs, and may also cause numbness or tingling and reduced reflexes. Symptoms worsen for more than 8 weeks or come and go; treatment such as immune globulin or steroids can improve symptoms, but may be needed long term.

topics.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic kidney disease means that reduced kidney function or other signs of kidney damage last at least 3 months. Early disease often causes no symptoms. As it worsens, waste and fluid can build up in the body and cause tiredness, nausea, itching, swelling, anemia, and bone problems. Advanced disease may require dialysis or a kidney transplant.

topics.name: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
topics.clinical_significance: CLL is a cancer of B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. These abnormal cells build up in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen. It often grows slowly and may cause no symptoms at first; later it can cause enlarged lymph nodes, tiredness, repeated infections, anemia, or low platelets. Treatment is often delayed until the disease causes symptoms or progresses.

topics.name: Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, also called Hashimoto thyroiditis, is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system inflames the thyroid. It may enlarge the thyroid and often gradually reduces thyroid hormone production, causing symptoms such as tiredness, feeling cold, and weight gain. Some people need lifelong thyroid hormone replacement.

topics.name: Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited immune disorder causes persistent or repeated Candida yeast infections of the mouth, skin, nails, and other moist body surfaces, often starting in infancy. Some forms also cause autoimmune hormone problems. Antifungal medicines usually control the infections.

topics.name: Chronic Myelocytic Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic myelocytic leukemia, also called chronic myeloid leukemia, is a blood cancer that makes the bone marrow produce too many white blood cells, especially granulocytes. It is usually driven by the Philadelphia chromosome, which creates the BCR::ABL1 gene. Without effective treatment, it can progress to a fast-growing phase; targeted medicines called tyrosine kinase inhibitors often control it and prolong life.

topics.name: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic myelogenous leukemia is another name for chronic myeloid leukemia, a blood cancer that causes the bone marrow to make too many granulocytes, a type of white blood cell. It is usually driven by the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR::ABL1 gene. Targeted medicines often control the disease and prolong life, but untreated disease can progress to a fast-growing phase.

topics.name: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), also called chronic myelogenous leukemia, is a cancer of blood-forming cells that causes too many granulocytes, a type of white blood cell. Most cases are driven by the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR::ABL1 gene. Without effective treatment, it can advance to a fast-growing phase resembling acute leukemia; targeted medicines greatly improve disease control and survival.

topics.name: Chronic Obstructive Bronchitis
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic obstructive bronchitis is chronic bronchitis with lasting airflow blockage, a form of COPD. It causes a mucus-producing cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 years, along with airflow obstruction on breathing tests. It can also cause breathlessness and flare-ups.

topics.name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: This topic group covers COPD, a long-term lung disease with persistent airflow blockage, and related conditions such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. COPD often causes ongoing cough, phlegm, and shortness of breath. Severe disease can lead to repeated flare-ups, respiratory failure, or right-sided heart failure.

topics.name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
topics.clinical_significance: COPD is a long-term lung disease that causes lasting, often worsening blockage of airflow because of damage to the airways, air sacs, or both. It commonly causes a cough with phlegm and shortness of breath, and symptoms can flare up. Severe COPD can lead to respiratory failure or right-sided heart failure. Tobacco smoke is a common cause; other inhaled toxins and inherited conditions can also contribute.

topics.name: Chronic Pancreatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term inflammation permanently scars the pancreas and gradually reduces its ability to make digestive enzymes and hormones such as insulin. It often causes upper-abdominal pain; reduced digestion can lead to oily stools, poor nutrition, and weight loss, while loss of insulin production can cause diabetes. Heavy alcohol use and smoking are major risk factors.

topics.name: Chronic Paronychia
topics.clinical_significance: Repeated or long-lasting inflammation of the skin around a nail, usually a fingernail. Ongoing exposure to water or other irritants is a common cause; Candida may be present but is not usually the main cause. The nail fold may become red and tender, the cuticle can be lost, and the nail may become misshapen over time.

topics.name: Chronic Pelvic Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic pelvic pain is pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis that lasts more than 6 months. In women, it can come from reproductive organs, the urinary or digestive tract, pelvic muscles, or nerves. It may affect emotional and sexual well-being, and finding the cause can be complex.

topics.name: Chronic Progressive Chorea
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic progressive chorea is another name for Huntington disease, an inherited brain disorder caused by extra repeats in the HTT gene. It causes involuntary movements, changes in mood or behavior, and worsening memory and thinking, usually beginning in adulthood. The disease gets worse over time; treatment helps manage symptoms but does not stop its progression.

topics.name: Chronic Relapsing Polyneuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic relapsing polyneuropathy is another name for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP). This immune-related nerve disorder damages the protective covering of nerves, causing weakness in the arms and legs and sometimes numbness or tingling. Symptoms last more than 8 weeks and may worsen slowly or return after periods of improvement. Treatment can help, but may be needed for a long time.

topics.name: Chronic Renal Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic renal failure is another name for chronic kidney disease: reduced kidney function or signs of kidney damage lasting at least 3 months. Early disease often has no symptoms. As kidney function worsens, waste and fluid can build up and cause tiredness, nausea, itching, swelling, anemia, and bone problems. Advanced disease may require dialysis or a kidney transplant.

topics.name: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE)
topics.clinical_significance: CTE is a progressive brain disorder that may develop after repeated head injuries or blast exposure. It can cause changes in mood and behavior, worsening memory and thinking, and movement problems. The risk after a given amount of head trauma is not known, and a definite diagnosis can currently be made only by examining the brain after death. There is no specific treatment.

topics.name: Chronic Venous Insufficiency and Post-Thrombotic Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic venous insufficiency occurs when blood does not flow back from the legs to the heart well, often because vein valves are damaged or veins are blocked. It can cause leg aching or heaviness, swelling, skin changes, and sores that may be slow to heal. Post-thrombotic syndrome is chronic venous insufficiency that develops after a deep vein blood clot and can cause long-term symptoms or leg ulcers.

topics.name: Chronic Widespread (Centralized) Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic widespread, or centralized, pain is pain that continues or returns for more than 3 months, sometimes after an injury has healed. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can make the body more sensitive, even when there is no clear ongoing tissue damage. The pain may affect many areas and can occur with conditions such as fibromyalgia.

topics.name: Churg-Strauss Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Churg-Strauss syndrome, now called eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is a rare disease in which small and medium blood vessels become inflamed. It usually occurs in people with adult-onset asthma, sinus allergies, and high levels of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. It can damage the lungs, skin, nerves, digestive tract, kidneys, or heart; heart or nerve involvement can be severe. Treatment often includes corticosteroids and other medicines that suppress the immune system.

topics.name: Chédiak-Higashi Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is a rare inherited immune disorder that makes it hard for white blood cells to kill germs. It causes repeated infections and reduced pigment in the skin, hair, and eyes. Many people develop a severe phase with fever, enlarged liver and spleen, low blood-cell counts, bleeding, and nerve problems. A stem cell transplant can be curative.

topics.name: Chédiak-Higashi's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Chédiak-Higashi’s syndrome is another name for Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, a rare inherited immune disorder that makes white blood cells less able to kill germs. It causes repeated infections and reduced pigment in the skin, hair, and eyes. A severe phase can cause fever, enlarged liver and spleen, low blood-cell counts, bleeding, and nerve problems. A stem cell transplant can be curative.

topics.name: Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders occur when the body’s internal sleep-wake clock is out of sync with the day-night cycle or a person’s required schedule. They can make it hard to sleep at the desired time and cause too much sleepiness while awake. Examples include jet lag, shift work sleep problems, and sleep times that are consistently too early or too late.

topics.name: Cirrhosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cirrhosis is advanced liver scarring that distorts the liver and can reduce its function and blood flow. It may cause no symptoms for years; later it can cause tiredness, poor appetite, weight loss, jaundice, or swelling of the abdomen or legs. Increased pressure in liver blood vessels can cause serious bleeding, fluid buildup, or confusion. Cirrhosis can also lead to liver failure and increases the risk of liver cancer.

topics.name: CKD
topics.clinical_significance: CKD means chronic kidney disease: reduced kidney function or other signs of kidney damage that last at least 3 months. It often develops slowly and may cause no symptoms at first. As it worsens, waste and fluid can build up and lead to tiredness, swelling, anemia, bone problems, and eventually kidney failure.

topics.name: Classic Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Classic typhus, also called epidemic typhus, is a serious infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and usually spread by body lice. It causes a prolonged high fever, severe headache, and rash. Severe illness can damage blood vessels and organs and may be fatal without treatment; antibiotics are effective. The infection can rarely return years later as Brill-Zinsser disease.

topics.name: Clavi
topics.clinical_significance: Clavi, or corns, are small, sharply defined areas of thickened skin caused by repeated pressure or rubbing, often over the toes. Unlike broader calluses, corns have a firm central core and may be painful or tender when pressed.

topics.name: Clavicle Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A clavicle fracture is a break in the collarbone, usually from a fall onto the shoulder or a direct blow. It causes pain that worsens when the arm moves and may make the bone look misshapen. Most heal with a sling, but severe displacement, threatened skin, or certain fracture locations may need surgery; fractures near the breastbone can occur with chest injuries.

topics.name: Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate
topics.clinical_significance: These birth differences occur when the upper lip, the roof of the mouth, or both do not close fully before birth. A cleft can make feeding difficult and later affect speech, teeth, or hearing; cleft palate also raises the risk of ear infections. Treatment often includes surgery and ongoing dental and speech care.

topics.name: Clindamycin
topics.clinical_significance: Clindamycin treats selected bacterial infections, including some skin and anaerobic infections. A major risk is antibiotic-associated diarrhea, especially severe Clostridioides difficile colitis.

topics.name: Clinical Applications of Genetics
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic testing can help diagnose inherited disorders, identify people at risk, and guide screening of relatives and reproductive counseling. Genetic information can also help guide treatment, including the choice or dose of some medicines; screening is most useful when accurate results can change care.

topics.name: Clinical Decision Making
topics.clinical_significance: Clinical decision making combines a patient's history, examination, and test results to identify likely diagnoses and choose appropriate testing or treatment. It uses medical evidence and the patient's needs and preferences to balance the possible benefits, risks, and costs of care.

topics.name: Clinical Decision Making, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Clinical decision making uses a patient's history, examination, and test results to decide what information is needed, which diagnoses are likely, and what treatment to recommend. It helps clinicians address urgent problems while weighing uncertainty, patient risk, and cost.

topics.name: Clinical Decision-Making Strategies
topics.clinical_significance: Clinicians use the patient's symptoms, history, examination, and test results to form and revise possible diagnoses. These strategies help decide when testing or treatment is needed by weighing the chance of disease against the benefits and risks of care and considering the patient's preferences.

topics.name: Clonorchiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Clonorchiasis is infection with a liver fluke, usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Many people have no symptoms, but heavy or long-lasting infection can inflame or block the bile ducts and, rarely, lead to bile duct cancer.

topics.name: Closed-Angle Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: In closed-angle glaucoma, the iris blocks the eye's drainage angle, raising pressure and damaging the optic nerve. A sudden attack can cause severe eye pain and redness, blurred vision or halos, headache, and nausea or vomiting; it is an emergency because vision can be lost quickly without treatment.

topics.name: Clostridial Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Clostridial bacteria can cause illnesses ranging from food poisoning to toxin-related diseases such as tetanus and botulism, as well as severe tissue infections such as gas gangrene. Many infections are mild, but serious forms can destroy tissue, affect the nervous system, and be fatal.

topics.name: Clostridial Intra-Abdominal and Pelvic Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Clostridial infections in the abdomen or pelvis can cause severe pain, fever, and tenderness. Bacterial toxins can destroy tissue and lead to sepsis, rapid breakdown of red blood cells, organ failure, or death, so urgent antibiotics and surgery to remove infected or dead tissue may be needed.

topics.name: Clostridial Myonecrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) is a rapidly spreading muscle infection, usually after a deep or crush injury. Severe pain, swelling, blisters, skin discoloration, and gas under the skin may develop; toxins can cause shock, kidney failure, and death, so immediate surgery and antibiotics are needed.

topics.name: Clostridial Necrotizing Enteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Clostridial necrotizing enteritis is an infection that destroys tissue in the small intestine, usually caused by Clostridium perfringens type C. It may cause mild diarrhea or progress to severe abdominal pain, bloody stools, septic shock, and death, so prompt antibiotics and sometimes surgery are needed.

topics.name: Clostridial Soft-Tissue Infections
topics.clinical_significance: These infections usually follow an injury and can affect the skin, muscle, or deeper tissue; gas may collect in the affected area. The most severe form, gas gangrene, rapidly destroys muscle and can cause shock or kidney failure, so it needs immediate antibiotics and surgery.

topics.name: Clostridioides difficile Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Clostridioides difficile can multiply, especially after antibiotic use, and release toxins that inflame the colon and cause diarrhea. Illness can be severe or recur; stool testing is useful when a person has symptoms because some people carry the bacteria without being ill.

topics.name: Clostridium perfringens Food Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: This is usually a mild food poisoning caused by eating contaminated meat that was left warm too long. Watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps often start 6 to 24 hours later and usually clear within a day with supportive care.

topics.name: Cluster Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Cluster headache causes repeated, extremely severe pain around one eye or temple, usually on one side. Attacks last about 15 minutes to 3 hours and often recur daily for weeks, with tearing, eye redness, or a runny or blocked nose on the same side; the pain can be disabling.

topics.name: Cnidaria (Coelenterates, such as Jellyfish and Sea Anemones) Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Stings from jellyfish, sea anemones, and related animals usually cause immediate pain and itchy skin welts, but some also cause muscle cramps, nausea, or changes in heart rate. Trouble breathing or confusion can signal a medical emergency, and a few species can cause fatal stings.

topics.name: Coagulation Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Coagulation disorders interfere with normal blood clotting and can cause abnormal bleeding. They may be inherited or related to liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, certain medicines, or disseminated intravascular coagulation; blood tests help identify the cause.

topics.name: Coagulation Disorders Caused by Circulating Anticoagulants
topics.clinical_significance: Circulating anticoagulants are antibodies that interfere with clotting proteins. They usually cause abnormal bleeding, which can be life-threatening, but antiphospholipid antibodies may instead cause artery or vein clots; blood tests help identify these disorders.

topics.name: Coagulation Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Coagulation disorders affect blood-clotting proteins and can lead to abnormal bleeding. They may be inherited, such as hemophilia, or acquired from liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, certain medicines, or disseminated intravascular coagulation; clotting tests help guide diagnosis.

topics.name: Coagulation Disorders, Uncommon Hereditary
topics.clinical_significance: Most uncommon inherited clotting-factor disorders can cause bleeding after injury or surgery; factor XII deficiency is an exception and does not usually cause bleeding. Factor XIII deficiency can also impair wound healing, and some fibrinogen disorders can raise the risk of blood clots.

topics.name: Coal Worker Pneumoconiosis
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term inhalation of coal-mine dust can scar the lungs (black lung) and may also cause chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Early disease may have no symptoms, but progressive lung damage can cause cough, shortness of breath, and severe loss of lung function, even after exposure ends.

topics.name: Coarctation of the Aorta
topics.clinical_significance: Coarctation is a narrowing of the aorta present from birth that raises blood pressure in the arms and reduces blood flow to the lower body. Severe narrowing in a newborn can cause poor organ blood flow, heart failure, or shock; milder cases may appear later as high blood pressure or weak leg pulses, and repair is usually needed.

topics.name: Cocaine
topics.clinical_significance: Cocaine is a stimulant that raises heart rate and blood pressure and narrows blood vessels. Use can lead to dependence and life-threatening problems such as abnormal heart rhythms, heart attack, stroke, seizures, overheating, or aortic dissection.

topics.name: Coccidioidomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Valley fever is usually acquired by breathing Coccidioides spores in dusty soil. Most infections are silent or cause a mild lung illness, but people with weakened immune systems or other risk factors can develop severe pneumonia or spread of infection to the skin, bones, joints, or brain.

topics.name: Coccydynia
topics.clinical_significance: Coccydynia is pain in or around the tailbone, usually worse when sitting or rising from a chair. It often follows an injury, childbirth, or repeated pressure; persistent or unexplained pain may need evaluation for less common causes such as infection or tumor.

topics.name: Coccygeal Area Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain near the tailbone has many possible causes and may come from nearby pelvic or rectal structures rather than the coccyx itself. Persistent pain, or pain with bleeding, drainage, fever, or numbness, should be evaluated to identify the cause and help prevent chronic pain.

topics.name: Coccygodynia
topics.clinical_significance: Coccygodynia, also called coccydynia, is pain in and around the tailbone, usually worse when sitting, especially when leaning back, or when standing up. It often follows injury or repeated pressure; persistent pain can become chronic, while infection or tumor are uncommon causes.

topics.name: Coccyx Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Coccyx disorders usually cause midline tailbone pain that worsens with sitting and may follow injury, childbirth, or repeated pressure. Nearby pelvic structures can cause similar pain, so severe or persistent symptoms need assessment; untreated pain can become chronic, while infection and tumors are uncommon causes.

topics.name: Cod Worm Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Cod worm disease (anisakiasis) is caused by marine roundworm larvae in raw or undercooked saltwater fish or squid. It can cause sudden abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; intestinal involvement may resemble other abdominal disorders, and stomach larvae can be removed during endoscopy.

topics.name: Coenurosis (Taenia multiceps, Taenia serialis, or Taenia brauni Infection)
topics.clinical_significance: Coenurosis is a rare tapeworm infection acquired by accidentally swallowing eggs from dog feces. Larvae form cysts in the brain, muscles, skin, or eyes, causing symptoms such as seizures, neurologic problems, tender lumps, or vision loss depending on the site; symptomatic cysts are usually removed surgically.

topics.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
topics.clinical_significance: CoQ10 is a substance made by the body that helps cells produce energy and acts as an antioxidant. Supplements are promoted for conditions such as heart failure and muscle symptoms from statins, but evidence of benefit is uncertain; CoQ10 may reduce warfarin's effect.

topics.name: Cogan Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cogan syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease that inflames the cornea and inner ear, causing eye pain or redness, reduced vision, dizziness, ringing in the ears, or hearing loss. Without prompt treatment, it can cause permanent vision or hearing loss; in some people, inflammation of the aorta or other blood vessels can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Cogan's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cogan syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease that inflames the cornea and inner ear, causing eye pain or redness, reduced vision, dizziness, ringing in the ears, or hearing loss. Without prompt treatment, it can cause permanent vision or hearing loss; in some people, inflammation of the aorta or other blood vessels can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Cognitive Errors in Clinical Decision Making
topics.clinical_significance: Cognitive errors are unconscious flaws in clinical reasoning, often caused by relying too heavily on mental shortcuts or an early diagnosis. They can distort estimates of disease likelihood, narrow the list of possible diagnoses, and lead to unnecessary or insufficient testing and missed or delayed diagnoses.

topics.name: Cold, Common
topics.clinical_significance: The common cold is an acute viral infection of the upper respiratory tract that usually causes a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, and cough. It usually resolves on its own, but can worsen asthma or chronic bronchitis and may be followed by sinusitis or middle-ear infection.

topics.name: Cold Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Cold injury can lower core body temperature (hypothermia) or damage local tissues. Local injury may occur with freezing (frostbite) or without freezing, as in immersion foot and chilblains. Risk increases with moisture, exhaustion, dehydration, poor nutrition, or impaired cardiovascular function.

topics.name: Cold Injury, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cold exposure can lower core body temperature (hypothermia) or cause injury to a local area. Local tissue damage may occur with freezing (frostbite) or without freezing, as in frostnip, immersion foot, or chilblains. Exhaustion, poor nutrition, dehydration, low blood oxygen, impaired heart or circulation, and moisture increase susceptibility.

topics.name: Colic
topics.clinical_significance: In infants, colic is repeated, prolonged crying without a clear cause in an otherwise healthy baby. It often starts in the first month, peaks around 6 weeks, and resolves by 3 to 4 months. It has no known intestinal cause and usually causes no lasting harm, but other causes of crying should be considered if the history or examination is abnormal.

topics.name: Colles Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A Colles fracture is a break near the wrist end of the radius, with the broken part displaced or angled toward the back of the hand. It often follows a fall on an outstretched hand and is common in older adults. Pain, swelling, and deformity may occur; swelling or displacement can injure the median nerve, and joint involvement can lead to lasting stiffness, pain, or arthritis.

topics.name: Colon Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Colon cancer is a malignant tumor of the large bowel, most often an adenocarcinoma that develops from an adenomatous polyp. Early disease may cause no symptoms; right-sided tumors often cause hidden bleeding and anemia, while left-sided tumors may change bowel habits or obstruct the bowel.

topics.name: Colonic Diverticulitis
topics.clinical_significance: Colonic diverticulitis is inflammation of a pouch in the colon, with or without infection. It commonly causes lower abdominal pain and tenderness, often with fever or nausea. Complications can include an abscess, bowel perforation, an abnormal connection, or blockage; perforation can lead to peritonitis or sepsis.

topics.name: Colonic Diverticulosis
topics.clinical_significance: Colonic diverticulosis is the presence of one or more small pouches in the colon wall without active inflammation. It becomes more common with age, and most people have no symptoms. The pouches can bleed, sometimes causing significant painless rectal bleeding, or become inflamed (diverticulitis).

topics.name: Colorectal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Colorectal cancer affects the colon or rectum; most cases are adenocarcinomas, often arising in precancerous polyps. Early cancer may cause no symptoms. Right-sided tumors often cause hidden bleeding and anemia, while left-sided or rectal tumors may cause visible blood, changed bowel habits, or blockage. The cancer can spread, and outlook depends strongly on its stage.

topics.name: Colorectal Cancer Screening
topics.clinical_significance: Colorectal cancer screening looks for cancer or precancerous polyps before symptoms develop. For average-risk adults, screening generally begins at age 45 and continues through age 75; from ages 76 to 85, the decision is based on health and prior screening. Options include stool tests and colonoscopy, and an abnormal non-colonoscopy test needs follow-up colonoscopy.

topics.name: Coma and Impaired Consciousness
topics.clinical_significance: Coma is deep unresponsiveness in which a person cannot be awakened and keeps their eyes closed; impaired consciousness is a less severe reduction in awareness or response. Causes include brain injury or disease, infection, drug effects, and metabolic problems. These states can worsen, threaten breathing, and require urgent identification of the cause.

topics.name: Coma and Impaired Consciousness, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Coma is unarousable unresponsiveness with the eyes closed; impaired consciousness is a less severe loss of awareness or response. Both usually result from dysfunction of both cerebral hemispheres or the brainstem arousal system. Causes include structural brain injury and widespread metabolic, infectious, or drug-related illness; impaired consciousness can worsen to coma and brain death.

topics.name: Common Cold
topics.clinical_significance: The common cold is an acute, usually fever-free viral infection that causes a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, and cough; rhinoviruses cause about half of cases. Most symptoms resolve within 10 days, although cough may last longer. Colds can worsen asthma or chronic bronchitis, and thick or colored nasal mucus alone does not show a bacterial infection.

topics.name: Common Dental Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Common dental disorders include tooth decay and gum disease. Early disease may cause few symptoms, but progression can lead to tooth pain, infection, and tooth loss. Poor oral health can make chewing difficult and reduce food intake; severe dental infections can sometimes spread beyond the mouth.

topics.name: Common Liver Fluke Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Fascioliasis is infection by liver flukes acquired by eating contaminated watercress or other aquatic plants. As the flukes move through the liver, they can cause fever, abdominal pain, an enlarged liver, and increased eosinophils. Adult flukes in the bile ducts may cause recurrent pain, inflammation or blockage of the ducts, jaundice, or pancreatitis.

topics.name: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID)
topics.clinical_significance: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is an antibody deficiency with low IgG and low IgA, IgM, or both, and a weak response to vaccines. It causes recurrent sinus and lung infections and may lead to bronchiectasis. Autoimmune disease, intestinal problems, and an increased risk of lymphoma or stomach cancer can also occur.

topics.name: Common Viral Infections in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: This topic covers several distinct viral illnesses in children, including measles, mumps, rubella, roseola, and parvovirus B19 infection. They can cause fever and rash, but some also lead to serious complications. Rubella or parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy can harm the fetus.

topics.name: Communication Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Communication disorders affect a child's voice, hearing, speech, language, or a combination of these. They can interfere with learning and social relationships. Delays or loss of communication skills may also point to an underlying hearing, developmental, or neurologic condition.

topics.name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Community-acquired pneumonia is an infection of the lungs acquired outside a hospital, caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. It commonly causes cough, fever, phlegm, shortness of breath, and chest pain; diagnosis uses clinical findings and chest imaging. It can be mild or life-threatening, with greater danger for older adults and people who are already ill.

topics.name: Community-Based Adult Day Services
topics.clinical_significance: Community-based adult day services provide older adults with daytime medical, rehabilitation, cognitive, and social support, often with meals and transportation. They can give caregivers respite, help maintain daily function, and reduce isolation; some programs may delay or prevent nursing-home placement.

topics.name: Compartment Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Compartment syndrome is dangerous pressure in a closed muscle space that reduces blood flow. Worsening pain out of proportion to the injury, often increased by passive muscle stretch, is usually the earliest sign; numbness, weakness, pallor, or loss of pulse may develop later. Without urgent pressure relief, it can cause permanent muscle and nerve damage, limb loss, or death.

topics.name: Complement System
topics.clinical_significance: The complement system is a group of proteins in blood and on cell surfaces that work in a cascade to support immune defense. It coats microbes so immune cells can engulf them, promotes inflammation, helps remove immune complexes, and can form pores that kill susceptible microbes. Defects can cause recurrent infections and are linked to lupus and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.

topics.name: Complementary and Alternative Medicine, Types of
topics.clinical_significance: Complementary and alternative therapies are grouped into five types: whole medical systems, mind-body methods, biologically based practices, body-based practices, and energy medicine. Evidence and risks vary by therapy; some mind-body methods are used in standard care, while cupping, scraping, and moxibustion can leave marks that may be mistaken for injuries.

topics.name: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
topics.clinical_significance: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) causes regional nerve pain that is more severe and lasts longer than expected after tissue damage, often following an injury. It may also cause changes in skin color or temperature, sweating, swelling, touch sensitivity, weakness, stiffness, and changes in skin, hair, or nails. These problems can limit use of the limb and lead to lasting stiffness or contractures.

topics.name: Complications of Acute Coronary Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Acute coronary syndromes can cause dangerous problems with the heart's rhythm, electrical conduction, or pumping. Complications include heart failure or shock, damage or rupture of heart structures, recurrent loss of blood flow, clots inside the heart, and inflammation around the heart. These problems can cause severe illness or sudden death.

topics.name: Complications of Diabetes in Children and Adolescents
