topics.clinical_significance: Children and adolescents with diabetes can develop severe low blood sugar, diabetic ketoacidosis, or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state; these emergencies can cause seizures, brain injury, coma, or death. Over time, diabetes can damage the kidneys, eyes, nerves, and blood vessels, especially when glucose remains poorly controlled. Mental health problems and other autoimmune or metabolic disorders can also occur.

topics.name: Complications of Transfusion
topics.clinical_significance: Transfusion reactions range from mild fever or itching to life-threatening problems. Major complications include destruction of red blood cells, acute lung injury, fluid overload that strains the heart, severe allergy, and graft-versus-host disease; these can cause shock, kidney failure, or death. Bacterial contamination can cause sepsis, and infections may rarely be transmitted. Reactions may occur during transfusion or days to weeks later, causing fever, breathing problems, jaundice, falling hemoglobin, or low platelets. Large-volume transfusion can also impair clotting and disturb body temperature and electrolytes.

topics.name: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: A structured review of an older adult’s physical health, ability to manage daily tasks, memory and thinking, mood, medicines, and social and home environment. It can reveal health problems and barriers to independence that a routine examination may miss. The findings guide an individualized care plan and help the care team track changes over time.

topics.name: Compressive Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure on the optic nerve damages it and usually causes slowly worsening, painless vision loss, often in one eye. A mass near the pituitary gland can press on crossing nerve fibers and reduce outer vision in both eyes. Tumors are common causes, but inflammation and thyroid eye disease can also compress the nerve. Continued pressure may cause permanent vision loss, so identifying the cause is important because treatment may preserve or improve sight.

topics.name: Computed Tomography (CT)
topics.clinical_significance: Computed tomography (CT) uses x-rays taken from many angles to create detailed cross-sectional images, which can also be combined into 3D views. It is fast and helps find problems such as bleeding, fractures, kidney stones, tumors, infection, and blocked blood vessels. Some scans use contrast dye to make soft tissues and blood vessels easier to see; the dye can cause reactions in some people. CT exposes the body to ionizing radiation, so its risks are weighed against the benefit of the scan.

topics.name: Computed Tomography in Neurologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Neurologic CT provides fast, noninvasive images of the brain and skull. A scan without contrast can quickly detect bleeding and major structural changes, including after injury. IV contrast can help show tumors, abscesses, and blood-vessel problems; CT angiography is used when stroke is suspected. CT shows skull bone well, while MRI often gives more detail about brain and spinal cord tissue. Contrast can cause allergic reactions or kidney injury.

topics.name: Concepts in Pharmacotherapy
topics.clinical_significance: A medicine’s benefit and safety depend on the condition being treated and on the drug’s properties, including how well it works, its side effects, how it is given and cleared, and how often it is taken. A person’s age, other illnesses and medicines, pregnancy, and sometimes weight or genes can also affect the choice and response. Medication errors and drug interactions may reduce benefit or cause harm.

topics.name: Concussion, Sports-Related
topics.clinical_significance: A sports-related concussion is a mild brain injury that temporarily disrupts brain function. It can cause headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, or loss of consciousness, even when imaging shows no clear structural injury. Symptoms may last for days or weeks and sometimes longer. A repeat head injury before recovery can cause further harm, so return to sport is gradual after symptoms have resolved.

topics.name: Conduct Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Conduct disorder is a persistent pattern in a child or adolescent of aggression, property damage, lying or stealing, or serious rule-breaking that violates others’ rights and disrupts school, family, or social life. It is linked with other mental health and substance-use problems, and suicidal thoughts may occur. In some people, serious behavior continues into adulthood and may meet criteria for antisocial personality disorder.

topics.name: Condylomata Acuminata
topics.clinical_significance: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) are benign growths on or around the genitals or anus, usually caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 or 11. They may be painless or itchy and can enlarge, spread, or return after treatment. The HPV types that usually cause visible warts differ from the types that cause most HPV-related cancers.

topics.name: Confidentiality and HIPAA
topics.clinical_significance: In the United States, HIPAA sets rules to protect identifiable health information. It limits how health records may be used or shared, requires safeguards for electronic records, and gives patients rights to see and request corrections to their records. Necessary information may be shared for treatment, and some disclosures are required by law, so confidentiality is protected but not absolute. Improper disclosure can trigger breach reporting and penalties.

topics.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Caused by 11Beta-Hydroxylase Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited enzyme defect limits cortisol production and causes excess adrenal androgens and buildup of a salt-retaining hormone precursor. It can cause virilization or early puberty and often high blood pressure, sometimes with low blood potassium. Newborn girls may have atypical external genitalia, while boys may look typical at birth. Unlike the common 21-hydroxylase form, salt-wasting is not typical.

topics.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Caused by 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited enzyme deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. It lowers cortisol and may lower aldosterone, while increasing adrenal androgens. Severe forms can cause salt loss, dehydration, low blood pressure, and high blood potassium, leading to a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Androgen excess can cause atypical external genitalia in newborn girls or early puberty and rapid growth; milder forms may appear later with acne or excess hair.

topics.name: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a group of inherited enzyme disorders that reduce production of cortisol, aldosterone, or both. In the common forms, hormone precursors build up and are diverted into androgen production, which can cause excess masculinizing hormones and atypical genital development. Severe cortisol or aldosterone deficiency can cause salt loss and a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Rarer forms can also reduce androgen production.

topics.name: Congenital and Perinatal Cytomegalovirus Infection (CMV)
topics.clinical_significance: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common congenital viral infection. Many infected newborns have no signs at birth, but infection before birth can affect the brain, liver, eyes, and inner ear; hearing loss may appear later or worsen over time. Signs can include a small head, jaundice, skin spots, and an enlarged liver or spleen. Infection acquired around birth is usually mild in term infants but can be severe in premature infants.

topics.name: Congenital Cardiac Anomalies, Other
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes less common congenital heart problems, such as blocked or narrowed valves, a heart with only one working ventricle, and congenital heart block. Depending on the defect, blood flow to the lungs or body may be reduced, or the heartbeat may be too slow. Severe defects can cause blue skin, heart failure, or poor oxygen delivery and may need treatment soon after birth.

topics.name: Congenital Cardiovascular Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital cardiovascular anomalies are structural differences of the heart or major blood vessels that are present at birth. Some create abnormal openings or block blood flow. They may cause no symptoms or only a heart murmur, while severe defects can lower blood oxygen, cause heart failure, or lead to circulatory collapse, sometimes in the first days of life.

topics.name: Congenital Cardiovascular Anomalies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital heart disease affects nearly 1% of live births and is a leading cause of death from birth defects in infancy. Defects may cause abnormal blood flow or blockage; effects range from an incidental murmur to low blood oxygen, heart failure, or shock. Some critical defects have few early signs, so newborn screening and early diagnosis are important.

topics.name: Congenital Cataract
topics.clinical_significance: A lens opacity present at birth or soon after can block clear images during early visual development, causing amblyopia and lasting vision loss, especially when one eye is affected. Some cataracts occur alone; others are linked to inherited or chromosomal disorders, metabolic disease, or infection during pregnancy. Dense cataracts may need early removal and visual correction to support normal sight development.

topics.name: Congenital Craniofacial and Musculoskeletal Abnormalities, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital musculoskeletal abnormalities are differences in the muscles, soft tissues, or bones that arise from unusual development or positioning before birth. They may affect one body part or occur as part of a syndrome involving other organs. Looking for additional birth defects or developmental delays can help identify an underlying condition that affects prognosis and family counseling.

topics.name: Congenital Craniofacial Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital craniofacial anomalies are differences in the skull, facial bones, or soft tissues caused by abnormal development or positioning. Some are isolated or improve on their own; others are part of a genetic syndrome and can affect feeding, breathing, hearing, vision, or development. Identifying associated defects and an underlying syndrome helps guide care, prognosis, and family counseling.

topics.name: Congenital Ear Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: A congenital ear anomaly is an ear or ear canal that is absent, misshapen, or underdeveloped. Microtia or a closed ear canal may block sound and cause conductive hearing loss, which can affect speech and learning. Some findings, such as low-set ears or ear pits, may occur with a genetic syndrome or other birth defects, including kidney problems.

topics.name: Congenital Eye Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital eye anomalies are differences in eye size, structure, or spacing present at birth, including a small or absent eye and coloboma. They may impair vision or lead to problems such as amblyopia or glaucoma. Some occur with brain, craniofacial, or other birth defects as part of a genetic syndrome, so associated findings matter for prognosis and care.

topics.name: Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital gastrointestinal anomalies are structural defects of the digestive tract or abdominal wall that are present at birth. Many block the passage of food or stool, causing feeding problems, vomiting, abdominal swelling, or failure to pass stool in the first days of life. A diaphragmatic hernia can also impair lung development and breathing. Some anomalies occur with defects in other organs.

topics.name: Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Many congenital gastrointestinal defects block the digestive tract, causing feeding difficulty, vomiting, abdominal swelling, and failure to pass stool in the first days of life. Obstruction can lead to dehydration, aspiration of vomit, or breathing problems and may require urgent surgery. A congenital diaphragmatic hernia can limit lung development, and other organ defects often occur at the same time.

topics.name: Congenital Genitourinary Anomalies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital genitourinary anomalies are birth defects of the kidneys, urinary tract, or reproductive organs. Urinary defects can cause blockage or backflow of urine, repeated infections, kidney stones, or impaired kidney function. Genital defects can affect urination, sexual function, or fertility. Some are found before birth, while others appear later; many require surgery.

topics.name: Congenital Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital glaucoma (primary infantile glaucoma) is a rare defect in the eye’s drainage system that raises pressure inside the eye. The pressure can enlarge the infant’s eye, cloud the cornea, and damage the optic nerve, causing lasting vision loss or blindness if untreated. Tearing, light sensitivity, and frequent blinking may occur. Early surgery can help protect vision.

topics.name: Congenital Goiter
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital goiter is enlargement of the thyroid gland present at birth; it may be diffuse or nodular. Thyroid hormone levels can be low, normal, or high, so the size of the gland alone does not show how well it functions. A large goiter can press on the windpipe or esophagus and interfere with breathing or swallowing.

topics.name: Congenital Hydrocephalus
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital hydrocephalus is excess cerebrospinal fluid that enlarges the brain’s fluid-filled spaces (ventricles) and may raise pressure inside the skull. In infants, it can cause an enlarging head, a bulging soft spot, vomiting, irritability, or sleepiness. Ongoing pressure can harm vision and brain function. Mild cases may be monitored; progressive cases may need surgery to redirect or drain the fluid.

topics.name: Congenital Jaw Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital jaw anomalies are jaws that are missing, misshapen, or underdeveloped. Depending on the type and severity, they can cause airway blockage, feeding problems, hearing loss, poor bite, or facial asymmetry. They may occur with other birth defects or genetic syndromes, so evaluation can help identify related conditions and guide care.

topics.name: Congenital Knee Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital knee dislocation is present at birth and may leave the leg held straight and hard to bend. The rare form with the knee forced backward needs emergency assessment because it can reduce blood flow to the leg. A hip dislocation or an underlying condition, such as Larsen syndrome or arthrogryposis, may also be present. Early gentle bending exercises and a flexed splint often help an otherwise healthy infant develop a functional knee.

topics.name: Congenital Limb Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital limb anomalies are missing, incomplete, extra, or abnormally formed arms, legs, fingers, or toes present at birth. They can affect movement and daily function, and some occur with genetic syndromes or problems in other organs. Identifying associated conditions helps guide care; surgery or prostheses can improve function for some children.

topics.name: Congenital Megacolon
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) occurs when part of the lower bowel lacks the nerve cells needed to move stool. Stool builds up, causing blockage and enlargement of the bowel above the affected part. Newborns may not pass their first stool on time and can develop abdominal swelling or vomiting; older children may have severe constipation. Without timely treatment, serious bowel inflammation and infection can occur. Surgery is usually needed.

topics.name: Congenital Muscular Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital muscular anomalies are muscles that are missing or underdeveloped from birth. They may occur alone or as part of a syndrome. A missing chest muscle may occur with hand, breast, or nipple differences; missing abdominal muscles may occur with serious urinary tract problems and undescended testes in boys. Checking for related problems helps guide care. Treatment ranges from minimal intervention to reconstructive surgery.

topics.name: Congenital Musculoskeletal Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital musculoskeletal anomalies are differences in how bones, muscles, or soft tissues develop or take shape. They may affect one area or occur with other birth defects or developmental delays as part of a syndrome. Identifying related conditions and the cause can help guide treatment, prognosis, and family counseling.

topics.name: Congenital Musculoskeletal Anomalies, Overview of
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital musculoskeletal differences may be deformations caused by pressure or position, or malformations caused by abnormal development. Some improve on their own, while others need treatment. Because they can be part of a syndrome and occur with other birth defects or developmental delays, evaluation can help identify the cause, guide care, and inform prognosis and family counseling.

topics.name: Congenital Myopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital myopathies are inherited muscle disorders that usually cause low muscle tone and weakness from birth or infancy. Severity varies: weakness may remain stable or progress slowly, delay motor skills, and, in severe forms, weaken the breathing muscles. Some types increase the risk of a dangerous reaction to certain anesthetics called malignant hyperthermia. Supportive care, including physical therapy, can help preserve function.

topics.name: Congenital Neck and Back Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital neck and back problems may involve soft tissues or abnormal vertebrae. A neck muscle injury around birth can tilt the head and flatten one side of the skull. Vertebral defects can cause a spinal curve that worsens during growth and may occur with kidney or other birth defects. Rare neck spine abnormalities can injure the spinal cord. Imaging and follow-up help find related problems; a worsening curve may need bracing or surgery.

topics.name: Congenital Nephrotic Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital nephrotic syndromes are rare inherited kidney-filter disorders that begin in the first year of life. They cause protein loss in urine, low blood protein, and swelling. Severe forms can lead to poor growth and early kidney failure. Early diagnosis guides intensive treatment; some infants need dialysis or a kidney transplant.

topics.name: Congenital Neurologic Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital neurologic anomalies are problems in the development of the brain or spinal cord. Their effects range from none to severe or life-threatening and may include problems with movement, learning, or seizures. Prenatal imaging can detect many major defects, and diagnosis helps guide care and genetic counseling. Taking folate before and early in pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects.

topics.name: Congenital Neurologic Anomalies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital brain anomalies range from harmless to life-threatening and may cause problems with movement, learning, or seizures. Some develop when the neural tube does not close properly; others result from abnormal brain development. Prenatal ultrasound, sometimes followed by fetal MRI, can detect many major defects. Genetic counseling can help explain possible causes and recurrence risk. Folate before and early in pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects.

topics.name: Congenital Renal and Genitourinary Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital renal and genitourinary anomalies affect the kidneys, urinary tract, or reproductive organs. Urinary tract defects can block urine flow or cause urine to remain in the tract, raising the risk of infection, stones, and kidney damage. Genital differences may affect urination, sexual function, or fertility. Many are found before birth, and some require surgery.

topics.name: Congenital Renal Cystic Dysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital renal cystic dysplasia is abnormal development of one or both kidneys, sometimes with cysts or blocked urine drainage. It may occur alone or with other urinary tract or body abnormalities. Kidney function depends on how much healthy tissue remains; some children develop kidney failure. The condition is often found by ultrasound before birth or in early childhood.

topics.name: Congenital Renal Transport Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital renal transport abnormalities affect how kidney tubules handle salts and other substances; many are inherited. Depending on the defect, they can cause electrolyte problems and muscle weakness, cystine kidney stones, or weak bones and poor growth from phosphate loss. Early diagnosis helps guide treatment and reduce complications.

topics.name: Congenital Rubella
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital rubella occurs when rubella infects a fetus during pregnancy; infection in the first 12 weeks carries the greatest risk of developmental problems. It can cause fetal death, poor growth, cataracts, hearing loss, heart defects, and brain problems. Hearing, learning, or hormone problems may appear later, so affected children need ongoing follow-up. Vaccination before pregnancy helps prevent infection.

topics.name: Congenital Syphilis
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital syphilis occurs when the bacterium Treponema pallidum passes from a pregnant person to the fetus. An infected infant may look well at birth, then develop a rash, enlarged liver or spleen, bone disease, or nervous system problems. Later effects can include hearing loss, vision problems, and dental changes. Untreated infection can cause fetal or newborn death. Testing during pregnancy and penicillin treatment help prevent or treat the infection.

topics.name: Congenital Toxoplasmosis
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when the parasite Toxoplasma gondii passes from a pregnant person to the fetus. Infection early in pregnancy is less often passed on but can cause more severe disease. Many infants look well at birth, yet eye or brain problems may appear later, including eye inflammation, excess fluid or calcium deposits in the brain, and seizures. Severe cases can cause poor growth or early death, so ongoing eye and developmental follow-up is important.

topics.name: Congenitally Corrected Transposition of the Great Arteries
topics.clinical_significance: In congenitally corrected transposition, the heart’s lower chambers and the large arteries are connected in an unusual way, but blood still flows to the lungs and body in the correct order. Other heart defects are common, and the right ventricle must pump blood to the body; it may weaken over time. Depending on associated defects, infants may have blue skin, heart failure, or a slow heartbeat. Ongoing cardiology care is important.

topics.name: Congestive Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Congestive heart failure means the heart cannot fill or pump well enough to meet the body’s needs. Blood and fluid can back up into the lungs and tissues, causing breathlessness, fatigue, or swelling; reduced blood flow can also affect organs. It can worsen suddenly and needs prompt care. In some forms, the heart’s measured pumping strength remains normal.

topics.name: Congestive Hepatopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Congestive hepatopathy is blood backing up in the liver, usually because of right-sided heart failure. It often causes no symptoms, but may lead to a tender, enlarged liver, upper-right belly pain, jaundice, or fluid in the abdomen. Long-lasting severe congestion can scar the liver and progress to cirrhosis. It often reflects the severity of heart failure, so treatment focuses on the heart condition.

topics.name: Conjugate Gaze Palsies
topics.clinical_significance: Conjugate gaze palsy means both eyes cannot move together in one direction, most often side to side. It can signal damage to brain pathways, commonly from a stroke; tumors and progressive supranuclear palsy are other causes. Because some causes are serious, prompt assessment and treatment of the underlying condition are important.

topics.name: Conjunctival and Scleral Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect the conjunctiva, the clear lining over the eyelids and white of the eye, or the sclera, the eye’s tough white outer layer. Many cause redness, irritation, or discharge from infection or inflammation. Some, especially scleritis, can damage the eye and threaten vision, so accurate diagnosis is important.

topics.name: Conjunctival and Scleral Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The conjunctiva protects the eye and helps keep its surface moist; the sclera supports and protects the eyeball. Infection, allergy, irritation, or immune disease can inflame these tissues and cause similar redness or discharge, so symptoms alone may not show the cause. Episcleritis usually does not threaten sight, but scleritis can cause lasting eye damage and vision loss.

topics.name: Conjunctivitis, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal conjunctivitis is redness and watery or pus-like discharge from a newborn’s eye, caused by infection or chemical irritation from eye drops given at birth. Some infections pass from a pregnant person during delivery. Gonorrhea can quickly damage the cornea and cause blindness; chlamydia may also cause pneumonia, and herpes can spread beyond the eye. Prompt testing matters because treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Conjunctivitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Conjunctivitis causes eye redness and discharge, sometimes with itching, burning, or tearing. It may be caused by a contagious infection, allergy, or irritation, and treatment depends on the cause. Marked eye pain, sensitivity to light, or reduced vision is unusual in simple conjunctivitis and may signal a more serious eye problem.

topics.name: Conn Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Conn syndrome (primary aldosteronism) occurs when one or both adrenal glands make too much aldosterone. The hormone makes the kidneys retain salt and water and lose potassium, often causing high blood pressure that may be hard to control. Low potassium can cause weakness or cramps, but potassium levels may also be normal. Treatment depends on the cause: an adrenal growth may be removed, while overactivity in both glands is treated with aldosterone-blocking medicine.

topics.name: Connective Tissue Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Connective tissue disorders affect the body’s supporting tissues, including skin, joints, bones, and tissues around organs. Some are inherited and may affect several parts of the body; others develop from abnormal movement or overuse. Effects vary, and some problems that begin in childhood continue throughout life, so identifying the specific disorder helps guide care.

topics.name: Connective Tissue Disorders in Children, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Connective tissue forms the body’s supporting framework and helps protect organs. Disorders may be inherited, have no known cause, or develop from abnormal movement and overuse. They can affect bones, joints, skin, tendons, or other organs, so effects and care depend on the specific disorder.

topics.name: Consent and Surrogate Decision Making
topics.clinical_significance: Consent is a patient’s informed agreement to medical care. If an adult cannot make a decision, an authorized surrogate should follow the patient’s known wishes and values or, when these are not known, the patient’s best interests. A parent or guardian usually makes decisions for a child, with exceptions that vary by location. In an emergency, necessary care may proceed under presumed consent when the patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available; legal rules vary.

topics.name: Constipation
topics.clinical_significance: Constipation means hard or infrequent stools, difficulty passing stool, or a feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully. Bowel frequency varies, so less than one movement a day is not necessarily abnormal. Constipation may result from medicines or bowel, metabolic, or neurologic disorders; severe or ongoing cases can lead to fecal impaction.

topics.name: Constipation in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Constipation in children is usually functional, often because a child avoids passing stool after a painful bowel movement. Retained stool can become harder and stretch the rectum, worsening constipation; it may also cause anal fissures or stool leakage around an impaction. Constipation from birth or delayed passage of the first stool can point to an underlying disorder.

topics.name: Consumption Coagulopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Consumption coagulopathy, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), is widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting proteins. Tiny clots can block blood vessels and damage organs, while the loss of these clotting components can cause serious bleeding. Rapid DIC tends to cause bleeding and organ damage; slower DIC more often causes blood clots. It usually develops as a complication of another serious condition, such as infection, cancer, or an obstetric emergency.

topics.name: Contact Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Contact dermatitis is skin inflammation caused by direct contact with an irritant or an allergy-triggering substance. The rash appears where the skin touched the cause and may be itchy or painful, red, swollen, scaly, or blistered. The rash pattern can help identify the exposure.

topics.name: Contact Lenses
topics.clinical_significance: Contact lenses correct refractive errors such as nearsightedness, farsightedness, and astigmatism; some types also improve vision with an irregular cornea. Poor hygiene or wearing lenses overnight increases the risk of corneal infection, which can threaten vision. Contact lenses provide less protection from eye injuries than glasses.

topics.name: Continuous Hemofiltration and Hemodialysis
topics.clinical_significance: Continuous hemofiltration and hemodialysis remove excess fluid and waste products from the blood over time. They are used mainly for people with acute kidney injury who have unstable blood pressure or need large amounts of fluid removed. The slower removal can reduce sudden blood pressure drops compared with standard intermittent hemodialysis.

topics.name: Contraception and Pregnancy in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: When contraception is not used consistently, adolescents are at risk of unintended pregnancy; condoms also reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Pregnancy during adolescence is linked to less prenatal care and higher risks of anemia, preterm birth, and preeclampsia, as well as low birth weight in the baby. It can also affect emotional well-being, education, and finances.

topics.name: Contraception, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Contraception includes reversible methods and permanent procedures used to prevent pregnancy. How well a method works depends on the method and how consistently it is used. Condoms also reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections, including HIV; most other contraceptive methods do not. Emergency contraception may reduce the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex.

topics.name: Contrast Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Contrast nephropathy, now usually called contrast-induced acute kidney injury, is sudden kidney damage caused by iodinated contrast. A kidney injury that occurs after contrast exposure is called contrast-associated acute kidney injury; timing alone does not prove that contrast caused it. Most cases improve, but preexisting chronic kidney disease and other health problems raise the risk.

topics.name: Conventional Radiography
topics.clinical_significance: Conventional radiography uses X-rays to make images of the body. It is commonly used to detect fractures, lung disease, and some abdominal problems. It is widely available, but image detail is limited compared with CT or MRI, and it uses ionizing radiation.

topics.name: Conversion Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Older name for functional neurological symptom disorder (FND), which causes real, involuntary movement or sensory symptoms that do not fit recognized neurologic patterns. See Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder.

topics.name: COPD Exacerbation, Treatment
topics.clinical_significance: An acute COPD flare-up is a sudden worsening of breathing symptoms that can cause low blood oxygen, carbon dioxide buildup, or respiratory failure. Treatment aims to open the airways and keep oxygen and blood acidity at safe levels. It may include inhaled medicines that widen the airways, corticosteroids, antibiotics when bacterial infection is likely, and oxygen or breathing support for severe cases.

topics.name: COPD, Treatment of Stable
topics.clinical_significance: Treatment of stable COPD aims to ease symptoms, maintain physical function, and prevent flare-ups. It includes smoking cessation, inhaled medicines that open the airways, and pulmonary rehabilitation. Long-term oxygen and other medicines are used for selected patients; surgery may help some people with severe disease.

topics.name: Copper Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Copper deficiency may be acquired or inherited. Acquired deficiency can cause anemia that does not improve with iron, low neutrophil counts, and nerve or spinal cord damage that may resemble vitamin B12 deficiency. Causes include malabsorption, gastrointestinal surgery, and excessive zinc intake; inherited deficiency in infants is called Menkes syndrome and can cause severe developmental and bone problems.

topics.name: Copper Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Excess copper can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Large exposures may destroy red blood cells and damage the kidneys or liver, sometimes causing life-threatening illness. Copper can also build up in Wilson disease, an inherited disorder.

topics.name: Corkscrew Esophagus
topics.clinical_significance: Corkscrew esophagus is another name for distal esophageal spasm, in which the esophagus contracts abnormally. It can cause intermittent chest pain or trouble swallowing liquids and solids; the chest pain may resemble a heart attack, so heart disease must be excluded. A barium swallow may show the twisted pattern, while esophageal manometry gives a more specific diagnosis.

topics.name: Corneal Abrasions and Corneal Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: A corneal abrasion is a scratch on the clear front surface of the eye; a foreign body can cause one. These injuries often cause pain, a gritty feeling, tearing, and redness, and central abrasions can blur vision. Contact lens use, contaminated material, or an unrecognized penetrating injury raises the risk of serious infection and vision loss.

topics.name: Corneal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Corneal disorders affect the clear front surface of the eye and can cause one-sided pain, light sensitivity, a feeling that something is in the eye, or blurred vision. These symptoms can help distinguish corneal disease from simple conjunctivitis. Some conditions, such as corneal ulcers, can damage sight.

topics.name: Corneal Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in one eye, light sensitivity, a foreign-body feeling, or reduced vision can point to corneal disease, including keratitis or an ulcer. Fluorescein staining and slit-lamp examination help identify corneal damage; infection can threaten vision.

topics.name: Corneal Graft
topics.clinical_significance: A corneal graft is donor tissue used to replace a damaged or diseased cornea. Transplantation can restore corneal structure, relieve severe pain, or improve vision; possible complications include rejection, infection, and graft failure. See Corneal Transplantation.

topics.name: Corneal Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: Corneal transplantation replaces damaged corneal tissue with donor tissue, either in part or through the full thickness. It can improve vision when the cornea is scarred or cloudy, repair a perforation, or treat severe disease. Complications include infection, graft rejection, glaucoma, and graft failure; vision may take months to improve.

topics.name: Corneal Ulcer
topics.clinical_significance: A corneal ulcer is an open defect in the corneal surface with inflammation beneath it, usually caused by infection. Injury, contact lens use, severe dryness, poor eyelid closure, or vitamin A deficiency can also contribute. It may cause pain, redness, tearing, light sensitivity, or blurred vision; scarring can reduce sight, and a deep ulcer can perforate the eye.

topics.name: Cornification Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Cornification disorders affect how the skin’s outer layer forms or sheds, often causing thick, dry, or scaly skin. They include inherited and acquired conditions; some may be linked to an underlying illness or affect other organs.

topics.name: Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)
topics.clinical_significance: Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) uses a blood vessel graft to route blood around severely narrowed or blocked coronary arteries, restoring blood flow to heart muscle. It is used when stenting is unsuitable for the coronary disease. Possible complications include bleeding, stroke, heart attack, abnormal heart rhythms, and infection.

topics.name: Coronary Artery Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is reduced blood flow through the heart’s arteries, usually from atherosclerotic plaque; coronary spasm and small-vessel disease are less common causes. It may cause no symptoms, stable chest pain (angina), an acute coronary syndrome such as a heart attack, or sudden cardiac death.

topics.name: Coronary Artery Disease, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Coronary artery disease is reduced blood flow through the heart’s arteries, usually because fatty plaques narrow them; coronary spasm or small-vessel disease can also impair flow. It may be silent or cause stable angina, an acute coronary syndrome such as a heart attack, or sudden cardiac death. Major risk factors include smoking, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease.

topics.name: Coronary Syndromes, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Treatment of acute coronary syndromes aims to prevent further clots, restore blood flow, ease chest pain, and limit heart damage. It commonly uses antiplatelet and anticoagulant medicines; beta-blockers, nitrates, and statins may also be used. The drug plan depends on the type of syndrome and whether a procedure to reopen the artery is planned. Clot-dissolving drugs are used only for selected ST-elevation heart attacks when timely angioplasty is not available.

topics.name: Coronaviruses and Acute Respiratory Syndromes (MERS and SARS)
topics.clinical_significance: Coronaviruses cause illnesses ranging from common colds to severe pneumonia. MERS and SARS are distinct coronavirus infections that can cause respiratory failure and death; MERS spreads from camels to people and sometimes between people, while the 2002–2004 SARS outbreak was caused by SARS-CoV-1. SARS-CoV-2 is a different virus that causes COVID-19.

topics.name: Coryza
topics.clinical_significance: Coryza is inflammation of the lining of the nose that causes a runny or blocked nose. It commonly occurs with a viral upper respiratory infection, such as the common cold.

topics.name: Cough in Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Cough is a protective reflex that clears irritants and secretions from the airways, but a persistent or severe cough can disrupt daily life and signal disease. Common causes vary with duration and include respiratory infections, asthma, COPD, reflux, postnasal drip, and some medicines. Coughing up blood, shortness of breath, persistent fever, or weight loss can be warning signs of a serious cause.

topics.name: Cough in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Cough is a protective reflex that clears secretions and helps prevent objects from entering the airways, but it can also signal disease. In children, acute cough most often comes from a viral upper respiratory infection; cough lasting more than 4 weeks is chronic and commonly linked to asthma, reflux, or postnasal drip. A sudden cough may mean a child inhaled a foreign object, while breathing distress, blue lips or skin, stridor, or a very ill appearance are concerning signs.

topics.name: COVID-19
topics.clinical_significance: COVID-19 is a contagious illness caused by SARS-CoV-2. It may cause no symptoms or a mild respiratory illness, but can progress to pneumonia, low blood oxygen, respiratory failure, or death; it can also affect other organs. Older adults and people with weakened immunity or chronic illnesses are at higher risk of severe disease, and some people have symptoms that last for months after the infection.

topics.name: COVID-19 During Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: COVID-19 during pregnancy can increase the risk of severe illness, especially in people with other health problems, although severe illness remains uncommon overall. Moderate or severe infection is linked to higher risks of preterm birth, preeclampsia, cesarean birth, and stillbirth. Transmission of the virus to the fetus appears uncommon.

topics.name: COVID-19 Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: COVID-19 vaccines train the immune system to recognize SARS-CoV-2 and reduce the risk of severe illness and death. They do not prevent every infection. Soreness, fatigue, headache, or fever may occur for a few days; severe allergic reactions are rare.

topics.name: COVID-Related Neuropsychiatric Manifestations
topics.clinical_significance: COVID-19 can affect the brain and nerves during the illness or recovery. Severe illness may cause delirium or complications such as stroke or brain injury from low oxygen. After infection, some people have lasting problems with memory or concentration, sleep, mood, fatigue, or smell and taste that can interfere with daily life. New symptoms need evaluation for other possible causes.

topics.name: Crack Cocaine
topics.clinical_significance: Crack is a fast-acting form of cocaine that is smoked and can lead to dependence. High doses can cause dangerous heart rhythms, heart attack, stroke, seizures, overheating, severe agitation, or psychosis. Smoking cocaine can also injure the lungs and, in rare cases, cause breathing failure.

topics.name: Cranberry
topics.clinical_significance: Cranberry products may modestly reduce the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections in some people, but evidence varies and they do not treat an active infection. Cranberry may interact with warfarin, and sweetened juice can add substantial sugar.

topics.name: Cranial Arteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Giant cell arteritis is inflammation of large arteries, often involving branches of the carotid arteries in adults over 50. It can cause a new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain while chewing, or vision changes. Reduced blood flow to the eye can cause permanent blindness, so suspected disease needs prompt treatment. It is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

topics.name: Craniocervical Junction Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: These congenital or acquired problems where the skull meets the upper spine can narrow the space around the lower brain stem or upper spinal cord. They may cause neck or back-of-head pain, weakness, numbness, poor coordination, or other nerve problems. Sudden or worsening neurologic symptoms may signal compression and need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Craniosynostosis
topics.clinical_significance: Craniosynostosis occurs when one or more skull sutures close too early, restricting normal skull growth and changing head shape. Some children also have a genetic syndrome or learning and developmental difficulties, so specialist assessment is important. Surgery may be needed to correct the skull shape and support growth.

topics.name: Craniotubular Dysplasias
topics.clinical_significance: Craniotubular dysplasias are a group of rare inherited bone disorders that cause mild increases in bone density while bone shape remains mostly normal. Effects vary by type: skull and facial bone overgrowth can trap nerves and cause hearing loss or facial weakness, while other forms may cause limb deformity or bone fragility. Some people have few symptoms.

topics.name: Craniotubular Hyperostoses
topics.clinical_significance: Craniotubular hyperostoses are rare inherited bone disorders that cause excess bone growth and increased bone density. Depending on the type, they can cause bone pain or weakness, changes in the face, or trapped cranial nerves leading to hearing loss or facial weakness. Severe skull involvement may raise pressure around the brain, but some people have few symptoms.

topics.name: Creatine
topics.clinical_significance: Creatine is stored in muscle as phosphocreatine, which helps rapidly restore energy during short, intense muscle activity. Supplements may modestly improve high-intensity performance and muscle mass, but can cause weight gain and raise blood creatinine without necessarily indicating kidney damage.

topics.name: Creeping Eruption
topics.clinical_significance: Creeping eruption is a skin infection caused by animal hookworm larvae entering skin after contact with contaminated soil or sand. It causes a very itchy, winding rash; scratching can lead to a bacterial skin infection. The larvae usually cannot mature in people, and treatment can relieve itching and reduce the risk of infection from scratching.

topics.name: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD)
topics.clinical_significance: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare prion disease that causes rapidly worsening memory and thinking, often with muscle jerks and loss of coordination. It progresses quickly and is usually fatal within months; care is supportive because there is no curative treatment.

topics.name: Critical Care Patient, Monitoring and Testing
topics.clinical_significance: In critically ill patients, repeated or continuous checks of vital signs, oxygen level, heart rhythm, fluid balance, and selected blood tests help detect changes and guide treatment. The type and frequency of monitoring depend on the patient’s condition; invasive monitors can have complications, so their results must be interpreted in context.

topics.name: Critical Care Scoring Systems
topics.clinical_significance: Critical care scores combine measures such as vital signs, organ function, age, and prior health to estimate illness severity and survival. They are only moderately accurate for an individual patient, so they should not be used alone to predict that person’s outcome. Their main value is comparing groups of patients and assessing quality of care.

topics.name: Critically Ill Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Critically ill patients need rapid assessment and care in an intensive care unit. Treatment supports breathing and heart function, closely monitors vital signs, treats the underlying illness, and helps prevent complications such as infection, blood clots, and pressure sores. Pain relief, nutrition, and clear communication with the patient and family are also part of care.

topics.name: Critically Ill Patient, Introduction to Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Critical care is specialist hospital care for people who are seriously ill. In an intensive care unit, the team closely monitors patients, supports breathing and heart function, treats pain, and provides nutrition. Care also aims to prevent complications such as infection, blood clots, stomach ulcers, and pressure sores, while easing suffering and communicating with families.

topics.name: Crohn Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Crohn disease is a long-term, relapsing inflammation that can affect any part of the digestive tract, most often the lower small intestine or colon. It causes episodes of diarrhea and abdominal pain; inflammation through the bowel wall can lead to narrowing or blockage, abscesses, or abnormal tunnels called fistulas. Joint inflammation and other problems outside the gut can also occur.

topics.name: Cross-Dressing
topics.clinical_significance: Cross-dressing means wearing clothing traditionally associated with another gender and may have different personal or social meanings. By itself, it is not a psychiatric disorder and does not determine a person’s gender identity. Transvestic disorder is a separate diagnosis for recurrent, intense sexual arousal from cross-dressing lasting at least 6 months and causing significant distress or problems in daily life.

topics.name: Croup
topics.clinical_significance: Croup is usually a viral illness in young children, especially those 6 months to 3 years old. Swelling around the voice box and windpipe narrows the airway, causing a barking cough and hoarseness; stridor or difficulty breathing can signal more serious narrowing. Most children recover fully.

topics.name: Crow-Fukase Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: POEMS (Crow-Fukase) is a rare syndrome linked to an abnormal plasma-cell disorder. It causes peripheral nerve damage and abnormal monoclonal plasma cells, along with varying combinations of enlarged organs, hormone problems, skin changes, bone lesions, and fluid buildup. Nerve damage can progress and cause weakness or loss of sensation, so finding and treating the underlying plasma-cell disease is important.

topics.name: Crying in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Crying is a normal way for infants and young children to express needs, and usually lessens after 3 months of age. Persistent or unusual crying may reflect pain or illness and should be assessed; serious medical causes are uncommon, while colic is a common cause in otherwise healthy young infants. Prolonged crying can also strain caregivers, so support is important.

topics.name: Cryptococcosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cryptococcosis is a fungal infection acquired by inhaling Cryptococcus yeasts. It usually begins in the lungs and may be mild or silent in people with normal immune function. In people with weakened immunity, it can spread—especially to the brain and its coverings, causing life-threatening meningitis—and may also affect the skin or bones.

topics.name: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)
topics.clinical_significance: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is an uncommon lung disease with no known cause, in which healing tissue blocks small airways and air sacs. It can cause a persistent cough, shortness of breath, and flu-like symptoms, and may look like pneumonia that does not clear. Most people improve with glucocorticoid treatment, but the disease can return.

topics.name: Cryptorchidism
topics.clinical_significance: Cryptorchidism means one or both testicles have not moved into the scrotum. Some descend on their own during the first year of life. If a testicle remains undescended, early surgery can help protect fertility and lower the later risk of testicular cancer. Undescended testicles are also more prone to twisting.

topics.name: Cryptosporidiosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cryptosporidiosis is an intestinal infection caused by a parasite, usually spread by swallowing water or food contaminated with stool. It causes watery diarrhea and stomach cramps. Most healthy people recover, but the infection can cause severe, long-lasting diarrhea and dehydration in people with weakened immune systems. Infected people may spread the parasite for weeks after symptoms improve.

topics.name: Crystal-Induced Arthritides
topics.clinical_significance: Crystal-induced arthritis occurs when crystals collect in a joint and trigger inflammation. It can cause sudden pain, swelling, warmth, and redness. Common forms include gout from urate crystals and calcium pyrophosphate arthritis. Joint-fluid testing can identify the crystals, but their presence does not rule out a joint infection, which needs urgent treatment.

topics.name: Crystal-Induced Arthritides, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Crystal-induced arthritis happens when crystals build up in a joint and cause inflammation. The crystals may be urate, calcium pyrophosphate, or basic calcium phosphate; each can cause a painful, swollen joint. Testing joint fluid can identify most crystals. Finding crystals does not rule out a joint infection, which may occur at the same time and needs urgent care.

topics.name: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cubital tunnel syndrome is compression or stretching of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. It can cause pain at the elbow and tingling or numbness in the ring and little fingers. Long-lasting or severe nerve pressure may weaken the hand and, in advanced cases, cause a claw-shaped position of these fingers.

topics.name: Culture
topics.clinical_significance: A culture grows microorganisms from a specimen so they can be identified and, often, tested to see which antimicrobial drugs may work. Results depend on collecting and handling the specimen correctly. Because normal microbes or contamination can also grow, the result must be interpreted based on where the specimen came from; some organisms need special culture methods.

topics.name: Cupping
topics.clinical_significance: Cupping is a traditional practice in which cups create suction on the skin. It may ease neck or lower-back muscle pain for a short time, but the benefit may not last. Evidence for its use for other conditions is limited. Cupping can redden or burn the skin.

topics.name: Cushing Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cushing syndrome is caused by long-term exposure to excess cortisol or related glucocorticoids. It may result from glucocorticoid medicines or a hormone-producing tumor. Common signs include weight gain around the trunk, a rounded face, thin limbs, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. It can lead to high blood pressure, diabetes, weak bones, and infections. Cushing disease is the form caused by a pituitary tumor that makes too much ACTH.

topics.name: Cushing's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Cushing syndrome (also called Cushing’s syndrome) is caused by long-term exposure to excess cortisol or related glucocorticoids. It may result from glucocorticoid medicines or a hormone-producing tumor. Common signs include weight gain around the trunk, a rounded face, thin limbs, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. It can lead to high blood pressure, diabetes, weak bones, and infections. Cushing disease is the form caused by a pituitary tumor that makes too much ACTH.

topics.name: Cutaneous Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A cutaneous abscess is a pocket of pus in the skin, usually caused by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus. It causes a painful, tender, often red lump that may feel soft in the center. The infection can spread into nearby skin or cause fever. Treatment usually involves draining the pus; antibiotics are sometimes needed.

topics.name: Cutaneous Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous cysts are closed sacs under the skin, often filled with keratin. Common types include epidermal inclusion cysts, milia, and pilar cysts. They are usually benign and painless, though they may be noticeable or uncomfortable. If a cyst ruptures or becomes inflamed, it can swell quickly and become painful, sometimes looking like a skin abscess even when there is no infection.

topics.name: Cutaneous Larva Migrans
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous larva migrans is a skin infestation by dog or cat hookworm larvae picked up from contaminated soil or sand. It causes intensely itchy, raised, winding red tracks as the larvae move through the upper skin. The larvae usually cannot mature in people, and the rash often clears over several weeks. Scratching can lead to a bacterial skin infection.

topics.name: Cutaneous Leukocytoclastic Angiitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis is inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin, with white blood cell debris in the vessel walls. It often causes raised purple spots, especially on the lower legs. Medicines, infections, or systemic inflammatory diseases can trigger it. Some cases are part of a wider illness that affects internal organs.

topics.name: Cutaneous Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis is inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin. On biopsy, immune cells called neutrophils break down and leave debris in the vessel walls. It often causes raised purple spots, especially on the lower legs. It may be limited to the skin or occur with an infection, a medicine reaction, or a disease affecting other organs.

topics.name: Cutaneous Myiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous myiasis is infestation of the skin by fly larvae (maggots). It may cause a boil-like lump, slow-moving itchy tracks, or larvae in an open wound. Wound infestations can damage tissue and lead to a secondary infection. A painful or draining skin lesion with visible larvae is a key sign. The condition is more common in tropical regions.

topics.name: Cutaneous Necrotizing Venulitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous necrotizing venulitis is another name for cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, inflammation that damages small blood vessels in the skin. It often causes raised purple spots, especially on the lower legs. It may follow an infection or medicine exposure, or occur with a disease that also affects internal organs.

topics.name: Cutaneous Penile Lesions
topics.clinical_significance: Penile skin lesions can result from irritation, skin disease, infection (including sexually transmitted infections), or, less often, precancer or cancer. Harmless pearly penile papules can be mistaken for genital warts but are not caused by HPV. Some red, velvety patches are cancer in situ and can progress to invasive cancer, so biopsy is important when these lesions are suspected.

topics.name: Cutaneous Small Vessel Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis is inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin. It often causes raised purple spots (purpura), tiny red or purple dots (petechiae), or shallow sores. It may be limited to the skin or occur as part of a disease affecting other organs. Possible causes include medicines, infections, and immune disorders.

topics.name: Cutaneous T-cell Lymphomas (CTCL)
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas are uncommon non-Hodgkin lymphomas that mainly affect the skin. The main types are mycosis fungoides, which often begins as a long-lasting itchy rash and may progress to plaques or tumors, and Sézary syndrome, which can cause widespread red skin and lymphoma cells in the blood. The outlook depends on how far the disease has spread.

topics.name: Cutaneous Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous vasculitis is inflammation of small or medium blood vessels in the skin. It may stay limited to the skin or occur as part of a wider disease. It can cause raised purple spots, small red-purple dots, or sores. Medicines, infections, cancers, and immune disorders are possible causes. A skin biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Cutis Laxa
topics.clinical_significance: Cutis laxa is a group of inherited or acquired disorders in which abnormal elastic fibers make the skin loose, sagging, and slow to recoil when stretched. Other organs may be affected. Depending on the type, complications can include early lung damage (emphysema), abnormal or enlarged arteries, and problems involving the heart, gut, or joints.

topics.name: Cyclothymic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Cyclothymic disorder causes repeated periods of mild high-energy symptoms and mild depressive symptoms that do not meet the criteria for full mood episodes. In adults, the pattern lasts at least 2 years; in children and teens, at least 1 year. Mood changes may disrupt relationships, school, or work and can later develop into bipolar I or II disorder, though this does not happen in everyone.

topics.name: Cystic Fibrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease caused by disease-causing variants in both copies of the CFTR gene. Defective salt and water movement makes mucus thick, leading to repeated lung infections and progressive airway damage. It can also cause poor pancreatic digestion, poor growth, liver disease, and infertility in many males. Lifelong specialized care and CFTR-targeted medicines have improved survival.

topics.name: Cystic Fibrosis (CF)
topics.clinical_significance: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an inherited disease caused by disease-causing variants in both copies of the CFTR gene. Defective salt and water movement makes mucus thick, leading to repeated lung infections and progressive airway damage. It can also cause poor pancreatic digestion, poor growth, liver disease, and infertility in many males. Lifelong specialized care and CFTR-targeted medicines have improved survival.

topics.name: Cystic Hygroma
topics.clinical_significance: A cystic hygroma is a benign congenital malformation in which lymph vessels are abnormally enlarged, forming fluid-filled spaces. It usually affects the head or neck and is present at birth or appears in the first 2 years of life. Larger lesions may cause problems because of their location; some occur with syndromes that also affect blood vessels or other tissues.

topics.name: Cystic Kidney Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Cystic kidney disease is a group of conditions, present from birth or acquired later, in which cysts form in the kidneys. The effects vary: simple cysts are often harmless, while inherited forms such as polycystic kidney disease can cause high blood pressure and progressive kidney failure. Cystic disease after long-term dialysis is linked to a higher risk of kidney cancer.

topics.name: Cystic Kidney Disease, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cystic kidney diseases are congenital or acquired conditions in which cysts form in the kidneys. Their effects range from usually harmless single cysts to inherited disorders that can enlarge the kidneys, cause high blood pressure, and lead to kidney failure; some also affect other organs. Cysts that develop after long-term dialysis are linked to a higher risk of kidney cancer.

topics.name: Cystinuria
topics.clinical_significance: Cystinuria is an inherited kidney-tubule disorder in which the kidneys do not reclaim cystine normally, so too much passes into the urine and forms cystine stones. These stones often recur and can cause severe flank pain, blood in the urine, blockage, and urinary infection. Repeated or prolonged blockage can damage the kidneys.

topics.name: Cystoceles
topics.clinical_significance: A cystocele occurs when the bladder bulges into the front wall of the vagina because its pelvic support has weakened. It may cause a vaginal bulge, pelvic pressure, urine leakage, or trouble emptying the bladder; mild cases may have no symptoms. A cystocele often occurs with a urethrocele, in which the urethra also bulges into the vagina.

topics.name: Cystoisosporiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Cystoisosporiasis is an intestinal infection caused by the parasite Cystoisospora belli, usually acquired from contaminated food or water. It causes sudden, watery diarrhea with cramps, fever, nausea, or tiredness. The illness often clears on its own but may last for weeks. In people with severely weakened immune systems, it can cause prolonged, severe diarrhea and weight loss. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual treatment.

topics.name: Cystosarcoma Phyllodes
topics.clinical_significance: A phyllodes tumor is an uncommon breast tumor arising from connective tissue. Despite the older name cystosarcoma phyllodes, these tumors may be benign, borderline, or malignant. They often grow quickly and become large, may recur in the breast after removal, and malignant tumors can spread to distant organs, most often the lungs.

topics.name: Cystoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Cystoscopy uses a thin camera passed through the urethra into the bladder. It helps find problems such as bladder tumors or stones and can be used to take tissue samples, treat some urethral narrowings, or place ureteral stents. Possible complications include urinary infection, bleeding, and injury to the urethra or bladder.

topics.name: Cytomegalic Inclusion Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Cytomegalic inclusion disease is another name for cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV often causes no symptoms or a mild illness in healthy people, then remains dormant in the body. Infection before birth can cause severe liver or brain injury or fetal death. In people with a weakened immune system, CMV can damage the eyes, lungs, gut, or brain.

topics.name: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a common herpesvirus that remains dormant in the body after infection. Most healthy people have no symptoms or a mononucleosis-like illness. Infection before birth can cause severe liver or brain damage, stillbirth, or death after birth. In people with a weakened immune system, reactivated CMV can damage the eyes, lungs, gut, or brain; severe disease may need antiviral treatment.

topics.name: Dacryocystitis
topics.clinical_significance: Infection of the tear sac, usually caused by blockage of the tear duct. It causes pain, redness, and swelling at the inner corner of the eye; pus may drain from the tear openings, and an abscess can form.

topics.name: Dacryostenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing or blockage of the tear duct that carries tears into the nose. It may be present from birth or develop later and usually causes excessive tearing; congenital blockage may also cause sticky or pus-like discharge.

topics.name: Dancer's Fracture
topics.clinical_significance: A Dancer’s fracture is an avulsion fracture at the base of the fifth metatarsal, the bone along the outer side of the foot. It often follows a twisting injury as a tendon pulls off a small piece of bone, causing local pain, swelling, and tenderness. Unlike a Jones fracture, delayed healing or failure to heal is uncommon.

topics.name: Dandy Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Dandy fever is another name for dengue, a viral illness spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It typically causes sudden fever, headache, severe muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. Severe dengue can cause bleeding, fluid leakage, and shock.

topics.name: Daptomycin
topics.clinical_significance: A lipopeptide antibiotic used for selected serious infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE). It does not treat pneumonia. Important adverse effects include muscle injury and, rarely, eosinophilic pneumonia; kidney impairment affects dosing.

topics.name: Darmbrand
topics.clinical_significance: Darmbrand is clostridial necrotizing enteritis, a severe intestinal infection caused by toxin-producing Clostridium perfringens type C. It can cause severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea. Intestinal tissue may die or perforate, leading to septic shock and death.

topics.name: de Morsier Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A congenital brain disorder in which the optic nerves are underdeveloped, often with an absent or abnormal septum pellucidum (a membrane between parts of the brain) and an underdeveloped pituitary gland. It can cause reduced vision, abnormal eye movements, hormone deficiencies, seizures, or developmental problems.

topics.name: De Quervain Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: De Quervain syndrome is narrowing and inflammation of the tendon sheaths that guide the thumb tendons along the thumb side of the wrist. It causes pain and tenderness there, often worse with thumb or wrist movement.

topics.name: de Quervain Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: De Quervain thyroiditis (subacute thyroiditis) is a usually self-limited inflammation of the thyroid, often following a viral illness. It causes a tender, enlarged thyroid and fever; release of stored thyroid hormone can cause temporary hyperthyroidism, sometimes followed by temporary hypothyroidism. It usually resolves within months, but rarely causes lasting hypothyroidism.

topics.name: Death and Dying in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Palliative or hospice care can ease symptoms and provide practical and emotional support to a dying child and family. After a child’s death, family members may need support with grief; children’s understanding of death varies with their developmental level.

topics.name: Decompression Sickness
topics.clinical_significance: Decompression sickness occurs when gas dissolved in blood or tissues forms bubbles as pressure falls, usually during ascent after diving or work in compressed air. It may cause joint pain, skin changes, numbness or weakness, confusion, or breathing problems. Severe cases can be fatal; treatment uses recompression in a hyperbaric chamber.

topics.name: Decreased Erythropoiesis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Decreased erythropoiesis means the bone marrow makes too few red blood cells, causing hypoproliferative anemia and a low reticulocyte count. Causes include iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency; chronic inflammation or kidney disease; and bone marrow disorders. Red blood cell size helps narrow the cause.

topics.name: Decubiti
topics.clinical_significance: Decubiti is an older term for pressure injuries: damage to the skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony area, from prolonged pressure. Early injury may occur without an open sore; deeper wounds can become infected and extend to muscle or bone.

topics.name: Decubitus Ulcers
topics.clinical_significance: A decubitus ulcer is an open pressure injury, usually over a bony area, caused by prolonged pressure on the skin and underlying tissue. It can extend into deeper tissues and become infected; severe wounds may expose muscle or bone.

topics.name: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) Prevention
topics.clinical_significance: DVT prevention aims to reduce deep-vein blood clots, especially during hospitalization, after surgery, or with limited movement. Measures include early movement, anticoagulant medicines, or compression devices; the choice depends on clot risk and bleeding risk.

topics.name: Deep Venous Thrombosis, Medications for Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Anticoagulants are the main medicines used to treat deep venous thrombosis; they prevent clots from growing and new clots from forming while the body clears the clot. Options include heparins, direct oral anticoagulants, and warfarin. Bleeding is the main risk; clot-dissolving drugs are reserved for selected severe cases because they carry greater bleeding risk.

topics.name: Deer Fly Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Deer fly fever is another name for tularemia, an infection caused by Francisella tularensis. It can spread through bites from infected deer flies or ticks, contact with infected animals, or contaminated food, water, or aerosols. It often causes fever, a skin ulcer, and nearby swollen lymph nodes; inhalation can cause pneumonia.

topics.name: Defibrination Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Defibrination syndrome is another name for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), in which widespread abnormal clotting uses up platelets and clotting proteins. It can cause both blood clots and bleeding; rapidly developing cases may lead to severe bleeding and organ damage, while slower cases more often cause thrombosis.

topics.name: Definition of Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Dermatitis means inflammation of the skin and describes several conditions with similar inflammatory changes. It often causes redness, scaling, and itching; chronic inflammation can thicken the skin, and scratching can lead to sores, oozing, crusts, or infection. Eczema is often used as another name for dermatitis, though it sometimes refers specifically to atopic dermatitis.

topics.name: Definition of Diverticular Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Diverticular disease means that pouches (diverticula) in the digestive tract cause symptoms; the term describes symptomatic diverticulosis. Diverticulosis is the presence of one or more pouches, while diverticulitis is inflammation, with or without infection, of a pouch.

topics.name: Degenerative Joint Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Degenerative joint disease is another name for osteoarthritis, a chronic joint disorder with progressive loss of cartilage and changes in nearby bone and other tissues. It commonly causes pain with activity and brief stiffness after rest; later, movement and daily activities may become limited. Joint changes on imaging do not always cause symptoms.

topics.name: Dehydration and Fluid Therapy in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Children, especially infants, can become dehydrated when fluid loss exceeds intake, often because of vomiting or diarrhea. Dehydration also reduces electrolytes and, when severe, can impair circulation and cause shock. Fluid therapy replaces the deficit and ongoing losses, orally when possible or intravenously in severe cases.

topics.name: Dehydration in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Dehydration in children is a significant loss of body water and electrolytes, usually from vomiting, diarrhea, or poor fluid intake. It can cause thirst, dry mouth, tiredness, and reduced urination; severe dehydration may impair circulation and lead to low blood pressure or shock. Infants are especially vulnerable.

topics.name: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)
topics.clinical_significance: DHEA is a steroid made by the adrenal glands and a precursor to estrogen and androgen hormones. Supplements are marketed for effects on aging, mood, strength, and sexual function, but evidence for most claimed benefits is limited. Potential harms include acne, unwanted hair growth, and mood changes; DHEA may interact with anticoagulants, antidepressants, and hormone-blocking medicines.

topics.name: Delayed Puberty
topics.clinical_significance: Delayed puberty is absent or stalled sexual maturation; key thresholds are no breast development by age 13 in girls or testicular enlargement by age 14 in boys. A common cause is constitutional delay, in which puberty starts later but proceeds normally. Undernutrition, chronic illness, or disorders of the gonads, hypothalamus, or pituitary can also cause it.

topics.name: Delirium
topics.clinical_significance: Delirium is a sudden, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness, and thinking that develops over hours to days. It is often reversible and usually reflects an acute illness, medication effect, intoxication, or withdrawal; some causes are life-threatening. Unlike dementia, it begins quickly and mainly affects attention.

topics.name: Delirium and Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: Delirium and dementia are distinct causes of impaired thinking. Delirium begins suddenly, fluctuates, and mainly affects attention; it often follows acute illness or drug exposure and may be reversible. Dementia usually develops gradually and progressively affects memory and other thinking abilities. Delirium can also occur in someone who has dementia.

topics.name: Delirium and Dementia, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Delirium and dementia are major causes of cognitive impairment but differ in onset and course. Delirium causes a sudden, fluctuating loss of attention and awareness, often from illness or drugs, and is often reversible; dementia usually develops slowly, chiefly affects memory and thinking, and tends to progress. Delirium may occur on top of dementia, so a sudden change can signal an acute medical problem.

topics.name: Delivery, Management of Spontaneous
topics.clinical_significance: Care during spontaneous vaginal birth focuses on the safety of the mother and infant. Clinicians monitor both, support controlled delivery of the baby and placenta, check for tears and bleeding, and observe the mother closely after birth because postpartum hemorrhage is an important early risk.

topics.name: Delivery, Operative Vaginal
topics.clinical_significance: Operative vaginal delivery uses forceps or a vacuum extractor to help deliver the baby during the second stage of labor. It may be used when labor is prolonged, the baby may be compromised, or the mother cannot push effectively or should avoid pushing. The fetal head must be suitably positioned; risks include maternal tears and bleeding and injury to the baby.

topics.name: Delusional Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Delusional disorder involves one or more firmly held false beliefs lasting at least one month, without other prominent symptoms of psychosis or major impairment in overall functioning. Any hallucinations are usually related to the delusion. Medical conditions and substance use must be ruled out as causes.

topics.name: Delusional Infestation
topics.clinical_significance: Delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis) is a fixed false belief of being infested by parasites despite a lack of evidence. People may describe organisms moving on or under the skin and bring skin debris as proof. True infestation and other physical causes must be ruled out.

topics.name: Delusional Parasitosis
topics.clinical_significance: Delusional parasitosis (delusional infestation) is a fixed, mistaken belief that parasites are present on or in the body. A person may report organisms moving under the skin or bring skin debris as proof; actual infestation and other physical causes must first be ruled out.

topics.name: Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: Dementia is a chronic decline in one or more thinking abilities, such as memory, language, or judgment, that interferes with independent daily life. It usually progresses and is often caused by a brain disease; some conditions can cause a similar decline and may be treatable. Unlike delirium, it usually develops gradually and mainly affects memory.

topics.name: Dementia, Behavioral and Psychologic Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: Dementia may cause changes in behavior and mood, such as restlessness, wandering, shouting, sleep problems, depression, delusions, or hallucinations. These changes can reflect dementia, unmet needs, pain or illness, or unfamiliar surroundings, and may affect safety and caregiving. A sudden behavior change may signal physical illness or delirium.

topics.name: Dementia Pugilistica
topics.clinical_significance: Dementia pugilistica is an older name for chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a progressive brain disorder that may develop after repeated head impacts. It has been described in some boxers and other contact-sport athletes. Possible effects include changes in mood, behavior, thinking, memory, and movement; not everyone exposed to repeated head impacts develops CTE.

topics.name: Dementia with Lewy Bodies and Parkinson Disease Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: These are progressive dementias linked to Lewy bodies in the brain.
