Dementia with Lewy bodies usually begins around the same time as movement problems; Parkinson disease dementia develops years after Parkinson disease begins. Both can impair thinking and daily function, and may cause fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, and slowed or stiff movement.

topics.name: Demyelinating Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Demyelinating disorders damage myelin, the covering that helps nerve signals travel. Depending on the nerves affected, they can cause weakness, numbness, vision problems, poor coordination, or other neurologic symptoms. Causes include immune, infectious, inherited, metabolic, and toxic conditions; symptoms and treatment depend on the cause.

topics.name: Demyelinating Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Demyelination damages myelin, the covering that helps nerve signals travel through the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Symptoms depend on the affected areas and may include weakness, numbness, vision problems, or poor coordination. Causes include immune disease and other conditions such as infection, inherited or metabolic disease, poor blood flow, and toxins. Some damage can repair, but severe myelin loss may permanently injure nerve fibers.

topics.name: Dengue
topics.clinical_significance: Dengue is a virus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It often causes sudden fever, severe headache or pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. A small number of people develop severe dengue, with bleeding and fluid leaking from blood vessels that can lead to shock. Warning signs such as severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, or unusual sleepiness—often as fever falls—need urgent medical care.

topics.name: Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever/Dengue Shock Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a severe form of dengue that can cause blood vessels to leak and bleeding to occur. Fluid loss can lead to shock and organ failure (dengue shock syndrome), which may develop quickly. It often follows a previous dengue infection. Severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, or confusion are warning signs that need urgent hospital care.

topics.name: Dental Anatomy and Development
topics.clinical_significance: Teeth and their supporting gums, ligaments, and jawbone allow biting and chewing. Tooth eruption and oral development help clinicians assess oral health and growth; eruption timing can help estimate skeletal age or identify growth restriction. Recognizing normal mouth structures and harmless variations can prevent them from being mistaken for disease.

topics.name: Dental Appliances
topics.clinical_significance: Dental appliances replace missing teeth and can improve chewing, speech, appearance, and bite. Options include bridges, partial or complete dentures, and implants. Good fit and cleaning matter because appliances can irritate the gums or increase the risk of infection.

topics.name: Dental Emergencies
topics.clinical_significance: Dental emergencies include tooth infections, broken or knocked-out teeth, a dislocated jaw, and problems after tooth extraction such as bleeding or severe pain. Prompt care can relieve pain, treat infection, and help limit damage. Rapidly spreading infection or trouble breathing or swallowing needs emergency medical care.

topics.name: Dental Emergencies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Dental infections and injuries can cause severe pain or lasting damage. A knocked-out tooth, a dislocated jaw, or a spreading infection needs urgent care. Prompt assessment can treat infection and help save injured teeth; a physician may provide emergency care when a dentist is not available.

topics.name: Dental, Mask, and Eye Barotrauma
topics.clinical_significance: During diving, pressure changes can injure air spaces in teeth, behind a face mask, or under hard contact lenses. This may cause tooth pain or damage, bruising or bleeding around the eyes, and blurred vision. Divers can reduce risk by equalizing pressure inside the mask and avoiding goggles; severe or lasting pain or vision changes need medical assessment.

topics.name: Dental Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: A dental assessment helps identify tooth and gum problems, oral cancer, and signs of other illnesses that can appear in the mouth. Unexplained mouth, face, or neck pain or swelling and persistent dry mouth may need dental evaluation. Dental review before head or neck radiation, and often before chemotherapy, can help prevent or manage oral complications.

topics.name: Dental Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Dental evaluations can find tooth decay, gum disease, and oral cancer early. A history and exam of the teeth, mouth, and jaw may also reveal signs of other illnesses. Routine checks are generally recommended every 6 months, with more frequent visits for people at higher risk of dental disease.

topics.name: Dental Patient, Introduction to Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Oral health affects chewing, nutrition, and general health, especially in older adults, who may have dry mouth or trouble keeping dentures in place. Mouth exams can reveal oral cancer or signs of other illnesses. Dental review before head and neck radiation helps identify infection and lower the risk of jawbone injury.

topics.name: Dependent Personality Disorder (DPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Dependent personality disorder is a lasting pattern of excessive need for care that can cause submissive behavior, fear of separation, and difficulty making decisions or living independently. Fear of losing support may lead a person to tolerate unreasonable demands or abuse. Psychotherapy can help build confidence and independence; depression and anxiety may also occur.

topics.name: Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: This disorder causes repeated or ongoing feelings of being detached from one’s body, thoughts, or surroundings, which may seem unreal or dreamlike. The person knows these are feelings and that reality has not changed. Symptoms cause significant distress or interfere with daily life; other medical, substance-related, or mental causes must be ruled out.

topics.name: Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate
topics.clinical_significance: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) is a long-acting progestin shot given about every 3 months to prevent pregnancy; it works best when injections are on time. Irregular bleeding or no periods and weight gain are common. Bone density may decrease during use and usually recovers after stopping. Fertility can take months, sometimes up to 18 months, to return after the last injection.

topics.name: Depression, Medications for Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Antidepressants can reduce depression symptoms, and the choice depends on a person’s symptoms, health, and past response; they may be used with psychotherapy. Improvement often takes several weeks. Watch for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, especially in children and young adults and after starting or raising a dose. Many antidepressants should be tapered rather than stopped suddenly to reduce withdrawal symptoms.

topics.name: Depressive Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Depressive disorders cause persistent sadness, emptiness, or irritability that interferes with daily life. They may also cause loss of interest and changes in sleep, appetite, energy, or concentration, and can include suicidal thoughts. They are more than short-lived sadness after a difficult event. Treatment often includes psychotherapy, antidepressants, or both; clinicians also assess suicide risk and check for medical or substance-related causes.

topics.name: Depressive Disorders in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and teens, depression causes persistent sadness or irritability that interferes with daily life. Younger children may show school problems, withdrawal, or behavior changes instead of describing sadness. Loss of interest and changes in sleep, appetite, or energy may occur, and suicide risk needs assessment. Treatment may include psychotherapy, medicine, or both, with close monitoring.

topics.name: Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Dermatitis is a group of inflammatory skin conditions, including atopic and contact dermatitis. It often causes itching, redness, scaling, or thickened skin; scratching may lead to sores, oozing, crusts, or secondary infection. Symptoms and treatment depend on the specific type and cause.

topics.name: Dermatitis, Definition
topics.clinical_significance: Dermatitis means skin inflammation and describes several skin conditions with a similar inflammatory pattern. It commonly causes redness, itching, and scaling; long-lasting cases may thicken the skin, and scratching can cause sores, oozing, crusts, or infection. “Eczema” is often used as another name for dermatitis, though it may also refer specifically to atopic dermatitis.

topics.name: Dermatitis Herpetiformis
topics.clinical_significance: Despite its name, dermatitis herpetiformis is not caused by herpes. It is an intensely itchy autoimmune rash with grouped blisters, often symmetrically on the elbows, knees, buttocks, or scalp. It is strongly linked to celiac disease, which may cause no digestive symptoms, so people with this rash should be evaluated for celiac disease. A strict gluten-free diet helps control it; dapsone often relieves the rash quickly.

topics.name: Dermatitis of the Ear Canal (Chronic Otitis Externa)
topics.clinical_significance: This is long-lasting inflammation of the ear canal skin, often causing itching, redness, and flaking; clear drainage or skin cracks may also occur. It can result from contact allergy, irritants such as water or cotton swabs, or another skin condition. A secondary infection may develop and usually causes more pain than itching.

topics.name: Dermatofibromas
topics.clinical_significance: Dermatofibromas are common, benign, firm red-brown bumps, often on the legs. They usually cause no symptoms, though some itch or become irritated after injury. A rapidly growing bump should be assessed because a rare skin cancer can look similar.

topics.name: Dermatologic Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Skin problems are assessed by looking at the appearance and distribution of lesions and asking about their timing, changes, and possible triggers. A full skin exam can find skin cancer and clues to internal illness or widespread disease. Biopsy or other tests may be needed when the cause is unclear.

topics.name: Dermatologic Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Skin evaluation combines a history of when lesions began, how they changed, and possible triggers with close inspection of their appearance and distribution. Examining the whole skin, scalp, nails, and mouth can help detect skin cancer or clues to internal illness. Many conditions can be diagnosed this way; unclear cases may need a biopsy or other tests.

topics.name: Dermatologic Therapy, Topical, Principles of
topics.clinical_significance: Topical medicines treat skin conditions directly. Their effectiveness and safety depend on choosing the right medicine, strength, and form (such as cream or ointment) for the condition and body site. Strong medicines or coverings can increase absorption and side effects; topical steroids can thin the skin, especially when potent products are used for too long or on thin skin.

topics.name: Dermatophytid Reaction
topics.clinical_significance: A dermatophytid reaction is an itchy rash caused by the body’s response to a fungal skin infection elsewhere; the rash itself contains no fungus. It may cause blisters on the hands or feet or other widespread rash patterns. Treating the underlying fungal infection clears the reaction, while anti-inflammatory treatment may ease itching.

topics.name: Dermatophytoses, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Dermatophytoses (tinea or ringworm) are common fungal infections of the skin, hair, or nails. Symptoms depend on the site and may include itchy, scaly patches, scalp scaling with hair loss, or thickened, discolored nails. These infections can recur and spread through contact with infected people or animals. Skin infections often respond to antifungal creams, while scalp or nail infections usually need oral treatment.

topics.name: Description of Skin Lesions
topics.clinical_significance: Describing a skin lesion by its type, shape, texture, color, and distribution helps clinicians narrow possible diagnoses and communicate findings clearly. Patterns can point to infection, inflammation, bleeding, or cancer, but are not always conclusive. Skin color changes may look different across skin tones.

topics.name: Desquamative Inflammatory Vaginitis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, often recurring inflammation of the vagina, usually without a clear infection. It most often affects people around or after menopause and may cause yellow discharge, irritation, burning, pain during sex, or pain when urinating. Diagnosis includes an exam and vaginal-fluid testing to rule out infection; treatment may include vaginal clindamycin or hydrocortisone.

topics.name: Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP)
topics.clinical_significance: A rare type of interstitial lung disease, seen almost only in current or former cigarette smokers. It causes gradually worsening shortness of breath and a dry cough. Diagnosis is based on lung imaging and sometimes a lung biopsy; stopping smoking is central to treatment, and corticosteroids may also be used.

topics.name: Development, Childhood
topics.clinical_significance: Childhood development is the gradual growth of movement, language, thinking, social, and emotional skills. The timing of milestones varies, so progress is followed over time; a marked or persistent delay may need assessment to identify developmental or medical problems and provide support.

topics.name: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH)
topics.clinical_significance: An abnormal development of the hip joint in infants that can make the thighbone unstable, partly displaced, or fully dislocated. Early screening and treatment are important; if missed, the affected leg may become shorter and hip pain or walking problems may develop. Treatment often uses a harness, while persistent cases may need surgery.

topics.name: Devic Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Devic disease is another name for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, an autoimmune disease that mainly damages the optic nerves and spinal cord. Attacks can cause vision loss, weakness or numbness, and bladder problems, and may lead to lasting disability. It is distinct from multiple sclerosis; prompt treatment of attacks and prevention of relapses are important.

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus and Hypoglycemia
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes mellitus is a group of disorders that cause high blood glucose because insulin is lacking, insufficient, or does not work well; over time, it can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels. Hypoglycemia is low blood glucose, often caused by insulin or certain diabetes medicines; it can cause sweating and confusion and, when severe, seizures or loss of consciousness.

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus, Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term high blood glucose can damage small blood vessels, causing eye, kidney, and nerve disease and poor wound healing, especially in the feet. It also speeds narrowing of larger arteries, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and poor blood flow to the legs. Good glucose and cardiovascular risk-factor control can prevent or delay many complications.

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Drug treatment lowers blood glucose and helps prevent diabetes complications. Insulin is required for type 1 diabetes; type 2 diabetes may be treated with oral or injectable medicines, sometimes with insulin, alongside lifestyle measures. Insulin and some other medicines can cause low blood glucose, so treatment and monitoring are tailored to the person.

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes in children and adolescents causes high blood glucose from too little insulin or insulin resistance. Type 1, caused by immune damage to insulin-producing cells, is most common; type 2 also occurs. Symptoms may include thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss, and some children develop life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis. Treatment depends on the type and requires ongoing glucose monitoring.

topics.name: Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes during pregnancy may be present before conception or first develop during pregnancy (gestational diabetes). High blood glucose increases health risks for the pregnant person and baby, including preeclampsia, a large baby, difficult birth, and low blood glucose in the newborn. Poor control early in pregnancy also raises the risk of miscarriage and birth defects; close monitoring and treatment help reduce these risks.

topics.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetic nephropathy is progressive damage to the kidney filters caused by diabetes. It often has no symptoms early; albumin in the urine can be an early sign. Ongoing damage may lead to chronic kidney disease and kidney failure, but checking urine albumin and kidney function and controlling blood glucose and blood pressure can slow progression.

topics.name: Diabetic Retinopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetic retinopathy is damage to the retina's blood vessels caused by diabetes. Early disease often has no symptoms; leaking vessels can swell the central retina and blur vision. In advanced disease, fragile new vessels can bleed or form scar tissue that pulls the retina away, causing severe vision loss. Regular eye exams and control of blood glucose and blood pressure help prevent or limit damage.

topics.name: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Gastrointestinal Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal procedures help find disease or assess how the digestive tract works. They include imaging, endoscopy with tissue sampling, and tests of movement or acid levels. Some endoscopic procedures can also remove polyps or foreign objects, stop bleeding, widen narrowed areas, or place tubes or stents. Risks depend on the procedure; endoscopy may require sedation and can rarely cause bleeding or a tear in the digestive tract.

topics.name: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Pulmonary Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary procedures help diagnose lung and pleural disease or treat breathing problems. They include imaging and lung-function tests, bronchoscopy or biopsy to inspect airways and collect samples, and thoracentesis to test or drain fluid around the lungs. Risks depend on the procedure; invasive tests can cause bleeding, a collapsed lung, or problems related to sedation.

topics.name: Diagnostic Tests for Skin Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: When a skin problem is not clear from its appearance and examination, tests can help find the cause and guide treatment. Scrapings or cultures can check for infection, patch tests can identify contact allergy, a Wood light can help assess some color changes or infections, and a biopsy can examine skin tissue for inflammation or cancer. The test is chosen based on the suspected cause.

topics.name: Diaphragmatic Hernia
topics.clinical_significance: A birth defect in the diaphragm lets abdominal organs move into the chest and limits lung growth before birth. The underdeveloped lungs and high blood pressure in the lung arteries can cause severe breathing problems after birth. It requires urgent newborn care and surgical repair.

topics.name: Diarrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Diarrhea is loose or watery stool, often passed more often than usual. Causes include infections, medicines, food intolerance, inflammation, or poor absorption of nutrients. Severe or prolonged diarrhea can cause dehydration and loss of body salts; persistent diarrhea may be a sign of an underlying illness.

topics.name: Diarrhea in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Diarrhea in children is frequent loose or watery stools that differ from the child's usual pattern, which varies with age and diet. Gastroenteritis is a common cause. Severe or prolonged diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration, especially in infants, and long-lasting diarrhea can affect weight gain. Oral rehydration solution is effective in most cases; antidiarrheal medicines such as loperamide are not recommended for infants and young children.

topics.name: Diet Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Diet therapy uses special eating plans to try to prevent or treat disease or promote wellness; some plans are also promoted as ways to “detoxify” the body. Evidence varies by diet: some, such as the Mediterranean diet, are widely accepted, while many others have limited evidence. Highly restrictive diets can lead to poor nutrition.

topics.name: Dietary Supplements
topics.clinical_significance: Dietary supplements contain vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, or other substances and are taken to add to the usual diet. Evidence for benefit and safety varies, and products may differ in strength or contain undeclared ingredients. Supplements can cause harm or interact with medicines, so their use should be reviewed with a health professional.

topics.name: Dietary Supplements, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Dietary supplements include vitamins, minerals, herbs, and similar products taken to add to the diet. Evidence for benefit and safety varies; in the United States, manufacturers generally do not have to prove a supplement is safe and effective before sale. Product contents or amounts may vary, and supplements can cause harm or interact with medicines, so they should not replace proven treatment.

topics.name: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage
topics.clinical_significance: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is bleeding from small lung vessels into the air sacs, often due to an autoimmune disease but also caused by some heart or blood-clotting disorders, medicines, or infections. It can cause shortness of breath, cough, anemia, and coughing up blood, though blood may not be visible. Severe bleeding can quickly impair oxygen levels and become life-threatening, so urgent assessment and treatment of the cause are needed.

topics.name: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage and Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary-renal syndrome combines bleeding into the lung air sacs with inflammation of the kidney filters (glomerulonephritis), usually from an autoimmune disease affecting small blood vessels. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing up blood, blood in the urine, or swelling; lung and kidney symptoms may begin at different times. It can be life-threatening and needs urgent testing and treatment of the cause, often with medicines that suppress the immune system.

topics.name: Diffuse Esophageal Spasm
topics.clinical_significance: Diffuse (distal) esophageal spasm is a movement disorder in which the esophagus contracts too early or in an uncoordinated way. It may cause squeezing chest pain or difficulty swallowing liquids and solids, but can also cause no symptoms. Because the pain can resemble heart-related chest pain, heart disease must be ruled out; a barium swallow or esophageal pressure test can help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Diffuse parenchymal lung diseases are a broad group of conditions that mainly affect the tissue around the lung air sacs and may spread to other lung structures. Inflammation and scarring can make the lungs stiff and reduce oxygen transfer, causing shortness of breath and cough. Causes include autoimmune disease, workplace or environmental exposures, medicines, and unknown factors; tests and treatment depend on the cause.

topics.name: DiGeorge Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: DiGeorge syndrome is usually caused by a missing piece of chromosome 22 (22q11.2 deletion). An underdeveloped thymus can reduce T cells, which help fight infections, and underactive parathyroid glands can cause low blood calcium. Congenital heart defects are common. Some people also have palate, feeding, speech, hearing, or learning problems; features and severity vary.

topics.name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a heart-muscle disorder in which one or both lower chambers enlarge and contract weakly. Causes include inherited changes, infections, alcohol, some medicines, pregnancy, and other illnesses; sometimes no cause is found. Weak pumping can lead to heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms, and blood clots.

topics.name: Dimethyltryptamine
topics.clinical_significance: Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a hallucinogenic drug found in ayahuasca and also made synthetically. It can cause hallucinations and changes in perception and judgment. Reactions are unpredictable; toxicity from tryptamine-type hallucinogens can affect the heart and blood vessels, causing high blood pressure or reduced blood flow to the heart.

topics.name: Diminished Ovarian Reserve
topics.clinical_significance: Diminished ovarian reserve means that the ovaries have fewer eggs or eggs of lower quality. It can make pregnancy harder to achieve and reduce the response to fertility treatment. It becomes more common with age and may also follow ovarian surgery or injury. Pregnancy can still be possible.

topics.name: Diphtheria
topics.clinical_significance: Diphtheria is a contagious infection, usually caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Throat infection can form a thick coating that may block breathing, and the toxin can damage the heart and nerves. Vaccination protects against the toxin’s effects but does not prevent infection itself.

topics.name: Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: This combined vaccine helps protect against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (whooping cough). DTaP is the formulation used for young children; Tdap, which has lower doses of the diphtheria and pertussis components, is used mainly for adolescents and adults. Booster doses help maintain protection.

topics.name: Diphyllobothriasis (Fish Tapeworm Infection)
topics.clinical_significance: Diphyllobothriasis is an intestinal infection with fish tapeworms, usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Many people have no symptoms; others have mild abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, or weight loss. The tapeworm can use vitamin B12 from food, sometimes causing B12 deficiency and anemia; heavy infection rarely blocks the intestine.

topics.name: Diplopia
topics.clinical_significance: Diplopia is seeing two images of one object. Monocular diplopia occurs in one eye alone and often comes from an eye problem, such as cataract or an irregular cornea. Binocular diplopia occurs only when both eyes are open and often reflects eye misalignment from a nerve, muscle, or brain disorder.

topics.name: Dipylidium caninum Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Dipylidium caninum is a dog and cat tapeworm that can infect people who swallow an infected flea, usually young children. Infection is usually mild or symptom-free and often clears on its own. Tapeworm segments may be seen in the stool.

topics.name: Direct Current (DC) Cardioversion-Defibrillation
topics.clinical_significance: A direct-current shock can stop certain fast, dangerous heart rhythms and allow the heart’s normal pacemaker to restore an organized rhythm. Cardioversion times the shock with the heartbeat; defibrillation delivers it without timing, as used for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

topics.name: Dirofilariasis
topics.clinical_significance: Dirofilariasis is a rare infection spread to people by mosquitoes carrying dog heartworm or related worms. In humans, the larvae do not mature; they may form a nodule in the lung, often found by chance and sometimes mistaken for a tumor. Rarely, nodules form in the eye, brain, or testes.

topics.name: Discoid Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Discoid (nummular) dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition that causes one or more itchy, coin-shaped, scaly patches or raised plaques. It often affects the arms or legs and may occur with atopic dermatitis, but it can also affect people without it.

topics.name: Diseases of the Aorta and Its Branches
topics.clinical_significance: Diseases of the aorta and its branches include aneurysms, tears in the artery wall, inflammation, and blockages. They can cause rupture or reduce blood flow to organs such as the heart, brain, kidneys, intestines, or limbs, and may be life-threatening.

topics.name: Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: A dislocation occurs when the bones forming a joint are completely displaced from their normal positions; partial displacement is called a subluxation. It can damage ligaments, nerves, or blood vessels, and may occur with a fracture. Open dislocations also carry a risk of infection.

topics.name: Dislocations, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A dislocation is a complete separation of the bones at a joint; partial separation is a subluxation. It usually follows an injury and may occur with a fracture or damage to ligaments, nerves, or blood vessels. These injuries can threaten the affected limb or cause lasting joint problems; an open dislocation also risks infection.

topics.name: Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
topics.clinical_significance: Disorders of gut-brain interaction cause digestive symptoms through changes in gut movement or sensitivity and in how the brain processes signals from the gut. Changes in gut microbes and the gut lining or immune system may also contribute. Examples include irritable bowel syndrome, functional dyspepsia, and functional constipation.

topics.name: Disorders of Neuromuscular Transmission
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders interfere with signals passing from nerves to muscles, causing muscle weakness that may vary over time and usually does not affect sensation. Myasthenia gravis is the most common example. Severe weakness can affect swallowing or breathing.

topics.name: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
topics.clinical_significance: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is abnormal, widespread blood clotting triggered by another serious illness. Small clots can block blood flow and use up platelets and clotting factors, leading to organ damage or bleeding. Rapid-onset DIC often causes severe bleeding, while slower forms may mainly cause blood clots.

topics.name: Dissociative Amnesia
topics.clinical_significance: Dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important personal memories, usually linked to trauma or severe stress, that goes beyond normal forgetfulness. Memory gaps may cover a specific event or period; rarely, they include a person’s identity and life history. Other medical causes of memory loss must be excluded.

topics.name: Dissociative Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Dissociative disorders disrupt the usual integration of memory, identity, awareness, or perception. They may cause important memory gaps, changes in identity, or feelings of being detached from oneself or one’s surroundings, often after severe stress or trauma. Symptoms cause significant distress or interfere with daily life.

topics.name: Dissociative Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Dissociative disorders are conditions in which memory, identity, awareness, or a person’s sense of self or surroundings becomes disconnected. They may cause major memory gaps, detachment from oneself or the world, or a fragmented sense of identity. Unlike ordinary lapses, symptoms can disrupt daily life and often follow overwhelming stress or trauma.

topics.name: Dissociative Identity Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Dissociative identity disorder involves two or more alternating identity states and memory gaps for everyday events or important personal information that go beyond ordinary forgetfulness. Shifts in identity may affect a person’s sense of self, speech, emotions, and behavior and can disrupt daily life. The disorder is often linked to overwhelming childhood trauma.

topics.name: Dissociative Subtype of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: This form of posttraumatic stress disorder includes its usual symptoms plus repeated or ongoing episodes of depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself) or derealization (feeling that one’s surroundings are unreal). These symptoms can disrupt a person’s sense of self or surroundings and may make daily life and recovery harder.

topics.name: Distal Esophageal Spasm
topics.clinical_significance: Distal esophageal spasm is a movement disorder in which the lower esophagus contracts too early or without a normal pattern. It may cause squeezing chest pain and difficulty swallowing liquids or solids. Because the pain can resemble heart-related pain, heart causes must be excluded; a barium swallow or manometry can help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Distal Humeral Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Distal humeral fractures are breaks in the lower end of the upper arm bone near the elbow, common in children and often caused by a fall on an outstretched arm. They cause elbow pain, swelling, and limited movement. Displaced fractures can injure nearby arteries or nerves and reduce blood flow to the forearm.

topics.name: Distal Radius Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Distal radius fractures are breaks near the wrist, often after a fall on an outstretched hand and common in older adults. They may cause pain, swelling, and wrist deformity; swelling or displacement can injure the median nerve and cause numbness. Fractures that affect the wrist joint can lead to stiffness, lasting pain, or arthritis.

topics.name: DIV
topics.clinical_significance: DIV stands for desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, a chronic inflammation of the vagina without an identified infection. It occurs most often around or after menopause and can cause yellow or pus-like discharge, irritation, burning, and pain with sex or urination. Vaginal pH and microscopy help distinguish it from infectious vaginitis.

topics.name: Diverticular Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Diverticular disease means symptoms linked to diverticula, small pouches in the colon wall. It may cause abdominal pain or changes in bowel habits; complications can include bleeding or diverticulitis, which is inflammation of a pouch with or without infection. Diverticulosis means pouches are present; they often cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Diverticular Disease, Definition
topics.clinical_significance: A diverticulum is a pouch in the wall of a hollow organ. Diverticulosis means one or more pouches are present; diverticular disease means they cause symptoms. Diverticulitis is inflammation, with or without infection, of one or more pouches. These terms distinguish an incidental finding from symptomatic disease or inflammation.

topics.name: Diverticular Disease of the Stomach and Small Bowel
topics.clinical_significance: Stomach and small-bowel diverticula are usually found by chance and cause no symptoms, so they generally need no treatment. They can sometimes bleed, become inflamed or perforated, or allow bacterial overgrowth that causes diarrhea and poor nutrient absorption. Diverticula near the bile duct opening may also contribute to bile duct or pancreas problems. Vague digestive symptoms alone do not prove that a diverticulum is the cause.

topics.name: Diving Injuries, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Changes in pressure and gas levels during descent and ascent can injure the lungs and other tissues. Serious problems include barotrauma, decompression sickness, and gas bubbles blocking blood flow (arterial gas embolism); nitrogen narcosis and oxygen toxicity can also occur. These injuries can cause lasting harm or death, so suspected diving injuries need urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Diving Precautions and Prevention of Diving Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Training, equalizing pressure in the ears and mask, and ascending slowly help lower the risk of pressure injuries and decompression illness. Divers should not hold their breath while ascending, dive alone, or dive after alcohol or sedative drugs. Some heart, lung, neurologic, and other conditions can make diving unsafe because they may cause serious illness or loss of consciousness underwater.

topics.name: Dizziness and Vertigo
topics.clinical_significance: Dizziness can mean faintness, light-headedness, imbalance, or spinning; vertigo is the false sense that a person or their surroundings are moving. These are symptoms, not diagnoses. Causes include inner-ear problems, medicines, and changes in blood pressure or blood sugar; less often, a brain or blood-vessel disorder. Symptoms can impair walking and raise fall risk, especially in older adults. Sudden symptoms with severe imbalance, headache, fainting, or weakness need urgent assessment.

topics.name: DMT
topics.clinical_significance: Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a short-acting hallucinogenic drug. It can change perception and impair judgment; when smoked, its effects begin within minutes and usually last less than an hour. Intoxication may also affect the heart and blood pressure, with rare serious problems such as abnormal heart rhythms or reduced blood flow to the heart. Products sold as DMT may contain other drugs.

topics.name: DNA Variants and Mutations
topics.clinical_significance: A DNA change may have no effect, or it may alter how a gene or chromosome works and cause disease. Its effect depends on the change and which cells carry it. Changes in egg or sperm cells can be passed to children; changes in other cells may affect only part of the body. Some variants are common and harmless, while others can cause inherited disorders, cancer, or pregnancy loss.

topics.name: Dog Heartworm Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Humans can rarely acquire dog heartworm larvae from infected mosquitoes. Most people have no symptoms, but a larva may cause a small lung nodule that can look like a tumor on imaging; rarely, nodules occur in the eye, brain, or testis. Human infection usually resolves on its own, and antiparasitic treatment is not needed.

topics.name: Dominant Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Dominant optic neuropathy, also called dominant optic atrophy, is an inherited disorder that gradually damages the optic nerves. It usually causes slow, painless loss of central vision in both eyes, often beginning in childhood. Vision loss may be permanent, and optic nerve damage can be advanced before it is noticed. Genetic counseling and low-vision aids may help; there is no proven cure.

topics.name: Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) Orders and Portable Medical Orders
topics.clinical_significance: A do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order tells clinicians not to attempt CPR if a person has cardiac arrest. By itself, it does not refuse other treatment. Portable medical orders, such as POLST forms in the United States, record broader choices about life-sustaining care and can follow a person across care settings. Clear, valid orders help emergency teams follow the person’s wishes; forms and rules vary by location.

topics.name: Dose-Response Relationships
topics.clinical_significance: A dose-response relationship shows how a drug’s effect changes as its dose changes. It helps guide the dose and schedule needed for benefit while limiting harm. Drugs differ in how much is needed to work and in their maximum effect, and people can respond differently. For drugs with a narrow safety margin, even a small dose increase may raise the risk of toxicity; age, pregnancy, and organ function can also affect the response.

topics.name: Double Outlet Right Ventricle
topics.clinical_significance: In double outlet right ventricle, both the aorta and pulmonary artery connect to the right ventricle, and a hole between the lower chambers is almost always present. The hole’s position and any narrowing of blood flow to the lungs affect oxygen levels and heart strain, so symptoms can range from bluish skin to heart failure and high pressure in the lungs. Surgery is needed, and the repair depends on the heart’s anatomy.

topics.name: Double Vision
topics.clinical_significance: Diplopia is seeing two images of one object. If it occurs when looking with one eye alone, it often comes from an eye problem such as a cataract or corneal defect. If it disappears when either eye is closed, the eyes are misaligned; causes can include nerve, muscle, or brain disorders. New double vision needs medical assessment, especially with pain, a drooping eyelid, pupil changes, a bulging eye, or other neurologic symptoms.

topics.name: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
topics.clinical_significance: Down syndrome is caused by extra genetic material from chromosome 21. It affects learning and development to varying degrees and can be associated with heart or digestive tract defects, hearing or vision problems, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, and some blood cancers. These conditions do not affect everyone, so regular health checks and care tailored to each person are important.

topics.name: Down's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Down syndrome is caused by extra genetic material from chromosome 21. It affects learning and development to varying degrees and can be associated with heart or digestive tract defects, hearing or vision problems, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, and some blood cancers. These conditions do not affect everyone, so regular health checks and care tailored to each person are important.

topics.name: Dracunculiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Guinea-worm disease is acquired by drinking water containing infected tiny crustaceans. About a year later, a mature worm causes a painful skin blister or ulcer, usually on the lower leg, and emerges through it. The wound can become infected, and longer-lasting disease can inflame joints and cause lasting stiffness. The worm is removed slowly; safe drinking water prevents infection.

topics.name: Drivers, Older
topics.clinical_significance: Age alone does not determine whether a person can drive safely. Changes in vision, movement, thinking, health, or medicines can affect driving and increase crash risk; older adults are also more likely to be seriously hurt in a crash. An individual assessment can identify needed support, driving changes, or restrictions. An office test or memory screen should not be the only basis for deciding whether someone can drive.

topics.name: Drowning
topics.clinical_significance: Drowning is breathing impairment after submersion in liquid and may be fatal or nonfatal. Low oxygen can cause respiratory or cardiac arrest and damage the brain and other organs. Lung injury and low body temperature may also occur, and breathing problems can worsen after rescue. Anyone with symptoms after a drowning event needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Drug Absorption
topics.clinical_significance: Drug absorption is the movement of a medicine from where it is given into the bloodstream. It affects how quickly a medicine starts working and how much reaches the blood, so it can change the dose or route needed. The route, drug form, food, gut conditions, and blood flow can affect absorption. Medicines given into a vein enter the blood directly.

topics.name: Drug Bioavailability
topics.clinical_significance: Bioavailability is how much and how quickly a drug or active metabolite reaches the bloodstream. It affects how quickly a medicine works and the amount needed; an intravenous dose enters the blood fully. Oral bioavailability may be reduced by incomplete absorption or breakdown in the gut or liver. Food, illness, surgery, and the drug formulation can change it. Differences matter most for drugs with a narrow safety margin.

topics.name: Drug Categories of Concern in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Some medicines have greater risks for older adults because age-related changes, health conditions, and taking several medicines can increase side effects or drug interactions. Possible harms include falls, confusion, bleeding, low blood sugar, and kidney problems. The Beers Criteria help identify medicines that may need to be avoided, used with caution, or adjusted for kidney function. They guide an individual medication review; they do not mean every listed drug is always unsafe.

topics.name: Drug Distribution to Tissues
topics.clinical_significance: Drug distribution describes how a medicine moves from the blood into body tissues. It affects how much reaches its target and how long its effects last. Blood flow, tissue binding, and the ability to cross cell membranes all matter. A drug stored in tissues may be released slowly and prolong its effects, while the blood-brain barrier limits entry of many drugs into the brain.

topics.name: Drug Eruptions and Reactions
topics.clinical_significance: Drug-related skin reactions range from mild rashes to severe, sometimes life-threatening reactions that can affect the skin and internal organs. They may begin days or weeks after a medicine is started, so the full recent medication history matters. Blistering or peeling skin, sores in the mouth or eyes, facial swelling, trouble breathing, or fever can signal a severe reaction that needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Drug Excretion
topics.clinical_significance: Drug excretion removes medicines and their breakdown products from the body, mainly through the kidneys and also through bile. Reduced kidney function can slow removal, allowing some drugs to build up, last longer, and cause side effects; doses may need adjustment. Some drugs pass into breast milk and can affect a nursing infant.

topics.name: Drug Hypersensitivity
topics.clinical_significance: Drug hypersensitivity is an immune reaction to a medicine, not an ordinary dose-related side effect. It can cause rash or hives, fever, organ injury, or life-threatening anaphylaxis; some reactions begin days or weeks after exposure. Careful review and documentation of the reaction help prevent harmful re-exposure and avoid incorrectly labeling a person as allergic, since not every reported drug reaction is immune-mediated.

topics.name: Drug Interactions
topics.clinical_significance: A drug interaction changes a medicine’s effect when it is used with another drug, food, or supplement. It may increase effects and cause toxicity, or reduce effects so treatment does not work well. Interactions can add to a drug’s effects or change its absorption, metabolism, or removal from the body. Reviewing prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products is important, especially for drugs with a narrow safety margin.

topics.name: Drug Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: Drug metabolism is the body’s chemical processing of medicines, mainly in the liver. It may inactivate a drug, make it easier to remove, or activate a prodrug. Genes, liver disease, age, and interacting medicines can change how fast a drug is processed, leading to levels that are too high and harmful or too low to work well. This can affect the dose needed.

topics.name: Drug Testing
topics.clinical_significance: Drug testing looks for selected drugs or their breakdown products in samples such as urine, blood, saliva, breath, or hair. Tests detect only substances they are designed to find; results depend on the sample and time since use, and screening tests can be falsely positive or negative. A positive result alone may not show how much or how often a person used a drug or whether they are impaired; interpretation may require confirmatory testing and clinical context.

topics.name: Drug Treatment in Children, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Children absorb, process, and remove medicines differently from adults, and these changes vary with age and growth. A child’s dose and dosing schedule must be chosen for the specific medicine; they cannot be set by simply scaling an adult dose according to weight. Some medicines also have age-specific risks or limited safety data, so correct dosing is important to avoid treatment failure or harm.

topics.name: Drug-Induced Autoimmunity
topics.clinical_significance: Some cancer medicines called immune checkpoint inhibitors can trigger autoimmune disorders, especially in hormone-producing glands. Problems may include pituitary inflammation, overactive or underactive thyroid, type 1 diabetes, or adrenal insufficiency. Blood sugar, hormone, and electrolyte tests can help detect these effects; treatment may require replacing hormones that are low.

topics.name: Drug-Induced Ototoxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Ototoxic medicines can damage the inner ear, causing hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or problems with balance. The damage may be temporary or permanent, and early symptoms may not reliably warn of injury. Risk can rise with high or prolonged doses, kidney problems, or use of more than one ototoxic medicine. Hearing checks and, for some drugs, blood-level monitoring can help reduce harm.

topics.name: Drug-Induced Pulmonary Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Many medicines and other substances can injure the lungs in different ways, causing problems such as asthma, lung inflammation or scarring, fluid buildup, bleeding, or pleural effusion. New breathing symptoms or abnormal lung tests during treatment may be due to a drug and can sometimes be serious. Finding and stopping the causative medicine or substance is central to treatment.

topics.name: Drug-Related Gastroenteritis and Chemical-Related Gastroenteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines and chemicals can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Antibiotics can lead to C. difficile infection, which may be severe and continue after the antibiotic is stopped. Laxative misuse or heavy-metal exposure can also cause serious illness, including electrolyte loss. Reviewing medicines and possible exposures helps identify the cause and guide treatment.

topics.name: Drugs and the Liver
topics.clinical_significance: Liver disease can change how drugs are processed, sometimes making usual doses have stronger effects. Medicines and supplements can also injure the liver. Mild liver-enzyme increases may cause no symptoms, while serious injury is uncommon but can cause jaundice or liver failure. Drug effects vary, so they may be harder to predict in people with liver disease.

topics.name: Drug–Receptor Interactions
topics.clinical_significance: Many medicines work by binding to receptors on or inside cells and changing cell activity. Whether a medicine activates or blocks a receptor, how strongly it binds, and how long it remains bound help shape its effects and side effects. Receptor changes during long-term use can reduce a medicine’s effect or cause serious symptoms if certain drugs are stopped suddenly.

topics.name: Dry Eyes
topics.clinical_significance: Dry eye disease causes burning, gritty irritation, light sensitivity, and fluctuating blurred vision that can interfere with daily tasks. It results from too few tears or tears that evaporate too quickly, and may occur with Sjögren disease or other conditions. Long-lasting, severe dryness can damage the cornea and, rarely, cause scarring, infection, or vision loss.

topics.name: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Becker Muscular Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited X-linked disorders cause progressive muscle weakness because dystrophin is absent or reduced. Duchenne muscular dystrophy usually begins in early childhood and progresses faster; Becker muscular dystrophy usually starts later and is milder. Both can affect the heart and breathing muscles, causing serious complications, especially in Duchenne disease.

topics.name: Duchenne's Muscular Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an inherited X-linked disease caused by a severe lack of dystrophin. It causes progressive muscle weakness that usually begins between ages 2 and 3 and often leads to loss of walking ability. Heart and breathing muscles can also weaken, causing cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure, which are major complications.

topics.name: Duncan Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Duncan syndrome (X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome) is an inherited immune disorder in which boys can have a dangerously abnormal response to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Infection may cause severe or fatal mononucleosis and liver failure; survivors may develop lymphoma, bone-marrow failure, or antibody deficiency. Early diagnosis matters because stem-cell transplantation can be curative before irreversible complications develop.

topics.name: Duodenal Obstruction
topics.clinical_significance: Duodenal obstruction blocks food and fluid from passing through the first part of the small intestine. Congenital forms can cause feeding problems and sometimes green (bilious) vomiting in newborns; imaging may show a characteristic “double-bubble” sign. Duodenal atresia and stenosis are linked with Down syndrome and other birth defects, and usually require surgical repair.

topics.name: Dupuytren Contracture
topics.clinical_significance: Dupuytren contracture is a gradual tightening of tissue under the skin of the palm, usually pulling the ring or little finger toward the palm. It can make it difficult to straighten the finger or lay the hand flat, limiting hand use. The condition often progresses over time, though the nodules and cords are usually painless.

topics.name: Dying Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Recognizing that a seriously ill person may be nearing the end of life allows the care team to discuss the likely course, understand the person’s wishes, and plan for future decisions and symptom relief. The timing of death is often hard to predict, especially with heart or lung disease, dementia, and frailty. Palliative care can improve comfort and quality of life alongside other treatment.

topics.name: Dying Patient, Symptom Relief for
topics.clinical_significance: Pain, breathlessness, nausea, constipation, confusion, and emotional distress are common near the end of life. Regular assessment helps guide care toward comfort, using cause-specific treatment when useful and avoiding tests that add burden without changing care. Because worsening illness can change how the body handles medicines, symptom-relief medicines need frequent review.

topics.name: Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: This older term is now generally covered by abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB): bleeding in nonpregnant reproductive-age patients that is unusually heavy, prolonged, irregular, or occurs between periods. Causes include problems with ovulation, uterine growths such as fibroids or polyps, and bleeding disorders. Heavy or prolonged bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia; identifying the cause also helps detect conditions such as endometrial hyperplasia or cancer.

topics.name: Dyshidrotic Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Dyshidrotic dermatitis causes itchy small blisters on the palms, sides of the fingers, or soles. Blisters may merge or break, leaving raw, crusted skin that can become infected. Flares may be linked to eczema, contact allergy, or irritants such as frequent water and detergent exposure. Despite its name, the condition is not caused by abnormal sweating.

topics.name: Dyslexia
topics.clinical_significance: Dyslexia is a learning disorder that mainly affects word recognition, decoding, reading fluency, and spelling. It can make school and other reading tasks difficult, but it does not mean a person has low intelligence. Focused reading instruction can build skills, although difficulties may continue into adulthood.

topics.name: Dyslipidemia
topics.clinical_significance: Dyslipidemia is an abnormal level or pattern of blood fats, such as high LDL cholesterol or triglycerides, or low HDL cholesterol. High LDL contributes to artery plaque and raises cardiovascular risk; very high triglycerides can cause acute pancreatitis. Low HDL is associated with cardiovascular risk, although the HDL level itself may not be the cause.

topics.name: Dysmenorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Dysmenorrhea is menstrual pain, usually cramping in the lower abdomen and sometimes spreading to the back or legs; nausea, diarrhea, or headache may also occur. The pain can disrupt school, work, and daily activities. Pain that starts later in life, persists beyond menstruation, or is accompanied by other pelvic symptoms may be due to a condition such as endometriosis or fibroids.

topics.name: Dyspepsia
topics.clinical_significance: Dyspepsia is recurrent pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen, often described as indigestion, burning, bloating, early fullness, or fullness after eating. Causes include functional dyspepsia, reflux, ulcers, medicines, and other disorders. Upper abdominal discomfort can sometimes signal heart-related reduced blood flow; breathlessness, sweating, or a rapid heartbeat during an acute episode is concerning. Weight loss, vomiting, bleeding, or trouble swallowing may point to serious disease.

topics.name: Dysphagia
topics.clinical_significance: Dysphagia is difficulty moving food or liquid from the mouth to the stomach. It can cause choking or aspiration into the lungs, leading to pneumonia, and may result in weight loss and poor nutrition. Sudden swallowing difficulty with new weakness may be due to stroke; progressive difficulty can signal an obstruction, including esophageal cancer, and inability to swallow anything may indicate a complete blockage.

topics.name: Dysphagia Lusoria
topics.clinical_significance: Dysphagia lusoria is difficulty swallowing caused by an unusual blood vessel pressing on the esophagus, most often an aberrant right subclavian artery. Symptoms may begin in childhood or appear later, sometimes as age-related changes increase pressure on the esophagus. CT or MRI can confirm the cause; many adults need no treatment, but surgery may be considered for significant symptoms or related aortic problems.

topics.name: Dysplastic Nevus
topics.clinical_significance: A dysplastic nevus is a benign atypical mole with an irregular shape or border and uneven color. Having atypical moles, especially many of them, is a marker of increased melanoma risk, but most melanomas arise in previously normal skin. Because an atypical mole can resemble melanoma, a changing or highly unusual lesion may need examination and sometimes biopsy.

topics.name: Dyspnea
topics.clinical_significance: Dyspnea is an uncomfortable sensation of difficult breathing. It may result from lung or heart disease, pneumonia, a blood clot in the lung, anemia, poor physical conditioning, or anxiety. Sudden or rapidly worsening dyspnea can signal a life-threatening problem, including a pulmonary embolism or heart attack.

topics.name: Dysproteinemias
topics.clinical_significance: In plasma-cell disorders, dysproteinemia often refers to excess monoclonal protein made by one clone of plasma cells. It may be a stable, symptom-free finding, but can also occur in multiple myeloma and related diseases. The abnormal cells or protein can impair immunity, damage organs such as the kidneys or heart, weaken bones, cause anemia, or increase bleeding.

topics.name: Dysproteinemias Causing Vascular Purpura
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal blood proteins can weaken or inflame small blood vessels, causing purpura (purple spots from bleeding under the skin). Depending on the cause, purpura may point to amyloidosis, cryoglobulinemia, an immune disorder, or very high immunoglobulin levels. Some forms can also cause ulcers, tissue damage, or bleeding elsewhere, so the skin finding may signal a wider blood or immune-system problem.

topics.name: Dystonias
topics.clinical_significance: Dystonia causes involuntary muscle contractions that produce twisting movements or abnormal postures; it may affect one area or many. It can be inherited or result from a brain disorder or medicines, especially antipsychotics and some anti-nausea drugs, so sudden unexplained symptoms may signal a medication reaction. Severe or widespread dystonia can limit movement and daily activities.

topics.name: Dysuria
topics.clinical_significance: Painful or burning urination is often due to bladder infection or urethritis, sometimes from a sexually transmitted infection, but can also result from stones, irritation, genital inflammation, or other urinary disease. Fever or flank pain may signal kidney infection. Recurrent symptoms, blood in the urine, pregnancy, or dysuria in men call for closer assessment because the cause may be more complex than a simple bladder infection.

topics.name: E. coli
topics.clinical_significance: E. coli is a common bacterium in the large intestine; most strains are harmless. Some cause diarrhea, including bloody diarrhea that can lead to hemolytic-uremic syndrome and kidney injury, while E. coli is also a leading cause of urinary tract infections. Less often, it causes bloodstream or other invasive infections, especially in newborns; drug-resistant strains are an important concern.

topics.name: E. coli Gastroenteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Different E. coli strains cause watery or bloody diarrhea, often with abdominal cramps. Shiga toxin–producing strains can cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome, which damages the kidneys and blood cells, especially in children and older adults. Most cases are managed with fluids; antibiotics are generally avoided until these strains are ruled out because they may raise the risk of this complication.

topics.name: Ear and Sinus Barotrauma
topics.clinical_significance: Rapid pressure changes, especially while diving, can injure the ear or sinuses when internal pressure cannot equalize. It may cause ear fullness or pain, hearing loss, ringing, dizziness, or sinus pain and congestion; severe ear injury can rupture the eardrum or damage structures involved in hearing and balance. New hearing loss or vertigo may signal inner-ear injury, while sinus barotrauma can cause nosebleeds and rarely affect nearby nerves or vision.

topics.name: Ear Disorders, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Common ear symptoms include pain, hearing loss, discharge, ringing, and vertigo. Evaluation also checks nearby head-and-neck structures because pain can be referred from the teeth, throat, jaw, or sinuses, and may include hearing and balance tests. Audiometry, vestibular testing, or imaging can help identify inner-ear, nerve, or structural disease, especially when there is hearing loss, vertigo, facial weakness, trauma, or persistent unexplained pain.

topics.name: Ear Foreign Body
topics.clinical_significance: A foreign object in the ear canal can cause pain, itching, temporary hearing loss, or infection; a retained object may lead to foul-smelling drainage. This is common in children, and deep or smooth objects can be difficult to remove without injuring the canal, eardrum, or tiny hearing bones. Organic objects such as seeds can swell when wet, making removal harder.

topics.name: Ear Problems, Approach to the Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Common ear complaints include pain, hearing loss, discharge, ringing, and vertigo. A focused history and examination of the ear and nearby head-and-neck structures help distinguish ear disease from pain referred from the teeth, jaw, or throat. Hearing and balance tests, and sometimes imaging, can help identify inner-ear, nerve, or structural problems; persistent unexplained symptoms may need further evaluation.

topics.name: Earache
topics.clinical_significance: Pain felt in the ear may come from an ear infection or pressure problem, or be caused by disease in nearby areas such as the teeth, jaw, or throat. Ongoing pain with a normal ear exam may be from a jaw problem or migraine; less often, especially in older adults, it can be an early sign of head-and-neck cancer. Finding the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: Early Pregnancy Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Early pregnancy problems include miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, and molar pregnancy. Bleeding or cramps can occur; a ruptured ectopic pregnancy can cause life-threatening internal bleeding. Pregnancy hormone tests and ultrasound help identify the pregnancy’s location and whether it is developing.

topics.name: Early Repolarization Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Early repolarization on an ECG is common and usually occurs without symptoms. Early repolarization syndrome is different: it is linked to dangerous ventricular rhythms, including ventricular fibrillation, and can cause sudden cardiac arrest. The syndrome is considered when the ECG pattern occurs with a history of serious ventricular arrhythmia or cardiac arrest.

topics.name: Easy Bruising
topics.clinical_significance: Easy bruising from purpura simplex is common and usually harmless; it reflects fragile small blood vessels and often occurs without other bleeding. Platelet and clotting tests are usually normal, and this form does not raise the risk of serious internal or surgical bleeding. Aspirin, blood thinners, corticosteroid exposure, low body weight, and sun exposure can increase bruising.

topics.name: Eating Behavior in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Children’s eating habits often vary with age, but persistent disordered eating can harm health and growth. Growth charts help show whether a child is growing as expected. Weight loss or failure to gain when expected, unusually rapid weight gain, or ongoing distress about body shape or weight may signal an eating disorder; these changes warrant assessment.

topics.name: Eating Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Feeding and eating disorders involve lasting changes in eating that disrupt nutrition or daily life and can harm physical health. Effects may include poor nutrition, major weight changes, and social or emotional difficulties. Severe disorders can cause dangerous fluid or salt imbalances, abnormal heart rhythms, and death.

topics.name: Ebola Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Ebola vaccines help prevent Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus, especially during outbreaks and in people at high risk of exposure. Vaccination can support outbreak control by protecting contacts of infected people. These vaccines do not protect against other Ebola virus species or Marburg virus.

topics.name: Ebstein Anomaly
topics.clinical_significance: Severity ranges from mild symptoms to serious problems in newborns. The misplaced, abnormal tricuspid valve may leak and reduce the right ventricle’s ability to pump blood. This can cause low oxygen levels, heart failure, or abnormal heart rhythms; some people have no symptoms until adulthood.

topics.name: Ebstein's Anomaly
topics.clinical_significance: Severity ranges from mild symptoms to serious problems in newborns. The misplaced, abnormal tricuspid valve may leak and reduce the right ventricle’s ability to pump blood. This can cause low oxygen levels, heart failure, or abnormal heart rhythms; some people have no symptoms until adulthood.

topics.name: ECG
topics.clinical_significance: A 12-lead ECG records the heart’s electrical signals through skin electrodes. It is especially useful for detecting abnormal rhythms and conduction problems and for quickly assessing possible acute coronary syndromes. It may show signs of reduced blood flow or a past heart attack, but results are interpreted with other clinical findings.

topics.name: Echinacea
topics.clinical_significance: Echinacea is used in supplements for colds and claimed immune support, but studies have not consistently shown that it prevents colds or shortens symptoms. It can cause mild side effects, allergic reactions in people sensitive to related plants, and interactions with some medicines. Its immune effects may be a concern in people with autoimmune disease, weakened immunity, or organ transplants.

topics.name: Echinococcosis
topics.clinical_significance: The tapeworm larvae form cysts, most often in the liver or lungs, which may grow for years before causing symptoms. A cyst can cause pain or organ problems, and rupture can trigger a severe allergic reaction. The less common alveolar form grows into nearby liver tissue and can cause liver failure.

topics.name: Echocardiography
topics.clinical_significance: Echocardiography uses ultrasound to show the heart’s chambers, valves, pumping, and blood flow. It helps detect valve problems, weak heart function, structural defects, and abnormal blood flow. Changes in heart-wall movement may also point to reduced blood supply or a heart attack.

topics.name: Economic Analyses in Clinical Decision Making
topics.clinical_significance: Economic analyses compare the costs and health outcomes of tests or treatments. They help clinicians and health systems judge how limited resources may produce the greatest health benefit. Results depend on which costs and outcomes are counted, the time period, and the assumptions used, so they support but do not replace clinical judgment or patient preferences.

topics.name: Ecstasy
topics.clinical_significance: Ecstasy usually refers to MDMA, a stimulant drug. Toxicity can cause dangerously high body temperature, low blood sodium, agitation, seizures, and abnormal heart rhythms; severe cases can lead to organ failure or death. Pills sold as Ecstasy may contain other drugs, making their effects unpredictable.

topics.name: Ectopic Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube. It may cause pelvic pain or vaginal bleeding, but early on there may be no symptoms. If it ruptures, severe internal bleeding and shock can occur. Ultrasound and blood tests for pregnancy hormone help determine the pregnancy’s location.

topics.name: Ectopic Supraventricular Arrhythmias
topics.clinical_significance: These abnormal rhythms start in the atria or nearby tissue above the ventricles. Many cause no symptoms, while others can cause palpitations or a fast heartbeat and may be linked to heart or lung disease. Frequent premature atrial beats are associated with a higher risk of atrial fibrillation and stroke, though this link does not prove they cause these problems.

topics.name: Eczema
topics.clinical_significance: Eczema, also called dermatitis, describes several types of skin inflammation. It commonly causes itching, redness, and scaling; long-lasting disease can thicken or crack the skin. Scratching may lead to oozing, crusts, or infection. Eczema is not contagious, and the term is often used for atopic dermatitis, one specific type.

topics.name: ED
topics.clinical_significance: Erectile dysfunction is difficulty getting or keeping an erection sufficient for sexual activity. Causes include blood-vessel, nerve, hormonal, medication-related, and psychological problems. When caused by impaired blood flow, it can be an early sign of cardiovascular disease.

topics.name: Edema
topics.clinical_significance: Edema is swelling from excess fluid in body tissues. Swelling in both legs or throughout the body can signal heart, liver, or kidney disease; swelling in one area may result from a blood clot, vein or lymph blockage, or infection. The pattern of swelling and other symptoms help point to its cause.

topics.name: Edema of the Residual Limb
topics.clinical_significance: Swelling can occur in the remaining limb even long after amputation. It changes the limb’s size and can make the prosthetic socket fit poorly or make the prosthesis hard to put on. A poor fit can increase pressure and friction, raising the risk of skin injury.

topics.name: Edwards Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy 18 usually causes severe developmental delay and multiple birth defects, often including serious heart defects. Early death is common: more than half of affected infants die in the first week, and fewer than 10% survive beyond the first year, although outcomes vary.

topics.name: Effects of Life Transitions on Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Retirement, moving, and bereavement can change an older adult’s income, social ties, daily life, and health. Difficulty adjusting may lead to isolation or depression. Some anxiety and sleep problems during grief are common and usually ease within months, but prolonged, intense grief can disrupt daily life and is linked to suicide risk and declining health.

topics.name: Effects of Liver Disease on Drug Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: Liver disease can change how medicines are absorbed, processed, and cleared, so a drug’s level or effect may rise or fall. The change depends on the drug and cannot be predicted reliably from liver test results alone. In chronic liver disease, greater sensitivity to opioids and sedatives means even small doses can sometimes trigger confusion or hepatic encephalopathy.

topics.name: Egyptian Ophthalmia
topics.clinical_significance: Egyptian ophthalmia is another name for trachoma, a contagious conjunctival infection caused by certain strains of Chlamydia trachomatis. It spreads through contact with infected eye or nose discharge, contaminated hands or objects, and, in some areas, flies. Repeated infection can scar the eyelids and cornea, turn the eyelashes inward, and cause permanent vision loss or blindness; trachoma remains a leading preventable cause of blindness worldwide.

topics.name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited connective tissue disorders commonly cause very flexible joints, stretchy fragile skin, easy bruising, and slow wound healing. Joint sprains and dislocations are common. Severity varies by type; in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, fragile arteries or organs may rupture, which can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Ehrlichiosis and Anaplasmosis
topics.clinical_significance: These tick-borne bacterial infections usually cause sudden fever, headache, muscle aches, and weakness; blood counts may be low and liver tests abnormal. Rash is less common with anaplasmosis than with ehrlichiosis. Severe illness can cause bleeding problems, brain involvement, seizures, or failure of several organs, especially in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Eighth Nerve Tumor
topics.clinical_significance: An eighth-nerve tumor, usually called a vestibular schwannoma or acoustic neuroma, is typically benign and slow-growing. It often causes gradual hearing loss in one ear and may also cause ringing, dizziness, or imbalance. As it enlarges, it can press on nearby nerves or the brainstem.

topics.name: Eisenmenger Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Eisenmenger syndrome is a serious, usually irreversible complication of a large unrepaired congenital heart shunt. High pressure in the lung arteries eventually reverses blood flow, sending low-oxygen blood to the body. It can cause bluish skin, breathlessness, fainting, abnormal heart rhythms, and right-sided heart failure; long-term low oxygen can lead to thickened blood, clots, stroke, or brain abscess.

topics.name: Eisenmenger's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Eisenmenger syndrome is a serious, usually irreversible complication of a large unrepaired congenital heart shunt. High pressure in the lung arteries eventually reverses blood flow, sending low-oxygen blood to the body. It can cause bluish skin, breathlessness, fainting, abnormal heart rhythms, and right-sided heart failure; long-term low oxygen can lead to thickened blood, clots, stroke, or brain abscess.

topics.name: EKG
topics.clinical_significance: A 12-lead EKG records the heart’s electrical signals through skin electrodes. It helps identify abnormal rhythms and conduction problems and quickly assess possible acute coronary syndromes. It may also show heart chamber enlargement or signs of reduced blood flow or a past heart attack.

topics.name: Elbow Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: Most elbow dislocations are posterior and follow a fall onto an extended arm. They can occur with fractures or injury to the ulnar or median nerve and, less often, the brachial artery, which may threaten hand movement or blood flow. Later stiffness and reduced elbow movement are common concerns.

topics.name: Elder Abuse
topics.clinical_significance: Elder abuse includes physical or psychological mistreatment, sexual abuse, neglect, and financial exploitation; several forms may occur together. It is linked to injuries, poorer physical and mental health, repeated hospital stays, financial loss, and early death. Abuse can be hard to detect because signs may be subtle and an older person may be afraid or unable to disclose it.

topics.name: Elderly, Day Care for
topics.clinical_significance: Adult day services provide older adults with medical monitoring, rehabilitation, cognitive support, meals, and social activities for part of the day. They can help maintain function, reduce isolation, and give family caregivers respite, which may help an older adult continue living in the community.

topics.name: Elderly, Hospital Care and the
topics.clinical_significance: Hospitalized older adults face increased risks of delirium, falls, medication-related harm, pressure injuries, and loss of mobility or independence. These complications can prolong recovery and make it harder to return home. Illness may also appear in less typical ways, which can make diagnosis more difficult.

topics.name: Electrical and Lightning Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Electrical current can burn or damage deep tissues and cause muscle breakdown, dangerous heart rhythms, or breathing to stop; the injury may be severe even when skin burns look mild. Lightning more often affects the heart and nervous system, causing cardiac arrest, loss of consciousness, or lasting neurologic problems. Its force can also cause traumatic injuries.

topics.name: Electrical Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Electrical current can cause burns and hidden damage to muscles, nerves, and organs. It may trigger dangerous heart rhythms or stop breathing; severe muscle damage can harm the kidneys. Skin burns do not show how serious internal injury is, and strong muscle contractions or falls can cause fractures and other injuries.

topics.name: Electrocardiography
topics.clinical_significance: An ECG is central to diagnosing abnormal heart rhythms and quickly assessing possible acute coronary syndromes, including heart attack. It can also show conduction problems, signs of current or past heart muscle injury, and some inherited rhythm disorders. Many ECG changes have more than one cause, so results need clinical context.

topics.name: Electrocardiography (ECG) in Pulmonary Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: In lung disease, an ECG can show strain or enlargement of the right side of the heart, including changes linked to pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary embolism. It may also show low electrical signals in COPD when overexpanded lungs lie between the heart and the electrodes. ECG findings support evaluation but do not replace other lung tests.

topics.name: Electroencephalography
topics.clinical_significance: EEG is important for diagnosing seizures, especially when episodes of altered awareness are hard to explain.
