It can also show patterns linked to sleep disorders or brain dysfunction. Some abnormal patterns are nonspecific, and a routine EEG may be normal even when a seizure disorder is suspected.

topics.name: Electrolyte Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal levels of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, or phosphate can disrupt brain, nerve, muscle, and heart function. Depending on the electrolyte and how quickly its level changes, effects may range from weakness or confusion to seizures or dangerous heart rhythms. Severe abnormalities can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Electromyography and Nerve Conduction Studies
topics.clinical_significance: These tests help find the cause of weakness, numbness, or other nerve and muscle symptoms. They can show whether the problem is in a nerve, muscle, or connection between them, and help locate the affected area. Nerve conduction results can also help distinguish damage to a nerve’s myelin covering from damage to the nerve fiber.

topics.name: Electronic Cigarettes
topics.clinical_significance: Nicotine-containing e-cigarettes can cause nicotine addiction, including in people who did not previously smoke. The inhaled aerosol carries fine particles and chemicals into the lungs. Adulterated products, especially some THC products containing vitamin E acetate, have been linked to severe vaping-related lung injury (EVALI).

topics.name: Electronic Health Records (EHR) and Clinical Decision Support
topics.clinical_significance: Electronic health records make patient information easier to share and review. Clinical decision support can add alerts and guideline-based prompts that may help prevent medication errors and guide testing or treatment. These tools can also add documentation work or make important details harder to find, and their overall effect on patient care remains uncertain.

topics.name: Electrophysiologic Studies (EPS)
topics.clinical_significance: EPS helps diagnose serious, sustained, or hard-to-record abnormal heart rhythms and assess the risk of sudden cardiac death. It can locate the rhythm’s source, assess the effects of antiarrhythmic medicines, and guide catheter ablation.

topics.name: Elevated Factor VIII, IX, and XI Levels
topics.clinical_significance: High levels of clotting factors VIII, IX, or XI are linked to a higher risk of venous blood clots, such as deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. High factor VIII can also occur with chronic inflammation or other systemic illness and is linked to recurrent clots. An elevated level is one factor in assessing clot risk.

topics.name: Embden-Meyerhof Pathway Defects
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited defects in red-cell glycolysis cause red-cell destruction and nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the most common defect. Severity varies; anemia may be accompanied by jaundice and an enlarged spleen, and severe cases may require repeated transfusions.

topics.name: Emergency Contraception
topics.clinical_significance: Emergency contraception lowers the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure. Oral pills mainly prevent or delay ovulation; an intrauterine device is more effective and can provide ongoing contraception. It does not end an established pregnancy, and effectiveness depends on the method and timing.

topics.name: Emergency Treatment of Arrhythmias
topics.clinical_significance: An arrhythmia that causes poor circulation can quickly become life-threatening. Urgent treatment depends on the rhythm and the patient’s stability: unstable fast rhythms may need cardioversion, while slow rhythms may need pacing or medicine. Rapid recognition helps direct appropriate treatment.

topics.name: Emerging Paradigms in Precision Dosing
topics.clinical_significance: Precision dosing uses patient-specific data, drug levels, and models of how the body handles medicines to tailor doses. These methods can help optimize treatment earlier, especially when drug handling varies or a medicine has a narrow safe range, balancing effectiveness with the risk of toxicity.

topics.name: Emery-Dreifuss Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited muscular dystrophy causes early muscle tightness (contractures), weakness, and muscle wasting. Heart involvement may cause abnormal electrical conduction, heart block, or cardiomyopathy, which can lead to sudden death. Cardiac complications are a major health risk.

topics.name: Emphysema
topics.clinical_significance: Emphysema destroys the walls between air sacs, reducing lung recoil and causing air trapping and persistent airflow obstruction. It is a form of COPD and can cause gradually worsening breathlessness. Severe disease may lead to respiratory failure or pulmonary hypertension; rupture of enlarged air spaces can cause a collapsed lung (pneumothorax).

topics.name: Encephalitis
topics.clinical_significance: Encephalitis is serious inflammation of brain tissue, often caused by a virus or an abnormal immune reaction. It can cause fever, headache, confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic problems. Severe cases may lead to coma, lasting brain damage, or death; some causes, including herpes simplex virus, have specific antiviral treatment.

topics.name: Encephalocele
topics.clinical_significance: An encephalocele is a skull defect through which the brain’s coverings and sometimes brain tissue protrude. Hydrocephalus and other congenital anomalies often occur; seizures and developmental or learning difficulties may also result. Prognosis depends on the defect’s size and location, and neurologic problems may persist after repair.

topics.name: Encopresis
topics.clinical_significance: Encopresis is repeated passage of stool outside the toilet in a child old enough for bowel control. It most often results from constipation: hard stool stretches the rectum, and softer stool can leak around it without the child being able to control it. Less often, another medical or psychological condition is involved. The problem can distress the child and family.

topics.name: Endemic Hemoptysis
topics.clinical_significance: Endemic hemoptysis is lung fluke infection (paragonimiasis), usually acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish. It may cause a chronic cough, chest pain, breathlessness, and blood in the sputum, resembling tuberculosis. If flukes reach the brain, seizures or other neurologic problems can occur.

topics.name: Endocardial Cushion Defect
topics.clinical_significance: Endocardial cushion defect (atrioventricular septal defect) is a congenital defect of the central heart wall and atrioventricular valves. Small or partial defects may cause few symptoms, but complete defects can cause heart failure and poor growth in infancy and, if unrepaired, pulmonary hypertension. The complete form is strongly associated with Down syndrome.

topics.name: Endocarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Endocarditis affects the heart’s inner lining, usually a valve. It may be infective, usually from bacteria or fungi, or noninfective, with sterile clots on the valve. Both forms can impair valve function or send emboli into the bloodstream; infective endocarditis can also damage valves or cause abscesses, heart failure, or stroke.

topics.name: Endocarditis, Noninfective
topics.clinical_significance: Noninfective endocarditis forms sterile platelet-and-fibrin deposits (vegetations) on heart valves, often with cancer, lupus, or another condition that increases clotting. The deposits can break off and block arteries, especially in the brain, or sometimes impair valve function; valve damage is uncommon. It must be distinguished from infective endocarditis because the causes and treatment differ.

topics.name: Endocervical Polyps
topics.clinical_significance: Endocervical polyps are common, usually benign growths in the cervical canal. Most cause no symptoms; some cause bleeding between periods or after sex, and infection can cause discharge. They rarely become cancerous, but an atypical polyp or persistent symptoms may need further evaluation.

topics.name: Endocrine Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Hormone disorders in children can affect growth, puberty, metabolism, and blood-sugar control. Recognizing them early helps identify problems that may interfere with healthy development or cause serious illness.

topics.name: Endocrine Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Endocrine disorders cause too much or too little hormone, often because a gland or its control by the brain is not working properly. Symptoms may be vague, so blood or other hormone tests are often needed to find the cause.

topics.name: Endocrine System, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The endocrine system uses hormones to coordinate organs and keep body functions in balance. A problem with a gland, hormone, or target tissue can affect several functions; the hypothalamus and pituitary regulate many of the glands.

topics.name: Endocrinology, Principles of
topics.clinical_significance: Endocrine principles explain how hormones and feedback between the brain and glands keep body functions balanced. Understanding these pathways helps locate the cause of hormone excess or deficiency and guide testing and treatment.

topics.name: Endogenous Eczema
topics.clinical_significance: Endogenous eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a long-lasting skin condition that causes itchy, inflamed patches and repeated flares. Scratching can thicken the skin, and bacterial skin infections are a common complication.

topics.name: Endolymphatic Hydrops
topics.clinical_significance: Endolymphatic hydrops is an abnormal buildup of fluid in the inner ear. It occurs in Ménière disease but does not always cause symptoms; when symptoms occur, they can include attacks of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, ringing in the ear, and ear pressure.

topics.name: Endometrial Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Endometrial cancer starts in the lining of the uterus and often causes abnormal bleeding, especially after menopause. Such bleeding needs medical evaluation; diagnosis is confirmed with a sample of the uterine lining. Many cases are found early and have a good outlook.

topics.name: Endometriosis
topics.clinical_significance: Endometriosis occurs when tissue like the uterine lining grows outside the uterus. It can cause painful periods, ongoing pelvic pain, pain during sex or bowel movements, and difficulty becoming pregnant. Symptoms do not always reflect how extensive the disease is.

topics.name: Endophthalmitis
topics.clinical_significance: Endophthalmitis is usually a bacterial infection inside the eye, often after eye surgery or a penetrating injury and, less often, from spread through the blood. It can cause severe eye pain and reduced vision. It is an emergency because delayed treatment can lead to permanent vision loss.

topics.name: Endoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal endoscopy uses a flexible camera to examine the digestive tract. It can help find the cause of symptoms, take tissue samples, and treat some problems—such as bleeding or narrowing—during the same procedure.

topics.name: Endothelial Keratoplasty
topics.clinical_significance: Endothelial keratoplasty replaces the inner cell layer of the cornea when it no longer keeps the cornea clear. It is used for conditions such as Fuchs dystrophy or corneal swelling after cataract surgery and can improve vision while leaving most of the cornea in place.

topics.name: Enteral Nutrition
topics.clinical_significance: Enteral nutrition provides formula through a tube into the stomach or intestine when a person cannot eat enough by mouth but the digestive tract still works. It can help prevent or treat poor nutrition; possible problems include aspiration, diarrhea, or a misplaced or blocked tube.

topics.name: Enteric Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is a serious whole-body infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually spread through food or water contaminated with feces. It causes high fever and may cause abdominal pain; severe illness can lead to intestinal bleeding or perforation.

topics.name: Enteritis Necroticans
topics.clinical_significance: Enteritis necroticans is a serious infection, usually caused by Clostridium perfringens type C, that destroys tissue in the small intestine. It can cause severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea, then progress to shock or bowel perforation. It needs urgent antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

topics.name: Enterobiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Enterobiasis is a pinworm infection that spreads when eggs on hands or objects are swallowed, especially among school-age children and people in the same household. It commonly causes itching around the anus and sometimes the vagina.

topics.name: Enteroceles
topics.clinical_significance: An enterocele occurs when the small intestine and its lining bulge down into the upper vagina because pelvic support tissues have weakened. It may cause vaginal pressure or a bulge, especially with straining, though mild cases may cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Enterococcal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Enterococci normally live in the gut but can cause urinary, blood, heart-valve, abdominal, skin, or wound infections. Some strains resist several antibiotics, so treatment depends on testing which medicines will work.

topics.name: Enterovirus Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Enteroviruses spread through stool, respiratory secretions, and contact with skin or mouth sores. They cause illnesses ranging from hand-foot-and-mouth disease to meningitis, paralysis, or heart inflammation; severe infection is more likely in newborns and people with antibody deficiencies.

topics.name: Enteroviruses
topics.clinical_significance: Enteroviruses are a large group of viruses spread mainly through stool-to-mouth contact and respiratory secretions. They cause illnesses ranging from hand-foot-and-mouth disease to meningitis, heart inflammation, and polio-related paralysis.

topics.name: Entropion and Ectropion
topics.clinical_significance: Entropion turns an eyelid inward, making the lashes rub the eye and potentially damage or scar the cornea. Ectropion turns the lower eyelid outward, which can cause excessive tearing and dry-eye irritation.

topics.name: Environmental and Occupational Pulmonary Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing dusts, chemicals, gases, fumes, or air pollution can cause lung disease, including asthma, COPD, and scarring of lung tissue. Identifying harmful exposures at work or at home is important because reducing or stopping exposure can prevent further harm.

topics.name: Environmental Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Environmental illness (idiopathic environmental intolerance) describes recurring symptoms that a person links to low-level environmental exposures. Symptoms may affect several body systems, but examination may show no clear physical cause; clinicians assess the symptoms and rule out other conditions.

topics.name: Environmental Pulmonary Disease, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Work or environmental inhalants such as dust, fumes, gases, and chemicals can injure the airways, lung tissue, or pleura and cause illnesses such as asthma or lung scarring. A careful history of home and workplace exposures helps identify causes and prevent further harm.

topics.name: Eosinophil Production and Function
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophils are white blood cells that take part in responses to parasites and help regulate allergic reactions. When eosinophils remain high for a long time, proteins they release can damage tissues.

topics.name: Eosinophilia
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophilia means more than 500 eosinophils per microliter of blood. It is often linked to allergies, medicines, or parasitic infections, but can also signal a blood disorder. Mild elevation usually causes no symptoms; counts of 1,500 per microliter or higher may damage organs if they persist.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophilic disorders involve abnormally increased eosinophils, often due to allergies, parasites, medicines, or a blood-cell disorder. If the increase is marked or lasts, eosinophils can inflame and damage organs.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Esophagitis
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophilic esophagitis is long-term immune-driven inflammation of the esophagus. It often causes trouble swallowing or food getting stuck; ongoing inflammation can narrow the esophagus. Diagnosis is confirmed by taking tissue samples during endoscopy.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Fasciitis
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophilic fasciitis is a rare disease that causes rapid, usually symmetric swelling and hardening of the tissue around muscles, most often in the arms and legs. Tightening can limit movement and lead to joint contractures; blood eosinophils may be high.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Granuloma
topics.clinical_significance: In the linked MSD topic, eosinophilic granuloma refers to pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, a lung disease strongly linked to cigarette smoking. It can cause cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain; stopping smoking is the main treatment.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)
topics.clinical_significance: EGPA (formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome) is a rare disease in which small and medium blood vessels become inflamed. It often occurs in people with asthma, nasal allergies, and high eosinophil levels, and can damage the lungs, sinuses, nerves, heart, kidneys, skin, or gut.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Pneumonia, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare lung illness in which eosinophils quickly build up in lung tissue. It causes fever, cough, and shortness of breath and can worsen rapidly into respiratory failure. Steroids are usually effective, and the outlook is generally good.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Pneumonia, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare lung disease in which eosinophils build up over weeks or months. It can cause cough, fever, wheezing, and worsening shortness of breath, and may resemble community-acquired pneumonia. It often returns but usually responds well to corticosteroids.

topics.name: Eosinophilic Pulmonary Diseases, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Eosinophilic pulmonary diseases are different conditions in which eosinophils build up in lung tissue. Causes include allergies, medicines, parasites, inhaled toxins, and systemic diseases, though sometimes no cause is found. A normal blood eosinophil count does not rule out eosinophils in the lungs.

topics.name: Ependymomas
topics.clinical_significance: Ependymomas are usually malignant tumors that arise from the lining of the brain’s fluid spaces or the spinal canal. In children, they often occur near the back of the brain and can raise pressure in the skull, causing headache, vomiting, or balance problems. Spinal tumors may cause back pain or problems with bladder or bowel control.

topics.name: Epidemic Parotitis
topics.clinical_significance: Mumps is a contagious viral illness spread through saliva and respiratory droplets. It usually causes fever and painful swelling of the parotid salivary glands; it can also inflame the brain, testicles, or pancreas. People can spread the virus before the gland swelling begins, and vaccination helps prevent infection.

topics.name: Epidemic Pleurodynia
topics.clinical_significance: Epidemic pleurodynia is a febrile illness usually caused by group B coxsackievirus. It causes sudden, often intermittent severe pain in the lower chest or abdomen; pain may return for several weeks. Rare complications include meningitis, testicular inflammation, or inflammation around the heart.

topics.name: Epidemic Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Epidemic typhus is a serious infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and usually spread between people by body lice. It causes prolonged high fever, severe headache, and rash; without antibiotic treatment it can be fatal. The infection can rarely return years later as Brill-Zinsser disease.

topics.name: Epidermal Inclusion Cyst [Epidermoid Cyst]
topics.clinical_significance: An epidermal inclusion cyst is a common, noncancerous skin lump filled with keratin. It often has a small central pore and is painless, but if it ruptures or becomes inflamed it can swell and hurt like an abscess.

topics.name: Epidermolysis Bullosa
topics.clinical_significance: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of rare inherited disorders caused by defects in proteins that hold skin layers together. Minor rubbing can cause blisters and wounds on the skin or mucous membranes; severity ranges from mild to life-threatening, and severe forms need specialized supportive care.

topics.name: Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita
topics.clinical_significance: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is a rare acquired autoimmune blistering disease, not an inherited form of epidermolysis bullosa. Antibodies against type VII collagen make the skin prone to blisters after minor injury; blisters often heal with scars, and the mouth or eyes may also be affected.

topics.name: Epididymitis
topics.clinical_significance: Epididymitis is inflammation of the tube behind the testicle, usually causing gradually increasing pain and swelling on one side of the scrotum. It is often caused by bacteria, including sexually transmitted or urinary bacteria. Sudden scrotal pain needs urgent assessment to rule out testicular torsion.

topics.name: Epiglottitis
topics.clinical_significance: Epiglottitis is usually a rapidly progressing bacterial infection that swells the epiglottis and nearby tissue. It can suddenly block the airway and become fatal. Severe sore throat, fever, drooling, trouble swallowing, or noisy breathing needs emergency care; the throat should not be examined until breathing support is ready.

topics.name: Epiphora
topics.clinical_significance: Epiphora means excessive or overflowing tears. It occurs when the eyes make extra tears, often from allergies, infection, or dry-eye irritation, or when tear drainage is blocked by a duct or eyelid problem. Blocked drainage can lead to infection of the tear sac.

topics.name: Epiphysitis of the Calcaneus
topics.clinical_significance: Epiphysitis of the calcaneus (Sever disease) is overuse-related pain at the heel’s growth area in active children, usually ages 9 to 14. Running or standing on tiptoe can worsen pain; Achilles tendon stretching and heel cups or pads often help.

topics.name: Epiretinal Membrane
topics.clinical_significance: An epiretinal membrane is a thin, scar-like layer that forms on the retina, often over the macula. If it contracts, it can wrinkle the retina and blur or distort central vision, making straight lines look wavy. Mild cases often need no treatment.

topics.name: Episcleritis
topics.clinical_significance: Episcleritis is a usually self-limiting, sometimes recurring inflammation of the thin tissue over the white of the eye. It causes a localized red patch and mild irritation or watering and usually does not threaten vision. Severe pain or light sensitivity may point to deeper eye inflammation.

topics.name: Epistaxis
topics.clinical_significance: Most nosebleeds are minor and start near the front of the nose, often after dryness or minor injury. Less common bleeds from the back of the nose can be severe; heavy or persistent bleeding, especially in someone with a bleeding disorder or taking blood-thinning medicine, needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Epithelioid Angiomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Epithelioid angiomatosis (bacillary angiomatosis) is a Bartonella infection that occurs in people with weakened immune systems. It causes red or purple skin growths that bleed easily and can spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, or bones. Antibiotics treat the infection.

topics.name: Erectile Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Erectile dysfunction is difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection sufficient for sexual activity. It may result from blood-vessel, nerve, or hormone problems, medicines, or psychological factors, and can signal underlying disease such as atherosclerosis or diabetes.

topics.name: Erosive Gastritis
topics.clinical_significance: Erosive gastritis is damage to the stomach’s protective lining that creates shallow sores. Common causes include anti-inflammatory medicines, alcohol, and severe physical stress from illness or injury. Mild cases may have no symptoms, but the condition can cause stomach bleeding, sometimes severely.

topics.name: Erysipelas
topics.clinical_significance: Erysipelas is a superficial bacterial skin infection that affects lymph vessels, often on the face or legs. It causes a tender, raised red patch with a clear edge and may cause fever or chills. It can recur and lead to lasting swelling; antibiotics are used for treatment.

topics.name: Erysipeloid
topics.clinical_significance: Erysipeloid is a skin infection caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, usually entering through a cut while handling fish, shellfish, or animal products. It causes a slowly spreading, raised purple-red patch, often on a finger or hand, and is treated with antibiotics. Rarely, it affects the blood or heart valves.

topics.name: Erythema Infectiosum (Parvovirus B19 Infection)
topics.clinical_significance: Parvovirus B19 usually causes a mild illness in children, with a low fever followed by bright-red cheeks and a lacy rash. It can briefly stop red blood cell production and cause severe anemia in people with sickle cell disease or other red blood cell disorders. Infection during pregnancy can cause severe fetal anemia, miscarriage, or stillbirth. People with weakened immunity may develop long-lasting anemia.

topics.name: Erythema Multiforme
topics.clinical_significance: An immune reaction that usually follows a herpes simplex infection; other infections or medicines can also trigger it. It causes target-shaped spots, often on the hands, feet, or face, and sometimes painful sores in the mouth. The rash usually clears on its own but may return.

topics.name: Erythema Nodosum
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the fat under the skin causes tender red or purple lumps, usually on the shins. It may be a sign of an underlying problem, especially a strep infection, sarcoidosis, or inflammatory bowel disease; sometimes no cause is found. The lumps usually fade like bruises over several weeks without scarring.

topics.name: Erythrasma
topics.clinical_significance: A bacterial infection of warm, moist skin folds, often between the toes, in the groin, or under the arms. It causes pink or brown patches that may have fine scaling. Risk is higher with diabetes, obesity, or weakened immunity. Topical antibiotics usually treat limited infection; widespread infection may need oral antibiotics, and it can recur.

topics.name: Erythroblastosis Fetalis
topics.clinical_significance: Antibodies from the pregnant person cross the placenta and destroy the fetus’s or newborn’s red blood cells, usually because their blood groups are incompatible (often Rh). This can cause severe anemia, swelling, heart failure, or fetal death; newborns may develop severe jaundice. Blood-type and antibody screening, plus Rh immune globulin for eligible Rh-negative pregnant people, prevents many Rh-related cases.

topics.name: Erythrocytosis, Secondary
topics.clinical_significance: An increase in red blood cells caused by another problem, such as low oxygen from lung disease or smoking, certain medicines, or rarely a tumor. It may cause headache, blurred vision, or shortness of breath, but some people have no symptoms. Care focuses on treating the cause; blood removal is rarely needed.

topics.name: Erythroderma
topics.clinical_significance: A severe condition in which redness and scaling affect most of the skin (over 70% of the body). It may result from psoriasis, dermatitis, a medicine reaction, or lymphoma. Loss of body heat and fluids can lead to infection and other serious complications; hospital care is often needed.

topics.name: Erythromelalgia
topics.clinical_significance: Repeated attacks of burning pain, warmth, and skin color change, usually in the hands or feet and less often the face or ears. Increased blood flow through small arteries causes the symptoms. Heat or exercise often triggers attacks, and cooling may ease them. It can be inherited or linked to another condition, including a blood or nerve disorder, and severe symptoms may be disabling.

topics.name: Erythropoietic Protoporphyria and X-linked Protoporphyria
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited disorders cause protoporphyrin to build up in the body. Even brief sunlight can trigger severe burning pain, itching, redness, and swelling of exposed skin, usually without blisters or scars. Gallstones are common, and about 1 in 10 people develop chronic liver disease that can progress to liver failure. X-linked protoporphyria may cause more severe skin and liver problems.

topics.name: Escherichia coli Infections
topics.clinical_significance: E. coli normally lives in the intestine, but some strains cause watery or bloody diarrhea; bloody diarrhea can lead to hemolytic-uremic syndrome, which may damage the kidneys. E. coli is the most common cause of urinary tract infection. Bloodstream infection and meningitis are uncommon, except in newborns, especially those born early.

topics.name: Esophageal and Swallowing Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These conditions affect swallowing or the esophagus, the tube that carries food to the stomach. They may block food, disrupt its movement, or allow stomach contents to flow back up. Depending on the cause, symptoms may include trouble or pain swallowing, food coming back up, or choking; food can sometimes enter the lungs.

topics.name: Esophageal and Swallowing Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Swallowing depends on coordinated muscles that move food from the throat through the esophagus into the stomach and keep stomach contents from flowing back. Narrowing or poor muscle movement can cause difficulty swallowing, food coming back up, or food entering the lungs. Tests may be needed to find the cause.

topics.name: Esophageal Aperistalsis
topics.clinical_significance: Achalasia is a disorder in which the esophagus does not move food normally and its lower valve does not relax during swallowing. Food and liquid build up, causing increasing difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and weight loss. Regurgitation at night can send food into the lungs. Treatment opens or weakens the valve but does not restore normal movement.

topics.name: Esophageal Atresia
topics.clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the esophagus ends in a pouch instead of reaching the stomach. It often also has an abnormal connection to the windpipe. A newborn may drool, cough, or turn blue during feeds and may develop pneumonia if food or saliva enters the lungs. Surgery is needed, and other birth defects are common.

topics.name: Esophageal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer of the esophagus (food pipe). The main types are squamous cell cancer and adenocarcinoma. Early disease may cause no symptoms; later, swallowing often becomes progressively harder and weight loss may occur. Tobacco and alcohol raise the risk of squamous cell cancer, while long-term reflux and Barrett esophagus raise the risk of adenocarcinoma. Outlook depends on the stage.

topics.name: Esophageal Disorders, Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: Infections of the esophagus are most often caused by Candida yeast, herpes simplex virus, or cytomegalovirus. They occur mainly in people with weakened immunity and can cause painful swallowing and chest pain. Treatment depends on the germ and uses antifungal or antiviral medicine.

topics.name: Esophageal Diverticula
topics.clinical_significance: An abnormal pouch in the esophagus that may trap food. Many cause no symptoms, but some cause difficulty swallowing or bring swallowed food back up. If food is regurgitated during sleep, it can enter the lungs. Most need no treatment; large or troublesome pouches may need surgery or an endoscopic procedure.

topics.name: Esophageal Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: Food or another swallowed object can become stuck in the esophagus, causing sudden difficulty or pain swallowing, drooling, or inability to swallow saliva. A complete blockage, sharp object, or button battery needs urgent removal because it can injure or perforate the esophagus. Endoscopy is often used to move or remove the object.

topics.name: Esophageal Motility Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Disorders that interfere with the esophagus moving food toward the stomach. They can cause difficulty swallowing, chest pain, or heartburn. Causes include achalasia, esophageal spasm, eosinophilic esophagitis, and some diseases affecting the whole body. Testing and treatment depend on the cause.

topics.name: Esophageal Rupture
topics.clinical_significance: A tear through the wall of the esophagus can occur during a procedure or after forceful vomiting. Leakage of food, saliva, or stomach contents into the chest can cause severe infection, shock, and death. This is a medical emergency that needs immediate treatment with antibiotics and usually endoscopic or surgical repair.

topics.name: Esophageal Tumors, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Benign growths in the esophagus are often found by chance and cause no symptoms. Larger growths may make swallowing difficult or cause discomfort, bleeding, or weight loss. Growing or symptomatic tumors may need removal; some rare types can become cancerous.

topics.name: Esophageal Web
topics.clinical_significance: A thin membrane across the upper esophagus can narrow the passage and make solid food hard to swallow. It is often linked to severe iron-deficiency anemia (Plummer-Vinson syndrome) and may also occur with celiac disease or other conditions. Treating anemia may help; persistent narrowing can be widened during endoscopy.

topics.name: Essential Fatty Acid Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: A rare lack of essential fats in the diet, most often in infants fed diets with too little fat. It can cause a scaly skin rash, hair loss, and a low platelet count; in children, it may impair intellectual development. Adding essential fats to the diet reverses the deficiency.

topics.name: Essential Thrombocythemia
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic bone-marrow disorder that makes too many platelets. It can cause blood clots or bleeding, though many people have no symptoms. Small-vessel problems may cause headache, vision changes, or burning pain in the hands or feet. Extremely high platelet counts can increase bleeding risk.

topics.name: Essential Thrombocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic bone-marrow disorder that makes too many platelets. It can cause blood clots or bleeding, though many people have no symptoms. Small-vessel problems may cause headache, vision changes, or burning pain in the hands or feet. Extremely high platelet counts can increase bleeding risk.

topics.name: Ethical Controversies in Genetics
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic tests and treatments can raise questions about privacy, informed consent, and discrimination based on genetic results. Prenatal screening can identify serious inherited disorders, but may also be used to choose nonmedical traits. Embryo gene editing and mitochondrial replacement may affect future generations, and cloning raises major safety and ethical concerns.

topics.name: Etiology of Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia develops when blood is lost, the body makes too few red blood cells, or red blood cells are destroyed too soon. Causes include bleeding, nutrient deficiencies, chronic illness or kidney disease, bone marrow problems, and inherited or acquired red blood cell disorders. Identifying the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: European Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: European (epidemic) typhus is a serious infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and spread mainly by body lice. It causes prolonged high fever, severe headache, and a widespread rash; severe cases can lead to shock, organ failure, or death. Prompt doxycycline treatment is important. The infection can rarely recur years later as Brill-Zinsser disease.

topics.name: Euthyroid Goiter
topics.clinical_significance: An enlarged, noncancerous thyroid gland with usually normal thyroid hormone levels. Most people have no symptoms other than neck swelling, but a large goiter can cause throat pressure, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, or trouble breathing. Causes include iodine deficiency, medicines, or problems making thyroid hormone; care depends on the cause and size.

topics.name: Euthyroid Sick Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: During severe illness, injury, or starvation, thyroid blood tests may show low T3 and sometimes low T4 even though the thyroid gland is functioning normally. TSH is usually normal or low. These changes usually resolve as the illness improves; treatment targets the underlying illness, not the thyroid hormone levels.

topics.name: Evaluating Drug Efficacy and Safety
topics.clinical_significance: Drug evaluation weighs whether a medicine improves symptoms, function, or survival against its possible harms. Clinical trials test benefits and side effects, but rare or long-term harms may appear only after wider use, so safety monitoring continues after approval.

topics.name: Evaluation of Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia is a finding, not a diagnosis; it signals an underlying problem that should be identified, even when symptoms are mild. Evaluation uses symptoms and history, blood counts, red blood cell size and appearance, and immature red blood cell counts. These help distinguish blood loss, poor cell production, or early cell destruction and guide further tests.

topics.name: Evaluation of Anorectal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation helps find the cause of anal or rectal symptoms such as bleeding, pain, swelling, discharge, or leakage. It usually includes a history and gentle examination; anoscopy or sigmoidoscopy, samples, or imaging may be used when needed.

topics.name: Evaluation of Breast Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Breast symptoms such as a lump, pain, or nipple discharge are often benign, but evaluation is important because breast cancer can look similar. A history, examination, and appropriate imaging help assess the cause; a biopsy may be needed if findings are suspicious.

topics.name: Evaluation of Ear Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of ear pain, hearing loss, discharge, tinnitus, or vertigo helps identify the cause. Examination and hearing or balance tests can distinguish ear problems from pain referred from nearby areas; imaging may be needed for selected symptoms or findings.

topics.name: Evaluation of Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain assessment helps identify its cause and severity and shows how it affects daily activities, sleep, and mood. Chronic pain needs a broader assessment, including related health conditions, to guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Ankle
topics.clinical_significance: Ankle evaluation helps identify fractures, ligament or tendon injuries, joint inflammation, and problems with nerves or blood flow. Examination checks swelling, tenderness, movement, stability, sensation, and pulses; joint fluid may be sampled when needed.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Dental Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Dental and oral exams can detect tooth and gum disease, signs of systemic illness that may first appear in the mouth, and oral cancer at an earlier stage. Evaluation of symptoms and risk factors helps guide dental care and follow-up.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Dermatologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Many skin conditions can be recognized by how lesions look and where they occur. A history and full skin examination help narrow the cause, detect skin cancer, and find clues to widespread illness; biopsy or other tests may be needed when the cause is unclear.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Elbow
topics.clinical_significance: Elbow examination can help distinguish joint arthritis from tendon or bursa problems. Loss of full extension may be an early sign of arthritis, while swelling or nodules can point to bursitis, gout, rheumatoid arthritis, infection, or another disorder.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Foot
topics.clinical_significance: Foot examination can reveal deformities, injury, skin sores, and problems with sensation or blood flow. Checking carefully between and under the toes is especially important in people with diabetes or nerve damage, who may not notice sores.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Gastrointestinal Patient
topics.clinical_significance: A focused history and examination often help identify the cause of gastrointestinal symptoms and show whether tests are needed. Blood in stool, difficulty swallowing, ongoing vomiting, fever, anemia, or weight loss are warning signs that call for further evaluation.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Hand
topics.clinical_significance: Hand examination helps locate problems affecting the joints, tendons, nerves, or other tissues. Testing movement, strength, and sensation can reveal issues such as tendon injury, trigger finger, or nerve compression and guide further evaluation.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Hip
topics.clinical_significance: A hip exam helps distinguish pain from the joint from pain in nearby tissues. Limping, pain with passive hip movement, or reduced inward rotation can point to joint disease; tenderness over the outer hip may suggest a bursa or tendon problem.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Knee
topics.clinical_significance: Knee examination can identify swelling or joint fluid, muscle wasting, instability, and tenderness from structures around the joint. Joint fluid may occur with arthritis, gout, or injury; sampling it can help determine the cause when needed.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Obstetric Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Routine obstetric evaluation monitors the pregnant person’s health and fetal growth and helps detect or prevent complications. It includes review of medical and pregnancy history, examination, and recommended tests; higher-risk pregnancies may need closer follow-up.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Ophthalmologic Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Eye evaluation measures vision and checks the eye to find the cause of vision changes, pain, redness, or discharge. Vision loss, eye pain, flashes or many new floaters, double vision, or loss of side vision may signal serious disease and need careful assessment.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient With a Liver Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: A history and examination help identify risk factors and signs of liver or bile-duct disease and guide testing. Because symptoms and individual liver tests may be nonspecific, results are considered together to assess the cause and severity.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient With Joint Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Joint evaluation helps distinguish problems within a joint from problems in nearby tissues and can point to causes such as injury, osteoarthritis, gout, infection, or systemic disease. The pattern of symptoms and examination findings guides testing; an unexplained joint-fluid collection may need sampling.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient with Nasal and Pharyngeal Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of nasal or throat symptoms helps distinguish inflammation or infection from injury, structural problems, or tumors. Examination of the nose, throat, and neck may reveal polyps, masses, or enlarged lymph nodes that need further assessment; tobacco or alcohol use and symptoms such as fever or weight loss add important clues.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient With Pulmonary Issues
topics.clinical_significance: History, physical examination, and often a chest x-ray help assess cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest pain, or coughing blood and decide what tests are needed. Further tests can check lung function, oxygen levels, and lung structure.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient With Renal Issues
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney problems may cause few clear symptoms until they are advanced, so evaluation uses urine tests and blood tests for creatinine, estimated filtration rate, and electrolytes to assess kidney function and damage. Imaging or other tests may be needed when findings suggest stones, blockage, cysts, or masses.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Patient With Urologic Issues
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of urinary pain, blood, retention, or changes in urine flow helps locate problems in the kidneys or other parts of the urinary tract. Urinalysis is central; blood in urine needs full evaluation, and suspected infection or blockage may require cultures or imaging.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Shoulder
topics.clinical_significance: Shoulder evaluation helps identify common rotator cuff problems and distinguish them from joint, tendon, or bursa causes of pain. Movement and strength tests can reveal rotator cuff weakness, and checking the neck can find pain referred from the spine.

topics.name: Evaluation of the Wrist
topics.clinical_significance: Wrist examination can help identify fractures, tendon problems, and joint or ligament injuries. Tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox can raise concern for a scaphoid injury, while targeted tests can point to tendon inflammation or joint instability.

topics.name: Evidence-Based Medicine and Clinical Guidelines
topics.clinical_significance: Evidence-based medicine combines the best available research with clinical expertise and patient preferences to guide care. Guidelines support consistent decisions, but clinicians must check that they fit the individual patient’s circumstances and values.

topics.name: Evoked Potentials
topics.clinical_significance: Evoked potentials measure the brain’s electrical response to visual, sound, or touch signals. They can reveal slowed or hidden damage along sensory pathways, such as optic nerve injury in multiple sclerosis, and help assess brainstem function when needed.

topics.name: Evoked Responses (Potentials), Measurement
topics.clinical_significance: Measuring evoked responses records how quickly and strongly the brain responds to visual, sound, or touch signals, showing whether sensory pathways are working. The test can uncover hidden pathway damage, help locate a problem, or assess brainstem function and, in some cases, outlook after coma.

topics.name: Exanthem Subitum
topics.clinical_significance: Roseola, usually caused by human herpesvirus 6B and sometimes by human herpesvirus 7, causes sudden high fever in young children, followed by a short-lived rash as the fever falls. Febrile seizures can occur; encephalitis is rare.

topics.name: Excessive Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Prolonged bleeding after small cuts, frequent nosebleeds, heavy periods, or unexplained bruising can signal a problem with platelets, clotting factors, or blood vessels. Finding the cause matters because severe bleeding can be dangerous and treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Repeated skin picking can cause sores, scarring, bleeding, and skin infections. It may cause shame or distress and interfere with daily life; recognizing the disorder can help people get effective treatment.

topics.name: Exercise
topics.clinical_significance: Regular exercise can improve heart and lung fitness, strength, mood, and daily function, and lower the risk of some chronic diseases and falls. The type and amount should fit a person’s health and fitness because unsuitable or excessive exercise can cause injury or worsen some conditions.

topics.name: Exercise, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Regular exercise can improve strength, heart and lung fitness, blood sugar control, balance, and daily function. It can help prevent some diseases and support rehabilitation; exercise plans should fit a person’s health and fitness and allow enough recovery to reduce injury risk.

topics.name: Exercise Testing for Pulmonary Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Exercise tests help find why a person becomes short of breath or cannot tolerate activity. The 6-minute walk test measures overall walking ability, while cardiopulmonary exercise testing can help show whether heart, lung, metabolic, or muscle problems limit exercise and guide treatment, rehabilitation, or surgical assessment.

topics.name: Exercise-Induced Cardiac Remodeling
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term intense training can enlarge and thicken the heart and slow the resting pulse while heart function remains normal. Recognizing this usually harmless adaptation helps distinguish it from serious heart disease, which can cause similar findings and needs evaluation.

topics.name: Exfoliative Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: When redness covers more than 70% of the skin, heat and fluid loss can occur, and infection may develop. Erythroderma can be life-threatening, so prompt medical assessment is often needed to find and treat the cause, such as a skin disease or medicine reaction.

topics.name: Exhibitionism
topics.clinical_significance: Exhibitionistic interests alone do not mean a person has a disorder. Exhibitionistic disorder involves intense, repeated sexual urges about exposing oneself to an unsuspecting person for at least 6 months, with either acting on the urges toward someone who does not consent or significant distress or problems in daily life. Nonconsensual exposure can harm others.

topics.name: Exhibitionistic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: This disorder involves intense, repeated sexual urges about exposing oneself to an unsuspecting person for at least 6 months. It is diagnosed when the person acts on the urges with someone who does not consent or the urges cause significant distress or problems in daily life. Treatment may include psychotherapy and, in some cases, medicine.

topics.name: Exophthalmos
topics.clinical_significance: Bulging of one or both eyes can be a sign of thyroid eye disease, infection, bleeding, or a tumor. Sudden bulging, eye pain or redness, fever, double vision, or reduced vision needs urgent evaluation because the cause may threaten sight and the exposed cornea can dry or become damaged.

topics.name: Explosives and Blast Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Blast waves, flying debris, or being thrown can cause severe injuries, including lung damage, internal bleeding, brain injury, hearing loss, burns, and crush injuries. Some injuries are hidden or worsen later, so people exposed to a significant blast need prompt trauma assessment and monitoring.

topics.name: External Ear Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: External ear problems can cause pain, itching, discharge, or temporary hearing loss from infection, skin inflammation, or blockage. Severe infection can spread to the bone around the ear, especially in people with diabetes or a weakened immune system, so persistent severe pain or discharge needs medical assessment.

topics.name: External Ear Obstructions
topics.clinical_significance: Ear-canal blockage is most often due to earwax, but can also come from a foreign object, scar tissue, or a growth. It may cause itching, pain, or temporary hearing loss; careful removal is important because attempts can injure the canal or eardrum.

topics.name: External Ear Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Injury to the outer ear can cause cuts or a blood collection over the cartilage. A hematoma needs prompt drainage to protect the cartilage and prevent permanent deformity; bite wounds also carry a risk of serious infection.

topics.name: External Otitis (Acute)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute otitis externa is usually a bacterial infection of the ear canal, often after water exposure or canal injury. It causes ear pain and drainage, and swelling can temporarily reduce hearing. In older adults and people with diabetes or weakened immunity, infection can rarely spread to the bone around the ear and become dangerous.

topics.name: Extraintestinal Protozoa
topics.clinical_significance: Extraintestinal protozoa infect tissues or organs outside the gut and include malaria, Chagas disease, leishmaniasis, and toxoplasmosis. Some can seriously affect the brain, heart, liver, lungs, or skin; identifying the parasite and relevant exposures is important because these infections need different treatments.

topics.name: Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis (TB)
topics.clinical_significance: TB can spread beyond the lungs to lymph nodes, bones, kidneys, the abdomen, heart, or brain, so symptoms depend on the affected area. TB meningitis and widespread TB can be fatal; early diagnosis matters, and treatment usually requires several TB medicines for at least 6 months.

topics.name: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing in substances such as mold, bird proteins, or workplace dust can trigger an immune reaction that inflames the lungs. It may cause cough, shortness of breath, fever, or fatigue; continued exposure can cause lasting lung scarring, so finding and avoiding the trigger is important.

topics.name: Eye Defects and Conditions in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Some eye problems in children can interfere with vision development; untreated amblyopia can cause lasting vision loss. Early screening and assessment can detect treatable causes, such as misaligned eyes or cataracts, and identify rare serious disorders.

topics.name: Eye Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Eye pain can come from a surface injury or infection, inflammation inside the eye, glaucoma, or pain referred from nearby areas. Pain with reduced vision, strong light sensitivity, fever, a bulging eye, limited eye movement, or halos with nausea needs prompt assessment because some causes can threaten sight.

topics.name: Eye Symptoms, Other
topics.clinical_significance: Dryness, discharge, halos, color changes, and blind spots can come from surface problems, medicines, migraine, or eye disease. New blind spots or halos with pain, headache, or nausea need prompt assessment because causes such as acute glaucoma can threaten vision.

topics.name: Eye Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Eye trauma can damage the cornea, lens, retina, optic nerve, or tissues around the eye and may cause lasting vision loss, even when the injury looks minor. Chemical exposures need immediate flushing; suspected penetrating injuries need emergency care, with a protective shield and no pressure on the eye.

topics.name: Eye Trauma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Eye trauma can injure the eyeball, nearby tissues, or the orbit, and internal damage may threaten vision even when the outside looks relatively normal. Prompt assessment of vision, pupils, eye movement, and possible bleeding or foreign bodies helps identify injuries that need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Eyelid and Lacrimal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Eyelid and tear-drainage disorders can cause irritation, swelling, infection, excess tearing, or damage to the eye surface. Most are treatable, but a persistent eyelid lump needs assessment because some growths are cancers, and a blocked tear duct can lead to infection of the tear sac.

topics.name: Eyelid Contusions and Lacerations
topics.clinical_significance: A black eye is often mainly cosmetic, but severe trauma can cause bleeding behind the eye and pressure that threatens vision. Every eyelid injury needs an eye check; cuts through the lid edge, inner corner, or full thickness may damage eyelid or tear-drainage structures and need specialist repair.

topics.name: Eyelid Growths
topics.clinical_significance: Most eyelid growths are benign, but some are skin cancers. A persistent or treatment-resistant lump, especially one that ulcerates or causes eyelash loss, needs examination and may require biopsy.

topics.name: Eyelid Swelling
topics.clinical_significance: Eyelid swelling can result from allergy, local inflammation or infection, or fluid buildup from a systemic illness. Fever, a bulging eye, reduced vision, or painful or limited eye movement can signal a dangerous infection around the eye, so urgent assessment is needed.

topics.name: Fabry Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Fabry disease is an inherited lack of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, which causes a fatty substance to build up in cells. It can cause burning pain in the hands and feet, skin spots, and progressive kidney, heart, or brain blood-vessel problems; diagnosis matters because specific treatments are available.

topics.name: Fabry's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Fabry disease is an inherited enzyme deficiency that causes a fatty substance to build up in cells and can progressively damage the kidneys, heart, and blood vessels in the brain. Enzyme or DNA testing confirms the diagnosis and helps guide disease-specific treatment.

topics.name: Facial Nerve Palsy
topics.clinical_significance: Facial nerve palsy weakens the upper and lower parts of one side of the face. New facial weakness needs prompt assessment to distinguish a nerve palsy from stroke or other causes. If the eye cannot close, the cornea can dry and become damaged, so it needs protection.

topics.name: Facial Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Severe facial trauma can cause fractures, major bleeding, or swelling that blocks the airway, and may occur with eye, brain, or neck injuries. Rapid assessment prioritizes breathing and bleeding, then checks vision and facial bones for injuries needing urgent treatment.

topics.name: Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited muscle disease usually begins by age 20 with slowly worsening weakness of the face and shoulder muscles; severity ranges from mild to disabling. Hearing loss and retinal blood-vessel changes can also occur, so diagnosis and eye monitoring are important.

topics.name: Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another
topics.clinical_significance: A caregiver deliberately falsifies or causes illness in a person in their care, usually a child. This is a form of abuse that can cause serious injury or death; the diagnosis applies to the caregiver, while the affected person needs protection.

topics.name: Factitious Disorder Imposed on Self
topics.clinical_significance: A person deliberately fakes or causes symptoms in themselves without an obvious external reward, often to take on the sick role. Recognizing this mental health disorder can prevent repeated, unnecessary tests or treatment and support appropriate psychiatric care.

topics.name: Factor V Resistance to Activated Protein C (APC)
topics.clinical_significance: Factor V resistance to activated protein C weakens a natural brake on blood clotting and increases the risk of venous clots, such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The risk is greater when both copies of the factor V gene carry the mutation.

topics.name: Factors Affecting Gene Expression
topics.clinical_significance: Factors that affect gene expression help explain why people with the same gene change may have different symptoms, severity, or no symptoms. They can also make a genetic condition appear to skip a generation, so they matter when interpreting family histories and estimating inherited risk.

topics.name: Factors Affecting Response to Medications
topics.clinical_significance: Age, body size, genes, illness, food, and other medicines can change how a medicine is absorbed, processed, removed, or acts in the body. As a result, the same dose may be less effective or cause harmful effects in one person, making these factors important when choosing and dosing medicines.

topics.name: Factors Facilitating Microbial Invasion
topics.clinical_significance: Microbial traits that help pathogens attach, spread through tissue, or evade immune defenses can make infections more likely or severe. Antimicrobial resistance and weakened host defenses can also let infections persist or recur, which can make treatment harder.

topics.name: Failure to Thrive
topics.clinical_significance: Now usually called growth and weight faltering, this means a child is not gaining weight or growing as expected. It can signal inadequate nutrition due to a medical condition or environmental factors; if prolonged, especially in infancy, it can delay physical and cognitive development.

topics.name: Fallopian Tube Torsion
topics.clinical_significance: Twisting of the fallopian tube can interrupt its blood supply, causing ischemia and possible tissue damage. It is a gynecologic emergency that typically causes sudden, severe pelvic pain, often with nausea or vomiting, and may require urgent surgery.

topics.name: Falls in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Falls in older adults can cause fractures, head injuries, disability, and death. Even without major injury, fear of falling can reduce activity and independence, and a previous fall raises the risk of another fall.

topics.name: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited condition causes many precancerous polyps in the colon and rectum. Nearly all untreated people develop colorectal cancer, often before age 40; preventive colon surgery greatly reduces this risk, but ongoing checks are still needed because polyps and cancers can occur elsewhere in the digestive tract.

topics.name: Familial Endocrine Adenomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Familial endocrine adenomatosis, also called multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN), is a group of inherited syndromes in which several hormone-producing glands develop tumors or overgrowth. These can cause excess hormones, and some tumors are cancerous; early recognition helps identify affected relatives and detect tumors.

topics.name: Familial Hibernian Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Familial Hibernian fever, now called TNF receptor–associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS), is an inherited inflammatory disorder that causes recurrent, prolonged fever attacks with shifting muscle pain and rash, sometimes with abdominal or chest pain. Ongoing inflammation can lead to AA amyloidosis and kidney damage.

topics.name: Familial Mediterranean Fever
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited disorder causes short attacks of fever, often with severe abdominal pain and sometimes chest or joint pain. Repeated inflammation can cause amyloid protein to build up in the kidneys and damage them; daily colchicine prevents attacks and this complication in most people.

topics.name: Familial Periodic Paralysis
topics.clinical_significance: Familial periodic paralysis causes repeated attacks of muscle weakness or temporary paralysis, often after exercise or meals. Blood potassium may be low, high, or normal depending on the type; Andersen-Tawil syndrome, one form, can also cause dangerous abnormal heart rhythms.

topics.name: Family Caregiving for Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Family caregiving can help an older adult remain at home, but heavy care needs can cause caregiver stress, illness, exhaustion, and isolation, and may increase the risk of neglect or abuse. Support and respite services can help protect both the caregiver’s health and the older adult’s well-being.

topics.name: Family Planning
topics.clinical_significance: Family planning helps people decide whether and when to become pregnant. Contraception can prevent unintended pregnancy, while preconception care can identify health risks and support a safer pregnancy.

topics.name: Famine Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Famine fever is an older name for relapsing fever, a Borrelia infection spread by body lice or ticks. It causes repeated bouts of high fever with periods of improvement; louse-borne disease can be severe and may cause heart or liver complications.

topics.name: Fanconi Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: The kidney’s proximal tubules fail to reclaim glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate, amino acids, and salts, so these are lost in urine. This can cause blood acidity and electrolyte problems, rickets or weak bones, muscle weakness, and poor growth in children; some causes can lead to kidney failure.

topics.name: Fascioliasis
topics.clinical_significance: Infection with liver flukes, usually after eating contaminated watercress or other aquatic plants. During migration through the liver it can cause fever, abdominal pain, liver enlargement, and high eosinophils; chronic infection can inflame or block bile ducts, causing jaundice or pancreatitis.

topics.name: Fasciolopsiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Fasciolopsiasis is an intestinal infection with the fluke Fasciolopsis buski, usually acquired from contaminated water or aquatic plants. Many infections cause no symptoms, but heavy infection can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, poor nutrient absorption, and protein loss that leads to swelling or fluid in the abdomen.

topics.name: Fatal Drowning
topics.clinical_significance: Fatal drowning is death after breathing is impaired by submersion or immersion in liquid. The resulting lack of oxygen can injure the brain, heart, lungs, and other organs.

topics.name: Fatal Familial Insomnia
topics.clinical_significance: Fatal familial insomnia is a rare inherited prion disease that progressively disrupts sleep and brain function, causing problems with thinking, balance, and body functions such as heart rate and blood pressure. It is fatal, often within several years, and care is supportive.

topics.name: Fatal Insomnia
topics.clinical_significance: Fatal insomnia is a rare prion disease that occurs in inherited and sporadic forms. It causes worsening brain function and coordination, with severe sleep problems especially in the inherited form, and is fatal within months to years; care is supportive.

topics.name: Fatigue
topics.clinical_significance: Fatigue is a lack of energy that makes it hard to start or continue activities and creates a need to rest. It can follow exertion, stress, or too little sleep, but can also be a sign of anemia, infection, endocrine or organ disease, medication effects, or a mood disorder.

topics.name: Fatty Acid and Glycerol Metabolism Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: These rare inherited disorders disrupt the body’s use of fatty acids, glycerol, or ketones for energy. Depending on the defect, fasting can trigger dangerous low blood sugar, acid buildup, muscle or heart injury, or liver problems; metabolic crises can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Febrile Seizures
topics.clinical_significance: Febrile seizures occur in children 6 months to 5 years old who have a fever but no brain infection or previous seizure without fever. Most are simple and do not cause lasting neurologic problems, though they may recur and slightly increase the later risk of epilepsy; prolonged or complex seizures can injure the brain.

topics.name: Fecal Incontinence
topics.clinical_significance: Fecal incontinence is involuntary passage of stool. It may be temporary with diarrhea or stool blockage, or persistent because of injury or disease affecting the anus, rectum, spinal cord, nerves, or awareness of bowel movements.

topics.name: Feeding and Eating Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Feeding and eating disorders cause persistent changes in eating or eating-related behavior that can disrupt nutrition and harm physical health or daily functioning. The effects vary by disorder and may become serious.

topics.name: Felon
topics.clinical_significance: A felon is a bacterial infection in the soft tissue at the fingertip. It can form a closed pocket of pus that puts pressure on nearby tissue and can damage it; without prompt treatment, infection may spread to the bone, joint, or tendons.

topics.name: Female Circumcision
topics.clinical_significance: Female circumcision (female genital mutilation or cutting) is a nonmedical procedure that injures or removes genital tissue and has no health benefit. It can cause bleeding and infection, chronic pain, urinary or sexual problems, childbirth complications, and psychological harm.

topics.name: Female Genital Cutting
topics.clinical_significance: Female genital cutting is a nonmedical procedure that injures or removes genital tissue and has no health benefit. Depending on the procedure, complications may include bleeding, infection, menstrual or urinary problems, chronic pain, pain or injury during sex, tearing or heavy bleeding during childbirth, and psychological harm.

topics.name: Female Genital Mutilation
topics.clinical_significance: Female genital mutilation is a harmful procedure that injures or removes external genital tissue for nonmedical reasons. It has no health benefit. Depending on the procedure, it may cause bleeding, infection, menstrual or urinary problems, chronic pain, painful sex, childbirth injury or bleeding, and psychological harm.

topics.name: Female Orgasmic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Female orgasmic disorder is persistent absent, delayed, infrequent, or much less intense orgasm despite sexual arousal and adequate stimulation, when it causes personal or relationship distress. It may be linked to medicines, stress or relationship problems, or nerve or genital conditions.

topics.name: Female Pelvic Mass
topics.clinical_significance: A pelvic mass may be benign or cancerous and can arise from reproductive or other pelvic organs. It may cause no symptoms or cause pain, pressure, bleeding, or bowel or urinary changes, so evaluation is needed to find the cause and assess cancer risk.

topics.name: Female Pelvic Mass in Children
topics.clinical_significance: A pelvic mass in a child may be a cyst, infection, birth-related condition, or tumor; some tumors are cancerous. Evaluation is needed to find the cause and check for ovarian twisting, which may need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Female Pelvic Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic pain can come from reproductive organs, the bladder, bowel, or pelvic muscles and may be sudden or long-lasting. Pain lasting more than 6 months is considered chronic. Sudden pain can signal an emergency, such as an ectopic pregnancy or ovarian twisting, while ongoing pain needs evaluation to find its cause.

topics.name: Female Reproductive Endocrinology
topics.clinical_significance: Hormones from the brain and pituitary gland regulate ovarian estrogen and progesterone. These hormones control puberty, ovulation, menstrual cycles, and changes in the uterus, vagina, and breasts; problems in this system can affect menstruation and fertility.

topics.name: Female Sexual Function and Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Female sexual dysfunction includes problems with desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain during sex. It is considered a disorder when it causes personal or relationship distress. Physical, hormonal, medication, and emotional factors can contribute and often overlap.

topics.name: Femoral Head Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Femoral head fractures are uncommon, serious injuries often linked to hip dislocation. They can damage the bone’s blood supply or joint surface, leading to bone death (osteonecrosis), arthritis, and lasting loss of hip function. If the hip is dislocated, it needs urgent treatment.

topics.name: Femoral Neck Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Femoral neck fractures, especially when displaced, can interrupt blood flow to the femoral head, leading to bone death (osteonecrosis), failure to heal, or arthritis. They are common in older adults with osteoporosis; most need surgery so patients can move sooner and avoid serious problems from prolonged bed rest.

topics.name: Femoral Shaft Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Femoral shaft fractures usually follow severe trauma and can cause major bleeding into the thigh—up to 1.5 liters per fracture—and sometimes shock. The leg is often swollen, deformed, and unstable. Urgent splinting and surgery are usually needed, and clinicians check for other injuries.

topics.name: Femoral Torsion (Twisting)
topics.clinical_significance: Femoral torsion turns the thighbone inward or outward. It is common in newborns and often improves as children grow. Marked torsion that limits walking may need orthopedic care; pronounced outward torsion at birth should be checked for hip dislocation.

topics.name: Fertility Awareness‒Based Methods of Contraception
topics.clinical_significance: These methods track menstrual cycles or signs such as cervical mucus to estimate fertile days and avoid sex then. They need careful, ongoing tracking and have relatively high pregnancy rates with typical use; they do not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Fertilization and Development of the Embryo
topics.clinical_significance: Fertilization usually occurs in a fallopian tube, and the developing embryo later implants in the uterus. Most organs form early in pregnancy, when exposure to harmful substances can cause birth defects; the brain and spinal cord continue developing throughout pregnancy.

topics.name: Fetal Alcohol Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Fetal alcohol syndrome results from alcohol exposure before birth and can cause poor growth, characteristic facial features, and lasting cognitive problems, sometimes including severe intellectual disability. Prenatal alcohol exposure also increases the risks of miscarriage and low birth weight. No safe amount is known, so alcohol should be avoided during pregnancy.

topics.name: Fetal Demise
topics.clinical_significance: Fetal demise means fetal death before or during birth. At or after 20 weeks in the United States, or after 28 weeks by the World Health Organization definition, it is classified as stillbirth; earlier loss is generally called miscarriage. Causes may involve the mother, placenta, or fetus, but many stillbirths remain unexplained. A prior stillbirth raises the risk in a later pregnancy.

topics.name: Fetal Monitoring During Labor and Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Fetal heart rate monitoring, often alongside contractions, helps detect possible fetal distress so clinicians can respond or expedite delivery. In low-risk labor, routine continuous electronic monitoring has not been shown to reduce overall deaths and can increase cesarean delivery because of false alarms.

topics.name: Fetal Presentation, Position, and Lie (Including Breech Presentation)
topics.clinical_significance: These terms describe which fetal part leads and how the fetus lies in the uterus. Breech or transverse lie can make vaginal birth difficult and raise the risk of cord compression, injury, or low oxygen, so checking before delivery helps plan repositioning or cesarean birth.

topics.name: Fetishism
topics.clinical_significance: Fetishism is sexual arousal focused on an inanimate object or a specific non-genital body part. It is a disorder only when intense, recurring urges or behavior last at least 6 months and cause significant distress or interfere with daily life; many people with fetishes do not meet these criteria.

topics.name: Fetishistic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Fetishistic disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from an inanimate object or a specific non-genital body part. Diagnosis requires that this pattern last at least 6 months and cause significant distress or interfere with daily functioning; fetishism alone is not a disorder.

topics.name: Fetor Oris
topics.clinical_significance: Halitosis is frequent or persistent unpleasant breath odor. Most cases come from the mouth, especially bacteria on the tongue, plaque, or gum disease; dry mouth, smoking, and some foods can contribute. Less often, it is linked to nose, lung, or other medical conditions.

topics.name: Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Fever is a rise in body temperature caused by the brain’s thermostat raising its target, usually in response to infection. It can also occur with inflammation, some medicines, cancer, or autoimmune disease. Hyperthermia is overheating without this change in the target.

topics.name: Fever in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Most fevers in children are caused by infections, often viral. Fever in young infants—especially those under 3 months—can signal a serious infection and needs prompt assessment; clinicians judge risk using age, appearance, symptoms, and temperature together.

topics.name: Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)
topics.clinical_significance: Classic fever of unknown origin is a rectal temperature of at least 38.3°C (101°F) lasting more than 3 weeks, with no cause found after 3 days of hospital evaluation or at least 3 outpatient visits. Causes may include hidden infections, inflammatory diseases, cancer, or drug reactions, so evaluation is guided by the clinical findings.

topics.name: Feverfew
topics.clinical_significance: Feverfew is an herbal supplement used mainly to prevent migraine; evidence is mixed, with a possible small reduction in attacks. It can cause mouth sores or stomach upset and may increase bleeding, especially with blood thinners or anti-inflammatory medicines; stop it 2 weeks before surgery. It should not be used during pregnancy.

topics.name: Fibrillary and Immunotactoid Glomerulopathies
topics.clinical_significance: These rare diseases involve abnormal fibers or tiny tubes deposited in the kidney’s filtering units. They usually cause protein in the urine and may cause blood in urine, high blood pressure, and chronic kidney disease; fibrillary glomerulopathy can progress to kidney failure. Immunotactoid glomerulopathy may be linked to blood cancers or abnormal antibodies.

topics.name: Fibroids in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Fibroids usually cause no symptoms during pregnancy, but degeneration can cause pain. They can increase the risks of miscarriage, preterm labor, abnormal fetal position, placenta previa or placental separation, and heavy bleeding after birth.

topics.name: Fibromuscular Dysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Fibromuscular dysplasia is abnormal growth in artery walls that can narrow or weaken an artery, most often in the kidneys or neck. It often causes no symptoms, but kidney-artery narrowing can cause high blood pressure, and neck or brain artery involvement can lead to an artery tear (dissection), aneurysm, or stroke.

topics.name: Fibromyalgia
topics.clinical_significance: Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain and tenderness for at least 3 months, often with fatigue, poor sleep, stiffness, and trouble thinking clearly. Altered pain processing may contribute. Diagnosis is based on symptoms and examination because no specific test confirms it.

topics.name: Fibrosis and Cirrhosis
topics.clinical_significance: Liver fibrosis is scar tissue that builds up after repeated injury; when scarring disrupts the liver structure, it is cirrhosis. Cirrhosis can reduce liver function and block blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension, fluid buildup, bleeding from enlarged veins, confusion, liver failure, and a higher risk of liver cancer.

topics.name: Fibula Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A fibula fracture near the ankle can make the ankle unstable, especially when ligaments or other ankle bones are also injured.
