A fracture high on the fibula can signal a more serious ankle injury, so the whole leg and ankle need assessment; unstable fractures may need surgery, and poor alignment can lead to arthritis.

topics.name: Fiery Serpent
topics.clinical_significance: Guinea-worm disease spreads when people drink water containing infected tiny crustaceans. About a year later, an adult worm emerges through a painful skin sore, usually on the leg; the sore can become infected, and joint inflammation may cause lasting stiffness or disability.

topics.name: Fifth Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Fifth disease is usually mild, with fever and a rash in children. Parvovirus B19 can temporarily stop red blood cell production, causing severe anemia in people with sickle cell disease or other red blood cell disorders, and lasting anemia in people with weakened immune systems. During pregnancy, infection can cause severe fetal anemia, swelling, miscarriage, or stillbirth.

topics.name: Fifth Metatarsal Bone, Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: The fracture site matters because it affects healing and treatment. A Jones fracture in the shaft near the base may heal slowly or fail to unite because its blood supply can be limited; fractures at the base usually heal more reliably.

topics.name: Filarial Nematode Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Filarial worms spread through bites from mosquitoes or flies, and the effects depend on the species. Infection can damage lymph vessels and cause lasting swelling of the limbs or genitals; some species damage the skin or eyes and can lead to blindness.

topics.name: Finger Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: Finger dislocations can tear supporting ligaments and may occur with a fracture or tendon injury. Prompt realignment and checking joint stability help protect finger movement; a volar dislocation can tear an extensor tendon and lead to a lasting boutonnière deformity.

topics.name: Fingertip Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Fingertip fractures often injure the nail bed, causing blood to collect painfully under the nail. Severe nail-bed damage can permanently deform the nail, and major soft-tissue injury may leave lasting fingertip sensitivity.

topics.name: First Metatarsophalangeal (MTP) Joint Sprain
topics.clinical_significance: Turf toe is a sprain of the supporting tissues under the big toe joint, usually from forceful upward bending. Severe injury can limit push-off and walking, and untreated sprains may cause lasting pain and stiffness; complete tears sometimes need surgery.

topics.name: First Trimester Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding in the first trimester is fairly common and does not always mean pregnancy loss, but it can signal miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy can cause life-threatening internal bleeding, so the cause needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Fish Oil
topics.clinical_significance: Prescription omega-3 products can lower high triglyceride levels, but fish-oil supplements have not consistently reduced heart attacks or deaths. They may cause belching, nausea, or diarrhea; high doses can increase bleeding or atrial fibrillation risk and may interact with warfarin.

topics.name: Fish Poisoning and Shellfish Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Toxins in fish or shellfish can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, or affect the nervous system. Severe poisoning can cause muscle paralysis and breathing failure; ciguatera can also leave abnormal sensations for months.

topics.name: Fissure in Ano
topics.clinical_significance: An anal fissure causes sharp pain during or after bowel movements and may cause bleeding. A chronic fissure can persist because tightening of the anal sphincter reduces blood flow; a fissure away from the usual midline may point to Crohn disease or another underlying cause.

topics.name: Fistula in Ano
topics.clinical_significance: An anal fistula is a tunnel from the anal canal to the skin near the anus. It often develops after an abscess and can cause ongoing drainage or repeated abscesses; Crohn disease is another cause, and many fistulas need surgery to close.

topics.name: Fitting the Prosthesis
topics.clinical_significance: A well-fitted, properly aligned prosthesis helps provide comfort, stability, and safe movement. Changes in the residual limb or a poor fit can cause pain, skin damage, and falls, so the fit needs regular review and adjustment.

topics.name: Flail Chest
topics.clinical_significance: Flail chest occurs when at least three neighboring ribs are each broken in two or more places, leaving a loose section of the chest wall. Pain and abnormal chest movement can make breathing difficult, and the injury often includes lung bruising that raises the risk of breathing complications.

topics.name: Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) Avulsion
topics.clinical_significance: An FDP tendon avulsion prevents active bending of the fingertip joint, often after a bent finger is forcefully pulled straight. Prompt assessment and surgical repair by a hand specialist are needed to restore tendon function.

topics.name: Flexor Tenosynovitis, Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: This is an acute infection around a finger flexor tendon. It can spread and damage hand function, so it needs urgent treatment, usually surgical drainage and antibiotics.

topics.name: Floaters
topics.clinical_significance: Floaters are moving spots or strands, usually harmless shadows in the eye gel that become more common with age. A sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, or a curtain over vision can signal a retinal tear or detachment and needs urgent eye assessment.

topics.name: Flu
topics.clinical_significance: Influenza (flu) is a contagious infection caused by influenza A or B viruses. It often starts suddenly with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, and cough; it can cause pneumonia or worsen chronic illness. Severe illness is more likely in children under 5, adults 65 or older, people with chronic conditions or weakened immunity, and people in the second or third trimester of pregnancy.

topics.name: Fluid Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: Fluid and sodium balance keeps blood volume and sodium concentration within safe limits. Disruption can cause dehydration or fluid overload and abnormal sodium levels, which may impair circulation or brain function.

topics.name: Fluid Resuscitation, Intravenous
topics.clinical_significance: IV fluids are used to restore circulation in hypovolemic or distributive (including septic) shock and in severe dehydration. The amount must be monitored because excess can cause fluid buildup in the lungs; IV fluids are usually not appropriate in cardiogenic or obstructive shock.

topics.name: Fluid Volume, Disorders of, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Too little or too much body sodium changes the volume of fluid outside cells: depletion can reduce circulation, while excess can cause swelling or fluid in the lungs or abdomen. A blood sodium level alone does not show total body sodium or fluid volume; heart, kidney, and liver disease commonly cause fluid overload.

topics.name: Fluorine Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Low fluoride exposure increases the risk of tooth decay. It may also be linked to osteoporosis, but that link is uncertain.

topics.name: Fluorine Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term high fluoride exposure can cause fluorosis. In children whose teeth are developing, it can leave white or brown patches or pits in the enamel; years of very high exposure can also cause bone changes in adults.

topics.name: Fluoroquinolones
topics.clinical_significance: Fluoroquinolones treat selected bacterial infections, often when other suitable antibiotics are not appropriate. They can cause serious, sometimes lasting adverse effects, including tendon rupture, nerve or brain problems, abnormal heart rhythm, low blood sugar, and C. difficile diarrhea; they are also linked to aortic aneurysm or dissection.

topics.name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: FSGS is scarring in parts of some kidney filters. It often causes protein to leak into urine and may lead to swelling, high blood pressure, and kidney failure; it may have no known cause or be linked to genetic conditions, infections, medicines, or excess strain on the kidneys.

topics.name: Folate Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia, in which red blood cells are abnormally large, leading to fatigue and sometimes a sore tongue. During pregnancy, it increases the risk of neural tube defects in the fetus. Causes include low intake, alcohol use, malabsorption, increased need, and some medicines.

topics.name: Folic Acid
topics.clinical_significance: Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate (vitamin B9), which the body uses to make DNA and red blood cells. Supplements treat folate deficiency and, when taken before conception and during early pregnancy, reduce the risk of fetal neural tube defects.

topics.name: Folliculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, most often from infection, causing small itchy or tender red bumps or pus-filled spots. Bacteria (usually Staphylococcus) and sometimes fungi or viruses can cause it; friction and blocked skin raise risk, while ingrown hairs after shaving can look similar without infection.

topics.name: Food Additives and Contaminants
topics.clinical_significance: Food additives help process and preserve food, and permitted amounts are judged safe; a few, such as sulfites, can rarely trigger reactions in sensitive people. Contaminants such as pesticides or heavy metals can harm health depending on the substance and amount, while effects of very low, long-term exposure are often uncertain.

topics.name: Food Allergy
topics.clinical_significance: A food allergy is an immune reaction to a food, usually a protein. Reactions can affect the skin, gut, or breathing and can include life-threatening anaphylaxis; common triggers include milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, soy, and wheat.

topics.name: Foot and Ankle Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Foot and ankle problems can cause pain and make standing or walking difficult. In people with diabetes or peripheral artery disease, regular foot checks help find injuries early because nerve or blood-flow problems can hide them.

topics.name: Foot and Ankle Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Foot and ankle disorders usually arise from problems in local bones, joints, or other tissues, though systemic diseases can also affect them. They may cause pain and difficulty walking. Pressure, friction, and infection are common problems; in diabetes or peripheral artery disease, reduced sensation or blood flow can make foot injuries harder to notice or heal.

topics.name: Foreign Bodies in the Gastrointestinal Tract, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Many swallowed objects pass through the digestive tract on their own. If an object becomes stuck, it can block or damage the gut, causing ulcers, bleeding, or a hole in the wall. Endoscopy can remove most objects that are stuck; surgery is sometimes needed.

topics.name: Foreign Travel
topics.clinical_significance: Foreign travel can expose people to infections that are uncommon at home, as well as risks such as road crashes. Risk depends on the destination, activities, and traveler’s health; vaccines and other preventive steps can reduce some risks. A history of recent travel is an important clue when evaluating illness after a trip.

topics.name: Formula Feeding
topics.clinical_significance: During the first year, commercial infant formula is the nutritionally complete alternative to human milk. Water can cause dangerously low blood sodium and poor nutrition, while whole cow’s milk does not provide complete infant nutrition and may cause intestinal blood loss. Some infants with cow’s milk protein allergy need a specialized formula.

topics.name: Fosfomycin
topics.clinical_significance: Fosfomycin blocks bacterial cell-wall production. Oral fosfomycin is used for uncomplicated bladder infections caused by E. coli or enterococci; it does not reach reliable blood levels to treat kidney infection. Intravenous fosfomycin, available in some countries, may be used with other antibiotics for serious resistant infections. Nausea and diarrhea are common side effects.

topics.name: Fourth Cranial Nerve (Trochlear) Palsy
topics.clinical_significance: A fourth cranial nerve palsy weakens the superior oblique eye muscle, causing double vision in which one image appears higher and slightly to the side. It is often worse when looking down and inward, such as on stairs, and may cause a compensatory head tilt. Causes include head injury and small-vessel damage, especially with diabetes; tumors and multiple sclerosis are rare causes.

topics.name: Fractured and Avulsed Teeth
topics.clinical_significance: Fractured and knocked-out teeth are dental emergencies because deeper damage can expose the pulp or loosen the tooth, threatening its survival. Fractures that expose the pulp or involve a loose tooth need urgent dental treatment. A knocked-out permanent tooth has the best chance of survival when replaced quickly; primary teeth are not replanted because this can harm the developing permanent tooth.

topics.name: Fracture-Dislocation of the Midfoot (Lisfranc Injury)
topics.clinical_significance: A Lisfranc injury disrupts the joints or ligaments that connect the midfoot to the forefoot, often making the foot unstable. It causes midfoot pain and swelling; bruising on the sole may occur. X-rays can miss the injury, and delayed diagnosis can lead to chronic pain, arthritis, and disability, so prompt orthopedic assessment is important.

topics.name: Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Fractures vary from minor injuries to emergencies that threaten a limb or life. Severe breaks can damage nearby blood vessels, nerves, or soft tissues; open fractures are at higher risk of infection, and pelvic or large-bone fractures can cause major bleeding or embolism. Healing may be delayed, and fractures involving a joint can leave stiffness or arthritis.

topics.name: Fractures of the 5th Metatarsal Bone
topics.clinical_significance: These fractures cause focal pain, swelling, and tenderness along the outer foot. The site matters: shaft (Jones) fractures have a less reliable blood supply and may heal slowly or fail to unite, while fractures at the base usually heal more reliably. Because healing and treatment differ by location, accurate diagnosis is important.

topics.name: Fractures of the Mandible and Midface
topics.clinical_significance: Fractures of the jaw or midface can alter the bite, limit jaw movement, cause facial numbness, or affect eye position and movement. Orbital fractures may cause double vision or a sunken eye. Severe facial trauma can also involve the brain or neck, and bleeding or swelling may obstruct the airway.

topics.name: Fractures, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Fractures can result from major trauma, repeated stress, or a small force on weakened bone; a low-force fracture may point to osteoporosis, cancer, or bone infection. Some fractures are not visible on the first X-rays, so CT or MRI may be needed when suspicion remains high. Poor circulation, including from diabetes or vascular disease, can slow healing.

topics.name: Fragile X Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Fragile X syndrome is an inherited condition caused by more than 200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. It is a common inherited cause of intellectual disability and may also cause autism-related social and behavioral difficulties. Effects vary, and females are often less affected than males.

topics.name: Fragile X–Associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome (FXTAS)
topics.clinical_significance: FXTAS is a late-onset neurologic disorder linked to an FMR1 premutation. It mainly affects men and causes intention tremor and progressive loss of balance and coordination. Parkinsonism, cognitive decline, and nerve damage may also develop; symptoms in women are usually milder.

topics.name: Freiberg Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Freiberg disease is loss of blood supply to a metatarsal head, usually the second, causing the bone to flatten and the joint to break down. It leads to pain in the ball of the foot, especially when bearing weight or pushing off, and may cause swelling and limited joint movement.

topics.name: Freiberg Infraction
topics.clinical_significance: Freiberg infraction is another name for Freiberg disease, a loss of blood supply to a metatarsal head, usually the second. It causes pain in the ball of the foot when bearing weight and can flatten and damage the joint, limiting movement.

topics.name: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD)
topics.clinical_significance: Frontotemporal dementia is a group of progressive disorders affecting the frontal and temporal parts of the brain, often beginning in midlife. Changes in personality, social behavior, or language commonly appear before major memory loss and can interfere with daily life. Some people also develop movement problems or muscle weakness; symptoms and progression vary.

topics.name: Frostbite
topics.clinical_significance: Frostbite is freezing injury to the skin and deeper tissues, usually affecting fingers, toes, ears, or nose. Early numbness and skin changes can hide how severe the damage is; rewarming is often very painful. Severe injury can cause gangrene and permanent tissue loss, and cold sensitivity or numbness may persist.

topics.name: Frotteuristic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Frotteuristic disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from touching or rubbing against a person who has not consented. Diagnosis requires the pattern to last at least 6 months and either be acted on with a nonconsenting person or cause significant distress or problems in daily life.

topics.name: Fructose Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited enzyme defects in fructose metabolism range from harmless fructosuria to serious disease. Depending on the defect, fructose exposure or fasting and illness can trigger low blood sugar, vomiting, metabolic acidosis, or seizures. Severe or repeated episodes can damage the liver or kidneys and may be fatal.

topics.name: Fulminant Liver Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Fulminant liver failure is another name for acute liver failure: rapid loss of liver function with jaundice, impaired blood clotting, and brain dysfunction in a person without preexisting chronic liver disease. It can quickly cause brain swelling and failure of other organs and may be fatal, so intensive care and urgent transplant evaluation are often needed.

topics.name: Function and Dysfunction of the Cerebral Lobes
topics.clinical_significance: Different cerebral lobes support movement, sensation, language, memory, behavior, and vision, but most complex tasks use several brain areas. Damage can cause weakness, numbness, language or memory problems, behavior changes, neglect, or vision loss. The pattern depends on where the damage is, how large it is, and how quickly it develops, helping clinicians locate and investigate the cause.

topics.name: Functional Assessment of the Older Driver
topics.clinical_significance: Safe driving requires adequate vision, movement, and thinking skills. Functional assessment can identify problems linked to aging, illness, or medicines, but no single screening test can determine driving safety with certainty. Findings help guide specialist evaluation, rehabilitation, vehicle adaptations, or driving restrictions or cessation.

topics.name: Functional Gastrointestinal Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Functional gastrointestinal illness, now called a disorder of gut-brain interaction (DGBI), includes common conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, functional dyspepsia, and functional constipation. These conditions cause real digestive symptoms through interacting changes in gut sensitivity, movement, and brain-gut signaling, often without a visible structural cause.

topics.name: Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Functional neurological symptom disorder causes genuine, involuntary problems with movement or sensation, or episodes that resemble seizures. The symptoms show patterns that do not fit recognized neurologic diseases, and diagnosis requires assessment for other causes and significant distress or impaired daily functioning. Symptoms are not intentionally produced.

topics.name: Fungal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Fungal infections may be local, affecting the skin, mouth, or vagina, or spread to the lungs and other organs. Some fungi can cause illness in healthy people, while others mainly cause severe, rapidly progressing disease when immunity is weakened. Travel and residential history can help identify exposure to fungi found in particular regions.

topics.name: Fungal Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Primary fungal infections often begin when spores are inhaled; some spread from the lungs to other organs. Opportunistic infections mainly affect people with weakened immunity and can progress rapidly. Past travel or residence can point to fungi found in specific regions, and a positive sputum culture alone may not prove infection.

topics.name: Fungal Skin Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Fungal skin infections can affect the skin, hair, nails, and moist skin or mucosal folds; common causes include dermatophytes and Candida. Symptoms vary by site and may include itchy, scaly patches, scalp hair loss, nail changes, or a moist red rash. Dermatophyte infections are usually superficial but may recur; weakened immunity can raise the risk of Candida spreading beyond the skin.

topics.name: Fungal Urinary Tract Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Fungal urinary tract infections, usually caused by Candida, occur mainly in people with urinary catheters or obstruction, diabetes, or weakened immunity. Candida in urine is often harmless colonization, so a positive culture alone does not prove infection. True infection can cause painful or frequent urination, fever, or blood in the urine; kidney infection or fungal masses may obstruct urine flow and impair kidney function.

topics.name: Fungi, Miscellaneous Opportunistic
topics.clinical_significance: Uncommon yeasts and molds can cause widespread, life-threatening infection in people with severely weakened immunity, especially those with neutropenia or advanced HIV. Some also cause local infection in otherwise healthy people or bloodstream infection linked to medical devices. Identifying the exact fungus is important because drug resistance and effective treatment vary by species.

topics.name: Furuncles and Carbuncles
topics.clinical_significance: Furuncles (boils) are painful staph abscesses that start in hair follicles; carbuncles are larger, deeper groups of connected boils that may scar or cause fever. They can recur, especially in people with diabetes, obesity, or weakened immunity, and MRSA may be the cause.

topics.name: Fusospirochetosis
topics.clinical_significance: Fusospirochetosis (trench mouth) is a rapidly developing, painful gum infection that causes tissue death and punched-out ulcers between the teeth, with bleeding and sometimes bad breath, fever, or swollen lymph nodes. Smoking, poor oral hygiene, stress, poor nutrition, and weakened immunity increase risk.

topics.name: Gait Disorders in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: A change in walking speed, balance, or step pattern in an older adult can signal an underlying joint, nerve, brain, or other health problem. Gait problems raise the risk of falls and injury and can limit daily activities and independence; walking speed also helps predict future function and health.

topics.name: Galactosemia
topics.clinical_significance: Galactosemia is an inherited enzyme disorder that prevents the body from processing galactose, a sugar in milk. In classic disease, infants can quickly develop jaundice, vomiting, liver and kidney injury, poor growth, and life-threatening E. coli infection after milk feeding. Untreated disease can cause cataracts and lasting learning and movement problems; early dietary restriction prevents acute illness but may not prevent all long-term effects.

topics.name: Galactosylceramide Lipidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Galactosylceramide lipidosis (Krabbe disease) is a rare inherited enzyme deficiency that damages myelin, the covering around nerves. It can cause loss of skills, intellectual disability, weakness that progresses to paralysis, blindness, and deafness, and may lead to early death. Stem cell transplantation can prolong life and improve function in some early-onset forms.

topics.name: Gallbladder and Bile Duct Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Gallstones are a common cause of gallbladder and bile duct problems, though they often cause no symptoms. A stone or other blockage can stop bile flow and cause upper abdominal pain, jaundice, gallbladder inflammation, bile duct infection, or pancreatitis; severe blockage or infection can be dangerous.

topics.name: Gallbladder and Bile Duct Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Tumors of the gallbladder and bile ducts include benign polyps and uncommon cancers. Cancers may block bile flow, causing jaundice, itching, or pain; they are often found late and have a poor outlook, though surgery may cure some cancers found early.

topics.name: Gamekeeper's Thumb
topics.clinical_significance: Gamekeeper’s thumb is a sprain or tear of the ligament on the inner side of the thumb joint, often caused by the thumb being forced outward in a fall. It causes pain and tenderness; a severe tear can leave the joint weak or unstable and impair gripping or pinching.

topics.name: Gamma Hydroxybutyrate
topics.clinical_significance: Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) is a sedative; its prescription form, sodium oxybate, is used to treat narcolepsy. Misuse or overdose can cause severe drowsiness, poor coordination, coma, and slowed or stopped breathing, especially when combined with alcohol or other sedatives. Frequent use can lead to dependence, and withdrawal can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Ganglia
topics.clinical_significance: In this hand-disorder topic, ganglia are noncancerous, fluid-filled lumps that usually form near a wrist joint or tendon. They are a common cause of hand or wrist swelling; many need no treatment, but painful or tender cysts may be drained or removed.

topics.name: Ganglion Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: A ganglion cyst is a fluid-filled lump near a joint or tendon, most often on the wrist or hand. It may change in size and often needs no treatment, but a painful or tender cyst can be drained or surgically removed.

topics.name: Garlic
topics.clinical_significance: Garlic supplements have been studied for effects on blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar, but results vary and benefits are uncertain. Supplements may increase bleeding risk with warfarin or antiplatelet medicines and may interact with blood-pressure or diabetes medicines; high doses can irritate the stomach.

topics.name: Gas Exchange, Measurement
topics.clinical_significance: Gas-exchange tests check blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels and how well oxygen passes from the lungs into the blood. Pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas tests, and DLCO help detect low oxygen, ventilation problems, and lung or pulmonary blood-vessel disease. Standard pulse oximeters can give misleading readings in carbon monoxide poisoning or methemoglobinemia.

topics.name: Gas Gangrene
topics.clinical_significance: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is a rapidly spreading, life-threatening muscle infection, usually after severe injury. Severe pain, swelling, skin discoloration or blisters, and gas in the tissue can progress quickly to shock, kidney failure, and death; urgent surgery and antibiotics are needed.

topics.name: Gas Toxicity During Diving
topics.clinical_significance: At depth, high gas pressures or contaminated breathing air can cause oxygen or carbon dioxide toxicity, nitrogen narcosis, or carbon monoxide poisoning. These can cause confusion, poor coordination, seizures, or loss of consciousness and may lead to drowning; carbon monoxide poisoning can occur despite a normal standard pulse-oximeter reading.

topics.name: Gastric Acidity, Medication Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines that reduce or neutralize stomach acid are used for reflux, gastritis, and peptic ulcers; some are also part of treatment for H. pylori infection. They relieve symptoms and help ulcers heal, but drug choice matters: antacids can affect absorption of other medicines, and misoprostol can cause pregnancy loss.

topics.name: Gastric Analysis
topics.clinical_significance: Gastric analysis measures how much acid the stomach produces and is rarely used today. It may help assess recurrent ulcers after vagotomy or interpret high blood gastrin: high acid can suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, while low acid may point to pernicious anemia or atrophic gastritis.

topics.name: Gastric and Intestinal Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: Most swallowed objects pass through the digestive tract without harm. Sharp objects, batteries, multiple magnets, and drug packets can cause injury, blockage, perforation, or poisoning; they may need urgent medical assessment, removal, or close monitoring.

topics.name: Gastrinoma
topics.clinical_significance: A gastrinoma is a gastrin-producing tumor, usually in the duodenum or pancreas. Excess stomach acid causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, often with severe or recurrent ulcers and diarrhea. About half of gastrinomas are malignant, and 40–60% occur in people with MEN1.

topics.name: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining; it may cause no symptoms or indigestion and sometimes bleeding. Peptic ulcers are deeper sores in the stomach or duodenum, usually caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use, and can bleed, perforate, or block the stomach outlet. Treating H. pylori and reducing stomach acid help ulcers heal and prevent recurrence.

topics.name: Gastritis, Nonerosive
topics.clinical_significance: Nonerosive gastritis is usually linked to H. pylori infection and often causes no symptoms. Long-standing infection can damage the stomach lining and lead to gland loss or intestinal changes, increasing the risk of ulcers and stomach cancer; treating H. pylori reduces these risks.

topics.name: Gastritis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining. It may be caused by H. pylori, medicines such as NSAIDs, alcohol, severe illness, or autoimmune disease; many people have no symptoms, while others develop indigestion or bleeding. Long-standing atrophic gastritis can reduce intrinsic factor and lead to vitamin B12 deficiency.

topics.name: Gastritis Syndromes, Uncommon
topics.clinical_significance: Uncommon gastritis syndromes include Ménétrier disease, eosinophilic gastritis, and stomach MALT lymphoma. They can cause protein loss and low blood albumin, nausea or vomiting, or stomach outlet blockage; H. pylori treatment may cure MALT lymphoma limited to the stomach. Rare bacterial gastritis can progress rapidly and be life-threatening.

topics.name: Gastroenteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and intestines, usually from infection but sometimes from drugs or toxins. It causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort; fluid and salt loss can cause dangerous dehydration, especially in young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity or serious illness. Most cases improve with supportive care.

topics.name: Gastroenteritis, Drug-Related
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines or chemicals can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea; common drug causes include antibiotics, magnesium antacids, cancer drugs, colchicine, digoxin, and laxatives. Antibiotics can also trigger C. difficile infection, which may be more severe and persist after the drug is stopped. Heavy-metal poisoning or laxative misuse can cause dangerous fluid and salt loss.

topics.name: Gastroenteritis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Most gastroenteritis is infectious and gets better on its own, but vomiting and diarrhea can cause severe fluid and salt loss, especially in infants, older adults, and people with weakened immunity or serious illness. Some people develop lasting irritable-bowel symptoms or indigestion after infection. Most need supportive care, while some bacterial or parasitic infections need specific treatment.

topics.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
topics.clinical_significance: GERD occurs when stomach contents repeatedly flow back into the esophagus, causing heartburn or regurgitation. Ongoing reflux can inflame or ulcerate the esophagus, cause narrowing, or lead to Barrett esophagus, which can rarely progress to cancer. Treatment often includes lifestyle changes and acid-reducing medicine.

topics.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux in Infants
topics.clinical_significance: Spitting up after feeds is common in infants and usually resolves by 12–18 months; if the infant is growing well and has no other symptoms, it is usually normal reflux. Reflux is GERD when it causes problems such as poor growth, feeding refusal, esophagitis, bleeding, or breathing symptoms. Forceful or green (bile-stained) vomiting needs prompt evaluation for other causes.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal and Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may produce hormones or cause no hormone-related symptoms. Hormone-producing tumors can cause flushing and diarrhea, peptic ulcers, or low blood sugar; other tumors may cause pain, bleeding, or blockage. Some spread to the liver or nearby lymph nodes, and outlook depends on the tumor site, grade, and stage.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Barotrauma
topics.clinical_significance: Air swallowed during a dive can expand as the diver rises, causing temporary bloating, cramps, abdominal pain, belching, or gas. Rarely, this can rupture the digestive tract; severe pain, tenderness, or a rigid abdomen needs urgent medical evaluation.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal bleeding can occur anywhere from the mouth to the anus and may be visible or hidden. Vomiting blood, black tarry stools, or red blood in the stool can signal bleeding. Severe blood loss can cause shock, while slow, hidden bleeding can lead to anemia. Visible bleeding needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Bleeding, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal bleeding may be obvious, such as vomiting blood or passing black, tarry or red stools, or hidden and found only by testing. Slow, ongoing blood loss can cause anemia; heavy bleeding can cause shock. The appearance of the blood may suggest where bleeding starts, but it does not prove the source. Visible bleeding needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Disorders in Neonates and Infants
topics.clinical_significance: Digestive disorders in newborns and infants range from common reflux and infections to bowel obstruction, tissue damage, or perforation. Serious problems can worsen quickly. Green (bilious) vomit, a swollen belly, blood in the stool, unusual sleepiness, or poor feeding needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors and Carcinoid Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors vary in behavior and may spread. Only some release hormones that cause carcinoid syndrome, with flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. In some people, the syndrome also damages right-sided heart valves. It often develops when an intestinal tumor has spread to the liver.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: A careful history and examination can often point to the cause of digestive symptoms and show when tests are needed. Blood in the stool, anemia, trouble swallowing, persistent vomiting, fever, or unexplained weight loss may signal serious disease and need further evaluation.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs)
topics.clinical_significance: GISTs may cause bleeding, indigestion, or blockage, but are sometimes found by chance. Their chance of spreading depends partly on size, location, and how quickly the tumor cells divide. Some spread, most often to the liver, so these features help guide monitoring and treatment.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal Testing Procedures, Other
topics.clinical_significance: These tests can help find causes such as H. pylori infection, carbohydrate intolerance, bacterial overgrowth, or abnormal movement of food through the gut. Motility capsules measure gut transit. Electrical stimulation may help selected patients with persistent gastroparesis symptoms or fecal incontinence. The choice depends on the symptoms and suspected problem.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal-Related Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Belching, bloating, and excess gas are often linked to diet, swallowed air, or gut sensitivity, but may also occur with digestive disease. New, persistent symptoms, especially in older adults, or symptoms with weight loss or blood in the stool need medical assessment. Chest discomfort described as gas may be heart-related.

topics.name: Gastroschisis
topics.clinical_significance: The exposed bowel can become inflamed and swollen before birth, and it can lose fluid and heat after birth. The infant needs immediate care and surgical repair. Some infants also have bowel abnormalities or need several weeks of feeding support while the bowel recovers.

topics.name: Gaucher Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Gaucher disease can enlarge the liver and spleen, lower blood counts, and damage bones, causing pain or fractures. Some types also affect the brain and nerves. The types differ in severity and treatment; enzyme replacement is used for types I and III.

topics.name: Gaucher's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Gaucher disease can enlarge the liver and spleen, lower blood counts, and damage bones, causing pain or fractures. Some types also affect the brain and nerves. The types differ in severity and treatment; enzyme replacement is used for types I and III.

topics.name: Gender Incongruence and Gender Dysphoria
topics.clinical_significance: Gender incongruence by itself is a normal variation, not a mental disorder. Gender dysphoria is diagnosed when a marked incongruence has lasted at least 6 months and causes significant distress or difficulty functioning. Respectful, individualized care can address distress and other mental health needs; some people also seek gender-affirming medical care.

topics.name: General Principles of Medical Genetics
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic principles help explain inherited disease and how risk may pass through a family. Genetic testing can support diagnosis or risk screening, guide some treatments, and identify relatives who may benefit from testing or counseling. The meaning of a result depends on the condition and the person’s history.

topics.name: General Principles of Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Poisoning can cause life-threatening problems with breathing, heart function, or consciousness, and harmful effects may be delayed. Care first supports vital functions and identifies the substance. Most treatment is supportive, though specific antidotes are available for some poisons. Suspected significant poisoning needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: GAD involves excessive, hard-to-control worry about several areas of life on more days than not for at least 6 months, with symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, or sleep problems. It can disrupt daily life and often occurs with depression or other anxiety disorders. Psychotherapy, medication, or both can help.

topics.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and teens, generalized anxiety disorder involves hard-to-control worry about many parts of life for at least 6 months, causing distress or problems at school or with friends. It may appear as restlessness, poor sleep, fatigue, trouble concentrating, or physical complaints such as stomachaches or headaches. Relaxation-based therapy may help; some children also need medication.

topics.name: Generalized Hypopituitarism
topics.clinical_significance: Loss of several pituitary hormones can affect growth, fertility, and the thyroid and adrenal glands. ACTH or TSH deficiency can be life-threatening, so prompt testing and treatment are important. Care usually includes replacing deficient hormones and treating the cause, such as a tumor.

topics.name: Genetic Diagnostic Technologies
topics.clinical_significance: Different genetic tests detect different kinds of changes: some examine a specific DNA segment, while microarrays and sequencing can survey much more of the genome. Choosing the right test can help diagnose genetic conditions and guide care. Broad testing may find changes whose meaning is unclear, so results need clinical interpretation.

topics.name: Genetic Skeletal Dysplasias
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited disorders disrupt bone or cartilage growth, causing short stature and often uneven growth of the limbs and trunk. Severity varies widely: some types are mild, while others can cause joint or spine problems, spinal cord pressure, or severe breathing problems in newborns. Identifying the type helps predict complications and guide care and genetic counseling.

topics.name: Genetics, Clinical Applications of
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic information can help diagnose inherited conditions, screen people at increased risk, guide family or carrier counseling, and inform some treatments or drug choices. Screening is most useful when the test is reliable and an effective action is available.

topics.name: Genetics, Ethical Controversies in
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic testing and treatments raise questions about privacy, discrimination, and whether testing should be voluntary. Prenatal screening, cloning, and gene editing also raise concerns about choosing traits and passing genetic changes to future generations. These issues make careful counseling and safeguards important.

topics.name: Genetics, General Principles
topics.clinical_significance: Genes on chromosomes pass biological information through families. A person’s traits and disease risk depend on genetic variants, how genes are expressed, and environmental factors, so a variant does not always mean disease will develop or predict its severity. Understanding inheritance patterns helps estimate family risk and guide counseling.

topics.name: Genetics, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Genes are DNA instructions for making proteins or functional RNA, and they are carried on chromosomes. Changes in genes or chromosomes can affect health, but their effects vary because gene activity and environmental factors also shape traits. Genetic findings therefore need to be interpreted in the person’s clinical and family context.

topics.name: Geniculate Herpes
topics.clinical_significance: Shingles reactivation involving nerves for facial movement, hearing, and balance can cause severe ear pain, blisters in the ear, and weakness or paralysis on one side of the face. Vertigo, ringing in the ears, or hearing loss may also occur and can persist. Antivirals and steroids are used, but evidence that they improve outcomes is limited.

topics.name: Genital Herpes
topics.clinical_significance: Genital HSV-1 or HSV-2 remains dormant in nerves and can reactivate. It may cause repeated painful genital sores, but many people have no symptoms. The virus can spread through sexual skin-to-skin contact even when no sores are present. A new infection during pregnancy carries a higher risk of severe infection in the newborn, often during delivery. Antivirals may shorten or lessen episodes but do not eliminate the virus or prevent all recurrences.

topics.name: Genital Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Genital trauma can injure the penis, testes, scrotum, or urethra. Some injuries need prompt surgery. Complications can include infection, tissue loss, erectile problems, urethral scarring, or impaired sperm or testosterone production. Blood in the urine or inability to urinate may signal urethral injury.

topics.name: Genital Warts
topics.clinical_significance: Genital warts are usually caused by HPV types 6 and 11. These types differ from the HPV types that cause most cancers. Warts can return after treatment.

topics.name: Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Repeated or ongoing pain, fear, or pelvic muscle tightening during attempted vaginal penetration can cause significant distress and affect sexual activity. Symptoms must last at least 6 months for this diagnosis. Physical and psychological factors may contribute, so treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Genitourinary Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: These cancers affect the kidneys, bladder, prostate, testes, or other urinary and reproductive organs. They may cause blood in the urine, a lump, pain, or trouble urinating, though some cause few symptoms early. Outlook and treatment depend on cancer site, type, and stage.

topics.name: Genitourinary Disorders, Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Painful or frequent urination, trouble emptying the bladder, urine leakage, or flank pain can signal infection, stones, blockage, or other urinary tract problems. The pattern of symptoms helps identify the cause. Blood in the urine needs medical evaluation.

topics.name: Genitourinary Imaging Tests
topics.clinical_significance: Imaging can reveal stones, tumors, blockages, injuries, or structural problems; some tests also measure kidney function. The best test depends on what needs to be checked. CT gives detailed images but uses radiation; ultrasound avoids radiation, and MRI gives clearer soft-tissue views.

topics.name: Genitourinary Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: A careful history and examination help locate the problem and identify urgent causes. Urinalysis is a key test; urine culture, other tests, or imaging may be needed based on symptoms. Blood in the urine needs a full urologic evaluation.

topics.name: Genitourinary Tract Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Severe injuries can cause internal bleeding, urine leakage, infection, kidney damage, or lasting problems with urination or sexual function. Blood in the urine or at the urethral opening, or inability to urinate after trauma, can signal serious injury and needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Genu Varum (Bowlegs) and Genu Valgum (Knock-Knees)
topics.clinical_significance: In children, bowlegs usually improve by 18 months and knock-knees by about age 9. Severe, worsening, or persistent deformity may signal a bone or growth problem. If left untreated, either deformity can contribute to knee osteoarthritis in adulthood.

topics.name: Geriatric Care, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults often have several health and daily-living needs and may see many clinicians. Coordinated care that respects patient goals and includes them in decisions helps prevent gaps in care and supports safety and independence.

topics.name: Geriatric Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults may have several illnesses and take many medicines; illness may first appear as confusion, falls, or loss of function. Reviewing health, medicines, thinking, mobility, daily activities, and support can help find treatable problems, reduce medication harm, and guide care that protects independence.

topics.name: Geriatrics, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Age-related changes can lower physiologic reserve, so illness or injury may trigger problems such as confusion or falls. Care should distinguish normal aging from disease and base decisions on health, function, and patient goals, not age alone.

topics.name: German Measles
topics.clinical_significance: Rubella is usually mild, but it can spread even when symptoms are absent. Infection early in pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious birth defects. Vaccination helps prevent rubella and congenital rubella.

topics.name: Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker Disease (GSS)
topics.clinical_significance: GSS is a rare inherited brain disease that worsens over time. It often causes poor balance and coordination and may also affect speech and thinking. There is no curative treatment; care is supportive.

topics.name: Gestational Age
topics.clinical_significance: Gestational age helps estimate fetal maturity and the due date. At birth, it guides assessment of newborn risks and care needs; babies born before 37 weeks are preterm. When menstrual dates are uncertain, an early pregnancy ultrasound gives the most accurate estimate.

topics.name: Gestational Diabetes
topics.clinical_significance: Gestational diabetes can increase the risk of a large baby, difficult delivery, high blood pressure during pregnancy, and low blood sugar in the newborn. It also raises future type 2 diabetes risk. Monitoring and treating blood sugar lowers many pregnancy risks.

topics.name: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Gestational trophoblastic disease ranges from molar pregnancy, which can become cancerous, to rare cancers of placental tissue. It can cause bleeding and serious pregnancy complications. Follow-up blood tests for the pregnancy hormone hCG are important because disease can persist after pregnancy, but persistent disease is often treatable.

topics.name: GHB
topics.clinical_significance: GHB overdose can cause coma and dangerously slow breathing, especially when combined with alcohol or other sedatives. Repeated use can cause dependence, and withdrawal can be life-threatening. Prescription sodium oxybate is also used to treat narcolepsy.

topics.name: GI Disorders in Neonates and Infants, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: GI disorders in newborns and infants range from common infections and reflux to bowel blockage and surgical emergencies. Vomiting or diarrhea can cause dangerous fluid loss in very young children, so early recognition is important.

topics.name: GI Disorders, Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: GI symptoms such as abdominal pain, indigestion, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, and bloating can have many causes, including problems outside the digestive tract. Their pattern and warning signs help guide evaluation and identify serious disease.

topics.name: GI Symptoms, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: GI symptoms may come from physical illness or from disorders of gut-brain interaction, such as irritable bowel syndrome, even when tests show no structural problem. Grouping symptoms as upper or lower GI can help guide evaluation.

topics.name: Giant Cell Arteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Giant cell arteritis affects large arteries, usually in people over 50. A new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain while chewing, or vision change can be a warning sign. The disease can cause sudden, permanent blindness, so suspected cases need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Giant Cell Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Subacute (giant cell) thyroiditis causes a painful, tender thyroid and often follows a respiratory infection. Thyroid hormone levels may be high at first and temporarily low later. Most people recover within months, but rarely the condition causes lasting hypothyroidism.

topics.name: Giardiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Giardia can spread through contaminated water or food, or from person to person; people without symptoms can still spread it. Diarrhea can cause dehydration, especially in infants and pregnant people. Long-lasting infection may cause poor nutrient absorption and weight loss, and symptoms can continue after the parasite is gone.

topics.name: Gigantism and Acromegaly
topics.clinical_significance: Excess growth hormone, usually from a pituitary tumor, causes extreme height if it begins before growth plates close (gigantism) and enlarged bones and soft tissues in adults (acromegaly). It can lead to diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, sleep apnea, and colon polyps.

topics.name: Gingival Hyperplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Drug-related gum overgrowth may partly cover teeth and can recur. Careful oral hygiene can reduce recurrence; when possible, the prescriber may change the medicine, or a dentist may remove excess tissue. A persistent or unusual gum enlargement should be checked because oral cancer can look similar.

topics.name: Gingivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Gingivitis is usually caused by dental plaque and makes gums red, swollen, and prone to bleeding. It often improves with good oral hygiene and professional cleaning. It can progress to periodontitis, but this does not always happen.

topics.name: Ginkgo
topics.clinical_significance: Ginkgo supplements have limited proven benefit and do not prevent dementia. They may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners or around surgery and may reduce the effect of seizure medicines. Raw ginkgo seeds are toxic and can cause seizures or death.

topics.name: Ginseng
topics.clinical_significance: Evidence for the claimed benefits of ginseng is limited, and supplement products may contain little active ingredient. Ginseng can lower blood sugar and interact with medicines such as warfarin and diabetes drugs. It should not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

topics.name: Gitelman's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Gitelman syndrome is an inherited kidney disorder that causes loss of salt, potassium, and magnesium in urine. Low potassium or magnesium can cause tiredness, muscle cramps, or weakness, though some people have no symptoms. Treatment usually replaces these salts.

topics.name: Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve and can cause permanent vision loss. Eye pressure often contributes, but glaucoma can occur even when pressure is in the usual range. Early glaucoma may have no symptoms.

topics.name: Glaucoma, Angle-Closure
topics.clinical_significance: Angle-closure glaucoma happens when the iris blocks the eye’s drainage angle, raising pressure and damaging the optic nerve. It may develop slowly or as a sudden attack. A sudden attack can cause severe eye pain and redness, blurred vision or halos, headache, nausea, and vomiting; it needs immediate treatment to prevent permanent vision loss.

topics.name: Glaucoma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Glaucoma is a group of diseases that gradually damage the optic nerve and can cause permanent vision loss. Eye pressure is often high, but it may be normal. Early disease often has no symptoms, so eye exams can help find it before vision loss advances; treatment lowers pressure to slow damage.

topics.name: Glaucoma, Primary Open-Angle
topics.clinical_significance: Primary open-angle glaucoma slowly damages the optic nerve while the eye’s drainage angle remains open. It often causes no early symptoms; side vision is usually affected first, and lost vision cannot be restored. Eye pressure may be high or normal, and lowering it can slow further damage.

topics.name: Glenoid Labral Tear
topics.clinical_significance: A tear in the cartilage rim around the shoulder socket, which helps deepen and stabilize the socket. It may follow a fall or repeated overhead activity and can cause deep shoulder pain, clicking, or catching during movement.

topics.name: Gliomas
topics.clinical_significance: Gliomas are primary tumors that arise in brain tissue; types include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas. They may grow into nearby tissue and cause seizures or other problems that depend on where they are. Their growth and outlook vary by tumor type and molecular features.

topics.name: Globe Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Trauma to the eyeball from a blow or a penetrating object. It can cause bleeding, a wound or rupture, a foreign body, or damage to the retina or optic nerve. Severe injuries can lead to permanent vision loss and need urgent eye-specialist assessment.

topics.name: Globoid Cell Leukodystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Globoid cell leukodystrophy (Krabbe disease) is a rare inherited disorder caused by low activity of the enzyme galactocerebrosidase. It damages myelin, the covering around nerve fibers, and can lead to worsening problems with movement and thinking, paralysis, and loss of vision or hearing. Severe early-onset forms can be fatal.

topics.name: Globus Hystericus
topics.clinical_significance: Globus hystericus, now usually called globus sensation, is the feeling of a lump in the throat when no mass is present; it is not linked to swallowing. The cause is often unclear, though reflux or changes in throat muscle function may contribute. The older term does not mean the symptom is caused by hysteria.

topics.name: Globus Pharyngeus
topics.clinical_significance: Globus pharyngeus, also called globus sensation, is a feeling of a lump in the throat when no mass is present. It is unrelated to swallowing and differs from difficulty swallowing. The cause is often unclear, though reflux or changes in throat muscle function may contribute.

topics.name: Globus Sensation
topics.clinical_significance: Globus sensation is a feeling of a lump in the throat when no mass is present. It is unrelated to swallowing and differs from difficulty swallowing. The cause is often unclear, though reflux or changes in throat muscle function may contribute.

topics.name: Glomerular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Glomerular disorders affect the kidney’s tiny blood-filtering units. They can cause blood or protein in the urine and may reduce kidney function. Some mainly cause blood in the urine, while others cause heavy protein loss and swelling; causes may be limited to the kidney or linked to another disease.

topics.name: Glomerular Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Glomerular disorders affect the kidney’s filtering units and often cause protein or blood in the urine. A nephrotic pattern involves heavy protein loss, low blood protein, and swelling; a nephritic pattern features blood in the urine and may include high blood pressure, reduced urine, or worse kidney function. Some disorders show both patterns.

topics.name: Glossodynia
topics.clinical_significance: Glossodynia is burning or painful sensation of the tongue, sometimes affecting other parts of the mouth. In burning mouth syndrome, the mouth often looks normal and no cause is found; similar symptoms can also result from problems such as dry mouth, nutritional deficiency, infection, or medicine effects.

topics.name: Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia
topics.clinical_significance: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes repeated, brief bouts of severe, sharp pain in the back of the throat, tonsil area, base of the tongue, or ear. Swallowing, speaking, coughing, or chewing may trigger the pain. Rarely, it can slow the heartbeat and cause fainting.

topics.name: Glucagonoma
topics.clinical_significance: A usually malignant tumor of the pancreas that releases excess glucagon. It can cause high blood sugar and a characteristic skin rash called necrolytic migratory erythema; weight loss and anemia may also occur.

topics.name: Glucosamine
topics.clinical_significance: Glucosamine is a natural compound used to make parts of cartilage. It is taken as a supplement for osteoarthritis, but evidence of pain relief is mixed and may depend on the formulation and joint affected.

topics.name: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: G6PD deficiency is an inherited enzyme disorder that makes red blood cells more vulnerable to damage from oxidative stress. Infections, some medicines, or fava beans can trigger red blood cell breakdown, causing anemia, jaundice, and dark urine; severe episodes can injure the kidneys.

topics.name: Gluten Enteropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Gluten enteropathy (celiac disease) is an immune reaction to gluten, a protein in wheat, rye, and barley, in people with genetic susceptibility. It damages the small-intestine lining and can reduce nutrient absorption, causing diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, anemia, or poor growth; some people have few symptoms. A strict gluten-free diet usually improves symptoms and intestinal damage.

topics.name: Glycerol Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Glycerol metabolism disorders are rare inherited problems with processing glycerol. They can cause episodes of vomiting, sleepiness, weak muscle tone, low blood sugar, or acidosis. Some forms occur with adrenal insufficiency or Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

topics.name: Glycogen Storage Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Glycogen storage diseases are inherited enzyme disorders that disrupt how the body stores or breaks down glycogen, its stored form of sugar. Symptoms vary by type: liver forms can cause low blood sugar and an enlarged liver, while muscle forms can cause cramps and difficulty with exercise.

topics.name: Glycolytic Pathway Defects
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited defects in enzymes that help red blood cells break down glucose for energy. These defects can cause ongoing red blood cell destruction (hemolytic anemia), with symptoms such as anemia, jaundice, or an enlarged spleen; severity varies.

topics.name: Goiter, Simple Nontoxic
topics.clinical_significance: A noncancerous enlargement of the thyroid without thyroid inflammation or overactivity; thyroid function is usually normal. It often causes only visible neck swelling, but a large goiter can cause throat fullness, hoarseness, or difficulty swallowing or breathing. Causes include iodine deficiency, some medicines, or may be unclear.

topics.name: Goldenseal
topics.clinical_significance: Goldenseal is an herbal supplement containing berberine and hydrastine. Evidence for many claimed benefits is limited. It can cause nausea and interact with medicines; it may be harmful during pregnancy or breastfeeding and can cause jaundice in newborns.

topics.name: Golfer’s Elbow
topics.clinical_significance: Golfer’s elbow (medial epicondylitis) is an overuse injury of the tendons attached to the inner side of the elbow. Repeated forceful wrist bending or turning the palm down can cause pain and tenderness, especially when these movements are resisted.

topics.name: Gonadal Dysgenesis
topics.clinical_significance: Gonadal dysgenesis is incomplete development of the ovaries or testes. In Turner syndrome, the ovaries are often replaced by fibrous tissue with few or no follicles, leading to low sex-hormone levels, delayed or absent puberty, and infertility.

topics.name: Gonorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It often causes no symptoms, but can cause discharge or pain when urinating and can infect the genitals, rectum, or throat. Untreated genital infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility; rarely, infection spreads to joints or a newborn’s eyes. Antibiotic resistance is increasing.

topics.name: Goodpasture Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease) is a rare autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the supporting layers around kidney filters and lung air sacs. It can cause rapidly worsening kidney inflammation and bleeding into the lungs, leading to blood in the urine, coughing blood, or shortness of breath; either organ may be affected alone. The disease can progress quickly and be fatal without prompt treatment.

topics.name: Goodpasture's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Goodpasture’s disease (anti-GBM disease) is a rare autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the supporting layers around kidney filters and lung air sacs. It can cause rapidly worsening kidney inflammation and bleeding into the lungs, leading to blood in the urine, coughing blood, or shortness of breath; either organ may be affected alone. The disease can progress quickly and be fatal without prompt treatment.

topics.name: Gout
topics.clinical_significance: Gout is inflammatory arthritis caused by deposits of monosodium urate crystals in and around joints, usually linked to long-term high blood urate. Flares cause sudden severe pain, swelling, warmth, and redness, often in the big toe. Repeated attacks can damage joints and form firm deposits called tophi; uric acid kidney stones may also occur.

topics.name: Gram Negative Bacilli, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Gram-negative bacilli are a broad group of rod-shaped bacteria. Some normally live in the intestines, but others can cause diarrhea, urinary tract or abdominal infections, and bloodstream infections. Some species also cause serious diseases such as cholera, plague, and typhoid fever.

topics.name: Gram-Negative Bacilli
topics.clinical_significance: Gram-negative bacilli are rod-shaped bacteria that stain pink on a Gram stain because they have a thin cell-wall layer and an outer membrane. Some live normally in the gut, while others cause infections in the urinary tract, lungs, abdomen, or bloodstream.

topics.name: Gram-Negative Cocci and Coccobacilli
topics.clinical_significance: Gram-negative cocci are round bacteria, while coccobacilli are short, oval rods. This group includes Neisseria, which cause gonorrhea and meningococcal disease, and coccobacilli such as Haemophilus and Bordetella, which can cause respiratory infections.

topics.name: Gram-Positive Bacilli
topics.clinical_significance: Gram-positive bacilli are rod-shaped bacteria that stain violet in the Gram stain. This group includes bacteria that cause diseases such as anthrax, diphtheria, listeriosis, and nocardiosis.

topics.name: Granular Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Granular conjunctivitis (trachoma) is a chronic eye infection caused by certain types of \textit{Chlamydia trachomatis}. It spreads through contact with infected eye or nose secretions, contaminated objects, or flies. Repeated infections can scar the eyelid, turn it inward, and make the eyelashes rub the cornea, causing vision loss or blindness.

topics.name: Granulocytopenia
topics.clinical_significance: Granulocytopenia is a low number of granulocytes in the blood, usually neutrophils. When the neutrophil count is very low, serious bacterial and fungal infections are more likely, and fever may be the only clear sign.

topics.name: Granuloma Annulare
topics.clinical_significance: Granuloma annulare is a harmless, noninfectious skin condition that causes smooth bumps or raised patches, often forming rings with a clear or slightly sunken center. It usually affects the hands, feet, or legs and causes few symptoms. It often clears on its own, though this may take years.

topics.name: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
topics.clinical_significance: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a disease in which blood vessels become inflamed, most often affecting the nose and sinuses, lungs, and kidneys. It can damage lung tissue and cause kidney inflammation that may quickly reduce kidney function. Early treatment can bring the disease into remission, but it often returns.

topics.name: Granulomatous Amebic Encephalitis
topics.clinical_significance: Granulomatous amebic encephalitis is a very rare, usually fatal infection of the brain caused by free-living amoebae. It often affects people with weakened immunity, though Balamuthia can also infect healthy people. It can cause gradually worsening headache, confusion or behavior changes, seizures, and coma.

topics.name: Granulomatous Ileitis
topics.clinical_significance: Granulomatous ileitis is Crohn disease involving the ileum, the last part of the small intestine. It can cause repeated abdominal pain and diarrhea. Deep inflammation may narrow or block the bowel, or lead to abscesses or abnormal connections called fistulas. Granulomas are not found in every patient.

topics.name: Granulomatous Ileocolitis
topics.clinical_significance: Granulomatous ileocolitis is Crohn disease affecting the ileum and colon. It can cause repeated abdominal pain and diarrhea. Deep inflammation may narrow or block the bowel, or lead to abscesses or abnormal connections called fistulas. Granulomas may occur but are absent in most patients.

topics.name: Granulomatous Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Granulomatous thyroiditis (subacute thyroiditis) is a painful thyroid inflammation that often follows a viral illness. It can cause fever and neck pain. Thyroid hormone levels may be high at first, then temporarily low. The illness usually clears within months, but rarely causes lasting hypothyroidism.

topics.name: Green Tea
topics.clinical_significance: Green tea is generally safe in moderate amounts, but evidence for most claimed health benefits is limited. Caffeine may cause insomnia, anxiety, or a fast heartbeat. Green tea extracts have rarely caused liver injury, and green tea can affect the levels or effects of medicines such as warfarin, lithium, nadolol, and some statins.

topics.name: Growth and Development
topics.clinical_significance: Growth is an increase in body size; development is the growth of movement, language, thinking, and social and emotional skills. Both are shaped by genes, nutrition, and a child’s surroundings, and children progress at different rates. Tracking growth and milestones can help identify possible health or developmental concerns.

topics.name: Growth and Development, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Physical growth means an increase in body size; development means gaining abilities and skills. Both are shaped by a child’s genes, nutrition, and surroundings. Clinicians consider these factors and the child’s age when assessing progress.

topics.name: Growth and Weight Faltering in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Growth and weight faltering means a child’s weight or height is below what is expected or has fallen across growth-chart lines. It reflects inadequate nutrition, which may result from illness, feeding problems, or environmental stress. Finding the cause and restoring good nutrition helps protect growth and development.

topics.name: Growth Hormone Deficiency in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Growth hormone deficiency is a lack of pituitary hormone that causes children to grow more slowly than expected and may lead to short stature. Other pituitary hormones may also be low. Assessment helps identify the cause, and prescribed growth hormone treatment can improve growth.

topics.name: Growth Parameters in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: A newborn’s weight, length, and head size are measured and compared with standards for the pregnancy length. These measurements help identify babies who are smaller or larger than expected and may need closer checks. They also help track later growth and development.

topics.name: Guided Imagery
topics.clinical_significance: Guided imagery uses imagined sights, sounds, or other sensations to help a person relax. It may help ease pain, stress, or anxiety, including around medical procedures. Evidence of benefit varies by condition.

topics.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)
topics.clinical_significance: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an immune-related nerve disorder that can cause rapidly worsening weakness and tingling, often starting in the legs and moving upward. It may weaken the muscles used for breathing and affect heart rate or blood pressure, so urgent hospital care and close monitoring are needed. Most people improve over months, though some have lasting weakness.

topics.name: Guinea Worm Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Guinea worm disease is caused by a parasite acquired by drinking water containing infected tiny crustaceans called copepods. About a year later, a worm may emerge through a painful skin blister, usually on a lower leg. The wound can become infected, and joint inflammation may limit movement.

topics.name: Gynecologic Diagnostic Tests and Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic tests and procedures help investigate symptoms and detect infections, pregnancy, or cancer. They can also assess menstrual or hormone problems and fertility. Methods include laboratory tests, cervical screening, biopsies, ultrasound, and procedures that examine the uterus or pelvis; results help guide care.

topics.name: Gynecologic Disorders, Miscellaneous
topics.clinical_significance: This section groups several different gynecologic conditions, including cysts, cervical polyps or narrowing, adenomyosis, benign ovarian or tubal masses, and adnexal torsion. They may cause pain, abnormal bleeding, urinary symptoms, or no symptoms. Sudden severe pelvic pain may signal torsion and needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Gynecologic Evaluation, General
topics.clinical_significance: A gynecologic evaluation begins with a history of reproductive and overall health, including menstrual and sexual history, pregnancies, symptoms, past conditions and procedures, and medicines. This information helps explain symptoms, identify health risks, and guide any examination or tests.

topics.name: Gynecologic Evaluation in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic care for children and adolescents should fit their age, development, symptoms, and needs. Children are examined only for a medical reason, and an external exam is usually enough. Adolescent visits focus on education, menstrual health, prevention, and confidential counseling; an internal pelvic exam is done only when medically needed.

topics.name: Gynecologic Patient, Approach to the
topics.clinical_significance: A gynecologic visit combines reproductive and medical history with an examination and tests chosen for the patient’s symptoms, age, and health risks. This approach helps diagnose reproductive health concerns and guide prevention, such as screening and counseling.

topics.name: Gynecologic Preventive Care
topics.clinical_significance: Preventive gynecologic care is ongoing and tailored to a person’s age, health risks, symptoms, and needs. Visits may include cancer or STI screening, immunizations, and reproductive, sexual-health, or general health counseling. Routine pelvic exams are not needed for everyone.

topics.name: Gynecologic Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic tumors can affect the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, cervix, vagina, or vulva; this topic focuses mainly on cancers in these organs and related pregnancy tissue. Many cause abnormal vaginal bleeding or a pelvic mass, so these symptoms need medical evaluation. Cervical screening and HPV vaccination help prevent or detect some cervical cancers early.

topics.name: Gynecologic Tumors, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic cancers can arise in the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, cervix, vagina, or vulva; related cancers may also involve the tissue lining the abdomen or pregnancy-related tissue. Many cause abnormal vaginal bleeding or a pelvic mass. Cervical screening and HPV vaccination help prevent or detect cervical cancer early.

topics.name: Gynecomastia
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecomastia is enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males, not simply extra fat. It is common in newborns and during puberty, when it usually goes away on its own. In adults, medicines, hormone changes, or illness may cause it; new painful enlargement or a hard, one-sided lump should be checked.

topics.name: HACEK Infections
topics.clinical_significance: HACEK infections are caused by a group of slow-growing, hard-to-culture gram-negative bacteria. They most often cause infective endocarditis, especially in people at risk for heart-valve infection. Some species can also cause respiratory, wound, bone, or other infections. Endocarditis needs prompt diagnosis and antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Haemophilus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Haemophilus bacteria, especially H. influenzae, can cause ear, sinus, and lung infections. Some strains also cause serious infections of the blood, brain coverings, joints, or epiglottis, mainly in children. Hib vaccination greatly lowers the risk of serious type b infection, but does not prevent disease from other Haemophilus strains.

topics.name: Haemophilus influenzae Type b (Hib) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The Hib vaccine protects against serious infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, including meningitis, bloodstream infection, and epiglottitis. It is part of routine childhood vaccination and has greatly reduced these infections. It does not protect against other H. influenzae types.

topics.name: Hair Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Hair disorders can cause hair loss, patchy bald spots, unwanted hair growth, or bumps from ingrown hairs after shaving. Hair loss may be linked to aging, genes, medicines, infection, or another illness. Some scarring conditions can permanently damage hair roots.

topics.name: Hair Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Hair loss may affect a small area or be widespread, and may occur with or without scarring. It can be inherited or age-related, or caused by medicines, infection, stress, or illness. Because it can sometimes signal a health problem, its pattern and other symptoms help guide evaluation. Scarring hair loss can be permanent.

topics.name: Hair-Pulling Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Hair-pulling disorder (trichotillomania) involves repeatedly pulling out hair, often from the scalp, eyebrows, or eyelashes, causing hair loss. People try to stop or pull less but cannot, and the behavior causes distress or disrupts daily life. Swallowing pulled hair can rarely form a blockage in the stomach or intestine.

topics.name: Halitosis
topics.clinical_significance: Frequent or persistent unpleasant breath odor. It usually comes from bacteria on the tongue or from gum or tooth disease. Smoking, certain foods, and dry mouth can also contribute. Less often, an infection or another illness outside the mouth is responsible.

topics.name: Hallucinogens
topics.clinical_significance: Hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, and mescaline can alter perception and mood and impair judgment. Intoxication may cause anxiety, nausea, sweating, or poor coordination. Severe toxicity can cause dangerously high body temperature or abnormal heart rhythms. Some people have recurring visual disturbances or lasting psychotic symptoms after use.

topics.name: Hallux Valgus
topics.clinical_significance: Hallux valgus is a deformity in which the big toe angles toward the other toes, forming a bump at the base on the inner side of the foot (a bunion). Shoe pressure can cause pain, redness, or swelling. Arthritis may also develop and limit toe movement.

topics.name: Hamman-Rich Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, rapidly worsening lung disease with no known cause.
