It can begin suddenly with fever, cough, and shortness of breath, then progress to dangerously low blood oxygen and respiratory failure that may require a ventilator. The risk of death is high, though some survivors recover lung function.

topics.name: Hammer Toe Deformity
topics.clinical_significance: Hammer toe is a deformity, usually of the second toe, in which the middle joint bends and may become fixed. The toe can rub against shoes and cause pain, corns, or calluses. A rigid deformity can also increase pressure under the ball of the foot and make walking painful.

topics.name: Hamstring Strain
topics.clinical_significance: A partial tear of a muscle at the back of the thigh, usually where the muscle meets its tendon. It often causes sudden pain during running or sprinting. More severe strains may cause bruising, swelling, and weakness, and recovery can take several months.

topics.name: Hand and Foot Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the hands and/or feet that may be caused by irritants, allergy, or atopic dermatitis. It can cause redness, scaling, and thickened skin; some people also develop itchy blisters that may break and form sore or crusted areas. Frequent contact with water or detergents can trigger or worsen it.

topics.name: Hand Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Hand disorders can cause pain, swelling, stiffness, deformity, numbness, or limited movement. They include arthritis, tendon problems, nerve compression, cysts, and infections. Hand infections can spread into tendons, joints, or bones, so prompt medical evaluation helps prevent serious damage.

topics.name: Hand Disorders, Overview and Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Hand problems are assessed by asking about injury, pain, stiffness, or numbness and examining the hand’s shape, movement, sensation, strength, and blood flow. Imaging or other tests may be needed to find the cause. Suspected hand infections need prompt evaluation because they can spread into tendons, joints, or bones and cause lasting problems.

topics.name: Hand-Foot-and-Mouth Disease (HFMD)
topics.clinical_significance: A contagious viral illness that mainly affects young children. It causes fever, painful mouth sores, and spots or blisters on the hands and feet; mouth pain can make it hard to drink. Most cases are mild and short-lived, but some viruses, especially enterovirus A71, can rarely cause serious brain or nerve complications.

topics.name: Hansen Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A long-lasting infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae or M. lepromatosis that mainly affects the skin and nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Skin patches may lose feeling, and nerve damage can cause weakness, unnoticed injuries, ulcers, and lasting disability. The infection is not easily spread, and treatment quickly stops a person from passing it to others. Early treatment helps prevent further nerve damage.

topics.name: Hansen's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A long-lasting infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae or M. lepromatosis that mainly affects the skin and nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Skin patches may lose feeling, and nerve damage can cause weakness, unnoticed injuries, ulcers, and lasting disability. The infection is not easily spread, and treatment quickly stops a person from passing it to others. Early treatment helps prevent further nerve damage.

topics.name: Hantavirus Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Hantavirus infection is usually caught by breathing in particles from infected rodent urine, droppings, or saliva; rarely, it spreads through bites. Depending on the virus, it can cause kidney failure with bleeding or rapidly worsening fluid buildup in the lungs and respiratory failure. Andes virus can also spread between people. Severe illness can be fatal.

topics.name: Hartnup Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition in which the gut absorbs less tryptophan and the kidneys lose more amino acids in the urine. This can reduce niacin levels and cause attacks of sun-sensitive rash, poor coordination, or mood and thinking changes, often after poor nutrition or illness. Some people have no symptoms, and attacks often become less frequent with age.

topics.name: Hartnup's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited condition in which the gut absorbs less tryptophan and the kidneys lose more amino acids in the urine. This can reduce niacin levels and cause attacks of sun-sensitive rash, poor coordination, or mood and thinking changes, often after poor nutrition or illness. Some people have no symptoms, and attacks often become less frequent with age.

topics.name: Hashimoto Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid that can enlarge the gland and gradually reduce thyroid hormone production, causing hypothyroidism. Some people briefly have signs of excess thyroid hormone early in the illness. When hypothyroidism develops, long-term thyroid hormone treatment is often needed.

topics.name: HAT
topics.clinical_significance: Human African trypanosomiasis is a parasitic infection spread mainly by tsetse flies. It can cause fever, headache, body aches, and swollen lymph nodes, then spread to the brain and cause sleepiness, confusion, movement problems, or coma. Untreated disease can be fatal, and treatment depends on the parasite type and whether the brain is affected.

topics.name: Hay Fever Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Seasonal allergic inflammation of the clear membrane covering the eye, usually triggered by pollen or mold spores. It causes itchy, red, watery eyes and may occur with other hay fever symptoms. Severe forms can scar the cornea; vernal keratoconjunctivitis can cause corneal ulcers and reduced vision.

topics.name: Hb S Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Sickle cell disease is a group of inherited blood disorders involving hemoglobin S. Red blood cells can become rigid and sickle-shaped, break down early, and block small blood vessels. This causes chronic anemia and painful episodes and raises the risk of infection, stroke, acute chest syndrome, and organ damage.

topics.name: HDL levels, Elevated
topics.clinical_significance: HDL cholesterol above 80 mg/dL. It is usually linked to lower cardiovascular risk, but high HDL caused by some inherited conditions may not protect the heart. Unexpectedly high levels can be related to alcohol use, an overactive thyroid, liver disease, or medicines and may need evaluation.

topics.name: Head and Neck, Tumors of
topics.clinical_significance: Head and neck cancers can arise in the mouth, throat, voice box, nose, sinuses, or salivary glands. Tobacco and alcohol are major risks, and HPV is linked to some throat cancers. A lasting mouth sore, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or a neck lump may be an early sign. Spread to neck lymph nodes can worsen the outlook, so early assessment is important.

topics.name: Head and Neck Tumors, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Head and neck cancers can arise in the mouth, throat, or voice box. Tobacco and alcohol raise the risk, and HPV is linked to some throat cancers. A neck lump, lasting mouth sore, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing may be an early sign. The outlook depends on the tumor’s site and spread; early diagnosis improves the chance of successful treatment.

topics.name: Head Circumference
topics.clinical_significance: A newborn’s head measurement, used with length, weight, and gestational age to assess growth and help identify health risks. It is compared with growth charts; a measurement outside the expected range may need further assessment.

topics.name: Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in any part of the head, including the scalp and face. Most headaches are primary disorders, such as migraine or tension-type headache, but some are caused by another condition. A sudden severe headache, a worsening pattern, fever with neck stiffness, or new neurologic symptoms can signal a serious cause and needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Headache, Approach to the Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of headache looks for a primary disorder, such as migraine or tension-type headache, or a cause elsewhere in the body. The clinician reviews when the pain began, its pattern and related symptoms, and performs an examination; typical recurrent headaches often need no tests. Sudden severe pain, worsening headaches, a new headache after age 50, fever with neck stiffness, or neurologic changes may signal a serious cause and need prompt assessment.

topics.name: Health Care Issues in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Adolescence involves rapid physical and psychosocial development, creating opportunities for prevention and risks that need attention. Health care addresses injuries, substance use, mental health, sexual and reproductive health, obesity, and new or chronic illness. Education, screening, and early detection can reduce short- and long-term harm.

topics.name: Health Supervision of the Well Child
topics.clinical_significance: Well-child visits track a child’s growth and physical, cognitive, and social development. They support health through vaccinations and guidance for caregivers, and help identify illness, developmental problems, and other needs early. Regular examination and age-based screening can guide timely care.

topics.name: Hearing Impairment in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Hearing loss in children can delay speech and language development and affect learning and social relationships. Early detection helps identify treatable causes and supports timely hearing and language care, which can reduce these effects.

topics.name: Hearing Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Hearing loss can make speech harder to understand and affect communication and daily activities. Evaluation helps identify its type and cause, including treatable ear problems or less common neurologic disease, and guides hearing support. Sudden or one-sided hearing loss can signal a serious cause.

topics.name: Hearing Loss, Sudden
topics.clinical_significance: Sudden hearing loss, usually affecting one ear, can result from inner-ear injury, infection, medication effects, or another disorder. It needs urgent evaluation because finding a reversible cause and starting timely care may improve hearing recovery.

topics.name: Heart Disease in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy increases the heart’s workload and can worsen existing heart disease or reveal previously unrecognized disease. Severe disease can cause heart failure or abnormal rhythms and raises the risk of serious complications for the pregnant person and fetus. Risk assessment and close care during pregnancy and after birth are important.

topics.name: Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Heart failure causes shortness of breath, fatigue, and fluid buildup, and can limit daily activity. It can worsen over time, impair other organs, and become life-threatening. Finding its cause and type helps guide treatment and reduce symptoms and hospital stays.

topics.name: Heart Failure, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Heart failure medicines can ease symptoms, reduce hospital stays, and, for several key drug classes, improve survival, especially in people with reduced ejection fraction. The best combination depends on the type of heart failure and the person’s condition. Monitoring helps detect side effects, including changes in kidney function and blood salts.

topics.name: Heart Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: For carefully selected people with end-stage heart disease that remains severe despite other treatment, a transplant can extend life and improve daily function. It requires lifelong immune-suppressing medicines and follow-up because rejection, infection, and disease of the donor heart can occur.

topics.name: Heart Valve Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing or leakage of a heart valve can alter blood flow and strain the heart, sometimes before symptoms appear. More severe disease may cause shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling, or impaired heart function, and may need valve repair or replacement.

topics.name: Heat Cramps
topics.clinical_significance: Heat cramps are painful spasms in exercised muscles, often linked to heavy sweating, fluid or salt loss, and fatigue. They can temporarily prevent use of the affected muscles. Unlike heat stroke, body temperature is usually normal and other examination findings are generally unremarkable.

topics.name: Heat Exhaustion
topics.clinical_significance: Heat exhaustion causes weakness, dizziness, nausea, or fainting after heat exposure and is often accompanied by dehydration. Unlike heatstroke, it does not impair mental function and usually causes only a mild rise in body temperature. Severe cases can lead to muscle breakdown and kidney injury.

topics.name: Heat Illness
topics.clinical_significance: Heat illness ranges from muscle cramps and heat exhaustion to heatstroke, which can cause brain and other organ damage or death. It occurs when the body cannot lose heat fast enough; risk rises with strenuous activity, hot or humid conditions, dehydration, some medicines, and very young or older age. High body temperature with altered mental status suggests heatstroke.

topics.name: Heat Illness, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Heat illness ranges from muscle cramps and heat exhaustion to heatstroke. It develops when the body cannot lose heat fast enough, especially during exertion or in hot, humid conditions. Heatstroke impairs mental function and can cause multiple organ failure or death, so it is important to distinguish it from milder heat illness.

topics.name: Heatstroke
topics.clinical_significance: Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency marked by very high core temperature, usually above 40 °C, and altered mental status. It can rapidly damage the brain, muscles, kidneys, liver, lungs, and heart; sweating may still be present. Rapid cooling is critical to reduce the risk of death and lasting injury.

topics.name: Heavy Chain Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: These rare, often malignant plasma-cell disorders produce abnormal immunoglobulin heavy chains without light chains. They can resemble lymphoma and cause enlarged lymph nodes or organs, low blood counts, or repeated infections; the IgA form often affects the intestine and impairs nutrient absorption. Their course ranges from mild to rapidly progressive.

topics.name: Heavy Metal Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term exposure to heavy metals such as lead or cadmium can damage kidney tubules and cause progressive chronic kidney disease. Lead-related kidney injury may also cause high blood pressure and gout; tubular damage may not fully recover. Recognizing the exposure is important because further exposure can worsen kidney injury.

topics.name: Heimlich Maneuver
topics.clinical_significance: Abdominal thrusts, formerly called the Heimlich maneuver, can clear a life-threatening foreign-body airway blockage in a conscious adult or child older than 1 year. They are used only for severe obstruction; back or chest thrusts are alternatives in some situations. Rib or internal injury can occur.

topics.name: Helicobacter pylori Infection
topics.clinical_significance: H. pylori often causes long-lasting stomach inflammation and is a common cause of stomach and duodenal ulcers. Infection increases the risk of stomach cancer and a rare stomach lymphoma called MALT lymphoma, although many people have no symptoms. Eradicating the infection can prevent ulcer recurrence and can cure some cases of MALT lymphoma.

topics.name: Helminthic Brain Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Worm infections of the brain or spinal cord can cause seizures, meningitis, hydrocephalus, stroke, or other neurologic problems. Neurocysticercosis, usually caused by the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, is the most common form in the Western Hemisphere and can be fatal without treatment. These infections are important to consider in people from or returning from areas where they are common.

topics.name: Helomas
topics.clinical_significance: Helomas (corns) are small, deep areas of thickened skin caused by repeated pressure or friction, often over toe bones. They can be painful and may recur if the pressure remains. Foot lesions need careful assessment in people with diabetes or poor circulation.

topics.name: Hematospermia
topics.clinical_significance: Blood in semen is usually temporary and benign, often with no known cause or after a prostate biopsy. Bleeding that lasts more than a month, blood in urine, urinary symptoms, fever, or an abnormal prostate or epididymis finding may point to infection or another underlying disorder and needs further evaluation, especially in men over 40.

topics.name: Hematuria
topics.clinical_significance: Hematuria may be visible or found only on urine testing. It can result from infection, stones, kidney disease, or urinary tract cancer, and red urine is not always caused by blood. Persistent microscopic or unexplained visible blood, especially in older adults or with protein in urine, can signal serious disease and needs evaluation.

topics.name: Hematuria, Isolated
topics.clinical_significance: Isolated hematuria means red blood cells in urine without other urine abnormalities, such as protein or casts. Brief microscopic cases are often temporary and have no known cause, but persistent blood—especially in older adults or people with cancer risk factors—can signal kidney or urinary tract disease. Urine testing confirms the finding and helps guide evaluation.

topics.name: Hemifacial Spasm
topics.clinical_significance: Hemifacial spasm causes painless, involuntary contractions on one side of the face, often starting around the eye and spreading to the cheek or mouth. It usually results from a blood vessel pressing on the facial nerve; contractions may become nearly continuous. It can resemble a tic, eyelid spasm, or focal seizure.

topics.name: Hemochromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Excess iron can build up in the liver, heart, pancreas, and hormone-producing organs. Over time it may cause cirrhosis, diabetes, joint disease, hormone problems, or heart failure. It can be inherited or acquired, including after repeated blood transfusions.

topics.name: Hemodialysis
topics.clinical_significance: Hemodialysis removes waste, toxins, and excess fluid and helps correct electrolyte imbalances when the kidneys cannot do so. In kidney failure, it helps prevent complications of uremia and may prolong life or serve as a bridge to transplant, but usually requires ongoing sessions. Low blood pressure and infection or clotting of the blood-vessel access are important complications.

topics.name: Hemofiltration and Hemodialysis
topics.clinical_significance: Continuous hemofiltration and hemodialysis remove waste and excess fluid slowly, making them useful for critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, unstable blood pressure, or large fluid needs. Slower fluid removal can reduce the sudden blood-pressure drops seen with standard intermittent dialysis. These treatments require continuous blood circulation through a machine and anticoagulation to prevent clotting.

topics.name: Hemoglobin C Disease
topics.clinical_significance: People with two Hb C genes usually have mild ongoing breakdown of red blood cells, small red blood cells, and an enlarged spleen; anemia can sometimes be severe. Gallstones are the most common complication. People with one Hb C gene are usually well. Inheriting Hb C with Hb S causes a separate sickling disorder called HbSC disease.

topics.name: Hemoglobin E Disease
topics.clinical_significance: People with two Hb E genes usually have mild anemia with small red blood cells and no enlarged spleen. People with one Hb E gene are usually well. Inheriting Hb E with beta-zero thalassemia can cause a more serious anemia, similar to thalassemia intermedia or major, often with an enlarged spleen.

topics.name: Hemoglobin S-C Disease
topics.clinical_significance: HbSC disease is a type of sickle cell disease caused by inheriting Hb S from one parent and Hb C from the other. Anemia and symptoms are often milder than in HbSS disease, but life-threatening acute chest syndrome or organ failure can still occur. Retinal bleeding, blood in urine, and damage to the hip bone are also common.

topics.name: Hemoglobin S–Beta-Thalassemia Disease
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited disorder causes sickle cell disease symptoms together with small red blood cells. Severity depends on how much normal hemoglobin A is made: HbS-beta-zero can be as severe as sickle cell anemia, while HbS-beta-plus is usually milder.

topics.name: Hemoglobinopathies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Hemoglobinopathies are inherited disorders that change hemoglobin structure or production. They can cause anemia of varying severity. The effects depend on the specific disorder and gene copies inherited; some people have mild disease, while others develop serious problems such as sickle cell disease or severe thalassemia.

topics.name: Hemolytic Anemia, Autoimmune
topics.clinical_significance: The immune system makes antibodies that destroy red blood cells, causing anemia. This can lead to fatigue, shortness of breath, pale or yellow skin, or an enlarged spleen. Severe cases can be life-threatening. The cause and treatment depend partly on whether the antibodies act at warm or cold temperatures.

topics.name: Hemolytic Anemia, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are destroyed faster than the bone marrow can replace them. It can cause fatigue, weakness, dizziness, jaundice, and an enlarged spleen; red or dark urine may occur when cells break down in the bloodstream. Severe, rapid destruction can cause shock. Causes may be inherited or acquired.

topics.name: Hemolytic Anemia, Traumatic
topics.clinical_significance: Mechanical forces or turbulent blood flow can damage and fragment red blood cells, causing hemolytic anemia. This may happen in small blood vessels, around abnormal heart valves or medical devices, or after repeated impact. Blood tests may show red-cell fragments called schistocytes. Symptoms reflect the anemia and its cause, so treatment targets the underlying problem.

topics.name: Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Neonate
topics.clinical_significance: Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal or newborn red blood cells, often because of an Rh or other blood-group mismatch. This can cause severe fetal anemia, heart failure, or death; after birth, it can cause jaundice and brain injury from high bilirubin. Screening finds pregnancies at risk. Rh immune globulin can prevent most Rh-related cases in Rh-negative pregnant people who have not already made these antibodies.

topics.name: Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
topics.clinical_significance: HUS is a serious disorder in which small-vessel clots destroy red blood cells and platelets and can injure the kidneys. It causes hemolytic anemia, a low platelet count, and sudden kidney injury. In children, it often follows diarrhea caused by Shiga toxin–producing bacteria such as E. coli; other cases can result from problems with the complement system. Some people need dialysis.

topics.name: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
topics.clinical_significance: HLH is a rare, serious disorder in which immune cells become overactive and can damage organs. It may cause persistent fever, an enlarged liver or spleen, low blood cell counts, and neurologic problems. HLH can be inherited or triggered by infections, cancer, or immune disorders, and it needs prompt specialist treatment.

topics.name: Hemophilia
topics.clinical_significance: Hemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder, usually affecting males, caused by low clotting factor VIII (type A) or factor IX (type B). Bleeding severity depends on the factor level; it may follow minor injury or occur without an obvious cause when disease is severe. Bleeding into joints and muscles is common, and repeated joint bleeding can cause lasting damage. Bleeding in the brain or airway can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Hemophilus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Haemophilus bacteria cause illnesses ranging from ear, sinus, and lung infections to serious bloodstream infection, meningitis, or epiglottitis. Different species cause different diseases; H. ducreyi causes chancroid. Hib vaccination has greatly reduced invasive disease from H. influenzae type b, which can be life-threatening, especially in young children.

topics.name: Hemoptysis
topics.clinical_significance: Hemoptysis means coughing up blood from the airways or lungs. Small blood streaks can occur with infections such as bronchitis, but other causes include widened airways, tuberculosis, pneumonia, a lung blood clot, and cancer. Heavy bleeding can block breathing and become life-threatening.

topics.name: Hemorrhoids
topics.clinical_significance: Internal hemorrhoids often cause painless bleeding or tissue that protrudes during a bowel movement. A clot in an external hemorrhoid can cause a painful lump. Other bowel problems can also cause rectal bleeding, so bleeding should not automatically be blamed on hemorrhoids.

topics.name: Hemosiderosis
topics.clinical_significance: Hemosiderosis is a localized buildup of iron in tissue, often after bleeding or breakdown of red blood cells. It usually does not damage the tissue, unlike widespread iron overload. Blood loss or loss of iron in urine can still lead to iron-deficiency anemia.

topics.name: Hemostasis
topics.clinical_significance: Hemostasis stops bleeding after a blood vessel is injured: the vessel narrows, platelets form a plug, and fibrin strengthens it. The body later breaks down the clot as the vessel heals. Problems with this process can cause either abnormal bleeding or harmful clots.

topics.name: Hemostasis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: After a blood vessel is injured, it narrows to limit blood loss, platelets form a plug, and clotting proteins make fibrin to strengthen it. Natural controls keep the clot from growing too much, and the body later dissolves it as healing occurs. Problems with this balance can cause bleeding or harmful clots.

topics.name: Hemothorax
topics.clinical_significance: Blood collects in the space around a lung, usually after blunt or penetrating chest injury, and it may occur with a pneumothorax. A large collection can compress the lung, make breathing difficult, and cause shock from blood loss. Treatment usually requires urgent chest-tube drainage; ongoing severe bleeding may require surgery.

topics.name: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura
topics.clinical_significance: Henoch-Schönlein purpura, now called IgA vasculitis, inflames small blood vessels, mainly in children. It causes raised purple spots, often on the legs and buttocks, and may cause joint pain, abdominal pain or bleeding, and kidney inflammation. Most children recover, but symptoms can recur and kidney involvement may cause lasting damage, especially in adults.

topics.name: Hepatic and Biliary Disorders, Testing for
topics.clinical_significance: Blood tests can show liver-cell injury, poor bile flow, or reduced production of albumin and clotting proteins. Imaging helps find gallstones, blocked bile ducts, and liver masses; test patterns and results are interpreted with the person’s history, and some cases need further tests or a biopsy.

topics.name: Hepatic Artery Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatic artery aneurysms are uncommon bulges in the artery that supplies the liver. If one ruptures, bleeding into the bile duct can cause jaundice, upper digestive tract bleeding, and right upper abdominal pain; bleeding into the abdomen can be fatal. Treatment is usually artery embolization or surgery.

topics.name: Hepatic Artery Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: Blockage of the hepatic artery reduces oxygen-rich blood to the liver and usually causes liver tissue injury (infarction). It may cause no symptoms unless injury develops; then right upper abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice can occur. It is especially serious after a liver transplant or when portal vein blood flow is also blocked.

topics.name: Hepatic Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Most isolated simple liver cysts are harmless and found by chance. Very large or numerous cysts can cause pain or press on nearby organs; many liver cysts may occur with polycystic kidney disease. Some cyst-like liver lesions result from infection or tumors and need separate evaluation.

topics.name: Hepatic Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Some liver disorders arise during pregnancy, while others are present beforehand. Pregnancy-related cholestasis causes intense itching and raises the risk of premature birth or stillbirth; acute fatty liver and HELLP can cause severe, life-threatening illness. Hepatitis E may be more severe in pregnancy, and hepatitis B can pass to the newborn, but newborn vaccination and immune globulin help prevent infection. Chronic liver disease usually does not worsen, but cirrhosis can raise the risk of bleeding from enlarged veins.

topics.name: Hepatic Fibrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatic fibrosis is excess scar tissue that forms after long-term liver injury. It often causes no symptoms at first, but can distort blood flow through the liver, raise pressure in the portal vein, and progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Treating the cause may stop or partly reverse early fibrosis.

topics.name: Hepatic Granulomas
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatic granulomas are small clusters of immune cells in the liver. They usually cause no symptoms or liver damage themselves, but can signal an infection such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, a medication reaction, or another disease. Rarely, inflammation from the underlying cause leads to liver scarring or high pressure in liver blood vessels; treatment focuses on that cause.

topics.name: Hepatic Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Blunt or penetrating injury can tear or crush the liver and cause internal bleeding; severe bleeding can lead to shock or death. Symptoms may include right upper abdominal pain and tenderness, sometimes with pain felt in the right shoulder. Small injuries often stop bleeding on their own, but severe injuries may need embolization or surgery and can cause bile leaks or abscesses.

topics.name: Hepatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. It may be short-term or chronic and can result from viruses, alcohol, fatty liver disease, medications, or autoimmune disease. It may cause fatigue, nausea, upper abdominal pain, or jaundice; ongoing inflammation can scar the liver and lead to cirrhosis or liver failure.

topics.name: Hepatitis A
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis A is an acute liver infection spread when virus from stool is swallowed, often through contaminated food or water or close contact with an infected person. Young children may have no symptoms; older children and adults may have poor appetite, tiredness, nausea, fever, or jaundice. Most people recover fully. Chronic infection does not occur, but rare acute liver failure is more likely in people with existing liver disease. Vaccination helps prevent infection.

topics.name: Hepatitis A (HepA) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The hepatitis A vaccine prevents hepatitis A infection and gives long-term protection. It is routinely given to children in some immunization schedules and is recommended for people at higher risk, such as travelers to areas where hepatitis A is common and people with chronic liver disease. The usual vaccine series has two doses; schedules vary by product and local guidance.

topics.name: Hepatitis, Acute Viral, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Acute viral hepatitis is a short-term inflammation of the liver caused mainly by hepatitis viruses A, B, C, D, or E. It may cause poor appetite, nausea, tiredness, fever, pain under the right ribs, dark urine, or jaundice, though some people have no symptoms. Many cases resolve on their own, but hepatitis B, C, and D, and rarely E, can become chronic; acute liver failure is rare. Identifying the virus matters because transmission, prevention, and treatment differ.

topics.name: Hepatitis B, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute hepatitis B is a new infection of the liver caused by hepatitis B virus, spread through infected blood or body fluids, including during sex or childbirth. It may cause nausea, loss of appetite, tiredness, fever, or jaundice, but can also have few or no symptoms. Most adults recover, though acute liver failure can occur. Infection is much more likely to become chronic when acquired in infancy or early childhood; chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Vaccination prevents infection, and vaccine plus hepatitis B immune globulin may help after exposure.

topics.name: Hepatitis B, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic hepatitis B is a long-lasting infection with hepatitis B virus. Many people have no symptoms; others may feel tired or generally unwell. Without treatment, liver damage may progress to cirrhosis, and the infection raises the risk of liver cancer even without cirrhosis. Antiviral medicines can control the virus and lower the risk of complications, but usually do not cure the infection; ongoing monitoring is important.

topics.name: Hepatitis B (HepB) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The hepatitis B vaccine prevents hepatitis B infection and its later complications, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. It is made using a viral surface protein, so it cannot cause hepatitis B. It is routinely offered to children and unvaccinated adults according to local schedules; completing the recommended doses gives strong, long-lasting protection.

topics.name: Hepatitis B Infection, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal hepatitis B is usually passed from an infected mother to her baby during delivery. Most infected newborns have no symptoms, but up to 90% develop chronic infection, which can later cause cirrhosis or liver cancer. Some babies develop jaundice or poor growth, and severe liver failure is rare. Giving the newborn hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin soon after birth greatly helps prevent infection.

topics.name: Hepatitis C, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute hepatitis C is a new liver infection, usually spread through infected blood. It often causes no symptoms, but most people (about 65–85%) develop chronic infection, which can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Acute liver failure is very rare. Direct-acting antiviral medicines are started after diagnosis; they can lower the chance of chronic infection and reduce spread to others. No vaccine is available.

topics.name: Hepatitis C, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic hepatitis C is infection with hepatitis C virus that lasts more than 6 months. Many people have no symptoms until liver damage develops. Over time, 15–30% develop cirrhosis within 20 years; cirrhosis can lead to liver cancer. Direct-acting antiviral medicines clear the virus in more than 95% of patients. People with advanced liver scarring or cirrhosis may still need ongoing liver cancer screening after treatment.

topics.name: Hepatitis, Causes
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver and can have many causes. Common causes include hepatitis viruses, alcohol, metabolic fatty liver disease, and medicines; autoimmune and genetic disorders are less common causes. Identifying the cause matters because treatment and risk of spread differ. Many cases of acute viral hepatitis resolve, but some become chronic and can cause lasting liver damage.

topics.name: Hepatitis, Chronic, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic hepatitis is liver inflammation lasting more than 6 months. Common causes include hepatitis B or C, fatty liver inflammation linked to metabolic disease, alcohol, and autoimmune disease. It may cause no symptoms and first be found through abnormal liver blood tests. Ongoing inflammation can scar the liver and lead to cirrhosis and its complications. Treatment depends on the cause; advanced cirrhosis may require a liver transplant.

topics.name: Hepatitis D
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis D is caused by a virus that can reproduce only in someone who also has hepatitis B. It spreads through infected blood or body fluids. It can occur with a new hepatitis B infection or infect someone who already has chronic hepatitis B; the latter often leads to chronic hepatitis D and a more aggressive liver disease. Hepatitis B vaccination also prevents hepatitis D.

topics.name: Hepatitis E
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatitis E is usually an acute liver infection spread through contaminated water; some types spread from animals through undercooked meat. Most people recover without specific treatment, but severe illness and liver failure are more likely during pregnancy. Rarely, people with weakened immune systems develop chronic infection.

topics.name: Hepatitis, Fulminant
topics.clinical_significance: Fulminant hepatitis, now usually called acute liver failure, is a rapid and life-threatening loss of liver function. It can cause jaundice, poor blood clotting, confusion, coma, brain swelling, and kidney failure. It is a medical emergency requiring intensive care and urgent assessment for liver transplant. Medicines such as acetaminophen and some hepatitis viruses are possible causes; treatment depends on the cause and complications.

topics.name: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer. It usually develops in a scarred liver (cirrhosis); chronic hepatitis B can also raise the risk without cirrhosis. HCC often causes no early symptoms. Screening people at high risk can find small tumors that may be cured with surgery, ablation, or liver transplant. Advanced cancer or poor liver function makes the outlook worse.

topics.name: Hepatoma
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatoma is another name for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a cancer that starts in liver cells called hepatocytes. It is the most common primary liver cancer and often develops in a liver with cirrhosis.

topics.name: Hepatopulmonary Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a complication of chronic liver disease, usually with portal hypertension. Small blood vessels in the lungs widen, so blood receives too little oxygen. This causes low blood oxygen and shortness of breath, often worse when sitting or standing and better when lying down. Supplemental oxygen may help, and the condition can improve after liver transplant.

topics.name: Hereditary and Acquired C1 Inhibitor Deficiency or Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Too little or poorly working C1 inhibitor can cause repeated attacks of bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Swelling may affect the face, lips, tongue, gut, or throat and usually occurs without itching or hives. Throat swelling can block breathing and is an emergency; antihistamines and steroids usually do not help. The condition may be inherited or acquired, sometimes with a blood cancer or autoimmune disease.

topics.name: Hereditary Chorea
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary chorea usually refers to Huntington disease, an inherited brain disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. It causes involuntary movements, mood or behavior changes, and worsening thinking and memory, usually beginning in adulthood and progressing over time. There is no cure, but symptoms can be treated. Genetic counseling is important before relatives consider testing.

topics.name: Hereditary Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (Cryopyrinopathies)
topics.clinical_significance: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS) are rare autoinflammatory disorders, usually caused by an overactive NLRP3 gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. They cause repeated episodes of fever, rash, and other inflammation. Severe forms can damage hearing, joints, eyes, brain, or kidneys. Early treatment with medicines that block interleukin-1 can prevent lasting organ damage.

topics.name: Hereditary Hemochromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a group of genetic disorders that cause the body to absorb too much iron. Iron can build up and damage the liver, heart, pancreas, joints, and hormone-producing organs, sometimes causing cirrhosis, diabetes, heart disease, or arthritis. Symptoms may be subtle or appear only after organ damage. Early diagnosis and regular blood removal can reduce iron and prevent further damage; close relatives may need screening.

topics.name: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is an inherited disorder that causes fragile abnormal blood vessels in the skin, nose, gut, lungs, brain, and liver. Repeated nose or gut bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia. Abnormal vessels in internal organs can cause serious problems, including stroke or brain abscess, bleeding, or heart failure, so screening for them is important.

topics.name: Hereditary Intrinsic Platelet Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited platelet function disorders impair the platelets' ability to stop bleeding and cause a lifelong bleeding tendency. Bleeding may involve the skin or mucous membranes, such as easy bruising or nosebleeds, and can sometimes be severe. Platelet counts and routine clotting tests may be normal, so diagnosis often requires special platelet function tests. Platelet transfusion may be needed for serious bleeding.

topics.name: Hereditary Motor Neuropathy With Liability to Pressure Palsies (HNPP)
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP) is a rare, usually autosomal dominant disorder that makes peripheral nerves unusually sensitive to pressure or stretching. Pressure can cause repeated episodes of numbness or weakness, such as foot drop, ulnar nerve palsy, or carpal tunnel symptoms. Episodes may last from minutes to months; many people recover fully, while others have mild lasting symptoms. Avoiding pressure and using protective splints or pads can help.

topics.name: Hereditary Nephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary nephritis (Alport syndrome) is an inherited disorder of type IV collagen that damages the kidney's filtering membranes. It commonly causes blood in the urine, followed by protein in the urine, high blood pressure, and progressive chronic kidney disease that may lead to kidney failure. Hearing loss is common, and eye problems can also occur. Early kidney-protective treatment can slow the damage.

topics.name: Hereditary Neuropathies
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary neuropathies are genetic disorders of peripheral nerves. Depending on the type, they can cause slowly worsening weakness, muscle wasting, reduced sensation, foot deformities, or problems with automatic body functions. Severity ranges from mild to disabling. Braces, physical therapy, and occupational therapy can help maintain movement and daily function; treatment for some specific causes is available.

topics.name: Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by changes in genes that repair DNA. It greatly increases the risk of colorectal cancer, often at a younger age, and also raises the risk of endometrial, ovarian, stomach, urinary tract, and other cancers. Regular colonoscopy and surveillance for other related cancers are important. Genetic testing can identify relatives who also need screening.

topics.name: Hereditary Optic Neuropathies
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary optic neuropathies, including dominant optic atrophy and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, damage the optic nerve and cause progressive loss of central vision, usually in both eyes. They often begin in childhood or young adulthood; vision may worsen slowly or, in Leber disease, over several months, and the nerve damage is usually permanent. Leber disease can also affect the heart or nervous system. There is no proven treatment for most cases, so low-vision support and genetic counseling are important.

topics.name: Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary periodic fever syndromes are a group of autoinflammatory disorders that cause repeated attacks of fever and other inflammation without another clear cause. They usually begin in childhood, but the symptoms and complications vary by syndrome. Identifying the specific condition matters because treatment differs and some types can cause lasting organ damage if not controlled.

topics.name: Hereditary Periodic Fever Syndromes, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary periodic fever syndromes are autoinflammatory disorders that cause repeated, unexplained attacks of fever and other symptoms, usually starting in childhood. The group includes familial Mediterranean fever, cryopyrin-associated syndromes, hyper-IgD syndrome, TRAPS, PFAPA, and PAPA. Similar cases can occur without a family history. Recognizing the specific syndrome helps guide treatment and reduce the risk of complications.

topics.name: Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary spastic paraplegia is a group of rare genetic disorders that gradually damage the nerve pathways controlling leg movement. It causes increasing leg stiffness and weakness, making walking difficult; bladder urgency is also common, while sensation is usually preserved. Some forms affect thinking, vision, hearing, or other nervous system functions. Treatment eases symptoms and helps maintain mobility.

topics.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis and Hereditary Elliptocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: Hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis are inherited red blood cell membrane disorders that can cause the cells to break down too early. This may lead to anemia, jaundice, and an enlarged spleen; pigment gallstones are common in spherocytosis. Elliptocytosis is often milder. Viral illness can trigger a sudden drop in red blood cell production, and people with severe symptoms or complications may need spleen removal.

topics.name: Hernias of the Abdominal Wall
topics.clinical_significance: A hernia is a bulge of tissue, often bowel or fat, through a weak spot in the abdominal wall. It may cause no symptoms or mild discomfort. If the tissue becomes trapped or loses its blood supply, it can cause bowel obstruction or tissue damage and needs urgent surgery.

topics.name: Herpangina
topics.clinical_significance: Herpangina is an enterovirus infection, most common in children, that causes fever, sore throat, and small blisters or ulcers at the back of the mouth. Painful swallowing may reduce drinking and lead to dehydration. The sores usually heal within a week; care focuses on pain relief and fluids.

topics.name: Herpes Gestationis
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes gestationis, now called pemphigoid gestationis, is a rare autoimmune, very itchy blistering rash that occurs during pregnancy or soon after birth; it is not caused by herpesvirus. It often starts near the navel and may return in later pregnancies. Most babies are unaffected, but fetal growth may need monitoring because placental problems can increase risk.

topics.name: Herpes Labialis
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes labialis (cold sores) is a recurrent herpes simplex virus infection of the lips, usually caused by HSV-1. It causes painful clusters of blisters or ulcers and can spread through close contact, even when sores are not visible. Infection can be prolonged or spread in people with a weakened immune system; eye symptoms need prompt medical care.

topics.name: Herpes Simplex (HSV) Infection, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal HSV is usually acquired during birth and can affect the skin, eyes, mouth, brain, or multiple organs. It can progress quickly and cause death or lasting brain and nerve problems; some infants have no blisters. Suspected infection is an emergency and needs prompt testing and intravenous acyclovir.

topics.name: Herpes Simplex Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes simplex keratitis is an HSV infection of the cornea that often recurs. It can cause eye pain or a gritty feeling, tearing, redness, and light sensitivity; repeated or deep infection can scar or thin the cornea and permanently reduce vision. Prompt eye care and antiviral treatment help protect sight.

topics.name: Herpes Simplex Keratoconjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis is an HSV infection of the eye. It can cause a red, watery, painful eye and light sensitivity; when the cornea is involved, repeated infection can scar it and permanently reduce vision. Prompt eye care and antiviral treatment help protect sight.

topics.name: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Infections
topics.clinical_significance: HSV-1 and HSV-2 cause lifelong infections that can affect the mouth, genitals, skin, or eyes; either type can infect different body sites. The virus can spread through close contact even when sores are not visible and may reactivate to cause recurrent painful blisters. Infection of the eye, brain, or newborn, or widespread infection in a person with weak immunity, can be severe and needs prompt antiviral treatment.

topics.name: Herpes Zoster
topics.clinical_significance: Shingles is reactivation of the chickenpox virus, causing a painful, usually one-sided band of blisters. Nerve pain may last for months after the rash heals. A rash on the forehead or near the eye can threaten vision; antiviral treatment works best when started within 72 hours of the rash appearing.

topics.name: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is shingles affecting the forehead or eyelid in the nerve area that serves the eye. It can inflame the cornea or other parts of the eye, causing scarring and vision loss. A rash in this area needs prompt eye assessment and antiviral treatment, even if the eye seems unaffected.

topics.name: Herpes Zoster Oticus
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) is shingles affecting nerves near the ear. It causes severe ear pain and blisters in or around the ear, often with weakness on the same side of the face; dizziness or hearing loss may also occur, and some problems can persist. Antivirals and steroids are often used, although evidence that they improve recovery is limited.

topics.name: Herpes Zoster Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The recombinant shingles vaccine lowers the risk of shingles and its complications, including long-lasting nerve pain. The MSD Manual recommends 2 doses for adults 50 years and older and adults 19 years and older who are or will be immunocompromised. A sore arm, tiredness, muscle aches, headache, or fever are common short-term effects.

topics.name: Herpes Zoster Virus Ophthalmicus
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes zoster virus ophthalmicus is shingles affecting the nerve that serves the forehead and eye. It can inflame the cornea and other parts of the eye, causing scarring and lasting vision loss. A rash on the forehead or eyelid needs prompt eye assessment and early antiviral treatment, even if the eye seems unaffected.

topics.name: Herpesvirus Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Human herpesviruses cause lifelong infections that can become dormant and later reactivate; some can spread even when they cause no symptoms. They cause illnesses ranging from cold sores, chickenpox, and shingles to mononucleosis and serious brain, eye, newborn, or widespread infections, especially in people with weakened immunity. Epstein-Barr virus and HHV-8 can also cause certain cancers.

topics.name: Herpesviruses
topics.clinical_significance: Eight herpesvirus types are known to infect humans. They establish lifelong dormant infections that can reactivate and cause diseases such as cold sores, chickenpox, shingles, mononucleosis, or cytomegalovirus infection; Epstein-Barr virus and HHV-8 can also cause certain cancers.

topics.name: Herpetic Gingivostomatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Herpetic gingivostomatitis is usually the first HSV-1 infection in children. It causes fever, painful sores throughout the mouth, and inflamed gums; pain can make drinking difficult and lead to dehydration. The virus remains dormant in nerve cells and may later cause cold sores.

topics.name: Herpetic Whitlow
topics.clinical_significance: Herpetic whitlow is an HSV infection of the fingertip that causes intense pain, swelling, and blisters. It may look like a bacterial finger abscess, but usually clears on its own and can recur. Do not cut or drain it; cover open blisters to reduce spread.

topics.name: Herring Worm Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Herring worm disease (anisakiasis) follows eating raw or undercooked saltwater fish or squid containing parasite larvae. It often causes sudden abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; rarely, intestinal inflammation develops later and can resemble appendicitis or Crohn disease. Endoscopic removal of the larvae is curative, and proper cooking or freezing prevents infection.

topics.name: Heterophyiasis and Related Trematode Infections
topics.clinical_significance: These intestinal fluke infections usually follow eating raw or undercooked freshwater or brackish-water fish. Many infections cause no symptoms, but heavier infections can cause abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, poor nutrient absorption, and weight loss; rarely, eggs spread to the heart or other organs. Praziquantel treats the infection, and cooking fish helps prevent it.

topics.name: Hiatus (Hiatal) Hernia
topics.clinical_significance: A hiatal hernia occurs when part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest. Most cause no symptoms, but some worsen acid reflux. A less common type can become trapped or lose its blood supply, so symptomatic hernias may need medical or surgical treatment.

topics.name: Hiccough
topics.clinical_significance: Hiccough (hiccup) is usually brief and harmless, often triggered by stomach fullness or alcohol. Hiccups lasting more than 2 days are uncommon and may be linked to an underlying digestive, chest, or nervous-system problem; persistent hiccups, especially with neurologic symptoms, need medical evaluation.

topics.name: Hiccups
topics.clinical_significance: Hiccups are repeated involuntary spasms of the diaphragm followed by sudden closure of the airway opening. Brief episodes are common; hiccups lasting more than 2 days or more than 1 month are uncommon and distressing and may signal an underlying illness, so they need medical evaluation.

topics.name: Hidradenitis Suppurativa
topics.clinical_significance: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a long-lasting inflammatory disease of hair follicles in skin folds, such as the armpits, groin, and areas beneath the breasts. It causes recurrent painful lumps and abscesses that may drain, form tunnels under the skin, and scar; severe disease can limit daily life. The lesions are often not caused by bacteria, though a secondary infection can occur.

topics.name: HIDS
topics.clinical_significance: HIDS (mevalonate kinase deficiency) is a rare inherited disorder that causes repeated fever attacks, usually beginning in the first year of life and lasting 4 to 6 days. Attacks may include chills, stomach pain, vomiting or diarrhea, joint pain, swollen neck glands, rash, or mouth sores; blood IgD can be normal, so other tests may be needed. Attacks can continue through life but often become less frequent after adolescence; medicines that block interleukin-1 can prevent them.

topics.name: High-Risk Pregnancy, Overview of
topics.clinical_significance: A high-risk pregnancy means the pregnant person, fetus, or newborn has an increased risk of serious illness or death before, during, or after birth. Risk factors include chronic health conditions, multiple fetuses, past pregnancy complications, or problems that arise during the current pregnancy. Early identification allows closer monitoring and specialized care.

topics.name: Hip Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: A traumatic hip dislocation is an emergency, usually caused by a strong force. It can injure the sciatic nerve or damage the blood supply to the top of the thighbone, causing bone death; delay in putting the hip back in place raises this risk. Fractures often occur with it, so the hip should be reduced promptly and checked for associated injuries.

topics.name: Hip Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Hip fractures are common in older adults with weak bones and may follow a minor fall. They cause hip or groin pain and difficulty walking; in older adults, long bed rest can lead to serious problems such as blood clots, pneumonia, pressure sores, and death. Most are treated with surgery so the person can move sooner; some fractures also damage the blood supply to the top of the thighbone and cause bone death.

topics.name: Hip Surgery Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation begins as soon as possible after hip fracture repair or hip replacement. Gradual exercises and movement help rebuild strength and restore walking and daily activities while limiting muscle loss from immobility. Weight-bearing and precautions depend on the operation and the surgeon's instructions.

topics.name: Hirschsprung Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Hirschsprung disease is present from birth: part of the bowel lacks nerve cells, so stool cannot pass normally and the bowel above it may enlarge. Newborns may fail to pass their first stool and develop abdominal swelling, constipation, or vomiting. Without treatment, a dangerous bowel inflammation called enterocolitis can occur; surgery is usually needed.

topics.name: Hirsutism and Hypertrichosis
topics.clinical_significance: Hirsutism is coarse, dark hair growth in women in a pattern more typical of men; it is often linked to excess androgens, commonly from polycystic ovary syndrome. Sudden rapid growth or signs such as a deepening voice or missed periods may point to a hormone-producing tumor and need prompt evaluation. Hypertrichosis is increased hair growth anywhere on the body and may be caused by medicines or illness.

topics.name: Histiocytic Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Histiocytic disorders are an uncommon, varied group caused by abnormal growth of immune cells called histiocytes, including dendritic cells and macrophages. They include Langerhans cell histiocytosis, the most common type, as well as disorders such as Erdheim-Chester disease and hemophagocytic syndromes. Symptoms and treatment depend on the specific disorder.

topics.name: Histiocytic Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Histiocytic syndromes are a group of disorders involving abnormal growth of dendritic cells or macrophages, types of immune cells. They include Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Erdheim-Chester disease, hemophagocytic syndromes, and Rosai-Dorfman disease. Effects vary by the specific disorder and the organs involved.

topics.name: Histiocytosis X
topics.clinical_significance: Histiocytosis X is an older name for pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, a lung disease in which abnormal Langerhans cells build up, usually in people who smoke. It can cause shortness of breath, dry cough, and sometimes sudden lung collapse (pneumothorax). Stopping smoking is the main treatment.

topics.name: Histoplasmosis
topics.clinical_significance: Histoplasmosis is caused by inhaling Histoplasma spores from contaminated soil or dust, often where birds or bats roost. Many infections cause no symptoms or a short-lived flu-like lung illness, but chronic lung disease or spread to other organs can occur, especially in people with weakened immunity. Untreated disseminated disease can be fatal, and severe cases need antifungal treatment.

topics.name: History-Taking in the Older Adult
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults may underreport symptoms, show nonspecific signs such as confusion or weight loss, or show illness only as a loss of daily function. These changes should not be assumed to be normal aging. A careful history should cover function, memory, mood, social needs, and all medicines, and may use family or records when recall is limited; this can reveal treatable problems and help preserve independence.

topics.name: Histrionic Personality Disorder (HPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Histrionic personality disorder is a long-term pattern of strong emotional expression and a need for attention that can make relationships difficult. A person may feel uncomfortable when not the center of attention, show quickly changing emotions, or see relationships as closer than they are. Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, and psychotherapy is the main treatment.

topics.name: HIV Infection, Antiretroviral Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for everyone with HIV. A combination of medicines suppresses the virus to an undetectable level and helps restore CD4 immune cells, reducing HIV-related illness; it controls infection but does not cure it. Consistent use and regular monitoring help maintain viral control and check for side effects or drug interactions.

topics.name: HIV-Associated Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: HIV-associated nephropathy is kidney damage linked to HIV that often causes heavy protein loss in the urine and enlarged kidneys. Without effective treatment, kidney function may worsen quickly and lead to kidney failure within months. Antiretroviral therapy helps control HIV and limit kidney damage; medicines that protect the kidneys may also be used.

topics.name: Hives
topics.clinical_significance: Hives are raised, itchy welts that can move around the skin. They may be triggered by foods, medicines, infections, or physical factors; long-lasting hives often have no clear cause. Hives can occur with angioedema, a deeper swelling. Swelling of the tongue or throat can block breathing and needs emergency care.

topics.name: HIV-related Cholangiopathy
topics.clinical_significance: HIV-related cholangiopathy is narrowing of the bile ducts, usually due to an opportunistic infection in advanced HIV. It can block bile flow and cause upper-right abdominal pain, diarrhea, or jaundice. Antiretroviral therapy and treatment of the infection are important; an endoscopic procedure may relieve a blockage.

topics.name: HNPCC
topics.clinical_significance: HNPCC, also called Lynch syndrome, is an inherited change in genes that repair DNA. It greatly raises the risk of colorectal cancer and also increases the risk of endometrial, ovarian, stomach, urinary tract, and other cancers. Regular colonoscopy and screening for related cancers can help find cancer early. Genetic testing can identify relatives who also need screening.

topics.name: Hoarding Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Hoarding disorder causes lasting difficulty discarding possessions, even when they have little value, and distress when discarding them. Clutter can make living areas unusable, interfere with daily life, and create fire or fall risks. Treatment often includes therapy tailored to hoarding, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy.

topics.name: Hodgkin Lymphoma
topics.clinical_significance: Hodgkin lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes that usually starts in lymph nodes. It often causes painless enlarged nodes. Fever, night sweats, or major unintentional weight loss can affect its stage and outlook. A lymph node biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and treatment cures most cases.

topics.name: Hodgkin’s Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Hodgkin’s disease, also called Hodgkin lymphoma, is a cancer of lymphocytes that usually starts in lymph nodes. It often causes painless enlarged nodes. Fever, night sweats, or major unintentional weight loss can affect its stage and outlook. A lymph node biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and treatment cures most cases.

topics.name: Holy Basil
topics.clinical_significance: Holy basil (tulsi) is promoted for stress, blood sugar, and other uses, but good evidence of benefit in people is limited. It can cause nausea or diarrhea and may affect thyroid hormone or slow blood clotting, increasing bleeding risk with blood thinners or surgery. It may interact with thyroid medicines. Avoid it when trying to conceive; safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding is unclear.

topics.name: Home Health Care
topics.clinical_significance: Home health care brings health services to a person's home, often after hospital discharge or when illness or disability limits daily function. Services may include nursing, wound care, medication monitoring, and physical or occupational therapy. Care is planned around the person's needs, and coverage rules vary.

topics.name: Homeopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Homeopathy is based on the idea that “like cures like” and uses highly diluted remedies. Studies have not found reliable evidence that homeopathic remedies treat the conditions studied. Some products labeled homeopathic contain active ingredients that can cause side effects, so they should not replace proven treatment.

topics.name: Hookworm Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Hookworm larvae enter through skin that touches contaminated soil, then grow in the small intestine and feed on blood. Infection may cause an itchy rash or stomach symptoms. Heavy or long-lasting infection can cause iron-deficiency anemia, which may be severe in children. Stool testing can diagnose infection, and antiparasitic medicines can treat it.

topics.name: Horner Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Horner syndrome causes a slightly drooping eyelid and a smaller pupil on one side; sweating on that side may also decrease. It results from damage to the nerve pathway between the brain and eye. Causes include stroke, a tear in a neck artery, or a chest or neck tumor, so finding the cause is important.

topics.name: Horner's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Horner's syndrome causes a slightly drooping eyelid and a smaller pupil on one side; sweating on that side may also decrease. It results from damage to the nerve pathway between the brain and eye. Causes include stroke, a tear in a neck artery, or a chest or neck tumor, so finding the cause is important.

topics.name: Horton Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Horton disease, also called giant cell arteritis, is inflammation of large arteries, often in the head and neck, usually in people over 50. It can cause a new headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain while chewing. It can also cause sudden, permanent vision loss, so suspected disease needs urgent treatment with corticosteroids.

topics.name: Hospital Care and Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Hospital stays can treat serious illness, but older adults face added risks such as confusion, medication side effects, falls, pressure injuries, and loss of strength or independence. Early movement, careful medication review, and clear discharge planning help reduce these problems and support safe recovery.

topics.name: Hospital-Acquired Infection, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: A newborn may acquire an infection during a hospital stay, especially if premature, very small at birth, or needing a long stay with tubes or lines. Bloodstream infections and pneumonia are common and can become severe. Hand cleaning and careful care of tubes and lines help prevent infection.

topics.name: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops at least 48 hours after admission in a patient who is not on a ventilator and was not already developing pneumonia on arrival. It may cause fever, cough, trouble breathing, and low oxygen. Drug-resistant bacteria are common, so antibiotics are chosen with test results and local resistance patterns in mind.

topics.name: Host Defense Mechanisms Against Infection
topics.clinical_significance: The body fights infection with barriers such as skin, quick defenses such as inflammation and white blood cells, and targeted defenses such as antibodies and T cells. Weakness in any of these defenses can make some infections more likely or severe. A person's genes also affect which infections they are more likely to develop.

topics.name: Host Response to Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: The immune system can recognize and kill some tumor cells, mainly through T cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages. Some tumors evade or weaken these defenses and continue to grow; antibodies alone usually do little to stop tumor growth. These immune responses are important in cancer immunotherapy.

topics.name: How To Apply a Cast
topics.clinical_significance: A cast holds a broken or injured limb still to help it heal. It must fit and be padded properly; swelling or excessive tightness can reduce blood flow or cause dangerous pressure in the limb. Worsening pain, numbness, tingling, or color change below the cast needs urgent medical review.

topics.name: How To Apply a Femoral Traction Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A femoral traction splint temporarily holds a broken thigh bone straight before definitive treatment and may reduce pain and bleeding. It can injure nerves or blood vessels and should not be used with a pelvic fracture or injuries to the same-side knee, lower leg, ankle, or foot. Blood flow and feeling in the foot should be checked before and after application.

topics.name: How To Apply a Fixed Finger Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A finger splint holds an injured finger still to protect certain fractures, tendon injuries, dislocations, or sprains while they heal. Only the joints that need support should be immobilized, because unnecessary splinting can cause stiffness. Taping too tightly can reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Apply a Knee Immobilizer
topics.clinical_significance: A knee immobilizer is a removable brace used to keep the knee stable after selected fractures or ligament or tendon injuries when a cast is not needed. Prolonged use can cause stiffness and increase the risk of a leg blood clot, so follow-up and instructions about safe movement are important. Blood flow and feeling in the foot should be checked after fitting.

topics.name: How To Apply a Long Arm Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A long arm splint supports certain fractures or dislocations around the elbow and upper forearm by limiting elbow bending and straightening. It does not fully stop the forearm from turning. Poor fit or tight wrapping can cause pressure injury or reduce blood flow, so finger color, movement, and feeling should be checked.

topics.name: How To Apply a Posterior Ankle Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A posterior ankle splint temporarily stabilizes selected ankle or foot fractures, reduced dislocations, sprains that should not bear weight, or Achilles tendon rupture. It is often used while swelling settles or before further treatment. Most are not designed for walking or weight bearing, and tight wrapping can injure skin or reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Apply a Short Arm Cast
topics.clinical_significance: A short arm cast keeps the wrist and lower forearm still to help selected fractures heal, including some wrist bone fractures and children's buckle fractures. If swelling is expected, a splint is often used first because a tight cast can reduce blood flow or cause dangerous pressure. Increasing pain, numbness, tingling, or finger color change needs urgent medical review.

topics.name: How To Apply a Short Leg Cast
topics.clinical_significance: A short leg cast keeps the foot and ankle still for selected fractures of the foot, ankle, or lower shin. Significant swelling usually calls for a splint first because a tight cast can reduce blood flow or cause dangerous pressure. Most short leg casts cannot safely bear weight unless they are made as walking casts.

topics.name: How To Apply a Shoulder Sling and Swathe
topics.clinical_significance: A sling supports the arm after a shoulder dislocation is put back in place, a humerus fracture is splinted, or an AC joint separation. Adding the swathe holds the arm against the body to limit shoulder movement; a sling alone supports the arm but does not fully immobilize the shoulder. Prolonged use can cause stiffness, and a poor fit may press on a nerve at the elbow.

topics.name: How To Apply a Sugar Tong Arm Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A sugar tong splint holds the wrist and forearm still, limiting rotation, and is commonly used for fractures near the wrist in the radius or ulna. If it is too tight, it can injure the skin or nerves, reduce blood flow, or cause dangerous pressure in the arm. Finger color, movement, and feeling should be checked.

topics.name: How To Apply a Sugar-Tong Ankle Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A sugar-tong (U-shaped) ankle splint stabilizes the ankle after selected fractures, reduced dislocations, or sprains that should not bear weight. It limits ankle movement, including side-to-side turning. Most are not made for walking; tight wrapping can injure skin, reduce blood flow, or cause dangerous pressure.

topics.name: How To Apply a Thumb Spica Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A thumb spica splint keeps the thumb and nearby wrist still for injuries such as thumb or scaphoid fractures, thumb ligament injuries, or De Quervain tenosynovitis. It protects the area while it heals or awaits further treatment. If wrapped too tightly, it can cause dangerous pressure or reduce blood flow; worsening pain, numbness, or color change needs urgent review.

topics.name: How To Apply a Volar Arm Splint
topics.clinical_significance: A volar splint holds the wrist and hand still for selected wrist or hand fractures, severe wrist sprains, and some soft-tissue injuries. It does not stop the forearm from turning palm up or down. If wrapped too tightly, it can cause pressure injury or reduce blood flow, so finger color, movement, and feeling should be checked.

topics.name: How To Apply an Ulnar Gutter Splint
topics.clinical_significance: An ulnar gutter splint holds the ring and little fingers and the outer side of the hand still for fractures of those fingers or hand bones, and some fractures near the wrist end of the ulna. Tight wrapping can injure skin or nerves and reduce blood flow, so finger color, movement, and feeling should be checked. After a punch injury, a cut over a knuckle may be a tooth wound and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: How To Aspirate or Inject a Prepatellar Bursa
topics.clinical_significance: Fluid is removed from the bursa in front of the kneecap mainly to test for infection or crystals when bursitis is suspected. Infection must be ruled out before a steroid injection, which is used only rarely for persistent or recurring noninfectious bursitis. Injecting steroids when infection is present can make it worse.

topics.name: How To Aspirate or Inject an Olecranon Bursa
topics.clinical_significance: Fluid is removed from the bursa over the elbow tip mainly to test for infection or crystals; this is the most common site of septic bursitis. Steroid injections are usually avoided because the bursa lies close to the skin and injection can cause skin damage or infection. They may be considered rarely for large, painful, recurring bursitis after infection is ruled out.

topics.name: How To Assess Gait, Stance, and Coordination
topics.clinical_significance: Walking, balance, and coordination tests help detect problems in the movement, balance, or position-sensing pathways of the nervous system. Abnormal patterns can suggest weakness, cerebellar problems, muscle stiffness, or reduced awareness of foot position, which may increase fall risk. Findings help guide further evaluation but do not identify the cause by themselves.

topics.name: How To Assess Mental Status
topics.clinical_significance: A mental status exam checks alertness and thinking, including attention, orientation, memory, language, and judgment. It helps detect or track changes in mental function, such as confusion or cognitive decline. Attention is checked first because poor attention can make other results unreliable; abnormal findings need evaluation for a cause.

topics.name: How To Assess Muscle Strength
topics.clinical_significance: Muscle strength testing helps find and grade weakness, show which muscle groups are affected, and assess how weakness limits movement. Comparing both sides and watching tasks such as standing from a chair can reveal subtle problems. Pain, fatigue, or limited effort can affect the results, so they are considered with the person's symptoms and other exam findings.

topics.name: How To Assess Reflexes
topics.clinical_significance: Reflex testing checks the nerves, spinal cord connections, and brain pathways that control automatic muscle responses. Reduced reflexes can point to a problem in a nerve or nerve root; unusually brisk reflexes or an abnormal plantar response can point to a problem in pathways from the brain or spinal cord. Comparing both sides and the pattern of findings helps guide further evaluation.

topics.name: How To Assess Sensation
topics.clinical_significance: Testing sensation helps show where a problem may be in the sensory nerves or pathways of the brain and spinal cord. The pattern of changes in pain, temperature, touch, vibration, or position sense can point to a peripheral nerve, nerve root, spinal cord, or brain problem. Findings are considered with strength and reflex changes to guide further evaluation.

topics.name: How To Assess the Autonomic Nervous System
topics.clinical_significance: This exam looks for problems in automatic body functions, such as blood pressure and heart rate changes, sweating, and pupil changes. It also asks about bowel, bladder, sexual, sleep, thirst, and appetite problems. These findings can help detect autonomic nerve or related brain problems and guide further evaluation.

topics.name: How To Assess the Cranial Nerves
topics.clinical_significance: Testing cranial nerve functions, such as vision, eye movement, facial sensation, hearing, and swallowing, can show which nerve or nearby brain area may be affected. The pattern of findings can help locate a problem in the brainstem or along a nerve's path, and can guide further evaluation.

topics.name: How To Assess the Motor System
topics.clinical_significance: A motor exam checks strength, muscle tone and size, and involuntary movements. Weakness or changes such as muscle wasting, twitching, or stiffness can help locate a problem in the brain's movement pathways, spinal cord, nerves, or muscles. The findings help guide further tests.

topics.name: How To Buddy-Tape Fingers
topics.clinical_significance: Buddy-taping supports and protects a first-degree sprain or selected stable finger fracture or dislocation by attaching the injured finger to a neighboring finger, while allowing most finger joints to move. It is not suitable for unstable or displaced fractures, unstable dislocations, or tendon injuries. Tape that is too tight can reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Buddy-Tape Toes
