topics.clinical_significance: Buddy-taping supports and helps align an injured toe by attaching it to a neighboring toe. It can be used for many toe sprains, dislocations, and fractures, but an open fracture or some big-toe fractures need other care. Tape that is too tight can reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Care for Wounds and Lacerations
topics.clinical_significance: Cleaning and examining a wound, removing debris or dead tissue, and dressing it help lower contamination and support healing before closure. Careful assessment can find retained objects or injury to deeper tissues. Inadequate cleaning or overly aggressive care can increase infection risk or cause further damage.

topics.name: How To Catheterize the Bladder in a Female Child
topics.clinical_significance: In young girls who cannot urinate on command, catheterization provides a reliable urine sample for testing, including when a urinary infection is suspected. It can also drain urine when the bladder cannot empty. Sterile, gentle insertion helps prevent infection and injury to the urinary tract.

topics.name: How To Catheterize the Bladder in a Male Child
topics.clinical_significance: In young boys who cannot urinate on command, catheterization provides a reliable urine sample for testing, including when a urinary infection is suspected. It can also drain urine when the bladder cannot empty. Sterile, gentle insertion helps prevent infection and injury to the urinary tract.

topics.name: How To Cleanse, Irrigate, Debride, and Dress Wounds
topics.clinical_significance: Cleaning and rinsing a traumatic wound, removing debris or dead tissue, and dressing it help reduce contamination and support healing before closure. Careful examination can find foreign objects or damage to deeper tissues. Too little cleaning can raise infection risk, while overly aggressive care can cause more tissue damage.

topics.name: How To Debride and Dress a Burn
topics.clinical_significance: Burns damage the skin barrier, raising the risk of infection and fluid loss and making it harder to control body temperature. For superficial and partial-thickness burns, removing loose dead tissue and applying a dressing can reduce infection risk and pain while the wound heals. Major burns may need care at a burn center.

topics.name: How To Do a Digital Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A digital nerve block temporarily numbs a finger for treatment of injuries or procedures such as wound repair, fracture care, nail removal, or ring removal. Compared with injecting anesthetic around the wound, it usually causes less pain, gives better numbing, and does not distort the wound edges.

topics.name: How To Do a Median Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A median nerve block at the wrist numbs the thumb-side of the palm and fingers, plus the back of those fingertips except the thumb. It can provide pain relief for hand injuries, wound repair, or ring removal, often with less pain and less tissue distortion than injecting anesthetic around the injury.

topics.name: How To Do a Mental Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A mental nerve block numbs one side of the lower lip and chin, along with nearby gum and mouth lining. It is used for repairs or procedures in these areas. Because it does not swell or distort the tissue around a wound, it can help the clinician line up the wound edges accurately.

topics.name: How To Do a Percutaneous Cricothyrotomy
topics.clinical_significance: Percutaneous cricothyrotomy creates an emergency airway through the front of the neck when a person cannot be intubated or oxygenated by other methods. It can restore breathing in severe respiratory failure or impending respiratory arrest, but may cause serious bleeding or injury to the airway.

topics.name: How To Do a Percutaneous Needle Cricothyrotomy
topics.clinical_significance: Needle cricothyrotomy creates a temporary airway through the front of the neck when a person cannot be intubated or given enough oxygen by other methods. It is often preferred for young children because their airway structures are smaller. It is a short-term measure, so a more lasting airway is needed as soon as possible.

topics.name: How To Do a Radial Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A radial nerve block numbs the back of the thumb-side part of the hand, from the thumb to the thumb-side half of the ring finger, but not the fingertips. It can provide anesthesia for wounds or procedures in this area and for ring removal, often with less pain and less tissue distortion than injecting around the wound.

topics.name: How To Do a Supraperiosteal Infiltration
topics.clinical_significance: This injection numbs one tooth by placing anesthetic near its root. In adults it is mainly used for upper teeth; in children it can be used for any tooth. It can relieve pain during treatment of dental problems, but may not work well for lower teeth because the thicker jawbone limits how far the anesthetic spreads.

topics.name: How To Do Abdominal Thrusts and Back Blows in the Conscious Adult or Child Who Is Choking
topics.clinical_significance: Back blows and abdominal thrusts are emergency first aid to clear a severe airway blockage caused by an object in a conscious adult or child. Use them when the person cannot speak, cough, or breathe adequately; they are not for infants under 1 year. Chest thrusts are used instead for people who are obese or in late pregnancy. Because these maneuvers can injure ribs or internal organs, medical evaluation is advised afterward.

topics.name: How To Do an Auricular Block
topics.clinical_significance: An auricular block numbs the outer ear to reduce pain during repair of an ear cut, removal of a small lesion, or drainage of an ear hematoma. It can also relieve pain from nerve irritation in the ear. It may be more comfortable than injecting anesthetic directly into the ear.

topics.name: How To Do an Emergency Tooth Extraction
topics.clinical_significance: Emergency extraction removes a tooth that cannot be saved, especially when it has a serious infection or is so loose that it could be inhaled. A dentist usually performs the procedure when available. Good pain control and aftercare help limit injury and prevent dry socket, a painful problem caused by loss of the blood clot from the socket.

topics.name: How To Do an Inferior Alveolar Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: This common dental block numbs one side of the lower jaw, including the lower teeth and bone. It usually also numbs the lower lip, chin, and part of the tongue and mouth lining. It is used to control pain during treatment of lower-jaw problems; numbing the gum beside the lower back teeth may require an added buccal nerve block.

topics.name: How To Do an Infraorbital Nerve Block, Intraoral
topics.clinical_significance: An intraoral infraorbital nerve block numbs one side of the lower eyelid, upper cheek, side of the nose, and upper lip. It is used to reduce pain during repair of cuts or treatment of other lesions in the middle of the face. Because it does not swell or distort the wound, it can help the clinician line up the edges accurately.

topics.name: How To Do an Infraorbital Nerve Block, Percutaneous
topics.clinical_significance: A percutaneous infraorbital nerve block numbs one side of the lower eyelid, upper cheek, side of the nose, and upper lip. It can reduce pain during repair of cuts or treatment of other midface lesions, and it does not distort wound edges. This skin-side approach is used less often than the intraoral approach, which may hurt less and last longer.

topics.name: How To Do an Ophthalmic Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: An ophthalmic nerve block numbs one side of the forehead and front of the scalp, and sometimes the upper eyelid. It reduces pain during repair of cuts or treatment of lesions in these areas. Because it does not distort the skin around a wound, it can help the clinician line up wound edges accurately.

topics.name: How To Do an Ulnar Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: An ulnar nerve block numbs both the palm and back of the little-finger side of the hand, including the little finger and the little-finger side of the ring finger. It provides anesthesia for wounds, procedures, or ring removal in this area, often with less pain and less tissue distortion than injecting around the injury. Numbing the whole palm may require an added median nerve block.

topics.name: How To Do an Ultrasound-Guided Peripheral Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: Ultrasound lets the clinician see the target nerve, needle, and nearby structures while placing local anesthetic. This improves the chance that the block will work and can lower the risk of nerve or blood vessel injury. It is used for anesthesia during procedures and for acute pain, but requires equipment and trained staff, and some small or deep nerves may be hard to see.

topics.name: How To Do Anesthesia Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: This section covers ways to reduce pain or anxiety and numb an area so medical procedures can be done, including local anesthesia, nerve blocks, and procedural sedation. The best method depends on the procedure and the patient's risks. Sedation needs careful monitoring because it can slow breathing or lower blood pressure.

topics.name: How To Do Ankle Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Ankle arthrocentesis removes fluid from the joint so it can be tested for causes such as infection or crystal arthritis. It can also drain excess fluid or allow medicine to be injected into the joint to reduce pain. Testing the fluid is important when joint infection is possible.

topics.name: How To Do Anoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Anoscopy lets a clinician examine the anal canal to find causes of pain, itching, discharge, protrusions, or bright-red bleeding. It can show hemorrhoids, fissures, masses, or other lesions, and may allow selected problems to be sampled or treated.

topics.name: How To Do Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Arthrocentesis removes fluid from a joint with a needle. Testing the fluid helps identify the cause of joint swelling, including infection or crystal arthritis. Removing fluid can ease pressure, and medicine can sometimes be injected into the joint.

topics.name: How To Do Bag-Valve-Mask (BVM) Ventilation
topics.clinical_significance: Bag-valve-mask ventilation gives temporary breathing support to someone who has stopped breathing or cannot breathe adequately. It pushes air, often with added oxygen, through a face mask and can support breathing while a more secure airway is prepared.

topics.name: How To Do Basic Airway Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Basic airway procedures keep the breathing passage open, clear choking blockages, or help move air into the lungs. They are used when an airway blockage or poor breathing threatens the body's oxygen supply.

topics.name: How To Do Burn Escharotomy
topics.clinical_significance: Burn escharotomy makes cuts through tight, stiff burn tissue to relieve pressure. It can restore blood flow to a burned limb or allow the chest to expand for breathing when a deep burn constricts it.

topics.name: How To Do Bursal Aspiration and Injection
topics.clinical_significance: Bursal aspiration removes fluid from the sac around a joint so it can be tested for infection or crystals. In selected cases, medicine such as a steroid may be injected into the bursa to reduce inflammation and pain.

topics.name: How To Do Casting Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Casting holds a broken bone or other injured part still while it heals. It is used for fractures and some unstable sprains or dislocations to keep the injured area aligned, reduce pain, and prevent further injury.

topics.name: How To Do Central Vascular Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Central vascular procedures place a catheter in a large vein when regular IV access is not enough or long-term access is needed. The catheter can deliver large amounts of fluid or medicine, support dialysis, and allow monitoring of pressure in the circulation.

topics.name: How To Do Dental Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Emergency dental procedures can numb the mouth for treatment, drain a tooth abscess to relieve pain and limit spread, remove a tooth that cannot be saved, or treat a jaw dislocation.

topics.name: How To Do Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage (DPL)
topics.clinical_significance: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage samples fluid from the abdomen to detect internal bleeding or other abdominal contents after trauma and help decide whether surgery is needed. It is now rarely used where bedside trauma ultrasound or CT is available.

topics.name: How To Do Ear Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures treat common ear-canal and outer-ear problems. They can remove wax or foreign objects that block the canal or affect hearing, drain an outer-ear hematoma to help prevent cartilage deformity, and numb the ear for painful procedures.

topics.name: How To Do E-FAST Examination
topics.clinical_significance: E-FAST is a rapid bedside ultrasound after trauma that looks for fluid around the heart or in the abdomen, and air or blood around the lungs. A positive result can help guide urgent treatment, but a normal scan does not rule out injury.

topics.name: How To Do Elbow Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Elbow arthrocentesis removes joint fluid for testing to find causes of swelling, such as infection or crystal arthritis. It can also drain fluid or allow medicine to be injected to relieve symptoms.

topics.name: How To Do Eye Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Eye procedures can remove foreign objects, flush chemicals or debris from the eye, and relieve dangerous pressure around the eye after trauma. Some are urgent treatments that help protect vision.

topics.name: How To Do Femoral Artery Cannulation (Ultrasound Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: A femoral artery catheter allows continuous blood pressure measurement and repeated blood sampling, especially when severe shock makes cuff readings unreliable. Ultrasound helps locate the artery and guide catheter placement.

topics.name: How To Do Femoral Vein Cannulation (Landmark-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: A femoral vein catheter provides central access for fluids and medicines when peripheral access is not available, often during resuscitation. Because it has higher risks of infection and blood clots, it is generally temporary and replaced when another site is suitable.

topics.name: How To Do Femoral Vein Cannulation (Ultrasound-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: Ultrasound-guided femoral vein cannulation provides central access for fluids and medicines when other access is unavailable. Ultrasound helps place the catheter reliably, but femoral lines carry higher risks of infection and blood clots and are usually temporary.

topics.name: How To Do Flexible Laryngoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Flexible laryngoscopy uses a thin camera to examine the throat and voice box. It helps find causes of voice changes, swallowing or breathing symptoms, and assess vocal-cord movement or the airway before intubation.

topics.name: How To Do Gastrointestinal Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures help diagnose or treat gastrointestinal problems. They include examining the anal canal, testing or draining fluid from the abdomen, and placing a tube through the nose to empty, sample, or feed the stomach.

topics.name: How To Do Genitourinary Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures help diagnose or manage urinary and genital problems. Urinary catheters can collect urine, measure urine output, or drain a bladder that cannot empty; urgent reduction of paraphimosis helps prevent damage to the penis.

topics.name: How To Do Head Tilt–Chin Lift and Jaw-Thrust Maneuvers
topics.clinical_significance: The head tilt–chin lift and jaw thrust open an airway blocked by the tongue, which can happen in an unconscious person. They support emergency breathing, including bag-mask ventilation; if neck injury is possible, jaw thrust helps open the airway while keeping the neck still.

topics.name: How To Do Infraclavicular Subclavian Vein Cannulation (Landmark-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: This technique places a central venous catheter through the subclavian vein for treatment and monitoring. The site may be chosen when reducing catheter infection risk is important. Landmark-guided needle placement can puncture the nearby lung or vessels, causing pneumothorax or bleeding; the clavicle can make bleeding difficult to detect or control.

topics.name: How To Do Infraclavicular Subclavian Vein Cannulation (Ultrasound-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: Real-time ultrasound guides placement of a central catheter through the axillary vein beneath the clavicle. This provides long-term access, allows large fluid volumes or vein-irritating medicines to be given, and supports monitoring. Ultrasound improves placement success and reduces needle passes; it lowers the risk of arterial puncture and may lower the risk of a collapsed lung. Bleeding, infection, and blood clots can still occur.

topics.name: How To Do Internal Jugular Vein Cannulation (Landmark-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: Internal jugular cannulation places a central catheter for secure or long-term access, large-volume fluids, vein-irritating medicines, or circulation monitoring. This site can be compressed if bleeding occurs and has a lower risk of lung puncture than subclavian access. Landmark-guided placement can still cause arterial puncture and other complications; ultrasound guidance is preferred when available.

topics.name: How To Do Internal Jugular Vein Cannulation (Ultrasound-Guided)
topics.clinical_significance: Ultrasound-guided internal jugular cannulation places a central catheter for long-term access, large-volume fluids, vein-irritating medicines, or circulation monitoring. Ultrasound helps locate the vein and guide the needle, increasing placement success and reducing complications such as arterial puncture. The neck site can be compressed if bleeding occurs and has a lower risk of lung puncture than subclavian access, though bleeding, infection, and blood clots remain possible.

topics.name: How To Do Knee Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Knee arthrocentesis removes joint fluid for testing to find the cause of swelling, especially infection or crystal arthritis such as gout. Removing excess fluid can ease pain and pressure, and the procedure can also be used to inject medicine into the joint.

topics.name: How To Do Lateral Canthotomy
topics.clinical_significance: Lateral canthotomy with cantholysis is an emergency procedure that releases pressure around the eye in orbital compartment syndrome. This pressure can compress the optic nerve and its blood supply, causing rapid, permanent vision loss; prompt decompression can help preserve sight.

topics.name: How To Do Local Wound Infiltration
topics.clinical_significance: Local wound infiltration injects anesthetic into the edges of an open wound to numb the area before treatment. It reduces pain during wound cleaning and repair, foreign-body removal, or incision and drainage. Very large wounds may require unsafe amounts of anesthetic.

topics.name: How To Do Lumbar Puncture
topics.clinical_significance: Lumbar puncture collects cerebrospinal fluid (the fluid around the brain and spinal cord) to test for infection and other neurologic diseases. It can also measure fluid pressure or deliver medicine into the spinal fluid. If a brain mass is suspected, imaging may be needed first because lumbar puncture can trigger life-threatening brain herniation.

topics.name: How To Do Metacarpophalangeal and Interphalangeal Joint Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Aspiration of fluid from a finger joint can help identify infection or crystal arthritis. Removing excess fluid may relieve pain, and medicine can also be injected into the joint for treatment.

topics.name: How To Do Metatarsophalangeal Joint Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Aspiration of a joint at the base of a toe can identify causes of swelling, including infection or crystal arthritis such as gout. Removing fluid may relieve pain, and medicine can be injected into the joint as treatment.

topics.name: How To Do Mirror Laryngoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Mirror laryngoscopy uses a small mirror to view the throat and larynx, including the vocal folds. It helps assess symptoms such as persistent hoarseness, swallowing difficulty, and throat pain, and can reveal vocal-fold lesions or impaired movement.

topics.name: How To Do Nail Trephination
topics.clinical_significance: Nail trephination drains blood trapped under an intact nail after an injury, easing pressure and pain from a subungual hematoma. It is used for painful hematomas; it is not suitable if the nail is split or lifted from its bed, and may not work after 1 to 2 days when the blood has clotted.

topics.name: How To Do Needle Thoracostomy
topics.clinical_significance: Needle thoracostomy releases trapped air from around a lung during a tension pneumothorax, reducing pressure on the lung and major blood vessels. It is an emergency measure when a chest tube cannot be placed quickly; a chest tube is needed as soon as possible afterward.

topics.name: How To Do Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation
topics.clinical_significance: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation supports breathing through a tight-fitting mask without a breathing tube. It can reduce the work of breathing and help delay or avoid intubation, or support removal of a breathing tube. Because it does not protect the airway, it can increase the risk of aspiration in patients who cannot protect their airway.

topics.name: How To Do Nose Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Nasal procedures can remove foreign objects and control nosebleeds. Prompt removal of an object can prevent infection and damage to the nasal lining; cautery or packing can stop bleeding that continues despite simpler measures.

topics.name: How To Do Orotracheal Intubation Using Video Laryngoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Video laryngoscopy uses a camera to guide an endotracheal tube into the trachea, securing the airway for assisted breathing when breathing is inadequate or absent, or when airway protection is needed. The screen view can help with difficult intubation, but incorrect tube placement can be life-threatening and must be checked.

topics.name: How To Do Other Airway Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures open or secure the airway and help provide oxygen or assisted breathing. They range from basic positioning and mask ventilation to airway tubes and emergency surgical airways, and are used when breathing is blocked, absent, or inadequate.

topics.name: How To Do Other Emergency Medicine Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Emergency bedside procedures help rapidly identify and respond to life-threatening problems. Tests such as E-FAST or diagnostic peritoneal lavage can detect internal bleeding or chest injury after trauma and help guide urgent treatment or surgery.

topics.name: How To Do Other Orthopedic Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures remove rings trapped by finger swelling, relieving constriction and helping prevent reduced blood flow and tissue injury. A ring cutter is used when swelling is severe, circulation is threatened, or gentler removal methods fail.

topics.name: How To Do Paracentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Paracentesis samples abdominal fluid (ascites) to find its cause, including infection, or removes excess fluid to ease pain or breathing difficulty from tense ascites.

topics.name: How To Do Paraphimosis Reduction Without Dorsal Slit
topics.clinical_significance: Manual reduction returns a foreskin trapped behind the head of the penis to its normal position. This is urgent because constriction can reduce blood flow and cause tissue death; if manual reduction fails, urgent urologic treatment is needed.

topics.name: How To Do Pediatric Urologic Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures provide a reliable urine sample to diagnose urinary tract infection in young children, especially febrile infants, when a bag sample may be unreliable. Bladder catheterization can also drain urine in retention; suprapubic aspiration is an option when catheterization is not possible.

topics.name: How To Do Peripheral Vascular Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral vascular procedures provide vein access for IV fluids, medicines, or blood sampling, and artery access for continuous blood-pressure monitoring and repeated blood tests in critically ill patients. Ultrasound guidance can help when vessels are difficult to locate.

topics.name: How To Do Procedural Sedation and Analgesia
topics.clinical_significance: Procedural sedation and analgesia reduces pain and anxiety, relaxes the patient, and may limit memory of a distressing procedure. Because sedating medicines can slow breathing or lower oxygen levels and blood pressure, close monitoring and readiness to support breathing are essential.

topics.name: How To Do Pulmonary Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary procedures can sample fluid around the lungs to find its cause or ease breathlessness from a large fluid collection. A chest tube or catheter can drain air or fluid around the lungs, helping treat conditions such as pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

topics.name: How To Do Shoulder Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Shoulder arthrocentesis removes joint fluid to help find causes such as infection or crystal arthritis. It can also relieve fluid buildup and allow medicine to be injected into the joint.

topics.name: How To Do Skin, Soft Tissue, and Minor Surgical Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: These minor procedures treat skin and soft tissue problems such as abscesses, burns, ingrown nails, and blood trapped under a nail. Depending on the problem, they may drain pus or blood, remove damaged tissue, or relieve pressure and pain.

topics.name: How To Do Suprapubic Aspiration of the Bladder in a Child
topics.clinical_significance: Suprapubic aspiration collects urine directly from a child’s bladder through the lower abdomen. The sample is less likely to be contaminated than urine collected in a bag, helping doctors test for a suspected urinary tract infection.

topics.name: How To Do Thoracentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracentesis removes fluid from around the lung with a needle. The fluid can be tested to find the cause of a new or unexplained effusion, and removing a large amount may ease breathlessness.

topics.name: How To Do Throat Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Throat procedures can test for infections with a swab, examine the throat and voice box with laryngoscopy, or drain a pocket of pus near a tonsil. They help identify throat problems and treat a peritonsillar abscess.

topics.name: How To Do Tube and Catheter Thoracostomy
topics.clinical_significance: A chest tube or catheter drains air or fluid from the space around the lung. It is used for conditions such as pneumothorax and large or infected fluid collections, helping the lung expand and breathing improve.

topics.name: How To Do Ultrasound
topics.clinical_significance: Bedside ultrasound helps clinicians quickly look for problems such as fluid buildup, abscesses, or blood clots. It can also guide procedures such as placing an IV catheter or drawing fluid from a joint.

topics.name: How To Do Ultrasound-Guided Peripheral Intravenous Catheter Insertion
topics.clinical_significance: Real-time ultrasound helps place a peripheral IV catheter in a deep vein that is hard to see or feel. This provides IV access when suitable veins are difficult to find.

topics.name: How To Do Ultrasound-Guided Radial Artery Catheter Insertion
topics.clinical_significance: A radial artery catheter gives continuous blood pressure readings and allows repeated arterial blood samples, often needed in critically ill patients or during complex surgery. Ultrasound helps find the artery when it is hard to feel.

topics.name: How To Do Urethral Catheterization in a Female
topics.clinical_significance: A urethral catheter drains the bladder when a woman cannot empty it and allows urine output or leftover bladder urine to be measured. It can also collect a sterile urine sample, support lower urinary tract tests, or deliver bladder irrigation or medicine.

topics.name: How To Do Urethral Catheterization in a Male
topics.clinical_significance: A urethral catheter drains urine when a man cannot empty his bladder, including when the urethra or prostate blocks urine flow. It can also measure urine output and urine left after urination, support bladder tests, or deliver irrigation or medicine.

topics.name: How To Do Venous Blood Sampling
topics.clinical_significance: Venous blood sampling collects blood for laboratory tests. The results help diagnose or monitor a person’s health problems.

topics.name: How To Do Wrist Arthrocentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Wrist arthrocentesis removes joint fluid to help find its cause, such as infection or crystal arthritis. It can also remove excess fluid or allow medicine to be injected for treatment and pain relief.

topics.name: How To Drain a Peritonsillar Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: Needle aspiration can help confirm a suspected abscess beside the tonsil and remove pus. Incision and drainage removes pus from a clear abscess, helping treat the infection and ease severe pain or trouble swallowing.

topics.name: How To Drain a Tooth Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: Draining a tooth abscess releases pus from an infection around a tooth or gum. It relieves pain and helps limit the infection from spreading deeper into nearby tissues.

topics.name: How To Drain an Auricular Hematoma
topics.clinical_significance: Drainage removes blood trapped between the outer ear cartilage and its covering. Keeping these layers in contact helps prevent the blood from collecting again and lowers the risk of permanent ear-cartilage deformity.

topics.name: How To Fit and Walk With Underarm Crutches
topics.clinical_significance: Underarm crutches help a person walk when an injured leg cannot safely bear some or all of the person’s weight. Correct fit and use support walking while helping prevent nerve injury from pressure in the armpit.

topics.name: How To Incise and Drain an Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: Incision and drainage opens a pocket of pus in the skin or soft tissue so it can be emptied. This relieves pressure and helps treat the infection; some abscesses also need antibiotics.

topics.name: How To Inject a Subacromial Bursa
topics.clinical_significance: An injection of local anesthetic and/or corticosteroid may reduce inflammation and quickly relieve pain from persistent or recurrent subacromial bursitis. A corticosteroid injection is avoided when infection is suspected.

topics.name: How To Inject a Trochanteric Bursa
topics.clinical_significance: An injection near the greater trochanter may quickly relieve ongoing outer-hip pain (greater trochanteric pain syndrome). This pain often comes from nearby gluteal tendon problems, sometimes with bursitis; corticosteroid injection is avoided if infection is suspected.

topics.name: How To Insert a Laryngeal Mask Airway
topics.clinical_significance: A laryngeal mask airway is a temporary device placed above the voice box to deliver breaths to an unconscious person or someone without a gag reflex. It is used for rescue ventilation when intubation cannot be done and during some short operations under anesthesia.

topics.name: How To Insert a Nasogastric Tube
topics.clinical_significance: A nasogastric tube gives access to the stomach to drain it when it is distended, collect stomach contents for testing, or deliver medicines, contrast, or nutrients. A thinner feeding tube may be passed into the small intestine when needed.

topics.name: How To Insert a Nasopharyngeal Airway
topics.clinical_significance: A nasopharyngeal airway helps keep the upper airway open in a person who is breathing on their own but has noisy breathing from blockage by soft tissue and still has a gag reflex. It may also help with bag-mask ventilation.

topics.name: How To Insert a Peripheral Intravenous Catheter
topics.clinical_significance: A peripheral IV catheter provides access to a vein to give fluids or medicines. It can also be used when blood needs to be sampled repeatedly.

topics.name: How To Insert a Radial Artery Catheter
topics.clinical_significance: A radial artery catheter provides continuous blood pressure readings and allows repeated arterial blood gas and other blood tests. It is used for critically ill or unstable patients and during complex surgery when close monitoring is needed.

topics.name: How To Insert an Esophageal-Tracheal Double Lumen Tube or a Laryngeal Tube
topics.clinical_significance: Esophageal-tracheal double-lumen tubes and laryngeal tubes are temporary airways that deliver breaths when bag-mask ventilation is difficult or intubation has failed. They may need to be replaced with a more secure airway for ongoing support.

topics.name: How To Insert an Oropharyngeal Airway
topics.clinical_significance: An oropharyngeal airway helps keep the throat open when the tongue or soft tissues block airflow. It is used in unconscious people without a gag reflex, including to support bag-mask ventilation.

topics.name: How To Irrigate the Eye and Do Eyelid Eversion
topics.clinical_significance: Eye irrigation flushes harmful chemicals or particles from the eye surface. Turning the upper eyelid outward exposes its inner surface so trapped material can be found and removed.

topics.name: How To Measure Compartment Pressure in a Forearm
topics.clinical_significance: Measuring forearm compartment pressure helps assess suspected compartment syndrome, especially after trauma with severe or worsening pain. The result must be considered with the clinical examination; a normal reading does not rule out the condition.

topics.name: How To Measure Compartment Pressure in the Lower Leg
topics.clinical_significance: Measuring lower-leg compartment pressure helps assess suspected compartment syndrome, especially after trauma with severe or worsening pain. A normal reading does not rule it out, and repeat measurements may be needed.

topics.name: How To Place an Intraosseous Catheter, Manually and With a Power Drill
topics.clinical_significance: Intraosseous access provides a temporary route for fluids, medicines, and blood products when IV access is difficult, especially in emergencies such as shock or cardiac arrest. It is replaced with venous access when practical.

topics.name: How To Reduce a Lateral Patellar Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Manual reduction returns a laterally dislocated kneecap to its normal position. This restores alignment and allows the knee to be examined for related injuries.

topics.name: How To Reduce a Mandibular Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Reducing an anterior jaw joint dislocation puts the jaw back in place so the person can close their mouth. Prompt reduction matters because the jaw becomes harder to put back as time passes.

topics.name: How To Reduce a Posterior Elbow Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Prompt reduction restores the elbow joint to its normal position. Because an artery or nerve can be injured, blood flow and nerve function in the arm should be checked before and after reduction; fractures or signs of poor blood flow need urgent orthopedic care.

topics.name: How To Reduce a Posterior Hip Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: A posterior hip dislocation needs urgent reduction because delay, especially beyond 6 hours, increases the risk that poor blood supply will damage the head of the thigh bone. The sciatic nerve can also be injured, so prompt reduction and nerve checks are important.

topics.name: How To Reduce a Radial Head Subluxation (Nursemaid Elbow)
topics.clinical_significance: Successful reduction usually lets the child start using the arm again. Swelling, bruising, deformity, pain beyond the radial head, or poor circulation can signal a more serious injury that needs evaluation before reduction.

topics.name: How To Reduce an Ankle Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Ankle dislocations often occur with fractures and can threaten the skin, nerves, and blood flow to the foot. Prompt reduction restores alignment and may limit tissue and joint damage; poor blood flow or skin stretched tightly over a fracture makes it especially urgent.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using External Rotation (Hennepin Technique)
topics.clinical_significance: This gentle technique restores the joint position after an anterior shoulder dislocation. The axillary nerve is often affected, and weakness may improve after reduction, so blood flow and nerve function should be checked before and after the procedure.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using Scapular Manipulation
topics.clinical_significance: Scapular manipulation gently moves the shoulder socket to help put an anteriorly dislocated shoulder back in place, often with little force. Because the axillary nerve is commonly affected, nerve function and blood flow should be checked before and after reduction.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using the Davos Technique
topics.clinical_significance: The Davos technique lets a calm, cooperative patient use controlled pulling to put an anteriorly dislocated shoulder back in place, often without pain medicine. It is not suitable when there are signs of nerve or blood vessel injury or threatened skin; those need immediate care with another approach.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using the FARES Method
topics.clinical_significance: FARES is a gentle way to put an anterior shoulder dislocation back in place and may be done without pain medicine. Because nerves or blood flow can be affected, check arm function and circulation before and after reduction; those problems or threatened skin call for immediate care.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using the Stimson Technique
topics.clinical_significance: The Stimson method uses gradual weight traction to help return an anteriorly dislocated shoulder to its socket and does not require an assistant. It can take up to 30 minutes, and the prone position makes monitoring harder, so it is not suitable for some patients who need close monitoring.

topics.name: How To Reduce Anterior Shoulder Dislocations Using Traction-Countertraction
topics.clinical_significance: Traction-countertraction is a reliable way to put an anteriorly dislocated shoulder back in place, but it usually needs assistants and sedation. The pulling can worsen some fractures or rarely injure the axillary nerve, so check nerve function and blood flow before and after reduction.

topics.name: How To Reduce Dislocations and Subluxations
topics.clinical_significance: Reduction puts a fully or partly displaced joint back into its normal position. Prompt care can lower the risk of lasting nerve or blood vessel damage; clinicians also check for fractures and assess circulation and nerve function before and after reduction.

topics.name: How To Reduce Posterior Shoulder Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior shoulder dislocations are rare and can be missed, and associated fractures may be present. Delayed diagnosis can lead to lasting stiffness, pain, or joint damage; because forceful reduction can cause fractures, orthopedic advice is recommended before reduction.

topics.name: How To Remove a Cast
topics.clinical_significance: A cast is removed when the planned immobilization period ends or when tightness, damage, wetness, or a skin problem needs attention. Trained staff use proper tools to reduce the risk of skin injury; numbness, tingling, or increasing pain may mean the cast is too tight.

topics.name: How To Remove a Deep Fishhook
topics.clinical_significance: A deep barbed fishhook cannot be pulled straight back out and may be near a nerve, blood vessel, or tendon. Careful removal helps avoid further damage; infection and a lasting inflammatory lump can occur.

topics.name: How To Remove a Foreign Body From the External Ear
topics.clinical_significance: A foreign object in the ear canal should be removed carefully to avoid pushing it deeper or injuring the canal or eardrum. Button batteries and magnets can cause serious damage within hours and need prompt removal; irrigation is unsafe if the eardrum may be perforated.

topics.name: How To Remove a Foreign Body From the Eye
topics.clinical_significance: Foreign bodies can scratch the cornea or injure the conjunctiva, so careful removal helps prevent further eye damage. A penetrating injury or object inside the eye needs urgent ophthalmology care rather than routine removal.

topics.name: How To Remove a Foreign Body From the Nose
topics.clinical_significance: Nasal objects can cause bleeding or infection, and removal attempts may push them deeper or lead to inhalation into the airway. Button batteries and magnets need immediate removal because they can burn or perforate nasal tissue within hours.

topics.name: How To Remove a Ring Using a Manual Ring Cutter
topics.clinical_significance: A ring trapped by finger swelling can reduce blood flow and threaten the finger. Color change, severe pain, or very slow capillary refill calls for urgent removal; a manual cutter can cut soft-metal rings, with care to avoid skin injury.

topics.name: How To Remove a Ring Using the String Method
topics.clinical_significance: The string method can remove a ring trapped by finger swelling without cutting it. It can injure the skin or digital nerves, so it should be avoided when the finger has a cut, fracture, or deformity beyond the ring.

topics.name: How To Remove a Shallow Fishhook
topics.clinical_significance: A shallow fishhook has not reached the curve of the hook and can often be removed through its entry site after the barb is freed. Puncture wounds can become infected, so careful removal, wound care, and tetanus review are important; nearby nerves, blood vessels, or tendons must also be considered.

topics.name: How To Remove a Tick
topics.clinical_significance: Ticks can spread infections, so removing an attached tick promptly lowers the chance of disease transmission. Seek medical evaluation for fever, headache, joint pain, or worsening redness or swelling within 4 weeks after a bite.

topics.name: How To Remove a Zipper From a Penis
topics.clinical_significance: Trapped penile skin can tear if the zipper is pulled, and delay can increase swelling and the risk of tissue damage or tissue death. Prompt, careful release is important; suspected urethral injury needs urology assessment.

topics.name: How To Remove Cerumen Manually and With Irrigation
topics.clinical_significance: Earwax protects and moisturizes the ear canal, so routine removal is discouraged. Remove impacted wax when it causes symptoms or blocks examination; removal can injure the canal or eardrum, and irrigation is unsafe if the eardrum may be damaged.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Buried Deep Dermal Sutures
topics.clinical_significance: Buried deep dermal sutures bring deeper wound layers together and reduce pull on the skin edges in deep or high-tension cuts. This helps the edges heal together; surface stitches may still be needed for precise skin alignment.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Horizontal Mattress Sutures
topics.clinical_significance: Horizontal mattress sutures bring wound edges together while spreading tension over a wider area, which can help when simple stitches may cut through fragile skin. If tied too tightly, they can reduce blood flow and damage the skin.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Simple Interrupted Sutures
topics.clinical_significance: Simple interrupted sutures are commonly used to close uncomplicated cuts. Each stitch can be adjusted on its own, and if one fails the others remain secure; stitches should not be tied too tightly because they can cut the skin or reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Stapling
topics.clinical_significance: Staples quickly close straight cuts on the trunk, limbs, or scalp when appearance is less important. Poor edge alignment, overly tight staples, or leaving them in too long can harm healing or increase scarring.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Tissue Adhesive
topics.clinical_significance: Tissue adhesive quickly and painlessly closes small, shallow cuts with little tension, with cosmetic results similar to stitches. It is weaker during the first 4 days and the wound is slightly more likely to reopen, so it is not suited to deep or high-tension cuts.

topics.name: How To Repair a Laceration With Vertical Mattress Sutures
topics.clinical_significance: Vertical mattress sutures help align and turn outward wound edges that are hard to evert, while closing deeper and surface layers in one stitch. They suit wounds under moderate tension; if too tight, they can leave stitch marks or reduce blood flow to the skin.

topics.name: How To Replace and Splint an Avulsed Tooth
topics.clinical_significance: A knocked-out permanent tooth has a better chance of survival when put back within 30 minutes. Splinting holds it in place while the ligament around the root heals; baby teeth should not be reimplanted.

topics.name: How To Splint or Immobilize a Lower Limb
topics.clinical_significance: A lower-limb splint holds an injury still to reduce pain and prevent further tissue damage. A non-circumferential splint leaves room for swelling, but excess pressure can cause skin sores or reduce blood flow.

topics.name: How To Splint or Immobilize an Upper Limb
topics.clinical_significance: An upper-limb splint holds an injured arm or hand still to reduce pain and prevent further tissue injury while swelling settles. If it is too tight, it can cause pressure sores, nerve injury, or reduced blood flow, so finger color, sensation, and movement should be checked.

topics.name: How To Treat an Ingrown Toenail
topics.clinical_significance: An ingrown toenail presses into the skin beside the nail and can cause pain, swelling, and infection. Mild cases may improve when the nail edge is lifted; more severe inflammation, infection, or pain may need partial nail removal. People with diabetes, poor circulation, or nerve damage need close follow-up because infection can spread to bone.

topics.name: How To Treat Anterior Epistaxis With Cautery
topics.clinical_significance: Cautery can stop an anterior nosebleed when the bleeding point is visible and firm pressure has not worked. It can injure or perforate the nasal septum if applied too widely or on both sides; ongoing bleeding may need nasal packing.

topics.name: How To Treat Anterior Epistaxis With Makeshift Nasal Clip
topics.clinical_significance: A makeshift nasal clip can press on the sides of the nose to help stop a visible front-of-nose bleed when firm pressure has not worked and a commercial clip is unavailable. It may not apply enough pressure and can slip, cause skin or cartilage injury, or allow bleeding to restart.

topics.name: How To Treat Anterior Epistaxis With Nasal Packing
topics.clinical_significance: Nasal packing can control a front-of-nose bleed when the bleeding site cannot be seen or pressure and cautery have failed. It may injure the nasal lining, cause infection, move toward the throat or airway, or allow bleeding to restart when removed.

topics.name: How To Treat Posterior Epistaxis With a Balloon
topics.clinical_significance: A balloon can help stop a posterior nosebleed, which is less common but more dangerous than a front-of-nose bleed. Because the packing can move and affect breathing or lower oxygen levels, patients need hospital monitoring; tissue injury and infection can also occur.

topics.name: How To Treat the Choking Conscious Infant
topics.clinical_significance: Severe choking can block an infant’s airway, quickly causing low oxygen or loss of consciousness. For an infant under 1 year with severe blockage, back blows followed by chest thrusts can help dislodge the object; abdominal thrusts are avoided because they can injure the liver. A clinician should check the infant afterward for injury.

topics.name: HTLV-1–Associated Myelopathy/Tropical Spastic Paraparesis (HAM/TSP)
topics.clinical_significance: HAM/TSP is a slowly worsening spinal cord disease caused by HTLV-1. It causes stiffness and weakness in both legs, changes in foot sensation, and bladder urgency or leakage. No treatment is proven to stop the disease, so care focuses on symptoms and support.

topics.name: Human African Trypanosomiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Human African trypanosomiasis is a tsetse fly–borne infection that can progress from fever and swollen lymph nodes to brain disease, with changes in sleep, behavior, and movement. Without treatment it can lead to coma and death, so early diagnosis matters; treatment depends on the parasite type and whether the brain is involved.

topics.name: Human and Mammal Bites
topics.clinical_significance: Bites can cause deep tissue damage and infection. Hand bites, especially clenched-fist human bites and cat bites, can spread infection to tendons, joints, or bone; some mammal bites also pose a rabies risk. Wounds need prompt cleaning and assessment for deep injury and preventive care.

topics.name: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: HIV damages CD4 immune cells, weakening the body’s defenses. Without treatment, this can lead to serious infections and cancers; antiretroviral treatment can suppress the virus and help preserve or restore immune function.

topics.name: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Infection in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: HIV can weaken a child’s immune system, impair growth and development, and cause serious infections; it may progress faster in infants and children than in adults. Early combination antiretroviral treatment lowers these risks. Diagnosis uses viral genetic tests in children under 18 months and antibody tests in older children.

topics.name: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)–Associated Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: HIV-associated dementia can cause worsening problems with thinking, behavior, and movement that interfere with daily activities. New or rapid decline needs prompt assessment for other, sometimes treatable, brain disorders. Antiretroviral therapy is the main treatment and may stabilize or partly improve symptoms.

topics.name: Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) System
topics.clinical_significance: HLA molecules show protein fragments to T cells, helping the immune system recognize infections and abnormal cells. HLA differences are important when matching transplant donors and recipients, and some HLA variants are linked to a higher risk of autoimmune diseases.

topics.name: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Most HPV infections clear on their own, but persistent infection with high-risk types can cause cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers; some other types cause genital warts. Vaccination protects against many wart- and cancer-causing HPV types.

topics.name: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: HPV vaccination prevents infection with several HPV types that cause most genital warts and many cervical and anal cancers. It does not cover every cancer-causing type, so cervical cancer screening is still needed after vaccination.

topics.name: Humeral Fractures, Distal
topics.clinical_significance: A distal humerus fracture often occurs in children after a fall and can cause elbow pain, swelling, and limited movement. It may injure nearby nerves or the brachial artery, so prompt checks of hand circulation and nerve function and orthopedic assessment are important.

topics.name: Humeral Fractures, Proximal
topics.clinical_significance: A proximal humerus fracture causes shoulder and upper-arm pain and swelling and makes it hard to raise the arm. It can injure the nearby axillary nerve or artery, and keeping the shoulder still too long can cause stiffness. Most are treated with a sling and early movement.

topics.name: Huntington Chorea
topics.clinical_significance: Huntington disease is an inherited, gradually worsening brain disorder that often starts in midlife and causes involuntary movements, mood or behavior changes, and declining thinking. Each child of an affected parent has a 1-in-2 chance of inheriting it, so genetic counseling is important before testing. Treatment can ease symptoms but does not stop the disease.

topics.name: Huntington Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Huntington disease is an inherited, gradually worsening brain disorder that often starts in midlife and causes involuntary movements, mood or behavior changes, and declining thinking. Each child of an affected parent has a 1-in-2 chance of inheriting it, so genetic counseling is important before testing. Treatment can ease symptoms but does not stop the disease.

topics.name: Huntington's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Huntington’s disease is an inherited brain disorder that gradually worsens. It causes involuntary movements and changes in thinking, mood, or behavior, usually starting in adulthood. Each child of an affected parent has a 1-in-2 chance of inheriting it, so genetic counseling is important before testing. Treatment can ease symptoms but does not stop the disease.

topics.name: Hutchinson-Gilford Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria is a rare condition caused by a usually new change in the LMNA gene. Children develop aging-like changes and poor growth, and early heart and blood-vessel disease can shorten life. Lonafarnib treatment can lower the risk of death.

topics.name: Hyaline Membrane Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Also called neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, this condition is most common in premature babies whose lungs lack surfactant. The air sacs collapse, making breathing and oxygen transfer difficult; severe cases may need oxygen, breathing support, and surfactant treatment.

topics.name: Hydatid Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Hydatid disease is caused by tapeworm larvae that form slow-growing cysts, most often in the liver or lungs. Cysts can cause pressure symptoms or, if they rupture, a severe allergic reaction; the invasive form can destroy liver tissue. Treatment may include albendazole, cyst drainage, or surgery, depending on the cyst.

topics.name: Hydramnios
topics.clinical_significance: Hydramnios (polyhydramnios) is excess amniotic fluid, sometimes linked to diabetes or fetal conditions and sometimes without a clear cause. Severe cases can cause maternal breathing difficulty and preterm labor, and raise the risks of abnormal fetal position, cord prolapse, and bleeding after birth.

topics.name: Hydrocarbon Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Swallowing gasoline, kerosene, or solvents may have few whole-body effects, but if liquid enters the lungs it can cause severe chemical pneumonia. Breathing hydrocarbon vapors can trigger a sudden, sometimes fatal abnormal heart rhythm. Treatment is mainly supportive; making the person vomit can increase the risk of aspiration.

topics.name: Hymenolepis diminuta Infection
topics.clinical_significance: This rare tapeworm infection is acquired by accidentally eating infected grain or flour beetles. It usually causes no symptoms, but mild stomach or bowel symptoms may occur. The eggs can be found in stool, and treatment is usually praziquantel.

topics.name: Hymenolepis nana (Dwarf Tapeworm) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: The dwarf tapeworm spreads when eggs are swallowed, including from one person to another, and can multiply inside the gut. Many infections cause no symptoms, but heavy infection may cause stomach cramps, diarrhea, poor appetite, or anal itching. Eggs are found in stool, and praziquantel is the usual treatment.

topics.name: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy gives 100% oxygen in a pressurized chamber. It is used mainly for decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism, and in selected cases of carbon monoxide poisoning. Starting promptly improves the chance of recovery; pressure can injure the ears or sinuses and rarely cause seizures or lung injury.

topics.name: Hyperbilirubinemia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn jaundice is common and often temporary, but very high bilirubin can cause lasting brain damage. Treatment thresholds depend on the newborn’s age in hours, prematurity, and health; treatment may include phototherapy and, rarely, exchange transfusion.

topics.name: Hypercalcemia
topics.clinical_significance: High blood calcium is often caused by overactive parathyroid glands or cancer; vitamin D excess and some medicines can also cause it. Mild cases may have no symptoms, but more severe cases can cause thirst, frequent urination, constipation, weakness, kidney stones, confusion, abnormal heart rhythms, or coma.

topics.name: Hypercalcemia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: High blood calcium in a newborn is most often caused by excess calcium or vitamin D or incorrectly prepared formula. It can cause poor feeding, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, irritability, and lethargy; severe cases may cause seizures and need prompt treatment.

topics.name: Hyperemesis Gravidarum
topics.clinical_significance: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe pregnancy-related nausea and vomiting that causes weight loss, dehydration, and ketones in the urine, often with abnormal blood salts. It can prevent adequate food and fluid intake and may require hospital care, IV fluids, vitamins, and anti-nausea medicine.

topics.name: Hypereosinophilic Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is persistent high eosinophil levels that damage one or more organs after other causes are excluded. It often affects the heart, lungs, skin, and nerves; heart damage can be life-threatening. Treatment depends on the subtype and may include steroids or imatinib for certain gene changes.

topics.name: Hyperglycemia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: High blood sugar in newborns is most common in very-low-birth-weight infants, often from too much or too rapid IV dextrose, or from serious illness. It is linked to more complications and deaths from the underlying illness and can cause fluid and salt loss in urine, so glucose and hydration need close monitoring.

topics.name: Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism
topics.clinical_significance: Primary ovarian insufficiency is reduced ovarian function before age 40, causing low estrogen and high FSH. It may lead to irregular or absent periods, infertility, hot flashes, and bone loss; ovarian activity and the chance of pregnancy may remain.

topics.name: Hyperhidrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Sweating that is excessive for the situation, often affecting the underarms, palms, or soles. It can interfere with daily life; widespread sweating may be linked to medicines or conditions such as infection, cancer, or an endocrine disorder.

topics.name: Hyperhomocysteinemia
topics.clinical_significance: A high homocysteine level, often due to folate, vitamin B6, or vitamin B12 deficiency, or rarely an inherited enzyme problem. It may be linked to arterial or venous blood clots, but this link is uncertain, and lowering the level with vitamins has not been shown to prevent clots.

topics.name: Hyper-IgD Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited inflammatory disorder that causes repeated fever attacks, usually starting in infancy and lasting several days. Attacks may include chills, abdominal pain, diarrhea, joint pain, swollen lymph nodes, rash, or mouth ulcers; treatment can reduce or prevent attacks.

topics.name: Hyper-IgE Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder with very high IgE, severe itchy skin inflammation, and repeated skin abscesses and lung or sinus infections. Some forms also cause delayed loss of baby teeth, weak bones, and fractures.

topics.name: Hyper-IgM Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune deficiency in which IgM is normal or high but other antibodies are low or absent. This weakens protection against infection, often causing repeated lung and sinus infections; some people also develop severe opportunistic infections, chronic diarrhea, or low neutrophil counts.

topics.name: Hyperimmunoglobulin D Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited inflammatory disorder that causes repeated fever attacks, usually starting in infancy and lasting several days. Attacks may include chills, abdominal pain, diarrhea, joint pain, swollen lymph nodes, rash, or mouth ulcers; treatment can reduce or prevent attacks.

topics.name: Hyperimmunoglobulin E Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder with very high IgE, severe itchy skin inflammation, and repeated skin abscesses and lung or sinus infections. Some forms also cause delayed loss of baby teeth, weak bones, and fractures.

topics.name: Hyperkalemia
topics.clinical_significance: A high blood potassium level, often from kidney problems, certain medicines, tissue breakdown, or acidosis. It may cause muscle weakness or dangerous heart rhythm problems, and severe cases can cause cardiac arrest. A falsely high result from a damaged blood sample should be ruled out.

topics.name: Hyperlipidemia
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal blood fat levels, such as high cholesterol or triglycerides or low HDL cholesterol. It often causes no symptoms but can contribute to artery disease, heart attack, and stroke; very high triglycerides can cause pancreatitis. Causes may be inherited or related to illness, medicines, or lifestyle.

topics.name: Hypermagnesemia
topics.clinical_significance: A high blood magnesium level, usually due to kidney failure and sometimes after taking magnesium-containing antacids or laxatives. Severe levels can lower blood pressure, weaken reflexes, slow breathing, and cause cardiac arrest.

topics.name: Hypernatremia
topics.clinical_significance: A high blood sodium level caused by too little body water relative to sodium, usually from water loss or limited access to water. It causes thirst and, if severe, can affect the brain and lead to confusion, seizures, or coma.

topics.name: Hypernatremia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: High blood sodium in a newborn, usually from dehydration due to poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhea, or fever; rarely, it is caused by too much salt. It can cause lethargy, restlessness, or seizures and may lead to bleeding in the brain or kidney injury. Treatment must lower sodium slowly to avoid brain swelling.

topics.name: Hyperparathyroidism
topics.clinical_significance: Overactive parathyroid glands release too much parathyroid hormone (PTH). Primary disease usually raises blood calcium and can cause kidney stones and bone loss; secondary disease is a response to low calcium or chronic kidney disease. Long-standing secondary disease can become tertiary, with PTH release no longer controlled by blood calcium.

topics.name: Hyperphosphatemia
topics.clinical_significance: A high blood phosphate level, most often because diseased kidneys cannot remove enough phosphate. It is usually symptom-free, but when blood calcium is also low it can cause muscle spasms. In chronic kidney disease, it can contribute to bone disease and calcium deposits in blood vessels and soft tissues.

topics.name: Hyperpigmentation
topics.clinical_significance: Darkening of the skin from increased melanin or deposits of pigment. It may follow inflammation or injury, but widespread changes can be caused by medicines or illnesses such as Addison disease or hemochromatosis; some focal pigmented lesions are due to skin cancer.

topics.name: Hypersensitivity and Inflammatory Skin Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: An overview of skin disorders caused by immune hypersensitivity or other reactions to medicines, infections, or cancer. The group includes inflammatory rashes and, in some cases, severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

topics.name: Hypersensitivity and Reactive Skin Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A group of skin conditions involving immune hypersensitivity or other inflammatory reactions, sometimes related to medicines, infections, or cancer. They range from skin rashes to potentially life-threatening reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

topics.name: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis
topics.clinical_significance: An immune lung disease caused by repeatedly breathing an environmental substance after becoming sensitized to it; common sources include bird proteins, mold, and workplace materials. It can cause cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue, with fever or chills during acute attacks. Continued exposure can lead to permanent lung scarring.

topics.name: Hypersensitivity Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: An older, loosely used name for vasculitis affecting blood vessels in the skin, especially small vessels. It may cause raised purple spots, tiny red-purple spots, or ulcers and can be limited to the skin or occur with vasculitis in other organs. Despite the name, many cases are not due to hypersensitivity; causes can include medicines, infections, autoimmune disease, or cancer.

topics.name: Hypersplenism
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood cell counts caused by an enlarged spleen, which traps and destroys more red cells and often white cells and platelets. Low counts can cause anemia, raise infection risk, or increase bleeding, although they are often mild; symptoms may also come from the underlying disorder.

topics.name: Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Sustained high resting blood pressure, usually without symptoms. Over time it can damage blood vessels and the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes, increasing the risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney failure. Diagnosis relies on repeated, accurate measurements because blood pressure varies.

topics.name: Hypertension, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Drug treatment uses one or more medicines to lower blood pressure and reduce long-term damage to the heart, brain, and kidneys. Choice depends on blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, and other conditions; options include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and other drug classes, which can have important side effects.

topics.name: Hypertension in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Persistent high blood pressure in a child, often without symptoms. Before age 6, it is more likely to have a secondary cause such as kidney disease; after age 6, primary hypertension is more common. Severe hypertension can damage organs, and childhood hypertension is linked to higher cardiovascular risk in adulthood. In children under 13, blood pressure is judged by age, sex, and height, and repeated measurements help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Hypertension in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: High blood pressure that is present before pregnancy or develops during pregnancy. It may be chronic (present before 20 weeks) or gestational (starting after 20 weeks). Either type raises the risk of preeclampsia and serious complications for the pregnant person, including stroke and kidney failure, and for the fetus, including poor growth, low oxygen, or placental abruption.

topics.name: Hypertensive Arteriolar Nephrosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term, poorly controlled high blood pressure damages small kidney blood vessels and tissue, causing progressive chronic kidney disease. It may have no symptoms early and only rarely progresses to kidney failure; signs of blood pressure damage to other organs may also occur.

topics.name: Hypertensive Emergencies
topics.clinical_significance: A severe rise in blood pressure (often at least 180 systolic or 120 diastolic) with new or worsening damage to organs such as the brain, heart, aorta, or kidneys. It is a life-threatening emergency; a very high reading without organ damage is not by itself a hypertensive emergency.

topics.name: Hypertensive Retinopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Damage to the retina’s blood vessels from high blood pressure. It often causes no symptoms until advanced but can blur vision; an eye exam may show narrowed arteries, bleeding, cotton-wool spots, or optic disc swelling in severe disease. It also signals increased risk of high blood pressure damage to other organs.

topics.name: Hyperthyroidism
topics.clinical_significance: Excess thyroid hormone activity that speeds the body’s processes, usually because the thyroid makes too much hormone. It can cause weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, tremor, anxiety, frequent stools, and a fast or irregular heartbeat. Common causes include Graves disease, overactive nodules, and thyroid inflammation; severe cases can lead to life-threatening thyroid storm.

topics.name: Hyperthyroidism in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Excess thyroid hormone in infants, children, or teens. In newborns it is usually caused by thyroid-stimulating antibodies crossing the placenta from a mother with Graves disease and can be life-threatening; in older children, Graves disease is the most common cause. Symptoms may include a fast heartbeat, irritability, poor feeding or weight gain, heat intolerance, tremor, and sleep or school problems. Untreated disease can impair growth and, rarely, cause thyroid storm.

topics.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
topics.clinical_significance: A usually inherited heart muscle disorder in which the left ventricle becomes abnormally thick and stiff. The thickened muscle can make it harder for the heart to fill or block blood flow out of it. The condition may cause shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, or fainting, and can lead to dangerous heart rhythms or sudden death, especially in people at higher risk.

topics.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Arrhythmias
topics.clinical_significance: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause slow or fast abnormal heart rhythms, including atrial fibrillation and dangerous ventricular rhythms. These may cause palpitations or fainting; severe ventricular rhythms can cause cardiac arrest or sudden death. Atrial fibrillation can worsen heart filling and increase the risk of stroke.

topics.name: Hypertrophic Osteoarthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Osteoarthritis, also called hypertrophic osteoarthritis, is a chronic joint disorder in which cartilage gradually breaks down and bone at the joint margins may enlarge. It commonly causes pain with activity, stiffness after rest that usually eases within 30 minutes, and reduced movement. The severity of symptoms may not match changes seen on X-rays.

topics.name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Thickening of the muscle at the stomach outlet narrows or blocks the passage of food, usually in infants in the first weeks of life. It causes forceful vomiting without bile after feeds and can lead to dehydration, abnormal blood salt levels, and poor weight gain.

topics.name: Hyperventilation Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A breathing pattern in which a person breathes more than the body needs, lowering blood carbon dioxide and causing respiratory alkalosis. It can cause breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness, tingling, or hand stiffness and is often linked to anxiety. Other medical causes of rapid breathing must be excluded.

topics.name: Hypnotherapy
topics.clinical_significance: A mind-body treatment that uses relaxation and focused attention to help a person respond to therapeutic suggestions; the person remains aware of the surroundings. It can reduce pain and anxiety during medical procedures and may ease symptoms such as irritable bowel syndrome, headaches, or nausea.

topics.name: Hypnotics
topics.clinical_significance: Hypnotics are medicines used to help induce or maintain sleep. Some benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and related sedative drugs have this effect. They can impair alertness and coordination; high doses can slow breathing, and long-term use may lead to dependence and withdrawal symptoms such as agitation or seizures.

topics.name: Hypocalcemia
topics.clinical_significance: A lower-than-normal level of calcium in the blood. Causes include underactive parathyroid glands, vitamin D deficiency, and kidney disease. It can cause tingling, cramps, and muscle spasms; severe cases may cause seizures, heart failure, or abnormal heart rhythms. Low albumin can lower total calcium even when active (ionized) calcium is normal.

topics.name: Hypocalcemia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: A low blood calcium level in a newborn, most often in the first days after birth. It is more common in premature or small-for-gestational-age infants and in infants of mothers with diabetes; birth asphyxia and parathyroid disorders are other causes. It may cause poor feeding, jitteriness, muscle weakness, pauses in breathing, or seizures.

topics.name: Hypoglycemia
topics.clinical_significance: A low blood glucose level. In people taking medicines for diabetes, a level at or below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is considered hypoglycemia. It can cause sweating, shaking, hunger, and a fast heartbeat; severe episodes can impair brain function and cause confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Insulin and some diabetes medicines are common causes.

topics.name: Hypoglycemia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood glucose in a newborn; the cutoff depends on age, prematurity, and symptoms. It is more common in premature or small newborns and in babies of mothers with diabetes or after oxygen deprivation around birth. Many infants have no symptoms, but severe or prolonged low glucose can cause poor feeding, shakiness, breathing pauses, seizures, or coma.

topics.name: Hypogonadism in Children, Male
topics.clinical_significance: Reduced production of testosterone, sperm, or both in a boy, or rarely a poor response to testosterone. Depending on when it begins, it can affect genital development before birth or delay puberty. During puberty, it may cause small testes and penis, little body hair, and a high-pitched voice. The cause may lie in the testes or in hormone signals from the brain or pituitary gland.

topics.name: Hypogonadism, Male
topics.clinical_significance: Reduced testosterone with related symptoms, reduced sperm production, or both. It may result from problems in the testes or in the brain and pituitary signals that control them. Depending on its cause and when it begins, it can cause delayed puberty, low sex drive, erection problems, infertility, loss of muscle or bone, and mood changes.

topics.name: Hypohidrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Inadequate sweating, which may affect one area or more of the body. Causes include skin injury or disease, nerve damage such as diabetic neuropathy, anticholinergic medicines, and inherited conditions. Reduced sweating can impair body cooling and raise the risk of overheating, heat exhaustion, or heatstroke.

topics.name: Hypokalemia
topics.clinical_significance: A low blood potassium level (below 3.5 mmol/L), usually from loss through the kidneys or gut or movement of potassium into cells. Mild cases may cause no symptoms; lower levels can cause muscle weakness, cramps, or paralysis, and severe cases can disrupt heart rhythm or breathing. Diuretics, vomiting, and diarrhea are common causes.

topics.name: Hypomagnesemia
topics.clinical_significance: A low blood magnesium level (below 1.8 mg/dL or 0.70 mmol/L), often due to poor intake or losses through the gut or kidneys. It may cause weakness, tremor, or muscle spasms; severe deficiency can cause seizures or abnormal heart rhythms. It often occurs with low potassium or calcium and can make these levels hard to correct.

topics.name: Hyponatremia
topics.clinical_significance: A low sodium concentration in the blood, usually because the body has too much water relative to sodium. Causes include diuretics, vomiting or diarrhea, heart, liver, or kidney disease, and hormone disorders that cause water retention. Symptoms mainly affect the brain and may include nausea, headache, and confusion; severe or rapidly developing cases can cause seizures or coma.

topics.name: Hyponatremia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood sodium in a newborn (below 135 mmol/L), usually from sodium loss with vomiting or diarrhea. Replacing these losses with low-sodium fluids or giving overly diluted formula can worsen it; excess water retention is another cause. Severe hyponatremia can cause lethargy, weakness, seizures, or coma.

topics.name: Hypoparathyroidism
topics.clinical_significance: Too little parathyroid hormone, which usually causes low blood calcium and high phosphate. It often follows thyroid or parathyroid surgery but may result from autoimmune or inherited disorders. Low calcium can cause tingling around the mouth or in the hands, muscle cramps, and, when severe, muscle spasms (tetany).

topics.name: Hypophosphatasia
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited disorder caused by low activity of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, leading to poor mineralization of bones and teeth. Severity varies: some children lose baby teeth early, while others develop rickets or other bone problems. Severe disease can disrupt vitamin B6 function in the brain and cause seizures.

topics.name: Hypophosphatemia
topics.clinical_significance: A low blood phosphate level (below 2.5 mg/dL or 0.81 mmol/L). Mild cases often cause no symptoms, but severe or long-lasting deficiency can cause muscle weakness, weak bones, breathing or heart failure, seizures, or coma. Causes include poor intake, alcohol use, kidney phosphate loss, and shifts into cells during refeeding or recovery from diabetic ketoacidosis.

topics.name: Hypophosphatemic Rickets
topics.clinical_significance: Usually an inherited disorder in which the kidneys lose too much phosphate, lowering blood phosphate and weakening bone mineralization. In children, it can cause rickets, bowed legs, bone pain, fractures, and slow growth or short stature. Unlike nutritional rickets, it does not improve with vitamin D alone.

topics.name: Hypopituitarism, Generalized
topics.clinical_significance: Partial or complete loss of anterior pituitary function, causing deficiency of one or more hormones that control growth, thyroid, adrenal, and reproductive glands. Symptoms depend on which hormones are affected and may include fatigue, low blood pressure, cold intolerance, delayed puberty, infertility, or poor growth. ACTH deficiency can cause dangerously low cortisol.

topics.name: Hypoplastic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for aplastic anemia, a bone marrow failure disorder in which blood-forming cells and marrow activity are greatly reduced. It lowers two or more blood cell types (red cells, white cells, and platelets), causing fatigue, infections, or easy bruising and bleeding. Severe disease can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
