topics.clinical_significance: A severe congenital heart defect in which the left ventricle, aortic and mitral valves, and ascending aorta are underdeveloped. After birth, blood flow to the body depends on the ductus arteriosus, a fetal blood vessel; when it closes, the newborn can rapidly develop shock. Survival requires staged heart surgery or, in some cases, transplantation.

topics.name: Hypothermia
topics.clinical_significance: An abnormally low core body temperature (35°C or lower), when heat loss exceeds heat production. It slows brain, breathing, and heart function. Early signs include shivering and poor coordination; worsening hypothermia can cause confusion, unconsciousness, dangerous heart rhythms, and death.

topics.name: Hypothermia in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Core temperature below 36.5°C in a newborn. Premature and low-birth-weight infants are especially prone because they lose heat quickly; hypothermia may also result from illness such as sepsis. Persistent hypothermia raises energy and oxygen needs and can cause low blood sugar and metabolic acidosis, while increasing the risk of sepsis and death.

topics.name: Hypothyroidism
topics.clinical_significance: Deficiency of thyroid hormone, most often from autoimmune thyroid disease or thyroid treatment; less often from pituitary or hypothalamic disease. It slows body functions and can cause fatigue, cold intolerance, modest weight gain, constipation, and slowed thinking. Severe, untreated disease can lead to myxedema coma, a life-threatening state with reduced consciousness and low body temperature.

topics.name: Hypothyroidism in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Low thyroid hormone in an infant or child. It is usually congenital in infants and often due to autoimmune thyroid disease in older children. Infants may show few early signs, but untreated deficiency can impair brain development; in older children, it can slow growth and delay puberty. Many cases are found through newborn screening.

topics.name: Hypoxia in Hospitalized Patients
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood oxygen during hospitalization, often shown by an oxygen saturation below 90%. It can reduce oxygen delivery to organs. Causes include slow or blocked breathing, lung infection, a blood clot in the lungs, or heart failure. Severe or persistent hypoxia can threaten organ function and life.

topics.name: Hypoxic Hepatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Sudden, widespread liver injury caused by too little blood flow or oxygen. It often occurs with low blood pressure, heart failure, respiratory failure, or sepsis and causes a sharp rise in liver enzymes. Liver function usually recovers when blood flow is restored, but acute liver failure can occur, especially in people with cirrhosis.

topics.name: Ichthyosis
topics.clinical_significance: A group of skin disorders that cause persistent dry, thickened, scaly skin. Ichthyosis may be inherited or acquired; acquired cases can be linked to an underlying illness or medicine. Severe forms may affect much of the body and cause itching or tightness.

topics.name: Idiopathic Environmental Intolerance
topics.clinical_significance: A condition in which a person has recurring, varied symptoms attributed to low-level exposure to unrelated environmental substances. Symptoms may involve several body systems, but clear signs of organ damage are usually absent. Other medical causes are ruled out first. It was formerly called multiple chemical sensitivity.

topics.name: Idiopathic Hypersomnia
topics.clinical_significance: A sleep disorder marked by excessive daytime sleepiness, with or without unusually long sleep at night. People may have great difficulty waking and remain drowsy or slowed after waking (sleep inertia). Sleep testing helps distinguish it from other sleep disorders, including narcolepsy.

topics.name: Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies
topics.clinical_significance: A group of inflammatory muscle diseases, usually related to an autoimmune response. They cause weakness, often in the shoulders and hips; some forms also affect the skin, swallowing, lungs, or heart. Dermatomyositis is associated with increased cancer risk.

topics.name: Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A group of lung diseases of unknown cause that inflame and scar the tissue around the air sacs. They commonly cause shortness of breath and sometimes cough; severity and outlook differ by type. Chest CT and lung function tests help identify the type, and sometimes a biopsy is needed.

topics.name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: A disorder of increased pressure around the brain, without a mass or hydrocephalus. It often causes daily headaches, brief episodes of blurred vision, or a pulsing sound in the ears. Swelling of the optic nerves can lead to permanent vision loss.

topics.name: Idiopathic Pleuroparenchymal Fibroelastosis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, slowly progressive lung disease that causes scarring and thickening of the lining and outer tissue of the upper lungs. It can cause shortness of breath, dry cough, repeated lung infections, and pneumothorax (collapsed lung). The outlook is often poor.

topics.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)
topics.clinical_significance: A progressive scarring lung disease of unknown cause. It causes worsening shortness of breath with activity and a dry cough, and lung function often declines over time. Antifibrotic medicines can slow its progression, but the outlook is often poor.

topics.name: Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare disorder, mainly affecting young children, in which bleeding repeatedly occurs in the tiny air sacs of the lungs without a known cause. It can cause cough, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, and iron-deficiency anemia; repeated bleeding may scar the lungs.

topics.name: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
topics.clinical_significance: An older name for immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), an autoimmune disorder in which platelets are destroyed and their production may fall. The low platelet count can cause small red or purple skin spots, bruising, or bleeding; some people have no symptoms.

topics.name: IgA Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: An immune kidney disease in which IgA-containing deposits build up in the kidney filters (glomeruli). It often causes visible or microscopic blood in the urine, sometimes during or soon after a respiratory infection, and may also cause protein in the urine. It often progresses slowly, but some people develop chronic kidney disease or kidney failure.

topics.name: IgG4-RD
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic immune disorder that causes inflammation and scar tissue, often forming mass-like growths or painless enlargement in one or more organs. It can affect the pancreas, tear or salivary glands, lungs, kidneys, and other tissues; delayed diagnosis may lead to lasting organ damage. Blood IgG4 levels may be normal, and diagnosis usually requires a biopsy.

topics.name: IgG4-Related Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic immune disorder that causes inflammation and scar tissue, often forming mass-like growths or painless enlargement in one or more organs. It can affect the pancreas, tear or salivary glands, lungs, kidneys, and other tissues; delayed diagnosis may lead to lasting organ damage. Blood IgG4 levels may be normal, and diagnosis usually requires a biopsy.

topics.name: IgG4-Related Sclerosing Cholangitis
topics.clinical_significance: An immune-mediated disease that inflames and narrows the bile ducts, often with autoimmune pancreatitis. It may block bile flow and cause jaundice, abdominal pain, or weight loss. It can resemble primary sclerosing cholangitis or bile duct cancer, but often responds well to corticosteroids.

topics.name: Ileus
topics.clinical_significance: A temporary slowing or stoppage of intestinal movement without a physical blockage, most often after abdominal surgery. It can cause abdominal swelling, nausea, vomiting, and discomfort; little or no stool may pass. It must be distinguished from a mechanical bowel blockage because the causes and treatment differ.

topics.name: Illicit Drugs and Intoxicants
topics.clinical_significance: Illicit drugs, alcohol, and inhaled chemicals can alter brain and body function. Intoxication or overdose may cause severe injury or death; repeated use can lead to dependence, withdrawal, and lasting health problems. Injecting drugs can spread serious infections, including HIV and hepatitis.

topics.name: Illness Anxiety Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Persistent preoccupation and fear of having or developing a serious illness, despite no or only mild physical symptoms. The person may repeatedly check their body, seek reassurance, or avoid medical care. The preoccupation lasts at least six months and causes significant distress or disrupts daily life.

topics.name: Imaging Tests of the Liver and Gallbladder
topics.clinical_significance: Imaging tests help find gallstones, bile-duct blockage, and liver masses, and assess liver tissue and blood flow. Ultrasound is usually the first test for gallbladder and bile-duct problems; CT or MRI may clarify liver findings, while ERCP can also treat some blockages but is invasive.

topics.name: Immersion Pulmonary Edema
topics.clinical_significance: A sudden buildup of fluid in the lungs during swimming or diving, caused by changes in blood flow and pressure during immersion. It causes severe shortness of breath and cough, sometimes with frothy sputum and low blood oxygen; severe cases can be fatal.

topics.name: Immune System, Biology of
topics.clinical_significance: The immune system protects the body from infections and abnormal cells by recognizing harmful or foreign targets. Innate defenses respond quickly; adaptive immunity uses B and T cells to target specific antigens and form memory. Poor regulation can cause allergies, autoimmune disease, or tissue damage.

topics.name: Immune System, Cellular Components
topics.clinical_significance: Immune cells work together to detect and remove microbes and abnormal cells. B cells make antibodies; T cells coordinate responses or kill infected cells; phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages engulf microbes; dendritic cells alert T cells. Problems with these cells can weaken immune defenses or contribute to allergy and autoimmune disease.

topics.name: Immune System, Molecular Components of
topics.clinical_significance: Immune molecules include antibodies, cytokines, and acute-phase proteins. Antibodies recognize specific targets, while cytokines coordinate immune activity and acute-phase proteins help respond to infection or tissue injury; C-reactive protein is a nonspecific marker of inflammation. Excess or misdirected immune signaling can cause tissue damage or inflammatory disease.

topics.name: Immune System, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The immune system protects against infections and abnormal cells by distinguishing the body's own tissues from foreign or harmful targets. Innate defenses respond quickly; adaptive B- and T-cell responses target specific antigens and develop memory. Weak defenses raise infection risk, while excessive or misdirected responses can cause allergy, autoimmune disease, or tissue damage.

topics.name: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
topics.clinical_significance: An autoimmune bleeding disorder that lowers the platelet count by increasing platelet destruction and reducing platelet production. Many people have no symptoms; others develop small red or purple skin spots (petechiae), bruising, nose or mouth bleeding, or heavy menstrual bleeding. Severe cases can cause serious bleeding.

topics.name: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura
topics.clinical_significance: An older name for immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), an autoimmune bleeding disorder that lowers platelet counts by increasing platelet destruction and reducing platelet production. It may cause small red or purple skin spots (petechiae), bruising, or mucosal bleeding, though some people have no symptoms.

topics.name: Immunization
topics.clinical_significance: Immunization creates protection against infection. Active immunization uses a vaccine or toxoid to trigger the person's own immune response and memory; passive immunization gives ready-made antibodies for short-term protection, sometimes after exposure. Vaccination prevents many serious infections and has made some formerly common diseases rare or eliminated.

topics.name: Immunization, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Immunization protects against infection by stimulating the body's own immune response with a vaccine or toxoid (active immunization), or by giving ready-made antibodies (passive immunization). Passive protection acts quickly but is temporary. Vaccination has greatly reduced serious infections and eliminated smallpox.

topics.name: Immunization, Overview of
topics.clinical_significance: Immunization protects against infection by stimulating the body's own immune response with a vaccine or toxoid (active immunization), or by giving ready-made antibodies (passive immunization). Passive protection acts quickly but is temporary. Vaccination has greatly reduced serious infections and eliminated smallpox.

topics.name: Immunization, Passive
topics.clinical_significance: Short-term protection created by giving preformed antibodies against an organism or toxin. It acts quickly and can be used after exposure or when a person cannot make enough antibodies, but it does not create lasting immune memory.

topics.name: Immunodeficiency, Approach to Suspected
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment for immunodeficiency is considered when infections are unusually severe, frequent, hard to treat, occur in several body sites, or involve unusual germs, especially with a family history. Clinical assessment and immune tests help identify whether the cause is inherited or acquired and which part of the immune system is affected.

topics.name: Immunodeficiency Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Immunodeficiency can increase the risk of recurrent infections, autoimmune disorders, lymphoma, and other cancers. It may be inherited (primary) or acquired (secondary); acquired forms are more common. The effects and outlook depend on the specific disorder.

topics.name: Immunodeficiency Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders impair one or more parts of the immune system and can cause recurrent, severe, or unusual infections. Some also cause autoimmune disease or raise the risk of cancer. Primary forms are genetic and often appear in childhood; secondary forms are acquired and more common. Identifying the affected part of immunity helps guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: IgA immune complexes collect in the kidney filters, often causing blood and protein in the urine. Visible blood may appear soon after a respiratory or other mucosal infection. Kidney function is often normal at first, but the disease can slowly progress to chronic kidney disease.

topics.name: Immunoglobulin A–Associated Vasculitis (IgAV)
topics.clinical_significance: IgA-associated vasculitis inflames small blood vessels, often in the skin, gut, joints, and kidneys. It can cause a raised purple rash, joint pain, and abdominal pain; kidney involvement may cause blood or protein in the urine. It occurs mostly in children and usually settles, but rarely leads to chronic kidney disease.

topics.name: Immunologic Tests for Infectious Disease
topics.clinical_significance: These tests help diagnose infections by detecting either parts of a pathogen (antigens) or antibodies made by the patient. Different tests have different strengths, and results can depend on the type and stage of infection, so they are interpreted with the clinical picture and other test results.

topics.name: Immunotherapeutics
topics.clinical_significance: Immunotherapeutics use or change immune activity to prevent or treat disease. They include antibodies, cytokines, small molecules, and cell-based treatments, and are used for conditions such as cancer, autoimmune disease, and some infections or immune deficiencies. Their benefits and risks depend on the specific treatment; some can cause serious inflammation or autoimmune reactions.

topics.name: Immunotherapy of Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer immunotherapy helps the immune system recognize or attack cancer. Treatments include checkpoint inhibitors, antibodies, vaccines, and modified immune cells. These approaches can help control some cancers, but benefits depend on the cancer and treatment; immune-related treatment can also cause serious inflammation in healthy organs.

topics.name: Impedance Planimetry
topics.clinical_significance: Impedance planimetry uses an inflatable balloon probe to measure pressure and how much a digestive tract passage opens. It is especially useful for assessing the esophagus in achalasia and measuring response to treatment, including when manometry is inconclusive or not tolerated. Its role in other digestive disorders is still being studied.

topics.name: Imperforate Anus
topics.clinical_significance: A birth defect in which the anal opening is absent or blocked, so a newborn cannot pass stool normally. It can cause bowel blockage and abdominal swelling. Other birth defects are common, including problems of the spine, heart, kidneys, limbs, or digestive tract; surgical repair is needed.

topics.name: Impetigo and Ecthyma
topics.clinical_significance: Impetigo is a contagious, superficial skin infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococci. Ecthyma is a deeper form that reaches the dermis and can scar. Delayed treatment can allow infection to spread; certain streptococcal strains can rarely lead to kidney inflammation after the skin infection.

topics.name: Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillators (ICD)
topics.clinical_significance: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator detects dangerous ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation and uses pacing or an electric shock to stop it. It lowers the risk of sudden cardiac death in people with prior life-threatening rhythms or a high risk of them. It treats these episodes but does not prevent them, so other treatment may also be needed.

topics.name: Impotence
topics.clinical_significance: Impotence (erectile dysfunction) is the repeated inability to get or keep an erection adequate for sexual activity. It may be related to blood vessel, nerve, hormone, or psychological problems, or to medicines, and can affect mental health and relationships. New erectile dysfunction from reduced blood flow can be an early sign of cardiovascular disease.

topics.name: Inborn Metabolic Disorders Causing Hyperbilirubinemia
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited disorders of bilirubin processing can raise either unconjugated or conjugated bilirubin and cause jaundice. Many, including Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes, are mild and need no treatment. Crigler-Najjar type I can cause very high bilirubin soon after birth and lead to brain damage (kernicterus); type II is usually milder.

topics.name: Incendiary Chemical-Warfare Agents and Hydrogen Fluoride (HF)
topics.clinical_significance: Incendiary agents can cause severe burns and mass-casualty injuries; white phosphorus and magnesium may keep burning in tissue and cause effects throughout the body. Hydrofluoric acid can penetrate deeply, with delayed severe pain despite mild-looking skin. It can lower blood calcium and magnesium and cause dangerous heart rhythm problems.

topics.name: including Graves Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis) means that too much thyroid hormone is acting in the body; Graves disease is a common cause. It can cause weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety, and a fast or irregular heartbeat. Graves disease may also inflame the tissues around the eyes, and severe disease can strain the heart.

topics.name: Induction of Labor
topics.clinical_significance: Induction starts uterine contractions before spontaneous labor, usually to achieve vaginal birth. It may be recommended when delivery is safer than continuing pregnancy, or planned electively in selected cases. Medicines or mechanical methods can prepare the cervix and start contractions; excessive contractions can affect the fetus, so fetal monitoring is used.

topics.name: Infant Botulism
topics.clinical_significance: Infant botulism occurs when Clostridium botulinum spores grow in an infant’s intestine and produce toxin. Constipation may be followed by poor sucking, a weak cry, drooping eyelids, and floppy weakness; severe cases can impair breathing. It requires urgent hospital care. Honey can carry the spores and should not be given before age 1 year.

topics.name: Infantile Cataract
topics.clinical_significance: Clouding of the lens present at birth or soon after can block vision while the eyes and brain are developing, causing amblyopia and lasting vision loss. Prompt assessment by an eye specialist is important; significant cataracts may need early surgery.

topics.name: Infantile Eczema
topics.clinical_significance: Infantile eczema is another name for atopic dermatitis, a chronic, relapsing, itchy skin inflammation linked to skin-barrier and immune problems. In infants, it often affects the face, scalp, neck, and outer limbs. Scratching can damage the skin and increase the risk of infection.

topics.name: Infantile Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: A developmental problem with the eye’s drainage system raises pressure inside the eye. The eye may enlarge and the cornea may become cloudy. Without early treatment, high pressure can damage the optic nerve and cause blindness; surgery is usually needed to protect vision.

topics.name: Infantile Hemangiomas
topics.clinical_significance: Infantile hemangiomas are common, benign blood-vessel growths that appear early in life, grow quickly, and usually shrink over time. Ulcerated lesions may bleed, hurt, or scar. Lesions near the eye, airway, or openings for urine or stool can impair function and may need treatment; a large lower-back lesion can signal neurologic or urinary-tract abnormalities.

topics.name: Infantile Paralysis
topics.clinical_significance: Infantile paralysis is an older name for polio (poliomyelitis), a highly contagious infection caused by poliovirus that can affect people of any age. Most infections cause no or mild symptoms, but fewer than 1% damage motor nerves and cause flaccid weakness, which may be permanent; breathing muscles can also be affected. Vaccination prevents most cases.

topics.name: Infantile Spasms
topics.clinical_significance: Infantile spasms are brief seizures with sudden flexion or extension of the trunk and limbs, often occurring in clusters. Developmental delay may be present, or the child may lose skills after the spasms begin. Other types of epilepsy may follow, so prompt diagnosis and treatment are important.

topics.name: Infants and Children, Physical Growth
topics.clinical_significance: Weight, length or height, and head size are measured over time and compared with age-appropriate growth charts. The pattern and rate of growth can reveal poor or unusually rapid growth and help identify possible health or nutrition problems; trends are more useful than a single measurement.

topics.name: Infants and Children, Symptoms in
topics.clinical_significance: Symptoms such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, rash, or persistent crying can have many causes in infants and children. Their meaning and urgency depend on the child’s age and other signs. Red flags can point to serious illness and need prompt medical evaluation.

topics.name: Infected Bite Wounds of the Hand
topics.clinical_significance: Small bite punctures to the hand, especially human or cat bites, may reach tendons or joints and cause deep infection. Infection can spread to a tendon sheath, joint, or bone, causing septic arthritis or osteomyelitis and threatening hand function. A wound over a knuckle after punching someone may be a human bite, and delay in care can worsen infection.

topics.name: Infection by Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Other Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC)
topics.clinical_significance: Shiga toxin–producing E. coli, including O157:H7, can cause severe abdominal cramps and watery diarrhea that may become bloody, often with little fever. It can lead to hemolytic-uremic syndrome, with red blood cell destruction, low platelets, and acute kidney injury, especially in young children and older adults. Antibiotics are not recommended because they do not prevent this complication.

topics.name: Infection, Manifestations of
topics.clinical_significance: Infection may cause local signs, such as redness or an abscess, or whole-body signs, often including fever and a fast heart rate. Severe infection can affect the brain, blood, lungs, kidneys, liver, and other organs, and may progress to life-threatening sepsis or septic shock.

topics.name: Infections in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Newborns can acquire infections before, during, or after birth. Their immature immune defenses, especially in premature babies, make serious illness such as sepsis or meningitis more likely, and early signs may be subtle, such as poor feeding, sleepiness, or temperature changes. Infections before birth can also affect growth and development.

topics.name: Infections of Joints and Bones
topics.clinical_significance: Infection can affect joints, bones, or artificial joints. A joint infection can damage cartilage quickly, while a bone infection can destroy bone and spread to nearby tissue. Prompt diagnosis and treatment help prevent lasting damage and loss of function.

topics.name: Infectious Disease, Biology of
topics.clinical_significance: Infectious disease develops through interactions between microbes and the body’s defenses. Normal microbes often help protect the body, but may cause illness if defenses are weakened. Microbial traits and antimicrobial resistance affect how infection spreads, how severe it becomes, and which treatments may work.

topics.name: Infectious Disease in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Some infections during pregnancy can harm the pregnant person or pass to the fetus or newborn. They may cause pregnancy loss, preterm birth, birth defects, or serious newborn illness. Prenatal screening and prompt care can reduce these risks; medicine choices must account for safety during pregnancy.

topics.name: Infectious Disease, Laboratory Diagnosis of
topics.clinical_significance: Laboratory tests help identify the cause of an infection and guide treatment. Different tests detect the microbe or the body’s response, and some infections need specific tests because routine tests can miss them. Culture and resistance testing can help clinicians choose an effective antimicrobial.

topics.name: Infectious Diseases, Introduction to Biology of
topics.clinical_significance: The body’s normal microbes help protect against disease-causing organisms. These microbes can sometimes cause illness if the body’s defenses are disrupted. The mix of microbes differs by body site, so this balance helps explain how infection risk varies.

topics.name: Infectious Esophageal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Infections of the esophagus occur mainly in people with weakened immune defenses and are often caused by Candida, herpes simplex virus, or cytomegalovirus. They can cause painful swallowing and chest pain. Identifying the cause matters because treatment differs by organism.

topics.name: Infectious Flexor Tenosynovitis
topics.clinical_significance: This is an acute infection in the sheath around a finger’s flexor tendon, often after a puncture wound. Swelling, tenderness along the tendon, and pain when the finger is straightened are warning signs. Treatment requires surgical drainage and antibiotics.

topics.name: Infectious Mononucleosis
topics.clinical_significance: Epstein-Barr virus causes infectious mononucleosis, usually with fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue that can last weeks or months. The spleen may enlarge and rarely rupture, so heavy lifting and contact sports should be avoided during recovery. Most people recover with supportive care.

topics.name: Infectious Uveitis
topics.clinical_significance: Infectious uveitis is inflammation inside the eye caused by an infection. It can threaten vision, especially when the retina is involved or the person has weakened immunity. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are important because some infections can rapidly cause severe vision loss.

topics.name: Infective Endocarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart’s inner lining, usually involving a valve. Infected growths can damage valves or break off and travel to other organs, causing serious problems such as heart failure or stroke. Diagnosis uses blood cultures and heart imaging, and treatment requires prolonged antimicrobial therapy; surgery is sometimes needed.

topics.name: Inferior Calcaneal Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the small bursa under the heel causes sharp or throbbing pain, often worse when the heel first hits the ground. It can be confused with plantar fasciitis or heel-pad problems, which need different care. Cushioned footwear and heel support can help.

topics.name: Infertility and Recurrent Pregnancy Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Infertility is difficulty achieving a successful pregnancy and may have causes in either partner. Recurrent pregnancy loss, usually defined as two or more pregnancy losses, is a separate condition. Both may need medical evaluation to look for causes and possible treatment, and can cause significant emotional distress.

topics.name: Infertility, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Infertility means being unable to achieve a successful pregnancy or needing medical help to do so. Causes may involve either partner, so both may need evaluation; some causes can be treated. Evaluation is generally advised after 12 months of regular, unprotected sex if the female partner is under 35, and after 6 months if 35 or older. Infertility can also cause emotional distress.

topics.name: Infertility, Unexplained
topics.clinical_significance: Unexplained infertility means standard tests have not found a cause; semen, ovulation, eggs, fallopian tubes, and uterus appear normal. Further evaluation or fertility treatment may be considered. Treatments that stimulate ovulation can increase the chance of a pregnancy with more than one fetus.

topics.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines for Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis reduce gut inflammation, treat flares, and help keep the disease in remission. The choice depends on the disease type, location, and severity. Steroids are generally used for short-term control of flares, while other medicines help maintain remission. Some treatments weaken immune defenses, so screening and monitoring for side effects are important.

topics.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. These long-term conditions cause gut inflammation that flares and settles, often leading to diarrhea and abdominal pain. They can also affect joints, eyes, skin, and other organs. Long-standing inflammation in the colon requires regular screening for colorectal cancer.

topics.name: Inflammatory Bowel Disease, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammatory bowel disease mainly includes Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Both cause long-term inflammation that flares and settles, but Crohn disease can affect different parts of the digestive tract, while ulcerative colitis affects the colon. Both can also affect organs outside the gut. Long-term colon inflammation requires colorectal cancer screening.

topics.name: Inflammatory Breast Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammatory breast cancer is a rare, fast-growing cancer. It can cause rapid breast redness, swelling, warmth, and thickened, dimpled skin, often without a lump. Prompt assessment and biopsy are important; treatment usually begins with chemotherapy, followed by surgery and radiation.

topics.name: Inflammatory Orbital Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation in the tissues around the eye can cause pain, eyelid swelling and redness, a bulging eye, or double vision. In some cases, vision is threatened. Causes include thyroid eye disease and other inflammatory conditions; imaging helps distinguish inflammation from infection because treatment differs.

topics.name: Inflammatory Vaginitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammatory vaginitis, also called desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, is a rare vaginal inflammation without a clear infectious cause. It occurs most often around or after menopause and can cause discharge, irritation, painful sex, or painful urination. Testing helps distinguish it from infections because treatment differs.

topics.name: Influenza
topics.clinical_significance: Influenza (flu) is caused mainly by influenza A or B viruses. It often starts suddenly with fever, chills, cough, headache, body aches, sore throat, or a runny nose. It can cause pneumonia or worsen existing illness and can be severe, especially in young children, older adults, pregnant people, and those with chronic health problems. Annual vaccination helps prevent it, and antiviral medicines can shorten illness, especially in high-risk or severely ill people.

topics.name: Influenza Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Influenza vaccine is updated each year to match viruses expected to circulate and helps prevent seasonal flu. It is recommended yearly for eligible people. Several forms are available; age, pregnancy, immune status, and other health conditions affect which type is suitable. Some young children need two doses in one season.

topics.name: Informed Consent
topics.clinical_significance: Informed consent means a patient freely agrees to a medical intervention after understanding their condition, the proposed care, its possible benefits and harms, alternatives (including no treatment), and key uncertainties. For invasive or risky care, the patient must have decision-making capacity; otherwise, an authorized decision-maker may be needed. Patients may refuse care.

topics.name: Infrapatellar Tendinitis
topics.clinical_significance: This overuse injury affects the patellar tendon where it attaches to the lower tip of the kneecap, most often in active children who run or jump. It causes pain below the kneecap, especially with jumping, stairs, or forceful knee straightening. Treatment usually includes reducing painful activity and physical therapy.

topics.name: Ingrown Toenail
topics.clinical_significance: An ingrown toenail occurs when the nail edge presses into the skin beside it, causing pain and redness; swelling or infection can develop. Tight shoes and cutting the nail too short increase the risk. Mild cases may improve with wider shoes and simple measures to lift the nail edge; severe or recurring cases may need part of the nail removed.

topics.name: Inguinal Hernia
topics.clinical_significance: An inguinal hernia is a bulge of abdominal tissue through a weak spot in the groin wall. It may be painless or cause discomfort, often more noticeable when standing or straining. If it becomes trapped or loses its blood supply, it can block the bowel and cause severe pain and vomiting; urgent surgery may be needed.

topics.name: Inheritance, Multifactorial (Complex)
topics.clinical_significance: Many common traits and diseases result from the combined effects of multiple genes and environmental factors. They do not follow a simple inheritance pattern, but close relatives of an affected person may have a higher risk. Family history and other risk factors can help identify people who may benefit from prevention.

topics.name: Inheritance, Unusual Aspects of
topics.clinical_significance: Changes in genes or chromosomes can make a disorder appear in an unexpected way. A new mutation may cause disease in a child even when neither parent is affected, while mosaicism can make symptoms patchy or milder in a parent. Some chromosome changes or expanding DNA repeats can also affect the risk or severity of disease in later generations. Recognizing these patterns helps guide diagnosis and family risk assessment.

topics.name: Inherited Copper Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Wilson disease is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder of copper handling. Copper builds up in the liver, brain, and other organs, causing liver disease, movement or mood problems, and sometimes brown-gold rings at the edge of the cornea. Early diagnosis matters because lifelong treatment with medicines and a low-copper diet can prevent further damage; without treatment, the disease can be fatal.

topics.name: Inherited Disorders of Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited metabolic disorders are genetic conditions, often caused by enzyme problems that lead to harmful substances building up or needed substances being lacking. They can cause sudden illness in newborns or later problems with growth, development, or organ function. Newborn screening and early diagnosis are important because prompt treatment can prevent serious complications or death.

topics.name: Inherited Disorders of Metabolism, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited metabolic disorders can cause nonspecific signs such as poor feeding, vomiting, or seizures in newborns, or later problems with growth and development. These signs often have other causes, but early recognition matters because prompt treatment can prevent lasting harm or death. Newborn screening and targeted tests help identify the cause.

topics.name: Inherited Disorders of Metabolism, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Most inherited metabolic disorders result from enzyme defects that cause harmful substances to build up or needed substances to be lacking. There are hundreds of these conditions; each is rare, but together they affect many people. Newborn screening can identify some of them early, when treatment may help prevent serious harm.

topics.name: Inherited Epidermolysis Bullosa
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited epidermolysis bullosa makes the skin and sometimes mucous membranes fragile, causing painful blisters after minor rubbing or sometimes without injury. Severity ranges from mild to life-threatening. Widespread disease can lead to infection, poor nutrition, breathing problems, and scarring that limits movement.

topics.name: Inherited Muscular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited muscular disorders are genetic conditions that affect muscle structure or function. Many cause muscle weakness that worsens over time, while some cause stiffness or episodes of weakness. Symptoms and severity vary, so identifying the specific disorder helps guide care.

topics.name: Inherited Muscular Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited muscular dystrophies cause progressive muscle weakness, but the muscles affected, age of onset, and severity differ by type. Duchenne usually causes more severe disease than Becker. Some forms begin at birth and may affect breathing, heart function, feeding, and movement, so identifying the type helps guide supportive care.

topics.name: Inherited Platelet Function Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These rare inherited disorders impair platelet function and cause a lifelong tendency to bleed. Bleeding severity varies, and the platelet count may be normal or low, depending on the disorder. Serious bleeding may require platelet transfusion.

topics.name: Initial Evaluation and Preventive Care in the Healthy Term Newborn
topics.clinical_significance: Prompt assessment after birth checks how well a term newborn is adapting and identifies the need for resuscitation or closer monitoring. Preventive care, including warmth, early feeding, vitamin K, recommended eye infection prevention, indicated hepatitis B vaccination, and newborn screening, helps prevent complications and support a healthy start.

topics.name: Initial Psychiatric Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: An initial psychiatric assessment reviews symptoms, their effect on daily life, medical and substance-related causes, and risk of harm to self or others. It combines a health and personal history with a mental status examination. This helps avoid missed diagnoses and guide care; urgent situations need immediate assessment.

topics.name: Injection Drug Use
topics.clinical_significance: Injection drug use raises the risk of overdose and serious complications, including HIV or viral hepatitis from contaminated needles, skin abscesses, bloodstream infection, and endocarditis. Vein damage and harm from contaminants can also occur. Recognizing injection use helps clinicians check for complications and offer substance-use treatment and harm-reduction support.

topics.name: Injury During Diving or Work in Compressed Air
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure changes during diving or work in compressed air can injure body tissues and cause gas bubbles to form in the blood. These injuries can lead to severe pain, breathing or neurologic problems, and death. Prompt recognition matters because urgent oxygen and recompression treatment may be needed.

topics.name: Inner Ear Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: The inner ear is important for hearing and balance. Disorders can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, or unsteadiness. Some damage, such as injury to inner-ear hair cells from loud noise, can be permanent.

topics.name: Inner Ear Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: The inner ear turns sound into signals for hearing and senses head movement to help maintain balance and posture. Damage to its sensory hair cells, especially from loud noise, can cause lasting hearing loss and tinnitus.

topics.name: Insect Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Most insect stings cause temporary pain, redness, and swelling. In people sensitized to the venom, a sting can cause life-threatening anaphylaxis. Many stings can also cause severe toxic effects, even without an allergy; breathing or circulation problems need emergency care.

topics.name: Insomnia and Excessive Daytime Sleepiness (EDS)
topics.clinical_significance: Insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness can result from sleep disorders, medical or mental health conditions, medicines, or substance use. Excessive daytime sleepiness is a symptom, not a disorder. Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it.

topics.name: Insulin Resistance Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Insulin resistance syndrome is another name for metabolic syndrome: a cluster of excess abdominal fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar or insulin resistance, and abnormal blood fats. It is linked to higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so finding and treating each risk factor matters.

topics.name: Insulinoma
topics.clinical_significance: An insulinoma is a rare insulin-producing tumor in the pancreas. It usually causes low blood sugar during fasting, which can lead to sweating, shaking, confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness; symptoms improve after eating. Most insulinomas are noncancerous and can often be removed with surgery.

topics.name: Integrative, Complementary, and Alternative Medicine
topics.clinical_significance: Complementary care is used with standard treatment; alternative care is used instead; integrative care combines appropriate approaches. Evidence and safety vary among therapies. Supplements may interact with medicines or be contaminated, and replacing proven treatment for serious illness can be dangerous. Telling clinicians about these therapies helps them check for risks and interactions.

topics.name: Integrative, Complementary, and Alternative Medicine, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The benefits and safety of these therapies must be judged one by one: some have evidence for specific uses, while others have uncertain benefit or can cause harm. Supplements may interact with medicines or be contaminated, and replacing proven treatment for a serious illness can be dangerous. Patients should tell their clinicians about all therapies they use.

topics.name: Intellectual Disability
topics.clinical_significance: Intellectual disability begins during childhood and affects both learning and reasoning and everyday skills such as communication, self-care, and making choices. The level of support needed varies. Early assessment and tailored education and support can help build skills and independence.

topics.name: Interdigital Neuralgia
topics.clinical_significance: Interdigital neuralgia (Morton neuroma) is benign thickening of a nerve near the ball of the foot, usually from repeated irritation. It causes pain, burning, tingling, or a pebble-like feeling, often worse in tight shoes. Despite the name, it is not a tumor.

topics.name: Interdigital Neuroma
topics.clinical_significance: Interdigital neuroma (Morton neuroma) is noncancerous thickening of a nerve near the ball of the foot, often caused by repeated pressure from tight shoes. It can cause pain, burning, tingling, or a pebble-like feeling, especially when walking in narrow footwear.

topics.name: Intermediate Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Intermediate syndrome is an older name for unstable angina, a form of acute coronary syndrome. It causes new, worsening, or resting chest discomfort because blood flow to the heart is reduced, but there is no evidence of heart-muscle death. It can progress to a heart attack and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Intermittent Hemodialysis
topics.clinical_significance: Intermittent hemodialysis filters waste and extra fluid from the blood and helps correct electrolyte problems when the kidneys cannot do so adequately. It is given in repeated sessions and can sustain life while a person awaits a kidney transplant. Low blood pressure during treatment and infection or clotting of the blood-vessel access are important risks.

topics.name: Internal Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Derangement
topics.clinical_significance: Internal TMJ derangement occurs when the cartilage disc in the jaw joint moves out of its normal position. It may cause clicking or pain when chewing; if the disc stays displaced, the jaw may become painful and difficult to open. Treatment often starts with pain relief, jaw rest, and other nonsurgical care.

topics.name: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia
topics.clinical_significance: This brainstem pathway disorder prevents one eye from moving inward during side-to-side gaze, although it may still move inward when focusing on a near object. It can cause double vision and jerky movement of the other eye. Multiple sclerosis is a common cause in young people; stroke is common in older adults.

topics.name: Interstitial Cystitis
topics.clinical_significance: Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome) is noninfectious bladder inflammation that causes bladder or pelvic pain with urinary urgency or frequency. Symptoms often worsen as the bladder fills and ease after urinating. Diagnosis requires ruling out other causes, such as infection. Treatment can improve symptoms, but cure is uncommon.

topics.name: Interstitial Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Interstitial keratitis is chronic inflammation of the middle layer of the cornea, usually caused by infection. It can cause eye pain, tearing, sensitivity to light, and blurred vision; corneal clouding may leave lasting vision impairment. The cause needs to be identified so treatment can be directed appropriately.

topics.name: Interstitial Lung Disease, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Interstitial lung diseases are a varied group of conditions that affect the tissue around the lung air sacs and may spread to other parts of the lungs. Some cause progressive scarring (pulmonary fibrosis), which can reduce lung function. Causes include autoimmune disease, workplace or environmental exposures, medicines, and unknown factors, so identifying the cause helps guide care.

topics.name: Interstitial Lung Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Interstitial lung diseases are a broad group of conditions that inflame or scar lung tissue and may spread to other parts of the lungs. Scarring can make breathing harder and reduce lung function. Causes include autoimmune disease, workplace or environmental exposures, medicines, and unknown factors; the specific cause helps guide care.

topics.name: Intertrigo
topics.clinical_significance: Intertrigo is irritation and breakdown of skin where skin folds rub and trap moisture, causing a red, sore rash. Yeast or bacteria may infect the area. It is more common with high body weight, diabetes, or difficulty keeping skin folds clean and dry. Treatment focuses on drying the area and treating infection if present.

topics.name: Intertrochanteric Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: An intertrochanteric fracture is a break in the upper femur between its bony prominences. It often follows a low-impact fall in an older adult with osteoporosis and causes hip or groin pain and difficulty walking. It is usually repaired surgically so the person can move sooner and avoid complications of prolonged bed rest.

topics.name: Interventions With the Older Driver
topics.clinical_significance: When health or functional changes may make driving unsafe for an older adult, clinicians can address treatable problems and refer for a driving assessment, rehabilitation, or adaptive equipment. If driving remains unsafe, planning to limit or stop driving and arranging other transportation helps protect safety while reducing isolation and loss of independence.

topics.name: Intestinal Duplication
topics.clinical_significance: An intestinal duplication is a rare birth defect in which an extra tube or cyst is attached to the intestine and shares its blood supply. It may cause no symptoms or lead to blockage, pain, vomiting, bleeding, or rarely perforation. Some children also have other birth defects; symptomatic duplications are usually removed surgically.

topics.name: Intestinal Fluke Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Intestinal fluke infection is usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater or brackish-water fish containing the parasite. Many infections cause no symptoms, but heavy infection can cause abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, weight loss, or poor nutrient absorption. Rarely, parasite eggs can spread beyond the intestine.

topics.name: Intestinal Lipodystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Intestinal lipodystrophy is another name for Whipple disease, a rare bacterial illness that can affect many organs. It often causes joint pain first, followed by diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss from poor nutrient absorption. Without treatment it can be fatal, but long-term antibiotics usually help; relapse can occur.

topics.name: Intestinal Lymphangiectasia
topics.clinical_significance: Intestinal lymphangiectasia is a rare problem in the lymph vessels of the small intestine. It causes loss of protein and fat into the bowel, which can lead to low blood protein, swelling, diarrhea, and fatty stools; children may grow poorly. Treatment supports nutrition, often with a high-protein, low-fat diet and medium-chain fats.

topics.name: Intestinal Obstruction
topics.clinical_significance: A partial or complete blockage that stops intestinal contents from moving normally. Adhesions, hernias, and tumors are common causes; symptoms include cramping abdominal pain, swelling, and vomiting, and a complete blockage usually prevents passing stool or gas. This is an emergency because dehydration or loss of blood flow can damage the bowel or cause it to perforate.

topics.name: Intestinal Protozoa and Microsporidia
topics.clinical_significance: These intestinal parasite infections are usually spread through food or water contaminated with stool and can cause diarrhea and other digestive symptoms. They are more common where sanitation is poor, and some can become severe or prolonged in people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Intestinal Protozoan and Microsporidia Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: These infections are caused by several microscopic parasites and related microsporidia. They spread mainly through food or water contaminated with stool and can cause diarrhea and other gut illness; disease may be severe in people with weakened immune systems. Stool tests help identify the cause because symptoms alone are not enough to diagnose it.

topics.name: Intimacy and Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Intimacy, including sexual activity, can remain important and healthy in later life; age alone is not a reason to avoid it. Illness, pain, medicines, or lack of privacy may affect intimacy, and cognitive impairment can affect comfort and the ability to consent. Older adults with new partners still need protection from sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Intimate Partner Violence
topics.clinical_significance: Intimate partner violence includes physical, sexual, and emotional or psychological abuse by a current or former partner; it may also involve control or stalking. It can cause injury, sexual or reproductive health problems, and lasting mental distress, and may be fatal. Recognizing abuse and supporting patient safety are key clinical priorities.

topics.name: Intimate Partner Violence and Sexual Assault
topics.clinical_significance: Intimate partner violence and sexual assault can cause physical injury, sexually transmitted infections, unintended pregnancy, and lasting psychological distress; intimate partner violence can be fatal. Care includes treating injuries, assessing safety, and offering respectful support and follow-up for physical and mental health needs.

topics.name: Intra-Abdominal Abscesses
topics.clinical_significance: An intra-abdominal abscess is a pocket of infection in the abdomen, often after bowel perforation, abdominal infection, surgery, or injury. It can cause fever and abdominal pain, though symptoms may be mild or unclear. The infection can spread and cause sepsis; treatment usually requires drainage plus antibiotics.

topics.name: Intraamniotic Infection
topics.clinical_significance: An infection of the amniotic membranes, fluid, placenta, or fetus, usually during labor. It often causes maternal fever and may cause uterine tenderness or a fast maternal or fetal heartbeat. It raises the risk of preterm birth, newborn infection, and maternal complications, so suspected cases need prompt antibiotics and obstetric care.

topics.name: Intracerebral Hemorrhage
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding into brain tissue, most often when long-standing high blood pressure weakens and ruptures a small artery. It can cause sudden weakness or other neurologic problems, headache, vomiting, seizures, or reduced consciousness; headache may be mild or absent. This life-threatening type of stroke needs immediate hospital care.

topics.name: Intracranial Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: An intracranial aneurysm is a weak, bulging area in a brain artery. Many cause no symptoms, but a growing aneurysm can press on nearby nerves. If it ruptures, it can cause sudden, severe headache and bleeding around the brain, with loss of consciousness or seizures; rupture is an emergency and can be fatal.

topics.name: Intracranial Epidural Abscess and Subdural Empyema
topics.clinical_significance: These are pockets of pus inside the skull: an epidural abscess lies between the skull and dura, while a subdural empyema lies between the dura and arachnoid. They often follow a sinus or ear infection and can cause fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, or rapidly worsening neurologic problems. Without emergency drainage and antibiotics, they can quickly lead to coma or death.

topics.name: Intracranial Tumors, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Tumors inside the skull may start in the brain or spread there from another cancer; metastases are more common than primary brain tumors. Even noncancerous tumors can press on brain tissue and cause seizures, weakness, changes in thinking or behavior, headache, or increased pressure. Symptoms depend on tumor location, so new or worsening neurologic symptoms need medical assessment.

topics.name: Intracranial Venous Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Intracranial venous hypertension is an older name for idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised pressure around the brain without a mass or hydrocephalus. It often causes daily headache and swelling of the optic nerves; brief vision dimming or double vision may occur. If untreated, it can cause permanent vision loss.

topics.name: Intraepidermal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: A noninvasive form of squamous cell skin cancer, also called Bowen disease, that is limited to the outer skin layer. It often appears as a persistent red, scaly patch and can progress to invasive cancer, so biopsy and treatment are important.

topics.name: Intrapartum Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Problems arising during labor and delivery can threaten the pregnant patient or baby and need prompt recognition and treatment. Depending on the problem, care may include urgent operative delivery, fluids or blood, and preparation for newborn resuscitation. Anticipating risks and involving obstetric and neonatal teams can reduce harm.

topics.name: Intrapartum Complications, Introduction to
topics.clinical_significance: Complications during labor or delivery can put the pregnant patient or baby at risk. Recognizing risk factors and problems early allows preparation and treatment, which may include urgent vaginal or cesarean delivery, fluids or blood for the mother, and newborn resuscitation when needed.

topics.name: Intrauterine Device (IUDs; IUD)
topics.clinical_significance: An intrauterine device (IUD) is a highly effective, long-acting, reversible contraceptive placed in the uterus. Hormonal IUDs often reduce menstrual bleeding, while copper IUDs may increase bleeding and cramps. Rare risks include expulsion or uterine perforation; IUDs do not prevent sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Intrauterine Growth Restriction
topics.clinical_significance: A fetus that has not reached its growth potential, often identified by an estimated weight or abdominal size below the 10th percentile for gestational age. Some small fetuses are healthy and naturally small, but placental, maternal, fetal, or genetic problems can restrict growth. Growth restriction raises the risks of stillbirth and newborn problems such as low blood sugar, low body temperature, and oxygen deprivation, so close pregnancy monitoring is needed.

topics.name: Intravenous Fluid Management
topics.clinical_significance: IV fluid management means choosing the type and amount of fluid and monitoring the patient response. It can restore circulation in dehydration or some forms of shock, but too much fluid can harm the lungs and other tissues. Careful reassessment is essential.

topics.name: Intravenous Fluid Resuscitation
topics.clinical_significance: IV fluid resuscitation rapidly replaces circulating volume to improve blood flow to tissues in hypovolemic or distributive shock and severe dehydration. The fluid and rate must match the cause and be reassessed, because excess fluid can cause lung swelling and fluids are usually avoided in cardiogenic or obstructive shock. Severe blood loss may require blood products.

topics.name: Intravenous Fluid Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Intravenous fluid therapy gives fluids through a vein to treat severe dehydration or restore circulation in hypovolemic and some distributive shock. Clinicians choose and adjust the fluid based on the cause and response; too much or too rapid fluid can cause lung swelling, and major bleeding may require blood products.

topics.name: Intravenous Vitamin Therapy (Myers' Cocktail)
topics.clinical_significance: Myers cocktail is a high-dose IV mix of vitamins and minerals promoted for energy, immunity, and other health benefits. Evidence has not shown that it provides these benefits or treats disease in people without deficiencies. Risks include abnormal heart rhythms, low blood pressure, drug interactions, and serious infection if sterile technique is poor.

topics.name: Introduction to Bone Modeling Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Bone modeling disorders affect how bones form, grow, or take shape, often through problems in the growth plates or genetic conditions. Children may have short or uneven growth, unusual bone shape, and bone or joint pain; these are not mainly disorders of low bone density. Effects and treatment depend on the specific disorder.

topics.name: Introduction to Extraintestinal Protozoa
topics.clinical_significance: Extraintestinal protozoa are parasites that can infect organs beyond the gut, including the liver, lungs, brain, and skin. They spread by different routes, sometimes through insect bites, and can cause severe disease, especially in people with weakened immune systems. Knowing the exposure and organs affected helps guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Introduction to Metabolic Bone Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders impair mineralization of growing bones, often because calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, or parathyroid hormone balance is abnormal. In children, they can cause bone pain, fractures, poor growth, and rickets. Finding and treating the underlying mineral problem is important.

topics.name: Intubation, Drugs to Aid
topics.clinical_significance: For an awake patient, a sedative (and sometimes pain medicine) is given before a muscle relaxant to make emergency tube placement easier and less distressing. Drug choice matters: sedatives may lower blood pressure, and some muscle relaxants can cause dangerously high blood potassium or other serious reactions in certain patients. Sedation and pain relief are also needed after intubation.

topics.name: Intubation, Tracheal
topics.clinical_significance: Tracheal intubation places a tube through the mouth or nose into the windpipe to keep the airway open and allow ventilation when a person cannot breathe adequately or protect the airway. It can be lifesaving but may cause injury, oxygen loss, or aspiration; a tube placed in the esophagus can be fatal if missed. Correct placement must be confirmed and rechecked.

topics.name: Intussusception
topics.clinical_significance: One part of the intestine slides into the next, blocking the bowel and sometimes cutting off its blood supply. It most often affects infants and young children and can cause waves of severe abdominal pain and vomiting; bloody stool is a late sign and may not appear. It needs urgent care: ultrasound is used to diagnose it, and an air enema often treats it; surgery may be needed if the enema fails or the bowel is damaged.

topics.name: Involuntary Weight Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Unintentional loss of more than 5% of body weight or 5 kg over 6 months warrants evaluation. It can be a sign of cancer, infection, hormone problems, medication effects, depression, or poor nutrient absorption. Finding the cause matters because ongoing weight loss can lead to undernutrition and is linked to a higher risk of death.

topics.name: Iodine Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Iodine deficiency limits thyroid hormone production. Mild to moderate deficiency can enlarge the thyroid (goiter); severe deficiency can cause hypothyroidism. During pregnancy, severe deficiency can impair fetal growth and brain development and raise the risks of miscarriage, stillbirth, and infant death.

topics.name: Iodine Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term high iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function. It may trigger hyperthyroidism, especially in people who were iodine-deficient, or suppress thyroid hormone production and cause goiter or hypothyroidism. Very large amounts can irritate the mouth and gut; repeated exposure to iodine-containing contrast dye or amiodarone may require thyroid monitoring.

topics.name: IPEX Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: IPEX is a rare inherited immune disorder that usually affects boys in infancy. It can cause severe autoimmunity, including type 1 diabetes, persistent diarrhea with poor growth, eczema, and food allergies. Without treatment, it is often fatal in the first year of life; early diagnosis matters because stem cell transplantation can help.

topics.name: Iron Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Iron deficiency limits the body’s ability to make hemoglobin and can progress to anemia. It may cause tiredness, pica (craving nonfood items), spoon-shaped nails, or restless legs. Finding the cause matters: deficiency may result from low intake or poor absorption, but it can also signal ongoing blood loss, including bleeding from bowel cancer in middle-aged and older adults.

topics.name: Iron Deficiency Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: A common anemia caused by too little iron to make healthy red blood cells. It can cause tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath, and pale skin. Blood loss is the usual cause, so the source should be found; in men and postmenopausal women, hidden bleeding from the digestive tract, including cancer, must be considered.

topics.name: Iron Overload
topics.clinical_significance: Excess iron can build up because of inherited hemochromatosis, excess iron intake or absorption, or repeated blood transfusions. When iron deposits damage tissues, it can affect the liver, heart, pancreas, and other hormone-producing organs, causing problems such as cirrhosis, heart disease, or diabetes.

topics.name: Iron Overload, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Iron overload occurs when excess iron builds up throughout the body, often from inherited hemochromatosis, repeated blood transfusions, or excess iron absorption or intake. Widespread buildup can damage the liver, heart, pancreas, and other hormone-producing organs; small, localized deposits usually do not cause tissue damage.

topics.name: Iron Overload, Secondary
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary iron overload is excess iron from repeated blood transfusions, excess absorption, or too much iron taken by mouth, often in people with blood disorders. Iron can build up in organs and cause liver disease, heart problems, diabetes, joint pain, or sexual problems. Treatment to remove excess iron can prevent or delay organ damage.

topics.name: Iron Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Swallowing a large amount of iron, often from supplement tablets, can cause life-threatening poisoning, especially in children. It may begin with severe vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, then seem to improve before worsening to shock and liver failure. Urgent medical care is needed.

topics.name: Iron Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Too much iron can build up from excessive or prolonged supplements, repeated blood transfusions, alcohol-related liver disease, or inherited hemochromatosis. An acute overdose can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and damage to the gut and other organs; long-term buildup can also injure organs. Prompt evaluation is important.

topics.name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)
topics.clinical_significance: IBS causes recurring abdominal pain linked to bowel movements and changes in stool frequency or form. It may cause constipation, diarrhea, or both, often with bloating. Blood in the stool, weight loss, anemia, or diarrhea at night should be checked because they may signal another condition.

topics.name: Irritant Gas Inhalation Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing an irritant gas can inflame and injure the airways and lungs, causing cough, wheezing, or shortness of breath. Severe exposure can cause airway swelling, fluid in the lungs, or life-threatening respiratory failure. Some gases cause delayed lung injury, and lasting airway problems can follow; risk depends on the gas and how much and how long a person inhales it.

topics.name: Isaacs Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Isaacs syndrome is a rare peripheral nerve disorder that keeps muscles active, causing continuous twitching, cramps, stiffness, difficulty relaxing muscles, and sometimes excessive sweating. It is often autoimmune but can also be inherited or occur with other conditions, including thymoma, so evaluation for an associated disorder may be needed.

topics.name: Ischemic Cholangiopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Reduced blood flow from the hepatic artery damages the bile ducts, most often after liver transplantation. The injury can block bile flow and cause itching, dark urine, pale stools, bile duct infection, or multiple narrowings of the ducts; severe cases may require treatment for rejection or another transplant.

topics.name: Ischemic Colitis
topics.clinical_significance: A temporary drop in blood flow to the colon causes lower-left abdominal pain, often followed by rectal bleeding. It mainly affects older adults and often improves with supportive care, but severe injury can cause bowel tissue death and may require surgery.

topics.name: Ischemic Hepatitis
topics.clinical_significance: A sudden shortage of blood or oxygen damages liver cells, often during heart failure, very low blood pressure, respiratory failure, or sepsis. Liver enzyme levels can rise sharply; nausea, vomiting, or a tender enlarged liver may occur. Most people recover when blood flow is restored, but liver failure can develop, especially in people with cirrhosis.

topics.name: Ischemic Myelopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Ischemic myelopathy (spinal cord infarction) is sudden damage to the spinal cord from reduced blood flow. It often causes severe back pain followed within minutes by rapidly worsening weakness and loss of sensation on both sides, especially for pain and temperature. It is an emergency; MRI is used to confirm it, and treatment is mainly supportive while the cause is addressed.

topics.name: Ischemic Necrosis of Bone
topics.clinical_significance: Ischemic necrosis of bone (osteonecrosis) is death of bone tissue when its blood supply is reduced. It often affects the hip, knee, or shoulder and can cause pain and limited movement. If bone near a joint collapses, arthritis and loss of function can follow; early diagnosis may allow treatment that helps preserve the joint.

topics.name: Ischemic Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Reduced blood flow damages the optic nerve and causes sudden, painless vision loss, usually in one eye. The arteritic form, often due to giant cell arteritis, can threaten sight in the other eye and needs urgent treatment; treatment may protect that eye but usually cannot restore vision already lost. The nonarteritic form has no established treatment.

topics.name: Ischemic Stroke
topics.clinical_significance: A blocked artery cuts blood flow to part of the brain, causing sudden neurologic problems and permanent brain injury. Signs can include face or limb weakness, trouble speaking or seeing, poor balance, or confusion. These symptoms need emergency assessment, even if they improve, because treatment works best when started quickly.

topics.name: Isolated Elevated High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (HDL-C) Levels
topics.clinical_significance: An isolated HDL-C level above 80 mg/dL usually relates to lower cardiovascular risk, but very high HDL is not always protective, especially when caused by certain genetic or metabolic conditions. An unexpected high result may be linked to alcohol use, an overactive thyroid, primary biliary cholangitis, or some medicines, so the cause may need evaluation.

topics.name: Isolated Olecranon Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A break in the bony tip of the elbow, usually from a fall or direct blow. It causes pain and swelling and can make it hard to straighten the elbow; the nearby ulnar nerve can also be injured. Displaced or fragmented fractures often need surgery, and open fractures need urgent antibiotics and orthopedic care.

topics.name: Isolated Progressive Cardiac Conduction Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A usually inherited problem in the heart’s electrical system that worsens over time, even when the heart has no structural disease. It can slow or block heartbeats and raise the risk of sudden death; a pacemaker may be needed.

topics.name: Itching
topics.clinical_significance: Itching (pruritus) is an uncomfortable skin sensation that creates the urge to scratch. It can occur with or without a rash and may come from a skin condition, medicine, or illness such as liver or kidney disease. Repeated scratching can damage the skin and lead to infection.

topics.name: Jail Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Jail fever (epidemic typhus) is a serious infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and spread mainly by body lice. It causes prolonged high fever, severe headache, and a rash; severe illness can lead to shock, kidney problems, brain involvement, or death. Prompt doxycycline treatment is important.

topics.name: Jaundice
topics.clinical_significance: Jaundice is yellowing of the skin, whites of the eyes, or mouth lining caused by high bilirubin in the blood. It is a sign of an underlying problem, such as increased breakdown of red blood cells, liver damage, or blocked bile flow, and needs evaluation to find the cause. Fever with right upper abdominal pain, confusion, or bleeding can signal a serious complication.

topics.name: Jaundice in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Yellowing of a newborn’s skin and eyes from high bilirubin. It is common and often harmless, but very high or rapidly rising bilirubin can enter the brain and cause lasting injury. Risk depends on the baby’s age in hours, prematurity, and health; jaundice in the first 24 hours or lasting more than 2 weeks needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Jaw Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Jaw tumors may be benign or cancerous. They can cause swelling, pain, tenderness, or unexplained loose teeth, though some are found on dental X-rays. Evaluation is needed to identify the tumor; treatment ranges from observation to surgery, sometimes with reconstruction.

topics.name: Jejunoileal Atresia
topics.clinical_significance: Jejunoileal atresia is incomplete formation of part of the small intestine, causing a blockage in a newborn. It usually leads to abdominal swelling, vomiting, feeding problems, and failure to pass stool in the first day or two of life. Surgery is needed; short bowel problems and associated conditions such as cystic fibrosis may also need attention.

topics.name: Jersey Finger
topics.clinical_significance: Jersey finger is a tear of the tendon that bends the fingertip, usually when a bent finger is pulled straight during contact sports. The person cannot actively bend the fingertip joint. Prompt assessment by a hand specialist is important because the injury usually needs surgical repair; an X-ray checks for a broken bone fragment.

topics.name: Jikoshu-kyofu
topics.clinical_significance: Jikoshu-kyofu (olfactory reference disorder) is a persistent, distressing belief that one gives off an offensive body odor that other people do not notice or find only slight. It can lead to repeated washing or checking, attempts to hide the odor, and avoidance of social or work activities. Treatment may include cognitive-behavioral therapy and medicines such as SSRIs or clomipramine.

topics.name: Joint Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Joint disorders affect the joints or nearby tissues and may cause pain, swelling, warmth, stiffness, or limited movement. Causes include injury, wear, inflammation, crystal buildup, and infection, so treatment depends on the cause. A suddenly painful, hot, swollen joint needs prompt assessment because infection can damage the joint.

topics.name: Joint Pain, Multiple
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in several joints may occur without inflammation or with arthritis, which often causes warmth and swelling. Causes include infections, crystal deposits, osteoarthritis, and systemic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis; the pattern and timing help narrow the cause. A hot, swollen joint with fever needs prompt assessment because infection can damage the joint.

topics.name: Joint Pain, Single
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in or around one joint can come from injury, arthritis, infection, or nearby tendons or bursae. A hot, swollen joint, especially with fever, needs urgent assessment because infection can quickly damage the joint and spread to the blood.

topics.name: Joint Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Joint involvement by tumors is rare and often results from direct spread from nearby bone or soft tissue. Some benign growths of the joint lining cause pain, fluid buildup, and damage to cartilage or bone, and may recur. Despite its name, synovial sarcoma usually arises in soft tissue rather than the joint lining.

topics.name: Jones Fracture
topics.clinical_significance: A Jones fracture is a break in the shaft of the fifth metatarsal near its base. Its limited blood supply raises the risk of slow healing or failure to heal. It differs from a more common fracture at the bone’s base, called a pseudo-Jones fracture.

topics.name: Jumper’s Knee
topics.clinical_significance: This overuse injury affects the patellar tendon where it attaches below the kneecap, often in active children. It causes localized pain that worsens with jumping, stairs, or forceful knee straightening; repeated pulling can injure the tendon attachment.

topics.name: Juvenile Angiofibromas
topics.clinical_significance: This rare, noncancerous but highly vascular tumor grows in the back of the nose, usually in adolescent boys. It can cause nasal blockage and sometimes heavy nosebleeds, spread into the eye sockets or skull, and recur. Biopsy can cause severe bleeding.

topics.name: Juvenile Xanthogranuloma
topics.clinical_significance: This usually affects only the skin, causing one or more bumps that may disappear on their own. Rarely, it involves organs such as the liver, lungs, or bone marrow. It is also rarely associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 or juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia.

topics.name: Kaposi Sarcoma
topics.clinical_significance: This vascular cancer is caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Weakened immunity, especially from advanced HIV or organ transplantation, greatly raises its risk. It causes purple, red, or brown lesions on the skin or mouth and can affect lymph nodes, the gut, or lungs; gut lesions may bleed.

topics.name: Kaposi's Sarcoma
topics.clinical_significance: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular cancer caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Weakened immunity, especially advanced HIV or after an organ transplant, raises the risk; the HIV-associated form is often more aggressive. It causes purple, red, or brown lesions on the skin or mucous membranes and can affect lymph nodes or organs such as the gut and lungs.

topics.name: Kava
topics.clinical_significance: Kava is a South Pacific plant root used in products for anxiety and sleep. It can cause drowsiness, prolong the effects of sedatives, and interfere with some Parkinson medicines. It has also been linked to serious liver injury, including liver failure.

topics.name: Kawasaki Disease
