topics.clinical_significance: Kawasaki disease is a childhood vasculitis that usually causes prolonged fever, rash, red eyes, mouth changes, swollen hands or feet, and enlarged neck lymph nodes. It is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children because coronary artery aneurysms can form and lead to blood clots or heart attack. Incomplete cases also occur.

topics.name: Kawasaki's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Also called Kawasaki disease, this childhood vasculitis may affect the coronary arteries and lead to aneurysms, blood clots, or heart attack. Prolonged fever, rash, red eyes, mouth changes, and swollen lymph nodes are common, though incomplete cases occur.

topics.name: Keloids
topics.clinical_significance: Keloids are raised scars that grow beyond the edges of the original wound, unlike hypertrophic scars. They can itch or hurt, and large scars may limit movement or cause major cosmetic effects. They often recur after treatment.

topics.name: Keratitis Sicca
topics.clinical_significance: Keratitis sicca (dry eye disease) is chronic drying of the eye surface due to too little tear production or rapid tear evaporation. It can cause burning, irritation, a gritty feeling, light sensitivity, and fluctuating blurred vision. Severe, long-lasting disease can damage the cornea and rarely impair vision.

topics.name: Keratoacanthoma
topics.clinical_significance: A rapidly growing, dome-shaped skin nodule with a central plug of keratin, usually on sun-exposed skin. It may shrink on its own, but it can be hard to distinguish from squamous cell carcinoma, and some lesions are considered a form of that cancer. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy or removal of the lesion.

topics.name: Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca
topics.clinical_significance: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is chronic dryness of both the conjunctiva and cornea because the tear film is inadequate, either from low tear production or rapid evaporation. It can cause burning, gritty irritation, light sensitivity, and fluctuating blurred vision. Severe, long-term disease can damage the cornea and rarely impair vision.

topics.name: Keratoconus
topics.clinical_significance: Keratoconus makes the cornea thin and bulge into a cone, usually in both eyes but often unevenly. This causes irregular astigmatism and blurred or distorted vision that glasses may not fully correct. Progression can scar the cornea and greatly reduce sight; corneal collagen cross-linking can slow it.

topics.name: Keratomalacia
topics.clinical_significance: This severe eye complication of vitamin A deficiency often occurs with protein-calorie undernutrition. The cornea becomes dry and cloudy and may ulcerate and become infected, risking permanent vision loss. Night blindness and foamy Bitot spots on the conjunctiva may also occur.

topics.name: Keratosis Pilaris
topics.clinical_significance: Keratosis pilaris occurs when keratin plugs hair follicles, causing small, rough, sometimes red bumps, usually on the upper arms, thighs, or buttocks. It is mainly a cosmetic condition but may itch.

topics.name: Kernicterus
topics.clinical_significance: Kernicterus (chronic bilirubin encephalopathy) is lasting brain injury from unconjugated bilirubin collecting in the newborn brain, usually during severe jaundice. It can cause a movement disorder, hearing loss, intellectual disability, and difficulty looking upward.

topics.name: Ketamine and Phencyclidine
topics.clinical_significance: Ketamine and phencyclidine (PCP) are dissociative drugs that can cause detachment, confusion, hallucinations, and unpredictable behavior, increasing the risk of injury. Severe poisoning can cause dangerously high body temperature or blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, seizures, or coma; ketamine can also cause laryngospasm. Repeated ketamine use may impair memory and cause urinary symptoms.

topics.name: Khat
topics.clinical_significance: Khat is a shrub whose leaves contain cathinone, an amphetamine-like stimulant. Chewing the leaves can cause euphoria and increased alertness, but also raise blood pressure and heart rate and disrupt sleep. Synthetic cathinones derived from it can cause severe poisoning, including agitation, overheating, seizures, or dangerous heart rhythms.

topics.name: Kidney Replacement Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney replacement therapy supports people with kidney failure by removing waste and excess fluid and balancing salts and acids in the blood. It includes dialysis and kidney transplantation and is sometimes used for certain poisonings. It replaces the kidneys’ filtering work but not their hormone production.

topics.name: Kidney Replacement Therapy, Long-Term, Medical Aspects
topics.clinical_significance: People on long-term kidney replacement therapy often still develop anemia, heart and blood-vessel disease, poor nutrition, and mineral and bone problems. Phosphate and calcium imbalances can cause blood-vessel calcification and weak bones. A rare complication, calciphylaxis, causes painful skin and tissue damage and can be fatal.

topics.name: Kidney Replacement Therapy, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney replacement therapy uses dialysis or a kidney transplant to take over some kidney functions in kidney failure. Dialysis removes waste and extra fluid and balances blood salts and acids, but does not restore kidney hormone production. It is also used for some poisonings.

topics.name: Kidney Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: A transplant provides a donor kidney for end-stage kidney failure and often frees the recipient from dialysis. Lifelong medicines are needed to prevent rejection; they increase the risk of infection and some cancers. Rejection or other damage can eventually cause the transplanted kidney to fail.

topics.name: Kienböck Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Kienböck disease is loss of blood supply to the lunate, a small wrist bone, causing bone damage (avascular necrosis). It causes gradually worsening wrist pain and tenderness. The lunate may collapse, leading to wrist-joint arthritis and reduced movement.

topics.name: Kienböck's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Kienböck’s disease is loss of blood supply to the lunate, a small wrist bone, causing bone damage (avascular necrosis). It causes gradually worsening wrist pain and tenderness. The lunate may collapse, leading to wrist-joint arthritis and reduced movement.

topics.name: Kingella Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Kingella, especially K. kingae, can spread from the throat into the blood and cause invasive infection. It is an important cause of septic arthritis and bone infection in children 6 months to 4 years old. It can also cause bloodstream infection or endocarditis.

topics.name: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Serratia Infections
topics.clinical_significance: These intestinal bacteria rarely cause illness in healthy people but can cause hospital-acquired infections, especially in people with serious illness or catheters and other devices. They can cause pneumonia, urinary infections, and bloodstream or surgical-site infections that may progress to sepsis. Klebsiella can also cause severe pneumonia or liver abscess, and some strains resist multiple antibiotics.

topics.name: Klinefelter Syndrome (47,XXY)
topics.clinical_significance: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome condition in males, usually 47,XXY. Features vary, but small testes, low testosterone, and reduced fertility are common. Some have speech or learning difficulties; diabetes, thyroid disease, and breast cancer are more common.

topics.name: Klinefelter's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex-chromosome condition in males, usually 47,XXY. Features vary, but small testes, low testosterone, and reduced fertility are common. Some have speech or learning difficulties; diabetes, thyroid disease, and breast cancer are more common.

topics.name: Knee Extensor Mechanism Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: These injuries can damage the quadriceps tendon, patella, patellar tendon, or tibial tubercle. Complete tendon tears and transverse patellar fractures can interrupt the knee’s straightening mechanism, making it impossible to straighten the leg or raise it straight. Pain and swelling are common, and lasting stiffness or weakness may occur.

topics.name: Knee Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Knee pain may come from injury or overuse of the kneecap, tendons, ligaments, meniscus, or bone. Arthritis and pain referred from the hip, back, or foot can also be causes. Locking or catching may signal damage inside the joint; a knee that gives way may reflect ligament injury or kneecap instability.

topics.name: Knee Sprains and Meniscal Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Knee trauma can stretch or tear the collateral or cruciate ligaments, or tear a meniscus, the knee’s shock-absorbing cartilage. These injuries cause pain and swelling. Severe ligament tears can make the knee unstable, while some meniscal tears cause locking.

topics.name: Knee (Tibiofemoral) Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: A tibiofemoral dislocation usually tears several ligaments and can injure the popliteal artery or nerves. Artery damage may be hidden or persist after the joint returns to place, cutting off blood flow and threatening the limb. Nerve injury can cause weakness or foot drop.

topics.name: Korsakoff Amnestic Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Korsakoff amnestic syndrome is a chronic brain disorder that may follow Wernicke encephalopathy, often in severe alcohol use disorder. It causes severe difficulty forming new memories, loss of some past memories, confusion, and sometimes confabulation—unconsciously making up accounts to fill memory gaps.

topics.name: Korsakoff Psychosis
topics.clinical_significance: Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic brain disorder that may follow Wernicke encephalopathy, often in severe alcohol use disorder. It causes severe difficulty forming new memories, loss of some past memories, confusion, and sometimes confabulation—unconsciously making up accounts to fill memory gaps.

topics.name: Krabbe Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Krabbe disease is a rare inherited metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of an enzyme needed to maintain myelin, the protective covering of nerves. It progressively damages the brain and nerves, causing loss of developmental skills, stiffness, weakness or paralysis, and loss of vision or hearing; severe early-onset disease can be fatal.

topics.name: Krabbe's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Krabbe's disease is a rare inherited metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of an enzyme needed to maintain myelin, the protective covering of nerves. It progressively damages the brain and nerves, causing loss of developmental skills, stiffness, weakness or paralysis, and loss of vision or hearing; severe early-onset disease can be fatal.

topics.name: Kuru
topics.clinical_significance: Kuru is a rare, fatal prion disease that damages the brain. Historically, it spread through ritual cannibalism in Papua New Guinea. It causes tremors and worsening difficulty with balance and coordination, followed by involuntary movements and dementia; death usually occurs within two years after symptoms begin.

topics.name: Köhler Bone Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Köhler bone disease is a rare childhood condition affecting the navicular bone in the foot, usually in children ages 3 to 5. It causes pain, tenderness, and swelling along the inner arch, often making walking painful or causing a limp. It usually resolves without lasting problems.

topics.name: Köhler's Bone Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Köhler's bone disease is a rare childhood condition affecting the navicular bone in the foot, usually in children ages 3 to 5. It causes pain, tenderness, and swelling along the inner arch, often making walking painful or causing a limp. It usually resolves without lasting problems.

topics.name: Labor and Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Labor is a series of uterine contractions that thin and open the cervix and lead to delivery of the baby and placenta. Monitoring labor helps identify problems with its progress or with the health of the pregnant person or baby that may require intervention.

topics.name: Labor and Delivery, Abnormalities and Complications of
topics.clinical_significance: Complications during labor and delivery can endanger the pregnant person or baby and may need urgent intervention. Examples include labor that stops progressing, abnormal fetal position, infection, umbilical cord prolapse, shoulder dystocia, uterine rupture, and severe bleeding after birth.

topics.name: Labor and Delivery, Normal
topics.clinical_significance: Normal labor begins on its own in a low-risk pregnancy and progresses through cervical opening, birth of the baby in a head-first position, and delivery of the placenta. The pregnant person and baby are in good condition after birth.

topics.name: Labor, Induction of
topics.clinical_significance: Induction of labor uses medicines or procedures to start uterine contractions before labor begins on its own, usually to achieve vaginal birth. It may be medically recommended when continuing the pregnancy poses greater risk to the pregnant person or baby; some inductions are elective.

topics.name: Labor, Management of Normal
topics.clinical_significance: Management of normal labor includes checking the pregnant person's health, the baby's heart rate and position, and the progress of cervical opening and delivery. This helps detect problems early and supports timely care if labor stops progressing or concerns arise.

topics.name: Labor, Protracted or Arrested
topics.clinical_significance: Protracted labor means that the cervix opens or the baby moves down unusually slowly; arrested labor means labor has stopped progressing. Causes can include weak contractions or difficulty moving the baby through the pelvis. Additional measures may be needed, including medicines to strengthen contractions or assisted or cesarean delivery.

topics.name: Laboratory Diagnosis of Infectious Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Laboratory tests help identify the organism causing an infection through microscopy, culture, antigen or antibody tests, or genetic tests. Identifying the organism can guide treatment; culture may also show which antimicrobial medicines are likely to work. Test choice depends on the suspected organism, and no single test detects every infection.

topics.name: Laboratory Reference Ranges
topics.clinical_significance: Laboratory reference ranges show the values found in most healthy people and help clinicians interpret test results. They vary with the laboratory method and factors such as age, sex, and pregnancy; a result outside the range does not by itself prove disease.

topics.name: Laboratory Tests of the Liver and Gallbladder
topics.clinical_significance: Blood tests such as ALT and AST can show liver-cell injury, while alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin can point to impaired bile flow. Albumin and clotting tests help assess the liver's ability to make important proteins. Patterns of results help narrow the cause, assess severity, and monitor disease, but must be interpreted with other clinical findings.

topics.name: Laboratory Values, Normal
topics.clinical_significance: Normal laboratory values are results within the reference range set by the laboratory for a healthy comparison group. Ranges vary by laboratory method and factors such as age, sex, and pregnancy; a value within range does not always rule out disease, and one outside range does not by itself prove it.

topics.name: Labyrinthitis, Purulent
topics.clinical_significance: Purulent labyrinthitis is a bacterial infection of the inner ear, often a complication of a severe middle-ear infection. It can cause severe vertigo, nausea, hearing loss up to deafness, and loss of balance.

topics.name: Lacerations and Abrasions
topics.clinical_significance: Lacerations are cuts or tears in tissue; abrasions are scrapes of the skin. Both can cause pain, bleeding, and infection, while deep lacerations may damage tendons, nerves, or blood vessels. Wound assessment and cleaning help reduce infection risk and identify injuries that need repair.

topics.name: Lactic Acidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Lactic acidosis is a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by excess lactate in the blood. It can result from poor tissue blood flow, certain medicines, seizures, or reduced lactate clearance in liver disease. When caused by shock or severe oxygen shortage, it may signal life-threatening illness.

topics.name: Lamin A/C Cardiomyopathies (Cardiolaminopathies)
topics.clinical_significance: Lamin A/C cardiomyopathies are inherited heart disorders caused by changes in the LMNA gene. They can weaken and enlarge the heart and cause heart block or dangerous abnormal rhythms, increasing the risk of heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Some forms also cause skeletal muscle weakness.

topics.name: Landouzy-Dejerine Muscular Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Landouzy-Dejerine muscular dystrophy, also called facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, is an inherited disorder that causes slowly progressive weakness, usually beginning in the face and shoulder muscles. It often becomes noticeable by adolescence and can make it hard to close the eyes, whistle, or raise the arms. Severity varies, and hearing or retinal problems may also occur.

topics.name: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a disorder in which abnormal dendritic immune cells build up in one or more organs. It often affects bone or skin, but can also involve the lungs, pituitary gland, liver, spleen, or bone marrow; symptoms depend on the organs affected. Disease involving the liver, spleen, or bone marrow carries a worse prognosis.

topics.name: Laparoscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Laparoscopy is a minimally invasive procedure that uses a camera passed through small incisions to examine the abdomen or pelvis. It can help diagnose abdominal or pelvic problems, stage cancer, take tissue samples, or perform surgery. Possible complications include bleeding, infection, or injury to an internal organ.

topics.name: Large-for-Gestational-Age (LGA) Infant
topics.clinical_significance: An infant is large for gestational age (LGA) when birth weight is above the 90th percentile for the length of pregnancy. This percentile-based term differs from macrosomia, which means a term birth weight over 4,000 g. Maternal diabetes is a major cause; large size increases the risk of difficult birth and injury, while newborns—especially those of mothers with diabetes—are at risk of low blood sugar.

topics.name: Laryngeal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Most laryngeal cancers are squamous cell cancers of the voice box; smoking and heavy alcohol use increase risk. Symptoms depend on the tumor's location and may include hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, ear pain, a neck lump, or airway blockage. Hoarseness often appears early when the vocal cords are involved.

topics.name: Laryngeal Contact Ulcers
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngeal contact ulcers are sores over the vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, often caused by repeated voice strain or irritation from intubation, chronic cough, or reflux. They can cause hoarseness, a lump-in-the-throat feeling, and discomfort when speaking or swallowing. They often recur, and prolonged ulcers can develop into granulomas.

topics.name: Laryngeal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngeal disorders affect the voice box, vocal folds, or airway opening. They can change the voice or interfere with breathing or swallowing. Causes include inflammation, vocal-fold injury or paralysis, growths, and cancer; laryngoscopy helps identify the specific problem.

topics.name: Laryngeal Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The larynx contains the vocal folds, which produce voice and open to let air pass into the windpipe; they close during swallowing. Disorders such as inflammation, growths, paralysis, or narrowing can cause hoarseness or other voice changes and may interfere with breathing or swallowing.

topics.name: Laryngeal Dystonia
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngeal dystonia (spasmodic dysphonia) is a movement disorder in which involuntary spasms of the vocal-fold muscles disrupt speech. Depending on the type, the voice may sound strained and squeezed or have sudden breathy breaks; symptoms often vary with particular speech sounds.

topics.name: Laryngeal Papillomas
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngeal papillomas are usually benign, HPV-caused growths and the most common presentation of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. They can cause hoarseness or a weak cry, often return after removal, and may block the airway if severe. Rarely, they spread to the lungs or become cancerous.

topics.name: Laryngeal Tumors, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Benign laryngeal tumors are noncancerous growths, such as papillomas, hemangiomas, and fibromas. Depending on their size and location, they can cause hoarseness or interfere with swallowing or breathing. Papillomas and neurofibromas can sometimes become cancerous, and vocal-fold leukoplakia may signal precancerous change.

topics.name: Laryngitis
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngitis is inflammation of the voice box, most often caused by a viral respiratory infection or voice overuse. It can cause hoarseness, reduced voice volume, or temporary voice loss; reflux, smoke, and other irritants can also cause or prolong it. Acute viral laryngitis usually resolves on its own, but severe swelling can rarely impair breathing.

topics.name: Laryngoceles
topics.clinical_significance: A laryngocele is an abnormal pouch formed when an air-containing sac in the larynx enlarges. It can cause hoarseness, cough, or a lump sensation; an internal laryngocele may narrow the airway, while an external one can form a neck lump. If it fills with infected mucus, it is called a laryngopyocele.

topics.name: Laryngotracheal Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Laryngotracheal stenosis is narrowing of the airway in the larynx or upper trachea. It may be present from birth or develop after airway injury, prolonged intubation, or disease. It can cause shortness of breath, noisy breathing (stridor), cough, or voice changes; severe narrowing can threaten breathing.

topics.name: Laryngotracheobronchitis
topics.clinical_significance: Croup is usually a viral infection that inflames the larynx, trachea, and bronchi and narrows the airway below the vocal cords. It mainly affects young children, causing a barking cough and hoarseness; noisy breathing (stridor) may occur, and severe cases can cause breathing distress.

topics.name: Lassa Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Lassa fever is a viral infection found mainly in West Africa. People usually acquire it from food contaminated by infected rodents’ urine, saliva, or droppings; it can also spread through infected people’s body fluids. Most infections are mild, but severe disease can affect several organs, cause bleeding or shock, and be fatal.

topics.name: Lateral Epicondylitis
topics.clinical_significance: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is an overuse injury of the forearm tendons where they attach to the outer elbow. It causes pain and tenderness that may spread down the forearm and often worsens when extending the wrist against resistance or gripping.

topics.name: Late-Term and Postterm Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Late-term pregnancy lasts 41 weeks 0 days through 41 weeks 6 days; postterm pregnancy lasts 42 weeks or longer. As pregnancy continues, risks such as low amniotic fluid, a large fetus, birth complications, and stillbirth increase, so fetal monitoring and planning delivery are important.

topics.name: Lead Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Lead poisoning may cause few early symptoms but can lead to lasting brain and nerve damage, especially in children. It can also damage the kidneys, cause anemia, and affect fertility. Blood testing detects lead exposure; treatment starts by removing the source, with chelation used for selected severe cases.

topics.name: Learning and Developmental Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These conditions begin early in life and can affect learning, attention, communication, social interaction, or everyday independence. They may make school and daily activities harder. Identifying a child’s strengths and needs helps guide teaching, therapy, and other support.

topics.name: Learning Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A learning disorder makes specific academic skills, such as reading, writing, or math, harder than expected for a person’s abilities. It may also affect language, attention, memory, or how information is processed, making schoolwork difficult. Identifying the specific needs helps guide teaching and other support.

topics.name: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is an inherited mitochondrial disorder that damages the optic nerves. It usually causes painless loss of central vision in one eye, followed weeks or months later by the other; vision loss may be permanent. Some people also have heart rhythm or neurologic problems.

topics.name: Lefamulin
topics.clinical_significance: Lefamulin is an antibiotic used to treat community-acquired bacterial pneumonia caused by susceptible bacteria. It can prolong the heart’s QT interval and disturb heart rhythm, especially when taken with certain other medicines. Pregnancy safety data are limited, so alternatives may be considered.

topics.name: Leg Amputation Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation after leg amputation helps a person regain mobility and independence. It builds strength and balance, teaches safe use of a prosthesis or wheelchair, and supports care of the remaining limb. Starting when the person is medically stable helps prevent joint contractures and other problems.

topics.name: Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease occurs when blood supply to the growing end of a child’s thighbone is reduced, damaging the hip joint. It causes gradual hip pain and limping, sometimes with knee pain. The bone may heal out of shape, increasing the risk of hip osteoarthritis later.

topics.name: Legionella Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Legionella bacteria are usually acquired by breathing in mist from contaminated water. They can cause Legionnaires’ disease, a potentially severe pneumonia treated with antibiotics, or Pontiac fever, a milder flu-like illness that usually resolves on its own. Severe pneumonia is more common in older adults, smokers, and people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Legionnaires' Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Legionnaires’ disease is pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, usually after a person breathes in mist from contaminated water. It can cause fever, cough, and shortness of breath; older adults, smokers, and people with chronic lung disease or weakened immunity are at higher risk of severe illness. It requires treatment with antibiotics that work against Legionella.

topics.name: Leiomyomas
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are noncancerous growths in the muscle of the uterus, and many cause no symptoms. When symptoms occur, they may include heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes leading to anemia, pelvic pain or pressure, and urinary or bowel problems. Fibroids can also affect fertility or cause pregnancy complications.

topics.name: Length
topics.clinical_significance: In infants, length is measured lying down from the crown of the head to the heels. Compared with gestational-age growth charts and considered with weight and head circumference, it helps assess growth and identify newborns who may need closer evaluation.

topics.name: Leprosy
topics.clinical_significance: Leprosy (Hansen disease) is a chronic bacterial infection that affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and lining of the nose and upper airways. It can cause numb skin patches, weakness, and damage that may lead to injuries or deformity; the eyes and nose may also be affected. Early multidrug antibiotic treatment stops the infection from progressing and limits further damage, but may not reverse nerve damage already present.

topics.name: Leptospirosis
topics.clinical_significance: Leptospirosis is usually caught when broken skin or the eyes, nose, or mouth contact water or soil contaminated by infected animal urine. It often causes sudden fever, headache, muscle aches, and red eyes; symptoms may return in a second phase. Severe disease can cause jaundice, kidney or liver problems, bleeding, or meningitis. Early antibiotic treatment works best.

topics.name: Leukemia, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Leukemia is cancer of the blood-forming cells, usually in the bone marrow. Abnormal white blood cells build up and reduce the production of normal blood cells, which can cause anemia, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. The course varies by type: acute leukemias often progress quickly, while chronic types may develop more slowly.

topics.name: Leukemias
topics.clinical_significance: Leukemias are cancers of blood-forming cells, grouped by the affected cell type and how quickly the disease progresses. Abnormal cells can crowd out normal blood-cell production, causing anemia, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding. Acute forms often progress quickly, while some chronic forms develop more slowly.

topics.name: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is a rare inherited immune disorder that makes it hard for white blood cells to leave blood vessels and reach infected tissues. It causes repeated bacterial infections, often with little or no pus, poor wound healing, gum disease, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord. Severe disease can be life-threatening without treatment.

topics.name: Leukocytoclastic Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a pattern of small-vessel inflammation seen on skin biopsy. It often causes raised purple spots (palpable purpura) and may be limited to the skin or occur as part of a disease that affects other organs. Medicines, infections, or immune diseases can trigger it.

topics.name: Leukopenias
topics.clinical_significance: Leukopenia is a low white blood cell count, most often due to a low neutrophil count, though other white blood cell types may also be reduced. It can weaken immune defenses and raise the risk of infection, especially when neutrophil levels are very low; the risk depends on which cells are affected and how low the counts are.

topics.name: Leukopenias, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Leukopenias are low counts of one or more types of white blood cells, most often neutrophils. Their effect on immune defense depends on which cells are reduced and by how much. Severe neutropenia can greatly raise the risk of serious bacterial and fungal infections.

topics.name: Levator Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Levator syndrome causes episodic rectal pain from spasm of the levator ani pelvic-floor muscle. The pain is often unrelated to bowel movements and may occur while sitting; episodes are usually brief but can last for hours. The condition is benign, but other causes of rectal pain should be ruled out.

topics.name: Liberation from Mechanical Ventilation
topics.clinical_significance: Liberation from mechanical ventilation is stopping ventilator support once the cause of respiratory failure has improved enough for the patient to breathe without it. A spontaneous breathing trial checks whether breathing can be sustained; removing the breathing tube also requires adequate alertness, airway protection, and an open airway. Reducing support before recovery is sufficient can delay recovery.

topics.name: Lice
topics.clinical_significance: Lice are blood-feeding insects that infest the scalp, body, or pubic area and usually cause itching. Head lice spread mainly through close contact, pubic lice usually through sexual contact, and body lice through infested clothing or bedding. Unlike the other types, body lice can spread serious infections.

topics.name: Lichen Planus
topics.clinical_significance: Lichen planus is a recurring, noncontagious, immune-related inflammation that can affect the skin, mouth, genitals, nails, or scalp. It may cause itchy, flat-topped skin bumps or painful mouth or genital sores. Long-lasting erosive mouth lesions rarely become cancerous, and genital or scalp disease may cause scarring.

topics.name: Lichen Sclerosus
topics.clinical_significance: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that usually affects the genital or anal area. It can cause itchy, fragile, pale patches that thin, crack, bruise, and scar over time, sometimes distorting genital tissue. Long-term treatment and follow-up are important because the condition raises the risk of squamous cell carcinoma, especially in persistent thickened or ulcerated areas.

topics.name: Lichen Simplex Chronicus
topics.clinical_significance: Lichen simplex chronicus is thickened, leathery skin caused by repeated scratching or rubbing. It creates an itch–scratch cycle in which scratching worsens itching, often forming dry, scaly patches on reachable areas such as the legs, arms, neck, or genitals. An underlying cause of the itch may be present and should be addressed.

topics.name: Licorice
topics.clinical_significance: Natural licorice contains glycyrrhizin. Large or regular amounts can make the body retain salt and water and lose potassium, causing high blood pressure and low potassium; this can be dangerous, especially for people with heart disease or those taking digoxin or certain diuretics. Natural licorice should be avoided during pregnancy and by people with high blood pressure. Many licorice-flavored candies contain no real licorice.

topics.name: Liddle Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Liddle syndrome is a rare inherited kidney disorder, usually passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. The kidneys retain too much sodium and water and lose potassium, causing early high blood pressure, low potassium, and an overly alkaline blood state (metabolic alkalosis). Medicines that block kidney sodium channels are effective treatment.

topics.name: Lightning Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Lightning strikes can cause heart-rhythm or breathing arrest, loss of consciousness, and brain or nerve injury. Serious burns are uncommon, but a person may be thrown or injured in a fall. Some survivors have lasting problems with memory, attention, pain, or nerve function, so assessment for heart, brain, and other injuries is important.

topics.name: Limb Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in an arm or leg can come from injury, muscle or bone problems, nerve disorders, infection, or blood-flow problems. Sudden severe pain with a pale, cool limb or weak pulse may signal an urgent blockage of blood flow; arm pain with chest pain or shortness of breath may be from a heart problem. Treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Limb Prosthetics
topics.clinical_significance: A limb prosthesis replaces a missing part of an arm or leg after amputation and can help with movement, daily activities, and independence. Its fit and type are chosen to meet individual needs; rehabilitation and follow-up help improve function and prevent problems such as skin injury.

topics.name: Limb Prosthetics, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: After amputation, a well-fitted limb prosthesis can improve mobility and daily function. Success depends on health, strength, the condition of the remaining limb, and the fit of the prosthesis; rehabilitation and follow-up are needed. Poor fit can cause pain, swelling, or skin breakdown.

topics.name: Limb-Girdle Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited muscle disorders cause slowly worsening weakness, usually around the hips and shoulders, which can make walking, standing, or lifting the arms difficult. Some forms can also affect the heart or breathing muscles, so checks may be needed. Care aims to maintain function and prevent stiff, shortened muscles.

topics.name: Lincosamides, Oxazolidinones, and Streptogramins
topics.clinical_significance: These antibiotic groups stop bacteria from making proteins and treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Some, such as linezolid, are used for infections caused by resistant bacteria. Resistance to one drug can sometimes affect others, so treatment depends on the bacteria and its susceptibility. Clindamycin can cause serious antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

topics.name: Linear Immunoglobulin A (IgA) Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Linear IgA disease causes clusters of itchy or burning blisters on the skin and may also affect the mouth or other moist linings. Medicines or infections can trigger it. Finding and stopping a causative medicine may help; a skin biopsy with special antibody testing confirms the diagnosis.

topics.name: Linezolid and Tedizolid
topics.clinical_significance: These antibiotics can treat gram-positive infections, including some resistant infections such as MRSA; linezolid is also active against vancomycin-resistant enterococci. Linezolid can interact with medicines that raise serotonin and lower blood counts, especially with longer treatment, so medication review and blood monitoring may be needed.

topics.name: Lip and Tongue Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Lip and tongue problems can include pain, sores, color changes, or swelling. Causes range from irritation and infection to signs of a wider illness or cancer. Sudden swelling that affects the tongue, throat, or breathing can block the airway and is an emergency; persistent sores or patches need medical assessment.

topics.name: Lip Swelling
topics.clinical_significance: Lip swelling can result from allergies, medicines, weather exposure, or an underlying illness. Swelling limited to the lips is often not dangerous, but swelling of the tongue or throat, or trouble breathing, can signal airway-threatening angioedema and needs emergency care. Evaluation focuses on finding the cause.

topics.name: Lip Ulcers and Cheilitis (Lip Inflammation)
topics.clinical_significance: Lip sores and inflammation can result from infection, injury, medicines, allergy, or other illness. Sun-damaged lip tissue (actinic cheilitis) can develop into cancer, and some cancers may look like a sore. Persistent or unusual lip lesions need medical or dental assessment.

topics.name: Lipid Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Lipid disorders often cause no symptoms but can increase the risk of artery disease, heart attack, and stroke. Very high triglyceride levels can cause acute pancreatitis. Blood tests can detect abnormal lipid levels, and treatment can lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

topics.name: Lipid Metabolism, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The body uses fats to store energy and build cell membranes, but most fats cannot travel freely in blood. Lipoproteins carry them through the bloodstream. Abnormal lipid levels, especially high LDL cholesterol, can promote plaque buildup in arteries and raise the risk of heart and blood vessel disease.

topics.name: Lipoglycopeptides
topics.clinical_significance: These IV antibiotics kill gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA, and are used mainly for serious skin infections; telavancin is also used for certain hospital-acquired pneumonias. Some stay in the body for a long time and need less frequent dosing. Telavancin can harm the kidneys, so kidney function and dose need attention.

topics.name: Lipoid Nephrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Lipoid nephrosis is an older name for minimal change disease, a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It causes sudden, heavy protein loss in the urine and swelling, while kidney function is usually preserved. Most patients respond well to treatment, but the disease can relapse.

topics.name: Lisfranc Injury
topics.clinical_significance: A Lisfranc injury damages the joints or ligaments connecting the middle and front of the foot, which can make the foot unstable. It may be missed on initial X-rays. Delayed diagnosis can lead to lasting pain, arthritis, and disability, so suspected injuries need prompt imaging and orthopedic assessment.

topics.name: Listeria
topics.clinical_significance: Listeria is a group of bacteria; L. monocytogenes is the main species that causes human illness, usually through contaminated food. It can cause severe blood or brain infections, especially in pregnant people, newborns, adults over 65, and people with weakened immunity. Infection during pregnancy can harm or kill the fetus or newborn.

topics.name: Listeriosis
topics.clinical_significance: Listeriosis is a foodborne infection that may cause mild fever and diarrhea or serious illness, such as bloodstream infection or meningitis. It is most dangerous for pregnant people, newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with weakened immunity. During pregnancy, it can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious newborn infection.

topics.name: Listeriosis, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Newborns can acquire listeriosis before birth or during delivery. It may cause sepsis soon after birth, with breathing or circulation problems, or appear weeks later as sepsis or meningitis. It can be life-threatening, so prompt diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are important.

topics.name: Liver and Gallbladder, Imaging Tests
topics.clinical_significance: Imaging tests help find gallstones, bile duct blockage, and liver growths or structural changes. Ultrasound is usually the first test for gallbladder and bile duct problems; CT or MRI can provide more detail, while ERCP is mainly used when treatment, such as removing a bile duct stone, is needed.

topics.name: Liver and Gallbladder, Laboratory Tests of
topics.clinical_significance: Blood tests help detect liver-cell injury, poor bile flow, and reduced liver function, and can track disease and response to treatment. Patterns in liver enzymes, bilirubin, albumin, and clotting time help guide diagnosis, but results are not always specific and must be interpreted with the person’s history and, often, imaging.

topics.name: Liver Biopsy
topics.clinical_significance: A liver biopsy removes a small piece of liver tissue for examination under a microscope. It can help diagnose liver problems or measure scarring when less invasive tests do not provide enough information. Pain and bleeding are possible complications; a vein-based approach may be used for some people at higher risk of bleeding.

topics.name: Liver Cancer, Metastatic
topics.clinical_significance: Metastatic liver cancer is cancer that has spread to the liver from another organ, often the bowel, breast, lung, or pancreas. It may cause no early symptoms; later signs can include weight loss, poor appetite, or discomfort in the upper right abdomen. Imaging helps detect it, and biopsy may confirm the diagnosis and cancer type. Treatment depends on the original cancer and how far it has spread; widespread disease often needs symptom-focused care.

topics.name: Liver Cancer, Primary
topics.clinical_significance: Primary liver cancer starts in the liver. Most cases are hepatocellular carcinoma; less common types include bile-duct cancer and childhood liver cancer. Early symptoms are often vague, so diagnosis may be delayed. Treatment and outlook depend on the type and stage; some localized tumors can be removed, and transplant may suit selected patients.

topics.name: Liver Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: Liver cancer may start in the liver or spread there from another organ; spread from elsewhere is more common. The main primary liver cancer in adults is hepatocellular carcinoma, often linked to cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C. Early symptoms may be absent or vague. Diagnosis and treatment depend on the cancer type, its spread, and liver function; some small primary tumors confined to the liver may be curable.

topics.name: Liver Disease, Approach to Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of possible liver disease combines symptoms and medical and exposure history with a physical exam, blood tests, and imaging; a biopsy is sometimes needed. This helps find the cause and judge severity, since early disease may have few signs and no single test gives the full picture.

topics.name: Liver Disease, Effects on Drug Metabolism
topics.clinical_significance: Liver disease can change how some medicines are absorbed, processed, or cleared, and can make the brain more sensitive to opioids and sedatives. For some drugs, usual doses may then have stronger or toxic effects; in cirrhosis, even small doses may trigger confusion from hepatic encephalopathy. Effects vary by drug and person, so dose changes must be individualized; liver test results alone cannot predict them.

topics.name: Liver Disease, Systemic Abnormalities in
topics.clinical_significance: Liver disease, especially advanced cirrhosis, can affect circulation, blood sugar and hormones, blood counts and clotting, kidney function and body salts, and the lungs. Serious problems can include bleeding, low blood pressure, kidney failure, or low blood oxygen. Recognizing these complications guides treatment and may prompt transplant assessment.

topics.name: Liver Disorder, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of a possible liver disorder looks at symptoms and risk factors, such as jaundice, alcohol or medicine use, and family history. A physical exam may give clues, but signs can be absent until disease is advanced. Blood tests and imaging are interpreted together, and a biopsy is sometimes needed, because no single test reliably shows the cause and severity.

topics.name: Liver Failure, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute liver failure is a rapid loss of liver function in someone without known chronic liver disease. It can cause jaundice, poor blood clotting, and confusion. Medicines or toxins, especially acetaminophen, and viral hepatitis are common causes. It is a medical emergency that needs hospital care and urgent assessment at a liver transplant center.

topics.name: Liver Injury Caused by Drugs
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines, herbal products, and supplements can injure the liver. Liver-test changes are often mild and cause no symptoms, but serious injury can cause jaundice or liver failure. Early identification and stopping the harmful product often allow recovery; severe cases may need specialist care.

topics.name: Liver Masses and Granulomas
topics.clinical_significance: A liver mass may be a harmless cyst or benign tumor, or primary or metastatic cancer; imaging, and sometimes biopsy, helps identify the cause. Most benign lesions cause no symptoms, though some can bleed or rarely become cancerous. Liver granulomas are usually symptom-free but may reflect infection or another systemic illness, so treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Liver Structure and Function
topics.clinical_significance: The liver processes nutrients and medicines, makes bile, albumin, and blood-clotting proteins, and removes waste from the blood. Liver damage can cause jaundice, abnormal blood sugar, bleeding, greater risk of infection, or confusion from waste buildup. Symptoms and test results help show which liver functions are affected.

topics.name: Liver Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: A liver transplant replaces a severely diseased or failing liver with a donor liver. It may be used for end-stage liver disease, acute liver failure, or selected liver cancers. It can be lifesaving, but rejection and other serious complications can occur, so recipients typically need anti-rejection medicines and close follow-up.

topics.name: Liver Tumors, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Most benign liver tumors are found by chance, cause no symptoms, and need no treatment. Some, especially large liver adenomas, can bleed or rarely become cancerous, so imaging helps identify the type and whether treatment is needed.

topics.name: Loa loa Filariasis
topics.clinical_significance: Loiasis is a Loa loa worm infection spread by day-biting deerflies in parts of West and Central Africa. Many people have no symptoms; others develop temporary localized swelling (Calabar swelling) or see a worm move across the eye. Heavy infection can affect the brain, and treatment can trigger life-threatening brain dysfunction if the worm level is high, so it must be measured before treatment.

topics.name: Lobular Glomerulonephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Lobular glomerulonephritis (membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis) is a pattern of kidney-filter injury seen on biopsy. It can cause blood and protein in the urine, swelling, and reduced kidney function, and may progress to kidney failure. It is often linked to another condition, such as chronic infection, an immune disorder, or a blood cancer, so treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Locked-In Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A person with locked-in syndrome is awake and aware but cannot move the limbs or speak, often after a stroke affecting the brainstem. They may communicate by blinking or moving the eyes up and down. Recognizing this is important because they can understand and make decisions.

topics.name: Lockjaw
topics.clinical_significance: Lockjaw (trismus) is difficulty opening the mouth because of jaw-muscle stiffness or spasm. It is a common early sign of tetanus, which can progress to whole-body spasms and breathing failure and needs emergency care. Lockjaw can also have other causes.

topics.name: Loeffler Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Loeffler syndrome is usually a mild, short-lived lung reaction with a dry cough, temporary shifting spots on chest imaging, and increased eosinophils in the blood. Migrating parasitic worms are a common cause, though sometimes no cause is found. It usually clears within about a month.

topics.name: Loiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Loiasis is a Loa loa worm infection spread by day-biting deerflies in parts of West and Central Africa. Many people have no symptoms; others develop temporary Calabar swellings or see a worm crossing the eye. In heavy infection, killing the worms with treatment can trigger dangerous brain dysfunction, so the worm level must be checked first.

topics.name: Long QT Interval Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Long QT syndromes delay the heart’s electrical recovery and can trigger a dangerous fast rhythm called torsades de pointes. This may cause palpitations, fainting, or sudden cardiac arrest. The condition may be inherited or caused by certain medicines or low potassium or magnesium, so finding and managing the cause helps lower risk.

topics.name: Long-Term Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term high blood sugar can damage small and large blood vessels and nerves. This can harm the eyes and kidneys, cause numbness or pain, and raise the risk of foot ulcers, infection, heart attack, stroke, and poor blood flow to the legs. Regular screening and control of blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol can prevent or delay some complications.

topics.name: Loosening of the Prosthesis
topics.clinical_significance: A loose limb-prosthesis socket may result from changes in the remaining limb or a faulty suspension or seal. It can let the prosthesis slip, injure the skin, and increase the risk of falls. If the fit does not improve with the usual adjustments, a prosthetist should check it.

topics.name: Lou Gehrig Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Lou Gehrig disease is another name for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a progressive disease that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscles. It causes worsening muscle weakness and wasting, eventually affecting movement, speech, swallowing, and breathing; sensation is usually spared. Breathing muscle failure is the main life-threatening complication.

topics.name: Louse-Borne Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Louse-borne typhus (epidemic typhus) is a serious infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and spread mainly by body lice. It causes prolonged high fever, severe headache, and a rash, and can be fatal without treatment. Doxycycline is the recommended antibiotic.

topics.name: Lower Esophageal Ring
topics.clinical_significance: A lower esophageal ring (Schatzki ring) is a thin band of tissue that narrows the lower esophagus. It can cause episodes of difficulty swallowing solid food, especially meat or dry bread, and food may get stuck. A tight ring may need to be widened during endoscopy.

topics.name: Lower-Extremity Edema During Late Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Swelling of both legs is common in late pregnancy and is often harmless. Sudden or severe swelling, high blood pressure, headache, or vision changes may signal preeclampsia; swelling, redness, warmth, or pain in one leg may signal a blood clot. Shortness of breath can indicate a serious heart or lung problem, so these symptoms need prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: LSD
topics.clinical_significance: LSD can cause altered perceptions, intense mood changes, and poor judgment for many hours, sometimes leading to panic or injury. Serious toxicity can cause dangerously high body temperature or abnormal heart rhythms. Recurrent visual disturbances or persistent psychosis may occur after use.

topics.name: Ludwig Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Ludwig angina is a fast-spreading infection in the floor of the mouth, often caused by an infected lower molar. Swelling can raise the tongue and block the airway within hours, making this a medical emergency. Treatment focuses first on keeping the airway open, with IV antibiotics and surgical drainage.

topics.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation
topics.clinical_significance: Many lumbar disc herniations cause no symptoms. When a herniated disc presses on a nerve, it can cause low-back pain that travels down a leg, with tingling, numbness, or weakness; most cases improve without surgery. New trouble urinating, loss of bladder or bowel control, or worsening weakness can signal severe nerve compression and require urgent assessment.

topics.name: Lumbar Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
topics.clinical_significance: A lumbar herniated nucleus pulposus (herniated disc) occurs when the soft inner part of a lower-back disc pushes through its outer layer. It may press on a nerve and cause back pain that travels down a leg, tingling, numbness, or weakness. Most cases improve without surgery, but new bladder or bowel problems or worsening weakness need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Lumbar Puncture
topics.clinical_significance: A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) collects cerebrospinal fluid from the lower back to help diagnose infections, bleeding, and other brain or spinal cord disorders. It can also measure or lower fluid pressure or deliver medicine. Headache occurs in about 1 in 10 patients. Bleeding problems or a mass causing high pressure in the skull can make the procedure unsafe, so clinicians assess these risks first.

topics.name: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Lumbar spinal stenosis is narrowing of the lower spinal canal that can compress nerves. It often causes pain, tingling, or weakness in the buttocks or legs when standing or walking, with relief when sitting or bending forward. New bladder or bowel problems, numbness around the groin, or severe leg weakness can signal serious nerve compression and need urgent medical care.

topics.name: Lumbosacral Radiculopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Lumbosacral radiculopathy occurs when a lower-spine nerve root is irritated or compressed, often by a herniated disc or spinal narrowing. It can cause pain that travels from the lower back or buttock down the leg, sometimes with tingling, numbness, weakness, or reduced reflexes. New bladder or bowel problems, numbness around the groin, or worsening leg weakness may signal severe nerve compression and need urgent care.

topics.name: Lump in Throat
topics.clinical_significance: Globus is a feeling of a lump in the throat that is not linked to swallowing and occurs without an actual mass. It is usually harmless; reflux or throat muscle tension may contribute. Seek medical assessment for pain, difficulty swallowing, food sticking, weight loss, a visible lump, or worsening symptoms, as these may point to another disorder.

topics.name: Lung Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A lung abscess is a pocket of pus formed when infection destroys lung tissue and creates a cavity. It often follows inhalation of bacteria from the mouth, especially in people with impaired swallowing or consciousness. It can cause a lasting cough with sputum, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and sometimes foul-smelling sputum. Treatment usually requires several weeks of antibiotics; some abscesses also need drainage.

topics.name: Lung and Heart-Lung Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: Lung transplantation may be considered for severe lung failure that remains life-threatening despite treatment. One or both lungs may be replaced; a heart-lung transplant may be needed when severe lung disease occurs with irreversible heart dysfunction. Recipients need lifelong anti-rejection medicines and face risks such as infection and rejection of the transplant.

topics.name: Lung Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer death and may spread before symptoms appear. It can cause a lasting cough, chest pain, coughing up blood, breathlessness, or weight loss. Smoking causes most cases, but people who have never smoked can also develop it. Small-cell and non-small-cell cancers differ in how they spread and are treated; imaging can find a suspicious growth, but biopsy is needed to confirm cancer.

topics.name: Lung Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Lung carcinoma is cancer that starts in the lungs or airways. It may cause no symptoms early and can spread to other organs. Smoking is the main risk factor, though it also occurs in people who have never smoked. The main types are small-cell and non-small-cell; biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and treatment depends on the type and stage.

topics.name: Lung Fluke Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Lung fluke infection (paragonimiasis) is caught by eating raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish. Many people have no symptoms; lung infection can cause a lasting cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood. In some cases, flukes affect the brain; praziquantel is the usual treatment.

topics.name: Lung Tumors, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Lung tumors may start in the lung or spread there from cancer elsewhere. Primary lung tumors can be benign or malignant. A benign growth can still block an airway; a malignant tumor can invade nearby tissue or spread. Knowing the tumor type and where it began helps guide care.

topics.name: Lungs, Tumors of
topics.clinical_significance: Tumors of the lungs and airways may begin there, grow into them from nearby tissue, or spread from cancer elsewhere. They can be benign or cancerous. Depending on their size and location, they may block airflow and cause cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, or repeated pneumonia; some cause no symptoms. The tumor type and extent guide treatment.

topics.name: Lupus Anticoagulant Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Lupus anticoagulant syndrome (antiphospholipid syndrome) increases the risk of blood clots, even though the antibody can prolong some clotting tests. It can cause clots in veins or arteries and pregnancy complications, including recurrent pregnancy loss. It can occur with or without lupus; diagnosis requires a related clot or pregnancy complication and antibodies that remain positive on repeat testing at least 12 weeks later.

topics.name: Lupus Nephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Lupus nephritis is kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus erythematosus. It may cause blood or protein in the urine, but can have few symptoms. Severe or ongoing disease can damage kidney function and lead to kidney failure. A kidney biopsy helps identify the type and activity of the disease and guide treatment.

topics.name: Lyme Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Lyme disease is a bacterial infection caused by Borrelia and spread by infected Ixodes ticks. An expanding rash is a common early sign, but it may be absent. Untreated infection can later affect the joints, nervous system, or heart. Antibiotics treat the infection, though joint inflammation can sometimes persist after the bacteria are cleared.

topics.name: Lymphadenitis
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphadenitis is inflammation of one or more lymph nodes, most often due to infection. The nodes are usually enlarged, painful, and tender; nearby skin may be red or warm, and an abscess can form. Less often, autoimmune disease, cancer, or a drug reaction is the cause. Treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Lymphadenopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphadenopathy means abnormal enlargement of one or more lymph nodes. Localized swelling is often a short-lived response to infection, while widespread swelling can signal an infection, autoimmune disease, or cancer. Persistent, hard, fixed, or collarbone-area nodes need medical assessment; treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, slowly progressive disease, mainly affecting women, in which abnormal smooth-muscle cells form cysts in the lungs and damage lung function. It can cause breathlessness, fluid around the lungs, or spontaneous lung collapse (pneumothorax); benign kidney growths may also occur. Severe disease can lead to respiratory failure.

topics.name: Lymphangioma
topics.clinical_significance: A lymphangioma (lymphatic malformation) is a benign congenital cluster of enlarged lymph vessels. It is usually present at birth or appears by age 2, often in the head or neck, as a soft swelling. Large lesions can distort nearby tissue, but treatment is often unnecessary; bothersome lesions may be treated with sclerotherapy.

topics.name: Lymphangioma Circumscriptum
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a benign, congenital microcystic malformation of skin lymph vessels. It appears as clusters of small, clear or pink fluid-filled bumps that may leak clear or blood-tinged fluid, bleed, or become infected. Treatment is often unnecessary unless the lesions cause problems.

topics.name: Lymphangitis
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphangitis is an acute infection of lymph vessels, usually caused by bacteria entering through a wound or skin infection; parasites are a less common cause. It causes warm, tender red streaks that spread toward nearby lymph nodes. Fever and chills may develop quickly, and the infection can enter the bloodstream, so prompt treatment is important.

topics.name: Lymphatic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphatic disorders affect the vessels and nodes that drain fluid and help fight infection. Blockage or damage can cause swelling (lymphedema) or fluid leaks; infection, inflammation, and cancer can also affect these structures. Causes and treatment vary, so care targets the underlying problem.

topics.name: Lymphatic Malformations
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphatic malformations are benign congenital defects in which lymph vessels form abnormally and widen, creating localized or widespread cyst-like lesions. They are usually present at birth or appear by age 2, often in the head or neck. Many need no treatment; larger or troublesome lesions may be treated with sclerotherapy.

topics.name: Lymphatic System, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The lymphatic system is a network of vessels, nodes, and organs that returns excess tissue fluid to the blood and helps defend against infection and cancer. Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain immune cells. Blockage or damage can cause fluid buildup (lymphedema), while infection or cancer can affect the nodes.

topics.name: Lymphedema
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphedema is chronic swelling caused by underdeveloped, blocked, or damaged lymph vessels. It usually affects an arm or leg and may be inherited or develop after cancer surgery or radiation, injury, or filariasis. Long-term swelling can thicken the skin and raise the risk of skin infection; treatment can reduce swelling and complications but rarely cures it.

topics.name: Lymphocytic Choriomeningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis is a rodent-borne virus infection, usually caught from dust or food contaminated with mouse or hamster urine or feces. Most infections cause no or mild illness, but some lead to a flu-like illness or meningitis; brain inflammation is rare. Infection during pregnancy can cause serious fetal problems, including hydrocephalus and eye damage, or fetal death. Treatment is mainly supportive.

topics.name: Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonitis
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphocytic (lymphoid) interstitial pneumonia is a rare lung disease in which immune cells build up in lung tissue. It may occur with Sjögren syndrome, other autoimmune diseases, or immune deficiency, and can cause gradually worsening cough and shortness of breath. Some cases progress to lung scarring and respiratory failure; rarely, lymphoma develops. Treatment depends on the cause and may include corticosteroids.

topics.name: Lymphocytopenia
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphocytopenia is a low blood lymphocyte count. It is often temporary during infections, severe illness, stress, or corticosteroid use, but can also result from HIV, undernutrition, autoimmune disease, cancer, other medicines, or an inherited immune disorder. It may cause no symptoms, but persistent or severe deficiency can weaken immune defenses and lead to recurrent or unusual infections.

topics.name: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by certain strains of Chlamydia trachomatis. A small genital sore may go unnoticed, followed by painful swollen groin or pelvic lymph nodes; after anal exposure, it can cause severe rectal inflammation. Without treatment, it may cause abscesses, draining tracts, rectal scarring, or lasting genital swelling. Antibiotics treat the infection, but late tissue damage may remain.

topics.name: Lymphoid Interstitial Pneumonia (LIP)
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP), also called lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis, is a rare lung disease in which immune cells collect in the air sacs and their walls. It may be linked to autoimmune disease, especially Sjögren syndrome, or to immune deficiency, and can cause gradual cough and shortness of breath. It may resolve, but can also progress to lung scarring and respiratory failure or, rarely, lymphoma.

topics.name: Lymphoma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphomas are cancers of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and include Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types. They often cause painless enlarged lymph nodes but can also affect the bone marrow, blood, spleen, or other organs. Behavior and treatment vary by subtype and stage, so biopsy and accurate classification are important; many types respond well to treatment.

topics.name: Lymphomas
topics.clinical_significance: Lymphomas are cancers of immune cells called lymphocytes. They may begin in lymph nodes or other organs and can involve the blood or bone marrow. They often cause painless swollen lymph nodes; fever, drenching night sweats, or unexplained weight loss may also occur. Growth rate and treatment vary widely, so biopsy and accurate classification are essential.

topics.name: Lymphomas, Primary Brain
topics.clinical_significance: Primary brain lymphoma is a rare cancer that starts in the brain or other central nervous system tissue, usually in B cells. It can cause neurologic symptoms and is more common in older adults and people with weakened immune systems. MRI and sometimes spinal-fluid tests or brain biopsy are used to diagnose it; treatment usually includes chemotherapy and may include radiation.

topics.name: Lynch Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Lynch syndrome is an inherited disorder of DNA mismatch repair that greatly raises the risk of colorectal cancer, often at a younger age, and also increases the risk of endometrial, ovarian, and other cancers. Genetic testing and counseling can identify affected relatives who need regular colonoscopy and screening for other cancers.

topics.name: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide
topics.clinical_significance: LSD can cause long-lasting changes in perception and mood, poor judgment, and impaired coordination. Severe toxicity may cause dangerously high body temperature or heart problems; some people later develop flashbacks or ongoing psychosis. Acute intoxication is treated with supportive care.

topics.name: Lysosomal Storage Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Lysosomal storage disorders are inherited conditions in which a missing or faulty lysosomal enzyme or other component causes substances to build up in cells. The buildup can damage the nervous system and organs such as the liver, spleen, bones, and heart. Symptoms and severity vary by disorder, and some types progress over time. Identifying the specific disorder matters because some have disease-specific treatments.

topics.name: Löffler Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Löffler syndrome is a usually short-lived lung condition marked by increased eosinophils in the blood and temporary lung opacities that move over time. Symptoms are often mild, such as a dry cough or wheezing. Parasitic infection is a common cause, although no cause is found in some people; the condition usually resolves within a month.

topics.name: Macrocephaly
topics.clinical_significance: Macrocephaly is a head circumference more than 2 standard deviations above the average for age and sex. It may be a harmless family trait, but can also signal a brain, blood vessel, or genetic condition, including hydrocephalus. Megalencephaly specifically means that the brain itself is enlarged.

topics.name: Macroglobulinemia
topics.clinical_significance: Macroglobulinemia (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) is a B-cell cancer in which abnormal cells produce excess monoclonal IgM protein. Many people have no symptoms at first; in others, the protein can thicken the blood and cause vision changes, bleeding, headache, or nerve problems. The disease may also cause anemia, infections, or enlargement of lymph nodes, liver, or spleen.

topics.name: Macrolides
topics.clinical_significance: Macrolides are antibiotics that usually stop bacteria from growing by blocking protein production at the 50S ribosome. Azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin treat selected infections, including some atypical respiratory infections. Some macrolides can cause stomach upset, affect heart rhythm by prolonging the QT interval, or interact with other medicines; bacterial resistance limits their use for some infections.

topics.name: Macrophage Activation Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Macrophage activation syndrome is a life-threatening form of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that can occur with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and other rheumatic diseases. Uncontrolled immune activation causes persistent high fever, low blood counts, and inflammation that may lead to bleeding, liver or spleen enlargement, confusion, seizures, shock, or failure of multiple organs.

topics.name: Macular Pucker
topics.clinical_significance: A thin fibrous membrane forms on the retinal surface and may contract, wrinkling the macula. It can blur or distort central vision, although many cases cause little visual trouble.

topics.name: Madura Foot
topics.clinical_significance: Madura foot (mycetoma) is a chronic, slowly worsening infection of the skin and deeper tissues, usually in the foot, caused by fungi or bacteria entering through a skin injury. It causes swelling and draining channels that release tiny grains of organisms; over time, it can damage nearby muscle and bone and deform the limb.

topics.name: Maduromycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Maduromycosis is another name for mycetoma, a chronic, slowly progressive infection caused by fungi or bacteria, usually after they enter through a skin injury. It causes swelling and draining channels that release tiny grains of organisms; over time, it can spread into nearby muscle and bone and deform the affected limb.

topics.name: Magnesium Concentration, Disorders of, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Magnesium helps nerves, muscles, the heart, and many enzymes work normally. Low blood magnesium can cause weakness, tremor, muscle spasms, seizures, or abnormal heart rhythms and often occurs with low potassium or calcium. High magnesium, usually due to kidney failure, can weaken reflexes and slow breathing and heart function.

topics.name: Magnet Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Magnet therapy uses static magnets or pulsed electromagnetic fields in an attempt to reduce pain or improve healing. Static magnets have not shown clear benefit for several pain conditions, while some pulsed-field treatments may help in selected uses. Magnets may interfere with implanted cardiac devices, insulin pumps, or medicine patches.

topics.name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Neurologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: In neurologic disorders, MRI gives more detailed images of brain and spinal cord tissues than CT, especially in the brainstem, posterior part of the brain, and spinal cord. It helps detect problems such as early stroke, multiple sclerosis plaques, tumors, abscesses, and spinal cord compression.

topics.name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
topics.clinical_significance: MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to make detailed images without ionizing radiation. It is especially useful for viewing soft tissues, the brain and spinal cord, joints, and some tumors, and for detecting early stroke. Some metal objects or implanted devices can make MRI unsafe, and contrast may need extra caution in severe kidney disease.

topics.name: Magnets
topics.clinical_significance: Medical magnet therapies use permanent magnets or pulsed electromagnetic fields. Permanent magnets have not shown reliable benefit for pain, while pulsed-field treatments have evidence for some uses, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for post-stroke depression. Magnetic devices may interfere with pacemakers and other implants, insulin pumps, or medicine patches.

topics.name: Major Neurocognitive Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) is a significant decline in thinking abilities, such as memory, language, or judgment, that interferes with independent daily life. It often develops gradually and may result from Alzheimer disease, vascular disease, or other brain disorders; some causes of cognitive decline are treatable. Unlike mild cognitive impairment, it affects independence and is distinct from sudden confusion (delirium).

topics.name: Mal de Mer
topics.clinical_significance: Mal de mer (motion sickness) is nausea and related symptoms triggered by motion or conflicting signals from the inner ear, vision, and body-position senses. It may cause vomiting, dizziness, pallor, sweating, and abdominal discomfort; prolonged vomiting can lead to dehydration.

topics.name: Malabsorption, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Malabsorption occurs when the body cannot properly digest, absorb, or transport nutrients from food. It can cause chronic diarrhea, greasy stools, bloating, weight loss, and deficiencies of vitamins, minerals, or other nutrients. It may affect one nutrient or many.

topics.name: Malabsorption Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Malabsorption syndromes are disorders that prevent the body from properly digesting or absorbing nutrients. They can cause chronic diarrhea, greasy stools, bloating, weight loss, and nutrient deficiencies that may lead to anemia or other health problems. Some affect only one nutrient, while others impair absorption of many nutrients.

topics.name: Malaria
topics.clinical_significance: Malaria is a potentially life-threatening infection caused by \textit{Plasmodium} parasites, usually spread by bites from infected female \textit{Anopheles} mosquitoes. After multiplying in the liver, the parasites infect red blood cells, causing fever, chills, sweating, headache, and anemia. Severe malaria, especially from \textit{P. falciparum}, can cause seizures, coma, kidney or breathing failure, and death. \textit{P. vivax} and \textit{P. ovale} can relapse because parasites may remain dormant in the liver.

topics.name: Male Hypogonadism
topics.clinical_significance: Male hypogonadism is low testosterone with related symptoms or signs, reduced sperm production, or both. It can result from problems in the testes or in the hypothalamus or pituitary gland. Effects depend on when it begins and can include impaired sexual development, delayed puberty, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, loss of muscle or bone mass, and infertility. Testosterone treatment may ease symptoms but does not restore fertility.

topics.name: Male Hypogonadism in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Male hypogonadism in children is low production of testosterone, sperm, or both, or a reduced response to testosterone. Depending on when it begins, it may cause incomplete genital development before birth, undescended testes, or delayed or incomplete puberty; fertility may later be affected. Hormone tests help distinguish testicular causes from problems in the brain’s hormone-control system and from temporary delay of puberty.

topics.name: Male Reproductive Endocrinology
topics.clinical_significance: Male reproductive hormones are controlled by signals from the hypothalamus and pituitary to the testes. Luteinizing hormone stimulates testosterone production, while follicle-stimulating hormone and testosterone support sperm production. Disruption can affect sexual development, puberty, sexual function, or fertility; testosterone also helps maintain muscle and bone. Testosterone tends to decline gradually with age, but age alone does not establish hypogonadism.

topics.name: Male Reproductive Endocrinology and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect the hormones that control male sexual development, testosterone and sperm production, and sexual function. Problems in the testes or in the brain’s hormone-control system, as well as some medicines and other conditions, can lead to delayed puberty, low testosterone, infertility, or sexual dysfunction.

topics.name: Male Sexual Function and Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Male sexual dysfunction is a problem with sexual desire, erection, ejaculation, or orgasm that interferes with sexual activity. It may result from physical illness, hormone or nerve problems, psychological factors, or medicines. Erectile dysfunction can be an early sign of blood vessel disease, including cardiovascular disease.

topics.name: Malformed Cerebral Hemispheres
