topics.clinical_significance: Cerebral hemisphere malformations are developmental abnormalities that can change the size, symmetry, or folds of the brain. They may result from genetic changes or problems during fetal development, such as infection or interrupted blood or nutrient supply. Effects vary, but may include seizures, movement difficulties, learning or intellectual disability, and an unusually small or large head.

topics.name: Malignant External Otitis
topics.clinical_significance: Malignant external otitis (necrotizing otitis externa) is a serious infection of the ear canal, most often affecting older adults with diabetes or weakened immunity; Pseudomonas is a common cause. It can spread into the temporal bone and skull base, causing bone infection, cranial nerve damage, or rarely infection inside the skull. Despite its name, it is not cancer.

topics.name: Malignant Hyperthermia
topics.clinical_significance: Malignant hyperthermia is a life-threatening reaction in genetically susceptible people, usually triggered by certain inhaled anesthetics together with the muscle relaxant succinylcholine. Overactive muscle metabolism can cause muscle rigidity, rising carbon dioxide and body temperature, acid buildup, and muscle breakdown that may damage the kidneys. It can occur during or soon after anesthesia.

topics.name: Malignant Melanoma
topics.clinical_significance: Melanoma is a cancer of pigment-producing cells. It usually begins in the skin but can also develop in the eye or mucous membranes. It may appear as a new or changing spot with uneven shape or color, though some melanomas have little or no pigment. It can spread through lymph or blood, and the chance of spread rises as it grows deeper.

topics.name: Mallet Finger
topics.clinical_significance: Mallet finger is an injury in which the tendon that straightens the fingertip pulls away from the end bone. The fingertip droops and cannot be actively straightened. The tendon may also pull off a small piece of bone.

topics.name: Mallory-Weiss Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a shallow tear in the lining where the lower esophagus meets the stomach, usually after forceful vomiting or retching. It can cause blood in vomit and upper digestive tract bleeding. Most bleeding stops on its own, but some cases need treatment to control it.

topics.name: Malocclusion
topics.clinical_significance: Malocclusion is abnormal contact or alignment between the upper and lower teeth when the jaws close. Uneven biting forces can cause abnormal tooth wear, fractures, or loose teeth. Severe cases may affect chewing or speech.

topics.name: Malrotation of the Bowel
topics.clinical_significance: Malrotation is an abnormal position of the bowel caused by incomplete rotation before birth. It may cause a blockage or let the bowel twist and lose its blood supply. This twisting, called volvulus, is a surgical emergency and can lead to bowel death.

topics.name: Mammography
topics.clinical_significance: Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to image the breast. It is used to screen people without symptoms and to assess breast symptoms or abnormal screening results. Dense breast tissue can make abnormalities harder to see, and an abnormal result may need more imaging or a biopsy.

topics.name: Management of Adverse Effects of Cancer Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer and its treatment can cause low blood cell counts, digestive problems, pain, anxiety, and serious syndromes such as tumor lysis or cytokine release. Recognizing and managing these problems helps prevent complications and maintain quality of life.

topics.name: Management of Normal Labor
topics.clinical_significance: Care during uncomplicated labor tracks cervical opening, contractions, the baby’s position and heartbeat, and the pregnant person’s health. Monitoring helps confirm that labor is progressing and detect problems that may need additional care.

topics.name: Management of Spontaneous Vaginal Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Care during spontaneous vaginal birth monitors the mother and baby, supports delivery, and checks for bleeding or injury afterward. Careful management after birth helps prevent postpartum hemorrhage, a major cause of serious maternal illness.

topics.name: Mandible and Midface, Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Fractures of the lower jaw or midface can change how the teeth fit together, limit mouth opening, or cause facial numbness or double vision. Severe swelling or bleeding can threaten breathing, and major facial trauma may also injure the brain or neck.

topics.name: Mandibular Condylar Hyperplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Mandibular condylar hyperplasia is continued overgrowth of the rounded end of the lower jaw at the jaw joint, usually on one side. It can slowly shift the chin and teeth, causing facial asymmetry and a crossbite. The growth eventually stops on its own.

topics.name: Mandibular Condylar Hypoplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Mandibular condylar hypoplasia is underdevelopment of the upright part of the lower jaw near its joint. It can make the face uneven, shift the chin toward the affected side, and cause the teeth to meet abnormally.

topics.name: Mandibular Dislocation
topics.clinical_significance: Mandibular dislocation occurs when the jaw joint slips out of place, often after the mouth is opened widely. The mouth becomes stuck open and cannot be closed. It is a dental emergency; the longer the jaw stays dislocated, the harder it is to put back and the more likely it is to dislocate again.

topics.name: Manganese Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Manganese is a trace mineral needed for healthy bones and for several enzymes. Manganese deficiency has not been clearly confirmed in people; in one study, severe restriction caused skin inflammation and low blood cholesterol.

topics.name: Manganese Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term excessive manganese exposure, often in mining or ore refining, can cause nervous system symptoms similar to parkinsonism and may affect heart and blood vessel function. Contaminated food or water can also be a source of harmful exposure.

topics.name: Manifestations of Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Infections may cause local signs, such as skin redness or an abscess, or body-wide effects such as fever and a fast pulse. Severe infection can affect several organs and progress to sepsis or septic shock, which can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Manometry
topics.clinical_significance: Manometry measures pressure and contractions in parts of the digestive tract, such as the esophagus, stomach, or rectum. It helps identify movement or sphincter problems, including causes of swallowing difficulty, constipation, or fecal incontinence, especially when other tests have not found a structural cause.

topics.name: Mansonellosis
topics.clinical_significance: Mansonellosis is infection with Mansonella filarial worms, spread by biting midges or blackflies. Many infections cause no symptoms; others may cause itching, rash, swollen lymph nodes, joint pain, or fever. Symptoms vary by worm species.

topics.name: Marburg and Ebola Virus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Ebola and Marburg are different viruses that can cause similar, severe illnesses. They spread through contact with body fluids from a person who has symptoms and can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, shock, and organ failure. The infections can be fatal.

topics.name: Marchiafava-Bignami Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Marchiafava-Bignami disease is a rare disorder in which myelin is damaged in the corpus callosum, the bundle connecting the brain’s two halves. It is linked to long-term alcohol use and poor nutrition. It can cause confusion, memory loss, trouble walking, seizures, or coma and can be fatal.

topics.name: Marfan Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Marfan syndrome is an inherited connective tissue disorder usually caused by a change in the FBN1 gene. It can affect the heart and blood vessels, eyes, and skeleton. The aorta may enlarge and tear, a life-threatening complication. Other features can include long limbs and fingers and a displaced eye lens.

topics.name: Marginal Keratolysis
topics.clinical_significance: Marginal keratolysis, also called peripheral ulcerative keratitis, is inflammation and ulceration at the edge of the cornea. It is often linked to active or long-standing rheumatic disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis. It can cause eye irritation, light sensitivity, and blurred vision, and may threaten sight.

topics.name: Marijuana (Cannabis)
topics.clinical_significance: Cannabis’s main intoxicating chemical, THC, can cause euphoria or sedation and temporarily impair attention, coordination, and reaction time. Frequent use can cause repeated episodes of nausea and vomiting (cannabinoid hyperemesis) and psychological dependence. Heavy long-term use is associated with cognitive problems and psychosis.

topics.name: Marine Bites and Stings, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Some marine animal bites and stings inject venom and can cause severe illness. Wounds can become infected with bacteria from seawater, including Vibrio species. Shark bites may cause major tissue damage or amputation.

topics.name: Massage Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Massage therapy uses pressure and movement of soft tissues to ease muscle tension, pain, and stress. It may provide short-term relief for some musculoskeletal symptoms. Bruising or bleeding can occur in people with low platelet counts or bleeding disorders.

topics.name: Mass-Casualty Weapons
topics.clinical_significance: Mass-casualty weapons include biological agents, chemicals, explosives, radiation sources, and toxins that can harm many people at once. The resulting emergencies can overwhelm medical resources and require rapid recognition, triage, and a coordinated response.

topics.name: Mass-Casualty Weapons, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A mass-casualty weapon incident can expose many people to biological agents, chemicals, radiation, explosives, or toxins and overwhelm medical services. Effects may be local or affect the whole body, and some exposures are hard to recognize at first. Rapid recognition, triage, and decontamination when needed help limit harm and protect responders.

topics.name: Mast Cell Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Mast cell disease can cause itching, flushing, stomach and bowel symptoms, and, in some people, severe allergic reactions with fainting or shock. In systemic disease, mast cells may build up in organs and damage them. Symptoms depend on the type and severity of the disease.

topics.name: Mastalgia (Breast Pain)
topics.clinical_significance: Breast pain is common and is often linked to hormonal changes, especially when it affects both breasts. Pain in one area may be due to a cyst or infection. Breast cancer usually does not first appear as pain, but a breast lump, nipple change, skin change, or signs of infection need medical assessment.

topics.name: Mastitis
topics.clinical_significance: Mastitis is painful breast inflammation, usually with infection, and often occurs during breastfeeding. It can cause a red, swollen, warm, tender area and fever. Rarely, infection forms a breast abscess.

topics.name: Mastocytosis and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Mastocytosis involves a buildup of mast cells in the skin or organs. Mast cell activation syndrome causes mast cells to release chemicals too easily, usually without a buildup. Both can cause itching, flushing, stomach upset, and sometimes severe allergic reactions with fainting or shock. Systemic mastocytosis can damage organs.

topics.name: Mastoiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Mastoiditis is usually a bacterial complication of middle-ear infection. It causes ear pain, fever, and swelling and tenderness behind the ear. The infection can damage hearing or spread to the blood or brain, causing sepsis or meningitis, so prompt treatment is important.

topics.name: Maternal Mortality and Perinatal Mortality
topics.clinical_significance: Maternal mortality counts deaths from pregnancy-related causes during pregnancy or within 42 days after it ends. Perinatal mortality counts late fetal deaths and deaths soon after birth; the exact definition varies. These rates show the risks around pregnancy and birth and help identify where better care and prevention are needed.

topics.name: MDMA
topics.clinical_significance: MDMA is a stimulant that can also change perception and increase feelings of emotional closeness. Toxicity can cause dangerously high body temperature, low blood sodium, seizures, abnormal heart rhythms, and organ failure. Repeated use may lead to dependence, psychosis, or problems with memory and thinking.

topics.name: Measles
topics.clinical_significance: Measles is extremely contagious and causes fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a rash that spreads from the face downward. It can lead to ear or lung infections, brain inflammation, and weakened immune defenses that raise the risk of other infections for months or years. Complications can be fatal, especially in young children, pregnant people, and people who are malnourished or have weakened immune systems.

topics.name: Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps, and rubella and helps prevent outbreaks and serious complications. Rubella protection is especially important because infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage or severe birth defects. Because MMR is a live vaccine, it is not given during pregnancy or to people with severe immune weakness.

topics.name: Measurement of Evoked Responses
topics.clinical_significance: Evoked response tests record the brain’s electrical response to visual, sound, or touch signals. They can reveal hidden damage or delay in sensory pathways, such as optic nerve damage in multiple sclerosis, help assess sensory pathways in infants, and sometimes help estimate outcome after coma.

topics.name: Measurement of Gas Exchange
topics.clinical_significance: Gas exchange tests show how well oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide is removed. Pulse oximetry estimates blood oxygen, an arterial blood gas measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acidity, and DLCO measures gas transfer from the air sacs into the blood. These tests help detect and assess breathing problems; pulse oximetry can give a falsely reassuring result in carbon monoxide poisoning.

topics.name: Mechanical Ventilation, Liberation from
topics.clinical_significance: Liberation from a ventilator is considered when the cause of respiratory failure has improved. A spontaneous breathing trial checks whether the patient can breathe without the machine. Passing the trial does not alone mean the breathing tube can be removed; alertness, airway protection, and an open airway also matter.

topics.name: Mechanical Ventilation, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Mechanical ventilation supports breathing when a person cannot keep oxygen levels adequate, remove enough carbon dioxide, or protect the airway. It can be given through a mask or a breathing tube and can be life-saving, but it may cause lung injury, low blood pressure, or pneumonia. Careful settings and stopping support when it is no longer needed help limit harm.

topics.name: Meckel Diverticulum
topics.clinical_significance: Meckel diverticulum is a pouch in the lower small intestine that is present from birth; most people have no symptoms. It can cause painless rectal bleeding, especially in children, or lead to bowel inflammation or blockage. These problems can be hard to distinguish from other causes of bleeding or abdominal pain, and symptomatic diverticula usually need surgery.

topics.name: Meckel's Diverticulum
topics.clinical_significance: This congenital pouch in the small intestine usually causes no symptoms. If it contains stomach tissue, the acid can cause ulcers and painless bleeding, often in children; it may also cause bowel inflammation or blockage. Symptomatic cases usually need surgery.

topics.name: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Meconium aspiration syndrome occurs when a newborn breathes meconium-stained fluid into the lungs around birth. The material can block airways and inflame the lungs, causing breathing difficulty and low oxygen. Severe cases can lead to high pressure in the lung blood vessels, air leaks, and a need for a ventilator; they can be fatal.

topics.name: Meconium Ileus
topics.clinical_significance: Meconium ileus is a blockage of a newborn’s lower small intestine by thick first stool. It is often the first sign of cystic fibrosis and can cause a swollen belly, green vomit, and failure to pass stool soon after birth. The blockage can lead to bowel twisting or perforation and needs prompt medical care.

topics.name: Meconium Plug Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A plug of thick first stool can block a newborn’s colon, causing failure to pass stool, a swollen belly, and vomiting. The blockage often clears with a contrast enema, but the condition can be linked to Hirschsprung disease or cystic fibrosis, which may need further testing.

topics.name: Medial and Lateral Plantar Nerve Entrapment
topics.clinical_significance: Compression of these foot nerves causes often constant pain around the inner heel or nearby arch, even when the foot is not bearing weight. Running and even standing can worsen the pain and make walking difficult. The condition can be mistaken for plantar fasciitis, but numbness and tingling are usually absent.

topics.name: Medial Collateral Ligament Tear
topics.clinical_significance: The medial collateral ligament helps keep the inner knee stable. A tear usually causes pain and swelling along the inner knee; a severe tear can make the knee unstable and may occur with an anterior cruciate ligament or meniscus injury. A blow or other force that pushes the knee inward is a common cause.

topics.name: Medial Epicondylitis
topics.clinical_significance: Medial epicondylitis, also called golfer’s elbow, causes pain where the forearm muscles attach to the inner elbow. Pain is often brought on by bending the wrist or turning the palm down against resistance. Repeated throwing, golfing, or similar arm movements can trigger it and make sport or daily tasks difficult.

topics.name: Mediastinal and Pleural Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect the lining around the lungs or the space between the lungs. Fluid or air around a lung can keep it from expanding fully and cause breathlessness or chest pain. A mass or infection in the space between the lungs can press on nearby airways, blood vessels, or the esophagus and may be serious.

topics.name: Mediastinal Masses
topics.clinical_significance: Mediastinal masses include cysts and tumors, some of which are cancerous. Many cause no symptoms, but a mass can press on the airways, major blood vessels, or esophagus, causing breathing or swallowing problems. Children are more likely than adults to have airway symptoms, so imaging and sometimes a biopsy are needed to find the cause and guide treatment.

topics.name: Mediastinitis
topics.clinical_significance: Acute mediastinitis is a serious inflammation, often due to infection, in the center of the chest. It usually follows a tear in the esophagus or infection after chest surgery and can cause severe chest pain, fever, and difficulty breathing. It can become life-threatening and needs urgent treatment; the chronic form can scar and narrow nearby airways or blood vessels.

topics.name: Mediastinoscopy and Mediastinotomy
topics.clinical_significance: These procedures let surgeons examine or sample lymph nodes and masses in the center of the chest and help stage cancers such as lung or esophageal cancer. Mediastinotomy can reach some lymph nodes that mediastinoscopy cannot. Complications are uncommon but can include bleeding, infection, lung collapse, or injury to the nerve that controls a vocal cord.

topics.name: Medical Aspects of Long-Term Kidney Replacement Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: People on long-term kidney replacement therapy often develop anemia, heart and blood vessel disease, bone and mineral problems, and nutrition or fluid problems. These need ongoing monitoring and treatment. Heart and blood vessel disease is a major cause of illness and death in people receiving hemodialysis, and calciphylaxis is a rare but often fatal complication.

topics.name: Medical Aspects of Travel
topics.clinical_significance: Travel can worsen some health conditions and expose people to infections, pressure and oxygen changes during flights, dehydration, motion sickness, or blood clots from long periods of sitting. Reviewing a traveler’s health and destination in advance helps guide vaccines, infection prevention, medicines, and plans for medical care. Road crashes are a major cause of death among travelers; heart attack and stroke are leading causes among older travelers.

topics.name: Medical Assessment of the Older Driver
topics.clinical_significance: Health problems and medicines can affect an older adult’s vision, movement, thinking, or alertness and make driving unsafe. Reviewing medical conditions, medications, falls, and physical and cognitive function helps identify risks and decide whether treatment changes or a formal driving assessment is needed.

topics.name: Medical Assessment of the Patient With Psychiatric Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: New or changed psychiatric symptoms can be caused or worsened by a medical illness, medication, or substance use. Even a person with a known mental disorder may also have a physical illness that needs care. Reviewing health history, medicines, and substance use, along with a physical and neurologic examination and any needed tests, helps find these causes.

topics.name: Medical Examination of the Rape Victim
topics.clinical_significance: After rape, a medical examination can identify and treat injuries, assess risks of pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, and offer prevention. Forensic evidence may be collected if the patient agrees. Care should be trauma-informed and support the patient’s emotional and psychological health.

topics.name: Medical Examination of the Sexual Assault Victim
topics.clinical_significance: After sexual assault, a medical examination can identify and treat injuries, assess risks of pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, and offer prevention. Forensic evidence may be collected if the patient agrees. Trauma-informed care also supports the patient’s emotional and psychological health.

topics.name: Medical Malpractice
topics.clinical_significance: Medical malpractice claims arise when a patient is harmed because a health professional’s care fell below the standard expected in similar circumstances. In the United States, a successful lawsuit also requires a professional relationship between the patient and clinician. Fear of lawsuits can lead to unnecessary tests or treatments, which may expose patients to avoidable harm and cost.

topics.name: Medical Radiation, Risks
topics.clinical_significance: Medical imaging that uses ionizing radiation can increase cancer risk, especially after repeated scans and in children. Fetal risk depends on the dose and stage of pregnancy. Clinicians weigh these risks against the need to diagnose or treat disease and limit exposure, but should not withhold a needed test.

topics.name: Medication Errors
topics.clinical_significance: Medication errors can cause ineffective treatment, adverse effects, serious injury, or death, though some cause no harm. They may occur when a drug is prescribed, dispensed, stored, or taken incorrectly, or when medication information is not shared accurately during care transitions. Clear instructions and medication reconciliation help prevent errors.

topics.name: Medication Overuse Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Frequent use of medicines for acute headaches can make headaches more frequent and turn episodic migraine or tension-type headache into a chronic headache. The diagnosis is considered when headache occurs on at least 15 days a month with regular overuse of headache medicine for more than 3 months. Treatment usually involves stopping the overused medicine and preventing the underlying headache; symptoms may worsen briefly during withdrawal.

topics.name: Medication Side Effects
topics.clinical_significance: Medication side effects are unintended effects that are unpleasant or harmful. They range from mild symptoms to severe or life-threatening reactions, so clinicians weigh a medicine’s benefits against its risks and may need to adjust or stop it. Risk is higher in older adults, people taking several medicines, and people with kidney or liver problems.

topics.name: Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (MRONJ)
topics.clinical_significance: MRONJ is a rare but potentially disabling problem in which exposed jawbone fails to heal for at least 8 weeks, often after dental extraction, in people taking antiresorptive or antiangiogenic medicines. It may be painless at first but can later cause pain and infection and can be difficult to treat. Good oral hygiene and regular dental care are important; the risk with oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis is very low, so needed treatment should not be stopped without medical advice.

topics.name: Medication-Related Problems in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults are at increased risk of medication-related harm because age-related changes, multiple medicines, other illnesses, and complex regimens can lead to side effects, drug interactions, dosing problems, or ineffective treatment. These problems can cause confusion, falls, hospitalization, or undertreated disease. Regular medication review, accurate medication lists during care transitions, and appropriate dosing and monitoring help reduce risk.

topics.name: Medications for Acute Coronary Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Acute coronary syndrome is a medical emergency, so medicines are started quickly along with reopening blocked arteries when needed. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs limit clot formation; nitrates and selected beta-blockers help reduce chest pain and heart workload. Statins and other medicines help lower the risk of future heart problems. Drug choice depends on the type of acute coronary syndrome and bleeding risk. Clot-busting drugs are used only for selected ST-elevation heart attacks when timely angioplasty is unavailable; they can worsen unstable angina and non-ST-elevation heart attacks.

topics.name: Medications for Arrhythmias
topics.clinical_significance: Antiarrhythmic drugs are used when an abnormal rhythm causes symptoms or poses a serious risk. The choice depends on the rhythm and the patient’s heart condition. These drugs can slow the heart or help restore and maintain a normal rhythm, but some can also cause new or worse arrhythmias, so careful selection and monitoring are important. Cardioversion, ablation, a pacemaker, or an implantable defibrillator may be needed instead of or along with medication.

topics.name: Medications for Deep Venous Thrombosis
topics.clinical_significance: Anticoagulants are the main treatment for deep venous thrombosis. They prevent the clot from growing and reduce the risk of pulmonary embolism and another clot while the body gradually breaks down the existing clot. Bleeding is the main treatment risk. Clot-dissolving drugs are reserved for a small number of people with extensive or limb-threatening clots because they can cause serious bleeding.

topics.name: Medications for Diabetes Mellitus Treatment
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes medicines lower blood glucose and help prevent complications. Insulin is essential for type 1 diabetes; treatment for type 2 may include oral or injectable medicines, sometimes with insulin. Some medicines also lower heart and kidney risks. Low blood glucose is an important risk, especially with insulin and some other drugs, so treatment and monitoring are tailored to the person.

topics.name: Medications for Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Heart-failure medicines can reduce symptoms, hospital stays, and risk of death; the survival benefit is strongest for certain treatments in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Diuretics reduce fluid buildup and breathlessness but mainly control symptoms. Drug choice depends on the type of heart failure and other health conditions. Blood pressure, kidney function, and blood salts such as potassium need monitoring.

topics.name: Medications for Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Antihypertensive medicines lower blood pressure and reduce the long-term risk of stroke, heart disease, and kidney damage. The choice depends on blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, other illnesses, and possible side effects; many people also need lifestyle changes or more than one medicine. Taking treatment regularly and monitoring blood pressure, kidney function, and blood salts can help ensure safe, effective control.

topics.name: Medications for Hypertension in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Blood pressure medicine may be needed for children with symptoms, stage 2 hypertension, organ damage, certain chronic illnesses, or blood pressure that remains high despite lifestyle changes. Treatment helps limit damage to the heart, kidneys, and other organs. The medicine and dose are chosen for the child; ACE inhibitors and ARBs can protect the kidneys in some children but must be avoided when pregnancy is possible. Blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium should be monitored.

topics.name: Medications for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammatory bowel disease medicines reduce intestinal inflammation to control flares and maintain remission. The choice depends on whether the disease is Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, where it affects the gut, and how severe it is. Mesalamine is mainly used for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis; steroids can treat flares but are generally not used to maintain remission. Immune-suppressing and targeted medicines can control more difficult disease but may increase infection risk, so screening and monitoring may be needed.

topics.name: Medications for the Treatment of Gastric Acidity
topics.clinical_significance: Acid-lowering medicines are used for gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcers, and some forms of gastritis; some are combined with antibiotics to treat Helicobacter pylori. Proton pump inhibitors are often used when strong, sustained acid reduction is needed, while antacids provide short-term symptom relief. The choice and duration depend on the cause, other medicines, and the patient’s health.

topics.name: Medications for Treatment of Bipolar Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Medicines help control manic and depressive episodes and reduce the chance of relapse. Treatment commonly uses mood stabilizers, atypical antipsychotics, or both; the choice depends on symptoms, medical history, and past response. Lithium requires regular blood tests and checks of kidney and thyroid function. Some mood stabilizers, especially valproate, can harm a developing fetus. Antidepressants may be added in selected cases but are generally not used alone.

topics.name: Medications for Treatment of Depression
topics.clinical_significance: Antidepressants reduce depressive symptoms and help prevent relapse; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are often a first choice, and psychotherapy may be combined with medication. Benefit usually takes several weeks. Monitor for side effects and worsening suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment and in children and young adults. Many antidepressants should be tapered rather than stopped suddenly.

topics.name: Medications to Aid Intubation
topics.clinical_significance: During medication-assisted intubation, a short-acting sedative, sometimes with pain medicine, reduces awareness and discomfort, while a muscle-relaxing drug can make tube placement easier and more likely to succeed on the first attempt. Drug choice depends on the patient’s condition: some medicines can lower blood pressure, and succinylcholine can dangerously raise potassium in people with certain injuries or neuromuscular disorders. Sedation and pain relief may need to continue after intubation.

topics.name: Medicolegal Issues
topics.clinical_significance: Medicolegal issues affect patient rights and clinicians’ duties, including informed consent, decision-making capacity, advance directives, professional licensing, and malpractice. Clear communication and documentation help support safe care, but legal requirements vary by location. Complex cases may need advice from an ethics committee or legal professional.

topics.name: Meditation
topics.clinical_significance: Meditation is a mind-body practice that trains a person to direct attention and observe thoughts or feelings. It may help with stress and emotional distress; evidence supports its use for depression, while benefits for many physical symptoms are less certain. It can complement care but should not replace needed medical treatment.

topics.name: Mediterranean Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Mediterranean anemia is another name for thalassemia, a group of inherited disorders rather than one distinct type. Reduced hemoglobin production causes small red blood cells and anemia. Severity ranges from an asymptomatic carrier state to severe anemia that may require regular transfusions and iron-chelation treatment.

topics.name: Medullary Sponge Kidney
topics.clinical_significance: Medullary sponge kidney is a usually benign disorder in which collecting ducts in the kidney medulla are dilated and form small cysts. Many people have no symptoms, but kidney stones and urinary infections are more common and can cause flank pain, blood in the urine, or painful urination. A stone that blocks urine flow can temporarily impair kidney function.

topics.name: Medulloblastoma
topics.clinical_significance: Medulloblastoma is a fast-growing malignant brain tumor that mainly affects children and develops in the back of the brain near the cerebellum. It can cause increased pressure in the skull and problems with balance or coordination, leading to headache, vomiting, visual changes, or unsteady walking. Treatment usually combines surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy; very young children who survive may have lasting problems with learning and thinking.

topics.name: Medulloblastomas
topics.clinical_significance: Medulloblastomas are fast-growing tumors that usually arise in the back of the brain. They can block the flow of cerebrospinal fluid, causing hydrocephalus, and can spread through that fluid to other parts of the central nervous system. Treatment depends on the tumor type, the patient’s age, and whether it has spread; it usually includes surgery and chemotherapy, with radiation used in some patients.

topics.name: Megaesophagus
topics.clinical_significance: In achalasia, weak esophageal contractions and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax cause the esophagus to widen and food to collect. This leads to gradually worsening trouble swallowing both liquids and solids and regurgitation of undigested food; aspiration into the lungs and weight loss can occur. Treatment aims to open the sphincter but does not restore normal esophageal movement.

topics.name: Megaloblastic Macrocytic Anemias
topics.clinical_significance: These anemias usually result from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which disrupts DNA production in blood cells. In addition to anemia, white blood cell and platelet counts may fall. Vitamin B12 deficiency can also cause nerve problems, such as numbness or trouble walking, which may become permanent if treatment is delayed. Check for B12 deficiency before treating with folate alone, because folate can improve the anemia while nerve damage continues.

topics.name: Melanocytic Nevi
topics.clinical_significance: Most melanocytic nevi (moles) are harmless, and any one mole is unlikely to become melanoma. Their main clinical importance is telling ordinary moles from melanoma and recognizing people at higher risk, such as those with many or atypical moles or a family history of melanoma. A mole that is asymmetric, has an irregular border or varied color, is larger than about 6 mm, or is new or changing should be assessed for melanoma.

topics.name: Melanoma
topics.clinical_significance: Melanoma is a cancer of pigment-making cells that most often starts in the skin but can also arise in the eye or mucous membranes. It can spread to lymph nodes and distant organs, and outcomes are worse after spread. A new or changing pigmented spot, especially one with an uneven shape or color, should be checked promptly because early diagnosis and treatment can be lifesaving.

topics.name: Melatonin
topics.clinical_significance: Melatonin is a hormone made by the pineal gland that helps regulate the body's daily rhythms, including the sleep–wake cycle. Supplements are used short term for jet lag and some sleep problems, but may cause drowsiness and can interact with medicines such as warfarin and sedatives.

topics.name: Melioidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, usually acquired from contaminated soil or water in endemic areas through broken skin, inhalation, or ingestion. It most often affects the lungs but can cause abscesses in the skin or other organs; bloodstream infection can be rapidly fatal. Symptomatic disease needs prolonged antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is a pattern of injury to the kidney's filtering units, not a single disease. It often causes both blood and protein in the urine and may reduce kidney function. Causes include immune disorders, chronic infections, and abnormal proteins made by blood cells; finding the cause matters because treatment is often directed at it.

topics.name: Membranous Glomerulonephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Membranous glomerulonephritis (membranous nephropathy) occurs when immune deposits thicken the kidney's filtering membrane. It often causes heavy protein loss in the urine and swelling; kidney function may be normal at first. The cause is often unknown, but some cases are linked to medicines, infections, autoimmune disease, or cancer. Some patients develop chronic kidney disease or kidney failure.

topics.name: Membranous Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Membranous nephropathy (also called membranous glomerulonephritis) occurs when immune deposits thicken the kidney's filtering membrane. It often causes heavy protein loss in the urine and swelling; kidney function may be normal at first. The cause is often unknown, but some cases are linked to medicines, infections, autoimmune disease, or cancer. Some patients develop chronic kidney disease or kidney failure.

topics.name: Memory Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Memory loss is difficulty learning or recalling information. It is common with aging and often does not mean dementia, but it can also result from depression, medicines, delirium, dementia, or treatable problems such as thyroid disease or vitamin B12 deficiency. Sudden or worsening memory loss, or problems with daily tasks, needs medical assessment.

topics.name: MEN 2
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 2 is an inherited syndrome caused by changes in the RET gene. Both MEN 2A and MEN 2B greatly increase the risk of medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma. MEN 2A may also cause overactive parathyroid glands, while MEN 2B can cause mucosal neuromas and skeletal changes. Genetic testing helps guide screening and preventive care.

topics.name: Meniere Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Meniere disease is a chronic inner-ear disorder that causes repeated attacks of spinning vertigo, often with nausea, fluctuating hearing loss, ringing in the ear, and ear pressure or fullness. Attacks usually last 20 minutes to 12 hours, and hearing loss can become lasting over time. Hearing tests and sometimes MRI help rule out other causes.

topics.name: Meniere's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Meniere's disease (Meniere disease) is a chronic inner-ear disorder causing repeated spinning attacks that last 20 minutes to 12 hours, often with nausea, fluctuating hearing loss, ringing in the ear, and pressure or fullness in the affected ear. Hearing loss may become persistent and worsen over time; hearing tests and sometimes MRI help rule out other causes.

topics.name: Meningiomas
topics.clinical_significance: Meningiomas are tumors of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. Most are noncancerous, but they can press on nearby brain tissue and cause problems such as seizures, vision changes, weakness, or memory and thinking changes, depending on where they grow. Some become malignant; small tumors without symptoms may be monitored, while growing or symptomatic tumors may need treatment.

topics.name: Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes and fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord. It is usually caused by infection, but medicines and other disorders can also cause it. Headache, fever, neck stiffness, light sensitivity, or confusion may occur, but symptoms can be incomplete. Bacterial meningitis can worsen quickly and is an emergency: antibiotics must start promptly, without waiting for test results. Cerebrospinal-fluid testing helps identify the cause when it is safe to do.

topics.name: Meningitis, Acute Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Acute bacterial meningitis is a rapidly worsening infection of the membranes and fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord. It often causes fever, headache, neck stiffness, and confusion, but some people have few typical signs. It is a life-threatening emergency: antibiotics and usually corticosteroids must be started promptly when it is suspected, without waiting for test results. Complications can include brain injury, hearing loss, sepsis, and death.

topics.name: Meningitis, Chronic and Subacute
topics.clinical_significance: Subacute meningitis develops over days to weeks; chronic meningitis lasts 4 weeks or longer. It causes slowly developing inflammation around the brain and spinal cord, often from infections such as tuberculosis or fungal disease, but cancer and autoimmune disorders can also be causes. Diagnosis may be difficult and can require repeated spinal-fluid tests; treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Meningitis in Infants Over 3 Months of Age, Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial meningitis in infants older than 3 months is a serious infection of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. Early signs may be vague, such as fever or low temperature, poor feeding, irritability, or unusual sleepiness; neck stiffness may be absent. It needs urgent hospital treatment with antibiotics. Spinal-fluid testing helps confirm the diagnosis when safe, but antibiotics should not be delayed if testing must wait. Survivors may have lasting problems such as hearing loss, seizures, or other nervous-system damage.

topics.name: Meningitis, Neonatal Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal bacterial meningitis is a serious bacterial infection of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, often occurring with bloodstream infection (sepsis). Newborns may show general signs such as unstable temperature, breathing problems, jaundice, or unusual sleepiness; neck stiffness and a bulging soft spot are uncommon. Spinal-fluid testing helps confirm the diagnosis, and antibiotics must be started urgently. Without treatment, the infection is almost always fatal; survivors may have lasting problems such as hearing loss or hydrocephalus.

topics.name: Meningitis, Noninfectious
topics.clinical_significance: Noninfectious meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord caused by a medicine, vaccine, cancer, or another disorder rather than an infection. It can cause headache, fever, and neck stiffness, so testing is needed to rule out infectious causes, especially bacterial meningitis. Treatment focuses on stopping a causative medicine or treating the underlying disorder.

topics.name: Meningitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Meningitis is inflammation of the membranes and fluid spaces around the brain and spinal cord, caused by infection or sometimes by medicines or other disorders. It often causes headache, fever, light sensitivity, and neck stiffness, but signs may be subtle in infants, older adults, or people with weakened immune systems. Severity depends on the cause: bacterial meningitis can worsen rapidly and needs immediate antibiotics, while viral and noninfectious forms are often self-limited; spinal-fluid testing helps identify the cause.

topics.name: Meningitis, Recurrent
topics.clinical_significance: Recurrent meningitis is repeated episodes of inflammation around the brain and spinal cord. Causes include recurrent viral infection, often due to herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2); a skull or spine defect that lets bacteria enter; a rare complement-system deficiency; or a medicine that triggers inflammation. Finding the cause is important because treatment is directed at it.

topics.name: Meningitis, Viral
topics.clinical_significance: Viral meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord caused by a virus, most often an enterovirus. It commonly causes headache, fever, and neck stiffness and is usually milder than bacterial meningitis; most cases improve with supportive care, though herpes-related disease may need antiviral treatment. Spinal-fluid tests help distinguish it from bacterial meningitis, which must be ruled out; 'aseptic meningitis' is a broader term and is not always viral.

topics.name: Meningococcal Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Meningococcal disease is an infection caused by Neisseria meningitidis, most often leading to meningitis or bloodstream infection (meningococcemia). It spreads through close contact with respiratory secretions and can worsen rapidly, causing shock, bleeding problems, organ failure, or death. It needs immediate antibiotic treatment; close contacts may need preventive antibiotics, and vaccination helps prevent disease.

topics.name: Meningococcal Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Meningococcal vaccines protect against selected serogroups of Neisseria meningitidis, which can cause meningitis and life-threatening bloodstream infection. MenACWY vaccines cover serogroups A, C, W, and Y; MenB vaccines cover serogroup B. Vaccination is recommended for adolescents and people at increased risk, but the vaccine and schedule depend on age, health risks, and local guidance.

topics.name: Meniscus Injury
topics.clinical_significance: A meniscus injury is damage to one of the two cartilage pads inside the knee that absorb shock and help stabilize the joint. It often follows twisting while bearing weight and can cause pain along the joint line, swelling, and sometimes locking of the knee. Treatment depends on the tear; large or complex tears, or those causing ongoing swelling or disabling symptoms, may need surgery.

topics.name: Menopause
topics.clinical_significance: Menopause is the permanent end of menstrual periods due to loss of ovarian follicle function, confirmed after 12 months without a period when no other cause explains it. It is a normal life stage, but changing and falling estrogen levels can cause hot flashes, night sweats, sleep problems, and vaginal or urinary symptoms. Bone loss speeds up during the first years after menopause.

topics.name: Menstrual Abnormalities, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Menstrual abnormalities include absent or irregular periods, heavy or between-period bleeding, painful periods, and premenstrual symptoms. Causes vary, so abnormal bleeding needs assessment; pregnancy should be checked in reproductive-age patients, and bleeding after menopause must be evaluated for possible gynecologic cancer.

topics.name: Mental Health in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Depression and anxiety often begin or become apparent during adolescence, so routine screening is important. Occasional sadness or worry can be normal, but persistent symptoms that disrupt school, relationships, or home life may signal a disorder. Screening should also identify suicide risk and concerns such as eating disorders or ADHD so support can be offered.

topics.name: Mental Symptoms, Approach to Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Mental symptoms can result from psychiatric disorders, medical illness, medicines, or substance use. A careful history, physical examination, and mental status examination help identify the cause and detect urgent problems such as delirium or infection. New or worsening symptoms in a person with a known psychiatric disorder still need medical assessment.

topics.name: Mental Symptoms, Medical Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: New psychiatric symptoms, or a major change in familiar symptoms, may be caused by medical illness, medicines, or substance use. Medical history and examination, with tests guided by the findings, can identify treatable causes and other health problems. Do not assume that new symptoms are due to a known psychiatric disorder.

topics.name: Merkel Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare but aggressive skin cancer that can spread to lymph nodes and distant sites. It often appears as a rapidly growing, painless red or bluish nodule, especially on sun-exposed skin in older adults or people with weakened immune systems. Prompt biopsy and staging are important because treatment and outlook depend on how far it has spread.

topics.name: Mesangiocapillary Glomerulonephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis, also called membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, is a pattern of kidney-filter injury rather than one single disease. It can cause blood and protein in the urine and reduced kidney function. Causes include immune-complex disease, abnormal complement activity, chronic infection, and some blood disorders; finding the cause guides treatment, and some cases progress to kidney failure.

topics.name: Mescaline
topics.clinical_significance: Mescaline is a hallucinogen found in peyote. Intoxication can cause visual hallucinations, distorted perception, mood changes, and poor judgment, which may lead to panic or accidental injury. Nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations, and poor coordination can occur; high body temperature or a dangerously fast or irregular heartbeat requires urgent care.

topics.name: Mesenteric Ischemia, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a life-threatening loss of blood flow to the intestines. Severe abdominal pain with few early examination findings is a key warning sign. Rapid diagnosis and restoration of blood flow are critical because delay can lead to bowel infarction, organ failure, and death.

topics.name: Mesothelioma
topics.clinical_significance: Malignant mesothelioma is an aggressive cancer of the lining of body cavities, most often the pleura around the lungs. Most cases are linked to asbestos exposure, and the cancer may appear decades after exposure. It can cause breathlessness, chest pain, and fluid around the lung; diagnosis usually requires a tissue biopsy, and the outlook is poor.

topics.name: Metabolic Acidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic acidosis is a primary fall in blood bicarbonate; the blood pH may be low or near normal if breathing compensates or another acid-base disorder is present. It can result from acid buildup, poor kidney acid removal, or bicarbonate loss. Severe acidemia may cause deep breathing, nausea, low blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, or coma. Finding and treating the cause is essential.

topics.name: Metabolic Alkalosis
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic alkalosis is excess bicarbonate in the blood, often caused by repeated vomiting, diuretic use, or loss of body fluid. Mild cases may cause few symptoms, but severe alkalemia or low potassium can lead to weakness, muscle cramps, confusion, seizures, or abnormal heart rhythms. Treatment addresses the cause and corrects fluid and electrolyte problems.

topics.name: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic and bariatric surgery changes the stomach, intestine, or both to produce weight loss in people with obesity. It can improve type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, and other obesity-related conditions. Because surgery can cause serious complications and nutritional deficiencies, careful patient selection and regular follow-up, including vitamin supplements when needed, are important.

topics.name: Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Liver Disease (MASLD)
topics.clinical_significance: MASLD is excess fat in the liver in a person with at least one metabolic risk factor, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, or abnormal blood fats. Many people have no symptoms, but some develop liver inflammation (MASH), scarring, and cirrhosis; the risk of serious liver disease rises with scarring. Weight loss and control of metabolic risks can reduce progression.

topics.name: Metabolic, Electrolyte, and Toxic Disorders in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Newborns can develop serious problems from abnormal blood sugar, bilirubin, calcium or sodium levels, and exposure to drugs before birth. Signs may be subtle, but untreated disorders can cause seizures, brain injury, severe dehydration, or death. Careful monitoring, timely testing, and treatment help prevent these complications.

topics.name: Metabolic Nephropathies
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic disturbances can injure the kidney tubules and nearby tissue. Depending on the cause, they may lead to sudden kidney injury, kidney stones, or gradual scarring and loss of kidney function. Finding and correcting the underlying metabolic problem early can prevent or limit lasting kidney damage.

topics.name: Metabolic Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic syndrome is a group of risk factors: excess abdominal fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar or insulin resistance, high triglycerides, and low HDL cholesterol. It is commonly diagnosed when at least 3 are present and raises the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Lifestyle changes and treatment of each risk factor can lower these risks.

topics.name: Metacarpal Neck Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Metacarpal neck fractures cause pain and swelling and may misalign a finger, especially if the bone is rotated. A small wound over a knuckle after punching someone in the mouth can be contaminated with oral bacteria and needs prompt care to prevent infection. Most fractures are splinted; some need the bone realigned first.

topics.name: Metachromatic Leukodystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an inherited enzyme deficiency that causes sulfatides to build up and damage myelin in the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. It leads to progressive loss of movement and thinking abilities, with age of onset and rate of progression varying by form. Early diagnosis matters because stem cell transplantation may stabilize some mildly affected patients, while advanced disease has no effective treatment.

topics.name: Metastatic Bone Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Cancers, especially those of the breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid, and colon, can spread to bone. These tumors often cause worsening bone pain and weaken the bone, sometimes leading to a fracture during ordinary activity. Bone symptoms may appear before the original cancer is found; identifying the spread guides cancer treatment and ways to relieve pain and prevent fractures.

topics.name: Metastatic Carcinoma of Unknown Primary Origin
topics.clinical_significance: This diagnosis means metastatic cancer has been found, but evaluation has not identified where it began. Biopsy and other tests can help determine the cancer type and guide treatment. Some subtypes respond well to specific treatment, but many have limited treatment response and a poor outlook.

topics.name: Metastatic Liver Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Liver metastases are more common than primary liver cancer and often arise from cancers of the digestive tract, breast, lung, or pancreas. They may cause no early symptoms or only weight loss and upper-right abdominal discomfort, and can be the first sign of the original cancer. Imaging helps detect them; treatment depends on the cancer type and how widely it has spread.

topics.name: Metatarsalgia
topics.clinical_significance: Metatarsalgia is a general term for pain around the joints at the ball of the foot, not a diagnosis by itself. Causes include stress fracture, Morton neuroma, joint disorders, sesamoiditis, and loss of the cushioning fat pad. Identifying the cause is important because treatment differs.

topics.name: Metatarsophalangeal Joint Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in the metatarsophalangeal joints often results from abnormal foot mechanics and can make walking painful. Pain with weight bearing and morning stiffness may be an early sign of rheumatoid arthritis. Marked warmth, redness, or swelling raises concern for gout, another inflammatory arthritis, or infection and needs evaluation.

topics.name: Methamphetamine
topics.clinical_significance: Methamphetamine is a powerful stimulant with high potential for dependence. Toxicity can cause agitation, high blood pressure, overheating, seizures, dangerous heart rhythms, stroke, or kidney injury from muscle breakdown. Repeated use can lead to paranoia or psychosis; stopping after chronic use may cause fatigue, sleep changes, and depression.

topics.name: Methionine Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited disorders of methionine and sulfur metabolism have varied effects. Some cause homocysteine buildup, which can lead to blood clots and harm the eyes, skeleton, or nervous system; others alter methionine or sulfite levels and may be mild or severe. Early diagnosis matters because some of these disorders can be treated to reduce serious complications.

topics.name: Methylenedioxymethamphetamine
topics.clinical_significance: MDMA is a stimulant that can raise heart rate, blood pressure, and body temperature. Toxicity can cause seizures and dangerous heart rhythms; it can also cause severe low blood sodium, sometimes with brain swelling, especially when a person drinks too much water. Repeated use may lead to psychosis or cognitive problems.

topics.name: Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: This finding can point to serious problems such as TTP, HUS, DIC, or damage to a heart valve. When it is part of a small-vessel clotting disorder, the clots can lower platelet counts and injure organs. Prompt evaluation is important because some causes, especially TTP, need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Microcephaly
topics.clinical_significance: Microcephaly can reflect abnormal brain growth due to genetic conditions, prenatal infection or exposure, or other developmental causes. It is associated with a higher risk of neurologic and developmental problems, such as seizures, intellectual disability, and spasticity; effects vary with the cause and severity.

topics.name: Microdeletion and Microduplication Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Small missing or extra chromosome segments can affect several nearby genes, causing birth defects, developmental or learning difficulties, and other health or behavior problems. The effects depend on which genes are involved and can vary widely. The significance of some duplications is still uncertain.

topics.name: Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)
topics.clinical_significance: MPA is a rare inflammation of small blood vessels that can damage the kidneys, lungs, and nerves. Kidney inflammation may progress rapidly to kidney failure, and bleeding into the lungs can be life-threatening. Other effects may include skin rash, nerve problems, fever, and joint or muscle pain.

topics.name: Microscopy
topics.clinical_significance: Microscopy can quickly show pathogens or abnormal cells in a specimen and help guide diagnosis and treatment. Results depend on specimen quality and the examiner's skill; some organisms are hard to see, and findings may need confirmation with culture or other tests.

topics.name: Microsporidiosis
topics.clinical_significance: In people with healthy immune systems, microsporidiosis may cause no symptoms or short-lived diarrhea, but it can also inflame the eye. In people with weakened immunity, especially advanced HIV, it can cause persistent diarrhea, weight loss, eye disease, or infection that spreads to several organs; widespread infection can be fatal.

topics.name: Microvascular Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Microvascular angina causes chest pain and reduced blood flow because the heart's small vessels do not widen normally, even when the major coronary arteries are not blocked. Symptoms may recur for years, and the risk of major cardiovascular events is higher than in the general population.

topics.name: Middle Ear and Tympanic Membrane Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Problems of the middle ear or eardrum can cause ear pain, drainage, or conductive hearing loss by blocking the passage of sound. Infection, pressure problems, and injury are common causes. Some chronic infections or complications, such as cholesteatoma, can lead to permanent hearing loss.

topics.name: Middle Ear and Tympanic Membrane Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Middle ear problems may follow infection, blockage of the eustachian tube, or injury. They can change eardrum movement and sound transmission, causing ear pain, pressure, drainage, or conductive hearing loss. Ear examination and hearing tests help identify the cause.

topics.name: Migraine
topics.clinical_significance: Migraine causes recurrent attacks of moderate-to-severe headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light or sound; some people also have a temporary neurologic aura. Severe attacks can disrupt daily life, and frequent attacks may become chronic. Acute and preventive treatments can reduce symptoms and attacks. A sudden thunderclap headache or clear change in pattern can signal another serious cause.

topics.name: Milia
topics.clinical_significance: Milia are benign, tiny cysts filled with keratin, often seen on newborns' faces and around the eyes or cheeks in older people. They usually cause no symptoms; milia in newborns often fade within weeks, while lesions in others may persist and are mainly a cosmetic concern.

topics.name: Miliaria
topics.clinical_significance: Blocked sweat ducts trap sweat in the skin, causing small blisters or bumps that may itch, sting, or hurt. Miliaria is common in hot, humid conditions or when skin stays covered; cooling and drying the skin helps the rash improve.

topics.name: Milk Thistle
topics.clinical_significance: Milk thistle (silymarin) is used as a supplement for liver and other conditions, but clear benefit for liver disease has not been established. It may cause stomach upset or allergy and can interact with medicines such as warfarin and some blood sugar drugs.

topics.name: Mineral Deficiency and Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Minerals are needed for normal bone, muscle, heart, and brain function. Too little or too much can cause illness; effects vary by mineral and may include anemia, poor growth, nerve or heart problems, and organ damage. Imbalances may result from diet, inherited conditions, or medical treatments.

topics.name: Minerals, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Minerals support bone and tooth formation, blood production, hormone and enzyme activity, and normal nerve, muscle, heart, and fluid balance. Too little or too much can disrupt these functions and cause serious problems, including anemia, abnormal heart rhythm, or developmental effects. Risk is higher with restrictive diets, some illnesses or treatments, and excessive supplements.

topics.name: Minimal Change Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children older than 1 year. It causes sudden, heavy protein loss in urine and swelling, while kidney function is usually normal. Most patients respond well to corticosteroid treatment, and progression to kidney failure is rare.

topics.name: Miscarriage
topics.clinical_significance: Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks, most often in the first trimester and commonly due to chromosomal problems. Bleeding and cramps may occur, but bleeding alone does not confirm pregnancy loss. Tissue left in the uterus can cause ongoing bleeding or infection; ultrasound and pregnancy hormone tests help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Bacterial Infections in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial infections in infants and children range from local illness to life-threatening infections of the blood or brain. Young infants may show only vague signs, such as fever, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness, and some infections can worsen quickly. Vaccines prevent several important causes.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Ear, Nose, and Throat Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Many ear, nose, and throat problems in children are common and temporary, but hearing loss or enlarged tonsils and adenoids can affect speech, learning, breathing, or swallowing. Early recognition of hearing problems matters because untreated hearing loss can hinder language and social development.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Gynecologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders include cysts, benign growths, and other abnormalities of the reproductive organs. They may cause pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, pressure, or pain during sex. Rarely, an ovarian mass can twist and cut off its blood supply, or a growth can be cancerous.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Opportunistic Fungi
topics.clinical_significance: Invasive disease from these fungi mainly affects people with weakened immune systems and can spread through the blood to other organs. Some species also cause superficial infections in healthy people. Because fungi differ in their resistance to antifungal medicines, identifying the exact species helps guide treatment.

topics.name: Miscellaneous Surgical Emergencies in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: These rare conditions can quickly become life-threatening. An inguinal hernia can become trapped, while a hole in the stomach or bowel or a blocked intestinal artery can cause severe infection or tissue death. Prompt assessment and often surgery are needed.

topics.name: Mite Bites
topics.clinical_significance: Most mite bites cause an itchy skin rash. Scabies mites burrow into the skin and cause an infestation that can spread between people. In parts of Asia and Australia, chiggers can transmit scrub typhus. Some mites linked to itchy reactions do not bite; dust mites cause allergy rather than bites.

topics.name: Mite-Borne Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Mite-borne typhus (scrub typhus) is a bacterial infection spread by chigger bites in parts of the Asia-Pacific region. It causes sudden fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash; a dark scab may form at the bite site. Severe illness can damage organs or cause shock, but early antibiotic treatment greatly improves recovery.

topics.name: Mitochondrial DNA Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: Mitochondrial DNA changes can disrupt the cell's energy production, especially affecting muscle, heart, and brain. Effects vary widely and may cause muscle, nerve, vision, or heart problems. These changes are passed through the mother’s side of the family, and the wide range of symptoms can make diagnosis difficult.

topics.name: Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Genetic changes can impair mitochondria’s ability to make ATP, the cell’s usable energy. The brain, nerves, eyes, and muscles are often affected, causing problems such as seizures, muscle weakness, vision or eye-movement problems, or heart disease. Lactic acid may also build up in the blood.

topics.name: Mitral Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Mitral insufficiency (regurgitation) occurs when the mitral valve does not close fully, so blood leaks backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium when the heart contracts. It may cause breathlessness or palpitations; severe or long-lasting leakage can lead to heart failure or abnormal heart rhythms.

topics.name: Mitral Regurgitation
topics.clinical_significance: Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve does not close fully, so blood leaks backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium when the heart contracts. It may cause breathlessness or palpitations; severe or long-lasting leakage can lead to heart failure or abnormal heart rhythms.

topics.name: Mitral Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Mitral stenosis narrows the valve opening and obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle. It usually results from rheumatic fever and may cause breathlessness and other heart-failure symptoms. Complications include an irregular heartbeat, high blood pressure in the lungs, and blood clots.

topics.name: Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP)
topics.clinical_significance: Mitral valve prolapse occurs when one or both valve flaps bulge into the left atrium as the heart contracts. It is usually harmless and causes no symptoms, but it can make the valve leak (mitral regurgitation). Less common complications include infection of the valve and rupture of its supporting cords.

topics.name: Mixed Anaerobic Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Mixed anaerobic infections involve anaerobic bacteria, often together with other bacteria. They can occur when normal bacteria infect damaged tissue and may cause serious illness that spreads locally or through the blood. Symptoms depend on the site; treatment usually includes antibiotics and may require drainage or removal of dead tissue.

topics.name: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)
topics.clinical_significance: MCTD is an uncommon rheumatic disease with features of lupus, systemic sclerosis, and inflammatory muscle disease. High levels of anti-RNP antibodies help identify it. It may cause swollen hands, Raynaud symptoms, joint pain, muscle inflammation, and lung or esophageal disease; symptoms can change over time.

topics.name: Molecular Components of the Immune System
topics.clinical_significance: Antibodies recognize specific targets, cytokines coordinate immune responses, and acute-phase proteins change during infection or tissue injury. C-reactive protein is a common marker of inflammation, but it does not show the cause. Excess cytokines can trigger a life-threatening immune reaction called cytokine storm.

topics.name: Molluscum Contagiosum
topics.clinical_significance: This contagious poxvirus infection causes small, smooth, firm bumps that often have a central dimple. It spreads through skin contact, scratching or touching the bumps, shared items, and bath water. It is usually limited to the skin but can be widespread in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Mollusk Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Mollusk injuries range from local pain or wounds to dangerous venom effects. Cone-snail stings and blue-ringed octopus bites can cause paralysis and breathing failure; severe cases may be fatal and need urgent supportive care.

topics.name: Molybdenum Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Molybdenum deficiency is rare and can reduce the activity of enzymes that process sulfites and other compounds. Inherited cofactor disorders can cause severe neurologic problems even when molybdenum intake is adequate. Deficiency during long-term intravenous nutrition has caused headache, rapid heart rate and breathing, vomiting, and coma.

topics.name: Molybdenum Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Excess molybdenum exposure has been linked to high uric acid and gout-like joint pain in some adults. However, the evidence is limited, and it is not clear that molybdenum caused these problems.

topics.name: Moniliasis
topics.clinical_significance: Moniliasis (candidiasis) is a yeast infection, usually affecting the skin or mucous membranes such as the mouth and genital skin. It often develops in warm, moist areas, and symptoms depend on the site. In people with weakened immunity, Candida can cause invasive, life-threatening infection.

topics.name: Monitoring and Testing the Critical Care Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Monitoring tracks vital signs, oxygen levels, fluid balance, and other measures to detect changes and guide care in critically ill patients. Blood tests help assess blood counts, electrolytes, and organ function. The type and frequency of monitoring depend on the patient’s condition, because invasive devices and repeated blood draws can cause harm.

topics.name: Mono
topics.clinical_significance: Mono (infectious mononucleosis) is usually caused by Epstein-Barr virus and causes fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue that may last weeks or months. Rare serious complications include airway blockage and spleen rupture. Treatment is usually supportive.

topics.name: Monobactams
topics.clinical_significance: Aztreonam is the only monobactam currently available. It treats some infections caused by aerobic gram-negative bacteria and may be used in people with serious allergy to other beta-lactam antibiotics, though cross-allergy with ceftazidime or cefiderocol is possible. It does not treat gram-positive bacteria or anaerobes, so other antibiotics may be needed.

topics.name: Monoclonal Gammopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Monoclonal gammopathies involve excess production of one type of antibody (M protein) by a single cell clone. They range from stable, symptom-free conditions to progressive blood cancers such as multiple myeloma. In some cases, the protein or cell growth can weaken immunity or damage the kidneys, bones, heart, or other organs.

topics.name: Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)
topics.clinical_significance: MGUS is a usually symptom-free condition in which noncancerous plasma cells produce a monoclonal protein. Some people develop nerve problems or bone loss, and a minority later develop myeloma or another blood disorder. Regular follow-up is needed to check for progression.

topics.name: Monocytopenia
topics.clinical_significance: Monocytopenia is a blood monocyte count below 200 cells per microliter. It can increase the risk of some infections and may occur with chemotherapy, certain infections or medicines, or blood and bone marrow disorders. Its significance depends on the cause and other blood cell counts.

topics.name: Monogenic Forms of Diabetes
topics.clinical_significance: Monogenic diabetes is a rare form caused by a change in a single gene. It often begins at a young age, may run in families, and can be mistaken for type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Genetic testing can identify the subtype, which matters because treatment varies; some types need no medicine, while others respond to specific drugs or require insulin.

topics.name: Mononeuritis Multiplex
topics.clinical_significance: Mononeuritis multiplex is damage to two or more separate peripheral nerves, often causing uneven areas of pain, tingling or numbness, and weakness. It is usually linked to another illness, such as vasculitis, diabetes, sarcoidosis, or infection, so finding and treating the cause is important.

topics.name: Mononeuropathies
topics.clinical_significance: A mononeuropathy affects one peripheral nerve, causing pain, tingling or numbness, or weakness in the area that nerve supplies. Injury or compression, such as in carpal tunnel syndrome, is a common cause. Treatment depends on the cause and may include surgery for severe nerve compression.

topics.name: Monosomy X
topics.clinical_significance: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is the complete or partial loss of one X chromosome, usually in phenotypic females. It commonly causes short stature and underdeveloped ovaries, which can lead to low estrogen, delayed puberty, and infertility. Heart or kidney defects, hearing problems, and learning difficulties may also occur; features vary, especially in mosaic forms.

topics.name: Mood Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Mood disorders are mental illnesses involving prolonged, severe changes in mood—depression, mania, or both—that interfere with daily functioning. They include depressive and bipolar disorders and are commonly treated with psychotherapy, medication, or both.

topics.name: Mood Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Mood-disorder symptoms usually occur in episodes of depression, mania, hypomania, or a mix of these. Their severity, duration, combination, and effect on daily life help distinguish a disorder from normal mood changes and identify the specific diagnosis. Episodes may resolve or shift to a different type.

topics.name: Moraxella catarrhalis Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Moraxella catarrhalis can cause middle-ear infections in children, sinusitis, and lower respiratory infections, especially COPD flare-ups in people with chronic lung disease. It can also live in the upper airway without causing illness. Nearly all strains make beta-lactamase, which affects antibiotic choice.

topics.name: Morbilli
topics.clinical_significance: Morbilli (measles) is a highly contagious viral infection that causes fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, white spots inside the mouth, and a rash that spreads from the face downward. Pneumonia or brain inflammation can be severe or fatal, especially in young children, pregnant people, and those who are malnourished or have weakened immunity. Vaccination prevents measles.

topics.name: Morton Neuralgia
topics.clinical_significance: Morton neuralgia (interdigital neuroma) is a benign thickening around a nerve between the toes, usually near the ball of the foot. It can cause burning or sharp pain, tingling, or a feeling of a pebble in the shoe, often worsened by tight footwear. Despite its name, it is not a tumor.

topics.name: Morton Neuroma
topics.clinical_significance: Morton neuroma is a benign thickening around a nerve near the ball of the foot, most often between the third and fourth toes; it is not a tumor. It can cause burning pain, tingling, or a feeling of a pebble in the shoe, often worsened by narrow footwear. Changing footwear may help.

topics.name: Motion Sickness
topics.clinical_significance: Motion sickness is a normal response to certain movements or conflicting signals from the eyes, inner ear, and body-position senses. It usually causes nausea and may also cause dizziness, pallor, sweating, abdominal discomfort, or vomiting. Behavior changes or medicines can help prevent or control symptoms.

topics.name: Movement and Cerebellar Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect control or coordination of movement.
