They may cause movement that is slow or reduced, extra involuntary movements such as tremor or tics, or poor coordination and balance from cerebellar problems. The pattern helps guide diagnosis of the underlying nervous system disorder.

topics.name: Movement and Cerebellar Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Smooth, purposeful movement depends on motor pathways, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum. Problems in these systems can cause movement that is slow or reduced, unwanted movements such as tremor or tics, or poor coordination, balance, walking, or eye control. The pattern helps clinicians identify which part of the nervous system may be affected.

topics.name: Moxibustion
topics.clinical_significance: Moxibustion is a traditional Chinese medicine practice in which dried mugwort is burned above, or sometimes directly on, acupuncture points. It is used for pain and other symptoms, but benefit varies by condition. It can cause round burns or blisters.

topics.name: Mpox (Monkeypox)
topics.clinical_significance: Mpox is an orthopoxvirus infection that causes a painful blistering or pus-filled rash, often with fever, feeling unwell, and swollen lymph nodes. It spreads through prolonged close contact, especially contact with lesions or body fluids, and can also spread through contaminated clothing or bedding. Severity varies; treatment is usually supportive, and vaccination helps prevent infection.

topics.name: Mpox Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Mpox vaccination helps prevent disease in people at high risk and may be recommended after a recent exposure. In the United States, the replication-limited MVA vaccine is the first-line option for high-risk adults. A live replication-competent vaccine is also available but is not first-line and may cause more adverse effects.

topics.name: MPX
topics.clinical_significance: MPX is another name for mpox (monkeypox), an orthopoxvirus infection that causes a painful blistering or pus-filled rash, often with fever, feeling unwell, and swollen lymph nodes. It spreads through prolonged close contact, including contact with lesions, body fluids, or contaminated clothing and bedding.

topics.name: MPX Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Mpox vaccines help prevent disease in people at high risk and may be used after recent exposure. In the United States, the replication-limited MVA vaccine is first-line; one study found moderate protection after a single dose. A live replication-competent vaccine is also available but is not first-line and can cause more adverse effects.

topics.name: MRON of the Jaw
topics.clinical_significance: MRON of the jaw is a rare condition in which exposed jawbone fails to heal for at least 8 weeks in someone taking certain medicines, such as bisphosphonates, denosumab, or antiangiogenic drugs, without prior head or neck radiation. It may follow a tooth extraction, be painless at first, and later cause pain or infection; it can be difficult to treat.

topics.name: Mucormycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Mucormycosis is an aggressive mold infection that mainly affects people with weakened immunity or poorly controlled diabetes, especially diabetic ketoacidosis. It often starts in the nose or sinuses and can spread to the eye or brain; it can also affect the lungs, skin, or other organs. It can progress quickly and is often life-threatening, requiring urgent antifungal treatment and surgery to remove dead tissue.

topics.name: Mucosal Neuroma Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Mucosal neuroma syndrome is another name for MEN 2B, a genetic condition that causes neuromas on the lips, tongue, or other mucous membranes. These may be an early sign of the syndrome, which is strongly linked to aggressive medullary thyroid cancer, often present by age 1, and sometimes pheochromocytoma. Prompt genetic testing and evaluation for tumors are important.

topics.name: Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
topics.clinical_significance: Mucous membrane pemphigoid is a chronic autoimmune disease. When it affects the eyes, it can progressively scar and shrink the conjunctiva and damage the eyelids and cornea, leading to vision loss or blindness. Early signs may be mild redness and irritation, so prompt eye-specialist care is important.

topics.name: Multifactorial (Complex) Inheritance
topics.clinical_significance: In multifactorial inheritance, many genes and environmental influences combine to affect a trait or disease. Conditions such as high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes can follow this pattern. They do not follow a simple inheritance rule, but close relatives may have higher risk, so family history can help guide prevention.

topics.name: Multifetal Gestation
topics.clinical_significance: Multifetal gestation means more than one fetus is present in the uterus. It increases risks for the pregnant person, including anemia, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and postpartum bleeding, and for the babies, including poor growth, preterm birth, stillbirth, or death soon after birth. Prenatal care includes closer monitoring of fetal growth and complications.

topics.name: Multiple Chemical Sensitivity
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple chemical sensitivity, also called idiopathic environmental intolerance, describes recurring, varied symptoms that a person attributes to low-level exposure to unrelated chemicals. Physical findings are often absent, and the definition is not universally accepted. Other possible causes should be ruled out; specific triggers may be difficult to identify.

topics.name: Multiple Congenital Contractures
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple congenital contractures (arthrogryposis) are stiff or fixed joints present at birth, caused by limited movement before birth. This is a finding shared by many different disorders, not one specific disease. The underlying cause affects prognosis and whether other problems, including developmental or intellectual difficulties, are present; identifying it helps guide care and genetic counseling.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Adenomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple endocrine adenomatosis is an older name for the inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes. These genetic conditions cause overgrowth or tumors in several hormone-producing glands, such as the parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas, thyroid, or adrenal glands; some tumors are cancerous. Early identification of affected relatives helps guide monitoring and treatment.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are genetic conditions that cause overgrowth or tumors in several hormone-producing glands. The pattern differs by type; tumors may affect the parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary, thyroid, or adrenal glands, and some can be cancerous. Because these syndromes often run in families, early identification and screening of relatives can help find tumors before complications develop.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia, Type 1 (MEN 1)
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 1 is an inherited syndrome that causes overgrowth or tumors mainly in the parathyroid glands, pancreatic or duodenal neuroendocrine cells, and pituitary gland. High blood calcium from overactive parathyroid glands is common; some tumors can be cancerous. Genetic screening of family members and ongoing monitoring can help detect tumors early.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia, Type 2A (MEN 2A)
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 2A is an inherited syndrome linked to RET gene mutations. Almost all affected people develop medullary thyroid cancer, often in childhood; some also develop adrenal pheochromocytomas, which can cause episodes of severe high blood pressure, or overactive parathyroid glands with high blood calcium. Genetic testing and regular screening can help detect tumors early.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia, Type 2B (MEN 2B)
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 2B is a genetic syndrome often caused by a new RET mutation, so a family history may be absent. Early signs can include neuromas on the lips or tongue. Medullary thyroid cancer is usually aggressive and almost always present by age 1; some people also develop pheochromocytoma and intestinal nerve growths. Early genetic diagnosis and tumor screening are important.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia, Type 4 (MEN 4)
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 4 is a rare inherited syndrome caused by a CDKN1B gene mutation. It resembles MEN 1 but usually begins later and has a slower course. It can cause parathyroid overactivity and high blood calcium, as well as tumors of the pancreas or pituitary gland. Hormone tests and imaging help find and monitor tumors.

topics.name: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasias (MEN), Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The MEN syndromes are four genetic conditions that often follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Each causes a different, sometimes overlapping mix of overgrowth or tumors in endocrine glands; some tumors are cancerous, and symptoms may begin at any age. Identifying affected people and relatives early supports monitoring and treatment.

topics.name: Multiple Mononeuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple mononeuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) affects at least two separate peripheral nerves, causing patchy pain, tingling or numbness, or weakness, often unevenly. It usually results from an underlying condition such as vasculitis, sarcoidosis, infection, or a metabolic disease, so identifying and treating the cause is important.

topics.name: Multiple Myeloma
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells that build up in bone marrow and make an abnormal single type of antibody protein. It can damage bone, causing pain or fractures, and may cause anemia, repeated infections, kidney injury, and high blood calcium.

topics.name: Multiple Personality Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple personality disorder is now called dissociative identity disorder. It involves two or more alternating identity states and memory gaps for everyday events, important personal information, or stressful events beyond normal forgetfulness. These changes can cause distress and interfere with daily life; treatment usually involves long-term psychotherapy.

topics.name: Multiple Sclerosis (MS)
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic disease of the central nervous system marked by scattered areas of damage to myelin in the brain and spinal cord. It can cause episodes of visual changes, numbness or tingling, weakness, stiffness, balance problems, and bladder dysfunction; symptoms may relapse and improve or worsen gradually. Accumulated nerve damage can lead to lasting disability.

topics.name: Multiple System Atrophy
topics.clinical_significance: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement and automatic body functions. It can cause slowness and stiffness or poor coordination and balance, along with problems such as low blood pressure on standing, urinary dysfunction, and constipation. Symptoms worsen over time and can lead to severe disability.

topics.name: Mumps
topics.clinical_significance: An acute contagious infection caused by mumps virus and spread through saliva or respiratory droplets. It usually causes fever and painful swelling of the salivary glands, especially the parotid glands. Complications can include inflammation of the testes or ovaries, pancreas, or brain and its coverings; permanent hearing loss is rare. MMR vaccination prevents most cases.

topics.name: Munchausen Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: An older name for factitious disorder imposed on self, especially when symptoms are dramatic or severe. The person deliberately falsifies or causes illness and presents as sick without an obvious external reward. The deception can lead to repeated investigations or harmful, unnecessary procedures.

topics.name: Munchausen Syndrome by Proxy
topics.clinical_significance: A former name for factitious disorder imposed on another. A caregiver deliberately falsifies or causes physical or psychological illness in someone in their care and presents that person as ill. The diagnosis applies to the caregiver; the person targeted may suffer serious harm from induced illness or unnecessary treatment.

topics.name: Mupirocin
topics.clinical_significance: A topical antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis. It treats impetigo and minor infected skin lesions and can clear Staphylococcus aureus from nasal carriage, although carriage may return. Prolonged use can select mupirocin-resistant bacteria.

topics.name: Murine (Endemic) Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: A flea-borne infection caused by Rickettsia typhi or R. felis, usually passed from rodents or other animals to people. It causes fever, chills, headache, and sometimes a rash. Illness is usually milder than epidemic typhus, but it can be more serious in older adults. Doxycycline is effective treatment.

topics.name: Muscle Cramps
topics.clinical_significance: A sudden, brief, involuntary, painful tightening of a muscle or group of muscles. Cramps are common in healthy people and often occur during or after exercise, at rest, or at night. Many are benign or exercise-related, but dehydration, electrolyte changes, medicines, and some neurologic or metabolic conditions can also contribute.

topics.name: Mushroom Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Illness caused by eating toxic mushrooms; effects vary by species and toxin. Vomiting and abdominal pain are common, while some toxins cause neurologic effects or delayed liver or kidney failure. Symptoms that begin several hours after eating a mushroom can signal more dangerous poisoning, although timing alone cannot determine toxicity.

topics.name: MUTYH Polyposis Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited, autosomal recessive condition caused by disease-causing variants in both copies of the MUTYH gene. It can cause many colorectal polyps and greatly raises the risk of colorectal cancer; polyps and cancers can also occur in other organs. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and guides cancer surveillance.

topics.name: Myasthenia Gravis
topics.clinical_significance: An autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction that causes fluctuating muscle weakness, which worsens with activity and improves with rest. It often affects the eye muscles, causing drooping eyelids or double vision, and may weaken muscles used for speech, swallowing, limb movement, or breathing. Severe swallowing or breathing weakness can cause a life-threatening myasthenic crisis.

topics.name: Mycetoma
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic, slowly progressive infection caused by fungi or bacteria that enter through a skin injury. It causes swelling and draining tunnels that release clumps of organisms called grains. The infection can spread into nearby muscle and bone, damaging and deforming the affected limb.

topics.name: Mycobacteria
topics.clinical_significance: A genus of acid-fast bacteria with waxy cell walls; many species grow slowly. It includes the causes of tuberculosis and leprosy, as well as environmental species that can infect the lungs, skin, lymph nodes, or other organs, especially when host defenses are weakened.

topics.name: Mycoplasmas
topics.clinical_significance: A group of bacteria that lack a cell wall, making them difficult to see with Gram stain and naturally resistant to antibiotics that target cell-wall formation, such as penicillins. Some species cause respiratory infections, including atypical pneumonia, or sexually transmitted urethritis; others may be part of normal urogenital flora.

topics.name: Mycosis Fungoides
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic T-cell lymphoma that mainly affects the skin. It may begin as a persistent, itchy rash and develop into patches, thicker plaques, or tumor nodules that can ulcerate. Advanced disease may involve lymph nodes or other organs.

topics.name: Myelodysplasia and Iron-Transport Deficiency Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: This topic covers two causes of reduced red-cell production. Myelodysplastic syndromes often cause normocytic or macrocytic anemia because the bone marrow makes blood cells abnormally. Iron-transport deficiency is a separate, rare cause of microcytic anemia; the inherited form called iron-refractory iron-deficiency anemia responds poorly to oral iron.

topics.name: Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)
topics.clinical_significance: A group of bone marrow disorders in which abnormal blood-forming cells make blood cells ineffectively. Low red-cell, white-cell, or platelet counts can cause fatigue, infections, or easy bruising and bleeding. Some cases progress to acute myeloid leukemia.

topics.name: Myelofibrosis, Primary
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic blood cancer in which abnormal blood-forming cells cause scarring in the bone marrow and disrupt normal blood-cell production. Blood formation may shift to the spleen, which often enlarges; anemia is common. The disease can progress to bone marrow failure or acute leukemia.

topics.name: Myeloma Cast Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: A kidney complication of multiple myeloma in which excess light-chain proteins combine with other proteins inside kidney tubules to form obstructing casts. These plugs injure the tubules and can cause severe kidney dysfunction or kidney failure.

topics.name: Myeloma Kidney
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for myeloma cast nephropathy: kidney injury in multiple myeloma caused when excess light-chain proteins combine with other proteins to form obstructing casts in kidney tubules. This can impair kidney function and progress to kidney failure.

topics.name: Myeloma-Related Kidney Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney injury linked to multiple myeloma, most often from excess abnormal light-chain proteins. These proteins can block kidney tubules as casts or build up in other kidney tissues; high blood calcium can also worsen kidney function. Severe injury can lead to kidney failure and affects prognosis.

topics.name: Myelomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells that often produces abnormal monoclonal proteins and damages bone. It may cause bone pain or fractures, anemia, kidney dysfunction, high blood calcium, and recurrent infections.

topics.name: Myelophthisic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia caused when tumor cells, scar tissue, or other abnormal tissue replaces normal bone marrow and reduces blood-cell production. Metastatic cancer is the most common cause. Blood smears may show immature red and white cells and teardrop-shaped red cells; other blood-cell counts may also be low.

topics.name: Myeloproliferative Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A group of bone marrow stem-cell disorders, now usually called myeloproliferative neoplasms, in which abnormal cells produce excess red cells, white cells, or platelets. The group includes polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis, and chronic myeloid leukemia; some forms can progress to acute leukemia.

topics.name: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A group of bone marrow disorders caused by abnormal clones of blood-forming stem cells. They can raise red-cell, white-cell, or platelet counts; some also cause marrow scarring or blood-cell production outside the marrow. Main types include essential thrombocythemia, polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis, and chronic myeloid leukemia; some can progress to acute leukemia.

topics.name: Myocardial Infarction
topics.clinical_significance: Death of part of the heart muscle due to reduced blood flow, usually when a clot blocks a coronary artery after a plaque ruptures. It may cause chest pressure or pain, breathlessness, sweating, or nausea, but can occur without clear symptoms. Diagnosis uses ECG findings and cardiac troponin blood tests. STEMI and NSTEMI are classified by ECG findings and evidence of heart-muscle injury, not simply by complete versus partial blockage. Complications include dangerous heart rhythms and heart failure.

topics.name: Myocarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the heart muscle, sometimes with injury or death of heart-muscle cells. Causes include infections, medicines or toxins, and inflammatory diseases, though many cases have no known cause. It may cause fatigue, breathlessness, swelling, or palpitations, but can also be silent or lead to heart failure, dangerous heart rhythms, or sudden death.

topics.name: Myocarditis and Pericarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation may affect the heart muscle (myocarditis), the sac around the heart (pericarditis), or both. Myocarditis can weaken the heart's pumping or cause dangerous heart rhythms. Pericarditis often causes chest pain and may lead to fluid around the heart; a large or rapidly collecting effusion can compress the heart and cause tamponade.

topics.name: Myoclonus
topics.clinical_significance: A brief, shocklike involuntary muscle jerk or sudden loss of muscle tone. It can occur normally when falling asleep or with hiccups, but may also result from medication effects, low oxygen, metabolic problems, epilepsy, or other neurologic disorders.

topics.name: Myomas
topics.clinical_significance: Benign growths of uterine muscle, also called uterine fibroids or leiomyomas. Many cause no symptoms; others cause heavy or irregular bleeding, anemia, pelvic pressure or pain, or urinary or bowel symptoms. Depending on their location, they may affect fertility or pregnancy.

topics.name: Myotonia Congenita
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited muscle disorder that causes delayed relaxation after contraction and muscle stiffness, usually beginning in childhood. Stiffness may ease with repeated movement, and the muscles may become enlarged. Some people, especially those with Becker disease, also have weakness; symptoms vary by type.

topics.name: Myotonic Dystrophy
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited muscle disease that causes delayed muscle relaxation, progressive weakness, and muscle wasting, often starting in adolescence or adulthood. Weakness can affect walking and hand use. The disease may also affect the heart, breathing, swallowing, digestion, eyes, and hormone function; effects vary by type. A severe form present from birth can cause feeding and breathing problems.

topics.name: Myringitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the eardrum, often with small fluid-filled blisters or bleeding. It can cause sudden ear pain and often occurs with a middle-ear infection. Hearing loss or fever may suggest a bacterial cause.

topics.name: Myxedema
topics.clinical_significance: In hypothyroidism, myxedema is swelling and thickening of the skin and tissues from a buildup of mucopolysaccharides, often causing facial puffiness. Long-standing, severe hypothyroidism can rarely lead to myxedema coma, a life-threatening emergency with very low body temperature, reduced alertness, and slowed breathing.

topics.name: N-acetyl-para-aminophenol
topics.clinical_significance: Acetaminophen (paracetamol; APAP) is a common medicine for pain and fever. An overdose can cause severe liver damage and liver failure, even when early symptoms are mild or absent; prompt treatment with N-acetylcysteine can prevent or limit the injury.

topics.name: Nail Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Nail changes can result from injury, infection, inflammation, skin disease, or conditions affecting the whole body. In people with diabetes or poor blood flow, toenail problems need attention because injury can lead to skin breakdown or infection.

topics.name: Nail Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Nail changes may result from injury, infection, inflammation, or genetic or whole-body conditions. In older adults and people with diabetes or poor blood flow, careful toenail care can help prevent skin breakdown and infection.

topics.name: Nail Dystrophies
topics.clinical_significance: Nail dystrophy means a change in nail texture or structure. Causes include fungal infection, injury, inflammatory skin disease, inherited conditions, and, rarely, cancer. These causes can look alike, so testing may be needed to guide treatment.

topics.name: Nail Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Nail injuries may cause pain, bleeding under the nail, temporary nail loss, or lasting nail deformity. A crush injury can also damage the nail bed or the bone beneath it; repeated trauma may lead to nail changes or infection.

topics.name: Nail-Patella Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder affecting the nails, kneecaps, elbows, and pelvic bones; the kneecaps may be small, misshapen, or absent. Some people develop kidney disease, which can progress to kidney failure, and glaucoma can also occur.

topics.name: Nanomedicine
topics.clinical_significance: Nanomedicine uses tiny particles and other nanotechnology to deliver drugs, diagnose disease, and image tissues. Nanoparticles can change where a drug travels and how long it stays in the body; their size and material affect how the body distributes and clears them, which can change their effects and safety.

topics.name: Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD)
topics.clinical_significance: A lasting pattern of exaggerated self-importance, a strong need for admiration, and difficulty recognizing other people’s feelings. It can strain relationships and may occur with depression or substance-use disorders; psychotherapy is the main treatment.

topics.name: Narcolepsy
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic disorder of sleep and wakefulness that causes severe daytime sleepiness and may cause sudden sleep attacks, even after a full night's sleep. Some people, especially those with type 1, also have brief emotion-triggered muscle weakness (cataplexy), sleep paralysis, or vivid hallucinations when falling asleep or waking. It can interfere with daily activities and increase the risk of injury, including vehicle crashes.

topics.name: Nasal and Pharyngeal Disorders, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation uses the person's symptom history and examination of the nose, throat, and neck; a flexible scope may be needed to see deeper areas. This helps identify causes such as infection, inflammation, injury, or a tumor.

topics.name: Nasal and Pharyngeal Symptoms, Approach to Patient With
topics.clinical_significance: Nasal and throat symptoms include congestion, sneezing, nasal discharge or bleeding, loss of smell or taste, mouth or throat pain or sores, and trouble swallowing or speaking. Causes range from infection and inflammation to injury or tumors, so examination helps identify the cause.

topics.name: Nasal Congestion and Rhinorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Stuffy nose and runny nose commonly occur together, most often with an upper respiratory infection or allergies. One-sided bloody or foul-smelling discharge, facial pain, or clear watery drainage after a head injury needs medical assessment because it may signal a foreign body, sinus disease, or a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Frequent use of decongestant nasal sprays can cause rebound congestion.

topics.name: Nasal Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: A foreign object in the nose, most common in young children, often causes one-sided foul-smelling, bloody, or pus-like discharge. Prompt removal helps prevent infection or tissue damage; button batteries need emergency removal because they can quickly burn nasal tissue, and an object pushed backward may block the airway.

topics.name: Nasal Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A break in the nasal bones or cartilage can cause pain, swelling, bruising, nosebleed, deformity, or blocked breathing. A blood collection inside the nasal septum needs immediate drainage to prevent cartilage damage and permanent deformity; clear watery drainage after facial trauma may signal a cerebrospinal fluid leak.

topics.name: Nasal Infections, Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial infection at the nostril opening, often caused by staph bacteria, can cause crusts, soreness, redness, swelling, and bleeding. A deeper infection of a nasal hair follicle can form a boil and spread to the skin of the nose; rarely, it can cause a dangerous blood clot in a nearby vein.

topics.name: Nasal Polyps
topics.clinical_significance: Soft, usually noncancerous growths from the chronically inflamed lining of the nose or sinuses. They can block airflow, cause postnasal drainage and reduced or lost smell, and often occur with chronic sinusitis, asthma, or allergies. A growth on only one side needs evaluation because it may be a different kind of mass, including a tumor.

topics.name: Nasogastric Intubation or Intestinal Intubation
topics.clinical_significance: A tube passed through the nose into the stomach or intestine can remove contents, relieve stomach or bowel distension, collect samples, give certain treatments, or provide nutrition. Incorrect placement can lead to lung aspiration; insertion can also rarely injure or perforate the nose, throat, esophagus, or stomach.

topics.name: Nasopharyngeal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: This cancer, usually a squamous cell carcinoma, may first appear as a neck lump or hearing loss caused by blockage near the ear. Other signs include nasal blockage or bleeding, ear pain, and facial numbness. It can spread to neck lymph nodes and nearby nerves; diagnosis requires examination and biopsy, and treatment usually includes radiation and chemotherapy.

topics.name: Naturopathy
topics.clinical_significance: A whole-person health system that emphasizes prevention, healthy living, and the body's natural healing abilities. It may use nutrition, exercise, herbs, acupuncture, massage, and other therapies. Evidence for many methods is limited or low quality, although some approaches may help in specific situations.

topics.name: Nausea and Vomiting
topics.clinical_significance: Nausea is the unpleasant feeling of needing to vomit; vomiting is the forceful expulsion of stomach contents. Causes range from infection, medicines, or pregnancy to bowel blockage or brain illness. Severe or ongoing vomiting can cause dehydration and salt imbalance; blood in the vomit, severe abdominal pain or swelling, confusion, stiff neck, or signs of dehydration need prompt assessment.

topics.name: Nausea and Vomiting During Early Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Nausea and vomiting are common in early pregnancy and can occur at any time of day, not only in the morning. Persistent, severe vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum) can prevent enough food and fluid intake, causing dehydration, abnormal blood salts, ketosis, and weight loss; it needs medical assessment and treatment.

topics.name: Nausea and Vomiting in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Vomiting in children is commonly caused by viral gastroenteritis, but causes vary by age and can include intestinal blockage or serious infection. Fluid loss can cause dehydration, especially in infants. Green vomit, repeated or forceful vomiting in a young infant, unusual sleepiness, a swollen abdomen, or ongoing vomiting with poor growth needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Neck and Back Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Most neck and back pain comes from mechanical problems in the spine. If a nerve is affected, pain may spread into an arm or leg with tingling, numbness, or weakness; rarely, the cause is infection, cancer, fracture, or another serious illness. Fever, new weakness, bladder or bowel problems, unexplained weight loss, or severe night pain need prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Neck Mass
topics.clinical_significance: Most neck masses are enlarged lymph nodes, often related to infection, but cysts and cancers are also possible. A hard, fixed mass, a new mass in an older adult, or a mass with trouble swallowing or persistent hoarseness needs prompt medical evaluation.

topics.name: Necrotizing Cellulitis
topics.clinical_significance: A rapidly spreading, life-threatening bacterial infection that destroys tissue beneath the skin and often the fascia. Pain can be much worse than the early skin changes suggest. It requires urgent antibiotics and surgery to remove dead tissue; delays can lead to gangrene and death.

topics.name: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
topics.clinical_significance: A life-threatening intestinal disease, most common in premature or sick newborns, in which inflammation destroys part of the bowel wall. It can cause feeding problems, a swollen abdomen, green vomit, bloody stools, unusual sleepiness, temperature changes, or pauses in breathing, and may lead to bowel perforation, sepsis, or death; urgent neonatal care is needed.

topics.name: Necrotizing Fasciitis
topics.clinical_significance: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly spreading, life-threatening bacterial infection beneath the skin that usually involves the fascia. Pain may be much worse than the visible skin changes suggest. Urgent antibiotics and surgery to remove dead tissue are needed to prevent gangrene and death.

topics.name: Necrotizing Otitis Externa
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, serious infection of the ear canal, often caused by Pseudomonas bacteria, that can spread to the temporal bone and skull base. It causes severe deep ear pain and foul-smelling drainage and mainly affects older adults and people with diabetes or weakened immunity. Spread can damage facial or other cranial nerves and, rarely, reach the brain, so prompt treatment with systemic antibiotics is needed.

topics.name: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection
topics.clinical_significance: A severe bacterial infection that spreads quickly through tissue under the skin and often the fascia, causing swelling and severe pain that may be much worse than the skin looks. It is an emergency requiring urgent antibiotics and surgery to remove dead tissue; without early treatment, it can lead to gangrene and death.

topics.name: Necrotizing Subcutaneous Infection
topics.clinical_significance: A rapidly spreading, life-threatening bacterial infection that destroys tissue beneath the skin and often the fascia. Severe pain may be much worse than early skin changes suggest. Urgent antibiotics and surgery to remove dead tissue are needed; without early treatment, the affected area can become gangrenous.

topics.name: Needle Decompression
topics.clinical_significance: An emergency procedure that releases trapped air from around a lung in tension pneumothorax, relieving pressure on the lung and major blood vessels. It can be life-saving when a chest tube cannot be placed quickly, but is a temporary measure and is followed by chest-tube placement.

topics.name: Nematodes (Roundworms)
topics.clinical_significance: Parasitic roundworms can infect the intestine or move through body tissues. Depending on the species and where it lives, infection may cause no symptoms or lead to digestive problems, anemia, lung symptoms, or skin, eye, or lymphatic disease. Diagnosis and treatment depend on the type of worm.

topics.name: Neonatal Bacterial Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: A serious infection of the membranes around a newborn's brain and spinal cord, often occurring with sepsis. Signs may be subtle and include unusual sleepiness, irritability, vomiting, unstable temperature, pauses in breathing, or seizures; neck stiffness or a bulging soft spot may be absent. It needs urgent hospital treatment with antibiotics and can cause death or lasting problems such as hearing loss.

topics.name: Neonatal Cholestasis
topics.clinical_significance: Reduced bile flow or bilirubin release from a newborn's liver causes direct bilirubin buildup and jaundice. Dark urine, pale stools, or an enlarged liver are important clues. It is never normal and needs prompt assessment because causes such as biliary atresia may need early treatment; ongoing cholestasis can impair fat and vitamin absorption, growth, and liver function.

topics.name: Neonatal Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation or infection of the conjunctiva during the first month of life, causing red eyes and watery or pus-like discharge. Causes include bacteria or viruses acquired around birth and irritation from eye drops. Gonococcal infection can quickly damage the cornea and cause blindness, while chlamydia or herpes may spread beyond the eye, so a newborn with eye redness or discharge needs prompt assessment and cause-specific treatment.

topics.name: Neonatal Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Newborns usually acquire hepatitis B from an infected mother during birth and often have no symptoms at first. Infection at birth often becomes chronic, raising the later risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Prompt vaccination and hepatitis B immune globulin help prevent infection in newborns of infected mothers.

topics.name: Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: HSV infection in a newborn, usually acquired during delivery, can affect the skin, eyes, and mouth or spread to the brain and other organs. Brain or widespread disease can be fatal or cause lasting neurologic problems, so suspected cases need urgent testing and intravenous acyclovir.

topics.name: Neonatal Hospital-Acquired Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Hospital-acquired infections mainly affect premature or medically ill newborns, especially those with very low birth weight or tubes and catheters. They can cause bloodstream infection or pneumonia. Careful hand hygiene and proper care of medical devices help prevent them.

topics.name: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
topics.clinical_significance: Jaundice is common in newborns, but early, rapidly worsening, or prolonged jaundice may signal an underlying problem. Very high bilirubin can damage the brain and cause lasting movement or sensory problems. Bilirubin levels are checked and treated based on the baby’s age, prematurity, and health; phototherapy helps prevent brain injury.

topics.name: Neonatal Hypercalcemia
topics.clinical_significance: High blood calcium in a newborn can cause poor feeding, vomiting, constipation, and dehydration; severe cases may cause lethargy or seizures. It often results from too much calcium or vitamin D, or too little phosphate in feeds, so finding and correcting the cause is important.

topics.name: Neonatal Hyperglycemia
topics.clinical_significance: High blood sugar in newborns often occurs in very premature or very low-birth-weight infants receiving IV glucose, or during serious illness. It can cause excess urination and loss of fluid and salts, and is linked to worse outcomes from the underlying illness; close glucose and fluid monitoring is important.

topics.name: Neonatal Hypernatremia
topics.clinical_significance: High sodium in a newborn usually reflects water loss and dehydration, often from poor feeding or illness. Dehydration may be more severe than it looks; severe cases can cause seizures, bleeding in the brain, or kidney injury. Sodium must be lowered gradually during rehydration to avoid brain swelling.

topics.name: Neonatal Hypocalcemia
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood calcium in a newborn is often linked to prematurity, small size at birth, maternal diabetes, or low oxygen during birth. Mild cases may have no symptoms, but severe cases can cause poor feeding, jitteriness, pauses in breathing, muscle spasms, or seizures.

topics.name: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
topics.clinical_significance: Babies born early or small, and babies of mothers with diabetes, are at higher risk of low blood sugar after birth. Many have no symptoms, but severe or prolonged low levels can cause poor feeding, shakiness, pauses in breathing, seizures, or coma. At-risk babies need prompt glucose checks and treatment.

topics.name: Neonatal Hyponatremia
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood sodium in a newborn often follows vomiting or diarrhea, especially when lost fluids are replaced with liquids that contain little salt. Severe cases can cause seizures or coma. Sodium must be corrected slowly to prevent harmful fluid shifts in the brain.

topics.name: Neonatal Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn infections can pass from the mother before or during birth or spread after birth. Premature babies are at higher risk, and signs may be subtle, such as poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, fever, or low temperature. Because infection can worsen quickly, suspected cases need prompt testing and treatment.

topics.name: Neonatal Listeriosis
topics.clinical_significance: Listeriosis can pass to a baby before or during birth, often after the mother eats contaminated food. It may cause sepsis or pneumonia soon after birth, or meningitis or sepsis later. Early infection can cause breathing or circulation failure and may be fatal, so prompt testing and antibiotic treatment are important.

topics.name: Neonatal Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumonia in a newborn may be part of a bloodstream infection, especially when it begins soon after birth; later cases often occur in infants on breathing tubes in intensive care. It can cause breathing problems and may progress to shock or death, so prompt evaluation for sepsis and antibiotic treatment are important.

topics.name: Neonatal Resuscitation
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal resuscitation is urgent support for newborns who do not breathe effectively or have a very slow heart rate. About 1 in 10 need breathing assistance, but fewer than 1 in 100 need extensive resuscitation. Prompt warming, airway support, and assisted breathing can restore breathing and circulation; some infants also need chest compressions.

topics.name: Neonatal Seizure Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Seizures in a newborn often signal an urgent problem, such as low oxygen, bleeding in the brain, infection, or low blood sugar. They can be subtle or have no visible signs, so prompt testing is needed to find and treat the cause. Long-term effects range from none to developmental problems or epilepsy.

topics.name: Neonatal Sepsis
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal sepsis is a life-threatening infection in a newborn, often bacterial, that may begin before, during, or after birth. Early signs can be subtle, such as poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, breathing pauses, or temperature changes. Because it can worsen quickly, suspected sepsis needs urgent testing and antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Neonatal Wet Lung Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: This causes temporary fast breathing and breathing difficulty in a newborn, usually because lung fluid clears slowly after birth. It is more common after cesarean birth without labor and in premature infants; oxygen or other breathing support may be needed. It usually resolves within 2 to 3 days, but infection and other serious causes of breathing difficulty must be ruled out.

topics.name: Neonates, Caring for Sick
topics.clinical_significance: Sick or premature newborns may need special care, but once stable, contact with parents is usually safe with appropriate precautions. Skin-to-skin contact can support survival, stability, growth, and development. Including parents in daily care and feeding also helps prepare them to care for the baby at home.

topics.name: Neonates, Infections in
topics.clinical_significance: Newborns can get infections before, during, or after birth; premature babies are at higher risk. Signs are often vague, such as poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, breathing problems, or changes in temperature. Some infections can become severe or spread to the blood or brain, so prompt evaluation and treatment are important.

topics.name: Nephritic Syndrome, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Nephritic syndrome is inflammation of the kidney’s filters, often causing blood and some protein in the urine. It may also cause swelling, high blood pressure, less urine, and worsening kidney function. Some forms can progress to kidney failure within weeks, so prompt assessment of the cause and kidney function is important.

topics.name: Nephroblastoma
topics.clinical_significance: Nephroblastoma, also called Wilms tumor, is a kidney cancer that mostly affects children under 5. It often appears as a painless lump in the belly; some children also have high blood pressure or blood in the urine. Treatment usually includes surgery and chemotherapy, and most children can be cured.

topics.name: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus
topics.clinical_significance: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the kidneys cannot respond to vasopressin and pass large amounts of dilute urine. People who cannot drink enough, especially infants, can become severely dehydrated and develop high blood sodium, which may cause seizures or coma. Untreated inherited disease in infants can cause lasting brain injury, so reliable access to water and early treatment are important.

topics.name: Nephrolithiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney and urinary stones may cause sudden severe side or back pain, nausea, and blood in the urine, especially when a stone blocks urine flow. A blockage with infection needs urgent treatment, and prolonged blockage can damage the kidney. Stones may recur; low fluid intake and some metabolic disorders increase risk.

topics.name: Nephronophthisis and Autosomal Dominant Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (ADTKD)
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited kidney disorders cause the kidneys to lose salt and become unable to concentrate urine, leading to frequent urination and thirst. Kidney function gradually worsens and may eventually fail. Nephronophthisis usually causes kidney failure in childhood, while ADTKD often progresses to kidney failure in adulthood and may cause early gout. Early diagnosis helps manage complications and plan for dialysis or transplant.

topics.name: Nephrotic Syndrome, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Nephrotic syndrome occurs when damaged kidney filters let large amounts of protein leak into the urine, causing low blood protein and swelling. It also raises the risk of serious infections and blood clots, and may reduce kidney function. Finding and treating the cause helps limit complications; the outlook varies by cause.

topics.name: Nerve and Muscle Biopsy
topics.clinical_significance: Nerve and muscle biopsies are usually done together to investigate nerve or muscle problems. Nerve biopsy can help distinguish types of nerve damage or detect rare infections when other tests are inconclusive; muscle biopsy can confirm muscle disease. The sample site is chosen based on the affected area.

topics.name: Nerve Chemical-Warfare Agents
topics.clinical_significance: These agents disrupt nerve signaling and can quickly cause excess secretions, breathing difficulty, muscle twitching, weakness or paralysis, seizures, and death. Exposure may occur by breathing vapor or through skin contact. Suspected exposure is a medical emergency requiring immediate decontamination and antidote treatment.

topics.name: Nerve Root Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure on a nerve root can cause shooting pain, tingling or numbness, and weakness in the area supplied by that nerve, often due to a herniated disc. New or worsening weakness or loss of bladder or bowel control may signal serious spinal compression. These symptoms need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Neuroblastoma
topics.clinical_significance: Neuroblastoma is a cancer of immature nerve cells and the most common cancer in infants. It usually starts in an adrenal gland or nearby nerve tissue; symptoms depend on where it starts and whether it has spread. Some tumors regress on their own, while others spread and need intensive treatment, so the outlook varies with age, stage, and tumor features.

topics.name: Neurocutaneous Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Neurocutaneous syndromes affect the skin and nervous system and may also involve the eyes or other organs. Skin changes can be clues to problems such as seizures, learning or developmental difficulties, vision problems, or tumors; the risks vary by syndrome. Early diagnosis and regular monitoring help detect complications.

topics.name: Neurodermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Neurodermatitis (atopic dermatitis) is a long-term skin condition that causes recurring inflammation and itching. Scratching can thicken and damage the skin and increase the risk of infection. Moisturizing, avoiding triggers, and treating flares help control symptoms and reduce complications.

topics.name: Neuroendocrine Skin Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive skin cancer that often grows quickly and can spread to lymph nodes and distant organs. It may appear as a painless, firm, red or bluish lump, often on sun-exposed skin, especially in older or immunosuppressed people. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and tests to find how far it has spread help guide treatment. The outlook is worse when the cancer has spread.

topics.name: Neuroendocrine Tumors of the Lungs
topics.clinical_significance: Lung neuroendocrine tumors vary in behavior, but tumors in the airways are often cancerous. About half cause no symptoms; others can block airways, causing cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, or repeated pneumonia. Some release hormones that cause problems such as Cushing syndrome or carcinoid syndrome. Imaging and biopsy help find and classify these tumors because treatment and outlook depend on their type and spread.

topics.name: Neurofibromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Neurofibromatosis is a group of genetic disorders that cause nerve tumors and can also affect the skin, eyes, bones, or hearing. NF1 often causes café-au-lait skin spots and other nerve tumors; NF2-related schwannomatosis can cause hearing and balance problems, while other schwannomatosis often causes lasting pain. Some tumors can press on nerves or become cancerous, so regular checks help find complications early.

topics.name: Neurogenic Arthropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Neurogenic (neuropathic) arthropathy can develop when nerve damage reduces pain and position sense, often from diabetes or stroke. Repeated unnoticed injuries can rapidly damage and deform a joint, even when pain is mild; swelling and instability are common. Early diagnosis and protecting the joint can limit damage. Infection must also be considered, especially in people with diabetes.

topics.name: Neurogenic Bladder
topics.clinical_significance: Nerve damage can make the bladder weak or overactive, causing urine leakage or retention. Depending on the pattern, repeated infections, high bladder pressure, or urine backing up toward the kidneys can cause kidney damage. In people with a high spinal cord injury, bladder overfilling can trigger a dangerous rise in blood pressure.

topics.name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic medicines and some nausea medicines; it can also follow stopping certain Parkinson medicines. Confusion, severe muscle stiffness, high fever, fast heartbeat, and unstable blood pressure may develop over days. It needs immediate hospital treatment because muscle breakdown, kidney injury, and death can occur.

topics.name: Neurologic Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Neurologic disorders in children can affect the brain, spinal cord, or nerves. They may cause seizures, weakness, unusual movements, or delays or loss of developmental skills. Some need urgent treatment, and early evaluation can identify treatable causes and connect children with support for learning and movement.

topics.name: Neurologic Disorders, Introduction, Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Neurologic symptoms can affect movement, sensation, vision, hearing, balance, sleep, awareness, or thinking. Because many disorders can cause similar symptoms, their pattern and speed of onset help guide examination and testing. Sudden weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, vision loss, or reduced alertness may signal an emergency.

topics.name: Neurologic Disorders, Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: Symptoms such as weakness, numbness, pain, balance problems, seizures, or changes in speech and vision can have many causes. Their location, timing, and combination help clinicians identify which part of the nervous system may be affected and choose appropriate tests. Sudden new neurologic problems may need emergency evaluation.

topics.name: Neurologic Examination
topics.clinical_significance: A neurologic examination checks mental function, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and walking. The pattern of findings helps locate the problem and narrow possible causes; repeat examinations can show whether it is changing or responding to treatment.

topics.name: Neurologic Examination, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: The neurologic examination checks whether the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and related muscles and senses are working normally. Matching abnormal findings to their location helps narrow the cause of symptoms, and repeat examinations can track the illness or response to treatment.

topics.name: Neurologic Imaging Studies, Other
topics.clinical_significance: Other imaging tests answer specific questions about the brain, blood vessels, or spine. Angiography and Doppler ultrasound can show problems in blood vessels; bedside ultrasound can detect bleeding or excess fluid in young infants. CT myelography can show the spinal cord and nearby bones when MRI is unavailable. The test is chosen based on the suspected problem and its risks.

topics.name: Neurologic Patient, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: A careful history and neurologic examination help locate whether symptoms come from the brain, spinal cord, nerves, or muscles. This narrows the possible causes and helps clinicians choose the right tests, reducing the risk of missed diagnoses and unnecessary testing.

topics.name: Neurologic Tests and Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Neurologic tests help find and locate problems in the brain, spinal cord, nerves, or muscles. Depending on the symptoms, imaging, brain-wave tests, nerve and muscle tests, or spinal-fluid tests can help detect structural problems, seizures, nerve or muscle disease, and infection or inflammation. The history and examination guide which tests are needed.

topics.name: Neuromuscular Junction Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders disrupt signals between nerves and muscles, causing fluctuating weakness without loss of feeling. Weakness may affect the eyes, speech, swallowing, limbs, or breathing; breathing or swallowing problems can be life-threatening and need urgent care. Causes include autoimmune diseases, botulism, and medicines or toxins; Lambert-Eaton syndrome can be linked to small-cell lung cancer.

topics.name: Neuromuscular Transmission, Disorders of
topics.clinical_significance: Disorders of neuromuscular transmission interfere with signaling at the nerve-muscle connection, usually causing fluctuating weakness while sensation remains normal. Eye, face, swallowing, and breathing muscles may be affected; severe swallowing or breathing weakness is an emergency. Causes include myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, botulism, and drugs or toxins; Lambert-Eaton syndrome may be linked to small-cell lung cancer.

topics.name: Neuromyelitis Optica
topics.clinical_significance: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an immune-mediated disorder that mainly affects the optic nerves and spinal cord. Attacks can cause severe vision loss, weakness, numbness, muscle spasms, or bladder problems and may lead to lasting disability. NMOSD is different from multiple sclerosis, so accurate diagnosis and the right immune treatment help prevent further attacks.

topics.name: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
topics.clinical_significance: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an immune-mediated disease that mainly affects the optic nerves and spinal cord. Attacks may cause severe vision loss, weakness, numbness, muscle spasms, or bladder problems and can leave lasting disability. NMOSD is distinct from multiple sclerosis; MRI and antibody tests help tell them apart, and immune treatment can reduce attacks.

topics.name: Neuromyotonia
topics.clinical_significance: Neuromyotonia (Isaacs syndrome) causes continuous muscle twitching and can also cause cramps, stiffness, delayed muscle relaxation, and excess sweating. It may be inherited or acquired and can occur with autoimmune disease or tumors such as thymoma, so evaluation for associated conditions is important. Nerve and muscle electrical tests help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Neuro-Ophthalmologic and Cranial Nerve Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Problems in the visual pathways or cranial nerves may cause vision loss, double vision, drooping eyelids, abnormal pupils, facial weakness or pain, hearing or balance changes, or trouble swallowing. Causes range from diabetes and inflammation to stroke, aneurysm, or tumors, so prompt examination is important because some causes need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Neuro-ophthalmologic and Cranial Nerve Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Problems in eye pathways or cranial nerves can affect vision, eye movement, pupil size, facial movement or feeling, hearing, balance, speech, or swallowing. The pattern helps locate the affected nerve or brain pathway and may point to serious causes such as stroke, aneurysm, or tumor. A focused examination and often CT or MRI help find the cause; some sudden problems need urgent treatment.

topics.name: Neuropathic Arthropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Neuropathic arthropathy occurs when nerve damage reduces pain and joint-position sense, so injuries may go unnoticed and the joint can rapidly break down. Swelling, instability, and deformity may be severe despite mild pain, often in people with diabetes or stroke. Early diagnosis and protecting the joint can slow damage; infection should also be considered.

topics.name: Neuropathic Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Neuropathic pain comes from damage or dysfunction in the nerves, spinal cord, or brain rather than direct tissue injury. It may feel burning, tingling, shooting, or electric, sometimes with numbness or pain from light touch, and can persist after the original injury heals. Finding and treating the cause matters; treatment often differs from that for tissue-injury pain.

topics.name: Neurotransmission
topics.clinical_significance: Neurotransmission is how nerve cells communicate through electrical signals and chemical messengers. Changes in this process can cause neurologic or psychiatric symptoms, and many medicines work by changing how neurotransmitters are made, released, received, or removed.

topics.name: Neutropenia
topics.clinical_significance: Neutropenia is a low blood neutrophil count. Severe neutropenia raises the risk and seriousness of bacterial and fungal infections, and signs such as redness or swelling may be less clear. Fever may be the only warning of a serious infection and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Nevi (Moles)
topics.clinical_significance: Most moles are harmless. Their clinical importance is that melanoma can resemble a mole, and people with many or atypical moles or a family history of melanoma have a higher risk. A mole that is uneven in shape, has irregular edges or varied colors, changes, or bleeds should be checked by a clinician.

topics.name: Nevus Araneus
topics.clinical_significance: A few spider angiomas are common and often harmless. Many or prominent lesions can occur with liver disease, including cirrhosis. They may also appear during pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use and often fade after pregnancy or stopping the medication.

topics.name: Newborns and Infants, Care of
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn and infant care includes early health checks, recommended screening and preventive care, feeding and growth support, safe sleep, and follow-up. These steps help find health problems early, check feeding and jaundice, and reduce preventable illness or injury.

topics.name: Niacin Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Severe niacin deficiency causes pellagra, which can affect the skin, mouth, digestive tract, and brain. It may cause a sun-sensitive rash, diarrhea, and confusion or other changes in thinking. Treatment with niacin usually works; other nutritional deficiencies may also need attention.

topics.name: Niacin Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Toxicity usually follows high-dose niacin supplements or medicines, not usual food intake. It can cause flushing and stomach upset; higher doses may injure the liver, worsen blood sugar, or trigger gout. Niacin supplements are not recommended to prevent cardiovascular disease because they have not reduced risk and can cause harm.

topics.name: Nicotinic Acid Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: High-dose nicotinic acid can cause flushing and, less often, liver injury. Toxic doses may also cause jaundice, stomach discomfort, blurred vision, raise blood sugar, or trigger gout; some sustained-release forms carry greater liver risk.

topics.name: Niemann-Pick Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Niemann-Pick disease refers to rare inherited disorders in which fats build up in cells. Different forms can affect the liver, spleen, lungs, blood cells, or nervous system; some cause severe neurologic decline in early childhood, while others progress more slowly. Enzyme or genetic testing helps identify the form because the course and care differ.

topics.name: Nil Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Nil disease, also called minimal change disease, is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It causes sudden heavy protein loss in urine and swelling, often while kidney function remains normal. Most patients respond to corticosteroids and have a good outlook, though relapses can occur.

topics.name: Nipple Discharge
topics.clinical_significance: Most nipple discharge has a benign cause, such as a growth inside a milk duct or widened ducts. Discharge that starts on its own from one breast, especially if bloody or accompanied by a lump or skin change, needs medical evaluation because a small proportion of cases are due to cancer. Milky discharge from both breasts can be linked to hormone changes, medicines, or other health conditions.

topics.name: Nitrofurantoin
topics.clinical_significance: Nitrofurantoin treats or prevents uncomplicated bladder infections because it reaches high levels in urine. It does not treat kidney or bloodstream infections. Nausea is common; prolonged use can cause lung or liver injury, and nerve damage may occur, especially with kidney impairment.

topics.name: Nocardia
topics.clinical_significance: Nocardia are environmental bacteria that can cause pneumonia or skin infection and may spread to the brain or other organs. Risk is higher in people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease, though healthy people can also be affected. Treatment usually requires prolonged antibiotics guided by species identification and susceptibility testing.

topics.name: Nocardiosis
topics.clinical_significance: Nocardiosis is usually acquired from soil by inhaling the bacteria or through a skin wound. It often affects the lungs or skin and can spread to the brain or other organs, especially in people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease. Disseminated infection can be life-threatening and needs prolonged antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Nociplastic Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Nociplastic pain is linked to changes in how the nervous system processes pain and can continue even when there is no ongoing tissue injury. It may occur along with pain from tissue damage or nerve injury. Care often combines gradual physical activity, symptom-focused medicines, and psychological support.

topics.name: Nonadherence in Children
topics.clinical_significance: When children do not take medicines as prescribed, treatment may not work well and illness may worsen. Barriers include unpleasant taste, trouble swallowing, complex schedules, cost, school routines, or concerns and misunderstandings in the child or caregiver. Finding these barriers can help families and clinicians make treatment easier to follow.

topics.name: Nonallergic Rhinitis
topics.clinical_significance: Nonallergic rhinitis is inflammation inside the nose that causes congestion or a runny nose without an allergic cause. It is often due to a virus; irritants, strong odors, cold or dry air, and changes in temperature or humidity can also trigger symptoms. Treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Nonatheromatous Arteriosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: This is thickening and stiffening of artery walls without atherosclerotic plaque. It often causes no symptoms, but small-vessel disease can reduce blood flow to organs, and weakening of larger arteries can lead to aneurysm or dissection. Calcified, stiff arteries may also cause blood pressure readings to appear falsely high.

topics.name: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis forms sterile platelet-and-fibrin clots on heart valves, often with cancer, severe illness, lupus, or a clotting disorder. The clots can break off and block arteries, causing stroke or damage to other organs. It must be distinguished from infective endocarditis because treatment differs.

topics.name: Noncholera Vibrio Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Noncholera Vibrio bacteria from warm coastal water or seafood can cause diarrhea or wound infections. Vibrio vulnificus can cause rapidly severe wound infection or bloodstream infection, especially after seafood exposure in people with chronic liver disease or weakened immunity; prompt treatment is important.

topics.name: Non-Compaction Cardiomyopathy
topics.clinical_significance: True non-compaction cardiomyopathy can weaken the heart, cause heart failure or abnormal rhythms, and allow clots to form and cause stroke. Some patients are at risk of sudden cardiac death. Extra heart-muscle ridges on imaging alone can be a normal finding, so diagnosis depends on the full clinical assessment.

topics.name: Nonerosive Gastritis
topics.clinical_significance: Nonerosive gastritis is often linked to Helicobacter pylori infection, and many people have no symptoms. Long-lasting inflammation can thin or change the stomach lining, sometimes leading to vitamin B12 deficiency or a higher risk of stomach cancer. Treating H. pylori can reduce cancer risk.

topics.name: Nonfatal Drowning
topics.clinical_significance: Nonfatal drowning is breathing impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid in a person who survives. Lack of oxygen can injure the brain and other organs, while aspiration can damage the lungs. Breathing problems may appear or worsen after rescue, so medical assessment and observation are important.

topics.name: Nonfreezing Tissue Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: These injuries result from cold exposure without tissue freezing. Frostnip and chilblains are usually temporary, but prolonged exposure to wet cold can cause immersion (trench) foot, with nerve and small-vessel injury, skin breakdown, and pain, numbness, or cold sensitivity that may persist.

topics.name: Nonfunctional Adrenal Masses
topics.clinical_significance: These adrenal growths are often found by chance, and most are benign. However, some make small amounts of hormones without obvious symptoms, and some are cancerous. Hormone tests and imaging help assess these risks and guide whether the mass needs monitoring or surgery.

topics.name: Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas
topics.clinical_significance: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a broad group of cancers of lymphocytes; some grow slowly, while others grow quickly. It often causes painless swollen lymph nodes but can also affect organs or blood. Biopsy and subtype testing guide care because outlook and treatment vary; some slow-growing cases can be monitored, while aggressive types often need prompt treatment.

topics.name: Noninfectious Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Noninfectious meningitis is inflammation of the tissues around the brain and spinal cord from causes such as autoimmune disease, cancer, or medicines. It can cause headache, fever, and a stiff neck, like infectious meningitis, so infection must be ruled out promptly. Care focuses on treating the cause or stopping the medicine responsible.

topics.name: Noninfective Endocarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Noninfective endocarditis forms sterile platelet-and-fibrin deposits on heart valves, often linked to cancer, clotting disorders, lupus, or blood-vessel inflammation. Deposits can break off and cause stroke or other organ damage, or sometimes become infected. Heart imaging and blood cultures help distinguish it from infective endocarditis, which needs different treatment.

topics.name: Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV)
topics.clinical_significance: NIPPV supports breathing by delivering pressurized air through a tight-fitting mask, avoiding a breathing tube in suitable patients. Because the airway remains unprotected, it is unsafe when a patient cannot protect their airway or is unstable; worsening breathing may require prompt intubation.

topics.name: Noninvasive Prenatal Fetal Screening Tests
topics.clinical_significance: These tests estimate the chance of certain fetal chromosome conditions or birth defects; they do not diagnose them. A high-risk result usually needs confirmation with diagnostic testing such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, while a low-risk result cannot rule out every condition. Blood tests and ultrasound avoid the procedure-related risks of invasive testing.

topics.name: Non-Nucleic Acid–Based Identification Methods for Infectious Disease
topics.clinical_significance: These methods identify infectious organisms without testing their genetic material. They use features such as appearance, growth, biochemical reactions, antibodies or antigens, and protein patterns. Correct identification helps guide treatment and infection-control steps, but some methods take days or depend on good-quality cultures.

topics.name: Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP)
topics.clinical_significance: NSIP is an uncommon lung disease that causes cough and shortness of breath over months or years. It may occur without a known cause or be linked to autoimmune disease, certain medicines, or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, so these causes should be checked. Many patients improve with steroid treatment, but outlook is worse when there is more lung scarring.

topics.name: Nonspecific Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue, fever, or weight loss, can occur in many conditions and do not identify a cause by themselves. They may still be an early sign of serious illness, so persistent, worsening, or concerning symptoms need assessment guided by the history and examination.

topics.name: Nonsuicidal Self-Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Non-suicidal self-injury is deliberate harm to the body without intent to die and is a behavior, not necessarily a disorder. It can signal significant distress and is linked to increased future suicide risk, so assessment should include injury severity, mental health, and suicidal thoughts.

topics.name: Nonsuicidal Self-Injury (NSSI) in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and teens, self-injury without intent to die may be a way to cope with distress, but it can occur with mental health conditions and is linked to higher suicide risk. Every episode needs clinical assessment of the injuries, emotional distress, and suicidal thoughts, even when the young person says they do not intend to die.

topics.name: Nonthrombotic Pulmonary Embolism
topics.clinical_significance: Nonthrombotic pulmonary embolism occurs when material other than a blood clot, such as air, fat, infected material, or tumor cells, blocks pulmonary arteries. Depending on the cause, it can lead to severe low oxygen, pulmonary hypertension, or sudden cardiovascular collapse, so prompt recognition and cause-specific care are important.

topics.name: Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Nontuberculous mycobacteria are found in the environment and usually do not spread from person to person. Finding them in a sample does not always mean they are causing illness; true infection can affect the lungs, skin, lymph nodes, or wounds, and may need species-specific testing and specialist care because many strains resist standard tuberculosis drugs.

topics.name: Nontyphoidal Salmonella Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Nontyphoidal Salmonella usually causes foodborne diarrhea that improves with supportive care. Infection can spread to the blood or other sites, especially in infants, older adults, and people with hemoglobin disorders or weakened immunity; antibiotics are generally reserved for high-risk or invasive illness because they may prolong bacterial shedding.

topics.name: Normal Laboratory Values
topics.clinical_significance: Laboratory reference ranges help compare a test result with values seen in a healthy population. Ranges vary by laboratory method and factors such as age, sex, and pregnancy; a result outside the range does not by itself prove disease, and a result within it does not always rule disease out. Interpret results using the range on the report and the clinical context.

topics.name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
topics.clinical_significance: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus can cause a slow, unsteady walk, loss of bladder control, and declining thinking, but these problems also occur in other conditions. Specialist evaluation matters because selected patients may improve after a shunt drains cerebrospinal fluid, especially in walking and bladder control.

topics.name: Norovirus Gastroenteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Norovirus spreads easily and often causes sudden vomiting, cramps, and diarrhea that resolve within 1 to 3 days. Fluid loss can cause dehydration, especially in young children; replacing fluids is the main treatment, and antibiotics do not help.

topics.name: Nose and Paranasal Sinus Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Nose and sinus disorders can cause congestion, nasal discharge, nosebleeds, facial pressure, or reduced smell and may interfere with breathing. Causes include inflammation, infection, injury, and growths such as polyps; ongoing or recurrent symptoms may need medical assessment.

topics.name: Nose, Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A nasal fracture may cause swelling, bruising, bleeding, deformity, or blocked nasal airflow. A blood collection inside the nasal septum needs immediate drainage to prevent cartilage damage; clear watery drainage after injury may signal a cerebrospinal fluid leak and needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Nosebleeds
topics.clinical_significance: Most nosebleeds come from small vessels near the front of the nose and stop with pressure; dryness and minor injury are common causes. Heavy, persistent, or repeated bleeding may need medical care, especially in people taking blood thinners or with a bleeding disorder. High blood pressure can make bleeding persist but is usually not its cause.

topics.name: Nuclear Gastrointestinal Scans
topics.clinical_significance: Nuclear gastrointestinal scans use a small amount of radioactive tracer to answer specific questions, such as where active lower intestinal bleeding is coming from, how quickly the stomach empties, or whether ectopic stomach tissue is present in a Meckel diverticulum. Delayed stomach emptying alone cannot distinguish slow motility from a physical blockage, so further testing may be needed.

topics.name: Nucleic Acid–Based Identification Methods for Infectious Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Molecular tests detect genetic material (DNA or RNA) from infectious organisms and can identify many infections quickly, including organisms that are hard to grow in culture. Results can guide targeted treatment, but the right test and a properly collected specimen are essential; contamination can cause false positives, and false negatives can still occur.

topics.name: Numbness
topics.clinical_significance: Numbness is partial or complete loss of sensation and may result from temporary pressure or disease affecting nerves, the spinal cord, or the brain. Sudden numbness, especially with weakness or other neurologic symptoms, needs urgent assessment because it can signal stroke or spinal cord injury; ongoing numbness can affect balance and hide injuries.

topics.name: Nummular Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Nummular dermatitis causes intensely itchy, coin-shaped patches of inflamed, scaly skin. It often occurs with atopic dermatitis, but fungal infection and psoriasis can look similar, so diagnosis matters; treatment usually includes skin care and topical corticosteroids.

topics.name: Nursemaid's Elbow
topics.clinical_significance: Radial head subluxation, or nursemaid elbow, usually follows a pull or twist on the arm of a young child. The child may refuse to use the arm, but a clinician can usually restore movement with a reduction maneuver. Persistent pain or limited use after reduction needs reassessment for an occult fracture or incomplete reduction.

topics.name: Nursing Homes
topics.clinical_significance: Nursing homes provide nursing care, rehabilitation, and help with daily activities for people who need more support than can be provided at home. Care may be short term after illness or injury or long term; residents can also face risks such as infection, pressure injuries, medication problems, and loss of function, so care should match individual needs.

topics.name: Nutrient-Drug Interactions
topics.clinical_significance: Food and nutrients can change how medicines are absorbed or broken down, and medicines can affect appetite or nutrient levels. These interactions may make a medicine less effective or increase harmful effects; for example, grapefruit changes the breakdown of some drugs, and tyramine-rich foods can cause a dangerous blood pressure rise with certain antidepressants called MAO inhibitors. Follow food instructions for medicines and check before making major diet or supplement changes.

topics.name: Nutrition and Feeding in Infants
topics.clinical_significance: Infants need frequent, age-appropriate feeding to meet their high fluid and calorie needs during rapid growth. Adequate intake is monitored through wet diapers and steady weight gain; excessive newborn weight loss, poor growth, or vomiting that lasts over 48 hours or contains bile needs medical evaluation.

topics.name: Nutrition: General Considerations
topics.clinical_significance: Adequate nutrition provides energy and essential nutrients for growth, tissue repair, and normal body function. Too little can cause undernutrition and nutrient deficiencies, while excess calories or some nutrients can contribute to chronic disease or toxicity; needs vary with age, health, and activity.

topics.name: Nutrition in Clinical Medicine
topics.clinical_significance: Nutrient deficiencies can worsen health and recovery, while some illnesses cause poor nutrient absorption.
