Excess nutrition can contribute to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Checking nutritional status helps identify harmful deficiencies or excess, especially in children, older adults, and people with ongoing illness.

topics.name: Nutrition, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Nutrition supplies energy and essential nutrients for growth, tissue maintenance, and normal body processes. Inadequate intake can cause undernutrition and deficiency, while excess calories can lead to obesity and excessive intake of some vitamins or minerals can be toxic; needs vary with age and health.

topics.name: Nutritional Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Nutritional optic neuropathy is damage to the optic nerve, often from deficiencies of B vitamins or folate, causing painless, usually gradual loss of central vision in both eyes. Early correction of the deficiency may improve vision, but prolonged damage can be permanent, so prompt eye and medical assessment is important.

topics.name: Nutritional Requirements
topics.clinical_significance: Nutritional needs vary with age, body size, activity, health, and life stage, so intake targets are guides and should be individualized. Matching energy and nutrients to need helps maintain a healthy body weight and prevent deficiencies; unnecessary supplements can cause harm.

topics.name: Nutritional Support for Patients Who Are Dying or Have Severe Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: For people near the end of life or unable to eat because of advanced dementia, tube feeding has not been shown to prolong life or improve comfort or function. Tube or IV nutrition may cause discomfort and is usually not indicated in these situations; care often focuses on food and sips as tolerated, mouth care, and support guided by care goals and palliative care.

topics.name: Nutritional Support, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Nutritional support may be needed when undernutrition, critical illness, poor appetite, or impaired absorption prevents adequate food intake. It aims to maintain or rebuild lean body mass; the route and amount are tailored to individual needs, and response is monitored through clinical recovery, wound healing, strength, and endurance.

topics.name: Nystagmus
topics.clinical_significance: Nystagmus is rhythmic, involuntary eye movement that can arise from inner-ear balance pathways or the brain and can help distinguish peripheral vertigo from a central neurologic cause. Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, especially with other neurologic signs, raises concern for a central disorder and needs prompt assessment.

topics.name: Obesity
topics.clinical_significance: Obesity is a chronic, complex condition involving excess body fat that may harm health. In adults, BMI of 30 kg/m² or higher is commonly used for screening, but BMI alone does not show body fat distribution or health effects. Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart and blood vessel disease, sleep apnea, fatty liver disease, osteoarthritis, and some cancers; many biological, behavioral, medication, and environmental factors can contribute.

topics.name: Obesity and the Metabolic Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of abdominal fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar or insulin resistance, high triglycerides, and low HDL cholesterol. Having at least three features raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so each risk factor should be identified and managed.

topics.name: Obesity in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In adolescents, obesity is assessed using BMI percentiles for age and sex (usually at or above the 95th percentile), not adult BMI cutoffs. It often persists into adulthood and raises the risk of high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes; weight-related teasing and stigma can also harm mental health and increase social isolation.

topics.name: Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes disorders marked by intrusive worries and rituals, intense concern about appearance, difficulty discarding possessions, or repeated hair pulling or skin picking. These problems can cause distress and interfere with daily life and relationships. Psychotherapy and, for some disorders, medication can help.

topics.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder and Related Disorders in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and adolescents, obsessive-compulsive disorder causes unwanted, upsetting thoughts or urges and repetitive rituals. Related disorders include intense concern about appearance, hoarding, hair pulling, and skin picking. These problems can cause distress and interfere with school, friendships, and daily life. Cognitive behavioral therapy and medicines such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors can help.

topics.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
topics.clinical_significance: OCD causes unwanted, recurring thoughts, images, or urges and/or repetitive actions or mental rituals that a person feels driven to do to reduce anxiety. These can take much time, cause serious distress, and disrupt school, work, or relationships. Exposure and response prevention therapy and medicines such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or clomipramine often help.

topics.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)
topics.clinical_significance: OCPD is a lasting pattern of perfectionism, order, and control with little flexibility. Attention to rules and details can slow work, interfere with finishing tasks, and strain relationships. Unlike OCD, it usually does not involve unwanted intrusive thoughts and rituals done to reduce anxiety. Psychotherapy can help; evidence for medicines is limited.

topics.name: Obstetric and Gynecologic History
topics.clinical_significance: This history records menstrual and sexual health, pregnancies and their outcomes, reproductive conditions, procedures, and treatments. It helps assess current symptoms and identify past pregnancy complications or reproductive conditions that may affect future pregnancies or long-term health.

topics.name: Obstetric Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation before and during pregnancy reviews health and pregnancy history, estimates pregnancy dates, and uses examinations and tests to assess the pregnant patient and fetus. Regular prenatal checks monitor growth and screen for conditions or complications that could affect either one, helping guide care and reduce risk.

topics.name: Obstructive Disorders of the Esophagus
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders narrow or block the esophagus, often causing difficulty swallowing solid food. Causes include narrowing or growths in the esophagus and pressure from nearby structures. A sudden, complete blockage from stuck food or an object is an emergency and needs urgent endoscopy.

topics.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
topics.clinical_significance: OSA causes repeated narrowing or closure of the upper airway during sleep, leading to pauses in breathing and disrupted sleep. It may cause snoring and daytime sleepiness, which can impair concentration and raise the risk of crashes or other injuries. Untreated OSA is linked to high blood pressure, abnormal heart rhythms, and heart failure; treatment can reduce symptoms and risks.

topics.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) in Children
topics.clinical_significance: In children, OSA causes repeated narrowing or closure of the upper airway during sleep. It may cause snoring, restless sleep, poor concentration, or hyperactivity. If untreated, it can affect learning, behavior, and growth, and sometimes strain the heart and lungs. Treatment often includes removing enlarged tonsils and adenoids.

topics.name: Obstructive Uropathy
topics.clinical_significance: A partial or complete blockage of urine flow anywhere in the urinary tract. Stones, scarring, an enlarged prostate, tumors, or urinary tract abnormalities may cause it. Severe or long-lasting blockage, especially when it affects both kidneys, can impair kidney function; infection behind a blockage can become serious.

topics.name: Occlusive Thromboaortopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Also called Takayasu arteritis, this is inflammation of the aorta and its major branches. Narrowing or blockage can reduce blood flow, causing weak or unequal pulses, different blood pressures between limbs, limb pain with use, or vision and other neurologic problems. The inflamed arteries may also widen and form aneurysms.

topics.name: Occult Bacteremia and Fever Without Apparent Source in Infants and Young Children
topics.clinical_significance: Occult bacteremia means bacteria are in the blood of a febrile young child who appears well and has no clear infection source. It is now uncommon in routinely immunized children, but can be an early sign of serious infection, such as sepsis or meningitis. Risk is higher in very young infants and children who are underimmunized or have weakened immune systems; age and condition guide testing.

topics.name: Occupational Asthma
topics.clinical_significance: New asthma caused by exposure to an allergen or irritant at work. It can cause cough, wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath that often worsen during or after work and may improve away from work, though symptoms can persist after exposure ends. It differs from pre-existing asthma that is only worsened by work conditions.

topics.name: Occupational Therapy (OT)
topics.clinical_significance: Occupational therapy helps people with illness, injury, or disability carry out daily activities more safely and independently. It builds or adapts movement, thinking, and self-care skills and may use practice, new routines, home changes, or assistive devices to support work, leisure, and social life.

topics.name: Ocular Burns
topics.clinical_significance: Heat burns usually affect the eyelids, while chemical burns can injure the eye surface, including the cornea and conjunctiva. Severe burns can cause scarring, corneal perforation, eyelid damage, or permanent loss of vision. Chemical burns to the eye surface are an emergency because immediate irrigation can limit injury.

topics.name: Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid
topics.clinical_significance: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, also called ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, is a chronic autoimmune disease that scars the conjunctiva, usually in both eyes. Scarring can damage the eyelids and cornea, leading to reduced vision or blindness. Early disease may look like lasting eye redness and irritation; progressive disease often needs treatment that suppresses immune activity.

topics.name: Ocular Larva Migrans
topics.clinical_significance: Ocular larva migrans (ocular toxocariasis) occurs when larvae of animal roundworms, usually Toxocara, migrate to the eye after eggs are swallowed. It usually affects one eye and causes little illness elsewhere, but inflammation and retinal damage can impair or permanently reduce vision. It can resemble an eye tumor, including retinoblastoma.

topics.name: Ocular Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid
topics.clinical_significance: This chronic autoimmune disease scars and shrinks the conjunctiva, usually in both eyes. Scarring can damage the eyelids and cloud the cornea, leading to reduced vision or blindness. Early signs may be lasting eye redness and irritation; progressive disease often requires medicines that suppress immune activity.

topics.name: Older Adult, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of an older adult considers how several illnesses, medicines, and changes in memory or daily function may affect one another. Finding problems early can help prevent decline, reduce medication-related harm, and preserve independence and quality of life. Frail or medically complex patients may need a comprehensive assessment by a care team.

topics.name: Older Adults, Alternative Living Arrangements
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults may live with partners, friends, siblings, or in other arrangements beyond living alone or with a spouse or adult child. Knowing a person's living situation and chosen support network helps clinicians plan care that respects the person's wishes and includes the right people. LGBTQ+ older adults may face added barriers when partners or caregivers are not recognized.

topics.name: Older Adults, Drug-Related Problems
topics.clinical_significance: Medication-related problems in older adults include side effects, drug interactions, incorrect or ineffective doses, unnecessary treatment, and difficulty taking medicines as prescribed. Multiple illnesses, many medicines, and age-related changes can increase the risk of confusion, falls, bleeding, and hospitalization. Regular review can catch problems while helping avoid both harmful treatment and undertreatment.

topics.name: Older Adults, Effects of Life Transitions
topics.clinical_significance: Retirement, moving, and bereavement can change an older adult's roles, finances, familiar surroundings, and social support. Adjustment difficulties may lead to isolation, depression, or loss of function. Grief that remains intense and impairs daily life for over a year may meet criteria for prolonged grief disorder. Bereavement is linked with increased suicide risk, so recognizing these changes helps clinicians assess mental health and support needs.

topics.name: Older Adults, Family Caregiving
topics.clinical_significance: Family caregiving can help older adults with chronic illness or disability remain at home, but intensive care can strain caregivers' health, finances, and social lives. Caregiver strain may cause fatigue, depression, isolation, or burnout and can sometimes contribute to neglect or abuse. Training, respite, and practical or emotional support can ease the burden and help sustain safe care.

topics.name: Older Adults Living Alone
topics.clinical_significance: Living alone does not by itself mean an older adult is isolated or unable to manage. However, health problems or sensory loss may go unnoticed, treatment routines and meal preparation may be harder, and loneliness or poor nutrition can occur. Care planning considers social support and daily needs while respecting the person's wish for independence.

topics.name: Older Adults, Quality of Life in
topics.clinical_significance: Quality of life is an older adult's own view of physical, emotional, social, and meaningful activities, shaped by health, abilities, relationships, and personal values. It varies between people and can change over time. Including it in care planning helps set goals that reflect what matters to each person.

topics.name: Older Adults, Social Issues in
topics.clinical_significance: Living arrangements, relationships, finances, transportation, daily activities, and caregiver support can affect an older adult's health and access to care. Understanding these social factors helps care teams identify needs and plan timely, appropriate support.

topics.name: Older Driver, Functional Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment checks the vision, movement, and thinking skills needed for safe driving. Problems from aging, illness, or medicines can impair driving, but age alone does not determine whether a person can drive safely. Office screening can flag the need for fuller evaluation; no single test predicts safety perfectly, and findings may guide rehabilitation, vehicle adaptations, or driving limits.

topics.name: Older Driver, Interventions
topics.clinical_significance: Interventions may treat problems that impair driving or use rehabilitation, vehicle adaptations, and driving limits. If driving remains unsafe, stopping protects the driver and others, but can reduce independence and increase isolation or depression. Planning other transportation helps maintain access to daily activities and social life.

topics.name: Older Driver, Medical Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment reviews illnesses and medicines that can impair vision, movement, thinking, or consciousness and raise crash risk. Examples include sedating medicines, fainting or seizures, diabetes-related problems, sleep disorders, and alcohol or drug use. Identifying these risks helps guide treatment and decisions about driving fitness.

topics.name: Older Driver, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Safe driving depends on vision, movement, and thinking skills, which may be affected by aging or illness. Impairment can raise crash risk, and older adults are more vulnerable to serious injury in a crash. Stopping driving can also reduce independence, so assessment should focus on each person's abilities and balance safety with mobility.

topics.name: Olfactory Reference Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Olfactory reference disorder is a distressing preoccupation with emitting a bad body odor that others do not notice or find only slight. Repeated checking, washing, or masking the perceived odor can lead to shame, social avoidance, and major problems at work or in daily life. Severe cases can be disabling, and suicidal thoughts may occur.

topics.name: Oligella Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Oligella infections are uncommon and usually affect the urinary tract, especially in people with long-term urinary catheters. O. urethralis may be present without causing illness, so culture results need to be considered with symptoms. O. ureolytica may contribute to urinary stone formation; rare infections can spread to the blood or other sites.

topics.name: Oligohydramnios
topics.clinical_significance: Amniotic fluid is lower than expected for the stage of pregnancy. Causes include leaking or ruptured membranes, reduced placental blood flow, some medicines, pregnancy past the due date, or fetal problems that reduce urine production. It can restrict fetal growth, affect lung or limb development if it begins early, and make labor harder for the fetus. Risk depends on the cause and severity, so ultrasound and fetal monitoring are used.

topics.name: Oliguria
topics.clinical_significance: Oliguria means urine output below 500 mL in 24 hours in an adult, or below 0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults and children (below 1 mL/kg/hour in newborns). It may result from reduced blood flow to the kidneys, kidney injury, or blocked urine flow. It can signal acute kidney injury or serious illness and needs prompt assessment of kidney function, fluid status, medicines, and urinary drainage.

topics.name: Omphalocele
topics.clinical_significance: Abdominal organs protrude through an opening at the base of the umbilical cord and are covered by a thin membrane. About two-thirds of affected infants have other birth defects, such as heart or chromosome problems. At birth, the exposed organs need protection from drying and infection, and the infant needs prompt specialist care and surgical repair.

topics.name: Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)
topics.clinical_significance: A parasitic worm infection spread by blackflies. It can cause itchy skin, rash, and nodules; eye inflammation and scarring can lead to vision loss or blindness. Ivermectin is the main treatment and reduces the small larval forms (microfilariae), but does not kill adult worms. People exposed to Loa loa in Central Africa need assessment for that infection before ivermectin because treatment can cause severe reactions.

topics.name: Onychocryptosis
topics.clinical_significance: The nail edge presses into the skin beside it, usually at a great toe, causing pain, redness, and swelling. Tight shoes, abnormal walking, or cutting the nail too short can contribute. Infection around the nail may develop.

topics.name: Onychomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: A fungal infection of the nail plate, nail bed, or both; toenails are affected much more often than fingernails. The nail may thicken, turn yellow or white, collect debris underneath, or separate from the nail bed. It can increase the risk of cellulitis in the lower leg. Other nail disorders can look similar, so confirm a fungal cause before treatment.

topics.name: Onycho-Osteodysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Also called nail-patella syndrome, this rare inherited disorder affects the nails, kneecaps, elbows, and pelvic bones. Kidney problems occur in about 30–50% of people and can progress to kidney failure; glaucoma may also develop. Ongoing kidney and eye checks help detect these complications.

topics.name: Open Pneumothorax
topics.clinical_significance: A chest wall wound lets outside air enter the space around the lung. If the opening is large, it can severely impair breathing and lead to respiratory failure. This is a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate wound dressing and chest-tube treatment.

topics.name: Operative Vaginal Delivery
topics.clinical_significance: Forceps or a vacuum device helps deliver the baby during the second stage of labor when pushing is prolonged, the baby may be in distress, or maternal illness or exhaustion makes pushing unsafe. The baby's head must be low and its position known. Risks include severe tears or bleeding in the mother and bruising or other injury in the baby.

topics.name: Ophthalmia Neonatorum
topics.clinical_significance: Conjunctivitis in a newborn, with watery or pus-like eye discharge, can be caused by infection acquired during birth or by irritation from eye drops. Chlamydia is a common cause; gonorrhea can quickly damage the cornea and cause blindness, while chlamydia can also cause pneumonia. Prompt testing and treatment for the cause are important.

topics.name: Ophthalmic Disorders, Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: Eye symptoms such as pain, redness, blurred or sudden vision loss, flashes, new floaters, double vision, or loss of side vision can have many causes, some serious. Sudden vision loss, severe pain, or new flashes and many floaters may signal an emergency such as retinal detachment or acute glaucoma and need urgent eye assessment.

topics.name: Ophthalmic Herpes Zoster
topics.clinical_significance: A one-sided shingles rash on the forehead, eyelid, or nose can involve the eye. Eye inflammation may scar the cornea or cause other problems that threaten vision; a blister on the tip of the nose signals higher risk. Prompt eye assessment and early antiviral treatment help reduce complications.

topics.name: Ophthalmologic Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment of an eye problem starts with when symptoms began and any pain, redness, discharge, or change in vision, followed by a focused eye examination. Sudden vision loss, eye pain, flashes or many new floaters, double vision, or loss of side vision may signal serious disease and need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Ophthalmologic Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: A full eye evaluation measures vision in each eye and examines the pupils, eye movements, cornea, visual fields, eye pressure, and retina. These checks can reveal sight-threatening problems such as glaucoma or retinal detachment. Sudden vision loss, eye pain, flashing lights, or many new floaters need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Opioid Toxicity and Withdrawal
topics.clinical_significance: Opioid overdose can slow or stop breathing, causing dangerously low oxygen and death; very small pupils and severe sleepiness may occur. It is an emergency treated with naloxone and breathing support. Withdrawal after stopping opioids can cause anxiety, yawning, runny nose, watery eyes, large pupils, aches, and stomach upset. It is usually not life-threatening but can be severe; treatment may include buprenorphine or methadone and supportive care.

topics.name: Opioid Use Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: A persistent pattern of compulsive opioid use for nonmedical reasons despite harm. Diagnosis requires at least 2 of 11 symptoms within 12 months, such as craving, inability to cut down, or continued use despite problems. Tolerance or withdrawal alone does not establish the disorder when opioids are taken as prescribed. Ongoing treatment with buprenorphine, methadone, or long-acting naltrexone, with social support, can reduce relapse and fatal overdose risk; withdrawal management alone carries a high risk of relapse.

topics.name: Opisthorchiasis
topics.clinical_significance: A liver-fluke infection usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Many infections cause no symptoms, but long-lasting infection can inflame or block bile ducts and, rarely, lead to gallstones, cholangitis, or bile-duct cancer. Praziquantel or albendazole can treat the infection; thoroughly cooking or freezing freshwater fish helps prevent it.

topics.name: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)
topics.clinical_significance: A persistent pattern of irritability, arguing, defiance, or spiteful behavior toward authority that is severe and disruptive. Diagnosis requires at least 4 symptoms for 6 months; occasional defiance alone is not enough. Check for related problems such as ADHD, anxiety, or depression. Behavior therapy involving the child and family is the main treatment; ongoing symptoms can harm school, work, and relationships.

topics.name: Optic Nerve Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: The optic nerves carry visual signals from the eyes to the brain. Damage can cause partial or complete vision loss or blind spots. Causes include inflammation, reduced blood flow, pressure on the nerve, inherited disease, or toxic or nutritional injury; vision loss may be permanent. Sudden vision changes need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Optic Neuritis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the optic nerve usually causes pain with eye movement and vision loss in one eye, sometimes with reduced color vision. It can be the first sign of multiple sclerosis or related immune disorders; infection is another possible cause. Examination and MRI help identify the cause. Many people recover vision over a few months, but outcome depends on the cause.

topics.name: Optic Pathway
topics.clinical_significance: The optic pathway carries visual signals from the retina through the optic nerves and brain pathways to the visual area at the back of the brain. Damage at different points causes distinct patterns of vision loss or blind spots. These patterns help clinicians locate the problem and may point to causes such as optic nerve disease, glaucoma, stroke, or a tumor.

topics.name: Options for Limb Prostheses
topics.clinical_significance: Prosthesis choice after amputation is tailored to the level of limb loss, the remaining limb, a person's abilities, and daily or sports goals. A well-fitted device can support hand use, standing, or walking, but fit, comfort, balance, and gait need individual assessment and adjustment with a prosthetist. Counseling may help people adjust to upper-limb loss.

topics.name: Oral Contraceptives
topics.clinical_significance: Hormone pills containing estrogen and progestin, or progestin alone, prevent pregnancy when taken correctly. They may also reduce painful or irregular bleeding and lower the risk of ovarian and uterine lining cancer. Common effects include nausea, headache, and breast tenderness. Estrogen-containing pills raise blood-clot risk and may be unsafe with some conditions, so medical history and blood pressure should be reviewed before use.

topics.name: Oral Dysesthesia
topics.clinical_significance: Daily burning, tingling, or numb pain in the mouth, often affecting the tongue, lips, or palate despite normal-looking tissue. Dry mouth or altered taste may occur. It is diagnosed after other causes are checked, including nutritional deficiency, diabetes, thrush, dry mouth, medication effects, or allergy. Some cases have no identifiable cause and can be difficult to treat.

topics.name: Oral Growths
topics.clinical_significance: Most oral growths are benign, but some are precancerous or cancerous. A persistent white or red patch that cannot be wiped away, a fast-growing or easily bleeding lesion, a neck lump, trouble swallowing, or unexplained weight loss needs prompt assessment. Because cancer can be hard to identify by appearance alone, a lasting or suspicious lesion may need biopsy. Tobacco, alcohol, and oral HPV raise cancer risk.

topics.name: Oral Malodor
topics.clinical_significance: Frequent or persistent bad breath, usually caused by bacteria on the tongue or between teeth, gum disease, smoking, or certain foods. Dry mouth can contribute; sinus, lung, digestive, or other medical causes are less common. Persistent odor should prompt an oral and dental check, especially if there is fever, pus-like nasal discharge or sputum, or a visible mouth lesion. Mouthwash alone usually helps only briefly.

topics.name: Oral Mucositis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation or painful ulcers in the mouth can make eating and drinking difficult, leading to dehydration or poor nutrition. Causes include infection, injury or irritants, medicines, cancer treatment, and systemic illness; secondary infection is more likely in people with weakened immunity. Fever, skin blisters, eye inflammation, or inability to drink needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Oral Rehydration Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: A balanced oral rehydration solution replaces water and salts lost with diarrhea or vomiting. It is safe and effective for children with mild to moderate dehydration who can drink. Soda, juice, and sports drinks have too much sugar and too little salt and may worsen fluid loss. Copious vomiting or a suspected bowel blockage needs medical assessment because oral treatment may not be suitable.

topics.name: Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: This is the most common cancer of the mouth lining. Early cancer may cause no symptoms, so regular mouth checks can help find it early. Tobacco and alcohol are major risks. A sore or red or white patch that does not heal, or a firm lump, should be checked; suspicious areas need a biopsy. The cancer can spread first to nearby neck lymph nodes and later to the lungs.

topics.name: Orbital Disease, Inflammatory
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation in the eye socket can cause eyelid swelling and redness, eye pain, bulging eyes, or double vision. Thyroid eye disease is a common cause, but infection and other immune conditions can look similar, so medical assessment and imaging may be needed. Rarely, pressure on the optic nerve or damage to the exposed eye surface can threaten sight; sudden vision changes need urgent care.

topics.name: Orbital Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Orbital disorders affect the eye socket and its contents. Causes include injury, infection, inflammation, tumors, and thyroid disease. They may cause eyelid swelling, eye pain, a bulging eye, double vision, or vision loss. Pain with eye movement, a bulging eye, fever, or reduced vision can signal a serious infection or pressure; these signs need urgent eye care.

topics.name: Orbital Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Orbital tumors may be benign or cancerous and can start in the eye socket or spread there from nearby or distant sites. They may push the eye out of place, causing bulging, pain, double vision, or vision loss; some cause few symptoms. New bulging of an eye or changes in vision need prompt assessment. CT or MRI is used to find the tumor, and a biopsy may be needed to identify it.

topics.name: Orchitis
topics.clinical_significance: Orchitis is infection of one or both testes, usually caused by a virus such as mumps; bacterial cases usually spread from an infection of the epididymis. It causes testicular pain and swelling, and mumps affecting both testes can reduce fertility. Sudden scrotal pain needs urgent assessment to rule out testicular torsion; antibiotics are used only for bacterial infection.

topics.name: Organophosphate Poisoning and Carbamate Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: These insecticides block cholinesterase, causing a dangerous buildup of acetylcholine. Exposure by swallowing, breathing, or skin contact can cause drooling, tearing, sweating, vomiting or diarrhea, pinpoint pupils, muscle twitching or weakness, and trouble breathing. Severe poisoning can cause seizures, coma, or death; nerve or muscle weakness may also appear days or weeks later. Suspected exposure is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

topics.name: Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Most cancers of the tonsils, base of the tongue, and nearby throat are squamous cell cancers. Many are linked to human papillomavirus (HPV), though tobacco and alcohol also raise the risk. A persistent sore throat, painful or difficult swallowing, or a neck lump needs medical assessment because spread to neck lymph nodes is common. HPV-related tumors generally have a better outlook.

topics.name: Oroya Fever and Verruga Peruana
topics.clinical_significance: This sandfly-borne Bartonella infection occurs in parts of the Andes and can have two stages. The first, Oroya fever, can cause severe anemia and may be fatal without treatment; other bloodstream infections can also occur. After recovery, verruga peruana may cause raised red-purple skin bumps that can persist or return. Prompt diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are important.

topics.name: Orthostatic Hypotension
topics.clinical_significance: A drop of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing is orthostatic hypotension. It may cause dizziness, blurred vision, confusion, or fainting and can increase the risk of falls. It is a sign of poor blood pressure regulation, often due to dehydration, medicines, prolonged bed rest, or autonomic nerve problems; repeated symptoms, fainting, or falls need medical assessment.

topics.name: Osgood-Schlatter Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A growth-related problem at the bony bump just below the kneecap, where the kneecap tendon attaches to the shinbone. Repeated pulling during growth causes local pain, swelling, and tenderness, often in children ages 10 to 15. It usually settles within weeks or months; pain or swelling beyond this spot, or redness and warmth, may point to another problem.

topics.name: Osgood-Schlatter's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: This is a growth-related problem at the bony bump just below the kneecap, where the kneecap tendon attaches to the shinbone. Repeated pulling during growth causes local pain, swelling, and tenderness, often in children ages 10 to 15. It usually settles within weeks or months; pain or swelling beyond this spot, or redness and warmth, may point to another problem.

topics.name: Osler-Weber-Rendu Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited disorder that causes small abnormal blood vessels and larger abnormal connections between arteries and veins. Recurrent nosebleeds or bleeding in the digestive tract can cause iron-deficiency anemia. Lung vessel malformations can allow clots or bacteria to reach the brain, causing stroke or brain abscess; brain malformations can bleed, and liver malformations can strain the heart. Screening for internal malformations is important even when symptoms seem mild.

topics.name: Osteitis Deformans
topics.clinical_significance: Osteitis deformans, or Paget disease of bone, causes unusually rapid bone breakdown and rebuilding in limited areas, leaving bone enlarged but weak. Many people have no symptoms; others develop bone pain or bending, hearing loss if the skull is affected, nearby joint arthritis, fractures, or pressure on nerves. New or severe pain in affected bone needs assessment because bone cancer can rarely develop there.

topics.name: Osteoarthritis (OA)
topics.clinical_significance: Osteoarthritis is a chronic joint disease in which cartilage is gradually lost and nearby bone changes. It often causes pain that worsens with activity and stiffness after rest that usually eases within 30 minutes. Knees, hips, hands, and the spine are commonly affected; some people have joint changes on X-rays but no symptoms. Advanced disease can limit movement and daily activities.

topics.name: Osteoarthritis of the Hand
topics.clinical_significance: Hand osteoarthritis commonly affects the finger joints and base of the thumb, causing pain and stiffness. Bony enlargements may form at the middle finger joints (Bouchard nodes) or the joints near the fingertips (Heberden nodes), sometimes without symptoms. The wrist is usually spared unless it was injured before; severe disease can deform joints and limit hand use.

topics.name: Osteoarthrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Osteoarthrosis is another name for osteoarthritis, a chronic joint disease in which cartilage is gradually lost and nearby bone changes. It often causes pain that worsens with activity and stiffness after rest that usually eases within 30 minutes. Knees, hips, hands, and the spine are commonly affected; some people have joint changes on X-rays but no symptoms. Advanced disease can limit movement and daily activities.

topics.name: Osteochondrodysplasias (Osteochondrodysplastic Dwarfism)
topics.clinical_significance: A large group of usually inherited conditions that disrupt bone or cartilage growth, often causing short stature with uneven growth of the limbs and trunk. Severity varies widely: some mainly affect height and joint function, while severe forms can narrow the chest and impair breathing in newborns. Identifying the specific type helps guide care, prognosis, and family planning.

topics.name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited disorder, usually involving type I collagen, that makes bones fragile and prone to repeated fractures and deformity. Severity ranges from mild to life-threatening; severe forms can cause fractures before birth and chest or spine problems that impair breathing. Blue-gray whites of the eyes, loose joints, brittle teeth, or hearing loss may also occur.

topics.name: Osteomalacia
topics.clinical_significance: Osteomalacia is poor mineralization of adult bone, which makes bones soft and weak. It is often caused by vitamin D deficiency but can also result from low phosphate or kidney disorders. It may cause bone pain, muscle weakness, and fractures, including hip fractures after minor injury; finding the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: Osteomyelitis
topics.clinical_significance: A bone infection, usually caused by bacteria but sometimes by fungi or mycobacteria, that can destroy bone. It causes localized pain and tenderness; acute infection may also cause fever and fatigue, while chronic infection may cause recurring pain or a draining wound. Infection of the spine can form an abscess and press on the spinal cord or nerves.

topics.name: Osteonecrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Osteonecrosis is death of bone tissue after its blood supply is reduced or cut off. It most often affects the hip and can also involve the knee or shoulder. It may cause no symptoms at first, but can lead to pain, limited movement, collapse of the joint surface, and osteoarthritis; early diagnosis may help preserve the joint.

topics.name: Osteonecrosis (ON)
topics.clinical_significance: Osteonecrosis (ON), also called avascular necrosis, is death of bone tissue after its blood supply is reduced or cut off. It most often affects the hip and can also involve the knee or shoulder. It may cause no symptoms at first, but can lead to pain, limited movement, collapse of the joint surface, and osteoarthritis; early diagnosis may help preserve the joint.

topics.name: Osteo-Onychodysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder affecting the nails, kneecaps, elbows, and pelvic bones. Nails may be small, misshapen, or absent, and kneecaps may be small, absent, or displaced. Kidney involvement can cause protein or blood in the urine and high blood pressure, and can sometimes progress to kidney failure; glaucoma may also occur.

topics.name: Osteopetroses, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Osteopetroses are inherited disorders in which bone-resorbing cells do not work properly, leaving bones unusually dense and abnormally shaped. Severe forms can crowd out the bone marrow, lowering blood cell counts, or cause bone overgrowth that presses on nerves or raises pressure inside the skull. The conditions range from mild to progressive and life-threatening.

topics.name: Osteoporosis
topics.clinical_significance: A progressive bone disease that lowers bone density and weakens bone structure, making fractures more likely after minor or no injury. It often has no symptoms until a fracture occurs; common sites are the spine, hip, and wrist. Spinal fractures may cause back pain, loss of height, or a stooped posture.

topics.name: Osteoporosis in Children
topics.clinical_significance: In children, low bone density together with a significant history of fractures indicates osteoporosis. It may result from chronic illness, medicines, immobility, or poor nutrition; rarely, no cause is found. Fragile bones can break after minor injury, especially long bones or the spine. Spinal fractures may be silent or cause back pain, loss of height, or a curved spine.

topics.name: Osteosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: In this pediatric context, osteosclerosis is a form of inherited osteopetrosis in which bone becomes unusually hard and dense because bone-resorbing cells do not work properly. In some forms, bone overgrowth crowds the marrow and lowers blood cell counts; it may also press on nerves. Severity ranges from mild to life-threatening.

topics.name: Otalgia
topics.clinical_significance: Ear pain that may come from the ear itself or be felt there because of a problem in nearby areas, such as the teeth, jaw, or throat. When the ear looks normal, common causes include jaw joint problems and migraine; persistent pain can sometimes signal a head or neck cancer.

topics.name: Other Arbovirus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: These infections are caused by several viruses usually spread by mosquitoes, ticks, or biting midges. They often cause fever, headache, and muscle or joint pain. Some can also cause brain inflammation, bleeding, eye problems, or complications during pregnancy; the likely infection depends on the region and type of exposure.

topics.name: Other Arthropod Bites
topics.clinical_significance: Bites from non-tick arthropods often cause itchy bumps, swelling, or pain; some cause skin ulcers. More serious problems include infection of the bite, a severe allergic reaction, or disease spread by mosquitoes, such as malaria or viral infections.

topics.name: Other Carbohydrate Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect enzymes that help the body process carbohydrates. Depending on the enzyme, they may impair glucose production and cause symptoms like some glycogen storage diseases, or lead to red blood cell breakdown and anemia.

topics.name: Other Congenital Cardiac Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: This group covers several heart problems present from birth, including blocked or narrowed blood flow to the lungs, a single working ventricle, and complete heart block. Depending on the defect and its severity, blood flow may be poor, causing bluish skin or heart failure.

topics.name: Other Eye Symptoms
topics.clinical_significance: Dryness and discharge often come from problems on the eye surface or conjunctivitis. Halos can occur with cataracts or corneal swelling, including acute glaucoma; blind spots or flashes can result from migraine or other problems in the visual pathway.

topics.name: Other Gastrointestinal Testing and Therapeutic Procedures
topics.clinical_significance: Breath tests help find problems such as Helicobacter pylori infection, sugar intolerance, or bacterial overgrowth. A swallowed wireless capsule measures movement through different parts of the gut. Electrical stimulation is used for selected problems, including severe gastroparesis symptoms and fecal incontinence.

topics.name: Other Neurologic Imaging Studies
topics.clinical_significance: These tests give detailed views of brain or spinal blood vessels and structures. Depending on the test, they can detect narrowed or blocked arteries, aneurysms, abnormal vessel connections, bleeding or fluid buildup in infants, and spinal canal problems. Catheter angiography can also guide some treatments.

topics.name: Other Primary Liver Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: These are uncommon cancers that start in the liver, such as bile duct cancer, hepatoblastoma, and angiosarcoma. Early symptoms are often vague, so diagnosis may be delayed, and the outlook is usually poor. Some localized tumors can be removed, which may extend survival.

topics.name: Other Schizophrenia Spectrum and Psychotic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These diagnoses describe distressing psychotic symptoms, such as hearing voices, fixed false beliefs, or disorganized thinking, that disrupt daily life but do not fit a specific psychotic disorder. They may be an early stage of another disorder, or remain unspecified when there is not enough information to classify them.

topics.name: Other Spotted Fever Rickettsioses
topics.clinical_significance: These tick-borne bacterial infections usually cause fever, headache, a small scab at the bite, swollen nearby lymph nodes, and a rash. They are often milder than Rocky Mountain spotted fever, but severe blood-vessel inflammation can occur.

topics.name: Other Types of Respiratory Failure
topics.clinical_significance: After surgery, lung tissue may collapse (atelectasis), causing respiratory failure and raising the risk of pneumonia. Poor blood flow can also limit oxygen delivery to the breathing muscles, especially when they are under extra strain, and lead to respiratory failure.

topics.name: Other X Chromosome Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: These conditions involve extra X chromosomes in females. Trisomy X (47,XXX) often causes no obvious physical signs, but may be linked to mild learning difficulties; menstrual irregularity or infertility occurs in some. Having more than three X chromosomes raises the risk of intellectual disability and congenital differences.

topics.name: Otic Barotrauma
topics.clinical_significance: A rapid change in outside pressure can cause ear pain or damage to the eardrum, especially when the Eustachian tube cannot equalize pressure. Severe cases may rupture the eardrum or injure the inner ear, causing hearing loss or vertigo.

topics.name: Otic Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: These rare benign or cancerous tumors can cause hearing loss, dizziness, or imbalance. Some block the ear canal; tumors near the middle ear may cause pulse-like tinnitus, and invasive tumors can affect nearby cranial nerves.

topics.name: Otitis Media (Acute)
topics.clinical_significance: Acute otitis media is a bacterial or viral infection of the middle ear, often accompanying a cold. It commonly causes ear pain and may cause fever or hearing loss, especially in young children. Rarely, the infection spreads to nearby tissues or the brain.

topics.name: Otitis Media (Chronic Suppurative)
topics.clinical_significance: This is a long-lasting middle-ear infection with a hole in the eardrum and pus draining for more than 6 weeks. It often causes painless discharge and hearing loss. Ongoing infection can damage ear structures or lead to cholesteatoma and, rarely, spread to nearby areas or the brain.

topics.name: Otitis Media (Serous)
topics.clinical_significance: Fluid remains behind the eardrum without an active infection, often after an ear infection or a cold. It may cause ear pressure and reduced hearing; if hearing loss lasts, it can delay speech and language development in young children. Most cases clear within a few months.

topics.name: Otitis Media with Effusion
topics.clinical_significance: Otitis media with effusion is fluid behind the eardrum without an active infection, often after an ear infection or cold. It can cause ear pressure and reduced hearing; if hearing loss lasts, it may delay speech and language development in young children. Most cases clear within a few months.

topics.name: Otorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Otorrhea is fluid draining from the ear; it may be clear, blood-tinged, or pus-like. Common causes include outer-ear infection or middle-ear infection draining through a perforated eardrum. After major head injury, clear or bloody drainage may be cerebrospinal fluid; persistent bloody discharge can signal ear cancer.

topics.name: Otosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal bone growth around the inner ear can fix the stapes, a small middle-ear bone, and slowly reduce hearing. Hearing loss is usually due to blocked sound transmission, but may also involve the inner ear.

topics.name: Ototoxicity, Drug-Induced
topics.clinical_significance: Drug-induced ototoxicity is inner-ear damage from certain medicines. It can cause hearing loss, ringing in the ears, dizziness, or balance problems; effects may be temporary or permanent. Risk can rise with higher or longer doses, kidney problems, or combinations of ototoxic medicines.

topics.name: Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Peritoneal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Ovarian, fallopian tube, and peritoneal cancers share similar features and often cause no symptoms or vague signs, such as bloating or feeling full quickly. They are often found at an advanced stage, when the outlook is poor and the cancer may be fatal.

topics.name: Ovarian Insufficiency, Primary
topics.clinical_significance: Ovarian follicles become depleted or stop working before age 40, lowering estrogen and disrupting or stopping periods. It can cause hot flashes, infertility, and bone loss, but ovarian activity may continue intermittently, so pregnancy is not always impossible.

topics.name: Ovarian Masses, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Benign ovarian masses include fluid-filled cysts and noncancerous tumors. Many cysts related to the menstrual cycle resolve on their own and cause no symptoms. Others can cause pelvic pain, or sudden severe pain if a cyst bleeds, ruptures, or twists (torsion).

topics.name: Ovarian Torsion
topics.clinical_significance: Twisting of an ovary, sometimes with the fallopian tube, interrupts its blood supply. It causes sudden, severe pelvic pain that may be localized or diffuse, often with nausea or vomiting. Prolonged loss of blood flow can damage the ovary or tube, so this is a gynecologic emergency usually treated with surgery.

topics.name: Overview of Arrhythmias and Conduction Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Arrhythmias and conduction disorders are problems with the heart's electrical signals that make the heartbeat too fast, too slow, or irregular. They may cause no symptoms or lead to palpitations, fainting, or, in severe cases, cardiac arrest.

topics.name: Overview of Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathies
topics.clinical_significance: These heart muscle disorders make abnormal heart rhythms more likely; some involve scar tissue in the heart. Many are genetic. They can cause heart failure, palpitations, fainting, or cardiac arrest, and may lead to sudden death.

topics.name: Overview of Arteriosclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Arteriosclerosis means that artery walls become thick and stiff and lose flexibility. Atherosclerosis, its most common form, involves fatty deposits in the walls and can lead to coronary artery disease, stroke, or peripheral artery disease.

topics.name: Overview of Beta-Lactams
topics.clinical_significance: Beta-lactams are antibiotics that block bacterial cell-wall formation. This group includes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams. Bacterial enzymes called beta-lactamases can inactivate many of these drugs and are a major cause of antibiotic resistance.

topics.name: Overview of Channelopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Channelopathies are disorders in which abnormal ion channels disrupt the heart's electrical signals, even when heart structure is normal. They may be genetic, autoimmune, or inflammatory and can cause dangerously slow or fast rhythms, fainting, or sudden cardiac death.

topics.name: Overview of Congenital Craniofacial Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: These are differences in the skull, facial bones, or soft tissues caused by abnormal development or unusual pressure and positioning before or after birth. Some occur with genetic syndromes and may be associated with other birth defects or developmental delays.

topics.name: Overview of Diabetes Mellitus
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes mellitus is a disease with high blood sugar because the body does not release enough insulin or cannot use it effectively. Over time, high blood sugar can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves, and blood vessels. Acute complications include diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar crisis.

topics.name: Overview of Diabetes Mellitus in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Diabetes in children and adolescents causes high blood sugar because the body makes too little insulin or cannot use it well. Type 1 is the most common form and may first appear as diabetic ketoacidosis; type 2 is also increasing. Long-term high blood sugar can damage blood vessels, eyes, kidneys, and nerves.

topics.name: Overview of Evaluation of the Older Adult
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of older adults considers multiple chronic illnesses, medicines, memory, mobility, and ability to manage daily activities. Symptoms may be subtle or appear as changes in behavior, and drug interactions or immobility can cause harm. A broad assessment can uncover treatable problems and help preserve function.

topics.name: Overview of Heart Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Heart failure occurs when a heart problem prevents the heart from meeting the body's needs or causes pressure to rise in the heart. Left-sided failure often causes breathlessness and fluid buildup in the lungs; right-sided failure often causes swelling in the legs or fluid in the abdomen. Both sides can be affected, and the condition can reduce blood flow to organs.

topics.name: Overview of High-Risk Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: A high-risk pregnancy is one in which the pregnant person, fetus, or newborn has a higher chance of serious health problems or death before, during, or after birth. Risks may come from chronic illness, carrying more than one fetus, past pregnancy complications, or problems that arise during pregnancy. Closer monitoring and specialist care may be needed.

topics.name: Overview of Illicit Drug Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Toxicity from illicit drugs can range from mild effects to life-threatening poisoning. The effects depend on the substance, amount, route of exposure, other substances taken, and underlying health. Poisoning can occur even without a large overdose if the body cannot clear a substance normally, and symptoms may be hard to identify when several substances are involved.

topics.name: Overview of Neck and Back Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Neck and back pain are common and usually come from mechanical problems in the spine and nearby muscles. The cause may be difficult to identify, and changes on imaging do not always explain the pain. Nerve involvement can cause pain, numbness, or weakness in an arm or leg. Less often, pain is due to a serious problem such as infection, cancer, fracture, spinal cord compression, or disease in a nearby organ.

topics.name: Overview of Revascularization for Acute Coronary Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Revascularization restores blood flow to heart muscle that is not receiving enough oxygen. In acute coronary syndromes, it can limit further heart muscle damage, reduce abnormal heart rhythms, and improve outcomes. The method and timing depend on the type of syndrome, when symptoms began, and the location and extent of coronary artery disease.

topics.name: Overview of Toxicity of Illicit Substances
topics.clinical_significance: Toxicity from illicit substances can cause short-term or lasting harm, and the effects vary with the substance, amount, route of exposure, and underlying health. Poisoning means exposure that causes clinically important harm; it can occur without an overdose if the body clears the substance poorly and it builds up. An overdose can affect different organs or body systems, not just intensify the usual effects.

topics.name: Ovulatory Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Ovulatory dysfunction means ovulation is irregular or absent. It often causes irregular or missing periods and can make pregnancy difficult. Common causes include polycystic ovary syndrome and problems with hormone control by the brain or pituitary gland; thyroid disease, high prolactin levels, major weight changes, and some medicines can also contribute. Finding the cause helps guide care and may allow ovulation to return.

topics.name: Oxygen Desaturation
topics.clinical_significance: Oxygen desaturation is a low or falling level of oxygen in the blood, usually measured by pulse oximetry. In hospitalized patients, oxygen saturation below 90% is a sign of hypoxia. It can result from poor ventilation or impaired oxygen transfer, with causes such as pneumonia, a blood clot in the lung, a collapsed lung, or heart failure. The reading points to a problem that needs to be identified and assessed.

topics.name: Oxyuriasis
topics.clinical_significance: Oxyuriasis, also called pinworm infection or enterobiasis, is an intestinal worm infection that spreads when eggs are swallowed. Most infected people have no symptoms; some develop itching around the anus, often at night, and pinworms can sometimes cause vaginal itching or inflammation. The infection is usually not harmful, but it spreads easily and reinfection is common.

topics.name: Paget Disease of Bone
topics.clinical_significance: Paget disease is an adult bone disorder in which bone is broken down and rebuilt too quickly in certain areas, leaving it enlarged but weak. Many people have no symptoms; others develop bone pain or deformity. Weakened bone can fracture, and nearby joints may develop arthritis. Enlarged bone can also press on nerves, sometimes affecting hearing or the spinal cord.

topics.name: Paget Disease of the Breast
topics.clinical_significance: Paget disease of the breast is a rare cancer that affects the nipple and areola, usually on one side. It can look like eczema, with redness, scaling, crusting, itching, or burning. About 90% of cases are linked to cancer in the breast ducts, which may be in situ or invasive, so the skin change can signal an underlying breast cancer.

topics.name: Paget Disease of the Nipple
topics.clinical_significance: Paget disease of the nipple is a rare cancer that affects the nipple and areola, usually on one side. It can look like eczema, with redness, scaling, crusting, itching, or burning. About 90% of cases are linked to cancer in the breast ducts, which may be in situ or invasive, so the skin change can signal an underlying breast cancer.

topics.name: Paget's Disease of Bone
topics.clinical_significance: Paget disease of bone, also called osteitis deformans, is a chronic adult disorder in which bone is remodeled too quickly in certain areas, making it enlarged but weak. It often causes no symptoms; when present, bone pain or deformity may occur. Complications include fractures, arthritis in nearby joints, and pressure on nerves; skull involvement can affect hearing.

topics.name: Paget's Disease of the Nipple
topics.clinical_significance: Paget disease of the nipple is a rare cancer that affects the nipple and areola, usually on one side. It can look like eczema, with redness, scaling, crusting, itching, or burning. About 90% of cases are linked to cancer in the breast ducts, which may be in situ or invasive, so the skin change can signal an underlying breast cancer.

topics.name: Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or possible tissue damage. It is personal and shaped by biological, psychological, and social factors, so the level of pain does not always match the amount of tissue injury. Pain can continue after tissue healing or occur without clear tissue damage.

topics.name: Pain and Inflammation, Rehabilitative Measures for
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitative measures such as therapeutic exercise, heat or cold, electrical stimulation, massage, traction, and acupuncture may be used to ease pain and inflammation and improve movement and muscle coordination. They are usually added to a broader rehabilitation plan rather than used alone. Their benefits vary by condition and treatment method.

topics.name: Pain, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic pain persists or recurs for more than 3 months and may continue after tissue heals or without clear ongoing injury. The linked MSD topic focuses on chronic widespread (nociplastic) pain, which can occur with long-term illness, injury, or primary pain conditions such as fibromyalgia; more than one pain mechanism may contribute. Chronic pain can limit daily function and may occur with anxiety or depression.

topics.name: Pain, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Pain evaluation looks for the cause and assesses the pain pattern, severity, and effects on daily activities, mood, thinking, and sleep. A history and physical examination guide any tests; chronic pain calls for a broader review of function, other health problems, and emotional and social factors. When a person can communicate, their own report is the main measure of pain; behavior changes can help identify pain in people who cannot.

topics.name: Pain Following Amputation
topics.clinical_significance: Pain after amputation may occur in the remaining limb or be felt in the missing limb (phantom limb pain); it is distinct from a painless phantom limb sensation. Causes include nerve injury, infection, poor blood flow, and pressure or poor fit from a prosthesis. Persistent pain in the remaining limb can limit prosthesis use, rehabilitation, and quality of life, and may signal a serious problem.

topics.name: Pain in and Around a Single Joint
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in or around one joint may come from the joint itself or nearby tendons, bursae, or other tissues. Common causes include injury, infection, and crystal arthritis; osteoarthritis is a frequent cause in older adults. A warm, swollen joint, especially with fever, may signal joint infection, which can quickly damage the joint and cause serious illness.

topics.name: Pain in and Around Joints
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in and around joints may come from the joint itself or nearby tendons, bursae, muscles, or bone. Joint pain without inflammation is called arthralgia; warmth and swelling may indicate arthritis. Pain in several joints can signal an infection or a systemic inflammatory disease, while injury and osteoarthritis are common causes. A new swollen joint must be assessed for infection, which can quickly damage the joint.

topics.name: Pain in Multiple Joints
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in several joints (polyarthralgia) may come from the joints or nearby tissues and may occur with or without inflammation. Warmth and swelling suggest arthritis, which may be due to infection or a systemic inflammatory disease; acute cases are often linked to viral infection, gout, or a flare of an inflammatory disorder. Chronic pain may be due to rheumatoid arthritis or a related disease, while osteoarthritis is a common noninflammatory cause. The pattern of affected joints and symptoms elsewhere in the body help identify the cause.

topics.name: Pain, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pain is a personal sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or possible tissue damage. Its intensity does not always match the amount of injury, and it is shaped by biological, psychological, and social factors. Pain may arise from tissue injury (nociceptive), nerve injury (neuropathic), or altered pain processing (nociplastic), and several mechanisms can occur together. Chronic pain can persist after tissues heal or without clear ongoing damage.

topics.name: Pain, Treatment
topics.clinical_significance: Pain treatment is tailored to its cause, duration, and type. It may combine medicines with rehabilitation, psychological support, or procedures; chronic pain care often uses a team approach focused on daily function and quality of life. Opioids can relieve acute, cancer, and end-of-life pain, but their long-term benefit for chronic noncancer pain is uncertain and risks include physical dependence, opioid use disorder, overdose, and slowed breathing.

topics.name: Painless Scrotal Mass
topics.clinical_significance: Most painless scrotal masses are due to benign causes such as hydrocele, inguinal hernia, or varicocele. Less often, a mass is testicular cancer; although uncommon, cancer is the most concerning cause and often responds well to treatment when found early. A solid mass in or attached to the testis needs evaluation for cancer.

topics.name: Palm Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A palm abscess is a deep bacterial pocket of pus in the palm, usually caused by staphylococci or streptococci. It causes severe throbbing pain, swelling, and tenderness, and can spread between deep spaces of the hand or onto its back. Because the infection can spread around important hand structures, prompt drainage and antibiotics are usually needed.

topics.name: Palmar Fibromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren contracture) is progressive thickening and shortening of the fascia beneath the skin of the palm. A firm cord forms and gradually bends the ring or little finger toward the palm, making it harder to straighten the fingers or open the hand.

topics.name: Palmoplantar Keratodermas
topics.clinical_significance: Palmoplantar keratodermas are a group of rare inherited or acquired disorders that cause thickening of the skin on the palms and soles. Some affect only these areas, while others occur as part of syndromes that can involve other organs. Skin infections are common, and acquired forms may be linked to chronic skin or systemic disease and, sometimes, cancer.

topics.name: Palpitations
topics.clinical_significance: Palpitations are the feeling that the heart is pounding, racing, fluttering, or skipping. They may reflect normal heartbeat awareness or a rhythm problem; causes include stimulants, anxiety, anemia, thyroid disease, and heart conditions. Many are harmless, but some rhythm problems are serious. Fainting, chest pain, or shortness of breath with palpitations needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Pancreas Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: Pancreas transplantation can restore insulin production and improve blood sugar control in selected people with diabetes, most often those with type 1 diabetes and kidney failure who also need a kidney transplant. It may help stabilize some diabetes complications, but carries risks of rejection, infection, surgery-related problems, and lifelong immunosuppressive medicines.

topics.name: Pancreatic Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Most pancreatic cancers are ductal adenocarcinomas. They often cause few early symptoms and are frequently found after spreading, so the outlook is often poor. Symptoms can include upper abdominal pain that spreads to the back, weight loss, and jaundice; tumors can also cause diabetes or poor digestion. Surgery is possible only for some cancers, often with chemotherapy.

topics.name: Pancreatic Islet Cell Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: Islet cell transplantation places insulin-producing cells in the liver to help control blood sugar. It may be used after pancreas removal for chronic pancreatitis or, in selected cases, for difficult-to-control type 1 diabetes. The treatment is still developing, and insulin independence may not last; repeat infusions may be needed. Donor-cell transplants require long-term immune-suppressing medicines and can cause bleeding or a clot in the portal vein.

topics.name: Pancreatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas. Gallstones and alcohol are common causes of acute pancreatitis, which usually causes sudden upper-abdominal pain, often with nausea or vomiting. Most mild cases improve, but severe cases can cause tissue death, infected fluid collections, shock, or organ failure. Chronic pancreatitis causes permanent damage and may lead to ongoing pain, poor digestion, weight loss, or diabetes.

topics.name: Pancreatitis, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often triggered by gallstones or alcohol. It usually causes severe upper-abdominal pain, often with nausea or vomiting. Many cases are mild and improve, but severe disease can cause pancreatic tissue death, shock, or organ failure. Repeated attacks can lead to lasting pancreatic damage.

topics.name: Pancreatitis, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic pancreatitis is lasting inflammation that permanently scars the pancreas and gradually reduces its ability to make digestive enzymes and insulin. It often causes upper-abdominal pain; poor digestion can lead to greasy stools and weight loss, and loss of insulin can cause diabetes. Heavy alcohol use and smoking are major risk factors; some cases are inherited, autoimmune, or due to blocked ducts. Chronic pancreatitis also raises the risk of pancreatic cancer.

topics.name: Pancreatitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas. Acute pancreatitis often resolves, but severe cases can cause tissue death or organ failure. Chronic pancreatitis causes permanent, progressive damage that can reduce its ability to make digestive enzymes and insulin, leading to poor digestion, weight loss, and diabetes.

topics.name: Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: A panic attack is a sudden, brief episode of intense fear with symptoms such as a pounding heart, shortness of breath, sweating, or dizziness. Panic disorder means repeated unexpected attacks followed by ongoing worry about more attacks or avoiding situations because of them. New chest or breathing symptoms may need medical assessment because other conditions can cause similar symptoms. Panic disorder can be treated with therapy, medicines, or both.

topics.name: Panic Disorder in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Panic disorder in children and teens causes repeated, unexpected attacks of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heart, shortness of breath, or dizziness. Children may avoid places or activities linked to attacks, disrupting school and social life. Because medical problems such as asthma can cause similar symptoms, they should be considered during assessment. Treatment, often cognitive behavioral therapy and medicine, usually improves the outlook.

topics.name: Panniculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Panniculitis is inflammation of the fat under the skin. It usually causes tender red or purple lumps, often on the limbs, and may also cause fever or feeling unwell. Causes include infection, inflammatory or autoimmune disease, cold or injury, pancreatic disease, and rarely lymphoma. Treatment depends on the cause; a skin biopsy may help confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: PAPA Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: PAPA syndrome is a rare inherited inflammatory disorder caused by changes in the PSTPIP1 gene. It can cause episodes of joint inflammation, often starting in childhood and sometimes damaging the joints, as well as poorly healing skin ulcers and severe cystic acne that can scar. Not everyone has all three features; skin problems often become more prominent after puberty.

topics.name: Papilledema
topics.clinical_significance: Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc due to increased pressure inside the skull, usually affecting both eyes. Vision may seem normal at first, but ongoing pressure can damage the optic nerve and cause permanent vision loss. It can signal a serious problem, such as idiopathic intracranial hypertension, a brain mass, bleeding, or infection, so the cause needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Paracentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Paracentesis removes fluid (ascites) from the abdomen with a needle or catheter. Testing a fluid sample can help find the cause of the fluid buildup, and removing a large amount can ease pain or breathing problems caused by tense ascites. Bleeding is the most common complication.

topics.name: Paracetamol Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Paracetamol poisoning can cause few or no early symptoms, even after a dangerous overdose. Liver injury may develop over the next 1 to 3 days and progress to liver failure or death. Prompt treatment with the antidote N-acetylcysteine can prevent or limit liver damage, so a suspected overdose needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Paracoccidioidomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Paracoccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection acquired by inhaling spores, mainly in rural parts of Central and South America. Many infections cause no symptoms, but active disease can progress and affect the lungs, mouth or skin, lymph nodes, and internal organs. Chronic lung disease can cause scarring; active disease is treated with antifungal medicines, sometimes for a long time.

topics.name: Paradoxical Vocal Cord Motion
topics.clinical_significance: Paradoxical vocal cord motion occurs when the vocal folds close during inhalation, narrowing the airway. It can cause noisy breathing, throat tightness, choking, or shortness of breath and may be mistaken for asthma; asthma medicines may not help when this is the cause. Education, speech therapy with breathing techniques, and treatment of related problems such as reflux can help.

topics.name: Paragonimiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Paragonimiasis is a lung-fluke infection acquired by eating raw, pickled, or undercooked freshwater crab or crayfish. Many infections cause no symptoms; others cause chronic cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood, and can resemble tuberculosis. Rarely, flukes spread to the brain or other organs and cause serious problems such as seizures. The infection can be treated with antiparasitic medicine.

topics.name: Parainfluenza Virus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Parainfluenza viruses cause respiratory infections ranging from a common cold to croup, bronchiolitis, or pneumonia, especially in children. Most infections are mild, but croup can rarely cause severe airway blockage, and lower lung infections can be serious in young infants or people with weakened immune systems. Treatment is mainly supportive.

topics.name: Paralytic Ileus
topics.clinical_significance: Paralytic ileus is a temporary stop in intestinal movement without a physical blockage, most often after abdominal surgery. It can cause abdominal swelling, nausea, vomiting, and discomfort, and can resemble a blocked intestine. Medicines, inflammation, or problems such as low potassium can also trigger it; treatment is supportive and addresses the cause.

topics.name: Paranasal Sinus Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Paranasal sinus cancer is rare and usually grows for some time before causing symptoms. Later signs can include ongoing nasal blockage or discharge, nosebleeds, facial pain or numbness, double vision, or loose upper teeth. It is often found at an advanced stage, so the outlook is generally poor, but earlier treatment improves it. Regular exposure to certain wood, leather, or metal dusts and smoking increase risk.

topics.name: Paraneoplastic Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Paraneoplastic syndromes are problems in body parts away from a tumor, caused by substances made by the cancer or by immune responses that affect healthy tissues. They can involve many body systems and may appear before the cancer is found. Treating the underlying cancer often helps, though some symptoms also need specific treatment.

topics.name: Paranoid Personality Disorder (PPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Paranoid personality disorder is a long-term pattern of unwarranted distrust and suspicion, with repeated assumptions that others intend harm or deception. This can make relationships and treatment difficult, and other mental health conditions often occur alongside it. Psychotherapy may be tried, and medicines may help specific symptoms, but no treatment has been proved effective.

topics.name: Parapharyngeal Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A parapharyngeal abscess is a deep infection beside the throat, often spreading from an infection in the tonsils, throat, or teeth. It can cause fever, painful swallowing, neck swelling, and difficulty opening the mouth. Swelling may block the airway, and infection can spread to major neck blood vessels, so urgent treatment with IV antibiotics and usually surgical drainage is needed.

topics.name: Paraphilias
topics.clinical_significance: Paraphilias are intense sexual interests focused on atypical objects, situations, or targets. An unusual interest alone is not a mental disorder; it is considered a paraphilic disorder when it is persistent and causes significant distress or problems in daily life, or involves harm or risk to others. This distinction helps avoid labeling consensual interests as illness while identifying when support or treatment may be needed.

topics.name: Paraphilias and Paraphilic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A paraphilic interest is not a disorder simply because it is unusual. A paraphilic disorder involves an intense, persistent pattern that causes significant distress or disrupts daily life, or harms or risks harming another person. Some patterns involve people who have not consented, so assessment considers safety as well as the person’s distress and functioning. Treatment may include psychotherapy and, in some cases, medication.

topics.name: Paraphilic Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Paraphilic disorders involve recurrent, intense sexual fantasies, urges, or behaviors focused on atypical objects, situations, or targets. An unusual interest alone is not a disorder: the pattern must be persistent and cause significant distress or problems in daily life, or involve harm or risk to others. Assessment considers consent, safety, and effects on the person’s functioning.

topics.name: Paraproteinemias
topics.clinical_significance: Paraproteinemia is the presence of an abnormal monoclonal protein in the blood or urine, usually made by a clone of plasma cells. It can occur in a stable condition, such as MGUS, or in a progressive blood cancer, such as multiple myeloma. Depending on the cause, the protein or growing cells can damage the kidneys or bones, lower blood counts or normal antibodies, or increase bleeding risk. Evaluation helps determine whether monitoring or treatment is needed.

topics.name: Parapsoriasis
topics.clinical_significance: Parapsoriasis causes chronic, thin, scaly patches or plaques that can look like psoriasis, but it is a different group of skin diseases. Small-plaque parapsoriasis is usually benign; large-plaque disease has a higher risk of progressing to cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Periodic skin checks, and sometimes biopsies, can help detect this change.

topics.name: Parasitic Infections, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Parasitic infections can affect the gut, blood, skin, or internal organs and may be caused by single-celled parasites, worms, or parasites that live on the skin.
