Symptoms and exposure history, such as travel, food or water, soil, freshwater, or insect bites, help guide testing; infection can also occur without travel. Diagnosis requires tests suited to the suspected parasite and the right sample, sometimes from more than one sample. Finding the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: Parasitic Skin Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Parasitic skin infections occur when parasites or their larvae infest or enter the skin. They often cause itching, bumps, rashes, or visible tracks, and some can spread through close contact or exposure to contaminated soil. Scratching or untreated lesions may lead to a skin infection. The cause guides treatment, and close contacts may also need care for some infestations.

topics.name: Parasomnias
topics.clinical_significance: Parasomnias are unwanted behaviors or experiences that occur while falling asleep, during sleep, or while waking. Some, such as sleepwalking or acting out dreams, can cause injury or disrupt sleep. In older adults, REM sleep behavior disorder can sometimes be an early sign of a brain disorder such as Parkinson disease. The pattern and timing of episodes help guide diagnosis and treatment.

topics.name: Parathyroid Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Parathyroid disorders can disrupt the body’s calcium balance. Too much parathyroid hormone can raise blood calcium and weaken bones or cause kidney stones. Too little hormone can lower calcium, causing tingling and muscle cramps; severe cases can cause painful muscle spasms. Blood calcium and hormone tests help identify the problem and guide treatment.

topics.name: Parathyroid Function, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) helps keep blood calcium and phosphate levels steady. When calcium falls, PTH raises it by acting on the kidneys, bones, and vitamin D; it also increases phosphate loss in urine. Because abnormal PTH can affect bones, muscles, nerves, and kidneys, clinicians interpret PTH blood tests together with calcium and kidney results.

topics.name: Parathyroid Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most parathyroid tumors are benign, but they can release too much parathyroid hormone and raise blood calcium. High calcium may cause kidney stones and bone loss, though many people have no symptoms. Parathyroid cancer is rare and can cause more severe hormone and calcium problems. Blood tests help detect the problem, and surgery to remove the tumor is often the main treatment.

topics.name: Parenchymatous Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Parenchymatous (interstitial) keratitis is inflammation in the middle layer of the cornea, often linked to an infection such as syphilis. It can cause eye pain, tearing, sensitivity to light, and blurred vision. Corneal clouding may leave lasting vision problems, so prompt assessment by an eye specialist and treatment of the underlying cause are important.

topics.name: Parenteral Nutrition (PN)
topics.clinical_significance: Parenteral nutrition (PN) supplies nutrients directly into a vein when the digestive tract cannot be used or needs rest. It can prevent or treat malnutrition, but a central line can cause infection or other complications. PN can also alter blood sugar, fluid, and electrolyte levels and affect the liver, so the formula and patient need close monitoring.

topics.name: Paresis
topics.clinical_significance: Here, paresis means ileus: a temporary slowing or stopping of intestinal movement without a physical blockage. It often occurs after abdominal surgery, but inflammation, low potassium, or some medicines can also cause it. Bloating, nausea, vomiting, and constipation may result. It can resemble a bowel obstruction, so the cause needs careful assessment.

topics.name: Parkinson Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Parkinson disease is a slowly progressive brain disorder that affects movement. It causes slowness and stiffness, often with shaking at rest; later, walking and balance problems can increase the risk of falls. Sleep, mood, memory, swallowing, bowel, or blood pressure problems may also occur. Medicines can ease symptoms, but regular care is often needed as the disease changes over time.

topics.name: Parkinson's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Parkinson’s disease is a slowly progressive brain disorder that affects movement. It causes slowness and stiffness, often with shaking at rest; later, walking and balance problems can increase the risk of falls. Sleep, mood, memory, swallowing, bowel, or blood pressure problems may also occur. Medicines can ease symptoms, but regular care is often needed as the disease changes over time.

topics.name: Paronychia, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic paronychia is repeated or long-lasting inflammation of the skin around a nail, usually a fingernail. It often follows ongoing exposure to water or irritants and is usually an inflammatory problem rather than a primary fungal infection. The nail fold may become red and tender, and the nail can become distorted over time. Avoiding moisture and irritants helps prevent ongoing damage.

topics.name: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)
topics.clinical_significance: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare acquired blood disorder in which the immune system destroys red blood cells. This can cause anemia and sometimes dark urine, and it raises the risk of serious blood clots, often in unusual veins. Bone marrow problems may also lower white blood cell and platelet counts. Flow cytometry confirms the diagnosis, and complement-blocking medicines can reduce red blood cell destruction and clot risk.

topics.name: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia
topics.clinical_significance: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) causes sudden episodes of a very fast, usually regular heartbeat that starts and stops abruptly. Episodes may cause pounding in the chest, shortness of breath, chest discomfort, or light-headedness. An ECG helps confirm the rhythm. Frequent or bothersome episodes can often be treated successfully with catheter ablation.

topics.name: Passive Hepatic Congestion
topics.clinical_significance: Passive hepatic congestion occurs when right-sided heart failure raises pressure in the veins draining the liver, causing blood to back up in the liver. It may cause no symptoms at first, but can lead to an enlarged, tender liver, abdominal discomfort, or, when severe, jaundice and fluid buildup. Long-term congestion can scar the liver. It is a sign of the heart failure’s severity, so treatment focuses on the heart problem.

topics.name: Passive Immunization
topics.clinical_significance: Passive immunization gives a person ready-made antibodies to help prevent or lessen an infection or toxin-related illness. It can be used after exposure or when a person cannot make enough antibodies. It acts quickly, but protection is temporary and does not create lasting immune memory.

topics.name: Patau Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 13. It often causes severe brain and heart defects, other birth differences, and profound developmental disability. Most affected infants die in the first weeks of life, although some survive longer. Care is supportive and tailored to the child and family.

topics.name: Patellar Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: A patellar dislocation occurs when the kneecap slips out of place, usually toward the outer side of the knee. It may return to place on its own, but pain and swelling can remain, and an associated bone or cartilage injury must be checked for with X-rays. Some people have repeated dislocations or ongoing knee instability; joint damage can lead to osteoarthritis.

topics.name: Patellar Tendon Tear
topics.clinical_significance: The patellar tendon connects the kneecap to the shinbone and helps straighten the knee. A tear causes pain and swelling and may make it impossible to straighten the leg or lift it while keeping it straight. A complete tear usually needs surgical repair; weakness and reduced movement can persist.

topics.name: Patellofemoral Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Patellofemoral syndrome (runner’s knee) causes pain around or behind the kneecap, often when climbing or descending stairs, doing sports that load the knee, or sitting with the knee bent for a long time. It may involve softened, swollen cartilage beneath the kneecap or poor kneecap tracking, and usually causes no visible swelling. Physical therapy to improve knee mechanics is a main treatment.

topics.name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
topics.clinical_significance: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a fetal blood vessel between the aorta and pulmonary artery (the artery to the lungs) that stays open after birth. A small PDA may cause no symptoms, but a large one can send too much blood to the lungs and strain the heart, causing breathing or feeding problems, poor growth, or heart failure. If severe and untreated, it can lead to high pressure in the lung arteries. Echocardiography shows the size and effect of the opening; some close on their own, while others need treatment.

topics.name: Paterson-Kelly Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Paterson-Kelly syndrome is linked to a thin membrane (web) in the upper esophagus, often with severe iron-deficiency anemia. The web can make solid food hard to swallow. Treating the anemia may improve the web; if swallowing problems persist, endoscopic stretching can open it.

topics.name: Pediatric Cancer, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Childhood cancer includes many different cancers, so treatment and outlook depend on the cancer type and its extent. Many children survive, but chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery can affect growth, learning, heart health, or fertility and may raise the risk of another cancer later. Care at a center experienced in childhood cancer and long-term follow-up help manage these effects.

topics.name: Pediatric Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: Pediatric cancers include leukemia, brain tumors, lymphomas, and cancers seen mainly in children, such as Wilms tumor and neuroblastoma. Treatment and outlook depend on the cancer type and extent. Many children survive, but treatment can affect growth, learning, heart health, or fertility and may increase the risk of another cancer later. Specialist care and long-term follow-up are important.

topics.name: Pediatric Physeal (Growth Plate) Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A growth plate fracture breaks the area of growing bone near the end of a child’s bone. Because the growth plate controls bone growth, damage can slow or stop growth and lead to a difference in limb length or shape. Some fractures are hard to see on the first X-ray, so a child may need follow-up if pain and tenderness continue. Treatment depends on the fracture and may include realigning and immobilizing the bone or surgery.

topics.name: Pediculosis
topics.clinical_significance: Pediculosis is an infestation with lice on the scalp, body, or pubic area. It often causes itching and skin sores from scratching. How it spreads depends on the type: head lice pass mainly through close contact, pubic lice usually through sexual contact, and body lice through infested clothing or bedding. Body lice can also spread serious infections such as epidemic typhus.

topics.name: Pedophilia
topics.clinical_significance: Pedophilia means a recurrent sexual interest in prepubescent children. A diagnosis of pedophilic disorder has added criteria: the pattern lasts at least 6 months, the person has acted on the urges or is distressed or impaired by them, and the person is at least 16 and at least 5 years older than the child. Sexual activity between an adult and a child is abuse and can cause serious harm; protecting children is essential.

topics.name: Pedophilic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Pedophilic disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual fantasies, urges, or behaviors focused on prepubescent children, lasting at least 6 months. Diagnosis also requires that the person has acted on the urges or is greatly distressed or impaired by them, is at least 16 years old, and is at least 5 years older than the child. Sexual activity between an adult and a child is abuse and can cause serious harm.

topics.name: Peliosis Hepatis
topics.clinical_significance: Peliosis hepatis causes multiple blood-filled spaces to form in the liver and often causes no symptoms. It has been linked to some medicines and chemicals, including anabolic steroids. Rarely, a space can rupture and cause serious bleeding, or the condition can lead to jaundice, liver enlargement, or liver failure. Most cases do not need treatment.

topics.name: Pellagra
topics.clinical_significance: Pellagra results from niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency. It can cause a rash on sun-exposed skin, a sore or inflamed mouth, digestive problems such as diarrhea, and changes in memory, behavior, or awareness. Severe untreated deficiency can be life-threatening, but it usually responds to nicotinamide and treatment of the cause of the deficiency.

topics.name: Pelvic Congestion Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic congestion syndrome, now included under pelvic venous disorders, can cause chronic pelvic pain linked to enlarged pelvic veins from backward blood flow or a blockage. Pain often worsens after prolonged standing or intercourse and may ease when lying down. Enlarged veins on imaging alone do not confirm the disorder, because they can be present without symptoms; other causes of pelvic pain must be considered. Treatment is considered when pain is severe and persistent.

topics.name: Pelvic Examination
topics.clinical_significance: A gynecologic pelvic examination may include looking at the external genitals, using a speculum to view the vagina and cervix, and feeling the pelvic organs by hand. It can help assess symptoms such as pelvic pain, unusual bleeding, or discharge and may allow cervical testing. It is not needed as a routine screening test for every person without symptoms; the clinician should explain each part and get consent.

topics.name: Pelvic Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic fractures range from stable breaks after a minor fall to unstable injuries after major trauma. Unstable fractures can cause severe internal bleeding and shock; injuries to the bladder, urinary tract, bowel, or nerves may also occur. Prompt assessment checks the fracture’s stability and for related injuries. Stable fractures may need only pain relief, while unstable ones need urgent stabilization.

topics.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection of the upper female reproductive tract. It is often caused by sexually transmitted bacteria and may cause few or no symptoms. Prompt antibiotic treatment helps prevent long-term problems such as infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain.

topics.name: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POP)
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when weakened pelvic support lets the uterus, vagina, bladder, or rectum bulge into or through the vagina. It can cause vaginal pressure or a bulge, trouble urinating, or difficulty passing stool. Treatment depends on symptoms and may include pelvic floor exercises, a pessary, or surgery.

topics.name: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POP), Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Weakening of the muscles and tissues that support the pelvic organs can cause the uterus, vaginal walls, or vaginal vault to descend. Prolapse often affects more than one area. Vaginal birth, aging, obesity, pelvic surgery, and chronic straining increase risk. Severity is graded with the POP-Q system, and treatment depends on symptoms.

topics.name: Pelvic Pain During Early Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic pain in early pregnancy can result from normal pregnancy changes, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or other pelvic and abdominal problems. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy can cause severe bleeding and shock, so assessment should promptly rule it out and check for other urgent causes.

topics.name: Pelvic Venous Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic venous disorders can cause chronic pelvic pain linked to blocked or backward blood flow in pelvic veins. Pain often worsens with standing or after sex, and varicose veins may be present near the ovaries. Dilated pelvic veins can also be symptom-free, so imaging alone does not confirm the disorder; symptoms and other causes of pain must be assessed.

topics.name: Pelvic Venous Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Pelvic venous syndrome describes chronic pelvic pain linked to blocked or backward blood flow in pelvic veins. Pain often worsens after standing or sex, but enlarged veins may cause no symptoms. Diagnosis depends on the symptoms and assessment for other causes; imaging alone does not confirm the syndrome.

topics.name: Pemphigoid Gestationis
topics.clinical_significance: Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare autoimmune, very itchy blistering rash that occurs during pregnancy or after birth, often starting around the navel. Most fetuses are unaffected, but placental problems can impair fetal growth; a small number of newborns have a temporary rash. Corticosteroids treat the rash, and fetal growth may need monitoring.

topics.name: Pemphigus Foliaceus
topics.clinical_significance: Pemphigus foliaceus is an autoimmune skin disease that causes fragile, shallow blisters. They often break quickly, leaving crusted, sore patches, usually on the face, scalp, or upper body; mouth sores are uncommon. Treatment depends on severity and may use steroid creams or steroid tablets.

topics.name: Pemphigus Vulgaris
topics.clinical_significance: Pemphigus vulgaris is a rare, serious autoimmune disease that causes fragile blisters, often in the mouth and on the skin. The blisters break into painful raw areas; mouth sores can make eating and drinking difficult. Widespread sores can cause infection and fluid loss, and the disease can be fatal without treatment.

topics.name: Penetrating Keratoplasty
topics.clinical_significance: Penetrating keratoplasty is a full-thickness corneal transplant used to replace a severely damaged, scarred, or cloudy cornea, restore the eye, or improve vision. Vision may take up to 18 months to reach its full potential. Complications include graft rejection, infection, glaucoma, and graft failure.

topics.name: Penicillins
topics.clinical_significance: Penicillins are antibiotics used to treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Which bacteria they treat depends on the specific drug and bacterial resistance. Side effects include rash, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; rarely, allergy causes life-threatening anaphylaxis. They should not be used after a serious allergic reaction to penicillin.

topics.name: Penile and Scrotal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Penile and scrotal disorders include skin changes, foreskin problems, pain, swelling, and masses. Some need urgent care: paraphimosis can cut off blood flow to the penis, and sudden scrotal pain may be testicular torsion, which can lead to loss of the testis without prompt treatment.

topics.name: Penile Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Penile anomalies include abnormal curvature, a tight foreskin, and differences in penile size or structure; some occur with urethral defects. They may affect function and sometimes need surgery. Paraphimosis, when a retracted foreskin is trapped behind the glans, needs urgent treatment because swelling can restrict blood flow.

topics.name: Penile Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Most penile cancers are squamous cell cancers. They may appear as a sore that does not heal, a thickened skin area, or a growth; a biopsy is needed to diagnose them. Early cancer can often be cured, but advanced cancer can spread to groin lymph nodes and be fatal. Risk is higher with HPV, smoking, chronic inflammation, or poor hygiene, especially in uncircumcised men.

topics.name: Penile Curvature
topics.clinical_significance: Scar tissue in the penis can cause it to bend during an erection, sometimes with pain or difficulty with penetration. Mild cases may improve over months and may not need treatment if sexual function is unaffected. More troublesome curvature can be treated with injections, traction devices, or surgery, but results vary.

topics.name: PEP Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: PEP (POEMS) syndrome is a rare disorder linked to a plasma cell disease. It causes peripheral nerve damage and may also cause enlarged organs, hormone problems, abnormal bone lesions, skin changes, fluid buildup, or swelling of the optic nerve. Treatment targets the plasma cell disease.

topics.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Peptic ulcers are deep sores in the lining of the stomach or upper small intestine, usually caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or anti-inflammatory medicines such as NSAIDs. They may cause burning upper-abdominal pain or no symptoms. Bleeding, perforation, or blockage are serious complications. Treatment includes acid-reducing medicine and, when present, treatment of H. pylori.

topics.name: Percutaneous Coronary Interventions (PCI)
topics.clinical_significance: PCI uses a balloon catheter, usually with a stent, to reopen a narrowed or blocked heart artery. It can quickly restore blood flow during a heart attack and relieve angina that persists despite medicine. Risks include bleeding, artery damage, and later re-narrowing or clotting in the stent; antiplatelet medicines help prevent clots.

topics.name: Perennial Allergic Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Perennial allergic conjunctivitis is year-round inflammation of the eye surface, often triggered by indoor allergens such as dust mites or animal dander. It causes itchy, red, watery eyes and may cause eyelid swelling or stringy discharge. Severe long-lasting cases can scar or damage the cornea and affect vision.

topics.name: Perforation of the GI Tract, AcutePerforation of the GI Tract, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: An acute hole in the digestive tract can let stomach or intestinal contents leak into the abdomen, causing severe inflammation, infection, and shock. It is a medical emergency that usually needs immediate surgery, IV fluids, and antibiotics.

topics.name: Periarteritis Nodosa
topics.clinical_significance: Periarteritis nodosa, also called polyarteritis nodosa, is a rare inflammation that damages medium-sized arteries and reduces blood flow to organs. It often affects the skin, kidneys, nerves, muscles, and gut, causing problems such as skin sores, weakness or numbness, abdominal pain, and high blood pressure. It can damage organs; the lungs and kidney filters are usually spared.

topics.name: Pericarditis
topics.clinical_significance: Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart. It often causes sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths or lying down and eases when sitting up and leaning forward. Fluid may collect around the heart; rarely, pressure or scarring can limit heart filling and lower blood flow. Causes include infections, heart injury, autoimmune or kidney disease, cancer, and some medicines, though often no cause is found.

topics.name: Perichondritis of the Ear
topics.clinical_significance: Perichondritis is inflammation of the tissue covering the outer-ear cartilage, causing pain, redness, and swelling; an abscess may form. It can follow cartilage injury or piercing, spread from a skin infection, or result from an inflammatory disease, so it is not always an infection. Separation of the covering from the cartilage can cut off its blood supply and cause cartilage death and lasting ear deformity.

topics.name: Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions
topics.clinical_significance: Peri-implant conditions affect the gum and jawbone around dental implants. Plaque-related mucositis causes gum swelling and bleeding and may improve when plaque is removed. Peri-implantitis can destroy the supporting bone and threaten implant stability. Gum or bone deficiencies can also affect long-term implant success and may need grafting.

topics.name: Perilunate and Lunate Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: Perilunate and lunate dislocations are serious wrist injuries, usually caused by a fall on an outstretched hand or a crash. They cause pain, swelling, and deformity. Without prompt reduction and specialist care, they can injure the median nerve or damage the wrist bones and joint, reducing hand function. Most need surgical repair.

topics.name: Perinatal Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Low red blood cell levels around birth may reflect the normal early drop in hemoglobin, especially in preterm infants, but can also result from blood loss, red-cell breakdown, or poor red-cell production. Severe or rapid anemia reduces oxygen delivery and can cause breathing or heart-rate problems, shock, or fetal swelling (hydrops); red-cell breakdown can cause jaundice. Treatment depends on the cause and severity, and severe or symptomatic cases may need a transfusion.

topics.name: Perinatal Hematologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Anemia and polycythemia are the most common blood disorders found at birth. Too few red blood cells can limit oxygen delivery; too many can make blood thick and slow its flow, sometimes causing clots, heart failure, or brain problems. Depending on the cause and severity, affected infants may develop jaundice, breathing or feeding problems, or shock. Treatment depends on the disorder and may include transfusion or other supportive care.

topics.name: Perinatal Physiology
topics.clinical_significance: At birth, a baby must shift quickly from placental support to independent breathing, circulation, feeding, and waste removal. Immaturity, especially in preterm infants, can disrupt oxygen exchange, bilirubin clearance, immunity, kidney function, or glucose control, leading to problems such as breathing difficulty, jaundice, infection, or low blood sugar.

topics.name: Perinatal Polycythemia and Hyperviscosity Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: In newborns, too many red blood cells can make blood thick and slow its flow. Severe cases may reduce blood flow to organs or cause blood clots, breathing problems, poor feeding, low blood sugar, jaundice, or seizures. Prompt assessment matters because some affected infants need treatment to lower the blood thickness.

topics.name: Perinatal Problems
topics.clinical_significance: Perinatal problems include complications related to a newborn’s growth and gestational age, breathing, birth injuries, and temperature control. Some can quickly become life-threatening or cause lasting harm, so early recognition and care are important.

topics.name: Perinatal Respiratory Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing problems around birth may appear at once or develop hours later, and they are a common reason newborns need intensive care. Fast or irregular breathing, grunting, chest pulling in, pauses in breathing, or bluish skin can signal poor oxygenation. Prompt assessment is important because causes range from temporary lung fluid to serious lung, heart, or other illness.

topics.name: Perinatal Tuberculosis (TB)
topics.clinical_significance: TB can pass to a baby before or during birth, or spread through the air after birth. In newborns it may affect several organs and look like sepsis, with signs that are easy to mistake for other illnesses. Prompt testing and treatment are important because TB can be severe in young infants, and preventive treatment may be needed after exposure.

topics.name: Periodic Abstinence
topics.clinical_significance: Periodic abstinence uses cycle dates or body signs to estimate fertile days and avoid intercourse during that time to prevent pregnancy. Because fertile days can be hard to predict and pregnancy rates are relatively high with typical use, it may not suit people who strongly need to avoid pregnancy. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Periodic Limb Movement Disorder (PLMD) and Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
topics.clinical_significance: Restless legs syndrome causes an urge to move, often with unpleasant leg sensations that worsen at rest and near bedtime. Periodic limb movement disorder causes repeated kicking or twitching during sleep. Both can disrupt sleep and lead to daytime tiredness; checking for iron deficiency or other related problems may help guide care.

topics.name: Periodontal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Periodontal disorders affect the gums and other tissues around or supporting the teeth. Gingivitis can cause red, swollen, bleeding gums and may improve with dental cleaning and good oral hygiene. More advanced disease can damage the bone that supports teeth, causing them to loosen or fall out, so early dental care helps limit harm.

topics.name: Periodontitis
topics.clinical_significance: Bacteria in dental plaque trigger chronic inflammation that damages the gums and the ligament and bone supporting the teeth. The disease often causes little pain, so it may go unnoticed as gums recede and teeth loosen; advanced disease can lead to tooth loss. Dental care can help slow further damage.

topics.name: Perioperative Management
topics.clinical_significance: Perioperative care is planned around the operation, a person’s health problems, and their medicines, which can affect bleeding, blood clots, blood sugar, and response to anesthesia. Reviewing these risks and checking the patient, procedure, and surgical site help prevent avoidable problems and support better outcomes.

topics.name: Perioral Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: This long-lasting facial rash causes small red bumps, and sometimes pus-filled spots, usually around the mouth while leaving a narrow area next to the lips clear. Steroid medicines, fluoridated toothpaste, and some skin products can trigger or worsen it. Identifying and avoiding triggers can help; topical or oral medicines may also be needed.

topics.name: Periorbital Cellulitis
topics.clinical_significance: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis is an infection of the eyelid and nearby skin, causing swelling, redness, and tenderness. Eye movement and vision are usually normal. Pain with eye movement, a bulging eye, or reduced vision may signal deeper orbital infection, which can threaten sight and spread into the brain and needs urgent care.

topics.name: Periorificial dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Periorificial dermatitis, also called perioral dermatitis, causes small red bumps and sometimes pus-filled spots around the mouth; it may also affect the skin around the eyes or forehead. Steroid medicines and fluoridated dental products can trigger or worsen it. Avoiding triggers and using prescribed skin treatments can help.

topics.name: Peripheral Artery Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral artery aneurysms often cause no symptoms, but a clot can block blood flow to a hand or foot. Sudden pain, coldness, pale skin, numbness, or loss of a pulse may signal acute limb ischemia, which needs urgent treatment. Rupture is less common.

topics.name: Peripheral Artery Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral artery disease is usually caused by fatty plaque that narrows arteries supplying the limbs and reduces blood flow. It may cause no symptoms or leg pain while walking that eases with rest; severe disease can cause wounds that do not heal, tissue death, or limb loss. It also signals increased risk of heart and blood vessel problems elsewhere.

topics.name: Peripheral Artery Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral artery disorders affect arteries that carry blood to the limbs and other parts of the body. Depending on the cause, arteries may narrow, become blocked, or widen abnormally. Reduced blood flow can cause pain, cold or discolored skin, sores that heal slowly, or tissue loss; sudden loss of blood flow needs urgent care.

topics.name: Peripheral Nervous System and Motor Unit Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, the nerve-to-muscle connection, or the motor system that controls movement. Depending on what is affected, they can cause pain, numbness, weakness, cramps, or loss of movement. Severe weakness may affect swallowing or breathing, so new or worsening symptoms need assessment.

topics.name: Peripheral Nervous System Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral nerve disorders can disrupt feeling, movement, or automatic body functions. They may cause pain, tingling, loss of sensation, weakness, or paralysis. Causes include injury, diabetes, infection, inflammation, toxins, and inherited conditions; some disorders worsen over time, and severe weakness can affect swallowing or breathing. Finding the cause helps guide treatment and limit further harm.

topics.name: Peripheral Rheumatoid Ulceration
topics.clinical_significance: This serious ulcer forms at the outer edge of the cornea, the clear front of the eye. It often occurs with active, long-standing rheumatoid arthritis or another rheumatic disease and can cause irritation, light sensitivity, and reduced vision. It may signal serious inflammation of blood vessels, so prompt eye-specialist assessment and treatment of the underlying disease are important.

topics.name: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis causes inflammation and an open sore at the outer edge of the cornea, leading to eye irritation, light sensitivity, and reduced vision. It is often linked to active systemic rheumatic disease, but infection must also be ruled out. Prompt eye-specialist assessment is important because vision is at risk and the underlying illness may be serious.

topics.name: Peripheral Vascular Disease
topics.clinical_significance: In this MSD usage, peripheral vascular disease means peripheral artery disease: plaque buildup narrows arteries, usually in the legs, and reduces blood flow. It may cause no symptoms or leg pain while walking that eases with rest. Severe disease can cause pain at rest, sores that do not heal, tissue death, or limb loss. It is also linked with disease in the heart or brain arteries.

topics.name: Peripheral Venous Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Venous disorders can impair blood return from the limbs or cause clots in the veins. Long-term poor return can lead to leg swelling, aching, skin changes, and ulcers. A deep vein clot can travel to the lungs and cause a life-threatening pulmonary embolism, so prompt assessment is important when a clot is suspected.

topics.name: Peritoneal Dialysis
topics.clinical_significance: Peritoneal dialysis treats kidney failure by using the lining of the abdomen as a filter. Dialysis fluid enters through a catheter, takes up waste and extra water, then drains out. It can be done at home and offers flexibility, but requires careful sterile technique because infection of the abdominal lining or catheter site can occur.

topics.name: Peritonsillar Abscess and Cellulitis
topics.clinical_significance: This infection beside a tonsil can cause severe one-sided throat pain, fever, trouble swallowing, difficulty opening the mouth, a muffled voice, and a uvula pushed to one side. An abscess often needs drainage as well as antibiotics. Severe swelling may require hospital care and airway monitoring.

topics.name: Permanent Contraception
topics.clinical_significance: Permanent contraception prevents pregnancy by cutting or blocking the tubes that carry sperm or eggs, or by removing the fallopian tubes. It is highly effective but should be considered permanent; reversal may not restore fertility. Rare failure after a tubal procedure can lead to an ectopic pregnancy. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Peroxisomal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited disorders prevent peroxisomes, cell structures that process certain fats and other substances, from forming or working normally. Depending on the type, they can affect the brain and nerves, vision, hearing, adrenal glands, liver, or bones. Severity ranges from milder adult-onset disease to severe illness in infancy; early diagnosis matters because some types have specific treatments.

topics.name: Persistent Ductus Arteriosus
topics.clinical_significance: The ductus arteriosus is a normal blood vessel before birth that usually closes soon after delivery. If it stays open, extra blood may flow to the lungs and strain the heart. A small opening may cause no problems, but a large one can lead to poor feeding, slow growth, heart failure, or worsening breathing problems, especially in premature infants.

topics.name: Persistent Genital Arousal Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: This rare disorder causes unwanted genital sensations, such as tingling or throbbing, without sexual desire. Symptoms can last for hours or days and cause severe distress or embarrassment. The cause and best treatment are not yet clear, but pelvic floor physical therapy may help some people.

topics.name: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)
topics.clinical_significance: In this newborn condition, lung blood vessels remain too tight after birth, so too little blood reaches the lungs for oxygen. Oxygen-poor blood may then circulate through the body, causing severe low oxygen, fast or labored breathing, and bluish skin that may not improve with oxygen. The extra strain can weaken the right side of the heart, so urgent intensive care is needed.

topics.name: Persistent Sexual Arousal Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Persistent sexual arousal disorder, also called persistent genital arousal disorder, causes unwanted genital sensations such as tingling or throbbing without sexual desire. Sensations may last for hours or days and cause severe distress. The cause and best treatment are unclear, but pelvic floor physical therapy may help some people.

topics.name: Persistent Truncus Arteriosus
topics.clinical_significance: This serious heart defect occurs when the aorta and pulmonary artery fail to form as separate vessels, leaving one large vessel to carry blood from the heart. A hole between the lower heart chambers is usually also present, so oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood mix. This can lower oxygen levels, send too much blood to the lungs, and cause heart failure in early infancy; early surgery is usually needed.

topics.name: Personality Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Personality disorders involve long-lasting, rigid patterns of thinking, feeling, and relating that cause serious distress or problems in relationships, work, or daily life. These patterns usually begin by adolescence or early adulthood and may become less severe over time.

topics.name: Personality Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Personality disorders involve long-lasting, rigid patterns of thinking, feeling, relating, or controlling impulses that cause distress or interfere with work and relationships. They usually become clear by early adulthood, and many become less severe over time. Psychotherapy is the main treatment.

topics.name: Pertussis
topics.clinical_significance: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection that causes severe coughing fits lasting for weeks; the cough may continue for months. It can cause breathing problems, seizures, or death, especially in young infants. Vaccination helps prevent it. Antibiotics can lessen illness if started early, limit spread, and help protect some close contacts.

topics.name: Pestis
topics.clinical_significance: Pestis, or plague, is a severe infection caused by Yersinia pestis, usually spread to people by flea bites from infected rodents. It can cause swollen, painful lymph nodes, severe pneumonia, or infection of the blood. Pneumonic plague can spread between people, and untreated plague can be fatal, so rapid diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are essential.

topics.name: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an inherited condition that causes dark spots on the lips and mouth, hands, or feet and noncancerous polyps in the digestive tract. The polyps can bleed or block the bowel, and affected people have a higher risk of several cancers, so ongoing cancer checks are important.

topics.name: Peyronie Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Peyronie disease is scar tissue inside the penis that can make it bend during an erection. It may cause pain or make penetration difficult. Mild cases that do not affect sexual function may need no treatment; treatment may be considered when symptoms interfere with sexual activity.

topics.name: Peyronie's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Peyronie's disease is scarring inside the penis that can make it bend during an erection. It may cause pain or make penetration difficult. Mild cases that do not affect sexual function may need no treatment, and some cases improve over time.

topics.name: PFAPA Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: PFAPA causes repeated bouts of fever, often every 3 to 4 weeks, with mouth ulcers, sore throat, or swollen neck glands, usually in young children. Children are generally well and grow normally between episodes. The episodes often become milder and stop by about age 10, but other causes of recurring fever should be ruled out.

topics.name: pH Monitoring, Ambulatory
topics.clinical_significance: Ambulatory pH monitoring records acidity in the esophagus, usually for 24 hours, while a person goes about daily activities. It helps confirm or rule out acid reflux, link symptoms to reflux episodes, and assess treatment or the need for antireflux surgery. When combined with impedance testing, it can also detect nonacid reflux.

topics.name: Phaeohyphomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Phaeohyphomycosis is an infection caused by dark-colored fungi. It can affect the skin or tissues under it and may also spread to the brain, lungs, sinuses, or other organs. Widespread infection is more common in people with weakened immune systems and can be life-threatening; treatment may require surgery and long courses of antifungal medicine.

topics.name: Phantom Limb Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Phantom limb pain is real pain felt in the part of a limb that has been amputated. It may feel burning, aching, shooting, or squeezing and often becomes less severe over time. It differs from phantom limb sensation, which is feeling the missing limb without pain.

topics.name: Phantom Limb Sensation
topics.clinical_significance: Phantom limb sensation is feeling part or all of an amputated limb as if it were still there, without pain. It is common after amputation and may help a person sense the position of a prosthesis, but it can sometimes lead to falls if the person forgets the limb is missing.

topics.name: Pharmacists and Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults often take several medicines and have a higher risk of harmful interactions, duplicate medicines, and dosing errors. A pharmacist can review the medication list, check for problems, explain how to use medicines, and help make the treatment plan safer and easier to follow.

topics.name: Pharmacodynamics
topics.clinical_significance: Pharmacodynamics describes what a drug does to the body, including how it produces its effects and how the body responds at different drug levels. Age, illness, and other medicines can change this response, helping explain why the same dose may affect people differently.

topics.name: Pharmacodynamics in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults may respond more strongly or weakly to a drug than younger people, even at the same drug level. They are especially sensitive to medicines with anticholinergic effects, which can cause confusion, drowsiness, constipation, trouble urinating, blurred vision, or low blood pressure; these medicines should be avoided when possible.

topics.name: Pharmacodynamics, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pharmacodynamics explains how a drug acts on the body and how its dose and level in the body affect its effects. The response depends on how the drug interacts with its target and can change with age, illness, or other medicines.

topics.name: Pharmacogenetics
topics.clinical_significance: Inherited genetic differences can make people process some medicines faster or slower, changing how well the medicines work and the risk of side effects. For some medicines, genetic testing can help clinicians choose a suitable dose and reduce the risk of treatment failure or harm.

topics.name: Pharmacokinetics
topics.clinical_significance: Pharmacokinetics describes how a medicine moves into, through, and out of the body: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. These processes affect how quickly it starts working, how strong its effects are, and how long they last, and help guide dosing.

topics.name: Pharmacokinetics in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Children absorb, process, and remove medicines differently as they grow because these body functions mature over time. Doses often depend on age and weight, but two children of the same age and size may still need different doses. Careful dosing is especially important in newborns and infants to prevent drug levels from becoming too high or too low.

topics.name: Pharmacokinetics in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: With age, the body may absorb, distribute, break down, and remove medicines differently. Slower liver metabolism and kidney removal can let some drugs build up and cause delayed harm, so doses or dosing intervals may need adjustment based on the person's kidney function and response.

topics.name: Pharmacokinetics, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pharmacokinetics follows how a medicine is absorbed, moves through the body, is broken down, and is removed. These processes affect how quickly a drug works, how strong its effect is, and how long it lasts. Age, kidney or liver function, and other factors can change drug levels and dosing needs.

topics.name: Pharmacologic Therapy in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Medication use in older adults is complicated by multiple illnesses and age-related changes in how medicines work and leave the body. Taking many medicines raises the risk of side effects, interactions, and missed doses, but needed treatments can also be underused. Regularly reviewing each medicine's benefit, dose, interactions, and continued need helps keep treatment safe and effective.

topics.name: Pharmacologic Therapy in Older Adults, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults often need several medicines, and aging or chronic illnesses can change how they respond to them. Good treatment balances using medicines that are needed and effective with avoiding unnecessary drugs, harmful interactions, and incorrect doses. Too much and too little treatment can both cause harm, so the full medication plan should be reviewed regularly.

topics.name: Pharmacologic Treatment of Asthma
topics.clinical_significance: Asthma medicines are chosen and adjusted step by step to control symptoms and prevent attacks while limiting side effects. Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and are the main treatment; bronchodilators ease narrowed airways, but a short-acting bronchodilator alone is not recommended. Severe asthma may need add-on medicines, and correct inhaler use is important.

topics.name: Pharmacotherapy, Concepts in
topics.clinical_significance: Pharmacotherapy uses medicines to treat a condition. Choosing a medicine depends on what is being treated, the drug's benefits and risks, how it is taken and removed, and patient factors such as age, other illnesses, and other medicines. Medication errors and interactions can change its effects or cause harm.

topics.name: Pharmacotherapy, Introduction to Concepts in
topics.clinical_significance: Choosing a medicine depends on the condition being treated, the drug's expected benefit and risks, how it is taken, and how often it is needed. Patient factors such as age, other illnesses, and other medicines also matter. Medication errors and drug interactions can reduce benefit or cause harm.

topics.name: Pharyngeal Bursa
topics.clinical_significance: A pharyngeal bursa (Tornwaldt cyst) is a rare, usually harmless cyst in the middle of the upper throat behind the nose. It often causes no symptoms, but if infected it can cause foul-smelling drainage or taste, sore throat, or blockage near the ear tube. Cysts without symptoms need no treatment; troublesome ones may be opened or removed.

topics.name: Pharyngitis
topics.clinical_significance: Pharyngitis is inflammation or infection of the throat, most often caused by a virus; group A strep is an important bacterial cause. It causes sore throat and pain with swallowing, sometimes with fever and swollen neck glands. Testing may be needed to identify strep, which is treated with antibiotics to reduce symptoms and prevent complications such as an abscess or rheumatic fever.

topics.name: Phenylketonuria (PKU)
topics.clinical_significance: PKU is an inherited disorder in which the body cannot properly break down phenylalanine, an amino acid in protein, so it builds up and can damage the brain. Without early treatment, it can cause severe problems with learning, development, and behavior. Newborn screening and lifelong control of phenylalanine in the diet can prevent most severe effects and give a very good outlook.

topics.name: Pheochromocytoma
topics.clinical_significance: A usually adrenal gland tumor that releases excess adrenaline-like hormones. It can cause persistent or sudden episodes of high blood pressure, often with headache, sweating, or a pounding heartbeat. It can strain the heart and blood vessels, but surgical removal after blood pressure is controlled is often curative.

topics.name: Phimosis and Paraphimosis
topics.clinical_significance: Phimosis is a foreskin that cannot be pulled back; in young children this is usually normal and often resolves by age 5. Paraphimosis occurs when the pulled-back foreskin gets trapped behind the head of the penis, causing swelling and cutting off blood flow. It is an emergency because the tissue can be damaged quickly.

topics.name: Phlyctenular Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an immune reaction to bacterial proteins that causes small inflamed bumps on the clear covering of the eye and sometimes the cornea, often in children. Corneal involvement can cause pain, light sensitivity, tearing, and blurred vision. Repeated or severe inflammation can scar the cornea and impair sight.

topics.name: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is an immune reaction to bacterial proteins that causes small nodules on the cornea or conjunctiva, often in children. Corneal involvement can cause pain, tearing, light sensitivity, and blurred vision. Repeated attacks can scar and cloud the cornea, reducing sight.

topics.name: Phlyctenulosis
topics.clinical_significance: Phlyctenulosis is an immune reaction in the eye, usually to staph bacteria, that forms small bumps on the conjunctiva or cornea. It is more common in children. Corneal involvement can cause pain, tearing, light sensitivity, and blurred vision; repeated attacks can scar the cornea and reduce sight.

topics.name: Phobic Disorders, Specific
topics.clinical_significance: A specific phobia is an intense, ongoing fear of a particular object or situation that is out of proportion to its actual danger and usually lasts 6 months or more. Facing or anticipating the trigger can cause strong anxiety and avoidance, disrupting daily life or preventing needed care. Exposure therapy is the main treatment.

topics.name: Phosphate Concentration, Disorders of, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Phosphate is needed for healthy bones and for cells to store and use energy. Low blood phosphate can cause muscle weakness and, when severe, breathing or heart problems, seizures, or coma. High phosphate, often caused by kidney disease, may lower blood calcium and lead to calcium deposits in tissues or blood vessels. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the imbalance.

topics.name: Photosensitivity
topics.clinical_significance: Photosensitivity is an unusually strong skin reaction to sunlight or ultraviolet light. It can cause sunburn-like redness and pain, an itchy rash, or blisters. It may be triggered by medicines or chemicals or linked to an inherited or other disease, such as lupus; new or severe symptoms may need medical evaluation.

topics.name: Phyllodes Tumor of the Breast
topics.clinical_significance: Phyllodes tumors are uncommon breast growths that can be benign or cancerous and may grow large. Some return after surgery, and a smaller number spread to other parts of the body, usually the lungs. Treatment is surgery to remove the tumor; the amount of tissue removed depends on its size and whether it is cancerous.

topics.name: Physical Changes With Aging
topics.clinical_significance: Many body functions gradually decline with age, which can affect strength, balance, vision, hearing, and how the body handles medicines. Normal aging alone usually does not cause major loss of daily function; illness is often the main cause. Regular physical activity can help older adults maintain strength, mobility, and independence.

topics.name: Physical Examination of the Newborn
topics.clinical_significance: A thorough exam soon after birth checks a newborn's growth and major body systems and looks for birth injuries or problems present at birth that may need early care. Abnormal findings may require prompt testing or follow-up. Screening tests are also needed because some conditions cannot be found by physical examination alone.

topics.name: Physical Examination of the Older Adult
topics.clinical_significance: A careful exam can find illness and changes in mobility, balance, vision, hearing, or ability to care for oneself. Checking blood pressure while lying and standing can reveal drops that may cause dizziness or falls. Findings should be considered with the person's history because some changes are normal with age, while new or worsening problems may need further evaluation.

topics.name: Physical Growth and Sexual Maturation of Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Tracking height, weight, and the order of pubertal changes helps show whether an adolescent is developing as expected. Timing varies, but very early, delayed, or out-of-sequence changes may point to a health problem and can affect final height, so evaluation may be needed. Reassurance and support matter because differences in timing can cause stress.

topics.name: Physical Growth of Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Regular measurements of weight, length or height, and head size show whether an infant or child is growing along an expected pattern. Changes in growth rate or an unusual pattern may point to feeding, nutrition, or other health problems and can prompt further evaluation. Repeated measurements on age-appropriate growth charts are more useful than a single measurement.

topics.name: Physical Therapy (PT)
topics.clinical_significance: Physical therapy uses exercises and movement training to improve joint motion, muscle strength, balance, and walking. It can help people regain function after illness, injury, surgery, or prolonged bed rest, making daily movement safer and supporting independence.

topics.name: Physiology of Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy causes normal changes in the heart and circulation, blood, kidneys, breathing, digestion, and hormones to support the fetus. Knowing these changes helps clinicians interpret symptoms and test results, distinguish expected changes from illness, and identify problems that need care. Most changes improve after delivery.

topics.name: Pica
topics.clinical_significance: Pica is persistent eating of nonfood, nonnutritive substances for at least 1 month when this is not appropriate for a person's developmental level or cultural practice; it is not diagnosed in children under 2 years. It often causes no serious harm, but some substances can lead to nutrient deficiencies, bowel blockage, lead poisoning, or parasitic infection. Pica is more common during pregnancy and with iron-deficiency anemia, and may occur with developmental or mental-health conditions.

topics.name: Pigbel
topics.clinical_significance: Pigbel is a severe form of Clostridium perfringens type C infection that damages tissue in the small intestine. It can cause severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, shock, or death, so prompt treatment with antibiotics is important; surgery may be needed if the bowel is badly damaged or blocked.

topics.name: Pigmentation Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pigmentation disorders cause patches or widespread areas of lighter, white, or darker skin because melanin has changed. They may follow skin injury or inflammation, or be linked to medicines, an internal illness, or cancer. Recognizing the pattern and finding the cause helps guide care and identify problems that need further evaluation.

topics.name: Pigmentation Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pigment changes may be limited to patches or affect larger areas, and may reflect reduced, absent, or increased melanin. Light patches often follow injury or skin inflammation, while widespread darkening can be linked to medicines, internal illness, or cancer. The pattern and medical history help identify the cause and whether further evaluation is needed.

topics.name: Pilar Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: A pilar cyst is usually a harmless, firm, painless lump, most often on the scalp, and may run in families. It can be removed if it causes discomfort or cosmetic concern; removing the entire cyst wall helps prevent it from returning. Malignant change is very rare.

topics.name: Piles
topics.clinical_significance: Piles (hemorrhoids) are enlarged blood vessels in the anal canal. Internal hemorrhoids may cause painless bleeding with bowel movements, while a clot in an external hemorrhoid can cause a painful lump. Rectal bleeding should not be assumed to be from hemorrhoids until more serious causes have been ruled out.

topics.name: Pilonidal Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Pilonidal disease is a pit or tunnel in the skin near the tailbone, often containing hair. It may cause no symptoms, but infection can lead to a painful abscess or a sinus that drains off and on. An abscess usually needs drainage, and a persistent sinus may need surgery.

topics.name: Pineal Region Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Pineal region tumors can block the flow of fluid in the brain and raise pressure inside the skull. They may also limit upward eye movement, affect pupil responses, or trigger early puberty, especially in boys. The tumor type guides treatment and outlook; germinomas often respond very well to radiation.

topics.name: Pinguecula and Pterygium
topics.clinical_significance: Both are benign growths on the clear covering of the eye and are linked to long-term sun exposure. A pinguecula stays beside the cornea and usually does not affect vision; a pterygium can grow over the cornea, distort it, and reduce vision. Eye irritation can occur, and protection from ultraviolet light may help slow pterygium growth.

topics.name: Pink Eye
topics.clinical_significance: Pink eye means visible redness of the eye, most often caused by conjunctivitis from infection or allergy. Some red eyes have more serious causes, such as corneal injury, uveitis, or glaucoma. Eye pain, marked light sensitivity, or reduced vision calls for prompt eye evaluation.

topics.name: Pinworm Infestation
topics.clinical_significance: Pinworm infection spreads when eggs are swallowed, often from contaminated hands or household objects, and is common in school-aged children and their households. Most infected people have no symptoms; some have itching around the anus at night, and less often vaginal itching. The infection is usually harmless, but reinfection is common and may require treating household members.

topics.name: Piriformis Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Piriformis syndrome is uncommon compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle, causing an ache in the buttock that may spread with tingling or numbness down the back of the leg. Pain can worsen with running or sitting. Because a spinal nerve problem can cause similar symptoms, it should be ruled out.

topics.name: Pituitary Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pituitary disorders can cause too little or too much of one or more hormones, affecting growth, reproduction, other hormone glands, or the body's water balance. Some pituitary growths can also press on nearby structures. Identifying which hormone or structure is affected helps guide evaluation and treatment.

topics.name: Pituitary Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: The pituitary gland controls other hormone glands and releases hormones that regulate growth, reproduction, and water balance. A pituitary disorder can make hormone levels too low or too high, causing problems throughout the body; a growth or other lesion may also press on nearby structures.

topics.name: Pituitary Lesions
topics.clinical_significance: A pituitary lesion may be found by chance or cause headaches, changes in thirst or appetite, loss of side vision, or too much or too little of one or more hormones. Because these lesions can affect vision and hormone function, they may need brain imaging and hormone tests to guide care.

topics.name: Pituitary Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most pituitary tumors are adenomas. Some release too much hormone; others can damage normal gland tissue and cause hormone shortages. Growing tumors can press on the optic nerves, causing headaches or loss of side vision, so hormone tests and MRI help guide treatment.

topics.name: Pityriasis Lichenoides
topics.clinical_significance: Pityriasis lichenoides is an uncommon inflammatory skin disorder. Its chronic form causes persistent scaly bumps; its acute form appears in crops and can ulcerate and sometimes scar. It can resemble other skin diseases, so a biopsy may be needed when the diagnosis is unclear. It may also be associated with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

topics.name: Pityriasis Rosea
topics.clinical_significance: Pityriasis rosea usually clears on its own in about 5 weeks. It often starts with one larger scaly patch, followed by smaller spots on the trunk, and may itch. Other skin conditions can look similar. When it occurs during the first 15 weeks of pregnancy, it has been associated with preterm birth or pregnancy loss; antiviral treatment has not been shown to prevent these outcomes.

topics.name: Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris
topics.clinical_significance: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a rare, often long-lasting inflammatory skin disease. Red-orange scaly patches and small bumps around hair follicles may spread widely, with islands of normal skin and thickened yellow skin on the palms and soles. It can resemble psoriasis and be hard to diagnose; symptoms may be difficult to control and can persist for years.

topics.name: Pityriasis Versicolor
topics.clinical_significance: Pityriasis versicolor, also called tinea versicolor, is a harmless, noncontagious yeast overgrowth that causes multiple finely scaly patches that may be lighter, darker, pink, or tan, usually on the trunk or neck. It often returns after treatment, and lighter patches may take months or longer to regain their color after the yeast clears.

topics.name: Placenta Accreta
topics.clinical_significance: The placenta is abnormally attached to the uterine wall and may not separate after birth. Trying to remove it can cause life-threatening bleeding, so delivery needs careful planning with an experienced team; a cesarean hysterectomy is often needed.

topics.name: Placenta Accreta Spectrum
topics.clinical_significance: Placenta accreta spectrum covers a placenta that attaches abnormally to the uterine muscle (accreta), grows into it (increta), or passes through it (percreta). The placenta may not separate after birth, and trying to remove it can cause severe bleeding. Planned delivery at an experienced center, often by cesarean hysterectomy, is usually needed.

topics.name: Placenta Previa
topics.clinical_significance: Placenta previa is when placental tissue covers the opening of the cervix. It can cause sudden, painless bleeding in the second half of pregnancy, sometimes severe. Ultrasound confirms the placental position; if it still covers the opening near delivery, cesarean birth is needed, and heavy bleeding or instability may require urgent delivery.

topics.name: Placental Abruption (Abruptio Placentae)
topics.clinical_significance: Placental abruption is early separation of the placenta from the uterus, usually after 20 weeks of pregnancy. It can cause abdominal or uterine pain and vaginal bleeding, but bleeding may be hidden. Separation can reduce the baby's oxygen supply and cause severe blood loss, shock, clotting problems, or fetal death, so urgent medical care and sometimes prompt delivery are needed.

topics.name: Plague and Other Yersinia Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, can cause painful swollen lymph nodes, severe pneumonia, or bloodstream infection and can be fatal without prompt antibiotics; pneumonic plague spreads through respiratory droplets. Other Yersinia species usually cause foodborne diarrhea or swollen abdominal lymph nodes that can mimic appendicitis, but may cause serious bloodstream infection, especially in people with chronic liver disease or iron overload.

topics.name: Plant Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Plant exposure can cause anything from mild skin or stomach irritation to seizures, abnormal heart rhythms, organ failure, or death. Most plant ingestions cause few or mild symptoms, but some plants are highly toxic. Identifying the plant and how much was involved helps guide treatment.

topics.name: Plantar Fasciitis
topics.clinical_significance: Plantar fasciitis (often called plantar fasciosis because inflammation is usually absent) is pain where the band of tissue under the foot attaches to the heel bone. Pain is often worst with the first steps after sleep or rest and may return with prolonged standing or walking.

topics.name: Plantar Fasciosis
topics.clinical_significance: Plantar fasciosis is heel pain where the plantar fascia attaches to the heel bone, usually from stretching or wear rather than inflammation. Pain is often worst with the first steps after sleep or rest and may return with prolonged standing or walking.

topics.name: Plantar Fibromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Plantar fibromatosis is a noncancerous growth of firm lumps in the band of tissue under the foot. The lumps may cause pain or swelling and sometimes make it hard to straighten the toes; shoe inserts can reduce pressure when walking.

topics.name: Plasma Cell Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Plasma cell disorders range from quiet conditions with an abnormal antibody protein to cancers such as multiple myeloma. The abnormal cells or protein can weaken bones, harm the kidneys, lower blood counts, or reduce normal immune defenses; sometimes an abnormal blood or urine protein is the first clue.

topics.name: Plasma Cell Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: In these disorders, one group of plasma cells makes too much of a single antibody protein. Some people have no symptoms, but the abnormal cells or protein can harm the kidneys, weaken immune defenses, affect bones and blood counts, or increase bleeding; abnormal protein in blood or urine may be the first clue.

topics.name: Plasma Cell Dyscrasias
topics.clinical_significance: Plasma cell dyscrasias, also called plasma cell disorders, range from stable conditions with an abnormal antibody protein to progressive cancers. They may be found on blood or urine tests before symptoms appear; some can damage bones, kidneys, blood cell production, or immune defenses.

topics.name: Plasma Cell Myeloma
topics.clinical_significance: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells that make an abnormal antibody. It can damage bones and bone marrow and may cause bone pain or fractures, kidney problems, high blood calcium, anemia, and repeated infections.

topics.name: Plasma Membrane Proteins
topics.clinical_significance: Plasma membrane transport proteins move drugs into and out of cells, affecting how drugs are absorbed, distributed, processed, and removed. When drugs compete for the same transporter, their levels or effects can change and cause harmful interactions; some transporters also help the kidneys remove drugs such as metformin.

topics.name: Platelet Disorders, Hereditary Intrinsic
topics.clinical_significance: These rare inherited conditions make platelets work poorly and cause a lifelong tendency to bleed. The platelet count may be normal or low; bleeding ranges from mild to severe, and serious bleeding may require a platelet transfusion.

topics.name: Platelet Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: A platelet disorder changes the platelet count or how well platelets work. Depending on the cause, it can raise the risk of blood clots or cause bleeding, often as easy bruising, tiny skin spots, nose or gum bleeding, heavy periods, or excess bleeding after surgery.

topics.name: Platelet Dysfunction, Acquired
topics.clinical_significance: Acquired platelet dysfunction can develop from medicines that reduce platelet activity, illnesses such as kidney failure, or heart-lung bypass surgery. It may cause unusual or prolonged bleeding; medicines such as aspirin are sometimes used for their antiplatelet effect but can increase bleeding risk.

topics.name: Pleural Biopsy
topics.clinical_significance: A pleural biopsy removes a small sample of the lining around the lungs to look for infection or cancer, often when tests of pleural fluid have not explained an effusion. It can cause a collapsed lung or bleeding into the chest.

topics.name: Pleural Effusion
topics.clinical_significance: Pleural effusion is fluid buildup in the space around the lungs. It may cause shortness of breath or chest pain, but some cases cause no symptoms; causes include heart failure, infection, cancer, and other diseases, so fluid testing may be needed to find the cause.

topics.name: Pleural Fibrosis and Calcification
topics.clinical_significance: Pleural fibrosis (scarring) and calcification (calcium buildup) are usually benign changes after inflammation or asbestos exposure. They often cause no symptoms and need no treatment, but extensive scarring can trap the lung and limit breathing; calcified plaques may be the only sign of past asbestos exposure.

topics.name: Pleuritis, Viral
topics.clinical_significance: Viral pleuritis is a viral infection of the lining around the lungs. It can cause chest pain that worsens with breathing; pneumonia or a blood clot in the lung may cause similar pain and sometimes need to be ruled out.

topics.name: Plumbism
topics.clinical_significance: Lead poisoning may cause few symptoms at first but can lead to lasting brain and nerve damage, kidney problems, anemia, and reproductive problems. Children are especially vulnerable to lasting effects on learning and development. Diagnosis uses a blood lead test; treatment starts by stopping exposure, with chelation for selected severe cases.

topics.name: Plummer-Vinson Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Plummer-Vinson syndrome combines iron-deficiency anemia with a thin tissue web in the upper esophagus, which can make swallowing solid food difficult. Treating the iron deficiency may improve the web; one that persists can be widened during endoscopy.

topics.name: Pneumococcal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumococcal bacteria commonly cause ear infections and pneumonia and can also cause life-threatening blood infection or meningitis. Severe disease is more likely in young children, older adults, and people without a working spleen or with weakened immunity. Vaccination helps prevent infection, and antibiotic treatment depends on the bacteria’s drug resistance.

topics.name: Pneumococcal Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumococcal vaccines protect against many, but not all, strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae. They lower the risk of serious infections such as pneumonia, bloodstream infection, and meningitis, as well as some ear infections; vaccination is especially important for children, older adults, and people with certain chronic illnesses or weakened immunity.

topics.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is an opportunistic lung infection, most often in people with severely weakened immunity, such as those with advanced HIV, organ transplants, or those taking steroids or other immune-suppressing medicines. It usually causes fever, dry cough, and worsening shortness of breath and can lower blood oxygen, so prompt diagnosis and treatment are important.

topics.name: Pneumomediastinum
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumomediastinum is air leaking into the space between the lungs, often from a ruptured air sac in the lung or a tear in the esophagus or bowel. It can cause chest pain and often needs no treatment itself, but doctors must check for an esophageal or bowel tear, which requires hospital care.

topics.name: Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumonia is an infection of the small airways and air sacs in the lungs that causes inflammation. It can make breathing difficult and range from mild to life-threatening; common symptoms include cough, fever, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Causes include bacteria and viruses, and less often fungi or parasites.

topics.name: Pneumonia in Immunocompromised Patients
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumonia in people with weakened immunity may be caused by common germs or unusual opportunistic infections and can be severe. Symptoms may be subtle or atypical; sometimes fever is the only sign. Prompt testing to identify the cause is important because treatment depends on the germ and the type of immune problem.

topics.name: Pneumonia, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal pneumonia is a lung infection in a newborn. It may begin soon after birth as part of sepsis or develop later, often in hospitalized infants on breathing machines. Signs may be limited to breathing difficulty or progress to shock, so prompt assessment and antibiotic treatment are important.

topics.name: Pneumonia, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pneumonia is an acute infection of the lower airways and air sacs in the lungs. It may be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites; likely causes and treatment depend on where the infection began, whether the patient is on a ventilator, and the person’s immune status.

topics.name: Pneumothorax
topics.clinical_significance: A pneumothorax is air in the space around a lung, causing it to partly or fully collapse. It may occur on its own or after an injury or medical procedure; it can cause sudden chest pain and shortness of breath, though small cases may cause no symptoms. A tension pneumothorax is life-threatening and needs immediate treatment.

topics.name: POEMS Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: POEMS is a rare syndrome linked to a plasma cell disorder. Nerve damage and an abnormal protein made by a group of plasma cells are central features; it may also cause enlarged organs, hormone problems, skin changes, bone lesions, fluid buildup, and swelling of the optic nerves.

topics.name: Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: Poisoning occurs when exposure to a substance causes harmful effects. It may follow swallowing, inhaling, injecting, or contact with the skin, eyes, or other body surfaces; effects can be delayed and range from mild to life-threatening, depending on the substance, amount, route, and person. Most cases need supportive care, while some have specific antidotes.

topics.name: Poisoning, General Principles of
topics.clinical_significance: Poisoning can cause different symptoms, sometimes after a delay; diagnosis relies mainly on exposure history and clinical signs, with targeted tests for some substances. Care first stabilizes breathing and circulation and is usually supportive; poison-center advice and a specific antidote may be needed.

topics.name: Poisons, Specific
topics.clinical_significance: Different poisons cause different symptoms and need different treatments; effects may be delayed and can be life-threatening. Identifying the substance, amount, and route of exposure helps guide care, and poison-center advice is recommended for all but mild, routine cases because some poisons require specific antidotes.

topics.name: Polio
topics.clinical_significance: Polio is an infection caused by poliovirus, an enterovirus spread mainly through the fecal–oral route and less often through the respiratory route. Most infections cause no symptoms or only a mild illness; some cause meningitis, and fewer than 1% cause paralytic disease with flaccid weakness that may leave lasting paralysis.

topics.name: Poliomyelitis
topics.clinical_significance: Poliomyelitis is a poliovirus infection that affects the nervous system. It can cause meningitis or sudden, limp muscle weakness; about two in three people with paralytic disease have lasting weakness, and brainstem involvement may impair breathing. Suspected cases should be reported promptly to public-health officials.

topics.name: Poliomyelitis Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Vaccination with inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) protects against polio, which can cause meningitis or permanent paralysis. Routine childhood vaccination has greatly reduced wild poliovirus, but vaccination remains important because the virus still circulates in some regions. Unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated people, and some adults with increased exposure risk, may need additional doses or a booster.

topics.name: Polyarteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Polyarteritis is another name for polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), a rare inflammation of medium-sized arteries. It can reduce blood flow and damage organs, especially the kidneys, skin, nerves, muscles, and gut. Kidney arteries may be affected, but inflammation of the kidney filters (glomerulonephritis) is not typical.

topics.name: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)
topics.clinical_significance: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a rare inflammation that damages medium-sized arteries and reduces blood flow to organs. It can affect the skin, nerves, muscles, kidneys, and digestive tract, causing problems such as skin ulcers, limb pain or weakness, abdominal pain, or high blood pressure. Kidney artery disease can injure the kidneys, but glomerulonephritis is not typical.

topics.name: Polycystic Ovary Syndromes [PCOS]
topics.clinical_significance: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) in the linked MSD topic, is a common hormone and metabolic disorder. It can cause irregular periods, excess facial or body hair, acne, and difficulty becoming pregnant. It is also linked to higher risks of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and thickening of the uterine lining. Ovarian cyst-like follicles are not present in everyone with the syndrome.
