topics.name: Polycythemia and Hyperviscosity Syndrome, Perinatal
topics.clinical_significance: In newborns, polycythemia means too many red blood cells. This can make the blood too thick (hyperviscosity), slow blood flow, and sometimes cause clots. Affected babies may have poor feeding, sleepiness, low blood sugar, jaundice, breathing problems, or seizures; severe cases can harm the brain, kidneys, or heart.

topics.name: Polycythemia Vera
topics.clinical_significance: Polycythemia vera is a long-term bone marrow disease that makes too many blood cells, especially red blood cells. It can thicken the blood and cause clots or bleeding; itching (often after a warm bath) and an enlarged spleen can also occur. Over time, it can lead to bone marrow scarring (myelofibrosis) or, rarely, acute leukemia.

topics.name: Polyendocrine Deficiency Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Polyendocrine deficiency syndromes are usually autoimmune disorders in which several hormone-making glands become underactive, either at the same time or over many years. Symptoms depend on which glands are affected. Untreated adrenal or parathyroid failure can be life-threatening, so long-term follow-up and replacement of missing hormones may be needed.

topics.name: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
topics.clinical_significance: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is a common hormone and metabolic condition. It can disrupt ovulation and periods, raise androgen levels (causing acne or excess facial and body hair), and make pregnancy harder. It is also linked with insulin resistance and higher risks of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and thickening of the uterine lining. Cyst-like ovarian follicles are not present in everyone with the syndrome.

topics.name: Polyglandular Deficiency Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Polyglandular deficiency syndromes are disorders in which two or more hormone-making glands become underactive, usually because of autoimmunity. The affected glands and symptoms vary, and problems may appear years apart. Untreated adrenal or parathyroid failure can be life-threatening, so long-term monitoring and hormone replacement may be needed.

topics.name: Polyhydramnios
topics.clinical_significance: Polyhydramnios is too much amniotic fluid around the fetus. It may cause no symptoms, but severe cases can stretch the uterus and cause shortness of breath or painful early contractions. It raises the risks of preterm birth, the fetus lying in an abnormal position, umbilical cord prolapse, and heavy bleeding after birth; risk is greater when more fluid builds up and depends on the cause.

topics.name: Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PUPPP) is a very itchy but benign rash, usually beginning in abdominal stretch marks late in pregnancy, especially a first pregnancy. It may spread to the thighs and buttocks and usually clears within about 2 weeks after delivery. Topical corticosteroids or antihistamines can relieve symptoms; a clinician may need to distinguish it from other pregnancy rashes.

topics.name: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
topics.clinical_significance: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes aching and morning stiffness in the shoulders, hips, and neck in adults over 50. It causes pain rather than true muscle weakness and usually improves quickly with low-dose corticosteroids. It is linked to giant cell arteritis; a new headache, jaw pain while chewing, or vision changes need urgent medical assessment because this condition can threaten sight.

topics.name: Polyneuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Polyneuropathy affects many peripheral nerves, often on both sides of the body. It can cause numbness, tingling or burning pain, reduced sensation, weakness, or poor reflexes, commonly starting in the feet and sometimes spreading upward. Causes include diabetes, vitamin problems, toxins or medicines, and immune disorders. Rapidly worsening weakness can become serious if breathing muscles are affected.

topics.name: Polypeptide Antibiotics: Bacitracin, Colistin, Polymyxin B
topics.clinical_significance: Bacitracin is used mainly on the skin for some superficial infections. Colistin and polymyxin B are reserved for severe infections caused by certain drug-resistant gram-negative bacteria when safer effective options are lacking. Their use is limited by kidney and nerve toxicity; they can also cause muscle weakness or breathing problems.

topics.name: Polyps of the Colon and Rectum
topics.clinical_significance: Many colon and rectal polyps are harmless and cause no symptoms, but some can bleed. Adenomatous polyps can become colorectal cancer over time, especially when they are large or have more advanced cell changes. Colonoscopy can find and remove polyps, and tissue examination helps determine their cancer risk.

topics.name: Polyuria
topics.clinical_significance: Polyuria is urine output over 3 liters a day in an adult. It means passing large volumes of urine, unlike urinary frequency, which is urinating often but in normal or small amounts. Common causes include diuretic medicines, uncontrolled diabetes, drinking excessive fluids, and problems with the hormone that helps the kidneys conserve water.

topics.name: Popliteal Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: A popliteal (Baker) cyst is a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee, often linked to arthritis or a knee injury. Small cysts may cause no symptoms; larger ones can cause pain, stiffness, and limited movement. If a cyst ruptures, fluid in the calf can cause swelling and warmth that resemble a blood clot, so medical assessment may be needed.

topics.name: Porencephaly
topics.clinical_significance: Porencephaly is a fluid-filled cavity in one side of the brain that forms before or after birth, often after a genetic problem, inflammation, or interrupted blood flow. Effects vary with its size and location: some children have mild signs, while others have developmental delay, weakness on one side, abnormal muscle tone, or seizures. Increased pressure in the brain or hydrocephalus can occur but is uncommon.

topics.name: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda
topics.clinical_significance: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is usually an acquired disorder in which low activity of a liver enzyme causes porphyrins to build up. Sun-exposed skin becomes fragile and may blister, break down, and scar. Iron overload, alcohol, smoking, estrogen use, and hepatitis C or HIV can contribute. Liver disease is common, and PCT is associated with cirrhosis and increased risk of liver cancer.

topics.name: Porphyrias, Cutaneous, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous porphyrias cause porphyrins to build up in the body and make the skin react to sunlight. Most cause fragile skin and blisters on exposed areas. Erythropoietic and X-linked protoporphyria more often cause burning pain within minutes or hours of sun exposure without blisters. Chronic liver problems are also common in these disorders.

topics.name: Porphyrias, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Porphyrias are rare disorders of heme production that cause porphyrins or their precursors to build up. Depending on the type, they can cause severe attacks with abdominal, nerve, or mental symptoms, sun-triggered skin problems, or both. Most are inherited, but porphyria cutanea tarda is often acquired. Some acute attacks can be triggered by medicines, fasting, alcohol, illness, or hormonal changes; blood, urine, or stool tests help confirm the type.

topics.name: Portal Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Portal hypertension is high pressure in the portal vein, which carries blood from the digestive organs and spleen to the liver. It is most often caused by cirrhosis, but can also result from a portal vein clot or other blood-flow problems. It may cause enlarged veins in the esophagus or stomach that can bleed severely, fluid buildup in the abdomen, an enlarged spleen, or confusion when blood bypasses the liver.

topics.name: Portal Vein Thrombosis
topics.clinical_significance: A clot in the portal vein may cause no symptoms at first, but it can raise pressure in the portal system and lead to an enlarged spleen or enlarged veins in the esophagus or stomach that can bleed severely. Causes include cirrhosis, cancer, surgery, infection, or a tendency to form blood clots.

topics.name: Portopulmonary Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Portopulmonary hypertension is high blood pressure in the lung arteries that occurs with portal hypertension, usually due to liver disease. It can cause shortness of breath and fatigue and strain the right side of the heart. Severe or uncontrolled disease raises the risk of complications during liver transplantation.

topics.name: Portosystemic Encephalopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Portosystemic encephalopathy (also called hepatic encephalopathy) is impaired brain function that can occur when liver disease or a shunt lets substances normally cleared by the liver reach the brain. It can cause changes in sleep, mood, or concentration, confusion, tremor, drowsiness, and, in severe cases, coma. Infection, gut bleeding, dehydration, electrolyte changes, or sedatives can trigger or worsen it; treating the cause often improves symptoms.

topics.name: Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
topics.clinical_significance: Positron emission tomography (PET) is an imaging test that uses a radioactive tracer to show how active tissues are. It is used mainly to stage some cancers and assess response to treatment, and can also help evaluate heart function and brain disorders such as seizures or dementia. PET/CT combines this activity map with detailed images of body structures.

topics.name: Postcholecystectomy Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Postcholecystectomy syndrome describes abdominal pain or other digestive symptoms that persist or develop after gallbladder removal. Symptoms are often nonspecific, such as bloating or indigestion. Causes vary and may include a retained bile duct stone, problems with the sphincter that controls bile flow, pancreatitis, reflux, or diarrhea from excess bile acids. Evaluation looks for both bile duct and other digestive causes; treatment depends on the cause.

topics.name: Posterior Achilles Tendon Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior Achilles tendon bursitis is inflammation of a small fluid-filled sac between the skin and Achilles tendon, usually where the back of a shoe presses on the heel. It can cause redness, warmth, pain, and a tender lump; long-term irritation may make the area firm. Shoes that reduce pressure on the heel are the main treatment.

topics.name: Posterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
topics.clinical_significance: A posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear is a knee injury that can cause pain, swelling, and instability. It may follow a direct blow to the front of the shin while the knee is bent or forceful knee hyperextension. A large blood-filled swelling or marked instability may signal a severe injury or knee dislocation with possible blood-vessel damage and needs urgent assessment. Treatment depends on tear severity and other knee injuries.

topics.name: Posterior Interosseous Nerve Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve palsy) affects the motor branch of the radial nerve in the forearm. It mainly causes weakness when straightening the fingers or thumb and sometimes the wrist, usually without loss of sensation. Aching pain near the outer elbow or forearm may also occur; weakness of the extensor muscles is the key sign of nerve palsy.

topics.name: Posterior Tibial Nerve Neuralgia
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior tibial nerve neuralgia (tarsal tunnel syndrome) is irritation or compression of the tibial nerve near the inner ankle. It causes pain, burning, or tingling behind the ankle and into the sole or toes, often worse with standing or walking. Swelling, scar tissue, arthritis, foot deformity, or a cyst can contribute. Treatment depends on the cause and may relieve pressure on the nerve.

topics.name: Posterior Tibial Tendon Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is wear or inflammation of the tendon behind the inner ankle. It can cause pain and swelling and make walking or standing on tiptoe difficult. Ongoing tendon damage may weaken or tear the tendon, allowing the foot arch to flatten and the heel to turn outward; later, this can lead to foot and ankle arthritis.

topics.name: Postextraction Problems
topics.clinical_significance: Problems after tooth removal range from expected soreness and swelling to complications such as persistent bleeding, dry socket, jaw infection, or jawbone damage. Dry socket occurs when the socket clot is lost, exposing painful bone. Worsening swelling after 3 days, severe pain, fever, or ongoing bleeding needs prompt dental assessment.

topics.name: Postgastrectomy Gastritis
topics.clinical_significance: After partial gastrectomy, bile reflux and other changes can cause long-term stomach inflammation and tissue loss. This can reduce stomach acid and intrinsic factor, leading to iron or vitamin B12 deficiency. Stomach cancer risk may rise 15 to 20 years later, though the overall risk remains low; new upper digestive symptoms or anemia should prompt evaluation.

topics.name: Postinfectious Glomerulonephritis (PIGN)
topics.clinical_significance: This kidney inflammation develops after an infection, often strep throat or a skin infection. It can cause blood and protein in the urine, swelling, high blood pressure, and reduced kidney function; severe cases may need dialysis. Most people recover kidney function with supportive care, but some develop rapidly worsening kidney damage.

topics.name: Postlumbar Puncture and Other Low–Pressure Headaches
topics.clinical_significance: These headaches result from low cerebrospinal fluid pressure, often after a lumbar puncture or a fluid leak. Pain usually worsens when sitting or standing and improves when lying flat; neck pain and vomiting may also occur. Persistent headache may need an epidural blood patch.

topics.name: Postoperative Care
topics.clinical_significance: After surgery, care protects breathing, maintains blood pressure and fluid balance, controls pain, and checks mental state and wound healing. Early safe movement and other measures help prevent blood clots and lung complications. Nausea, difficulty urinating, constipation, and infection also need attention.

topics.name: Postoperative Liver Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Mild liver test changes or jaundice can occur after major surgery and often resolve. Causes include reduced liver blood flow, low oxygen, transfusions, infection, medicines, or blocked bile flow. Severe or persistent jaundice needs evaluation for liver injury or a surgical complication; acute liver failure is rare.

topics.name: Postpartum Care
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum care supports recovery during the first 6 weeks after birth and helps detect complications early. It checks bleeding, blood pressure, infection, wound healing, urination, and mood, and supports feeding and contraception. Serious complications include heavy bleeding, infection, postpartum preeclampsia, blood clots, and depression or psychosis.

topics.name: Postpartum Care and Associated Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum disorders can cause serious illness in the weeks after birth. Important problems include heavy bleeding, infection, high blood pressure or preeclampsia, blood clots, wound complications, and depression or psychosis. Timely follow-up and prompt assessment of concerning symptoms help prevent severe harm.

topics.name: Postpartum Depression
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum depression is major depression during the first year after birth, with symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks and interfering with daily life. It may cause sadness, loss of interest, anxiety, sleep or appetite changes, difficulty caring for or bonding with the baby, or thoughts of self-harm. Early screening and treatment matter because it can affect both parent and infant.

topics.name: Postpartum Endometritis
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum endometritis is a uterine infection that is more likely after cesarean birth, especially after labor. Fever with lower abdominal pain or uterine tenderness, sometimes with foul-smelling discharge, needs prompt evaluation and antibiotic treatment. Rarely, the infection spreads and causes an abscess or sepsis.

topics.name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum hemorrhage is blood loss over 1 liter within 24 hours of birth, or less blood loss that causes signs of low blood volume. The most common cause is a uterus that does not contract well. It can quickly lead to shock and needs immediate obstetric treatment to stop the bleeding and replace lost fluid or blood.

topics.name: Postpartum Pyelonephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Postpartum pyelonephritis is a bacterial kidney infection, often caused by bacteria spreading upward from the bladder. It can cause fever, side or back pain, and feeling unwell, sometimes with painful urination. It needs prompt urine testing and antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Postpolio Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Years or decades after paralytic polio, a person may develop new weakness, muscle fatigue, and reduced endurance, often in muscles affected by the original illness. Muscle twitching or wasting may also occur. Care is supportive and focuses on managing symptoms and function.

topics.name: Postpoliomyelitis Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Postpoliomyelitis syndrome (postpolio syndrome) can cause new muscle fatigue, reduced endurance, weakness, twitching, or muscle loss years or decades after paralytic polio, often in muscles affected before. Supportive care helps manage symptoms and preserve function.

topics.name: Postterm Infants
topics.clinical_significance: A postterm infant is born at 42 weeks of pregnancy or later. These infants have a higher risk of low blood sugar, breathing problems from meconium aspiration, and low oxygen around birth. They should be monitored for these complications, especially if the placenta is not supplying enough oxygen and nutrients.

topics.name: Posttraumatic Iridocyclitis
topics.clinical_significance: After blunt eye injury, inflammation of the iris and nearby uvea may develop within 3 days. It can cause aching eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, tearing, and blurred vision; the pupil may look irregular. Prompt eye assessment is needed to confirm the cause and guide treatment.

topics.name: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
topics.clinical_significance: PTSD can develop at least a month after a traumatic event and may cause unwanted memories or nightmares, avoidance of reminders, persistent negative mood, and feeling constantly on guard or unable to sleep. It can disrupt daily life and relationships. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the main treatment; medication may also help.

topics.name: Potassium Concentration, Disorders of, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Blood potassium that is too high or too low can disrupt electrical signals in the heart and muscles. It may cause muscle weakness or dangerous heart rhythm problems, even when the change is small. Results must be interpreted with the person’s condition because shifts between blood and cells or a blood sample problem can affect the measured level.

topics.name: Pox Viruses
topics.clinical_significance: Poxviruses include viruses that cause mpox and smallpox. Mpox can cause fever and painful blisters or pustules and can spread through close contact, so recognizing it helps guide testing and infection control. Natural smallpox transmission has been eradicated, but smallpox was highly contagious and often fatal.

topics.name: Precocious Puberty
topics.clinical_significance: Puberty that begins earlier than average can cause rapid growth followed by early closure of the growth plates, which may limit adult height. It can also cause social or emotional stress. Evaluation checks whether puberty is progressing and looks for a cause, since some hormone or brain conditions need treatment.

topics.name: Preeclampsia and Eclampsia
topics.clinical_significance: Preeclampsia is new or worsening high blood pressure after 20 weeks of pregnancy, with protein in the urine or signs of organ damage; it can also develop after birth. Eclampsia is seizures linked to preeclampsia. These conditions can cause serious harm to the pregnant person and fetus, so close obstetric care is needed; severe disease requires urgent treatment and may require delivery.

topics.name: Pregestational Diabetes
topics.clinical_significance: Pregestational diabetes is type 1 or type 2 diabetes present before pregnancy. Pregnancy can make blood sugar harder to control. Poor control raises the risks of miscarriage and birth defects early in pregnancy, and later of a large baby, difficult delivery, preeclampsia, stillbirth, and newborn low blood sugar. Care before conception and close monitoring during pregnancy help lower these risks.

topics.name: Pregnancy, Cancer in
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer needs timely diagnosis and treatment during pregnancy, but some cancer medicines can harm the developing fetus, especially early in pregnancy. Delaying treatment can also put the pregnant person at risk. Oncologists and maternal-fetal specialists help plan care that weighs these risks and benefits.

topics.name: Pregnancy Complicated by Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy can change how a medical illness behaves and how it can be treated. Some diseases and their treatments can also affect the pregnant person and fetus. Care is tailored to the condition, with obstetric and medical specialists balancing disease control, medicine safety, and fetal monitoring.

topics.name: Pregnancy Complications, Risk Factors for
topics.clinical_significance: Health conditions, smoking or substance use, age or weight, multiple pregnancy, harmful exposures, and past pregnancy problems can raise the chance of complications for the pregnant person or fetus. Finding risk factors early helps guide screening, closer monitoring, and care to reduce risk.

topics.name: Pregnancy, Infectious Disease in
topics.clinical_significance: Many infections during pregnancy are mild, but some can seriously harm the pregnant person or fetus, cause pregnancy loss or preterm birth, or pass to the baby and cause birth defects or newborn illness. Prenatal screening and prompt assessment of symptoms help detect infections that need treatment. Medicines are chosen with pregnancy stage and fetal safety in mind.

topics.name: Pregnancy Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Spontaneous pregnancy loss before 20 weeks (miscarriage) may cause vaginal bleeding and cramping. Medical assessment confirms what is happening and checks for ectopic pregnancy, retained tissue, heavy bleeding, or infection. Early losses are often linked to chromosome problems, but the cause is usually unknown. Emotional support is important.

topics.name: Pregnancy of Unknown Location
topics.clinical_significance: This is a temporary finding: a pregnancy test is positive, but ultrasound has not yet located the pregnancy. Repeat ultrasound and serial blood hCG tests help distinguish an early uterine pregnancy, pregnancy loss, or ectopic pregnancy. Follow-up is essential because an ectopic pregnancy can rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding.

topics.name: Pregnancy, Physiology of
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy causes normal, usually reversible changes in nearly all maternal organ systems, including the heart and blood vessels, blood, kidneys, breathing, digestion, and hormones. Knowing these changes helps clinicians interpret symptoms and test results and distinguish normal adaptation from illness. Most changes move toward prepregnancy levels after delivery.

topics.name: Pregnancy, Symptoms During
topics.clinical_significance: Mild nausea, breast tenderness, fatigue, and leg swelling are often normal changes of pregnancy. Bleeding, leaking fluid, fever, severe or lasting pain, faintness, vision changes, or reduced fetal movement can signal a complication. Recognizing these warning signs helps clinicians assess the health of the pregnant patient and fetus.

topics.name: Pregnancy-Related and Postpartum Sexual Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy and childbirth can affect sexual function through physical changes, birth-related trauma, breastfeeding-related vaginal dryness, and psychological or relationship stress. These factors may cause pain during sex or reduce sexual interest and arousal. Postpartum depression and intimate partner violence can add risk, and sexual problems that began before pregnancy may continue afterward.

topics.name: Pregnant Woman and Prenatal Care, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Prenatal care uses medical history, examinations, and screening tests to check the pregnant patient’s health and the fetus’s growth. It helps find medical problems and pregnancy complications early, assess risks, and reduce harm to both. Follow-up visits also track symptoms and support health education.

topics.name: Preinfarction Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Preinfarction angina is another name for unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome caused by temporary reduced blood flow to the heart without a heart attack. Chest discomfort that is new, worsening, prolonged, or occurs at rest signals increased risk of a heart attack.

topics.name: Prelabor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)
topics.clinical_significance: Breaking of the amniotic sac before labor begins. If it happens before 37 weeks, it is called preterm rupture; a gush or continuing leak of fluid needs prompt obstetric assessment because infection and early birth may follow.

topics.name: Premacular Fibrosis
topics.clinical_significance: Premacular fibrosis (epiretinal membrane) is a thin layer on the retinal surface. If it contracts, it can wrinkle the macula and blur or distort central vision. Many cases need no treatment; surgery may be considered when vision is significantly affected.

topics.name: Premature Menopause
topics.clinical_significance: Premature menopause is an older term for primary ovarian insufficiency, in which ovarian function decreases before age 40. Periods may become irregular or stop, and low estrogen can cause hot flashes, vaginal dryness, infertility, and bone loss. Ovarian activity may vary, so periods and pregnancy can still occur.

topics.name: Premature Ovarian Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Premature ovarian failure is an older term for primary ovarian insufficiency, a decrease in ovarian function before age 40. It can cause irregular or absent periods, low-estrogen symptoms, infertility, and bone loss. Ovarian function may continue intermittently, so pregnancy can still occur.

topics.name: Premature Rupture of Membranes
topics.clinical_significance: Rupture of the amniotic sac before labor can lead to infection, placental separation, or an abnormal fetal position. If it happens before 37 weeks (preterm PROM), early birth is a major risk. At term, labor often begins within a day.

topics.name: Premature Ventricular Contraction
topics.clinical_significance: Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are early beats that start in the heart’s lower chambers. They are common and often harmless when the heart is otherwise healthy, but can signal heart disease. Very frequent PVCs can weaken the heart muscle.

topics.name: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a severe, recurring premenstrual disorder. Marked mood symptoms, such as depression, irritability, or anxiety, occur in the second half of the cycle and ease around menstruation. Symptoms can disrupt daily life, and suicidal thoughts may occur.

topics.name: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)
topics.clinical_significance: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) causes recurring emotional or physical symptoms during the days before a period, such as irritability, anxiety, headache, breast pain, or swelling. Symptoms usually ease soon after bleeding starts. Severe symptoms that disrupt daily life may be premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

topics.name: Premenstrual Tension
topics.clinical_significance: Premenstrual tension is another name for premenstrual syndrome (PMS): recurring emotional or physical symptoms, such as irritability, anxiety, headache, breast pain, or swelling, in the days before menstruation. Symptoms usually ease soon after bleeding starts; severe, disabling symptoms may be PMDD.

topics.name: Prenatal Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Prenatal complications are medical or pregnancy-related problems that can harm the pregnant patient, affect fetal growth, or lead to early birth. Recognizing them early helps clinicians identify risks and provide care that can reduce serious harm.

topics.name: Prenatal Drug Exposure
topics.clinical_significance: The effects of prenatal drug exposure depend on the substance and when it is used. Alcohol and illicit drugs can harm the placenta or fetus and may cause developmental problems or withdrawal in the newborn; some prescription medicines can also affect fetal development.

topics.name: Prenatal Genetic Counseling
topics.clinical_significance: Prenatal genetic counseling helps prospective parents understand inherited-condition risks, testing choices and limits, and possible results. It supports informed reproductive decisions before or during pregnancy and can cover ways to lower some birth-defect risks.

topics.name: Prenatal Genetic Counseling and Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Prenatal genetic evaluation uses family history and tests to assess whether a fetus may have a genetic or chromosomal condition. Screening estimates risk; diagnostic tests can identify specific conditions but may carry procedure-related risk. Counseling helps parents understand results and choices.

topics.name: Preoperative Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Preoperative evaluation estimates the risks of surgery and anesthesia by reviewing health conditions, medicines, allergies, prior anesthesia problems, and the planned procedure. It guides treatment of active problems, any needed monitoring, and changes to the surgical or anesthesia plan. Tests are chosen based on symptoms and risk, not done routinely for everyone.

topics.name: Preparing for a Limb Prosthesis
topics.clinical_significance: Preparation before and after limb amputation supports healing and successful prosthetic use. Functional assessment, exercise, care of the residual limb, and rehabilitation help maintain strength and mobility and guide prosthetic fitting as swelling settles.

topics.name: Preseptal and Orbital Cellulitis
topics.clinical_significance: Preseptal cellulitis infects the eyelid and skin in front of the orbital septum; orbital cellulitis infects tissues behind it. Both cause eyelid swelling and redness, but orbital cellulitis can impair eye movement or vision and spread infection into the skull.

topics.name: Pressure Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure injuries are skin or deeper tissue damage, usually over bony areas, from sustained pressure alone or with friction, shear, or moisture. They may begin before the skin breaks and can deepen or become infected, sometimes spreading to bone or the bloodstream.

topics.name: Pressure Injury
topics.clinical_significance: A pressure injury is localized skin or deeper tissue damage, usually over a bony area, caused by sustained pressure alone or with shear. The skin may remain intact at first even when deeper tissue is damaged; severe wounds can expose muscle or bone and become infected.

topics.name: Pressure Sores
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure sore is a common older name for a pressure injury caused by sustained pressure on skin and deeper tissues, often over a bony area. Early damage may leave the skin intact; deeper wounds can become infected and reach muscle or bone.

topics.name: Pressure Ulcers
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure ulcer is an older term for pressure injury, localized skin or deeper tissue damage from sustained pressure, usually over a bony area. Early injury may occur without an open wound; severe damage can reach muscle or bone and become infected.

topics.name: Preterm Infants
topics.clinical_significance: A preterm infant is born before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Immature lungs, brain, gut, and immune defenses raise the risk of breathing and feeding problems, infection, bleeding in the brain, bowel disease, and later developmental difficulties. These risks are generally greater the earlier the birth.

topics.name: Preterm Labor
topics.clinical_significance: Preterm labor is labor with regular contractions that change the cervix before 37 weeks of pregnancy. It can lead to early birth and related health problems for the infant; risk is greater when birth occurs earlier. Infection, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, cervical problems, and a prior preterm birth raise risk. Contractions alone do not always mean labor.

topics.name: Prevention in the Elderly, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Preventive care for older adults aims to prevent or delay disease and frailty, reduce accidents and treatment-related harm, and maintain the ability to manage daily activities. Measures should match the person’s health, independence, and frailty; nutrition, exercise, screening, and vaccination are common parts.

topics.name: Prevention of Disease and Disability in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Prevention in older adults aims to reduce disease, frailty, falls, treatment-related harm, and psychosocial problems while preserving daily function. Measures should fit the person’s health and level of independence and may include screening, vaccination, exercise, nutrition, and medication review.

topics.name: Prevention of Disease in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Disease prevention in older adults includes lowering risk before illness, finding disease early, and managing existing disease to prevent complications and loss of function. Vaccination, healthy habits, screening, and treatment may help, but choices should reflect the person’s health, function, life expectancy, and preferences.

topics.name: Prevention of Frailty
topics.clinical_significance: Frailty is loss of physiologic reserve that makes an older adult more vulnerable to disability after minor stress. Regular aerobic and strength exercise, a healthy diet, and adequate nutrition can help prevent or reduce frailty, preserve muscle and function, and lower the risk of falls.

topics.name: Prevention of Iatrogenic Complications in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults are at risk of harm caused by medical care, including drug reactions, falls, infections, pressure sores, delirium, and surgical problems. Risk rises with multiple illnesses, clinicians, or medicines and during hospitalization. Coordinated care and careful medication review can help prevent these complications.

topics.name: Prevention of Injuries in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Older adults are at risk of injuries from falls, driving, and hazards at home. Reviewing these risks with the person and caregivers, using fall-prevention measures when needed, driving safely, and checking the home for hazards can help prevent injuries.

topics.name: Prevention of Psychosocial Problems in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Depression and social isolation can harm older adults’ health. Screening can help identify depression for treatment. Support to build social connections and take part in meaningful activities may improve well-being and help prevent psychosocial problems and physical disability.

topics.name: Prevention of Surgical Site Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Preventing infection at the surgical wound lowers the risk of complications. Whether preventive antibiotics are needed depends on the operation and the patient’s risks; they are not needed for every procedure. If an infection is found during surgery, antibiotics are used to treat it rather than prevent it.

topics.name: Priapism
topics.clinical_significance: An erection lasting more than 4 hours without sexual desire or stimulation is priapism. The low-flow (ischemic) type is usually painful and needs urgent treatment because prolonged lack of blood flow can damage penile tissue and cause erectile dysfunction. The high-flow (nonischemic) type is usually painless but still needs medical assessment.

topics.name: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison Disease)
topics.clinical_significance: The adrenal glands make too little cortisol and aldosterone, causing fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, and often darkening of the skin; blood sodium may fall and potassium may rise. Illness or injury can trigger a life-threatening adrenal crisis with severe weakness and shock. Treatment usually requires lifelong hormone replacement, with higher steroid doses during illness.

topics.name: Primary Aldosteronism
topics.clinical_significance: The adrenal glands make too much aldosterone without normal control, usually because of a benign growth or enlargement of both glands. It commonly causes high blood pressure that may be hard to control; potassium may be low but can also be normal. Treatment may include surgery or medicines that block aldosterone.

topics.name: Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis
topics.clinical_significance: This rare brain infection is caused by Naegleria fowleri, usually when contaminated fresh water enters the nose. It can progress rapidly, causing severe brain inflammation and is usually fatal, so urgent diagnosis and treatment are critical.

topics.name: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)
topics.clinical_significance: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune disease that gradually damages the small bile ducts inside the liver. Bile builds up and can cause itching and fatigue; the disease may be silent at first but can progress to liver scarring, cirrhosis, and liver failure.

topics.name: Primary Biliary Cirrhosis
topics.clinical_significance: Older name for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), an autoimmune disease that damages the small bile ducts in the liver. The newer name is preferred because cirrhosis may develop only in later stages and is not present in everyone at diagnosis.

topics.name: Primary Brain Lymphomas
topics.clinical_significance: A lymphoma that begins in the brain or other central nervous system tissue, usually from B cells. It can form one or more brain tumors and cause neurologic symptoms. It is uncommon but serious; diagnosis often uses brain imaging and may require spinal fluid testing or biopsy, and treatment usually includes chemotherapy, sometimes with radiation.

topics.name: Primary Hemochromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited disorder in which the body absorbs too much iron, which can slowly damage organs. Iron buildup may cause liver scarring that can raise the risk of liver cancer, diabetes, heart problems, skin darkening, and joint disease, though symptoms can take years to appear. Early detection and regular blood removal can limit further iron buildup and organ damage.

topics.name: Primary Infantile Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: A developmental problem in the eye’s drainage angle raises pressure inside the eye. In infants and young children, this can stretch and enlarge the eye and damage the optic nerve, causing blindness if untreated. Early eye surgery is usually needed to protect vision.

topics.name: Primary Macroglobulinemia
topics.clinical_significance: Also called Waldenström macroglobulinemia, this uncommon B-cell cancer produces too much IgM antibody. Many people have no symptoms at first; others develop anemia, infections, bleeding, or thickened blood that can affect vision and brain function. Treatment may be delayed when there are no symptoms, but severe thickening of the blood needs urgent treatment.

topics.name: Primary Malignant Bone Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: These are uncommon cancers that start in bone, unlike the more common cancers that spread to bone from another site. They may cause persistent pain or swelling, weaken bone, and spread to other parts of the body, especially the lungs. Imaging and biopsy help identify the tumor type and guide treatment.

topics.name: Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF)
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic blood cancer in which scarring in the bone marrow disrupts normal blood-cell production. It can cause anemia, low platelet counts, and an enlarged spleen, and may progress to acute leukemia. The course varies; medicines can ease symptoms, while stem cell transplant is the only potentially curative treatment.

topics.name: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic disease that damages the optic nerve and gradually reduces side vision, usually without pain or early symptoms. Eye pressure is often high but can be normal. Treatment to lower the pressure can slow further damage, but vision already lost cannot be restored.

topics.name: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: When the ovaries lose function before age 40, estrogen levels fall and periods may become irregular or stop. This can cause hot flashes, infertility, and bone loss, but ovarian activity may continue at times, so pregnancy is not always impossible. Hormone therapy is usually used to treat low estrogen until the usual age of menopause, unless it is not suitable.

topics.name: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)
topics.clinical_significance: A chronic disease that inflames and scars the bile ducts, narrowing them and slowing bile flow. It can cause itching and fatigue and may progress to cirrhosis or liver failure. It is often linked to inflammatory bowel disease and raises the risk of bile duct and gallbladder cancers, so ongoing monitoring is important.

topics.name: Primary Small Cell Skin Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Primary small cell skin carcinoma is another name for Merkel cell carcinoma, a rare, aggressive skin cancer. It often appears as a painless, rapidly growing red or bluish nodule, usually on sun-exposed skin. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant sites, so prompt biopsy and staging are important.

topics.name: Primary Thrombocythemia
topics.clinical_significance: A bone marrow disorder that produces too many platelets. It can cause blood clots, bleeding (especially when platelet counts are extremely high), or symptoms such as headaches, visual changes, and burning pain in the hands or feet. Many people have no symptoms and may not need treatment.

topics.name: Principles of Cancer Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer treatment is chosen based on the cancer’s type and spread, the patient’s health, and the patient’s preferences. It may combine surgery or radiation with medicines that treat cancer throughout the body. Treatment can aim to cure or control the cancer, reduce the chance it returns, or ease symptoms when cure is not possible.

topics.name: Principles of Drug Treatment in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Children absorb, process, and remove medicines differently from adults, and these changes vary with age and growth. Doses often depend on a child’s age and size, but they cannot be worked out by simply scaling down an adult dose. Careful dosing and monitoring are important because some medicines can cause different or more serious side effects in children.

topics.name: Principles of Endocrinology
topics.clinical_significance: Endocrine disorders occur when glands make too much or too little hormone, or when the body does not respond to a hormone normally. Because hormones regulate functions such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, and water balance, problems can affect many parts of the body. Diagnosis often needs hormone tests, and treatment may replace missing hormones or reduce hormone excess.

topics.name: Principles of Radiologic Imaging
topics.clinical_significance: Radiologic imaging uses methods such as x-rays, CT, ultrasound, MRI, and nuclear scans to help find or assess disease. The best test depends on the clinical question and the patient. X-rays, CT, and nuclear scans use ionizing radiation, so unnecessary exposure should be avoided while making sure needed tests are not delayed.

topics.name: Principles of Topical Dermatologic Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Topical skin treatments are chosen for the condition and body site. The form of the medicine (such as a cream, lotion, or ointment) and any dressing can change how it works and how much is absorbed. Some medicines, especially strong steroid creams, can irritate or thin the skin, and coverings can increase absorption.

topics.name: Prinzmetal Angina
topics.clinical_significance: A temporary spasm of a heart artery reduces blood flow to the heart muscle, causing chest pain usually at rest and sometimes temporary ECG changes. Calcium channel blockers help prevent attacks, and nitroglycerin often relieves them. Coexisting coronary artery narrowing increases risk.

topics.name: Prion Disease Associated With Diarrhea and Autonomic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: This rare inherited prion disease mainly affects nerves outside the brain and spinal cord and other organs. It causes chronic watery diarrhea, problems with automatic body functions (such as blood pressure or bladder control), and sensory nerve damage; brain symptoms may appear later. Consider it when chronic diarrhea and neuropathy have no clear cause. Treatment is supportive.

topics.name: Prion Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Prion diseases are rare disorders in which an abnormal protein damages the nervous system. They may start spontaneously, be inherited, or rarely spread through contaminated tissue or food. They cause worsening neurologic problems and are usually fatal; no cure is available, so care focuses on comfort and support. Consider them in rapidly worsening neurologic illness.

topics.name: Prion Diseases, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Prion diseases occur when a normal protein folds abnormally and damages the nervous system. They may arise on their own, be inherited, or rarely be acquired through contaminated tissue, instruments, or food; they are not spread by casual contact. They cause progressive neurologic problems and are fatal, with no cure. Care is supportive, and contaminated instruments need special handling.

topics.name: Prion Protein Systemic Amyloidosis
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited prion disorder causes abnormal protein deposits in nerves outside the brain and in internal organs. It can lead to long-lasting watery diarrhea, nerve damage, and problems with automatic body functions such as blood pressure and bladder control; brain symptoms may develop later. Consider it when diarrhea and neuropathy have no clear cause. Treatment relieves symptoms.

topics.name: Procedural and Medical Abortion
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy can be ended with medicines that cause the uterus to contract or with a procedure that removes pregnancy tissue. The method depends mainly on how far the pregnancy has progressed and the person’s health. Follow-up may be needed to confirm completion and check for heavy bleeding or infection. Serious complications are uncommon with safe care, but risk rises later in pregnancy.

topics.name: Procedures for Prenatal Genetic Diagnosis
topics.clinical_significance: Procedures such as chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis can diagnose some genetic or chromosome conditions before birth. They are invasive and carry a small risk of pregnancy loss. The choice depends on the reason for testing, the stage of pregnancy, and the pregnant person’s informed preferences.

topics.name: Proctitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the rectal lining can cause a strong urge to pass stool, rectal discomfort, bleeding, or mucus. Causes include infections (including sexually transmitted infections), inflammatory bowel disease, and radiation treatment. Examination of the rectum and tests help find the cause, which guides treatment.

topics.name: Progeria
topics.clinical_significance: Progeria, usually Hutchinson-Gilford syndrome, is a rare genetic disease caused by a change in the LMNA gene, usually arising anew rather than being inherited. Children develop poor growth and signs of early aging. Heart and blood vessel disease is the main life-threatening complication and often causes early death. Lonafarnib treatment can lower the risk of death.

topics.name: Progestin Contraceptive Injections
topics.clinical_significance: Progestin shots, such as depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, provide effective birth control for several months per dose. Irregular bleeding or no periods and weight gain can occur. Bone density may decrease during use and usually recovers after stopping; fertility may take months to return after the last shot.

topics.name: Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)
topics.clinical_significance: PACE is a U.S. program for adults 55 or older who need nursing-home-level care but can live safely in the community with support. An interdisciplinary team coordinates medical, social, rehabilitation, home, and day-center services to help participants remain at home. It is available only in participating service areas and combines Medicare and Medicaid funding.

topics.name: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)
topics.clinical_significance: PML is a serious brain disease caused by reactivation of the JC virus, usually when cell-based immunity is weakened, such as in advanced HIV infection or during some immune-suppressing treatments. It causes progressive damage to brain white matter and worsening neurologic problems, and is often fatal. MRI and testing spinal fluid for JC virus help diagnose it; care focuses on restoring immune function and treating the underlying cause.

topics.name: Progressive Rubella Panencephalitis
topics.clinical_significance: This rare brain disorder can develop in adolescence in children born with congenital rubella, probably because the virus persists or becomes active again. It causes worsening movement problems, stiff muscles, loss of thinking ability, and seizures. There is no specific cure; treatment manages symptoms.

topics.name: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP)
topics.clinical_significance: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a degenerative brain disorder that causes difficulty moving the eyes (often looking down), slowed movement, stiffness, balance problems, and backward falls. Speech, swallowing, and thinking may worsen over time. There is no cure; treatment aims to ease symptoms, support mobility, and reduce falls.

topics.name: Prolactinoma
topics.clinical_significance: A prolactinoma is a noncancerous pituitary tumor that makes too much prolactin. It can cause breast milk discharge, menstrual changes, reduced sex hormones, and fertility problems; larger tumors may cause headache or vision problems. Dopamine-agonist medicines usually lower prolactin and shrink the tumor.

topics.name: Prolapsed Intervertebral Disc
topics.clinical_significance: A cervical disc herniates when its soft center pushes through a tear in its outer layer. Many herniations cause no symptoms; if a nearby nerve is irritated, pain may spread from the neck into an arm with tingling, numbness, or weakness. Spinal cord compression can cause serious problems and needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Proptosis
topics.clinical_significance: Proptosis is forward bulging of the eye and can signal disease in the tissues around it. In adults, a common cause is Graves-related eye disease; in children, orbital infection is a common cause. Sudden bulging, especially with pain, redness, fever, double vision, or vision loss, needs urgent assessment. Severe proptosis can dry and damage the cornea.

topics.name: Prostate Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A prostate abscess is a pocket of pus, usually caused by bacteria and arising as a complication of acute prostatitis. It can cause painful or frequent urination, difficulty emptying the bladder, and pain or pressure in the area between the scrotum and anus. Persistent or returning infection despite antibiotics should raise concern; treatment usually needs antibiotics and drainage.

topics.name: Prostate Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may cause no early symptoms, but some tumors spread to nearby tissues or bones. Older age, family history, and Black ancestry increase risk. A raised PSA or abnormal rectal exam can prompt evaluation, but a biopsy is needed to confirm cancer. Grade and stage guide care, from active monitoring for some low-risk tumors to surgery, radiation, or other treatment.

topics.name: Prostate Disease, Benign
topics.clinical_significance: Benign prostate disorders include enlargement, inflammation, and infection. They may cause a weak urine stream, frequent or urgent urination, difficulty emptying the bladder, or pelvic pain; infection may also cause fever. These symptoms can have other causes, including prostate cancer, so assessment may be needed. Long-lasting blockage can lead to urinary retention, infection, stones, or kidney damage.

topics.name: Prostatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Prostatitis includes acute or chronic bacterial infection and nonbacterial pelvic pain disorders. It can cause painful or frequent urination and pain in the pelvis or area between the scrotum and anus; acute bacterial infection may also cause fever, chills, or sepsis. Because many chronic cases are not bacterial, antibiotics help only when infection is present.

topics.name: Prosthesis, Fitting
topics.clinical_significance: Prosthesis fitting customizes the socket, suspension, and limb components to the person’s residual limb and functional needs. A well-fitted, properly aligned device protects the skin and improves comfort, stability, and movement. Trial fittings and adjustments are coordinated with physical and occupational therapy to support safe use.

topics.name: Prosthesis, Loosening
topics.clinical_significance: A prosthesis may loosen if the remaining limb changes shape or volume, or if its socket, straps, or suction system develops a problem. Slippage can injure the skin and reduce stability, increasing the risk of a fall. If basic troubleshooting does not fix it, a prosthetist should check and adjust the device.

topics.name: Prosthetic Components
topics.clinical_significance: A limb prosthesis includes a skin-protecting interface, a system that holds it on, a socket and connecting parts, and functional parts such as a hand or foot. The components are chosen and adjusted to the person’s needs. A comfortable, secure fit helps protect the residual limb and supports stable, efficient movement.

topics.name: Prosthetic Joint Infectious Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Infection of an artificial joint can occur soon after surgery or later if bacteria spread through the blood. It can cause joint pain, swelling, warmth, and reduced movement, and may lead to sepsis. Diagnosis usually requires testing joint fluid. Treatment involves prolonged antibiotics and often surgery to clean the joint, with the implant sometimes removed or replaced.

topics.name: Prosthetics, Limb
topics.clinical_significance: A limb prosthesis replaces part or all of a missing arm or leg. Its fit and components are tailored to the person’s health, remaining limb, and activity goals to improve comfort, stability, and daily function. Rehabilitation helps people learn to use it. Pain, swelling, or skin damage may signal a problem with the remaining limb or prosthesis.

topics.name: Proteeae Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Proteeae are gut bacteria that can cause opportunistic infections, especially after antibiotics disturb normal bacteria. They commonly affect the urinary tract and can sometimes cause deep infections or blood infection. Proteus can make urine more alkaline and promote struvite kidney or bladder stones. Antibiotic choice depends on the organism and its susceptibility.

topics.name: Protein C Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Protein C normally helps prevent excess blood clotting. Inherited or acquired deficiency raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; severe deficiency in newborns can cause purpura fulminans with widespread clots and skin injury. Starting warfarin without heparin in a person with protein C deficiency can trigger severe skin damage.

topics.name: Protein S Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Protein S helps protein C limit blood clotting. Inherited or acquired deficiency increases the risk of venous clots, such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; severe deficiency in newborns can cause purpura fulminans. Levels can also fall with liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin use, pregnancy, or estrogen use, so test results need clinical context.

topics.name: Protein Z Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Protein Z helps limit blood clotting. Its deficiency may raise the risk of venous clots, mainly when another clotting disorder is also present. The clinical importance is uncertain, testing is not part of routine clotting-disorder workups, and it is unclear whether the deficiency itself needs treatment.

topics.name: Protein-Energy Undernutrition (PEU)
topics.clinical_significance: Protein-energy undernutrition is a lack of calories and protein, often with shortages of other nutrients. It can result from too little food or from illness that limits digestion, absorption, or use of nutrients. It causes loss of fat and muscle, weakens immunity, and can impair many organs. Severe or prolonged cases need careful, gradual refeeding because rapid feeding can cause dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts.

topics.name: Proteinuria
topics.clinical_significance: Proteinuria is excess protein, usually albumin, in the urine. It can be temporary after fever or intense exercise, but persistent proteinuria may signal kidney disease and can further damage the kidneys. Heavy protein loss can lower blood protein levels and cause swelling. Repeat testing and evaluation help identify the cause.

topics.name: Prothrombin (Factor II) 20210 Gene Mutation
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited gene change raises blood prothrombin levels and increases the risk of venous clots, such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It does not appear to increase the risk of arterial clots that cause heart attack or stroke. The risk is higher when other clotting risk factors are present.

topics.name: Protracted or Arrested Labor
topics.clinical_significance: Protracted labor means cervical dilation or the baby’s descent is abnormally slow; arrested labor means progress has stopped. Causes include weak or poorly coordinated contractions and a mismatch between the baby’s size or position and the pelvis. Assessment of labor guides whether to wait, strengthen contractions with oxytocin, assist vaginal birth, or perform cesarean delivery.

topics.name: Providing Care to Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Care for older adults should consider multiple illnesses, medications, daily function, thinking, and social support together. Coordinated, person-centered care that includes the patient and, when appropriate, family or caregivers helps prevent gaps and errors when care moves between settings. The goal is to support health, safety, and independence.

topics.name: Proximal Humeral Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A fracture near the shoulder end of the upper arm bone causes pain and swelling and makes it hard to raise the arm. These fractures are common in older adults. Most are treated with a sling and early gentle shoulder movement to limit stiffness. More complex or displaced fractures may need surgery; rarely, nerves or blood vessels are injured.

topics.name: Prune-Belly Syndrome (Triad Syndrome)
topics.clinical_significance: Prune-belly syndrome is a birth condition marked by weak or missing abdominal muscles, urinary tract problems, and usually undescended testes in boys. Urinary problems can damage the kidneys; severe cases may lead to kidney failure and serious lung problems.

topics.name: Pruritic Urticarial Papules and Plaques of Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: This benign, very itchy rash usually starts in abdominal stretch marks late in pregnancy and may spread to the thighs and buttocks. It can disrupt sleep but usually clears within about 2 weeks after delivery; it rarely returns in a later pregnancy.

topics.name: Pruritus
topics.clinical_significance: Pruritus is the sensation of itching, often leading to scratching. It may occur with a skin condition or, sometimes without a visible rash, with an illness or medicine. Repeated scratching can damage the skin and cause infection.

topics.name: Pruritus Ani (Anal Itching)
topics.clinical_significance: Pruritus ani is itching of the skin around the anus. It is often linked to local irritation from stool, moisture, or cleansing; infections and anorectal or skin disorders are less common causes. Scratching can worsen irritation and damage the skin or cause infection.

topics.name: Pseudofolliculitis Barbae
topics.clinical_significance: Pseudofolliculitis barbae is a shaving-related skin reaction in which hairs grow back into the skin, causing inflamed bumps or pus-filled spots, usually in the beard area. It can resemble a bacterial infection of the hair follicles and may lead to scarring.

topics.name: Pseudogout
topics.clinical_significance: Pseudogout is joint inflammation caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals in or around joints. Sudden attacks often affect the knee or wrist and can resemble gout; long-lasting disease can damage joints. Crystal deposits may also be present without symptoms.

topics.name: Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type I
topics.clinical_significance: This rare inherited disorder makes the body resistant to aldosterone, so the kidneys lose too much salt and water and retain potassium. It can cause dehydration, low blood pressure, low blood sodium, and high blood potassium, especially in infants. Severe forms may also affect the skin and lungs.

topics.name: Pseudo-Jones Fracture
topics.clinical_significance: A pseudo-Jones fracture is a break at the base of the fifth foot bone, often caused when the foot rolls inward and pulls a small piece of bone away. It must be distinguished from a Jones fracture farther along the bone because pseudo-Jones fractures have a lower risk of delayed or failed healing.

topics.name: Pseudomembranous Colitis
topics.clinical_significance: Pseudomembranous colitis is inflammation of the colon caused by toxins from Clostridioides difficile, often after antibiotic use. It causes diarrhea and abdominal cramps and may recur; rarely, it leads to severe colon swelling, a hole in the colon, or sepsis.

topics.name: Pseudomonas and Related Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Pseudomonas and related bacteria can infect the skin, ears, eyes, lungs, urinary tract, bones, or blood. Severe infections are more common in hospitalized or weakened patients and can lead to sepsis. Antibiotic resistance is common, so treatment depends on testing the bacteria.

topics.name: Pseudorubella
topics.clinical_significance: Roseola is a common viral illness in young children, usually caused by human herpesvirus 6B and less often by human herpesvirus 7. Several days of high fever are followed by a brief rash as the fever falls; febrile seizures can occur.

topics.name: Pseudotumor Cerebri
topics.clinical_significance: Pseudotumor cerebri, also called idiopathic intracranial hypertension, is high pressure around the brain without a tumor or hydrocephalus. It can cause frequent headaches, brief dimming of vision, and swelling of the optic nerves; permanent vision loss is the most serious complication.

topics.name: Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited condition causes elastic fibers in the skin, eyes, and blood vessels to calcify and break down. It can cause yellow skin bumps, bleeding in the retina with gradual vision loss, early artery disease, and bleeding in the stomach or intestines.

topics.name: Psilocybin
topics.clinical_significance: Psilocybin is a hallucinogenic drug found in some mushrooms. It can change perception and impair judgment and coordination; adverse effects may include anxiety, a fast heartbeat, and, in severe toxicity, dangerously high body temperature or abnormal heart rhythms.

topics.name: Psoriasis
topics.clinical_significance: Psoriasis is a long-lasting inflammatory skin disease that causes raised, sharply defined scaly patches, often on the scalp, elbows, and knees. Their color can vary with skin tone, and nails may also be affected. About 3 in 10 people develop psoriatic arthritis, which can damage joints.

topics.name: Psoriasis and Other Papulosquamous Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes different skin diseases that cause raised spots or patches with scale, such as psoriasis, parapsoriasis, pityriasis rosea, lichen planus, and lichen sclerosus. They can look alike, but their causes, course, and risks differ, so identifying the specific disease is important.

topics.name: Psoriatic Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Psoriatic arthritis is long-term joint inflammation linked to psoriasis of the skin or nails, though joint symptoms may appear first. It can affect fingers, toes, the spine, and tendon attachments, causing pain and sausage-shaped swelling of digits. Ongoing inflammation can damage joints and cause disability.

topics.name: Psychiatric Disorders in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Child and adolescent psychiatric disorders are patterns of emotions or behavior that cause significant distress or interfere with daily life beyond what is expected for the child’s age. They can affect learning, relationships, and development; evaluation must consider the child’s development and surroundings because symptoms can overlap or resemble typical behavior.

topics.name: Psychiatric disorders in Children and Adolescents, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Mental health disorders that begin in childhood or adolescence include anxiety, mood, stress-related, obsessive-compulsive, behavior, and developmental disorders. They matter when symptoms cause serious distress or disrupt daily life beyond what is expected for the child’s age. Symptoms can overlap, so assessment considers development and family and social surroundings.

topics.name: Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions
topics.clinical_significance: This diagnosis applies when psychological or behavior factors worsen an existing illness or its outcome, such as when a person underestimates the illness or has difficulty following through with testing or treatment. These factors can worsen the illness and raise the risk of disability, emergency care, hospitalization, or death.

topics.name: Psychosocial Development in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Adolescence is a normal transition toward adulthood, with changes in thinking, emotions, social relationships, and independence. Some mood changes, conflict, and risk-taking are expected, but frequent or severe problems that disrupt daily life or put the adolescent or others at risk may need attention.

topics.name: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
topics.clinical_significance: This disorder involves hallucinations or delusions caused by a medical illness, such as a brain infection, stroke, seizure disorder, or metabolic disease. Identifying and treating the cause may reduce the psychotic symptoms; symptoms caused by drugs or delirium are classified separately.

topics.name: Pulmonary Air-Leak Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: These newborn conditions occur when air escapes from the lungs into nearby tissues or spaces, such as around the lungs or heart. They are more common in very premature infants and those with lung disease or breathing-machine support. Some cause no symptoms, but a large leak can worsen breathing or cause circulatory collapse.

topics.name: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis
topics.clinical_significance: This rare lung disorder occurs when surfactant builds up in the air sacs and interferes with oxygen transfer. It can cause worsening shortness of breath and fatigue; impaired lung defenses may also lead to infections.

topics.name: Pulmonary Barotrauma
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary barotrauma is lung injury from pressure changes, often during ascent while holding the breath after breathing compressed air. Ruptured air sacs can cause a collapsed lung or air around the heart and lungs; air entering the bloodstream can cause a dangerous gas embolism, including in the brain.

topics.name: Pulmonary Chemical-Warfare Agents
topics.clinical_significance: Inhaled chemical-warfare agents can injure the airways or the deeper parts of the lungs. They may cause immediate coughing and wheezing or delayed breathing difficulty as fluid builds up in the lungs. Severe exposure can block the airways or cause respiratory failure; some agents may also cause later lung scarring.

topics.name: Pulmonary Contusion
topics.clinical_significance: A lung bruise caused by chest trauma, with bleeding and swelling inside the lung but no tear. Breathing and oxygen levels may worsen over time; severe cases can lead to respiratory failure, pneumonia, or acute respiratory distress syndrome.

topics.name: Pulmonary Disease, Drug-Induced
topics.clinical_significance: A group of lung disorders caused by harmful reactions to medicines or other substances. Depending on the cause, the lungs may become inflamed or scarred, airways may narrow, or fluid or blood may collect in the lungs, leading to cough, breathlessness, or low oxygen.

topics.name: Pulmonary Disorders, Symptoms of
topics.clinical_significance: Common respiratory symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, wheezing, noisy breathing, and coughing up blood. They may arise from lung or other diseases; their timing, triggers, and accompanying signs help identify the cause and its seriousness.

topics.name: Pulmonary Edema
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary edema is fluid buildup in lung tissue and air sacs, often from acute left-heart failure or another heart problem. It interferes with oxygen exchange and can cause severe breathlessness, wheezing, and sometimes pink, frothy sputum. Sudden pulmonary edema can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Pulmonary Embolism
topics.clinical_significance: A pulmonary embolism is a blockage in a lung artery, usually from a blood clot that traveled from a deep vein in the leg or pelvis. It may cause sudden shortness of breath or sharp chest pain with breathing; severe cases can strain the right side of the heart, lower blood pressure, and cause collapse or cardiac arrest.

topics.name: Pulmonary Embolism, Nonthrombotic
topics.clinical_significance: A blockage of a lung artery by material other than a blood clot, such as air, fat, amniotic fluid, infected material, tumor cells, or cement. Effects depend on the material and may range from a small lung injury to severe oxygen loss, heart strain, or circulatory collapse.

topics.name: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is blockage of a lung artery by a clot, usually from a deep vein in the leg or pelvis. Small emboli may cause no symptoms, while larger ones can cause sudden breathlessness, sharp chest pain, and strain on the heart. Severe PE can lead to low blood pressure, collapse, or death; some people develop lasting breathlessness or chronic pulmonary hypertension.

topics.name: Pulmonary Function Tests, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) measure how well the lungs move air and exchange gases. They assess airflow, lung volumes, oxygen levels, and, in some tests, gas transfer and breathing-muscle function. Results help identify patterns of lung impairment, estimate its severity, and assess changes after a bronchodilator or over time.

topics.name: Pulmonary Granulomatosis X
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary granulomatosis X, also called pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is an uncommon lung disease linked mainly to cigarette smoking. It can cause cough, breathlessness, and chest pain, and scans may show lung nodules and cysts. A cyst can rupture and cause a collapsed lung; progressive disease can lead to high pressure in the lung arteries or respiratory failure.

topics.name: Pulmonary Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary hypertension is high blood pressure in the blood vessels of the lungs. It can result from heart or lung disease, long-term blood clots, or changes in the lung arteries. It often causes breathlessness with activity and tiredness; severe disease strains the right side of the heart and can lead to heart failure.

topics.name: Pulmonary Langerhans' Cell Granulomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary Langerhans cell granulomatosis, also called pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is an uncommon lung disease strongly linked to cigarette smoking. It can cause cough, breathlessness, fatigue, and chest pain. Lung cysts can rupture and cause a collapsed lung; progressive disease may lead to pulmonary hypertension or respiratory failure.

topics.name: Pulmonary Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is an uncommon lung disease in which abnormal Langerhans cells collect in the lungs; it is strongly linked to cigarette smoking. It may cause cough, breathlessness, fatigue, or chest pain, and sometimes has no symptoms. Lung cysts can rupture and cause a collapsed lung; progressive disease can lead to pulmonary hypertension or respiratory failure.

topics.name: Pulmonary Patient, Approach to
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluating a patient with possible lung disease starts with the symptoms, medical and exposure history, and physical examination; a chest X-ray is often part of the initial assessment. These findings help identify likely causes and determine whether tests such as lung-function testing, blood-gas analysis, CT imaging, or bronchoscopy are needed.

topics.name: Pulmonary Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of pulmonary symptoms combines the medical and exposure history with examination of breathing, oxygenation, and chest sounds; a chest X-ray is often included. Findings can point to lung disease or breathing distress and help determine which tests, such as lung-function tests, CT, or bronchoscopy, are needed.

topics.name: Pulmonary Procedures, Diagnostic and Therapeutic
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary procedures help diagnose lung and pleural disorders or treat problems in the airways and chest. Bronchoscopy allows doctors to view the airways and collect samples; thoracentesis removes pleural fluid for testing or symptom relief, while chest tubes can drain air or fluid. Some procedures have both diagnostic and therapeutic uses.

topics.name: Pulmonary Regurgitation
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary regurgitation occurs when the pulmonary valve does not close fully, allowing blood to flow back into the right ventricle. It is often mild and causes no symptoms; in adults it is commonly linked to pulmonary hypertension. Severe regurgitation can enlarge and weaken the right ventricle, causing breathlessness, reduced exercise ability, or heart failure.

topics.name: Pulmonary Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised program of exercise, education, and support for people with chronic respiratory disease. It can reduce breathlessness and improve exercise ability, daily function, and quality of life; for people with COPD, it may also lower the risk of hospital readmission after an exacerbation. It improves function but usually does not improve lung function itself.

topics.name: Pulmonary Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary stenosis is narrowing of the pulmonary valve or the nearby path from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery, which restricts blood flow to the lungs. It is usually present from birth; mild cases may cause no symptoms for years. More severe narrowing can strain and enlarge the right ventricle, causing breathlessness, chest pain, fainting, or reduced ability to exercise.

topics.name: Pulmonary Vascular Obstructive Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary vascular obstructive disease, also called Eisenmenger syndrome, can develop when a large congenital heart opening or abnormal connection sends extra blood to the lungs. Rising pressure and resistance in the lung vessels can reverse blood flow, sending low-oxygen blood into the body. This causes cyanosis and may lead to breathlessness, fainting, heart failure, blood clots, stroke, or other complications; the lung-vessel changes are usually irreversible.

topics.name: Pulmonary-Renal Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary-renal syndrome is the combination of bleeding into the air sacs of the lungs and inflammation of the kidney filters (glomerulonephritis), usually from an autoimmune disease. It can cause breathlessness or coughing blood along with blood in the urine or swelling. Lung and kidney problems may appear at different times, and the syndrome can rapidly threaten breathing and kidney function.

topics.name: Pulmonic Valve Regurgitation
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonic valve regurgitation, also called pulmonary regurgitation, occurs when the valve does not close fully and blood flows back into the right ventricle. It is often mild and causes no symptoms; in adults it is commonly linked to pulmonary hypertension. Severe regurgitation can enlarge and weaken the right ventricle, causing breathlessness, reduced exercise ability, or heart failure.

topics.name: Pulpitis
topics.clinical_significance: Pulpitis is inflammation of the soft tissue inside a tooth, usually from deep decay, trauma, or repeated dental procedures. Reversible pulpitis causes brief pain with cold or sweet foods; irreversible pulpitis can cause spontaneous or lingering pain and may progress to pulp death. Infection can then spread beyond the tooth and form a painful abscess.

topics.name: Pulsed Electromagnetic Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Pulsed electromagnetic therapy uses intermittent magnetic fields produced by an electromagnet. It differs from therapy with static magnets. Evidence of benefit varies by condition: it may reduce pain in some settings, but findings from one use cannot be assumed to apply to others.

topics.name: Pulseless Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Pulseless disease, also called Takayasu arteritis, is rare inflammation of the aorta and its major branches; the cause is unknown, though immune mechanisms may be involved. Arteries may narrow, close, or form aneurysms, reducing blood flow to the limbs or organs. This can cause weak or unequal pulses and blood pressure, limb pain with activity, dizziness, vision changes, stroke, or high blood pressure.

topics.name: PUPPP
