topics.clinical_significance: PUPPP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) is a benign, very itchy rash that usually begins in abdominal stretch marks late in pregnancy and may spread to the thighs and buttocks. The palms, soles, and face are usually spared. The rash generally clears within about 2 weeks after delivery.

topics.name: Pure Autonomic Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Pure autonomic failure is loss of nerve cells that control automatic body functions, especially blood pressure. The main problem is a drop in blood pressure on standing, which can cause dizziness or fainting. Other symptoms may include reduced sweating, heat intolerance, constipation, bladder problems, or sexual dysfunction. It occurs without the movement problems seen in multiple system atrophy, although some people later develop a related neurologic disorder.

topics.name: Pure Red Blood Cell Aplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Pure red blood cell aplasia is a bone marrow disorder in which red blood cell production is greatly reduced, while white blood cells and platelets are usually unaffected. It causes an isolated normocytic anemia with very low reticulocyte counts, leading to fatigue, pallor, and reduced exercise tolerance. Acquired cases may be linked to immune disease, medicines, parvovirus B19, or thymoma.

topics.name: Purine and Pyrimidine Metabolism Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Purine and pyrimidine metabolism disorders are usually inherited enzyme defects that disrupt the making, recycling, or breakdown of these DNA and RNA building blocks. Their effects depend on the specific defect and may include developmental or movement problems, immune deficiency, anemia, or kidney stones from abnormal waste products such as uric acid or xanthine.

topics.name: Purine Catabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Purine catabolism disorders are rare enzyme defects that disrupt the breakdown of purines, which normally ends in uric acid. Their effects vary: some cause severe immune deficiency and recurrent infections, some cause neurologic or exercise-related muscle symptoms, and others allow xanthine to build up and form kidney stones. Uric acid levels may be high or low, depending on the defect.

topics.name: Purine Nucleotide Synthesis Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Purine nucleotide synthesis disorders are rare inherited enzyme defects that affect the body’s production of purines, which are needed for DNA, RNA, and cell energy. Their effects vary: excess purine production can raise uric acid and cause gout as well as neurologic or developmental problems; other defects can cause severe developmental disability, autistic behavior, and seizures.

topics.name: Purine Salvage Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Purine salvage disorders are inherited enzyme defects that prevent the body from recycling purine bases. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome can cause high uric acid, gout, kidney stones, movement and developmental problems, and self-injury. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency causes 2,8-dihydroxyadenine kidney stones and kidney damage, even when blood uric acid is normal.

topics.name: Purpura Simplex
topics.clinical_significance: Purpura simplex is common, easy bruising caused by fragile small blood vessels. Bruises often appear on the thighs, buttocks, or upper arms without a remembered injury. Platelet counts and clotting tests are usually normal, and serious bleeding or a higher risk of internal bleeding does not occur.

topics.name: Purulent Labyrinthitis
topics.clinical_significance: Purulent labyrinthitis is a bacterial infection of the inner ear, often spreading from a severe middle-ear infection or meningitis. It can cause severe spinning dizziness, nausea, poor balance, ringing in the ears, and sensorineural hearing loss. Damage to the inner ear may leave lasting hearing or balance problems.

topics.name: Puss Moth Caterpillar (Asp) Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Puss moth caterpillar stings occur when its venomous hairs break off and lodge in the skin. They cause intense burning or throbbing pain and a red rash, which usually improve within hours to a day. Some people develop swelling, nausea, headache, or swollen lymph nodes; severe reactions can include shock or breathing problems.

topics.name: PVC
topics.clinical_significance: A premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is an early heartbeat that starts in a ventricle. PVCs are common and may cause a skipped or pounding beat, but isolated PVCs in a structurally normal heart are usually harmless. Very frequent PVCs can weaken the heart muscle, while PVCs that increase with exercise may signal reduced blood flow to the heart.

topics.name: Pyelonephritis, Chronic
topics.clinical_significance: Chronic pyelonephritis, also called reflux nephropathy, is kidney scarring and shrinkage after infection-related inflammation, usually in people with urine reflux or urinary blockage. It may cause few symptoms, but kidney damage can slowly progress to chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure. Recurrent infection can worsen the damage.

topics.name: Pyoderma Gangrenosum
topics.clinical_significance: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare, noninfectious inflammatory skin disease that often causes rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcers with a dusky purple edge. It is sometimes linked to inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, or blood disorders. Skin injury can trigger or worsen lesions, a response called pathergy.

topics.name: Pyogenic Granulomas
topics.clinical_significance: A pyogenic granuloma is a benign growth of small blood vessels, not an infection or a true granuloma. It usually grows quickly as a moist, bright-red nodule, often after minor skin injury, and bleeds easily. It can resemble a skin cancer, so removed tissue is examined under a microscope.

topics.name: Pyorrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Pyorrhea is an older name for periodontitis, a chronic gum disease triggered by bacteria in dental plaque. Inflammation damages the tissues and bone that support the teeth, forming deep gum pockets; teeth may loosen and eventually be lost. Gums may bleed or recede, while pain is uncommon unless an abscess develops.

topics.name: Pyridoxine Deficiency and Dependency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency can cause nerve damage, skin and mouth inflammation, anemia, confusion, and seizures; in infants, seizures may resist usual antiseizure medicines. Deficiency is usually secondary to poor nutrition, malabsorption, alcohol use disorder, or certain medicines. Rare inherited dependency can also cause seizures, developmental disability, and anemia.

topics.name: Pyridoxine Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Taking excessive pyridoxine (vitamin B6), usually in high-dose supplements, can damage sensory nerves. It may cause numbness, impaired sense of position and vibration, and poor balance or coordination. Recovery after the excess is stopped is slow and may be incomplete.

topics.name: Pyrimidine Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pyrimidine metabolism disorders are rare enzyme or immune-system defects that disrupt the making, recycling, or breakdown of pyrimidines, which are needed for DNA and RNA. Effects vary and may include anemia, recurrent infections, developmental delay, or seizures. One defect, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency, can cause severe or fatal reactions to the cancer drug 5-fluorouracil.

topics.name: Pyruvate Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pyruvate metabolism disorders are rare inherited enzyme defects that disrupt how the body uses pyruvate for energy or glucose production. Lactic acid can build up and cause lactic acidosis. Depending on the specific defect, effects may include abnormal brain development, developmental delay, seizures, or movement problems; severity ranges from episodic illness to life-threatening disease in infancy.

topics.name: Q Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Q fever is an infection caused by Coxiella burnetii, usually caught by breathing dust contaminated by infected sheep, goats, or cattle. It may cause fever, severe headache, and pneumonia or hepatitis, though some people have no symptoms. Rarely, infection persists and causes endocarditis, especially in people with abnormal heart valves.

topics.name: Quadriceps Tendon Tear
topics.clinical_significance: A quadriceps tendon tear is a serious knee injury that causes pain and swelling above the kneecap. A complete tear can make it impossible to straighten the knee or lift the straight leg; surgical repair is usually needed. The risk is higher in older adults and in people with certain medical conditions or who use some medicines, such as corticosteroids or fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

topics.name: Quality of Life in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Quality of life in older adults is each person’s own view of their physical, emotional, mental, social, and spiritual well-being. Symptoms, disability, memory problems, relationships, finances, and personal values can all affect it. Clinicians should ask what matters to the person and use that information when setting care goals and making treatment decisions.

topics.name: Quintan Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Quintan fever, also called trench fever, is an infection caused by Bartonella quintana and spread by body lice. It causes sudden fever that may return in episodes, often with severe headache, weakness, and shin or back pain. Bacteria may remain in the blood after symptoms improve, and rarely cause endocarditis (infection of the heart lining or valves).

topics.name: Quinupristin and Dalfopristin
topics.clinical_significance: Quinupristin and dalfopristin are intravenous antibiotics used for infections caused by certain bacteria, including vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium; they do not work against E. faecalis. They can cause muscle pain and inflammation of the infused vein, raise bilirubin, and interact with many medicines.

topics.name: Rabbit Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Rabbit fever, or tularemia, is an infection caused by Francisella tularensis. People can get it from infected animals (especially rabbits and hares), insect bites, contaminated food or water, or breathing in the bacteria; it does not spread from person to person. It often causes a skin sore and swollen nearby lymph nodes, but can also cause severe illness or pneumonia. Antibiotics are needed to treat it.

topics.name: Rabies
topics.clinical_significance: Rabies is a viral infection of the brain and spinal cord, usually spread when saliva from an infected mammal enters a bite, broken skin, or the eyes, nose, or mouth. It may begin with fever or unusual feelings near the bite, then cause brain inflammation or paralysis. Once symptoms begin, rabies is almost always fatal, but prompt post-exposure care can almost always prevent it.

topics.name: Radial Head Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A radial head fracture often follows a fall onto an outstretched arm and causes pain and swelling on the outer side of the elbow. Pain is often worse when turning the forearm palm up or down, and elbow movement may be limited. Small fractures can be hard to see on X-rays, so tenderness and joint swelling may still point to a fracture. Stable fractures are usually treated with a sling and early movement; unstable fractures or those that block movement may need surgery.

topics.name: Radial Head Subluxations
topics.clinical_significance: Radial head subluxation, or nursemaid’s elbow, is common in children about 2 to 3 years old and usually happens when the forearm is pulled. The child may suddenly stop using the arm, often with little tenderness. A clinician can usually return the joint to its normal position with a simple reduction maneuver, and the child soon moves the arm again. The injury can recur.

topics.name: Radial Tunnel Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Radial tunnel syndrome is pressure on the radial nerve near the elbow. It causes pain along the outer elbow and back of the forearm, often worse when straightening the wrist or fingers or turning the forearm palm up; numbness is uncommon. It can resemble tennis elbow. Splinting may help, while ongoing symptoms or marked weakness may require further care, sometimes surgery.

topics.name: Radiation Exposure and Contamination
topics.clinical_significance: Ionizing radiation can damage tissues. The effects depend on the dose, how quickly it is received, and how much of the body is exposed; they can range from local skin injury to severe whole-body illness, with a possible later increase in cancer risk. Radiation exposure alone does not make a person radioactive. Contamination means radioactive material is on or inside the body and may continue to expose the person or spread to others.

topics.name: Radiation Therapy for Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Radiation therapy uses focused radiation to damage cancer cells. It can cure some localized cancers, be combined with surgery or drug treatment, or relieve symptoms when cure is not possible. Nearby healthy tissue can also be injured, causing short-term effects such as fatigue or skin and mouth irritation, and sometimes late organ damage or a second cancer.

topics.name: Radiculopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Radiculopathy is a problem with a nerve root near the spine, often caused by a slipped (herniated) disc or bone changes. It can cause pain, tingling, numbness, or weakness in the body area served by that nerve; the pattern depends on which root is affected. Worsening weakness or loss of bladder or bowel control can signal serious spinal compression and needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Radiographic Contrast Agents and Contrast Reactions
topics.clinical_significance: Radiographic contrast agents make organs and blood vessels easier to see on imaging tests. Injected iodine-based contrast can cause reactions ranging from itching or rash to rare severe breathing or blood-pressure problems; a past contrast reaction raises the risk. Kidney injury can occur, especially in people with existing kidney problems or dehydration. Shellfish or iodine allergy alone does not increase the risk of a contrast reaction.

topics.name: Radiographs and Other Imaging Contrast Studies of the Gastrointestinal Tract
topics.clinical_significance: Contrast imaging studies outline the gastrointestinal tract on X-rays, moving fluoroscopy, or CT and help find masses, narrowings, and other structural problems. Moving images can also show how parts of the tract work, such as swallowing. Barium is avoided when a perforation is suspected because leaked barium can severely irritate nearby tissues; water-soluble contrast may be used instead.

topics.name: Radiography, Conventional
topics.clinical_significance: Conventional radiography uses X-rays to make flat images of the body. It is widely available and often the first imaging test for fractures, pneumonia, or bowel obstruction, but it may not show enough detail to locate or define some problems, so other tests may be needed. Fluoroscopy provides moving X-ray images for examining motion or guiding procedures and can involve higher radiation doses.

topics.name: Radiological Weapons
topics.clinical_significance: Radiological weapons can expose people to ionizing radiation, contaminate them with radioactive material, or do both. Clinicians need to tell radiation exposure from contamination and determine whether radioactive material is on the body or inside it, because this affects protection and treatment. Care is mostly supportive, but some radioactive materials inside the body have specific treatments.

topics.name: Radionuclide Scanning
topics.clinical_significance: Radionuclide scanning uses a radioactive tracer that collects in selected tissues; a camera detects its radiation to show where the tracer goes. These scans can help find bone cancer spread, infection, internal bleeding, and some thyroid or gallbladder problems. Radiation doses are generally low and reactions are rare, but images may have limited detail and scanning may take several hours.

topics.name: Radius Fractures, Distal
topics.clinical_significance: A distal radius fracture is a common wrist fracture, often caused by falling onto an outstretched hand, especially in older adults. It causes wrist pain and swelling and may make the wrist look crooked. Swelling can press on the median nerve, causing numbness in the thumb or fingers and weakness of the thumb. Fractures that affect the wrist joint or heal out of position can lead to lasting pain, stiffness, deformity, or arthritis.

topics.name: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Ramsay Hunt syndrome occurs when the shingles virus reactivates near the facial nerve. It causes severe ear pain, a blistering rash in or around the ear, and weakness or paralysis on the same side of the face. Vertigo, ringing in the ear, or hearing loss may also occur, and facial weakness or hearing loss can sometimes be permanent. Antiviral and steroid medicines may be used, but evidence that they improve outcomes is limited.

topics.name: Rape Victim, Medical Assessment
topics.clinical_significance: Medical care after rape or sexual assault should be private, compassionate, and guided by the person’s consent; they may accept or decline any part of the examination or evidence collection. The assessment checks and treats injuries, considers pregnancy and sexually transmitted infection risks, and offers prevention or treatment when appropriate, as well as emotional support and follow-up.

topics.name: Rash in Infants and Young Children
topics.clinical_significance: Rashes are common in infants and young children and are usually mild, often due to diaper irritation, eczema, or a viral infection. A rash with fever and a very ill or unusually irritable child, purple spots, blisters or peeling skin, sores in the mouth or eyes, or hives with breathing problems can signal a serious illness and needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Rat Lungworm
topics.clinical_significance: Rat lungworm infection is usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked snails, slugs, or certain animals that carry the parasite, or raw produce containing a small snail or slug. Angiostrongylus cantonensis can cause meningitis with severe headache and neck stiffness; Angiostrongylus costaricensis can cause abdominal pain and vomiting that may resemble appendicitis. Care is mainly supportive; anti-worm medicines may worsen inflammation.

topics.name: Rat-Bite Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Rat-bite fever is a bacterial infection usually acquired from a rat or other rodent bite; rarely, it follows drinking contaminated unpasteurized milk. It can cause fever, rash, and joint pain, or repeated bouts of fever with swollen lymph nodes. Serious complications such as joint infection or endocarditis are rare, but untreated disease can be fatal, so antibiotic treatment is important.

topics.name: Rat-Flea Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Rat-flea typhus, also called murine or endemic typhus, is caused by Rickettsia bacteria spread by fleas from rodents and some other animals. It usually causes fever, chills, and headache; about half of people develop a rash. It is generally milder than epidemic typhus but can be serious, especially in older adults, and is treated with doxycycline.

topics.name: Raynaud Phenomenon
topics.clinical_significance: Raynaud phenomenon is a temporary narrowing of small blood vessels, usually in the fingers or toes, triggered by cold or emotional stress. The affected digits may turn white or blue, then red as blood flow returns, and may feel cold, numb, or painful. Primary Raynaud phenomenon is usually mild; secondary Raynaud phenomenon, often linked to another disease, can cause painful ulcers or tissue loss.

topics.name: Raynaud Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Raynaud syndrome refers to secondary Raynaud phenomenon, in which cold- or stress-triggered narrowing of blood vessels in the fingers is linked to another condition or to a medicine or substance. Fingers may turn white or blue, then red as blood flow returns, and may feel numb or painful. Unlike primary Raynaud phenomenon, the secondary form can cause painful ulcers or tissue loss.

topics.name: Reactions to Sunlight
topics.clinical_significance: Sunlight, mainly its ultraviolet rays, can cause short-term skin effects such as sunburn and rashes from unusual sun sensitivity. Repeated exposure can cause premature skin aging, precancerous rough spots called actinic keratoses, and skin cancer. Some sunlight-triggered rashes are caused by medicines, chemicals, plants, or an underlying disease.

topics.name: Reactive Arthritis
topics.clinical_significance: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation triggered by an infection, usually in the gut or genital tract, and often begins after the infection. It usually affects a few joints unevenly, especially in the legs and toes, and may also cause eye inflammation, pain where tendons attach to bone, or sores and rashes. It often improves within a few months, but symptoms can return or last longer.

topics.name: Reactive Thrombocytosis (Secondary Thrombocythemia)
topics.clinical_significance: Reactive thrombocytosis is a high platelet count caused by another condition, such as infection, inflammation, bleeding, iron deficiency, cancer, or spleen removal. Platelet function is usually normal, and the high count usually does not increase the risk of blood clots or bleeding unless the person has arterial disease. Treating the underlying cause usually brings the platelet count back to normal.

topics.name: Recompression Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Recompression therapy gives 100% oxygen inside a pressurized chamber. It is used mainly for decompression sickness and gas bubbles in the arteries after diving, and also for carbon monoxide poisoning. The increased pressure shrinks gas bubbles, while the oxygen improves its delivery to tissues. Treatment works best when started early, but may still help if delayed.

topics.name: Rectal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Rectal cancer is usually an adenocarcinoma in the last part of the large intestine. Bleeding with a bowel movement is a common first sign; changes in bowel habits or a feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully may also occur. Diagnosis is confirmed by colonoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on the stage and often includes surgery; chemotherapy and radiation may be given before surgery for more advanced rectal tumors.

topics.name: Rectal Foreign Bodies
topics.clinical_significance: An object lodged in the rectum can cause pain or bleeding and may cut or perforate the rectal wall. Sudden severe pain during a bowel movement or frank bleeding can signal injury. Because removal can cause further harm, it should be done by a clinician skilled in removing rectal objects, sometimes with imaging or direct visualization.

topics.name: Rectal Prolapse and Procidentia
topics.clinical_significance: Rectal prolapse is protrusion of the rectum through the anus; procidentia means the full thickness of the rectum has prolapsed. The protrusion may appear during straining or even while standing. It is often painless, but bleeding and loss of bowel control can occur; pain may signal that the prolapse is trapped. Adults usually need surgery, while minor rectal-lining prolapse in infants often resolves with conservative care.

topics.name: Recurrent Aphthous Stomatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis causes repeated, painful, round or oval ulcers inside the mouth, commonly called canker sores. The cause is often unclear, and the ulcers are not herpes sores. They usually heal but may return; frequent or severe episodes can interfere with eating and may be linked to an underlying illness or nutrient deficiency. Topical steroid medicines can help reduce symptoms.

topics.name: Recurrent Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Relapsing fever is an infection caused by Borrelia bacteria spread by ticks or body lice. It causes sudden bouts of high fever, often with chills, headache, muscle and joint aches, nausea, or vomiting. Bouts are separated by days without fever, and untreated illness may recur several times.

topics.name: Recurrent Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Meningitis that returns after an earlier episode has resolved. Causes include infections, especially herpes simplex virus type 2 in recurrent viral cases; skull or spinal defects that allow bacteria to enter; some medicines; and, rarely, immune-system problems. Repeated episodes need evaluation to find and treat the cause.

topics.name: Recurrent Pregnancy Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Loss of two or more pregnancies. Causes may involve fetal chromosome changes, uterine or cervical problems, inherited factors, certain chronic illnesses, or antiphospholipid syndrome; often no cause is found. Reviewing each loss helps decide whether further evaluation is needed.

topics.name: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, usually noncancerous growth in the airway caused by human papillomavirus, most often affecting the voice box. The growths often return after removal and can cause hoarseness or, in severe cases, block breathing. They may rarely spread to the lungs or become cancerous.

topics.name: Red Blood Cell Production
topics.clinical_significance: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow. The kidneys release erythropoietin when oxygen is low, and production also needs iron, vitamin B12, and folate. Problems with this process can reduce red blood cell levels and cause anemia.

topics.name: Red Eye
topics.clinical_significance: Red eye is visible redness caused by widened blood vessels on the eye surface. It commonly occurs with conjunctivitis but may also result from corneal injury, inflammation inside or around the eye, or acute angle-closure glaucoma. Eye pain, light sensitivity, or reduced vision can signal a more serious cause.

topics.name: Reentrant (Paroxysmal) Supraventricular Tachycardias (PSVT)
topics.clinical_significance: PSVT is a sudden episode of a fast, usually regular heartbeat caused by an abnormal electrical loop in or above the heart ventricles. Episodes start and stop abruptly and may cause palpitations, breathlessness, chest discomfort, or light-headedness. Frequent episodes can often be treated with catheter ablation.

topics.name: Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy and Causalgia
topics.clinical_significance: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy and causalgia are older names for complex regional pain syndrome types I and II. Both cause lasting regional pain that is greater or longer than expected after an injury; type II involves a known nerve injury. The affected area may also become unusually sensitive, swollen, weak, stiff, or show changes in skin color, temperature, or sweating.

topics.name: Reflexology
topics.clinical_significance: A massage-based practice that applies pressure to specific points on the feet or hands, which practitioners believe correspond to other body parts. Studies mainly report general symptom relief, such as relaxation; evidence for pain relief is limited and low quality. It is not an established treatment for specific diseases.

topics.name: Reflux Nephropathy (Chronic Pyelonephritis)
topics.clinical_significance: Reflux nephropathy is kidney scarring and tissue loss caused by inflammation, usually when infected urine flows backward into the kidneys because of vesicoureteral reflux or a blockage. It may cause few symptoms but can slowly reduce kidney function and lead to chronic kidney disease.

topics.name: Refractive Error
topics.clinical_significance: A vision problem in which the eye does not focus light sharply on the retina, causing blurred vision at near or far. Types include nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, and age-related presbyopia. Glasses or contact lenses can usually correct the blur.

topics.name: Refractive Error, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Refractive errors blur vision because the cornea or lens does not focus light sharply on the retina. Nearsightedness blurs distant objects; farsightedness can blur near or distant objects; astigmatism can blur vision at any distance; and age-related presbyopia makes it harder to focus on near objects. Glasses or contact lenses can correct these problems.

topics.name: Refractive Surgery
topics.clinical_significance: Refractive surgery changes the shape of the cornea or uses an implanted or replacement lens to improve focus and reduce the need for glasses or contact lenses. It can correct nearsightedness, farsightedness, and astigmatism. Temporary dryness, glare, or halos may occur; less common complications include infection and too much or too little correction.

topics.name: Regional Enteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Regional enteritis is another name for Crohn disease, a chronic bowel disease with patchy, deep inflammation that can affect any part of the digestive tract, most often the ileum and colon. It can cause abdominal pain and diarrhea and may lead to bowel narrowing, fistulas, or abscesses.

topics.name: Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation is care that helps people recover lost function, reduce pain, and regain as much independence as possible after illness, injury, or surgery. It may combine physical, occupational, or speech therapy with pain care and psychological or social support.

topics.name: Rehabilitation for Other Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation for conditions such as arthritis, vision loss, brain or spinal cord injury, chronic pain, COPD, or severe weakness uses tailored exercise, training, devices, and symptom care to improve function and independence. It can also help prevent complications such as stiff joints and pressure sores.

topics.name: Rehabilitation, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Rehabilitation is team-based care that helps people recover function and reduce pain after illness or injury. Goals are tailored to the person and may include full recovery or regaining as many daily activities and as much independence as possible. Care may combine physical, occupational, or speech therapy with pain treatment and psychological or social support.

topics.name: Rehabilitative Measures for Treatment of Pain and Inflammation
topics.clinical_significance: Non-drug rehabilitation methods used to ease pain and inflammation and help movement include heat, cold, electrical stimulation, massage, ultrasound, traction, and acupuncture. The choice depends on the condition; these methods usually support, rather than replace, exercise-based rehabilitation, and evidence varies by method.

topics.name: Reiki
topics.clinical_significance: Reiki is a Japanese energy-healing practice in which practitioners place their hands on or near a person and intend to channel energy to promote healing. Evidence is mixed: some reviews suggest it may help pain or anxiety, but high-quality studies are limited and benefit for other conditions has not been shown.

topics.name: Reishi
topics.clinical_significance: Reishi (Ganoderma lucidum) is a mushroom sold as a supplement for claims such as boosting immunity or treating cancer, but evidence of benefit is limited; reishi alone has not been shown to treat cancer or improve survival. It may cause liver injury and can interact with blood-thinning, blood-pressure, or diabetes medicines.

topics.name: Relapsing Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Relapsing fever is an infection caused by Borrelia bacteria and spread by ticks or body lice. It causes bouts of high fever, often with chills, headache, muscle and joint aches, nausea, or vomiting, followed by periods of recovery. The number of relapses varies with the form of the disease.

topics.name: Relapsing Polychondritis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare immune-mediated disease that causes repeated inflammation of cartilage, most often in the outer ears and nose, but also sometimes in the eyes, joints, or airways. Ongoing damage can deform cartilage; airway collapse or heart and blood vessel complications can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Relaxation Techniques
topics.clinical_significance: Relaxation techniques are mind-body practices designed to ease tension and strain, sometimes alongside meditation, guided imagery, or hypnotherapy. Applied relaxation can reduce anxiety and some types of pain and may help depression, but many studies are small or low quality.

topics.name: Religion and Spirituality in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Religious and spiritual beliefs can affect how older adults cope with illness, find social support, and make health care decisions. They may support well-being but can also cause distress or conflict with medical care. Clinicians should ask about patients’ needs respectfully and not impose beliefs.

topics.name: Renal Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital kidney abnormalities vary in their effects. Some cause no symptoms and are found before birth or by chance; others can disrupt urine drainage, raise the risk of urinary infections, or reduce kidney function. The effects depend on the type and severity of the anomaly.

topics.name: Renal Artery Stenosis and Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing or blockage of an artery supplying a kidney reduces its blood flow. Chronic narrowing, usually from atherosclerosis or sometimes fibromuscular dysplasia, can cause hard-to-control high blood pressure and gradual kidney damage. Sudden blockage, often from a blood clot, can cause flank or abdominal pain, blood in the urine, and acute kidney injury.

topics.name: Renal Atheroembolism
topics.clinical_significance: Renal atheroembolism occurs when cholesterol-rich material from a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque blocks small kidney arteries, often after a procedure involving a large artery. It reduces kidney blood flow and can cause worsening kidney function; emboli may also affect the skin, eyes, or other organs.

topics.name: Renal Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: The most common kidney cancer, arising from kidney cells. It often causes no symptoms at first and is found by chance on imaging; later it may cause blood in the urine, flank pain, fever, or a mass, and can spread to other organs.

topics.name: Renal Cortical Necrosis
topics.clinical_significance: A rare condition in which injury to small kidney arteries destroys the outer kidney tissue (cortex), causing acute kidney injury. It often follows severe infection or pregnancy complications, especially in newborns or during or after pregnancy. Blood in the urine, flank pain, fever, and very low urine output may occur; lasting kidney failure is possible.

topics.name: Renal Cysts, Acquired
topics.clinical_significance: Acquired renal cysts are fluid-filled sacs that develop in the kidneys. Single simple cysts are usually found by chance and cause no problems; they may rarely bleed or become infected. Multiple cysts are more common in chronic kidney disease, especially after years of dialysis, and are associated with a higher incidence of kidney cancer.

topics.name: Renal Glucosuria
topics.clinical_significance: Glucose in the urine despite normal blood glucose, because the kidney tubules do not reabsorb all filtered glucose. It may be inherited, occur as part of a broader kidney-tubule disorder, or result from SGLT2 medicines. The isolated form is usually harmless and needs no treatment.

topics.name: Renal Glycosuria
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for renal glucosuria: glucose in the urine despite normal blood glucose, usually because kidney tubules do not reabsorb glucose fully. It is usually harmless when isolated, but can occur with broader kidney-tubule disorders or use of SGLT2 medicines.

topics.name: Renal Insufficiency in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney disease does not always worsen during pregnancy, but severe kidney impairment or uncontrolled high blood pressure raises the risk of complications, including poor fetal growth, stillbirth, preeclampsia, and early delivery. Close monitoring by kidney and pregnancy specialists is needed.

topics.name: Renal Metastases
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer that has spread to the kidneys from another site, commonly the lung, breast, stomach, bowel, or skin. It is usually found during evaluation of the original cancer or by chance on imaging, and often causes no symptoms or change in kidney function. Treatment usually focuses on the original cancer.

topics.name: Renal Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluation of possible kidney disease uses the medical history and physical examination, along with urine tests and blood tests such as creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Because symptoms may be mild or absent, these tests help detect kidney problems, assess function, and guide imaging or other tests to find the cause.

topics.name: Renal Pelvic and Ureteral Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: Cancers of the kidney’s collecting system (renal pelvis) or ureter, usually urothelial cancer. They often cause blood in the urine and sometimes pain. A tumor can block urine flow and cause cramping pain. Smoking, long-term cyclophosphamide use, chronic urinary irritation, and some chemical exposures raise the risk.

topics.name: Renal Transport Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: Renal transport abnormalities occur when kidney tubules do not handle substances such as salts, bicarbonate, glucose, or water normally. Depending on the disorder, this can upset fluid, electrolyte, or acid balance and may cause problems such as dehydration, muscle weakness, or poor bone growth.

topics.name: Renal Transport Abnormalities, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect how kidney tubules handle salts, acid, glucose, amino acids, and water. They may be inherited or acquired and can cause problems such as abnormal blood salt or acid levels, excess urination, kidney stones, or poor growth. Some begin in childhood; others can occur at any age.

topics.name: Renal Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney injury is common in urinary tract trauma. It is often caused by a blunt blow and is often mild, but severe injury can cause major bleeding or urine leakage. Blood in the urine may be a sign. Stable minor injuries are often monitored; severe or penetrating injuries may need a procedure or surgery.

topics.name: Renal Tubular Acidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Kidney tubules fail to remove enough acid or keep enough bicarbonate, causing chronic acid buildup and changes in blood potassium. Potassium may be low or high, depending on the type. Some people have no symptoms, but complications can include muscle weakness, kidney stones, bone problems, and chronic kidney disease; severe potassium changes can be dangerous.

topics.name: Renal Vein Thrombosis
topics.clinical_significance: A clot in one or both main kidney veins can reduce kidney function or cause sudden kidney injury. It may cause flank pain, blood in the urine, nausea, or less urine, and is often linked to nephrotic syndrome or cancer. Clots may also occur elsewhere, including in the lungs. Treatment usually includes blood thinners and care for the underlying cause.

topics.name: Renovascular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Renovascular disorders affect the blood vessels that supply or drain the kidneys. They can cause or result from high blood pressure and may reduce kidney function. A sudden blockage of an artery can cause acute kidney injury or kidney tissue death, while long-term vessel damage can lead to chronic kidney disease.

topics.name: Renovascular Hypertension
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing or blockage of a kidney artery can trigger high blood pressure by causing the kidney to release hormones that raise blood pressure. This uncommon cause should be considered when blood pressure starts suddenly, worsens quickly, is hard to control, or kidney function declines. Treatment usually uses medicines; selected patients may benefit from widening the artery.

topics.name: Reproductive Endocrinology, Male
topics.clinical_significance: Male reproductive hormones guide sexual development, puberty, testosterone production, and sperm formation. Problems in this system can cause delayed or atypical sexual development, low testosterone, reduced fertility, or sexual dysfunction. Testosterone tends to fall with age, but low levels indicate hypogonadism only when confirmed on repeat morning tests and accompanied by symptoms.

topics.name: Residential Care
topics.clinical_significance: Residential care provides housing and daily support for people, often older adults, who cannot live fully independently but may not need nursing-home care. Services may include meals, housekeeping, help with personal care or medicines, and supervision. The level and quality of care vary, so the setting should match the person’s needs and be checked for safety.

topics.name: Residual Limb Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain in the part of a limb that remains after amputation. Causes include pressure from a prosthesis, skin breakdown or infection, poor blood flow, bone problems, and nerve injury. Persistent pain can limit prosthesis use and rehabilitation, so it needs assessment to find treatable causes. It differs from phantom limb pain, which is felt in the missing part.

topics.name: Residual Limb, Skin Care
topics.clinical_significance: Skin under a prosthetic socket is at risk of pressure, friction, and moisture damage, which can lead to sores and infection. Poor circulation or reduced sensation, as in diabetes, increases risk and may hide early injury. Daily skin checks and a well-fitting prosthesis help prevent problems; pain, redness, sores, drainage, or a bad odor need prompt assessment.

topics.name: Respiratory Acidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Slow or shallow breathing traps carbon dioxide in the blood and usually makes it more acidic. Causes include lung disease, medicines or drugs that slow breathing, and weakness of the breathing muscles. Sudden or worsening cases can cause headache, confusion, and drowsiness; long-term cases may be partly compensated by the kidneys.

topics.name: Respiratory Alkalosis
topics.clinical_significance: Rapid or deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide in the blood and can raise its pH. Causes include low oxygen, fever, pain, anxiety, and some brain disorders. Sudden cases may cause light-headedness, confusion, tingling, cramps, or fainting. Since serious illness, including a blood clot in the lung, can also cause rapid breathing, the cause should be checked rather than assuming anxiety.

topics.name: Respiratory Arrest
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory arrest is the stopping of breathing. Without rapid help to restore breathing, oxygen levels fall, brain injury can occur within minutes, and cardiac arrest often follows. It is an emergency requiring immediate airway support and assisted breathing while the cause is treated.

topics.name: Respiratory Arrest, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory arrest is the stopping of breathing. It differs from cardiac arrest, but without prompt treatment it can lead to cardiac arrest within minutes and cause lasting brain injury. Causes include a blocked airway, medicines or drugs that slow breathing, and breathing-muscle weakness. Immediate airway support and assisted breathing are needed.

topics.name: Respiratory Bronchiolitis–Associated Interstitial Lung Disease (RBILD)
topics.clinical_significance: This smoking-related lung disease causes inflammation in small airways and scarring in nearby lung tissue. It can lead to cough and shortness of breath with activity. Stopping smoking and avoiding secondhand smoke are the main steps; the outlook is generally good when smoking stops.

topics.name: Respiratory Disorders in Young Children
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory infections and airway conditions are common in young children and can cause cough, wheezing, or difficulty breathing. Wheezing is often triggered by a virus and does not always mean asthma; other causes may need to be considered. Fast or labored breathing, chest pulling in, blue color, pauses in breathing, unusual sleepiness, or a silent chest can signal severe illness and need urgent assessment.

topics.name: Respiratory Distress Syndrome in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: This condition most often affects premature newborns whose lungs lack enough surfactant, so the air sacs collapse and blood oxygen falls. It causes fast, labored breathing soon after birth and can progress to respiratory failure. Treatment may include surfactant and breathing support; complications include air leaks and long-term lung disease.

topics.name: Respiratory Failure and Mechanical Ventilation
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory failure occurs when the lungs cannot add enough oxygen to the blood or remove enough carbon dioxide. It can be life-threatening and may require oxygen or machine-assisted breathing. Mechanical ventilation supports breathing through a mask or a tube in the airway while the cause is treated.

topics.name: Respiratory Failure, Other Types
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory failure can occur after surgery, often when parts of the lung collapse (atelectasis), which also raises the risk of pneumonia. Poor blood flow can deprive breathing muscles of oxygen and contribute to failure. Treating the cause, controlling pain, sitting upright, and moving early can help limit lung problems; some patients need breathing support.

topics.name: Respiratory Failure, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory failure means the lungs cannot keep enough oxygen in the blood, remove enough carbon dioxide, or do both. It is life-threatening and may cause severe breathlessness, rapid or labored breathing, bluish skin, or confusion. It needs urgent treatment of the cause and oxygen or breathing support when needed.

topics.name: Respiratory Muscle Function, Tests
topics.clinical_significance: These tests measure how strongly a person can breathe in and out and help assess weakness of the diaphragm or other breathing muscles. They can be useful when muscle or nerve disease is suspected. An abnormal result alone cannot confirm the cause because it may also reflect low effort or problems with lung mechanics.

topics.name: Respiratory Problems in Neonates
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing problems in newborns are a common reason for special or intensive care and may come from lung, heart, brain, blood, or metabolic conditions. Grunting, nostril flaring, chest retractions, fast or irregular breathing, pauses in breathing, or blue color are warning signs that need prompt assessment. Symptoms may start at birth or appear later.

topics.name: Respiratory Support in Neonates and Infants
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory support helps newborns who cannot keep oxygen levels up or remove carbon dioxide well enough on their own. Support ranges from extra oxygen and CPAP, which helps keep air sacs open, to a ventilator or, in severe cases, ECMO. Oxygen and ventilator settings must be carefully monitored because excess oxygen or pressure can harm developing lungs and eyes.

topics.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus Infections
topics.clinical_significance: RSV and human metapneumovirus are seasonal viruses that can cause bronchiolitis and, less often, pneumonia, especially in infants and young children. Illness may be mild or severe; babies under 6 months and people with heart, lung, or immune problems are at higher risk. In infants under 6 months, pauses in breathing can be an early sign of RSV. Treatment is mainly supportive.

topics.name: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: RSV vaccination helps prevent severe RSV illness: vaccination during pregnancy can pass protection to the newborn, and vaccination is recommended for older adults and some adults at higher risk. Eligibility and timing depend on age, health, pregnancy, and local guidance. The vaccine prevents illness; it does not treat an active RSV infection.

topics.name: Respiratory Viruses
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory viruses infect the nose, throat, or lungs and cause illnesses such as colds, bronchiolitis, croup, flu, and pneumonia. Most infections are mild, but infants, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease can become seriously ill. Viral illness can also worsen chronic conditions or lead to a bacterial infection. Care is usually supportive, though some viruses have vaccines or antiviral medicines.

topics.name: Respite Care
topics.clinical_significance: Respite care is temporary care from a substitute caregiver that gives the regular caregiver a break from the physical and emotional demands of caregiving. It may be provided at home, in a day program, or in a care facility. By supporting caregivers, it can help a chronically ill older adult continue living at home when appropriate.

topics.name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Restrictive cardiomyopathy makes the heart muscle stiff, so the heart cannot fill properly between beats. It can cause breathlessness, fatigue, and swelling in the legs or abdomen, and may lead to abnormal heart rhythms. Causes include amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, iron overload, and scarring; identifying the cause can guide treatment.

topics.name: Resuscitation, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Emergency care given at birth when a newborn is not breathing effectively or has a slow heart rate. It aims to establish breathing and circulation and may include keeping the baby warm, opening the airway, assisted breathing, and, if needed, chest compressions and medicines.

topics.name: Retinal Artery Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: A blocked retinal artery causes sudden, painless vision loss in one eye or part of its visual field. The vision loss may be permanent. The blockage may result from an embolus or blood vessel inflammation, and it is linked to increased stroke risk, so prompt assessment is important.

topics.name: Retinal Detachment
topics.clinical_significance: Retinal detachment occurs when the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye separates from the tissue beneath it. It may follow a tear, scar tissue pulling on the retina, or fluid collecting under it. Flashes, new floaters, or a curtain-like shadow can occur. Untreated detachment can cause lasting vision loss and needs urgent eye assessment.

topics.name: Retinal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: The retina detects light and sends visual signals to the brain. Diseases of the retina can reduce central, side, color, or night vision, and some can cause permanent vision loss.

topics.name: Retinal Vein Occlusion
topics.clinical_significance: A retinal vein blockage causes painless, often sudden vision loss. Blood and fluid can build up in the retina, and swelling of the macula (the central part of the retina) can blur central vision. High blood pressure, diabetes, and glaucoma are common risk factors. Abnormal new blood vessels can later cause bleeding or glaucoma.

topics.name: Retinitis Pigmentosa
topics.clinical_significance: A group of inherited diseases that slowly damage the light-sensing tissue at the back of both eyes. It often first causes difficulty seeing in dim light and gradual loss of side vision; central vision may also worsen later.

topics.name: Retinoblastoma
topics.clinical_significance: A cancer of the retina that mainly affects children younger than 2 years. Common signs are a white pupil or eyes that are not aligned. It may be inherited and affect both eyes; inherited cases also raise the risk of other cancers later in life. When found before it spreads beyond the eye, it can often be cured, and treatment may preserve vision.

topics.name: Retinol Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin A deficiency can cause poor night vision and dry, damaged eyes (xerophthalmia), which may progress to blindness. It also weakens immune defenses and increases infection risk, especially in children. Causes include low intake, poor fat absorption, and liver disease.

topics.name: Retinol Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Excess vitamin A can cause headache, nausea, and vomiting after a large dose. Long-term excess can cause dry skin, hair loss, bone pain, and liver damage. Very high doses during pregnancy can cause birth defects. Toxicity usually results from excessive supplements or vitamin A–related medicines.

topics.name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
topics.clinical_significance: Retinopathy of prematurity is abnormal growth of retinal blood vessels in premature infants, especially those born very early or at low birth weight. Mild cases often improve, but severe disease can pull the retina away and cause vision loss. It may have no early signs, so at-risk infants need eye exams.

topics.name: Retrocalcaneal Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the fluid-filled sac between the Achilles tendon and heel bone. It causes pain, swelling, and warmth near the back of the heel, which can make walking or wearing shoes difficult. Friction, injury, tight shoes, gout, or rheumatoid arthritis may cause it.

topics.name: Retrolental Fibroplasia
topics.clinical_significance: An older name for retinopathy of prematurity, in which retinal blood vessels grow abnormally in premature infants. Severe disease can pull the retina out of place and cause vision loss.

topics.name: Retronychia
topics.clinical_significance: Retronychia is a nail growth disorder, usually of the big toe, in which the nail grows into the skin fold at its base and new nail layers stack under old ones. It can cause pain, swelling, and yellowing, often after repeated toe injury or pressure from tight shoes.

topics.name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: A pocket of pus forms in the tissues behind the throat, usually after a bacterial infection. It occurs mainly in young children and can cause fever, severe throat or neck pain, trouble swallowing, a stiff neck, and noisy breathing. Swelling can block the airway and become life-threatening.

topics.name: Rett Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Rett syndrome is a rare genetic disorder of brain development that mainly affects girls. After early development, children often lose skills such as speech and purposeful hand use and develop repeated hand movements. Seizures, problems with walking or breathing, feeding difficulties, and scoliosis may also occur.

topics.name: Reye Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, life-threatening illness that causes brain swelling and liver injury, usually in children after a viral infection. Repeated vomiting may be followed by confusion, severe sleepiness, seizures, or coma. Aspirin use during the infection is strongly linked to increased risk.

topics.name: Reye's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Another name for Reye syndrome, a rare illness that causes sudden brain dysfunction and liver injury, usually in children after certain viral infections. Aspirin use during the infection is linked to increased risk. Severe cases can cause seizures, coma, or death.

topics.name: Rh Incompatibility
topics.clinical_significance: Rh incompatibility occurs when a pregnant person with Rh-negative blood carries an Rh-positive fetus. The pregnant person may form antibodies that cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, causing anemia and jaundice; severe cases can be life-threatening. Anti-D immune globulin can prevent antibody formation.

topics.name: Rhabdomyolysis
topics.clinical_significance: Rhabdomyolysis is breakdown of skeletal muscle that releases proteins and salts into the blood. It may cause muscle pain or weakness and dark urine, but these signs are not always present. Severe cases can disturb blood salts, cause dangerous heart rhythms, or damage the kidneys. Triggers include crush injury, extreme exercise, seizures, heat illness, and some medicines.

topics.name: Rhabdomyosarcoma
topics.clinical_significance: A cancer of immature cells that can develop into skeletal muscle. It occurs most often in children and can form almost anywhere in the body. It may spread to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, or bone marrow.

topics.name: RhD Alloimmunization
topics.clinical_significance: RhD alloimmunization happens when an Rh-negative person forms antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive blood, such as during pregnancy or transfusion. In a pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, these antibodies can cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, causing anemia and jaundice. Anti-D immune globulin can prevent sensitization.

topics.name: Rheumatic Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory illness that can develop after a group A strep throat infection, usually in children. It can cause painful, swollen joints, jerky movements, skin changes, and heart inflammation. Heart inflammation may permanently damage the valves.

topics.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
topics.clinical_significance: Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term autoimmune disease that causes painful swelling and stiffness in joints, often on both sides of the body. It can gradually damage cartilage and bone, leading to joint deformity and loss of function. It can also affect organs beyond the joints, including the lungs and heart.

topics.name: Rhinitis, Nonallergic
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the nasal lining that is not caused by an allergy. It can cause a stuffy or runny nose, sneezing, or mucus dripping down the throat. Triggers include viral infections and irritants such as smoke, strong odors, cold air, or dry air.

topics.name: Rhodiola
topics.clinical_significance: Rhodiola rosea is a plant whose root is used in herbal supplements claimed to reduce fatigue and improve mood, memory, or exercise performance. High-quality studies have not shown that it treats any health condition. It may cause dizziness or dry mouth and can interact with antidepressants, blood thinners, and some diabetes, blood pressure, or immune-suppressing medicines.

topics.name: Rhythm Method
topics.clinical_significance: The rhythm method uses past menstrual cycles to estimate when pregnancy is most likely and avoids sex during those days. Ovulation can shift, so the method can fail, especially with irregular cycles; in typical use, pregnancy rates are higher than with many other contraceptive methods. It does not prevent sexually transmitted infections.

topics.name: Rib Fracture
topics.clinical_significance: A broken rib causes localized pain and tenderness that worsens with deep breaths, coughing, or movement. Multiple fractures or fractures after a strong blow may occur with injuries to the lungs, blood vessels, or nearby organs.

topics.name: Riboflavin Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency often occurs with other B vitamin deficiencies. It can cause cracks at the corners of the mouth, a sore or swollen tongue, sore throat, scaly skin, eye irritation, and sometimes anemia.

topics.name: Rickets
topics.clinical_significance: Rickets is a disorder of growing bones in which they do not harden normally. It is most often caused by low vitamin D or calcium, but can also result from phosphate or inherited problems. It can cause bone pain, slow growth, bowed legs, and, in severe cases, fractures.

topics.name: Rickettsiae and Related Organisms
topics.clinical_significance: Rickettsiae and related organisms are bacteria that live inside host cells. Many spread through bites of ticks, mites, fleas, or lice and cause fever, headache, and sometimes a rash; some can damage blood vessels and cause severe illness.

topics.name: Rickettsial and Related Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Rickettsial and related infections are caused by bacteria that multiply inside human cells. Most spread from animals through ticks, mites, fleas, or lice. They often cause sudden fever and headache, sometimes with a rash; severe infections can damage blood vessels and organs and may be fatal.

topics.name: Rickettsialpox
topics.clinical_significance: Rickettsialpox is usually a mild infection caused by Rickettsia akari and spread by mites associated with mice and other rodents. A dark scab forms at the bite site, followed by fever and a scattered blister-like rash that can resemble chickenpox. Recognizing this pattern helps distinguish it from other febrile rashes.

topics.name: Rifamycins
topics.clinical_significance: Rifampin, rifabutin, and rifapentine are antibiotics used mainly with other drugs to treat tuberculosis; rifampin also treats some other infections. Rifaximin acts mainly in the gut and is used for some diarrheal infections. Rifampin can interact with many medicines by speeding their breakdown and can turn urine, sweat, tears, and other body fluids orange-red.

topics.name: Right Heart Failure and Cor Pulmonale
topics.clinical_significance: Right heart failure occurs when the right ventricle cannot pump blood effectively, causing blood to back up in the veins. It may lead to swollen legs, enlarged neck veins, or liver swelling; left heart failure is the most common cause. Cor pulmonale is right heart failure caused by lung disease and high pressure in the lung arteries. Treating the cause early can help limit lasting heart damage.

topics.name: Riot-Control Chemical Agents
topics.clinical_significance: Riot-control agents, including tear gas and pepper spray, quickly irritate the eyes, skin, and airways, causing pain, tearing, coughing, or wheezing. Effects usually ease after exposure ends and the agent is removed. Heavy exposure, especially in an enclosed space, can cause serious lung injury and fluid in the lungs and may be fatal.

topics.name: Risk Factors for Pregnancy Complications
topics.clinical_significance: Some factors raise the chance of problems during pregnancy or birth. These include health conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure, smoking or substance use, harmful exposures, carrying more than one fetus, maternal age or weight, and problems in past pregnancies. Finding risk factors early helps clinicians plan care and monitoring to protect the pregnant person and fetus.

topics.name: Risks of Medical Radiation
topics.clinical_significance: X-rays, CT scans, and some other tests use ionizing radiation, which may slightly raise a person’s future cancer risk. The risk increases with higher or repeated doses and is greater in children. During pregnancy, fetal risk depends on the dose, test, and stage of pregnancy. Most diagnostic doses are low, but these tests should be used when needed and exposure kept as low as practical.

topics.name: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF)
topics.clinical_significance: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne infection that can quickly damage blood vessels and organs. It causes sudden fever and severe headache; a rash often appears later, and a tick bite may not be noticed. Because delayed treatment can be fatal, suspected infection needs prompt doxycycline, including in children and pregnant patients.

topics.name: Rosacea
topics.clinical_significance: Rosacea is a long-lasting skin condition that can cause facial flushing, redness, visible small blood vessels, and acne-like bumps. It can also inflame the eyes. In some people, long-standing disease thickens the skin, often on the nose. Treatment can control symptoms, but does not cure the condition.

topics.name: Rosai-Dorfman Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Rosai-Dorfman disease is a rare disorder in which histiocytes, a type of immune cell, build up in the body. It often causes fever and large, painless lymph nodes in the neck, but can also affect other organs. It often improves without treatment; progressive disease may need treatment.

topics.name: Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease is another name for Rosai-Dorfman disease, a rare disorder in which histiocytes build up, usually causing fever and large, painless lymph nodes in the neck. Other organs can be affected. It often resolves without treatment, but progressive disease may need therapy.

topics.name: Roseola Infantum
topics.clinical_significance: Roseola infantum is a viral illness in young children, usually caused by human herpesvirus 6. It causes several days of high fever, followed by a brief rash as the fever falls. Febrile seizures can occur. The illness usually resolves on its own, and treatment is mainly to relieve symptoms.

topics.name: Rotator Cuff Injury/Subacromial Bursitis
topics.clinical_significance: Rotator cuff tendons can become irritated or torn, and nearby bursitis can cause shoulder pain, especially when lifting the arm overhead. A complete tear may cause marked weakness. Tendinitis, bursitis, and partial tears often improve with nonsurgical care, while severe tears may need repair.

topics.name: Rotavirus Gastroenteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Rotavirus causes highly contagious watery diarrhea and vomiting, especially in infants and young children. Fluid loss can lead to severe dehydration and may be life-threatening. Replacing fluids and salts is the main treatment. Infant vaccination greatly reduces severe illness and hospitalizations.

topics.name: Rotavirus Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: Oral rotavirus vaccine protects infants against severe diarrhea, vomiting, and dehydration caused by rotavirus and reduces hospitalizations. It is given in early infancy according to the local schedule. A very small risk of bowel telescoping (intussusception) has been reported; it should not be given to infants who have had intussusception or have severe combined immunodeficiency.

topics.name: Rubella
topics.clinical_significance: Rubella is a contagious viral illness that usually causes mild fever, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash. Infection during early pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or serious birth defects, including hearing, eye, and heart problems. Vaccination prevents rubella; the live MMR vaccine is not given during pregnancy.

topics.name: Rubeola
topics.clinical_significance: Rubeola, or measles, is a highly contagious viral illness that causes fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a spreading rash. It can lead to serious problems such as pneumonia or brain inflammation; rarely, a fatal brain disease develops years later. MMR vaccination is the main way to prevent measles.

topics.name: Rugby Finger
topics.clinical_significance: Rugby finger (jersey finger) is an avulsion of the tendon that bends the fingertip, sometimes pulling off a small piece of bone. The person cannot actively bend the fingertip joint. Prompt assessment is important because the tendon usually needs surgical repair.

topics.name: Rumination
topics.clinical_significance: Rumination is usually involuntary return of small amounts of food from the stomach, often 15 to 30 minutes after eating. The food is rechewed and usually swallowed again, without nausea or abdominal pain. It can rarely cause weight loss; behavioral techniques may help.

topics.name: Rumination Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Rumination disorder causes repeated return of food after eating, without nausea or forceful retching; it can be intentional or outside the person’s control. Spitting out food or restricting meals can lead to weight loss or poor nutrition. Other causes of regurgitation should be ruled out, and behavioral techniques may help.

topics.name: Runner's Knee
topics.clinical_significance: Runner’s knee is pain around or behind the kneecap, often linked to abnormal kneecap movement or imbalance in the thigh muscles. Running downhill, using stairs, or sitting with the knee bent may worsen the pain. Reducing painful activity and exercises to strengthen and stretch the thigh muscles often help.

topics.name: Ruptured Cervical Disc
topics.clinical_significance: A herniated disc in the neck may cause no symptoms. If it irritates or presses on a nerve, it can cause neck pain that spreads into the arm, numbness, tingling, or weakness. Pressure on the spinal cord can affect movement and needs prompt medical assessment. Many cases improve without surgery.

topics.name: Ruptured Lumbar Disc
topics.clinical_significance: A herniated lumbar disc may cause no symptoms or press on a nerve, causing low back pain that travels down a leg, tingling, numbness, or weakness. Most cases improve without surgery. New difficulty passing urine or loss of bladder control can signal pressure on the cauda equina nerves and needs urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: S-Adenosyl-L-Methionine
topics.clinical_significance: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAMe) is made naturally in the body and sold as a supplement for depression, osteoarthritis, and liver problems, but evidence for these uses is limited or mixed. It can trigger mania in people with bipolar disorder and may interact with antidepressants or levodopa, so medical advice is important before use.

topics.name: Salicylism
topics.clinical_significance: Salicylism is toxicity from aspirin or other salicylates after an overdose or repeated high doses. Early signs include ringing in the ears, nausea, vomiting, and rapid breathing. Severe poisoning can cause fever, confusion, seizures, acid-base problems, and organ failure. It can be life-threatening and needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Salivary Gland Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Most salivary gland tumors are benign and appear as a painless lump, often in the parotid gland. A lump that grows quickly or is fixed, painful, or associated with numbness or facial weakness may signal cancer. Biopsy and imaging help identify the tumor type and how far it has spread.

topics.name: Salivary Stones
topics.clinical_significance: Salivary stones are hardened mineral deposits that block saliva flow, most often in the gland under the jaw. They can cause pain and swelling during meals, when saliva production increases. Repeated blockage can lead to gland infection. Some stones pass on their own; others need removal.

topics.name: Salmonella Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Salmonella bacteria, often spread through contaminated food or water, can cause several illnesses. Many strains cause diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps; Salmonella Typhi causes typhoid fever. Some infections spread into the blood or other organs, especially in infants, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.

topics.name: SAMe
topics.clinical_significance: SAMe is the abbreviation for S-adenosyl-L-methionine, a substance made naturally in the body and also sold as a supplement. Evidence for its claimed uses, including depression and osteoarthritis, is limited or mixed. It can trigger mania in people with bipolar disorder and may interact with antidepressants or levodopa.

topics.name: San Joaquin Fever
topics.clinical_significance: San Joaquin fever (Valley fever) is a fungal infection caused by Coccidioides, usually caught by breathing spores in dust in parts of the southwestern United States and nearby regions. Many infections cause no symptoms or a mild lung illness. In some people, especially those with weakened immune systems, it can become severe or spread to the skin, bones, or membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

topics.name: Sarcoidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Sarcoidosis is an illness in which small clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomas) form in organs; its cause is unknown. It most often affects the lungs and nearby lymph nodes, but can also affect the eyes, skin, heart, nervous system, or other organs. Many people have no symptoms or improve without treatment, but lung, heart, or nervous system involvement can cause serious or lasting problems.

topics.name: SARS-CoV-2 Infection
topics.clinical_significance: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus that causes COVID-19, a respiratory illness. Infection may cause no symptoms or a mild illness, but can also lead to severe lung disease, blood clots, problems in other organs, or death. Some people have symptoms that continue for weeks or months after the infection.

topics.name: Saw Palmetto
topics.clinical_significance: Saw palmetto is a plant supplement often used for urinary symptoms from an enlarged prostate, but most studies find little or no benefit. It can cause headache or diarrhea, and the strength of products varies. It may reduce the effect of estrogen medicines; people taking warfarin should use caution because bleeding risk has been reported, although evidence is limited.

topics.name: Scabies
topics.clinical_significance: Scabies is a skin infestation caused by tiny mites that burrow into the outer skin. It causes an intensely itchy rash, often worse at night, and spreads mainly through prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Scratching can cause a bacterial skin infection, and close contacts may need treatment even if they have no symptoms.

topics.name: Scaphoid (Navicular) Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A scaphoid fracture is a break in a small wrist bone, often after a fall onto an outstretched hand. Early X-rays may not show the break. The fracture can reduce blood flow to part of the bone, leading to poor healing or bone death and, in some cases, lasting wrist pain and arthritis.

topics.name: Schatzki Ring
topics.clinical_significance: A Schatzki ring is a thin band of tissue that narrows the lower esophagus. It can cause episodes of difficulty swallowing solid foods, especially meat or dry bread, and food may get stuck. Narrow rings may need to be widened during endoscopy.

topics.name: Scheuermann Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Scheuermann disease usually begins during adolescence, and its cause is uncertain. Several spinal bones (vertebrae) grow into a wedge shape, creating a fixed rounded upper back (kyphosis) and sometimes mild, lasting back pain. Severe curvature can limit chest movement, but the condition is usually mild.

topics.name: Scheuermann's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Scheuermann disease usually begins during adolescence, and its cause is uncertain. Several spinal bones (vertebrae) grow into a wedge shape, creating a fixed rounded upper back (kyphosis) and sometimes mild, lasting back pain. Severe curvature can limit chest movement, but the condition is usually mild.

topics.name: Schistosomiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Schistosomiasis is caused by parasitic flatworms. Their larvae, released from freshwater snails, can penetrate the skin during contact with contaminated freshwater. Infection may cause an itchy rash, fever, belly pain, diarrhea, or blood in the urine or stool. Long-term infection can scar and damage the bowel, liver, or urinary tract; one form also raises the risk of bladder cancer.

topics.name: Schizoaffective Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Schizoaffective disorder combines psychosis (such as hallucinations or delusions) with major episodes of depression or mania. Mood episodes occur during much of the illness, but psychosis also lasts for at least 2 weeks without a major mood episode. This pattern helps distinguish the disorder from mood disorders with psychosis.

topics.name: Schizoid Personality Disorder (ScPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Schizoid personality disorder is a long-term pattern of little interest in close relationships and limited emotional expression. A person may prefer solitary activities and seem detached, which can make relationships difficult. It does not involve hallucinations or delusions, which are symptoms of psychosis.

topics.name: Schizophrenia
topics.clinical_significance: Schizophrenia is a long-term mental illness that can affect a person’s thoughts, perceptions, emotions, and ability to function. It may cause hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech or behavior, reduced motivation or emotional expression, and problems with thinking or memory. These symptoms can disrupt work, relationships, and self-care; treatment and social support can help manage them.

topics.name: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders, which can cause hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thinking and behavior. Some also involve major mood symptoms, reduced emotional expression or motivation, or difficulty with thinking. The disorders differ in their symptoms and course, so diagnosis depends on how symptoms develop and how long they last.

topics.name: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders can cause hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thoughts, speech, or behavior. They may also reduce motivation and emotional expression or affect attention, memory, and problem solving. Doctors distinguish these disorders by the pattern and course of symptoms; there is no single lab test that confirms them.

topics.name: Schizophrenia in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Schizophrenia in children and adolescents is rare and often begins gradually. It can cause hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech or behavior, and problems with motivation or emotional expression, affecting learning, relationships, and development. Careful assessment over time helps distinguish it from mood, developmental, or medical conditions with similar symptoms.

topics.name: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Psychotic Disorders, Other
topics.clinical_significance: These diagnoses apply when psychotic symptoms, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thinking, cause significant distress or problems with daily life but do not fit another specific psychotic disorder. They are called specified when the reason is described, or unspecified when it is not.

topics.name: Schizophreniform Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Schizophreniform disorder causes symptoms like schizophrenia, such as hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized speech, that last at least 1 month but less than 6 months. If symptoms continue longer, schizophrenia or another disorder may be diagnosed. Careful follow-up helps clarify the diagnosis and guide treatment.

topics.name: Schizotypal Personality Disorder (STPD)
topics.clinical_significance: Schizotypal personality disorder is a lasting pattern of discomfort with close relationships, unusual beliefs or perceptions, and eccentric behavior. People may be socially anxious, suspicious, or have unusual speech, which can make relationships difficult. These traits resemble schizophrenia but are usually less severe.

topics.name: School Avoidance
topics.clinical_significance: School avoidance is repeated difficulty attending or staying at school, often linked to anxiety or other emotional or social stress. Children may have real physical symptoms, such as stomachaches or nausea. Frequent absence can affect learning and may signal anxiety, depression, bullying, or problems with peers, family, or school.

topics.name: Sciatica
topics.clinical_significance: Sciatica is pain that travels from the buttock down the back of the leg, usually because a nerve in the lower spine is compressed by a herniated disk or narrowing of the spine. Tingling, numbness, or leg weakness may also occur. New loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the groin, or worsening leg weakness can signal severe nerve compression; these symptoms need urgent medical assessment.

topics.name: Scleritis
