topics.clinical_significance: Scleritis is severe inflammation of the sclera, the tough white outer layer of the eye. It causes deep, often intense eye pain, redness, tearing, and sensitivity to light, and can damage the eye or threaten vision. It is often linked to an autoimmune disease, though infection or other causes may be involved.

topics.name: Scleroderma
topics.clinical_significance: Scleroderma describes disorders in which excess scar tissue makes the skin hard and tight. Localized forms affect mainly the skin and tissue beneath it. Systemic sclerosis can also affect blood vessels, joints, and organs such as the esophagus, lungs, heart, and kidneys, sometimes causing serious problems. Its cause is not fully known.

topics.name: Sclerosing Cholangitis
topics.clinical_significance: Sclerosing cholangitis is long-term inflammation and scarring that narrow the bile ducts inside and outside the liver, slowing the flow of bile. It can cause itching and jaundice and may progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, or bile duct cancer. It may occur without a known cause or result from another disease, infection, or injury.

topics.name: Scorpion Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Most scorpion stings cause immediate pain, tingling or numbness, and little swelling. Some species have dangerous venom that can cause muscle spasms, unusual eye or head movements, sweating, drooling, agitation, or changes in heart rate and blood pressure. Severe illness is more likely in children and can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Scraping
topics.clinical_significance: Scraping (gua sha) is a practice in which a dull tool is rubbed over oiled or wet skin, often on the back, neck, or limbs. It has been studied for problems such as chronic back pain, headaches, and perimenopausal symptoms, but the evidence is limited and more reliable studies are needed. The practice commonly causes bruising.

topics.name: Screening for Sports Participation
topics.clinical_significance: Before sports participation, screening uses a health and family history and physical examination to look for conditions—especially heart problems—that could make intense exercise risky. Further tests may be needed if there are concerning symptoms or findings. Screening cannot detect every problem, and recommendations for ECG testing vary by country.

topics.name: Screening Tests for Infants, Children, and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Screening during well-child care can find health problems before symptoms appear. Depending on age and risk, tests may check hearing, vision, anemia, lead exposure, tuberculosis, or sexually transmitted infections. Which tests are needed and when depends on the child’s age, risk factors, and local recommendations.

topics.name: Screening Tests for Newborns
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn screening uses blood tests, hearing tests, oxygen checks, and bilirubin assessment to find serious conditions that may not cause symptoms at first. Early detection can allow prompt treatment and prevent death or long-term harm. The exact conditions screened for vary by region.

topics.name: Scrotal Mass, Painless
topics.clinical_significance: A painless scrotal lump is often due to a benign cause, such as a hydrocele, hernia, or varicocele, but it can also be testicular cancer. A firm lump in or attached to the testicle needs prompt evaluation, usually with ultrasound, because early recognition of testicular cancer is important.

topics.name: Scrotal Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Scrotal pain can be caused by testicular torsion, infection, injury, or a hernia. Sudden, severe pain may mean the testicle has twisted and lost its blood supply; this is an emergency because prompt treatment may save the testicle. Other serious causes also need rapid assessment.

topics.name: Scrub Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Scrub typhus is an infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by bites from infected chigger mites, mainly in the Asia-Pacific region. It causes sudden fever, chills, severe headache, and swollen lymph nodes; a dark scab (eschar) may form at the bite site, and a rash may follow. Severe illness can affect the lungs, heart, or brain and lower blood pressure.

topics.name: Scurvy
topics.clinical_significance: Scurvy is severe vitamin C deficiency, which disrupts collagen formation and weakens blood vessels and connective tissue. It can cause fatigue, swollen or bleeding gums, easy bruising, anemia, and poor wound healing. In children, it can also impair bone growth.

topics.name: Sea Urchin Stings
topics.clinical_significance: Sea urchin spines can pierce the skin and break off. Retained spines may move deeper and cause a firm inflammatory lump, or injure nearby bone or nerves; pain and skin irritation can also occur. Rare species can inject venom.

topics.name: Seal Worm Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Seal worm disease (anisakiasis) is infection with roundworm larvae from eating raw or undercooked saltwater fish or squid. The larvae burrow into the stomach or intestine, causing abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Intestinal infection can form an inflammatory mass that resembles appendicitis or Crohn disease.

topics.name: Seasickness
topics.clinical_significance: Seasickness is motion sickness caused by movement on a ship. It commonly causes nausea and may also cause vomiting, dizziness, pale skin, sweating, and abdominal discomfort. Prolonged vomiting can rarely lead to dehydration and low blood pressure.

topics.name: Seasonal Allergic Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is an allergic inflammation of the eye surface triggered by airborne pollen or mold spores. It causes itchy, red, watery eyes, sometimes with eyelid swelling or stringy discharge, and tends to recur during particular seasons.

topics.name: Seborrheic Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common inflammation of skin areas rich in oil glands, especially the scalp and face. It causes dandruff or greasy yellow scaling and may itch. It can be more severe in people with HIV or certain neurologic disorders; in infants, it may cause cradle cap.

topics.name: Seborrheic Keratoses
topics.clinical_significance: Seborrheic keratoses are common, benign skin growths, especially in older adults. They look waxy, scaly, or rough and seem stuck onto the skin; they are not precancerous. A sudden increase in many lesions can be a Leser-Trélat sign associated with internal cancer, but the sign is not specific.

topics.name: Second Trimester Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Vaginal bleeding from 20 weeks of pregnancy until birth may be a small blood-streaked mucus discharge as labor begins, or it may signal a serious problem such as placental abruption or placenta previa. These problems can threaten the pregnant person or fetus; in vasa previa, even a small amount of bleeding can cause severe fetal blood loss. Visible bleeding may be slight despite major internal blood loss.

topics.name: Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary adrenal insufficiency occurs when too little ACTH from the pituitary (or, less often, the hypothalamus) reduces cortisol production; long-term glucocorticoid use can also suppress this system. It causes fatigue, weakness, weight loss, nausea, and sometimes vomiting. Aldosterone is usually preserved, so high potassium and skin darkening are uncommon; severe cortisol deficiency can lead to adrenal crisis.

topics.name: Secondary Aldosteronism
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary aldosteronism is excess aldosterone production driven by increased renin, often because the kidneys receive too little blood flow. It can occur with renal artery disease, heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome. It may cause high blood pressure and, when potassium is low, weakness, tingling, cramps, or rarely temporary paralysis; swelling may occur with some causes.

topics.name: Secondary and Atypical Parkinsonism
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary and atypical parkinsonism cause movement problems like Parkinson disease, including slowness, stiffness, resting tremor, and poor balance. Secondary parkinsonism can result from medicines, toxins, stroke, or other brain disorders; atypical parkinsonism is caused by other degenerative brain diseases and often has additional neurologic problems. Atypical forms usually respond less well to levodopa and have a poorer outlook, while secondary symptoms may improve if their cause is treated.

topics.name: Secondary Erythrocytosis
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary erythrocytosis is an increase in red blood cells caused by low tissue oxygen or excess erythropoietin, which stimulates red cell production. Causes include chronic lung or heart problems, smoking, high altitude, some tumors, and certain medicines. Unlike polycythemia vera, it usually affects only red blood cells; it may cause headache, blurred vision, breathlessness, fatigue, or weakness.

topics.name: Secondary Hemochromatosis
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary hemochromatosis is acquired iron overload, often caused by repeated blood transfusions or disorders that prevent normal red blood cell production. Excess iron can build up in the liver, heart, and hormone-producing organs, causing liver disease, heart muscle damage, diabetes, joint problems, or reduced sexual function.

topics.name: Secondary Iron Overload
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary iron overload is excess iron that builds up from repeated transfusions, excess iron absorption or intake, or some disorders of blood cell production. If iron accumulates in organs, it can cause liver disease and cirrhosis, heart muscle damage or heart failure, diabetes, joint disease, and problems with sexual function. It is also called secondary hemochromatosis.

topics.name: Secondary Polycythemia
topics.clinical_significance: Secondary polycythemia, also called secondary erythrocytosis, is an increase in red blood cells caused by low tissue oxygen or excess erythropoietin. It usually affects red blood cells alone, unlike polycythemia vera, which often also raises white blood cells and platelets. It may cause headache, blurred vision, breathlessness, fatigue, or weakness, but some people have no symptoms.

topics.name: Secretory Otitis Media
topics.clinical_significance: Secretory otitis media (otitis media with effusion) is noninfected fluid behind the eardrum, often after an ear infection or a blocked eustachian tube. It can cause a feeling of fullness and temporary hearing loss; persistent hearing loss in young children may affect language development. Persistent fluid in adults can sometimes result from a growth blocking the eustachian tube.

topics.name: Sedatives
topics.clinical_significance: Sedatives are medicines that reduce alertness and anxiety or help cause sleep; examples include benzodiazepines and barbiturates. High doses can cause severe drowsiness, poor coordination, confusion, slowed breathing, coma, or death. Long-term use can cause dependence, and sudden withdrawal can cause agitation and seizures.

topics.name: Seizure Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A seizure is a sudden episode of abnormal electrical activity in the brain that disrupts brain function, causing changes in awareness, sensation, movement, or behavior. Epilepsy is a chronic seizure disorder defined by at least 2 unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart; a single seizure, especially one caused by a temporary illness or trigger, does not by itself mean epilepsy.

topics.name: Seizure Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Seizure disorders in pregnancy can affect both the pregnant person and fetus. Uncontrolled seizures may cause injury and are linked with higher risks of preeclampsia, poor fetal growth, and stillbirth; some antiseizure medicines also raise the risk of birth defects. Drug levels can change during pregnancy, so seizure control and medicine exposure both affect outcomes.

topics.name: Seizure Disorders, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal seizures are abnormal electrical discharges in a newborn’s brain, often caused by oxygen deprivation, stroke or bleeding in the brain, infection, or a metabolic problem. They may be hard to recognize and can appear as repeated small movements, unusual eye movements, changes in muscle tone, or changes in breathing or heart rate. The long-term outlook depends on the cause and ranges from normal development to developmental delay, intellectual disability, or epilepsy.

topics.name: Seizures, Drug Treatment of
topics.clinical_significance: Antiseizure medicines help prevent seizures, but the best choice depends on seizure type because no single medicine works for all types, and some can worsen certain seizures. Many people gain control with one medicine; seizures that continue despite adequate trials of two medicines are considered drug-resistant and may be evaluated for surgery. A single seizure caused by a temporary problem may not need long-term medicine.

topics.name: Selective Antibody Deficiency With Normal Immunoglobulins (SADNI)
topics.clinical_significance: Selective antibody deficiency with normal immunoglobulins (SADNI) is an immune disorder in which total antibody levels are normal, but the body makes too few antibodies against certain sugar molecules on bacteria while responding normally to protein antigens. It can lead to repeated sinus and lung infections, and sometimes allergy symptoms such as asthma or chronic rhinitis. Severity varies, and the disorder may resolve in some young children.

topics.name: Selective IgA Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Selective IgA deficiency is very low or absent immunoglobulin A (IgA) despite normal IgG and IgM levels. Many people have no symptoms, while others have repeated sinus, lung, or intestinal infections, allergies, or autoimmune disease. Rarely, antibodies against IgA can cause a severe allergic reaction to blood products containing IgA.

topics.name: Selective Pituitary Hormone Deficiencies
topics.clinical_significance: Selective pituitary hormone deficiency is loss of one or a few pituitary hormones while other pituitary functions remain. Effects depend on the hormone and may include poor growth, delayed puberty or infertility, low thyroid or cortisol levels, or inability to produce breast milk. It may be an early stage of broader pituitary failure and can occur with a pituitary tumor.

topics.name: Selenium Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Selenium deficiency is rare but can occur with very low intake or long-term intravenous feeding. It may cause muscle pain and tenderness; severe deficiency can increase the risk of Keshan disease, a heart muscle disorder, and Kashin-Beck joint and bone disease in growing children. Together with iodine deficiency, it may contribute to goiter and an underactive thyroid.

topics.name: Selenium Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Selenium toxicity results from taking in too much selenium, often from supplements. High intake (over 900 micrograms a day) can cause nausea or diarrhea, hair loss, brittle or abnormal nails, skin rash, tiredness, irritability, nerve problems, and garlic-smelling breath.

topics.name: Self–Neglect in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Self-neglect is when an older adult cannot or does not meet basic needs, such as getting enough food, maintaining hygiene and a safe home, or taking needed medicines and seeking medical care. It can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, untreated illness, or harm from unsafe living conditions. Memory or judgment problems, severe depression, chronic illness, and social isolation can increase risk. It can be hard to distinguish self-neglect from informed choices about how to live.

topics.name: Senile Macular Degeneration
topics.clinical_significance: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD), formerly called senile macular degeneration, damages the macula and causes painless loss or distortion of central vision, while side vision is usually preserved. Dry AMD usually progresses slowly; wet AMD can cause rapid, severe vision loss from abnormal blood vessels and bleeding under the retina. AMD is a leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults.

topics.name: Senile Purpura
topics.clinical_significance: Senile purpura is easy bruising on the backs of the hands and forearms in older adults, caused by fragile blood vessels and thinning skin from aging, sun damage, or some medicines. The purple patches fade over days but may leave brown marks. It is usually harmless and does not signal serious bleeding elsewhere.

topics.name: Separation Anxiety and Stranger Anxiety
topics.clinical_significance: Separation anxiety (distress when a caregiver leaves) and stranger anxiety (fear of unfamiliar people) are normal parts of infant development. They usually begin around 8 to 9 months; separation anxiety is strongest at 10 to 18 months, and both usually ease by age 2. Fear that is unusually intense or lasts much longer may signal an anxiety problem, especially if it interferes with a child’s development or daily activities.

topics.name: Separation Anxiety Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Separation anxiety disorder is an intense, persistent fear of being apart from a main caregiver that is not appropriate for the person’s age. In children, it may cause school refusal, excessive worry that the caregiver will be harmed, refusal to sleep alone, or headaches and stomachaches. Symptoms last at least 4 weeks and cause significant distress or interfere with daily activities; this differs from normal separation anxiety in infants.

topics.name: Sepsis and Septic Shock
topics.clinical_significance: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an abnormal, harmful response to infection. Septic shock is a severe form in which blood pressure remains dangerously low after fluid treatment, medicines are needed to raise it, and blood lactate is high, showing poor tissue perfusion. Both can quickly cause failure of several organs and death.

topics.name: Sepsis, Neonatal
topics.clinical_significance: Neonatal sepsis is an invasive infection, usually bacterial, during the first 28 days of life. Early-onset infection (within 3 days of birth) is usually acquired during birth; later infection is often acquired from the environment. Signs may be subtle, including poor feeding, reduced activity, unstable temperature, pauses in breathing, or breathing difficulty. The infection can spread to the brain coverings or cause shock and organ failure.

topics.name: Sepsis Neonatorum
topics.clinical_significance: Sepsis neonatorum is another name for neonatal sepsis: an invasive, usually bacterial infection during a newborn’s first 28 days. Early signs may be subtle, such as poor feeding, low activity, unstable temperature, or pauses or difficulty in breathing. The infection can spread to the brain coverings or lead to shock and organ failure.

topics.name: Septal Deviation and Perforation
topics.clinical_significance: A deviated nasal septum is common and often causes no symptoms. If it blocks airflow, it can cause nasal blockage, sinus infections, nosebleeds, or worsen obstructive sleep apnea. A hole in the septum (perforation) may cause crusting, repeated nosebleeds, or a whistling sound; causes include surgery, injury, drug or spray use, toxic exposure, and some infections or inflammatory diseases.

topics.name: Septic Abortion
topics.clinical_significance: Septic abortion is a serious infection of the uterus during or shortly before or after a miscarriage or induced abortion. Fever, chills, vaginal discharge, bleeding, or severe pelvic or abdominal pain may develop, often within 24 to 48 hours. The infection can spread and cause peritonitis, septic shock, and organ failure.

topics.name: Septo-Optic Dysplasia
topics.clinical_significance: Septo-optic dysplasia is a condition present from birth involving underdevelopment of the optic nerves and pituitary gland, often with an absent or abnormal septum pellucidum, a membrane in the brain. It can cause reduced vision or abnormal eye movements, pituitary hormone deficiencies, seizures, and developmental or learning difficulties.

topics.name: Sequelae of Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Cancer and its spread can cause pain, weight loss, fatigue, or blockage of organs. Spread to bones, nerves, or the spinal cord can cause pain or neurologic problems. Cancer can also raise the risk of blood clots and cause metabolic or immune-related problems; advanced disease may lead to organ failure.

topics.name: Seronegative Spondyloarthritides
topics.clinical_significance: Seronegative spondyloarthritides are a group of inflammatory joint diseases in which the rheumatoid factor blood test is usually negative. They can cause inflammatory back pain and arthritis, and may be linked with eye inflammation (uveitis), bowel symptoms, or skin rashes. Examples include ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

topics.name: Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Seronegative spondyloarthropathies are a group of inflammatory joint diseases in which the rheumatoid factor blood test is usually negative. They can cause inflammatory back pain and arthritis, and may be linked with eye inflammation (uveitis), bowel symptoms, or skin rashes. Examples include ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

topics.name: Serotonin Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Serotonin syndrome is a potentially life-threatening reaction to excessive serotonin activity, usually related to medicines and often triggered by a drug interaction or dose change. It can cause agitation or confusion, sweating and fever, and muscle twitching, tremor, stiffness, or overactive reflexes. Severe cases may cause seizures, muscle breakdown, kidney injury, or abnormal clotting.

topics.name: Sesamoiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Sesamoiditis is pain in the small sesamoid bones beneath the big toe joint, with or without inflammation or fracture. Pain often worsens when walking or bearing weight, especially in thin-soled or high-heeled shoes. It is common in dancers, runners, and people with high-arched feet or bunions.

topics.name: Sever Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Sever disease (calcaneal apophysitis) causes pain where the heel bone’s growth area joins the rest of the bone, before growth is complete. It usually affects active children aged 9 to 14 and causes pain along the sides of the heel, worse with running or standing on tiptoe. Symptoms may last for months but usually resolve as the heel matures.

topics.name: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)
topics.clinical_significance: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of inherited disorders in which T-cell immunity is absent or severely reduced, and B-cell function is also impaired. Infants are highly vulnerable to serious and unusual infections, often developing persistent infections, diarrhea, and poor growth in the first months of life. Without early diagnosis and treatment, SCID is usually fatal during infancy.

topics.name: Sever's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Sever’s disease (calcaneal apophysitis) causes pain where the heel bone’s growth area joins the rest of the bone, before growth is complete. It usually affects active children aged 9 to 14 and causes pain along the sides of the heel, worse with running or standing on tiptoe. Symptoms may last for months but usually resolve as the heel matures.

topics.name: Sex Chromosome Abnormalities, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Sex chromosome abnormalities are changes in the number or structure of the X or Y chromosomes, including extra or missing chromosome material or a mixture of cell patterns. Their effects vary widely: some people have few noticeable signs, while others have differences in growth, development, or fertility. Some abnormalities are not recognized until childhood or puberty.

topics.name: Sexual Dysfunction, Male
topics.clinical_significance: Male sexual dysfunction is a problem with sexual desire, erection, ejaculation, or orgasm that interferes with interest in or ability to have sex. It may result from physical or psychological conditions or from medicines.

topics.name: Sexual Function and Dysfunction, Female, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Female sexual dysfunction refers to distressing problems with sexual desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain during sexual activity. Several factors may contribute, including physical or emotional health, relationships, and medicines; more than one problem may occur at the same time.

topics.name: Sexual Function, Male, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Male sexual function includes sexual desire, erection, ejaculation, and orgasm. A problem with any of these that interferes with sexual interest or the ability to have intercourse is sexual dysfunction. Physical or psychological conditions and medicines may contribute.

topics.name: Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Female sexual interest/arousal disorder involves a marked loss or decrease in at least three areas of sexual interest or arousal, such as sexual thoughts, initiation, pleasure, or response to stimulation. For diagnosis, the symptoms last at least 6 months and cause significant distress. Health conditions, medicines, and emotional or relationship factors may contribute.

topics.name: Sexual Masochism Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Sexual masochism disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from being humiliated, bound, beaten, or made to suffer. The pattern must last at least 6 months and cause significant distress or problems in daily life. A consensual masochistic interest by itself is not a disorder.

topics.name: Sexual Sadism Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Sexual sadism disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from another person’s physical or emotional suffering. The pattern must last at least 6 months and cause significant distress or problems in daily life, or the person must act on the urges with someone who has not consented. Consensual sexual practices alone are not a disorder.

topics.name: Sexuality and Gender in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Adolescence is a time of sexual development and, for many, exploration of sexual orientation and gender identity. Supportive, open discussion can help teens build healthy relationships, understand contraception and sexually transmitted infection prevention, and recognize coercion or abuse. Some may face distress or bullying related to identity and need support.

topics.name: Sexuality, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Sexuality includes physical, emotional, and social aspects of sexual feelings, identity, and relationships. Consensual, nonharmful sexual behavior is not a medical disorder; care may be helpful when sexual difficulties cause distress or behavior causes harm. Nonjudgmental sexual health care can address safety, contraception, sexually transmitted infections, and sexual concerns.

topics.name: Sexually Transmitted Enteric Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Enteric infections can spread during sexual contact when fecal matter reaches the mouth, especially with oral-anal contact. They may cause diarrhea, fever, bloating, nausea, or abdominal pain, but some infections have no symptoms.

topics.name: Sexually Transmitted Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections spread through oral, anal, or genital sexual contact by body fluids or skin contact; the term sexually transmitted disease (STD) refers to illness caused by an STI. Many STIs cause no symptoms, while others cause sores, discharge, itching, or pain with urination or sex. Testing can detect infections without symptoms, and diagnosis and treatment help reduce complications and spread to partners.

topics.name: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
topics.clinical_significance: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections spread through oral, anal, or genital sexual contact by body fluids or skin contact; the term sexually transmitted disease (STD) refers to illness caused by an STI. Many STIs cause no symptoms, while others cause sores, discharge, itching, or pain with urination or sex. Testing can detect infections without symptoms, and diagnosis and treatment help reduce complications and spread to partners.

topics.name: Sheep Liver Fluke Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Sheep liver fluke infection (fascioliasis) is acquired by eating watercress or other aquatic plants contaminated with fluke larvae. As the parasites migrate through the liver, they may cause abdominal pain, an enlarged liver, fever, nausea, or high levels of eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. Later bile-duct infection can cause recurring pain, inflammation, blockage, or pancreatitis.

topics.name: Shigellosis
topics.clinical_significance: Shigellosis is a highly contagious infection of the intestine caused by Shigella bacteria, usually spread by fecal-oral contact. It causes diarrhea, abdominal cramps, urgency to pass stool, and sometimes fever; stools may become bloody or contain mucus. Severe illness can cause dehydration, and a toxin-producing strain can rarely cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome.

topics.name: Shin Bone Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Shin bone fever is another name for trench fever, a body-louse-borne infection caused by Bartonella quintana. It causes sudden fever that may recur, severe shin and leg pain, headache, and weakness; a rash may occur. Infection can persist or relapse and may sometimes lead to endocarditis.

topics.name: Shin Splints
topics.clinical_significance: Shin splints is a general term for lower-leg pain during running sports, often caused by repeated impact that overloads muscles and tendons around the shin. Pain may begin when exercise starts and ease as activity continues. Sometimes a specific cause, such as a tibial stress fracture or exercise-induced compartment syndrome, is present; often the exact cause is unclear.

topics.name: Shingles
topics.clinical_significance: Shingles is reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a sensory nerve, causing pain followed by a one-sided blistering rash in the area supplied by that nerve. Rash near the eye can lead to severe eye disease and needs prompt evaluation; ear involvement can cause facial weakness or vertigo. Some people, especially older adults, have nerve pain for months or longer after the rash heals (postherpetic neuralgia).

topics.name: Shingles Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The recombinant shingles vaccine helps prevent shingles and its complications, including long-lasting nerve pain (postherpetic neuralgia). The MSD Manual recommends 2 doses, 2 to 6 months apart, for adults aged 50 years or older and adults aged 19 years or older who are or will be immunocompromised.

topics.name: Shock
topics.clinical_significance: Shock is a life-threatening state in which circulatory failure reduces blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues, causing cell and organ injury. Causes include severe blood or fluid loss, heart failure, blocked blood flow, and widespread blood-vessel dilation, as in sepsis or a severe allergic reaction. Signs may include confusion, a rapid pulse or breathing, low urine output, and cool, clammy skin; blood pressure may still be normal early on. Shock requires immediate treatment.

topics.name: Shock and Fluid Resuscitation
topics.clinical_significance: Shock and fluid resuscitation covers emergency treatment to restore blood flow to tissues during circulatory failure. Intravenous fluids are often used for hypovolemic and distributive shock, including septic shock, but are usually avoided in cardiogenic or obstructive shock because they can worsen the condition. Severe bleeding may require blood products, and treatment is guided by the cause and response.

topics.name: Shock Liver
topics.clinical_significance: Shock liver (ischemic hepatitis) is widespread liver injury caused by too little blood flow or oxygen. It often follows heart failure, a sudden drop in blood pressure, respiratory failure, or sepsis and can cause nausea, vomiting, or a tender enlarged liver with very high liver enzyme levels. Liver function usually recovers when blood flow and oxygen supply improve, but liver failure can occur, especially in people with cirrhosis.

topics.name: Short Bowel Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Short bowel syndrome is poor absorption of nutrients, fluids, and electrolytes after extensive removal of the small intestine, usually more than two-thirds of its length. It can cause severe diarrhea, dehydration, and nutritional deficiencies. People with very little small intestine remaining may need long-term intravenous nutrition.

topics.name: Short QT Interval Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: Short QT interval syndromes are rare, usually congenital heart-channel disorders that shorten the QT interval on an electrocardiogram (ECG). They can cause atrial fibrillation or dangerous ventricular arrhythmias, leading to palpitations, fainting, cardiac arrest, or sudden death. Some affected people have no symptoms.

topics.name: Short-Lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform Headache With Conjunctival Injection and Tearing (SUNCT)
topics.clinical_significance: SUNCT is a rare headache disorder that causes many brief attacks of one-sided pain, usually around an eye, with eye redness and tearing on that side. Because other conditions can cause similar pain, imaging may be used to check for another cause.

topics.name: Shoulder Dislocation Reduction Techniques, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Shoulder reduction techniques put a dislocated shoulder joint back in place to relieve pain and restore function. The dislocation or the procedure can injure nerves or blood vessels, so clinicians check nerve and blood flow before and after reduction and reduce the joint promptly. No single method works for every case.

topics.name: Shoulder Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: A shoulder dislocation occurs when the upper arm bone comes out of its socket; most dislocations are toward the front. It causes pain and limits arm movement, and may also injure nerves, blood vessels, bone, or the rotator cuff. Repeat dislocations are common in younger people.

topics.name: Shoulder Dystocia
topics.clinical_significance: Shoulder dystocia occurs when the baby’s head is delivered during vaginal birth but a shoulder becomes stuck, preventing delivery of the body. It is an obstetric emergency: prompt maneuvers are needed because it can cause nerve or bone injury or lack of oxygen in the baby, and heavy bleeding or tears in the mother.

topics.name: Shoulder Fracture
topics.clinical_significance: A proximal humerus fracture breaks the upper arm bone near the shoulder, often after a fall and especially in older adults. It causes pain, swelling, and difficulty raising the arm. Most are treated with a sling and early movement; some displaced fractures need surgery. Rarely, nerves or blood vessels are injured, and keeping the shoulder still too long can cause stiffness.

topics.name: Shoulder Separation
topics.clinical_significance: A shoulder separation is a sprain of the joint between the collarbone and the top of the shoulder blade, usually after a fall onto the shoulder. It causes pain and tenderness at the joint; severe ligament tears can shift the collarbone out of place. Most injuries are treated with a sling and early movement, but some severe cases need surgery.

topics.name: Sialadenitis
topics.clinical_significance: Sialadenitis is inflammation or infection of a salivary gland. It causes painful, tender swelling, often on one side, and may cause fever or pus from the gland’s duct. Low saliva flow, a blocked duct or stone, infection, and autoimmune disease can contribute; an abscess may form.

topics.name: Sialolithiasis
topics.clinical_significance: A salivary stone is a hardened mineral deposit that can block a salivary duct, most often under the jaw. The blockage causes pain and swelling, especially during meals, and may ease when saliva drains. Repeated blockage can lead to gland infection, and some stones need removal.

topics.name: Sick Sinus Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sick sinus syndrome is a problem with the heart’s natural pacemaker. It can cause an abnormally slow heartbeat, pauses, or alternating slow and fast rhythms. Some people have no symptoms; others may feel tired, dizzy, faint, or notice palpitations. If symptoms are due to the rhythm and no reversible cause is found, a pacemaker may be needed.

topics.name: Sickle Cell Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder in which abnormal hemoglobin makes red blood cells fragile and rigid. The cells break down, causing chronic anemia, and can block blood flow, causing severe pain and organ damage. Serious complications include infection, stroke, and acute chest syndrome.

topics.name: Sideroblastic Anemias
topics.clinical_significance: Sideroblastic anemias are disorders in which developing red blood cells cannot use iron properly to make hemoglobin. This causes anemia even when iron is available, and iron may build up in the body. Causes may be inherited or acquired, including marrow disease, some medicines, alcohol, toxins, or vitamin and mineral deficiencies.

topics.name: Sideropenic Dysphagia
topics.clinical_significance: Sideropenic dysphagia refers to trouble swallowing solid food because of a thin membrane (web) in the upper esophagus, classically with severe iron-deficiency anemia (Plummer–Vinson syndrome). Treating the anemia may help the web; a web that persists can be widened during endoscopy.

topics.name: Silent Lymphocytic Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Silent lymphocytic thyroiditis is a painless autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid, often occurring after childbirth. It may first cause a temporary overactive thyroid, then an underactive thyroid. Most people recover, but some develop lasting hypothyroidism and need thyroid hormone replacement; the condition can recur after later pregnancies.

topics.name: Silicosis
topics.clinical_significance: Silicosis is permanent lung scarring caused by breathing crystalline silica dust, usually at work. It may develop slowly and progress to severe breathing problems. It also increases the risk of tuberculosis, COPD, and lung cancer.

topics.name: Silymarin
topics.clinical_significance: Silymarin is an extract from milk thistle seeds sold as a dietary supplement and often promoted for liver disease, but studies have not shown clear overall benefit. It may cause stomach upset or allergic reactions and can interact with warfarin and blood-sugar medicines.

topics.name: Simple Nontoxic Goiter
topics.clinical_significance: A simple nontoxic goiter is a noncancerous enlargement of the thyroid, usually with normal thyroid function and no inflammation. It often causes no symptoms, but a large goiter can cause throat fullness, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing or breathing. Causes include iodine deficiency and some medicines, but are often unknown.

topics.name: Simple Pneumothorax
topics.clinical_significance: A simple pneumothorax is air around a lung without major pressure shift or circulatory problems. It can cause chest pain and shortness of breath. Positive-pressure ventilation can turn it into a life-threatening tension pneumothorax. Small, stable cases may be watched, while larger or symptomatic cases often need a chest tube.

topics.name: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome is an overuse injury where the patellar tendon attaches to the lower tip of the kneecap, usually in active children ages 10 to 13. It causes pain that worsens with jumping, running, climbing stairs, or bending the knee. Activity changes and physical therapy usually help.

topics.name: Single-Gene Defects
topics.clinical_significance: Single-gene disorders result from a disease-causing change in one gene and may follow dominant, recessive, or X-linked inheritance patterns. Knowing the pattern helps estimate who in a family may be affected or carry the gene change, and the chance of passing it to children; genetic testing and counseling can guide family planning.

topics.name: Singultus
topics.clinical_significance: Singultus (hiccups) are repeated involuntary spasms of the diaphragm followed by brief closure of the voice box, making a sound. Short episodes are common and usually harmless. Hiccups lasting more than 2 days are uncommon and may need medical evaluation because they can be linked to an underlying problem.

topics.name: Sinus Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Paranasal sinus cancer is rare and may grow for a long time before causing symptoms, so it is often found late. It can cause nasal blockage or discharge, nosebleeds, facial pain or numbness, loose upper teeth, or double vision. Earlier diagnosis improves the chance of a better outcome.

topics.name: Sinus Histiocytosis With Massive Lymphadenopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy (Rosai–Dorfman disease) is a rare disorder in which immune cells build up, usually causing large, painless lymph nodes in the neck and sometimes fever. Other organs can be affected, but the disease often resolves without treatment; progressive cases may need treatment.

topics.name: Sinus Node Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Sinus node dysfunction (sick sinus syndrome) is a problem with the heart’s natural pacemaker. It can cause a slow heartbeat, pauses, or alternating slow and fast rhythms. Some people have no symptoms; others may feel weak or tired, have trouble exercising, feel dizzy or faint, or notice palpitations. If symptoms are due to the rhythm and no reversible cause is found, a pacemaker may be needed.

topics.name: Sinusitis
topics.clinical_significance: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, often with inflammation inside the nose. Most acute cases are viral; allergies, bacteria, or fungi can also cause it. Symptoms include nasal blockage or discharge, facial pain or pressure, headache, and reduced smell. Acute sinusitis lasts less than 4 weeks; chronic sinusitis lasts more than 12 weeks. Antibiotics are used when bacterial infection is likely, not for most viral cases.

topics.name: Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome is injury and blockage of tiny channels and small veins in the liver. It can follow stem-cell transplant, radiation, some cancer drugs, or exposure to certain toxins or herbal products. It may cause sudden jaundice, a painful enlarged liver, and fluid in the abdomen; severe cases can lead to liver failure.

topics.name: SIPE
topics.clinical_significance: SIPE (swimming-induced pulmonary edema) is sudden fluid buildup in the lungs during swimming or diving. It can cause severe shortness of breath, cough, and low blood oxygen; severe cases can be fatal. It may recur, so people who have had SIPE should be checked for underlying heart or lung problems before returning to swimming or diving.

topics.name: Sipple Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sipple syndrome is another name for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A), an inherited condition caused by a RET gene change. It carries a high risk of medullary thyroid cancer and can also cause adrenal tumors (pheochromocytomas) and overactive parathyroid glands. Genetic testing and screening of relatives can help find tumors early and guide preventive care.

topics.name: Sixth Cranial Nerve (Abducens) Palsy
topics.clinical_significance: A sixth nerve palsy weakens the muscle that moves an eye outward. The eye may turn inward, causing horizontal double vision, especially when looking toward the affected side. Small-vessel disease is a common cause, but the palsy can also signal increased pressure in the skull, infection, stroke, or a tumor, so the cause needs medical evaluation. Many palsies caused by small-vessel disease or an unknown cause improve within about 2 months.

topics.name: Sjögren Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sjögren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease that reduces tear and saliva production, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. It can also affect joints, lungs, kidneys, nerves, and other organs, and it greatly increases the relative risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, although lymphoma remains uncommon.

topics.name: Sjögren's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sjögren’s syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease that reduces tear and saliva production, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. It can also affect joints, lungs, kidneys, nerves, and other organs, and greatly increases the relative risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, although lymphoma remains uncommon.

topics.name: Skene Gland Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: A Skene gland cyst forms beside the urethral opening when the gland’s duct is blocked. Most are small and cause no symptoms, but a larger cyst can cause pain with sex or painful urination and, rarely, block urine flow. Infection can lead to an abscess or recurrent urinary tract infections.

topics.name: Skene's Gland Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: A Skene gland cyst forms beside the urethral opening when the gland’s duct is blocked. Most are small and cause no symptoms, but a larger cyst can cause pain with sex or painful urination and, rarely, block urine flow. Infection can lead to an abscess or recurrent urinary tract infections.

topics.name: Skier's Thumb
topics.clinical_significance: Skier’s thumb is a sprain or tear of the ligament on the inner side of the thumb’s main joint, often when the thumb is forced away from the hand. It causes pain and tenderness and can weaken pinch or grip. A severe tear may make the joint unstable or pull off a small bone fragment; treatment often uses a thumb splint, while lasting instability may need surgery.

topics.name: Skilled Nursing Facilities
topics.clinical_significance: Skilled nursing facilities provide nursing care, rehabilitation, and help with daily needs for people who need more support than they can get at home. They may offer short-term care after an illness or injury or long-term care. Residents are at risk of loss of function, poor nutrition, pressure injuries, infections, and other problems; attentive care can prevent some of them.

topics.name: Skin Cancer, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Skin cancer is common and includes basal cell and squamous cell cancers and melanoma. It often appears as a skin lesion that does not go away or that grows, hurts, or bleeds; such lesions need medical assessment and may need biopsy. Most skin cancers can be cured when found and treated early. Limiting ultraviolet (UV) exposure lowers risk.

topics.name: Skin, Cancers of
topics.clinical_significance: Skin cancers are common and include basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and rarer types. Basal cell carcinoma usually grows slowly and rarely spreads, but can damage nearby tissue; some other skin cancers can spread to other parts of the body. A skin spot that grows, bleeds, or does not heal should be checked; biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, and early treatment can often cure the cancer. Sun protection lowers the risk of many skin cancers.

topics.name: Skin Care of the Residual Limb
topics.clinical_significance: Skin under a prosthetic socket can break down from pressure, rubbing, or moisture and may become infected. Pain, redness, sores, or discharge are warning signs; reduced sensation can hide early problems. Daily skin checks, good hygiene, and a well-fitting socket help prevent injury, and persistent or unusual changes need medical review.

topics.name: Skin Disorders, Diagnostic Tests for
topics.clinical_significance: When a skin problem cannot be identified from the history and examination alone, targeted tests can help find its cause. Depending on the suspected condition, tests may include a skin biopsy, scraping, culture, Wood light examination, or allergy testing; the results help confirm a diagnosis and guide treatment.

topics.name: Skin Infections, Bacterial, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial skin infections range from small sores and abscesses to deeper infections such as cellulitis or a dangerous infection that destroys tissue. Staphylococcus and Streptococcus bacteria are common causes; antibiotic choice may depend on local resistance, including MRSA. Fever, confusion, a fast heartbeat, or rapid worsening can signal a severe infection that needs urgent medical care.

topics.name: Skin Lesions, Description
topics.clinical_significance: Describing a skin lesion by its type, shape, size, texture, color, and location gives clinicians a clear, shared record of what they see. These features can help narrow the possible causes and guide testing, though appearance alone may not confirm the diagnosis.

topics.name: Skin Manifestations of Internal Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Some skin changes can be clues to disease elsewhere in the body, including diabetes, thyroid or digestive disease, and sometimes cancer. The type, pattern, and timing of the skin change can guide further assessment, but most findings are not specific enough to diagnose an internal illness on their own.

topics.name: Skin Tags
topics.clinical_significance: Skin tags are common, soft, harmless growths, usually on the neck, armpits, or groin. They usually cause no symptoms but can become irritated. Having many skin tags may be linked to insulin resistance, so a clinician may consider checking for it; tags can be removed if they are bothersome.

topics.name: Skull Base Osteomyelitis
topics.clinical_significance: Skull base osteomyelitis is a serious infection that can spread from the ear canal into the bone at the base of the skull. It mainly affects older people and those with diabetes or weakened immunity. Deep, persistent ear pain and discharge need prompt medical assessment because the infection can damage nerves and, rarely, spread inside the skull. Treatment usually requires a long course of antibiotics.

topics.name: Slapped-Cheek Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Slapped-cheek disease (fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19 and is usually a mild illness in children, with red cheeks and a lacy rash on the arms, legs, or trunk. The virus can cause severe anemia in people with sickle cell disease or other blood disorders, and in people with weakened immunity. Infection during pregnancy can cause severe fetal anemia, pregnancy loss, or stillbirth; most otherwise healthy children need only symptom relief.

topics.name: Sleep and Wakefulness Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Sleep and wakefulness disorders can cause difficulty sleeping at night or excessive sleepiness during the day. They may affect mood, memory, alertness, and daily performance, and can increase the risk of accidents. They can also be caused or worsened by medical conditions, mental health problems, medicines, or disrupted schedules.

topics.name: Sleep and Wakefulness Disorders, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Assessment starts with questions about sleep times, awakenings, naps, daytime sleepiness, medicines, and health or mood problems. This can help identify the cause and decide whether a sleep test is needed. Falling asleep while driving, repeated sudden sleep attacks, or witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep are warning signs that need prompt medical attention.

topics.name: Sleep Apnea
topics.clinical_significance: Sleep apnea causes repeated pauses or shallow breathing during sleep. In obstructive sleep apnea, the airway closes; in central sleep apnea, the brain briefly fails to signal the muscles to breathe. These episodes interrupt sleep and may lower oxygen. Obstructive sleep apnea may cause loud snoring, gasping, or daytime sleepiness; if untreated, it raises the risk of high blood pressure, heart problems, and accidents from sleepiness. Sleep testing confirms the diagnosis.

topics.name: Sleep Problems in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Many sleep problems in children, such as occasional night waking, nightmares, night terrors, or sleepwalking, are temporary and need no treatment. Persistent or severe problems may need assessment; snoring with restless sleep can be a sign of obstructive sleep apnea. Infants should sleep in the same room as a caregiver but on a separate sleep surface to lower the risk of sleep-related death.

topics.name: Sleeping Behaviors in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: Infants usually develop a day-night sleep pattern by 4 to 6 months. Night waking and bedtime difficulty are often linked to age, routines, or stress; a steady bedtime routine and learning to fall asleep without being held may help. For safer sleep, place infants on their backs on a separate sleep surface in the caregiver’s room, rather than sharing a bed, to lower the risk of sleep-related death.

topics.name: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)
topics.clinical_significance: SCFE is a growth-plate injury in which the top of the thighbone slips at the hip, usually in adolescents; obesity is an important risk factor. It can cause hip, thigh, or knee pain and a limp, so knee pain may come from the hip. The slip can worsen and damage the blood supply to the bone. Keep weight off the affected leg and arrange urgent assessment, imaging, and surgical treatment.

topics.name: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)
topics.clinical_significance: SIBO occurs when too many bacteria grow in the small intestine, often because of altered anatomy or slow movement of intestinal contents. It can cause bloating, abdominal discomfort, gas, and diarrhea; severe or long-lasting overgrowth can cause fat malabsorption, vitamin B12 deficiency, and undernutrition. Breath tests or a small-bowel fluid culture can help confirm it; treatment uses antibiotics and addresses underlying problems and nutrient deficiencies.

topics.name: Small-Bowel Transplantation
topics.clinical_significance: Small-bowel transplantation is a rare option for life-threatening intestinal failure, especially when complications of long-term intravenous nutrition develop. It can restore intestinal function but has major risks, including rejection and serious infection. Recipients need ongoing medicines to prevent rejection and regular endoscopic checks of the transplanted bowel.

topics.name: Small-Bowel Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Small-bowel tumors are uncommon and may cause few symptoms at first. They can cause abdominal pain, bleeding, diarrhea, or bowel blockage; some cancerous tumors, especially neuroendocrine tumors, can spread to the liver. Unexplained bleeding or ongoing abdominal symptoms may need imaging or endoscopy, and treatment often involves removing the tumor.

topics.name: Small-for-Gestational-Age (SGA) Infant
topics.clinical_significance: An SGA newborn weighs below the 10th percentile for gestational age. Some are healthy and simply small; others had poor growth before birth. They need monitoring for low blood sugar, low body temperature, excess red blood cells, infection, and birth-related problems such as low oxygen or inhaling meconium. Care treats any underlying cause or complication.

topics.name: Smallpox
topics.clinical_significance: Smallpox is a highly contagious disease caused by variola virus. Classic smallpox caused severe illness and a widespread pustular rash, with a death rate of about 30%; a milder form was less often fatal. Natural spread has been eradicated, but suspected cases would be a public health emergency and require immediate isolation and notification of public health authorities.

topics.name: Smell and Taste Abnormalities, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Smell and taste are closely linked, so a problem with one can make food seem bland or taste different. Infections, nose or mouth problems, medicines, and aging can affect these senses; ongoing changes may reduce appetite and lead to poor nutrition. Loss of smell can also make it hard to notice smoke or gas, and sudden changes should be medically assessed.

topics.name: Smith Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A Smith fracture is an uncommon break near the wrist end of the radius in which the broken part shifts toward the palm, usually after a fall on a bent wrist. It causes wrist pain, swelling, and deformity and may injure the median nerve, causing numbness or thumb weakness. X-rays guide care; the bone usually needs to be realigned and splinted, and some fractures need surgery.

topics.name: Smoke Inhalation
topics.clinical_significance: Smoke inhalation can burn or irritate the airways and expose a person to toxic gases such as carbon monoxide or cyanide. Airway swelling may worsen over several hours and block breathing; lung injury can also appear later. After a fire, breathing trouble, confusion, soot in the sputum, or burns around the mouth or nose call for emergency care because early oxygen and airway support may be lifesaving.

topics.name: Smoking Cessation
topics.clinical_significance: Nicotine cravings and withdrawal make quitting difficult. Symptoms such as irritability, low mood, poor concentration, and trouble sleeping are often strongest in the first few days; most ease within 2 to 4 weeks, though cravings may last longer. Counseling combined with medicine, such as nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion, improves the chance of quitting; follow-up and repeated attempts may be needed.

topics.name: Snakebites
topics.clinical_significance: Venomous snakebites can cause severe swelling and tissue damage, bleeding or clotting problems, shock, or nerve effects that weaken breathing. Symptoms may be delayed, and some bites inject no venom, so an uncertain bite still needs prompt medical assessment and observation. Serious envenomation may require antivenom; do not cut the wound or apply a tourniquet.

topics.name: Snoring
topics.clinical_significance: Snoring is a common sound caused by soft tissues in the upper airway vibrating during sleep. It may disturb a bed partner, and many people who snore do not have sleep apnea. Loud, frequent snoring with breathing pauses, gasping or choking, morning headaches, or daytime sleepiness should be assessed for obstructive sleep apnea; snoring alone has no known harmful effects.

topics.name: Social Anxiety Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Social anxiety disorder causes a strong, persistent fear of being watched, judged, or embarrassed in social or performance situations. The fear lasts at least 6 months and leads a person to avoid these situations or face them with great distress, which can interfere with school, work, relationships, or daily life. Cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure therapy, can help; medicines are sometimes used.

topics.name: Social Anxiety Disorder in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and teens, a lasting fear of being embarrassed or judged by others can lead to avoiding school, class presentations, parties, or eating with others. It may show as crying, freezing, clinging, withdrawal, or repeated stomachaches or headaches; the fear must last at least 6 months and disrupt daily life to meet diagnostic criteria. Behavioral therapy is the main treatment, and an SSRI may be used in some cases.

topics.name: Social Issues in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Social conditions can affect an older adult’s health and access to suitable care. Reviewing living arrangements, social support, daily needs, finances, and caregiver capacity can reveal unmet care needs, isolation, or caregiver strain.

topics.name: Social Phobia
topics.clinical_significance: Persistent fear of being judged or embarrassed can lead to avoiding social situations and cause distress or problems at school, work, or in relationships. In children, it may also appear as school refusal or physical complaints such as stomachaches or headaches.

topics.name: Sodium Oxybate
topics.clinical_significance: Sodium oxybate is the prescription form of gamma-hydroxybutyrate used to treat narcolepsy. Misuse can cause severe sleepiness, poor coordination, vomiting, coma, or slowed breathing, especially with alcohol or other sedatives. Repeated use can cause dependence, and withdrawal can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Soft Fibromas
topics.clinical_significance: Skin tags are usually harmless but may become irritated by rubbing. Multiple skin tags can be associated with insulin resistance, so they may signal a need to consider metabolic risk.

topics.name: Solid Foods in Infancy
topics.clinical_significance: Solid foods add nutrients such as iron as infants grow and learn to handle thicker textures. They are usually started when an infant is ready, around 6 months and not before 4 months. Safe food texture helps prevent choking; honey before age 1 can cause botulism, and early introduction of allergenic foods can lower food-allergy risk.

topics.name: Solitary Pulmonary Nodule
topics.clinical_significance: Many solitary lung nodules are benign, but cancer and active infection must be considered. The chance of cancer depends on features such as size, shape, and growth, as well as age, smoking, and cancer history. Comparison with earlier scans and follow-up imaging help assess the risk and whether biopsy is needed.

topics.name: Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Repeated straining or rectal prolapse can injure the rectal lining, causing difficulty emptying the bowel and sometimes bleeding or mucus. The lesions may resemble other rectal disorders, so endoscopy and sometimes biopsy help confirm the diagnosis and check for prolapse.

topics.name: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders can cause distress, repeated health care visits, and problems with daily life. Physical symptoms are not necessarily imagined or intentionally produced, and a medical illness can coexist. New or changing symptoms still need appropriate medical evaluation.

topics.name: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders in Children
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders can cause real, distressing symptoms that interfere with a child’s school, family life, and daily activities; symptoms are not necessarily made up, and physical illness can coexist. Medical evaluation is important at first presentation and when symptoms change, while unnecessary repeated tests can add distress.

topics.name: Somatic Symptom Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Physical symptoms may or may not have a medical cause and are not intentionally produced. The disorder involves excessive worry, fear, or time spent on symptoms that causes distress or disrupts daily life. A medical illness can coexist, so new or clearly changing symptoms still need assessment.

topics.name: Somatization, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Somatization presents psychological processes as physical symptoms and often leads people to seek medical care. Symptoms may be involuntary, as in somatic symptom disorders, or intentionally produced in factitious disorder; malingering involves external gain and is a separate behavior. Distinguishing these patterns helps prevent mislabeling and supports appropriate assessment.

topics.name: Sore Throat
topics.clinical_significance: Most sore throats are caused by viral infections, but group A streptococcal infection can cause serious complications. Rare throat abscesses and epiglottitis can threaten the airway; drooling, breathing difficulty, noisy breathing, or a muffled voice are warning signs.

topics.name: Sparganosis
topics.clinical_significance: The larvae usually form slowly growing masses under the skin or in muscle. Rarely, they affect the brain or spinal cord, causing neurologic symptoms or seizures. Symptomatic masses are usually removed surgically; antiparasitic drugs are generally ineffective.

topics.name: Spasmodic Dysphonia
topics.clinical_significance: Spasms of the laryngeal muscles interrupt the voice during speech, causing a strained, squeezed voice or sudden breaks with air leakage. This can make speaking difficult and impair communication; the voice pattern depends on which muscles are affected.

topics.name: Spasmodic Torticollis
topics.clinical_significance: Involuntary neck-muscle contractions cause a painful, twisted or tilted head position and may cause tremor. Symptoms often worsen gradually before leveling off and can interfere with daily activities.

topics.name: Specific Cardiac Arrhythmias
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiac arrhythmias range from harmless extra beats to emergencies that disrupt blood flow or cause cardiac arrest. Atrial fibrillation can cause clots and stroke; very slow rhythms may cause fainting, and dangerous ventricular rhythms can lead to sudden death.

topics.name: Specific Phobias
topics.clinical_significance: Intense fear can cause avoidance, panic symptoms, and problems at work, school, or in daily life, especially when the feared situation is hard to avoid. Fear of needles may also cause a vasovagal reaction or lead someone to avoid needed medical procedures.

topics.name: Spectinomycin
topics.clinical_significance: Spectinomycin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that acts against gonorrhea bacteria. Where available, it is reserved for selected patients who cannot be treated with ceftriaxone; it does not work for gonorrhea in the throat.

topics.name: Speech Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Speech therapy helps people with language or speech problems communicate through exercises or communication aids, and can help restore a voice after laryngectomy. Speech-language pathologists also assess and treat swallowing problems.

topics.name: Sperm Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Sperm disorders can contribute to male infertility by reducing sperm number or quality or by blocking sperm release. A semen analysis helps identify problems, and finding the cause can guide treatment or assisted reproduction. Reduced sperm number or quality does not always prevent pregnancy.

topics.name: Spider Angioma
topics.clinical_significance: One or a few spider angiomas are common and harmless. Many prominent lesions can occur with liver disease, especially cirrhosis; they may also appear during pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use and often fade after pregnancy or stopping the medicine.

topics.name: Spider Bites
topics.clinical_significance: Most spider bites cause only local symptoms. Brown recluse bites can damage skin and rarely cause serious illness throughout the body; widow spider venom can cause severe muscle cramps and other widespread symptoms. Many suspected spider bites are misidentified, so other causes, especially skin infections, must be considered.

topics.name: Spider Nevus
topics.clinical_significance: One or a few spider nevi are common and harmless. Many prominent lesions can occur with liver disease, especially cirrhosis; they may also appear during pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use and often fade after pregnancy or stopping the medicine.

topics.name: Spina Bifida
topics.clinical_significance: Effects range from no symptoms to weakness or paralysis and loss of feeling below the spinal defect. More severe forms can affect bladder and bowel control, cause orthopedic problems or hydrocephalus, and lead to kidney damage from bladder dysfunction.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs)
topics.clinical_significance: These abnormal blood-vessel connections can compress the spinal cord, reduce its blood supply, or bleed. They may cause radiating pain and neurologic problems that worsen gradually or come and go. Rupture can cause sudden severe back pain and abrupt neurologic problems; rarely, it causes bleeding around the brain.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Autonomic Dysreflexia
topics.clinical_significance: After a spinal cord injury above T6, a stimulus below the injury—often a full bladder or bowel—can trigger sudden, dangerous high blood pressure, headache, flushing, and sweating. This can lead to brain bleeding, seizures, heart attack, or death, making autonomic dysreflexia a medical emergency.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Compression
topics.clinical_significance: Pressure on the spinal cord can cause back or radiating nerve pain, weakness, numbness, abnormal reflexes, and loss of bladder or bowel control. Acute compression can lead to sudden, sometimes irreversible loss of function, so new neurologic symptoms with spinal pain require immediate assessment.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Spinal cord disorders can cause weakness or paralysis, changes in sensation and reflexes, and loss of bladder, bowel, or sexual function. Some lead to permanent disability, but rapid diagnosis and treatment can limit damage, especially when symptoms begin suddenly.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Spinal cord disorders can affect movement, sensation, reflexes, and automatic functions such as bladder and bowel control; the pattern depends on the part of the cord involved. Sudden neurologic symptoms require emergency evaluation because rapid diagnosis and treatment may prevent permanent disability. MRI is the most accurate imaging test.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Infarction
topics.clinical_significance: Loss of blood flow to the spinal cord can cause sudden severe back pain, followed within minutes by weakness in both limbs and loss of sensation, especially for pain and temperature. Some neurologic problems may partly improve after the first few days, but the sudden onset requires urgent assessment.

topics.name: Spinal Cord Injury in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Children may injure the spinal cord without a visible bone injury on imaging, and weakness, tingling, or other neurologic signs may be delayed for hours or days. Because most childhood spinal injuries affect the neck, even brief neurologic symptoms after trauma can signal a serious injury and need prompt assessment.

topics.name: Spinal Epidural Abscess
topics.clinical_significance: An abscess in the space around the spinal cord can compress the cord or nerve roots, causing weakness, numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control. These problems can worsen over hours or days. Severe unexplained back pain, especially with fever or focal spinal tenderness, calls for urgent imaging even before neurologic symptoms appear.

topics.name: Spinal Muscular Atrophies (SMAs)
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited motor neuron disorders cause progressive muscle weakness and wasting. Severe early-onset forms can impair swallowing and breathing and may be fatal, while milder forms progress more slowly. Genetic testing confirms the type, and disease-modifying treatments can improve movement or delay disability and death.

topics.name: Spinal Stenosis, Cervical
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing can compress cervical nerve roots or the spinal cord. It may cause neck or arm pain and tingling; spinal cord compression can impair hand coordination and balance and cause weakness or stiffness in the limbs. Deficits from advanced cord damage may not fully reverse.

topics.name: Spinal Stenosis, Lumbar
topics.clinical_significance: Narrowing can compress the lower spinal nerve roots, causing back, buttock, thigh, or calf pain when standing or walking; sitting or bending forward often eases it. Numbness or weakness may also occur. Rarely, severe compression causes cauda equina syndrome, with numbness around the groin and loss of bladder or bowel control.

topics.name: Spinal Subdural or Epidural Hematoma
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding in the spinal canal can rapidly compress the spinal cord or nerve roots, causing severe back or radiating pain followed by leg weakness or paralysis that can worsen within minutes to hours. It is a neurologic emergency, especially after trauma or in people with a bleeding disorder or taking blood thinners.

topics.name: Spinal Tap
topics.clinical_significance: A spinal tap (lumbar puncture) samples cerebrospinal fluid to help diagnose infections, bleeding, and other neurologic conditions; it can also measure or lower pressure and deliver medicines. It may cause a post-procedure headache and can be unsafe when a mass or blocked fluid flow creates a risk of brain herniation.

topics.name: Spinal Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Spinal trauma can injure the vertebrae, ligaments, spinal cord, or spinal nerves. Cord injury may cause weakness or paralysis, loss of sensation, and problems controlling breathing, blood pressure, or bladder and bowel function, depending on its level and severity. Unstable injuries can worsen and cause lasting disability; prompt recognition helps prevent further damage.

topics.name: Spinal Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Spinal tumors may arise in the spinal cord or nearby tissues; tumors outside the dura are often metastases from cancers elsewhere. They can cause worsening back or radiating pain and compress the spinal cord or nerve roots, leading to weakness, sensory loss, or bladder and bowel problems. Cord compression can progress quickly and cause permanent disability.

topics.name: Spirochetes
topics.clinical_significance: Spirochetes are spiral-shaped bacteria; pathogenic genera include Treponema, Borrelia, and Leptospira. They cause infections such as syphilis, Lyme disease, relapsing fever, and leptospirosis. Depending on the infection, disease can affect the skin, joints, nervous system, heart, kidneys, or liver.

topics.name: Spleen Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Spleen disorders can affect blood filtering and immune defense. An enlarged spleen may trap and destroy blood cells, causing low red-cell, white-cell, or platelet counts. Injury can cause splenic rupture and severe bleeding. Loss or failure of spleen function increases the risk of serious infection, especially from encapsulated bacteria.

topics.name: Spleen, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The spleen helps fight blood-borne infections and filters old or damaged red blood cells. If it is absent or does not work, the risk of severe infection rises, especially from pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. Loss of spleen function can also allow abnormal red-cell remnants to remain in the blood.

topics.name: Splenic Injury
topics.clinical_significance: Splenic injury, often caused by blunt abdominal trauma, can lead to bleeding inside the abdomen. Severe bleeding may cause hemorrhagic shock, and a blood-filled hematoma may rupture later. An enlarged spleen can rupture after minor trauma. If the spleen must be removed, the risk of severe bacterial infection rises.

topics.name: Splenomegaly
topics.clinical_significance: Usually caused by another condition, such as infection, liver disease, a blood disorder, or cancer, splenomegaly may cause no symptoms or lead to early fullness and upper-left abdominal discomfort. An enlarged spleen can trap and destroy blood cells, causing low blood-cell counts (hypersplenism), and is more vulnerable to rupture, especially after trauma.

topics.name: Spondylolisthesis
topics.clinical_significance: Spondylolisthesis is slippage of one vertebra relative to the one below; forward slippage is more common than backward slippage. It often affects the lower back and may cause no symptoms or pain with prolonged standing or walking. It can narrow the openings for spinal nerves, but mild to moderate cases are usually stable.

topics.name: Spontaneous Abortion
topics.clinical_significance: Spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of gestation. It often causes crampy pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding, although bleeding in early pregnancy does not always mean pregnancy loss. Retained pregnancy tissue can cause continued bleeding or infection. Early losses are often linked to chromosomal abnormalities, but the cause is frequently unknown.

topics.name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
topics.clinical_significance: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is infection of ascitic fluid without a clear source, most often in people with cirrhosis. It may cause fever, diffuse abdominal discomfort, confusion, or worsening liver function, but signs can be mild. It can lead to sepsis, kidney failure, and death.

topics.name: Sporadic Fatal Insomnia
topics.clinical_significance: Sporadic fatal insomnia is a very rare prion disease that occurs without a disease-causing PRNP gene mutation. It causes rapidly worsening thinking and coordination; sleep disruption may be found on a sleep study even when sleep problems are not reported. The disease is fatal, and treatment is supportive.

topics.name: Sporotrichosis
topics.clinical_significance: Sporotrichosis is a skin infection caused by Sporothrix fungi, usually entering through a small break in the skin after contact with plants, soil, or infected cats. It often forms nodules that spread along lymph channels and may ulcerate. Rarely, infection spreads to the lungs, joints, or other organs, especially in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Sports and the Heart
topics.clinical_significance: Regular exercise benefits heart health, but intensive training can enlarge and thicken the heart and slow the resting heart rate; these normal changes can resemble heart disease. More rarely, exercise can trigger dangerous heart rhythms or sudden cardiac death in people with underlying heart disease. Screening helps identify athletes who may need further heart evaluation.

topics.name: Sports Injuries, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: Sports injuries result from repeated stress or sudden trauma and range from sprains and strains to fractures, dislocations, and concussion. Pain is typical; swelling, bruising, instability, or limited movement may also occur. Recognizing the type and severity of injury helps identify damage that needs specific care and supports safe recovery.

topics.name: Sports Injury
topics.clinical_significance: A sports injury is physical damage sustained during sport or exercise, caused by repeated stress or a sudden event. It may affect muscles, tendons, ligaments, cartilage, or bone, and range from overuse injuries to contusions, sprains, strains, fractures, dislocations, or concussion. Pain is typical; swelling, bruising, or limited movement may also occur.

topics.name: Sports Participation, Screening
topics.clinical_significance: Screening before sports aims to identify heart and other health conditions that may raise risk during activity. It uses medical and family history and a physical exam, with ECG or other tests selected when findings are concerning. Screening can miss disease or produce false alarms, so a normal result does not rule out all risk. Significant findings may affect sports participation.

topics.name: Sports-Related Concussion
topics.clinical_significance: A sports-related concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury that disrupts brain function; loss of consciousness is not required, and routine imaging may show no structural injury. Headache, confusion, memory problems, dizziness, or poor balance may follow and can persist. A repeat impact before recovery can cause severe brain swelling, and repeated concussions are associated with long-term brain disease.

topics.name: Spotted Fever
