topics.clinical_significance: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. It causes sudden high fever, severe headache, and muscle aches; a rash often appears later and may be absent. The infection damages small blood vessels and can injure the brain, lungs, heart, kidneys, or other organs. Delayed treatment increases the risk of severe illness and death.

topics.name: Spotted Fever Rickettsioses, Other
topics.clinical_significance: Other spotted fever rickettsioses are tick-borne infections caused by several Rickettsia species. They can cause fever, headache, a small sore at the bite site (eschar), nearby swollen lymph nodes, and a rash. Most are milder than Rocky Mountain spotted fever, but severe blood-vessel inflammation can occur; complications are more likely in older or debilitated people.

topics.name: Sprains and Other Soft-Tissue Injuries
topics.clinical_significance: Sprains are tears in ligaments, strains are tears in muscles, and tendons can also tear. These injuries cause pain and may limit movement; fractures or dislocations can occur at the same time. Severe tears can leave a joint unstable or cause lasting loss of function. Rarely, damage to blood vessels, nerves, or tissue pressure can threaten the limb.

topics.name: Sprains and Other Soft-Tissue Injuries, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Sprains are ligament tears, strains are muscle tears, and tendons can partly or completely rupture. Severity ranges from stretched fibers to complete tears, which may limit movement or make a joint unstable. Many partial tears heal, but severe injuries can cause lasting loss of function. Fractures, dislocations, and rare nerve or blood-vessel injuries may occur at the same time.

topics.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is a skin cancer of epidermal keratinocytes, often on sun-exposed skin. It may appear as a persistent scaly, crusted, or ulcerated sore or a firm nodule and can invade nearby tissue. Spread to lymph nodes or distant sites is uncommon but possible, especially in high-risk tumors.

topics.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Situ
topics.clinical_significance: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) consists of abnormal squamous cells confined to the epidermis, with no invasion into the deeper dermis. It often appears as a red-brown, scaly or crusted patch, commonly on sun-exposed skin. It is noninvasive but can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma; biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

topics.name: St. John’s Wort
topics.clinical_significance: St. John’s wort (Hypericum perforatum) is a herbal supplement that may help mild-to-moderate depression, but evidence varies by preparation. It can cause photosensitivity, dizziness, and other side effects, and has serious interactions with many medicines; some, including hormonal contraceptives, HIV drugs, cyclosporine, and anticoagulants, may become less effective. It can trigger mania in people with bipolar disorder.

topics.name: Stable Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Stable angina is predictable chest pressure or discomfort from temporary reduced blood flow to the heart, usually triggered by exertion or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. It signals heart muscle ischemia without heart muscle death. New, worsening, prolonged, or resting symptoms may indicate acute coronary syndrome.

topics.name: Staphylococcal Food Poisoning
topics.clinical_significance: This food poisoning is caused by a toxin already made by Staphylococcus aureus in contaminated food. Sudden nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and often diarrhea usually start within 30 minutes to 8 hours and improve within a day. Treatment is fluids to prevent or treat dehydration; antibiotics do not help.

topics.name: Staphylococcal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Staphylococci, especially Staphylococcus aureus, can cause skin abscesses and serious infections of the blood, lungs, bones, joints, or heart valves. Some strains release toxins that cause severe illness. Antibiotic resistance, including MRSA, is common, so cultures help guide treatment; abscesses may need drainage and infected devices may need removal.

topics.name: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A toxin from Staphylococcus aureus causes widespread superficial blisters and peeling, mainly in infants and young children. It usually spares the mouth and other moist linings, which helps distinguish it from some severe drug reactions. The damaged skin can cause fluid loss and infection, so prompt antibiotics and careful skin care are important; illness can be especially severe in adults.

topics.name: Stasis Dermatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Stasis dermatitis is an itchy, scaly rash on chronically swollen lower legs, often caused by poor blood flow back through the veins. The skin may become red or brown, ooze, or break down into ulcers that can become infected. Care focuses on reducing the swelling and protecting the skin; leg elevation and compression are often used when appropriate.

topics.name: Steele-Richardson-Olszewski Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome is another name for progressive supranuclear palsy, a disorder that gradually damages parts of the brain. It can cause difficulty looking up or down, stiffness, slowed movement, and early balance problems with falls; swallowing and thinking may worsen over time. Care focuses on symptoms, mobility, and safety.

topics.name: Steinert Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Steinert disease, or myotonic dystrophy type 1, is an inherited disorder in which muscles relax slowly and gradually weaken. It often affects the face, hands, and feet, and may also cause heart rhythm, breathing, swallowing, eye, or hormone problems. Heart and breathing complications can be serious, so ongoing medical follow-up is important.

topics.name: Stein-Leventhal Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Stein-Leventhal syndrome is an older name for polycystic ovary syndrome, now also called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome. The diagnosis is based on at least two of three findings: excess androgen effects (such as acne or extra facial hair), irregular ovulation, and polycystic-appearing ovaries. It can make pregnancy harder and is linked to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic problems.

topics.name: Stenosing Flexor Tenosynovitis
topics.clinical_significance: Stenosing flexor tenosynovitis (trigger finger) occurs when a swollen finger tendon catches as it moves through its sheath. It can cause palm pain and a finger that clicks, locks in a bent position, or suddenly snaps straight. It is more common in people with diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis; persistent symptoms may need an injection or surgery.

topics.name: Sterilization
topics.clinical_significance: In contraception, sterilization means a procedure intended to prevent pregnancy permanently, such as vasectomy or blocking or removing the fallopian tubes. It is highly effective but should be considered permanent. After vasectomy, another method is needed until testing confirms that no sperm remain in the semen. In infection control, sterilization instead means destroying all microbes, including spores, on equipment or materials.

topics.name: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)
topics.clinical_significance: SJS and TEN are severe reactions, usually to a medicine, that cause a painful rash, blisters, skin peeling, and sores in the mouth, eyes, or other moist linings. They are classified by how much skin is affected: under 10% of body surface area is SJS, over 30% is TEN, and 10% to 30% is overlap. These are medical emergencies that need hospital care and stopping the suspected cause; complications can include infection, fluid loss, eye damage, and death.

topics.name: Stiff-Man Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Stiff-man syndrome, now more often called stiff-person syndrome, is a rare disorder of the brain and spinal cord that causes gradually worsening muscle stiffness and spasms, usually starting in the trunk and abdomen. It is often linked to an autoimmune condition, such as type 1 diabetes, and can lead to disability. Treatment focuses on reducing stiffness and spasms.

topics.name: Stiff-Person Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare disorder of the brain and spinal cord that causes gradually worsening stiffness and muscle spasms, usually starting in the trunk and abdomen. It is often autoimmune and may occur with type 1 diabetes or other autoimmune diseases. It can spread and cause major disability; treatment aims to ease stiffness and spasms.

topics.name: Stillbirth
topics.clinical_significance: Stillbirth means death of a fetus before or during birth at 20 weeks of pregnancy or later in the United States; the World Health Organization uses a threshold after 28 weeks. Causes may involve the pregnant person, placenta, or fetus, but many cases remain unexplained. A previous stillbirth increases the risk of fetal death in a later pregnancy.

topics.name: Stingray Stings
topics.clinical_significance: A stingray’s venomous tail spine can cause a deep, jagged wound with sudden severe pain, bleeding, tissue damage, and risk of infection. Rarely, venom causes severe whole-body symptoms, breathing problems, or death; a wound to the chest or abdomen can injure internal organs. Medical care is needed to check for spine fragments and clean the wound.

topics.name: Stomach Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Stomach cancer is a malignant growth in the stomach; most cases are adenocarcinoma. Early symptoms may be vague, so the cancer is often found after it has spread; Helicobacter pylori infection is an important risk factor. Diagnosis requires endoscopy and biopsy, and treatment and outlook depend on how far the cancer has spread.

topics.name: Stomatitis
topics.clinical_significance: Stomatitis is painful inflammation of the mouth lining, causing redness, swelling, or ulcers; it may be mild or widespread. Causes include infection, injury or irritation, medicines, cancer treatment, or another illness, though many cases have no clear cause. Pain can make eating and drinking difficult, leading to dehydration or poor nutrition.

topics.name: Stomatocytosis and Anemia Caused by Hypophosphatemia
topics.clinical_significance: This topic covers two red blood cell problems that can cause anemia from early cell breakdown. In stomatocytosis, red blood cells have a slitlike center; the condition may be inherited or acquired and may cause no symptoms or anemia. Severe low phosphate makes red blood cells less flexible and more likely to break down; correcting the low phosphate can prevent or reverse this anemia.

topics.name: Stones
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary stones are hard deposits that form in the kidneys or elsewhere in the urinary tract. Some pass without symptoms; others cause severe side or back pain, blood in the urine, nausea, or blockage. A blocked stone can lead to infection, and fever or chills may signal this complication. Risk is increased by concentrated urine and some metabolic conditions.

topics.name: Stool Incontinence in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Stool incontinence (encopresis) is passing stool outside the toilet in a child older than 4 years, or at a similar developmental level. It is usually involuntary leakage around stool retained because of constipation, not misbehavior. It needs care because it can distress the child and family; treatment of constipation and ongoing bowel and toilet support often help, though recovery may take time.

topics.name: Strabismus
topics.clinical_significance: Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes, so they do not look in the same direction. It may cause double vision; in children, the brain may ignore the image from one eye, leading to amblyopia (reduced vision) and lasting vision loss if untreated. It is often related to focusing problems or eye-muscle imbalance, but can rarely signal a serious eye or nerve problem.

topics.name: Streptococcal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Streptococci cause infections ranging from strep throat and skin infections to pneumonia, blood infection, or heart valve infection. Group A strep can sometimes lead later to rheumatic fever or kidney inflammation, while severe invasive infection can cause shock. Testing helps identify the species or group so treatment can be chosen for the infection site.

topics.name: Stress Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Stress fractures are small, incomplete breaks caused by repeated weight-bearing stress, most often in the foot or lower leg. Pain starts with activity and may gradually begin earlier, worsen, or continue at rest. Early x-rays can be normal. Deep groin or thigh pain with weight-bearing may signal a femur stress fracture; fractures in the femur or pelvis can also point to weak bones.

topics.name: Stridor
topics.clinical_significance: Stridor is a high-pitched breathing sound, usually heard while breathing in, caused by narrowing or blockage of the upper airway. It can result from acute problems such as croup, an inhaled object, or an allergic reaction, or from longer-term airway or vocal-cord problems. Sudden or severe stridor can signal life-threatening airway blockage and needs urgent assessment, especially with breathing difficulty, drooling, bluish skin, or reduced alertness.

topics.name: Stroke
topics.clinical_significance: A stroke is sudden brain injury caused by a blocked blood vessel or bleeding in the brain. It can cause sudden weakness or numbness, often on one side, trouble speaking, vision problems, dizziness, confusion, or a severe headache. It is a medical emergency: prompt treatment can limit brain damage, while a stroke may cause lasting disability or death.

topics.name: Stroke, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Stroke is sudden brain injury from a blocked brain artery (ischemic stroke) or bleeding in the brain (hemorrhagic stroke). Symptoms vary by the area affected and may include one-sided weakness or numbness, speech or vision problems, dizziness, or loss of balance. It is a medical emergency: urgent brain imaging helps identify the type because treatment differs, and faster treatment can limit damage. High blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, and some heart disorders raise risk; prevention and rehabilitation are important parts of care.

topics.name: Stroke Rehabilitation
topics.clinical_significance: Stroke rehabilitation is team-based care that begins once the person is medically stable. It aims to regain or adapt movement, speech, swallowing, thinking, and daily activities so the person can function as safely and independently as possible. Physical, occupational, and speech therapy also help prevent problems such as stiff joints, falls, pressure sores, and food or liquid entering the airway.

topics.name: Strongyloidiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Strongyloidiasis is an infection with the roundworm Strongyloides stercoralis, usually caught when larvae in contaminated soil enter through the skin. It can persist for decades because the worm can reinfect the same person; symptoms may affect the skin, lungs, or gut, or be absent. Corticosteroids and other causes of weakened immunity can trigger life-threatening spread through the body, so identifying and treating infection before immune-suppressing treatment is important.

topics.name: Sturge-Weber Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a non-inherited condition present from birth, caused by abnormal blood vessels. It classically causes a port-wine birthmark on the face; abnormal vessels may also affect the tissues covering the brain or the eye. These changes can cause seizures, weakness, learning problems, glaucoma, or stroke-like episodes, so neurologic and eye checks are important.

topics.name: Subacute and Chronic Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Meningeal inflammation that develops over days to weeks or lasts 4 weeks or longer. Causes include tuberculosis, fungal infection, cancer, and autoimmune disease. It may injure cranial nerves or cause stroke, so finding the cause is important for treatment.

topics.name: Subacute Combined Degeneration
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin B12 deficiency can damage the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. It may cause numbness, weakness, poor balance, and difficulty walking; nerve damage can become permanent if treatment is delayed.

topics.name: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, delayed brain disorder thought to result from persistent measles virus infection, appearing months to years after measles. It causes progressive loss of mental and physical function, often with muscle jerks and seizures, and is usually fatal.

topics.name: Subacute Spongiform Encephalopathy
topics.clinical_significance: A prion disease, usually called Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, that causes rapidly worsening dementia, involuntary jerks, and poor coordination. It is usually fatal within months to a few years and has no cure. Instruments exposed to nervous tissue need special handling because routine sterilization may not destroy prions.

topics.name: Subacute Thyroiditis
topics.clinical_significance: Usually follows a viral illness and causes fever with pain and tenderness over the thyroid. Release of stored thyroid hormone can cause a temporary hyperthyroid phase, sometimes followed by temporary hypothyroidism. It usually resolves within months, though rarely thyroid underactivity persists.

topics.name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding into the space around the brain; most spontaneous cases are caused by a ruptured aneurysm. A sudden, severe headache that peaks within seconds is a medical emergency. The bleeding can cause loss of consciousness, stroke, seizures, or hydrocephalus and may be fatal.

topics.name: Subcapital Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A fracture through the femoral neck just below the femoral head, common in older adults after a fall. It can disrupt blood flow to the femoral head, causing bone death or failure to heal. Some impacted fractures are hard to see on X-rays, so further imaging may be needed if suspicion remains.

topics.name: Subconjunctival Hemorrhages
topics.clinical_significance: A patch of blood beneath the conjunctiva, often after minor trauma, coughing, or straining. It usually causes no pain or vision change and clears on its own within 1 to 3 weeks. Associated eye injury or a bleeding disorder needs assessment.

topics.name: Subdermal Contraceptive Implants
topics.clinical_significance: A small progestin-releasing rod placed under the skin that provides highly effective contraception for several years. Irregular bleeding is common, and some medicines can reduce its effectiveness. Fertility can return quickly after removal.

topics.name: Submandibular Space Infection
topics.clinical_significance: A rapidly spreading infection of the tissues under the tongue and jaw, usually starting from an infected lower molar. Swelling can lift the tongue and block the airway within hours, making this a medical emergency that needs immediate airway care and antibiotics.

topics.name: Substance Misuse
topics.clinical_significance: A harmful pattern of alcohol or drug use, especially when use continues despite serious problems. When diagnostic criteria are met, it is called a substance use disorder, a treatable medical condition. Screening can help identify overdose, withdrawal, and other health risks and connect people with care.

topics.name: Substance- or Medication-Induced Psychotic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Hallucinations or delusions caused by a substance, medication, or withdrawal, beyond the usual effects of intoxication and without delirium. Symptoms often improve after the cause clears but may last for weeks. Careful history and follow-up help identify the cause and distinguish it from an emerging primary psychotic illness.

topics.name: Substance Use Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A pattern of substance use that causes significant problems and continues despite them; illegal use alone does not mean a person has this disorder. It can harm health and daily life and may lead to overdose or withdrawal. Treatment is available and may include counseling, support, and medication.

topics.name: Substance Use in Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Even occasional alcohol or drug use can lead to overdose, crashes, injuries, or other risky situations. Regular use during adolescence is linked to mental health problems and poorer functioning later in life. Routine screening can identify risk early and guide age-appropriate support.

topics.name: Substance-Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: A group of conditions related to substance use or withdrawal, including use disorders, intoxication, withdrawal, and mental health symptoms. Effects range from problems with daily life to life-threatening overdose, so identifying the substance and condition guides urgent care and longer-term treatment.

topics.name: Substance-Related Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Substances can affect the brain reward system and cause intoxication, withdrawal, mental health symptoms, or a use disorder. Effects and risks vary by substance and how it is taken, so identifying what was used helps guide safe assessment and care.

topics.name: Substance-Related Psychiatric Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Substances or medicines can cause depression, anxiety, psychosis, or thinking problems during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal. Because these symptoms can resemble independent mental illnesses, clinicians check the timing, the suspected substance, and other possible causes before choosing treatment.

topics.name: Subtrochanteric Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A break in the upper thighbone below the trochanters. Hip fractures often follow a fall in older adults with weak bones and can make standing or walking difficult. Surgery and early rehabilitation help reduce serious problems from prolonged bed rest.

topics.name: Sucking Chest Wound
topics.clinical_significance: An open chest wound that lets air pass between the outside and the space around the lung; air may make a sucking sound with breathing. A large opening can impair ventilation and cause respiratory failure, so it needs immediate wound coverage and chest-tube treatment.

topics.name: Sudden Cardiac Death in Athletes
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, sudden collapse from a heart problem during exercise that may be fatal. In younger athletes, causes include inherited rhythm disorders and heart abnormalities; in older athletes, coronary artery disease is common. Rapid CPR and AED use can save lives, so screening and emergency plans are important.

topics.name: Sudden Hearing Loss
topics.clinical_significance: Moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss that develops within 72 hours, usually in one ear. It needs urgent assessment because some causes, such as infection, injury, or medication toxicity, are treatable, and early treatment may improve hearing recovery.

topics.name: Sudden Unexpected Infant Death and Brief, Resolved, Unexplained Events
topics.clinical_significance: This topic covers two distinct events: sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) and brief resolved unexplained events (BRUE). A BRUE is a brief episode in an infant under 1 year involving a change in color, breathing, muscle tone, or responsiveness, with no cause found after initial assessment. Risk assessment helps identify infants who need further evaluation; BRUE is not the same as SUID or SIDS.

topics.name: Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)
topics.clinical_significance: SUID is the broad term for a sudden, unexpected death in an infant under 1 year when the cause is not clear at first. It includes SIDS, deaths of undetermined cause, and accidental suffocation or strangulation in bed. SIDS is diagnosed only after a full medical, autopsy, and death-scene investigation finds no cause. Safe-sleep practices, including placing infants on their backs for every sleep, reduce risk.

topics.name: Suicidal Behavior
topics.clinical_significance: A range of experiences and actions, from thoughts or plans about suicide to preparatory acts and nonfatal attempts. Nonsuicidal self-injury is different but is linked to higher suicide risk. Prompt, nonjudgmental assessment and safety-focused care are important because risk can change quickly.

topics.name: Suicidal Behavior in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Suicidal thoughts, plans, or actions in a child or adolescent need prompt assessment by a trained clinician. Any attempt needs immediate crisis care and psychiatric referral. Depression, substance use, previous attempts, and family or social stress can raise risk, so warning statements and major behavior changes should be taken seriously.

topics.name: Sulfatide Lipidosis
topics.clinical_significance: Also called metachromatic leukodystrophy, this inherited disorder usually involves a deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase A. Sulfatides build up and damage myelin in the brain and peripheral nerves, causing progressive loss of movement and thinking skills. Onset and severity vary; severe early-onset forms can cause paralysis, dementia, and early death.

topics.name: Sulfonamides
topics.clinical_significance: Many sulfonamides are bacteriostatic antibiotics that block bacterial folate production; resistance is widespread. They can cause severe allergic or skin reactions, blood-cell problems, or kidney crystals. Use near delivery or in infants under 2 months can raise bilirubin and risk kernicterus.

topics.name: Sunburn
topics.clinical_significance: Skin inflammation from too much ultraviolet (UV) exposure, causing redness and pain; severe cases may blister, and widespread burns can cause fever, chills, or weakness. Sunburn increases later skin-cancer risk, so preventing further UV exposure and using sun protection are important.

topics.name: Sunlight, Chronic Effects of
topics.clinical_significance: Long-term ultraviolet (UV) exposure causes premature skin aging and actinic keratoses, which are precancerous, and raises the risk of skin cancers, including melanoma. Limiting sun and tanning-bed exposure and using protective clothing and sunscreen can reduce further damage.

topics.name: Sunlight Effects, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Ultraviolet (UV) rays from sunlight can cause sunburn and photosensitive skin reactions. Over time, UV exposure can cause early skin aging, precancerous spots, and skin cancer. Shade, protective clothing, and sunscreen help reduce damage; tanning is not safe.

topics.name: Superficial Punctate Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Superficial punctate keratitis is damage and inflammation of the cornea, the clear front of the eye. It can cause redness, tearing, a gritty feeling, light sensitivity, and slightly blurred vision. Causes include dry eye, infection, ultraviolet light, chemical injury, and contact lens overuse. Treatment depends on the cause; contact lens wearers should stop wearing them and have the eye checked.

topics.name: Superficial Venous Thrombosis
topics.clinical_significance: A clot in a vein near the skin can cause a painful, tender, warm, red, firm area along the vein. Some clots, especially those near where a leg vein joins a deep vein, can extend into deep veins and lead to a pulmonary embolism. Recurrent clots in different veins can sometimes signal an underlying cancer. Clots above the knee may need ultrasound to check for deep vein thrombosis.

topics.name: Supplemental Oxygen Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Supplemental oxygen gives extra oxygen when the blood level is too low. The amount is adjusted using oxygen measurements. People at risk of carbon dioxide buildup need close monitoring, and too much oxygen can cause harm.

topics.name: Suppurative Labyrinthitis
topics.clinical_significance: Suppurative labyrinthitis is a bacterial infection of the inner ear, often spreading from a serious middle-ear infection or meningitis. It can cause severe spinning dizziness, nausea, and hearing loss, which may be permanent. It needs urgent treatment with intravenous antibiotics and treatment of the source of infection.

topics.name: Supracondylar Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A supracondylar fracture is a break in the upper arm bone just above the elbow; it is common in children. The nearby artery and nerves can be injured, which may threaten blood flow, feeling, or movement in the hand. Prompt orthopedic assessment is important, especially for displaced fractures, and blood flow and nerve function should be checked.

topics.name: Supraglottitis
topics.clinical_significance: Supraglottitis is usually a rapidly developing bacterial infection that can swell and block the upper airway. Severe sore throat, trouble swallowing, drooling, high fever, or noisy breathing needs emergency hospital care. Examining the throat can trigger complete airway blockage, especially in children; treatment may require airway support and intravenous antibiotics.

topics.name: Supraorbital Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A supraorbital nerve block uses local anesthetic to numb one side of the forehead and front of the scalp, and sometimes the upper eyelid. It can control pain during repair of cuts or other procedures in this area without distorting the wound edges. Poor needle placement can injure the nerve or blood vessels, cause bleeding, or lead to anesthetic toxicity.

topics.name: Supratrochlear Nerve Block
topics.clinical_significance: A supratrochlear nerve block uses local anesthetic to numb the skin of the lower inner forehead and inner upper eyelid on one side. It can reduce pain during repair of cuts in this area without distorting the wound edges. Risks include bleeding, nerve irritation or injury, infection spread, and rare anesthetic toxicity.

topics.name: Supraventricular arrhythmias, ectopic
topics.clinical_significance: Ectopic supraventricular arrhythmias are abnormal heart rhythms that start in the upper chambers or nearby electrical tissue. Many cause no symptoms and need no treatment, but some cause palpitations, dizziness, or fainting. Frequent extra atrial beats are linked with higher risk of atrial fibrillation and stroke, though they may not cause these problems. A persistent fast rhythm can weaken the heart and lead to heart failure; treatment depends on the rhythm and its cause.

topics.name: Surgical Airway
topics.clinical_significance: A surgical airway creates an opening into the windpipe to move air past a blocked upper airway or when breathing support cannot be provided another way. Emergency cricothyrotomy can be lifesaving when a person cannot be intubated or ventilated; tracheostomy is used more often for long-term ventilation. Complications can include bleeding, air leaking into the chest, and lung collapse.

topics.name: Surgical Emergencies in Neonates, Miscellaneous
topics.clinical_significance: Newborn surgical emergencies include groin hernias that can trap bowel, holes in the stomach or small intestine, and rarely blocked blood flow to the intestine. A trapped hernia needs prompt surgical assessment. Sudden belly swelling or breathing trouble may signal a perforation, which needs emergency hospital care and often surgery; blocked intestinal blood flow can cause bowel death.

topics.name: Surgical Patient, Care of the
topics.clinical_significance: Care of a surgical patient includes preparation before surgery, care during the procedure, and recovery afterward. Reviewing health conditions, medicines, and surgery-related risks helps the team plan safe care. Monitoring after surgery helps detect problems such as bleeding, infection, breathing trouble, or blood clots early. Care is tailored to the procedure and the patient’s health.

topics.name: Susceptibility Testing
topics.clinical_significance: Susceptibility testing checks whether bacteria, fungi, or viruses are likely to be stopped by specific antimicrobial drugs. It helps clinicians choose treatment and detect drug resistance. A test result does not guarantee success, because drug levels at the infection site and the patient’s defenses also matter.

topics.name: Swan-Neck Deformity
topics.clinical_significance: Swan-neck deformity is a finger posture in which the middle joint bends backward and the fingertip joint bends toward the palm. It is often linked to rheumatoid arthritis, but can also follow tendon, ligament, or bone injury. The finger may not close fully, making grasping difficult; treatment targets the cause, with splints for mild cases and surgery for severe disability.

topics.name: Sweater Finger
topics.clinical_significance: Sweater finger is a tear of the tendon that bends the fingertip, often when a bent finger is pulled straight during sport. The person cannot actively bend the fingertip joint. X-rays check for a small piece of bone pulled off with the tendon; prompt repair by a hand specialist is usually needed.

topics.name: Sweating Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Sweating disorders include too much or too little sweating, blocked sweat ducts, and abnormal body odor. Sweat helps cool the body, so reduced sweating can raise the risk of overheating. Widespread excessive sweating may sometimes point to an illness or medication effect; the cause guides care.

topics.name: Sweating Disorders, Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Eccrine sweat glands cover most of the body and help cool it during heat or activity. Their disorders include excessive or reduced sweating and blocked ducts that cause heat rash. Apocrine gland disorders can cause abnormal body odor. The pattern helps identify which glands are involved and guide care.

topics.name: Sweet Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sweet syndrome causes a sudden outbreak of painful, swollen red or purple bumps or plaques, often with fever. It may be linked to infection, inflammatory illness, a medicine, or cancer; about 1 in 5 people with the condition have an underlying cancer, often a blood cancer. A skin biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis, and treatment usually includes corticosteroids and care of the underlying cause.

topics.name: Swimmer's Ear
topics.clinical_significance: Swimmer’s ear is usually a bacterial infection of the outer ear canal, often after swimming or irritation from cotton swabs. It causes ear pain, itching, and discharge; swelling can temporarily reduce hearing. Ear drops usually treat it. Rarely, especially in people with diabetes or weakened immunity, infection can spread to nearby bone and nerves.

topics.name: Swimming Pool Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Swimming pool conjunctivitis (adult inclusion conjunctivitis) is usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis acquired through sexual contact; spread from contaminated, poorly chlorinated pool water is rare. It often causes lasting redness and discharge in one eye and may occur with a genital infection. Oral antibiotics treat the eye and genital infection, and sexual partners also need treatment.

topics.name: Swimming-Induced Pulmonary Edema
topics.clinical_significance: Swimming-induced pulmonary edema is sudden fluid buildup in the lungs during swimming or diving. It can cause severe breathlessness, cough with frothy sputum, and low blood oxygen, and may be fatal. It needs immediate rescue from the water and emergency medical care, often with oxygen. It can recur, so affected people should be checked for heart, lung, and blood-pressure problems before returning to swimming or diving.

topics.name: Swine Flu
topics.clinical_significance: In people, swine flu is infection with influenza A viruses that circulate in pigs. It usually follows direct or indirect contact with infected pigs; spread from person to person is rare. Symptoms resemble seasonal flu, such as fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, headache, and muscle aches. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus had genes from swine, birds, and humans and now circulates as seasonal flu; properly cooked pork does not spread swine flu.

topics.name: Swine Influenza
topics.clinical_significance: Swine influenza is a respiratory disease of pigs caused by influenza A viruses. Some strains can infect people through direct or indirect contact with infected pigs; person-to-person spread is rare. In people, symptoms resemble seasonal flu. A history of pig exposure helps raise suspicion, and specialized testing may be needed to confirm infection; antiviral treatment is used for severe or high-risk cases.

topics.name: Sympathetic Ophthalmia
topics.clinical_significance: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare immune reaction in which penetrating injury or surgery to one eye causes inflammation inside the other eye. It often develops within weeks and can cause floaters and reduced vision, threatening sight. Prompt eye-specialist care is important; treatment usually uses corticosteroids and other medicines that suppress the immune system.

topics.name: Symptom Relief for the Dying Patient
topics.clinical_significance: Care of a dying patient aims to relieve physical, emotional, and spiritual distress, especially pain and breathlessness. Treat a reversible cause when doing so is useful and fits the patient’s goals; when tests or treatments would add burden without improving comfort, focus on symptom relief. Symptoms and medicine effects can change quickly, so care needs regular reassessment and support for the patient and family.

topics.name: Symptoms and Treatment of Specific Poisons
topics.clinical_significance: Symptoms and treatment vary with the poison, amount, and route of exposure; severe poisoning can cause organ failure or stop breathing. For anything beyond the mildest, routine exposure, contact poison control or emergency medical services promptly. Care may require poison-specific treatment, an antidote, or support for breathing and circulation.

topics.name: Symptoms During Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Many mild symptoms during pregnancy come from normal changes in the body. New, severe, or lasting symptoms may signal a complication, such as high blood pressure or infection, and should be discussed promptly with a pregnancy-care clinician. Recognizing warning signs helps protect both the pregnant person and the fetus.

topics.name: Symptoms in Infants and Children
topics.clinical_significance: In infants and children, symptoms and their risks depend on age; young children may show illness through changes in feeding, crying, activity, or breathing rather than clearly describe how they feel. A careful history and examination help identify common self-limited problems and serious illness. Warning signs such as unusual lethargy or trouble breathing need prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Symptoms, Nonspecific
topics.clinical_significance: Nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, fever, weight loss, or night sweats can occur with many different conditions, from minor to serious. Their duration, pattern, associated symptoms, and examination help narrow the cause. Persistent symptoms or warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, ongoing fever, or night sweats need medical evaluation.

topics.name: Symptoms of Cardiovascular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Cardiovascular disorders may cause chest discomfort, shortness of breath, palpitations, fainting or light-headedness, and leg swelling. These symptoms can have other causes, so their timing, triggers, associated signs, and the person’s health history help guide evaluation. New severe chest pain, breathlessness at rest, or fainting may signal an emergency.

topics.name: Symptoms of Dental and Oral Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Tooth pain, bleeding gums, bad breath, dry mouth, mouth sores, or difficulty chewing can signal dental or oral disease and may interfere with eating and speaking. Some mouth changes can also be the first sign of a wider health problem. Persistent sores or swelling, fever, or trouble swallowing need prompt dental or medical assessment.

topics.name: Symptoms of Gastrointestinal Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Gastrointestinal symptoms include abdominal pain, indigestion, trouble swallowing, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, gas, bloating, and rectal bleeding. They may be caused by digestive disease or by changes in gut movement or sensitivity, including disorders of gut-brain interaction. The symptom pattern and warning signs guide evaluation; ongoing symptoms, bleeding, trouble swallowing, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or unexplained weight loss need medical assessment.

topics.name: Symptoms of Genitourinary Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Genitourinary symptoms can include painful or frequent urination, difficulty passing urine, blood in the urine, flank or pelvic pain, genital pain or swelling, and discharge. Causes range from infections and kidney stones to urinary blockage, kidney or prostate problems, and sexually transmitted infections. The symptom pattern and tests help identify the cause. Fever with flank pain, inability to urinate, blood in the urine, or sudden severe testicular pain needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Symptoms of Gynecologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Gynecologic symptoms can include pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, changes in menstrual periods, unusual discharge, and vulvar or vaginal itching or pain. Causes range from normal changes to infection, endometriosis, fibroids, pregnancy-related problems, or cancer; age, pregnancy status, and the pattern of symptoms help guide evaluation. Sudden severe pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, fever with discharge, or any bleeding after menopause needs medical assessment.

topics.name: Symptoms of Neurologic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Neurologic symptoms can affect movement, strength, sensation, balance, speech, vision, memory, sleep, or awareness. They may result from problems in the brain, spinal cord, or nerves, and the pattern and speed of onset help guide evaluation. Sudden weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, vision loss, a seizure, or reduced alertness can signal a serious problem and should be assessed urgently.

topics.name: Symptoms of Ophthalmic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Eye symptoms can include blurred or lost vision, eye pain or redness, double vision, flashes or floaters, and discharge or itching. Causes range from common problems such as dry eye or infection to serious disease of the cornea, retina, optic nerve, or other parts of the eye. Sudden vision loss, a sudden increase in floaters or flashes, or severe eye pain can signal a serious problem; urgent assessment is needed.

topics.name: Symptoms of Pulmonary Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary symptoms commonly include cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, sputum, coughing up blood, and chest pain. They may be caused by lung or airway disorders, but heart problems and other conditions can cause similar symptoms, so the timing and associated signs help guide evaluation. Severe or sudden breathlessness, coughing up blood, or chest pain with breathing trouble needs prompt medical assessment.

topics.name: Syncope
topics.clinical_significance: Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness and postural tone caused by a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, followed by spontaneous recovery. It is often due to a reflex faint or a blood-pressure drop on standing, but heart rhythm or structural heart problems can be life threatening. Fainting during exercise or while lying down, or with chest pain, palpitations, or injury, raises concern for a serious cause; prolonged confusion may point to a seizure or another cause.

topics.name: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH)
topics.clinical_significance: In SIADH, antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) activity is not properly suppressed, so the kidneys retain too much water. This dilutes the sodium in the blood, usually without obvious fluid overload. Causes include some medicines, lung or brain disorders, and certain cancers. Symptoms depend on how low the sodium becomes and can include nausea, unsteadiness, and confusion; severe hyponatremia can cause seizures or coma.

topics.name: Syndrome of Inappropriate Sinus Tachycardia
topics.clinical_significance: In this condition, the heart’s normal pacemaker causes a persistently or intermittently fast heart rate (over 100 beats per minute, with a 24-hour average over 90) without another clear cause. It can cause distressing palpitations, especially when standing or exercising, as well as fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort. Diagnosis requires an ECG and ruling out other causes of a fast heart rate, such as infection, anemia, thyroid disease, or stimulants.

topics.name: Syndrome X
topics.clinical_significance: Syndrome X is another name for metabolic syndrome: a cluster that includes excess abdominal fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar or insulin resistance, high blood triglycerides, and low HDL cholesterol. It is usually diagnosed when at least 3 of these risk factors are present. This cluster raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

topics.name: Syrinx of the Spinal Cord or Brain Stem
topics.clinical_significance: A syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity in the spinal cord or brain stem. As it enlarges, it can damage nearby nerve pathways. In the spinal cord, it may cause weakness and wasting of the hands and arms and reduced pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders, arms, and back. A syrinx in the brain stem can affect balance, facial sensation, speech, or swallowing; MRI is used to diagnose it and look for a cause such as a Chiari malformation, past injury, or tumor.

topics.name: Systemic Abnormalities in Liver Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Advanced liver disease can affect circulation, hormone and reproductive function, blood counts and clotting, kidney function and blood salts, and the lungs. These problems may cause low blood pressure, anemia or bleeding, kidney failure (hepatorenal syndrome), or low blood oxygen. Some complications are serious and affect the need for specialist care or liver transplant evaluation.

topics.name: Systemic Asphyxiant Chemical-Warfare Agents
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic asphyxiants such as cyanide and hydrogen sulfide stop cells from using oxygen, even when oxygen reaches them in the blood. Exposure can quickly cause confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures, breathing failure, and death. Suspected exposure is a medical emergency that needs immediate airway and oxygen support and, for cyanide, prompt antidote treatment; rescuers must not enter a contaminated area without proper protection.

topics.name: Systemic Cancer Therapy
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic cancer therapy uses medicines that act throughout the body, including chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted drugs, and immune therapy. It can treat cancer cells beyond the main tumor, reduce the risk of cancer returning, or cure some cancers. Benefits and side effects vary by treatment; some medicines also affect healthy cells, hormones, or the immune system, so the choice and monitoring depend on the cancer and the patient.

topics.name: Systemic Disorders and the Mouth
topics.clinical_significance: Changes in the mouth can provide clues to illness elsewhere in the body, such as diabetes, vitamin or iron deficiency, infection, or a blood disorder. Systemic illness and its treatments can also affect oral health, healing, bleeding, and infection risk during dental care. Recognizing these links helps clinicians identify possible disease and plan dental procedures safely, sometimes with input from the patient’s physician.

topics.name: Systemic Rheumatic Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic rheumatic diseases are a varied group of autoimmune or inflammatory conditions that can affect joints, muscles, skin, blood vessels, and organs such as the lungs, heart, or kidneys. Some can cause lasting organ damage. The diseases and their treatments can also raise risks such as heart disease, serious infection, or bone loss, so care includes monitoring affected organs and treatment effects.

topics.name: Systemic Sclerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a chronic disease involving abnormal blood vessels and excess scar tissue. It can cause Raynaud symptoms, thick and tight skin, joint problems, and difficulty swallowing or reflux; it may also damage the lungs, heart, or kidneys. Lung, heart, or kidney complications can be life-threatening, so these organs need monitoring.

topics.name: Sézary Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Sézary syndrome is an uncommon cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that typically causes widespread red, itchy skin, often with cracking of the palms and soles. Cancerous T cells can be found in the blood, and lymph nodes may enlarge. Skin and blood tests help confirm and stage the disease; treatment often needs to act throughout the body.

topics.name: Taenia asiatica (Asian Tapeworm) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Taenia asiatica is an intestinal tapeworm acquired by eating raw or undercooked pork containing its larvae. Infection is often symptom-free or causes mild digestive symptoms; a person may notice tapeworm segments in the stool. It is not clear whether this species can cause cysticercosis in people.

topics.name: Taenia saginata (Beef Tapeworm) Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Taenia saginata is an intestinal tapeworm acquired by eating raw or undercooked beef containing its larvae. Infection is often symptom-free or causes mild digestive upset; some people notice a moving tapeworm segment in the stool. Stool testing can identify the infection, which is treated with antiparasitic medicine.

topics.name: Taenia Solium (Pork Tapeworm) Infection and Cysticercosis
topics.clinical_significance: Taenia solium causes two different infections. Eating undercooked pork containing larvae can lead to an adult tapeworm in the intestine, often with no symptoms or only mild digestive upset. Swallowing tapeworm eggs from human fecal contamination can cause cysticercosis, in which larvae form cysts in tissues. Cysts in the brain can cause seizures and other serious problems; their treatment needs specialist care because killing the cysts can trigger inflammation.

topics.name: Takatsuki Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Takatsuki disease, also called POEMS syndrome, is a rare disorder associated with abnormal plasma cells. It is marked by peripheral nerve damage and abnormal monoclonal plasma cells, and may also cause enlarged organs, hormone problems, skin changes, bone lesions, fluid buildup, or swelling of the optic nerve. It can affect several body systems and needs specialist assessment.

topics.name: Takayasu Arteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Takayasu arteritis is a rare inflammation of the aorta, its major branches, and sometimes the pulmonary arteries. It can narrow or block arteries, or weaken them and form aneurysms, reducing blood flow to organs and limbs. Common clues include weak or unequal pulses, different blood pressure between limbs, limb pain with activity, and high blood pressure; reduced blood flow can cause serious organ problems.

topics.name: Takayasu's Arteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Also called Takayasu arteritis, this is a rare inflammation of the aorta, its major branches, and sometimes the pulmonary arteries. It can narrow or block arteries, or weaken them and form aneurysms, reducing blood flow to limbs and organs. Clues include weak or unequal pulses, different blood pressure between limbs, pain in a limb with activity, or high blood pressure; reduced blood flow can cause serious organ problems.

topics.name: Talipes Equinovarus (Clubfoot) and Other Congenital Foot Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Clubfoot is a structural birth deformity in which the foot points downward and the heel and forefoot turn inward. Other congenital foot anomalies can change the foot’s position, arch, or flexibility; some are stiff and limit movement, and several are associated with developmental hip dysplasia.

topics.name: Tapeworm Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Tapeworms are parasitic flatworms, usually acquired by eating infected food. Adult worms in the intestine often cause few or no symptoms, though some cause abdominal symptoms or vitamin B12 deficiency. Larvae can spread to tissues and cause severe disease, including seizures when the brain is affected.

topics.name: Target Organs of Viral Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Different viruses tend to infect particular organs or cell types, a pattern called tissue or cellular tropism. This helps explain the symptoms they cause and group viral illnesses, such as those affecting the lungs, gut, skin, liver, or brain. Some viruses can spread to several organs.

topics.name: Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Compression of the posterior tibial nerve behind the inner ankle causes pain, burning, or tingling that may spread into the heel and sole. Symptoms often worsen with standing or walking. Tendon inflammation, swelling, scar tissue, a cyst, or foot deformity can contribute to the compression.

topics.name: Tay-Sachs Disease and Sandhoff Disease
topics.clinical_significance: These inherited disorders occur when enzymes that break down a fatty substance in the brain (GM2 ganglioside) are lacking, causing it to build up in brain cells. Tay-Sachs disease involves hexosaminidase A deficiency; Sandhoff disease involves deficiency of hexosaminidases A and B. The classic infantile forms cause progressive loss of movement and thinking skills, often with seizures and vision loss, and are usually fatal in early childhood; Sandhoff disease may also affect the liver and bones.

topics.name: Tearing
topics.clinical_significance: Excess tearing (epiphora) occurs when the eye makes too many tears or tear drainage is reduced. Dryness, allergy, or eye-surface irritation can trigger extra tears; tear-duct narrowing or blockage and eyelid misalignment can impair drainage. Persistent blockage can cause infection of the tear sac.

topics.name: Technique of Transfusion
topics.clinical_significance: Safe transfusion depends on confirming that the blood component is intended for the recipient and watching for reactions during and after infusion. Proper equipment, compatible fluids, and an appropriate infusion time help reduce risks such as red-cell damage, clotting, bacterial growth, and fluid overload.

topics.name: Teeth, Fractured and Avulsed
topics.clinical_significance: A broken tooth may expose sensitive inner layers; exposure of the pulp or a loose tooth signals a serious injury. A knocked-out permanent tooth is a time-sensitive dental emergency, and prompt replacement improves its chance of survival. A knocked-out baby tooth is not replaced because this can lead to infection or interfere with the permanent tooth coming in.

topics.name: Teething
topics.clinical_significance: Teething is the passage of new teeth through an infant’s or young child’s gums. It may cause tender, red gums, drooling, chewing, and fussiness, with at most a slight rise in temperature. It does not cause a true fever (38°C or higher); fever may point to another illness, such as an infection.

topics.name: Temper Tantrums
topics.clinical_significance: Temper tantrums are emotional outbursts, common in young children and often triggered by frustration, tiredness, hunger, or boredom. They are usually part of normal development, especially from ages 2 to 4. Episodes lasting over 15 minutes or occurring several times a day may point to an underlying mental, physical, or social problem.

topics.name: Temporal Arteritis
topics.clinical_significance: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is inflammation of large arteries, often affecting the temples and aorta, in adults over 50. It can cause a new headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain while chewing. Reduced blood flow to the eye can cause sudden, permanent vision loss, and aortic inflammation can lead to an aneurysm.

topics.name: Temporal Bone Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A temporal bone fracture, usually caused by severe head trauma, can injure the ear, balance organs, or facial nerve. It may cause bleeding from the ear, hearing loss, dizziness, or facial weakness; a leak of fluid around the brain and spinal cord can raise the risk of meningitis.

topics.name: Temporomandibular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Temporomandibular disorders are a group of problems affecting the jaw joints and chewing muscles. They can cause pain in the jaw, face, or neck, clicking or popping sounds, and limited jaw movement; headache or ear pain may also occur.

topics.name: Temporomandibular Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Temporomandibular disorders affect the jaw joints, chewing muscles, and nearby nerves and ligaments. They commonly cause pain in the jaw, face, or neck, clicking or popping, or limited jaw movement; headaches and ear pain may also occur. Because other problems can cause similar symptoms, assessment must consider these other causes.

topics.name: Temporomandibular Myofascial Pain Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: This muscle-related cause of jaw pain can occur even when the jaw joint is normal. Tension or fatigue in the chewing muscles causes tenderness and pain that may spread to the head or neck, and jaw movement may be limited. Clenching or grinding the teeth can contribute.

topics.name: Tendinopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Tendinopathy is a painful disorder involving damage and other degenerative changes in a tendon; it is usually not an inflammatory condition. Repeated loading or overuse may contribute, but sometimes the cause is unknown. Pain often worsens when the tendon is used or stressed, and long-term changes can limit movement.

topics.name: Tennis Elbow
topics.clinical_significance: Tennis elbow is injury to the tendons that straighten the wrist where they attach to the outer elbow. It causes tenderness and pain that may spread into the forearm, often worsened by gripping or straightening the wrist against resistance. Repeated or forceful forearm use can contribute.

topics.name: Tension Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Tension-type headache causes mild or moderate pressing pain, often on both sides of the head. Unlike migraine, it usually does not cause nausea or vomiting or worsen with physical activity. It may be occasional or occur on 15 or more days each month; chronic headaches can be linked to sleep problems, stress, neck pain, jaw disorders, or eye strain.

topics.name: Tension Pneumothorax
topics.clinical_significance: Air trapped around a lung builds pressure, compressing the lungs and reducing blood returning to the heart. This life-threatening emergency can rapidly cause shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure, and shock, often after chest injury or during mechanical ventilation; it requires immediate decompression.

topics.name: Tension-Type Headache
topics.clinical_significance: Tension-type headache causes mild or moderate, pressing pain, usually on both sides of the head. Unlike migraine, it usually does not cause nausea or vomiting and is not worsened by physical activity, light, or sound. It can be episodic or occur on 15 or more days each month (chronic).

topics.name: Testicular and Scrotal Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Common congenital anomalies include fluid around the testis (hydrocele), an undescended testis, and twisting of the testis (torsion). A hydrocele usually causes painless scrotal swelling and may resolve on its own. Torsion cuts off the testis’s blood supply and can destroy the tissue; although rare in newborns, it is an emergency.

topics.name: Testicular Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Testicular cancer is the most common solid cancer in males aged 15 to 35 and often appears as a painless lump or swelling. It can spread even when it seems limited to the testicle, but localized disease is often curable. Ultrasound, blood tumor markers, and scans help determine its extent.

topics.name: Testicular Torsion
topics.clinical_significance: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle twists on the spermatic cord, cutting off its blood supply. It causes sudden, severe pain and swelling on one side of the scrotum, often with nausea or vomiting. It is an emergency because the testicle can be permanently damaged or lost without rapid treatment.

topics.name: Testing for Hepatic and Biliary Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Blood tests, imaging, and sometimes liver biopsy help find liver or bile-duct disease, assess injury and function, and monitor change over time. Patterns in the results can help distinguish damage to liver cells from impaired bile flow, but results must be considered along with a person’s history and examination.

topics.name: Tests of Pulmonary Function (PFT)
topics.clinical_significance: Pulmonary function tests measure airflow, how much air the lungs hold, and how well gases move between the lungs and blood. They help identify and assess lung disorders, distinguish narrowed airways from restricted lung expansion, and track changes or response to treatment.

topics.name: Tests of Respiratory Muscle Function
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing pressure and airflow tests help assess the strength and reserve of the breathing muscles, including the diaphragm. They can help detect muscle weakness or diaphragm paralysis, but abnormal results are not specific and must be considered alongside the person’s effort and other findings.

topics.name: Tetanus
topics.clinical_significance: Tetanus is a serious illness caused when Clostridium tetani bacteria in a wound release a toxin that affects the nerves. It causes severe muscle stiffness and painful spasms, often starting with jaw stiffness. Spasms can interfere with breathing and may be fatal.

topics.name: Tetanus-Diphtheria Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The Td vaccine stimulates protection against tetanus and diphtheria. It is used for routine vaccination and booster doses; the related Tdap vaccine also protects against pertussis. Repeat doses help maintain protection over time.

topics.name: Tetracyclines
topics.clinical_significance: Tetracyclines are antibiotics that stop bacteria from making proteins. Drugs in this group, including doxycycline, treat infections such as Lyme disease, chlamydia, and rickettsial infections. Common effects include nausea, diarrhea, and increased sun sensitivity. Prolonged use in young children can affect developing teeth and bones, although short courses of doxycycline have not been shown to stain teeth.

topics.name: Tetralogy of Fallot
topics.clinical_significance: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect with four features: a hole between the ventricles, blockage of blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs, an aorta positioned over the hole, and a thickened right ventricle. Reduced blood flow to the lungs can cause low blood oxygen, blue skin, breathlessness, and poor growth; sudden severe “tet spells” can be life-threatening. Surgical repair is the definitive treatment.

topics.name: Thalassemia Major and Minor
topics.clinical_significance: “Minor” (thalassemia trait) usually causes no symptoms or only mild anemia with small red blood cells. “Major” causes severe anemia and often requires regular blood transfusions. Intermediate forms also occur; severe disease and repeated transfusions can lead to iron overload, an enlarged spleen, and bone or growth problems.

topics.name: Thalassemias
topics.clinical_significance: Thalassemias are inherited blood disorders in which the body makes too little of one part of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. They can cause small red blood cells and anemia, ranging from mild or symptom-free forms to severe anemia. Severe disease can lead to jaundice, an enlarged spleen, bone changes, poor growth, and iron overload, including from repeated transfusions.

topics.name: The Bends
topics.clinical_significance: The bends is a common name for decompression sickness, which occurs when dissolved gas forms bubbles in the blood or tissues as pressure falls, usually during ascent from a dive. It often causes deep joint or muscle pain, but bubbles can also harm the brain, spinal cord, or lungs, causing severe disability, breathing problems, collapse, or death.

topics.name: The Porphyrias
topics.clinical_significance: Porphyrias are rare disorders of heme production in which porphyrins or their precursors build up. Depending on the type, they can cause attacks of severe abdominal pain and nerve or mental symptoms, or skin sensitivity to sunlight with pain, fragile skin, or blisters; some types cause both. Severe acute attacks can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Therapeutic and Assistive Devices
topics.clinical_significance: Therapeutic and assistive devices support injured or weak body parts or help with movement. Braces and shoe inserts can support joints and reduce pain; canes, crutches, walkers, and wheelchairs can aid balance and mobility. Prostheses replace missing limbs and can help restore function.

topics.name: Therapeutic Apheresis
topics.clinical_significance: Therapeutic apheresis separates blood components and selectively removes harmful substances from plasma or excess or defective blood cells, returning the other components to the patient. It is used for selected blood and immune disorders. Possible complications include low blood pressure, low calcium, allergic reactions, and problems from the IV catheter.

topics.name: Therapeutic Objectives in Older Adults
topics.clinical_significance: When choosing tests or treatments for an older adult, weigh likely benefits—such as symptom relief, better function, or longer life—against risks and burdens that may affect quality of life. Decisions should reflect the person’s health, expected lifespan, and preferences; age alone should not determine care.

topics.name: Therapeutic Touch
topics.clinical_significance: Therapeutic touch is an “energy medicine” practice in which a practitioner moves their hands over or near the patient, usually without touching. It is sometimes used to promote well-being, but there is not enough evidence that it treats disease or heals wounds.

topics.name: Thiamine Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency can cause nerve damage (dry beriberi), heart failure (wet beriberi), or Wernicke-Korsakoff brain disease. It is often linked to severe malnutrition or alcohol use disorder. Untreated Wernicke encephalopathy can progress to coma or death, and lasting memory problems may remain after treatment.

topics.name: Thin Basement Membrane Disease
topics.clinical_significance: This inherited condition thins the filtering membrane in the kidneys and often causes microscopic blood in the urine, found incidentally. Kidney function is usually normal and the long-term outlook is excellent, though visible blood or protein in the urine can occur and progressive kidney failure is rare.

topics.name: Third Cranial Nerve (Oculomotor) Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Third nerve damage can make the eyelid droop, cause double vision, and limit the eye’s ability to move inward, up, or down. A suddenly enlarged pupil that reacts poorly to light can signal an aneurysm or pressure on the brain and needs urgent assessment. When the pupil is spared, reduced blood flow to the nerve, often related to diabetes or high blood pressure, is a more common cause.

topics.name: Third Trimester Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding in the third trimester may be a small blood-streaked mucus discharge as labor begins, but it can also signal placental abruption, placenta previa, vasa previa, or uterine rupture. These causes can lead to severe bleeding, shock, problems with blood clotting, or serious harm to the fetus. Visible bleeding may be slight even when blood loss inside the uterus is severe.

topics.name: Third Window Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Third window syndrome occurs when an abnormal opening or very thin area in the bone of the inner ear creates an extra pathway for sound and pressure. It can cause unusually loud perception of a person’s own voice or body sounds, dizziness triggered by sound or pressure, and hearing loss. The superior semicircular canal is the most common site.

topics.name: Thoracentesis
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracentesis uses a needle to remove fluid from the space around the lungs. The fluid can be tested to find the cause of a new or unexplained pleural effusion; removing fluid may ease shortness of breath caused by a large effusion.

topics.name: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms
topics.clinical_significance: A thoracic aortic aneurysm is an abnormal widening of the aorta in the chest. It often causes no symptoms until it enlarges or leads to complications. It can press on nearby organs, cause a clot to block blood flow, split the aortic wall (dissection), or rupture; dissection and rupture can be fatal.

topics.name: Thoracic Outlet Compression Syndromes (TOS)
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracic outlet compression syndromes cause pain, tingling, or numbness in the neck, shoulder, arm, or hand when nerves—and sometimes blood vessels—are compressed between the neck and chest. Nerve compression is most common. Blood vessel compression can cause arm swelling or color change and, rarely, tissue damage.

topics.name: Thoracic Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracic trauma is injury to the chest from a blunt or penetrating force. It can damage the lungs, ribs, heart, major blood vessels, or diaphragm and interfere with breathing or blood flow. A collapsed lung, bleeding into the chest, pressure around the heart, or a torn aorta can quickly cause shock or death.

topics.name: Thoracic Trauma, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracic trauma includes blunt or penetrating injuries to the chest. These injuries can damage the lungs, heart, major blood vessels, or chest wall and impair breathing or blood flow. A collapsed lung, severe bleeding, pressure around the heart, or aortic injury can cause rapid respiratory failure, shock, or death.

topics.name: Thoracoscopy and Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracoscopy uses a camera passed through the chest wall to examine the space around the lungs and, when needed, take tissue samples or treat disease. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is the surgical form, used for procedures such as treating recurrent pneumothorax or empyema and removing lung tissue. It can help diagnose pleural disease when less invasive tests are inconclusive.

topics.name: Thoracotomy
topics.clinical_significance: Thoracotomy is a surgical opening of the chest used to diagnose or treat chest disease when less invasive methods are inadequate. It provides access for major operations, such as removing part or all of a lung, often to treat lung cancer. Risks include bleeding, infection, pneumothorax, and an abnormal opening between the lung airways and pleural space (bronchopleural fistula).

topics.name: Threadworm Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Threadworm infection (strongyloidiasis) is a roundworm infection that can persist for decades because the parasite can reinfect the same person. It may cause no symptoms or cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash, or cough. In people taking corticosteroids or other immune-suppressing treatment, it can spread widely and cause life-threatening illness, including severe bacterial infection.

topics.name: Thromboangiitis Obliterans
topics.clinical_significance: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) causes inflammation and clots in small and medium arteries and some superficial veins, mainly in the hands and feet. It occurs almost only in people who use tobacco and reduces blood flow, causing coldness, numbness, pain, nonhealing ulcers, or gangrene. Continued tobacco use can lead to loss of fingers, toes, or a limb.

topics.name: Thrombocythemia, Essential
topics.clinical_significance: Essential thrombocythemia is a chronic bone marrow disorder that makes too many platelets. It may cause small-vessel symptoms such as headache, vision changes, or burning pain in the hands and feet; blood clots and bleeding can also occur. Extremely high platelet counts can increase the risk of bleeding. Many people have no symptoms, and life expectancy may be normal.

topics.name: Thrombocytopenia and Platelet Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: Thrombocytopenia means having too few platelets; platelet dysfunction means platelets do not work properly. Either problem can weaken clot formation and cause easy bruising, pinpoint skin spots (petechiae), nose or gum bleeding, or other abnormal bleeding. The effect depends on the platelet count, how well the platelets work, and the underlying cause.

topics.name: Thrombocytopenia Due to Splenic Sequestration
topics.clinical_significance: An enlarged spleen can hold onto more platelets than usual, lowering the number in the blood. This usually causes only mild thrombocytopenia and rarely causes bleeding when it is the only problem, because stored platelets can be released when needed. In advanced cirrhosis, low platelet counts are often mainly due to reduced platelet production linked to low liver thrombopoietin, not splenic trapping alone.

topics.name: Thrombocytopenia: Other Causes
topics.clinical_significance: Infections, medicines, autoimmune or blood disorders, sepsis, transfusion reactions, and pregnancy can lower the platelet count. This may cause pinpoint skin spots, bruising, or bleeding from the nose, gums, or other mucous membranes. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an important exception: despite the low count, it can trigger dangerous blood clots.

topics.name: Thrombocytosis, Reactive (Secondary Thrombocythemia)
topics.clinical_significance: Reactive thrombocytosis is a high platelet count caused by another condition, such as infection, inflammation, blood loss, iron deficiency, or cancer. Platelets usually work normally, and this condition generally does not increase the risk of blood clots or bleeding unless arterial disease is also present. The count usually returns to normal when the underlying cause is treated.

topics.name: Thromboembolic Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Pregnancy and the first 6 weeks after birth raise the risk of blood clots in the deep veins and lungs. Blood clots more easily during pregnancy, and blood flow in the leg veins slows. A pulmonary embolism can be life-threatening, and these disorders are a leading cause of maternal death. Many clots occur after delivery; cesarean birth adds risk.

topics.name: Thrombotic Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Thrombotic disorders cause harmful blood clots to form in veins, arteries, or the heart. A clot can block blood flow where it forms or travel elsewhere, causing problems such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, heart attack, or stroke. Inherited traits and acquired factors such as cancer, pregnancy, surgery, infection, or prolonged immobility can raise the risk.

topics.name: Thrombotic Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Thrombotic disorders develop when blood clots too readily, often because of inherited, acquired, or environmental factors. A clot may block a vessel where it forms or travel and block another, causing deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, heart attack, or stroke. Risk can rise with cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, surgery, pregnancy, prolonged immobility, severe infection, or inherited clotting conditions.

topics.name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
topics.clinical_significance: TTP is a life-threatening disorder usually caused by severe deficiency of the ADAMTS13 enzyme. Tiny platelet-rich clots form in small blood vessels, using up platelets and damaging red blood cells; this causes low platelets, hemolytic anemia, and reduced blood flow to organs, especially the brain and digestive system. Without prompt treatment, TTP is usually fatal.

topics.name: Thyroid Cancers
topics.clinical_significance: Thyroid cancers often first appear as painless nodules. Most papillary and follicular cancers grow slowly and have an excellent outlook, but anaplastic and poorly differentiated cancers can grow rapidly and are much more dangerous. Medullary thyroid cancer can run in families as part of an inherited syndrome.

topics.name: Thyroid Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Thyroid disease may change hormone production, making the gland underactive or overactive, or cause inflammation, enlargement, nodules, or cancer. Thyroid hormones regulate metabolism and support growth and development, so abnormal levels can affect energy, weight, temperature tolerance, and heart rate.

topics.name: Thyroid Disorders in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Thyroid disorders during pregnancy can affect both the pregnant person and fetus. Untreated or poorly controlled hyperthyroidism can cause fetal growth restriction, preeclampsia, or stillbirth; untreated hypothyroidism can increase miscarriage risk and impair the child’s intellectual development. In Graves disease, antibodies can cross the placenta and disrupt fetal thyroid function. Thyroid problems can also develop after birth.

topics.name: Thyroid Function, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The thyroid makes thyroxine (T4), which most body tissues convert to the active hormone triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones regulate metabolism throughout the body and are essential for normal brain and body development before and just after birth. Pituitary thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) helps control thyroid hormone levels, and TSH testing is the main way to assess thyroid function.

topics.name: Thyroid Nodule, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: A thyroid nodule is a growth within the thyroid; nodules are common and most are benign, but some are cancerous. Many cause no symptoms, while some produce excess thyroid hormone or press on nearby structures. Thyroid function tests and ultrasound help assess a nodule, and needle biopsy is used for nodules with suspicious features.

topics.name: Thyroiditis, Subacute
topics.clinical_significance: Subacute thyroiditis is an acute thyroid inflammation that is likely caused by a viral infection. It causes fever and a painful, tender thyroid. Release of stored hormone often causes temporary hyperthyroidism first, followed in some people by temporary hypothyroidism; rarely, thyroid damage causes permanent hypothyroidism. The condition usually resolves within a few months.

topics.name: Thyrotoxicosis
topics.clinical_significance: Thyrotoxicosis is the state of excess thyroid hormone in the body. It can result from increased hormone production by the thyroid, release of stored hormone (as in thyroiditis), or taking too much thyroid hormone. It speeds body processes and may cause palpitations, fast heartbeat, tremor, sweating, heat intolerance, anxiety, or weight loss; severe cases can cause life-threatening thyroid storm.

topics.name: Tibia Fractures
