topics.clinical_significance: Fractures of the distal tibia at the ankle usually involve the medial or posterior malleolus. They cause ankle pain and swelling; if the fracture disrupts the ankle’s stabilizing ring, the joint can become unstable. Poor alignment during healing can lead to ankle arthritis, so joint stability is important to the outcome.

topics.name: Tibial Torsion
topics.clinical_significance: Tibial torsion is inward or outward twisting of the shinbone, often present at birth. Inward twisting is common in infants and usually straightens as they grow, but excessive or persistent twisting can cause in-toeing and sometimes bowlegs; marked torsion may be linked to a neuromuscular problem or Blount disease. Outward twisting normally increases with growth and rarely causes problems.

topics.name: Tibialis Posterior Tendinosis and Tibialis Posterior Tenosynovitis
topics.clinical_significance: Tibialis posterior tendinosis is chronic damage to the tendon; tenosynovitis is inflammation of the sheath around it. Both commonly cause pain behind the inner ankle bone. Long-term tendon damage can weaken or tear the tendon, leading to a fallen foot arch, outward heel tilt, difficulty walking or standing on tiptoe, and eventually arthritis.

topics.name: Tic Disorders and Tourette Syndrome in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Tic disorders cause repeated, sudden, rapid, nonrhythmic movements or sounds that vary in type and severity and are not deliberate. Tourette syndrome is diagnosed when both motor and vocal tics persist for more than a year. Tics often lessen during adolescence; ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, and learning problems are common and may affect a child more than the tics.

topics.name: Tic Douloureux
topics.clinical_significance: Tic douloureux (trigeminal neuralgia) causes repeated bursts of very severe, brief, electric or stabbing pain on one side of the face along one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve, most often the maxillary branch. Chewing, brushing the teeth, or light touch can trigger an attack. The nerve is usually compressed near its entry into the brainstem by a blood vessel.

topics.name: Tick Bites
topics.clinical_significance: Tick bites are usually painless and cause only a small red bump, but some ticks transmit infections such as Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, or babesiosis. The chance of disease transmission increases the longer the tick stays attached. Local swelling or an allergic-type skin reaction can occur, and some tick species cause blisters or ulcers.

topics.name: Tick Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Tick fever (tick-borne relapsing fever) is an infection caused by Borrelia bacteria spread by ticks. It causes sudden episodes of high fever, chills, headache, nausea, and muscle and joint aches. The fever usually stops for several days before returning; several relapses may occur.

topics.name: Tick Paralysis
topics.clinical_significance: Tick paralysis is a rare illness caused by toxin in the saliva of a tick that has been attached for several days. It causes weakness that can spread upward and may affect breathing. Removing the tick usually allows recovery, though weakness may worsen for a day or two before it improves.

topics.name: Tick Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Tick typhus (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) is an infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and spread by ticks. It causes sudden high fever, severe headache, and often a rash that appears after several days. It can damage blood vessels and organs and may be fatal without prompt treatment.

topics.name: Tigecycline
topics.clinical_significance: Tigecycline is an IV antibiotic used for complicated skin, abdominal, and community-acquired lung infections, usually when other options are unsuitable. It can treat some drug-resistant bacteria, but its low blood levels make it a poor choice for bloodstream infections. It carries a warning about increased risk of death and commonly causes nausea and vomiting.

topics.name: Tilt Table Testing
topics.clinical_significance: Tilt table testing helps find the cause of unexplained fainting, dizziness, or falls after an initial evaluation. The patient is secured on a table that is tilted upright while heart rate and blood pressure are monitored for changes and symptoms. The test can help identify vasovagal fainting, delayed orthostatic hypotension, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

topics.name: Tinea Barbae (Barber's Itch)
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea barbae is a fungal infection of the beard area and hair follicles. It can cause scaly patches or inflamed bumps and pus-filled spots; severe inflammation may scar and lead to lasting hair loss. Treatment usually requires antifungal medicine taken by mouth.

topics.name: Tinea Capitis (Scalp Ringworm)
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea capitis is a contagious fungal infection of the scalp and hair, most common in children. It can cause scaly patches and broken hairs; severe inflammation may scar and cause permanent hair loss. Treatment requires antifungal medicine by mouth; shampoos may help reduce spread but are not enough on their own.

topics.name: Tinea Corporis (Body Ringworm)
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea corporis is a fungal infection of the skin on the body, arms, legs, or face. It often causes an expanding, ring-shaped scaly patch with a raised edge and clearer center. Mild cases are usually treated with antifungal cream; widespread or resistant cases may need antifungal medicine by mouth.

topics.name: Tinea Cruris (Jock Itch)
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea cruris is a fungal infection of the groin that causes an itchy, ring-shaped rash, often spreading onto the upper inner thighs. Heat and moisture make it more likely, and it can recur. Antifungal creams usually treat it; widespread or persistent infection may need antifungal medicine by mouth.

topics.name: Tinea Pedis (Athlete's Foot)
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) is a fungal infection of the feet, often between the toes. It can cause itching, scaling, or soft, cracked skin; some forms cause thickened soles or blisters. Broken skin may develop a bacterial infection such as cellulitis. Antifungal treatment and keeping the feet dry help, but the infection often recurs.

topics.name: Tinea Unguium
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea unguium is a fungal infection of the nails caused by dermatophytes and is more common in toenails. Affected nails may become thick, yellow or white, collect debris, and separate from the nail bed. It can cause discomfort and may increase the risk of cellulitis in the leg or foot; treatment may require prolonged antifungal medicine.

topics.name: Tinea Versicolor
topics.clinical_significance: Tinea versicolor is an overgrowth of yeast normally found on the skin. It causes multiple fine-scaled patches that may be white, tan, pink, or brown, usually on the trunk, neck, or upper arms. It is harmless and not contagious, but often returns; skin color may take months or longer to return to normal after treatment.

topics.name: Tinnitus
topics.clinical_significance: Tinnitus is hearing ringing, buzzing, or another sound when there is no outside sound; it is usually heard only by the affected person and often occurs with hearing loss. It may disturb sleep or cause distress. Tinnitus in one ear or in time with the heartbeat needs medical assessment because it can sometimes point to an underlying ear, nerve, or blood vessel problem.

topics.name: TNF Receptor–Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS)
topics.clinical_significance: TRAPS is a rare inherited inflammatory disorder caused by a change in the TNFRSF1A gene. It causes long attacks of fever with moving muscle pain, abdominal or chest pain, and a tender red rash; swelling around the eyes may also occur. Over time, a protein called amyloid can build up in the kidneys and cause damage.

topics.name: Tobacco Use
topics.clinical_significance: Tobacco use can quickly lead to nicotine dependence. Smoking greatly raises the risk of early death, heart and blood vessel disease, chronic lung disease, and many cancers. All tobacco products expose users to harmful chemicals, and secondhand smoke also harms others. Counseling and medicines can help people quit.

topics.name: Toe Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Toe fractures cause pain, swelling, and tenderness; a crush injury may cause bleeding under the toenail. Most fractures are stable and treated by taping the injured toe to a neighbor. Displaced or deformed fractures and some great-toe fractures may need X-rays, realignment, a stiff-soled shoe, or specialist follow-up.

topics.name: Toilet Training
topics.clinical_significance: Toilet training usually begins when a child shows readiness, often between 18 and 30 months. Bowel control commonly develops by age 2 to 3 years and daytime bladder control by age 3 to 4. Accidents and temporary setbacks can occur; pressure or punishment may increase resistance and cause regression.

topics.name: Tolerance and Resistance
topics.clinical_significance: Tolerance means a medicine or substance has less effect after repeated use, so a higher dose may be needed for the same effect. Resistance means microbes, cancer cells, or a disease no longer respond well to a medicine that used to work, making treatment less effective. Tolerance is a change in the body’s response; resistance is reduced response to treatment.

topics.name: Tomaculous Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Tomaculous neuropathy (HNPP) is a rare inherited disorder that makes peripheral nerves unusually sensitive to pressure and stretching. Pressure on a nerve can cause episodes of numbness and weakness, sometimes with foot drop, hand weakness, or carpal tunnel symptoms. Avoiding pressure and using pads or splints can help prevent repeat injury.

topics.name: Tongue Discoloration and Other Changes
topics.clinical_significance: Changes in tongue color or surface may be harmless, such as a geographic or hairy tongue, or may result from smoking, medicines, infection, dehydration, or nutrient deficiency. A pale, smooth tongue may occur with iron or vitamin B12 deficiency; a smooth, sore red tongue may reflect inflammation or niacin deficiency. Persistent white or red patches need assessment because some can be precancerous or cancerous.

topics.name: Tongue Discomfort
topics.clinical_significance: Tongue discomfort means pain or burning and is often caused by irritation, injury, dry mouth, ulcers, or oral thrush; iron or vitamin B12 deficiency can also cause a sore, burning tongue. Rarely, a deep infection under the tongue causes swelling that can block the airway and needs urgent care.

topics.name: Tongue Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Tongue injuries often result from biting or sharp teeth; minor cuts usually heal quickly because the tongue has a rich blood supply. Major injuries can bleed heavily, and swelling or bleeding may block the airway. Large, gaping, or persistently bleeding cuts may need repair, while many small cuts heal without stitches.

topics.name: Tonsillitis
topics.clinical_significance: Tonsillitis is inflammation or infection of the tonsils, usually as part of a throat infection. Most cases are caused by viruses; group A strep is an important bacterial cause. Symptoms include sore throat, painful swallowing, fever, swollen neck glands, and sometimes pus on the tonsils. Strep infection can cause an abscess or, rarely, rheumatic fever or kidney inflammation.

topics.name: Tonsillopharyngitis
topics.clinical_significance: Tonsillopharyngitis is an acute infection of the throat, the tonsils, or both. It is usually caused by a virus; group A strep is the most common bacterial cause. Symptoms include sore throat, pain when swallowing, fever, and swollen neck glands. Strep infection can cause an abscess or, rarely, rheumatic fever or kidney inflammation, so testing may be needed to guide treatment.

topics.name: Toothache and Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Toothache most often results from tooth decay or its complications, such as inflammation of the tooth pulp or an abscess; trauma and an infected wisdom tooth are other causes. Pain may be triggered by hot, cold, or sweet foods, chewing, or may persist without a trigger. Facial swelling or fever can signal spreading infection; swelling or tenderness under the tongue may indicate a dangerous deep infection that needs urgent care. Dental assessment is needed to treat the cause.

topics.name: Tornwaldt Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: A Tornwaldt cyst is a rare, benign cyst present from birth in the midline of the nasopharynx, the area behind the nose. It is often found by chance and causes no symptoms, but infection can lead to foul-smelling drainage, a bad taste, sore throat, or blockage of the tube connecting the back of the nose to the middle ear. Asymptomatic cysts need no treatment; symptomatic cysts may be opened or removed.

topics.name: Tornwaldt's Cyst
topics.clinical_significance: Tornwaldt’s cyst is a rare, benign cyst present from birth in the midline of the nasopharynx, the area behind the nose. It is often found by chance and causes no symptoms, but infection can lead to foul-smelling drainage, a bad taste, sore throat, or blockage of the tube connecting the back of the nose to the middle ear. Asymptomatic cysts need no treatment; symptomatic cysts may be opened or removed.

topics.name: Torsades de Pointes Ventricular Tachycardia
topics.clinical_significance: Torsades de pointes is a dangerous, rapid, irregular rhythm from the heart’s lower chambers, linked to a prolonged QT interval and sometimes caused by medicines or low potassium or magnesium. It can cause palpitations or fainting and may recur or progress to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. It requires emergency treatment.

topics.name: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR)
topics.clinical_significance: TAPVR is a congenital heart defect in which none of the pulmonary veins connect to the left atrium; instead, oxygen-rich blood returns to the right side of the heart and must cross an opening between the atria to reach the body. It can cause bluish skin and heart failure. If blood flow from the lungs is blocked, a newborn can develop severe breathing distress and fluid in the lungs. Surgical repair is required, urgently if flow is blocked.

topics.name: Total Parenteral Nutrition
topics.clinical_significance: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) supplies complete nutrition directly into a vein when the digestive tract cannot be used or needs rest. It provides fluid, calories, amino acids, fats, vitamins, and minerals. It requires close monitoring for catheter infection, blood sugar or electrolyte changes, fluid overload, and liver problems.

topics.name: Tourette's Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Tourette syndrome is diagnosed when a person develops multiple repeated movements and at least one repeated sound (tics) before age 18, and both types have been present for more than a year. Tics are sudden and involuntary; they can change in type and severity and often lessen during adolescence. ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, or learning disorders may also occur. Treatment is considered when tics interfere with daily activities or self-image.

topics.name: Toxic and Nutritional Optic Neuropathies
topics.clinical_significance: Toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy damages the optic nerve and usually causes gradual, painless loss of central vision and color vision, often in both eyes. Causes include toxins or medicines and undernutrition or deficiencies of vitamins B1, B12, or folate. Promptly removing the cause or correcting a deficiency may improve vision; established optic nerve damage may be permanent.

topics.name: Toxic Optic Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Toxic optic neuropathy is damage to the optic nerve from a medicine or chemical, such as ethambutol, methanol, or lead. It usually causes gradual, painless loss of central vision and color vision in both eyes. Promptly identifying and removing the cause may improve vision, but established nerve damage may be permanent.

topics.name: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)
topics.clinical_significance: Toxic shock syndrome is a life-threatening illness caused by toxins made by Staphylococcus aureus or group A strep bacteria. It can cause sudden high fever, low blood pressure, a widespread red rash, and failure of several organs, and may rapidly progress to shock and death. It requires immediate hospital treatment with antibiotics, removal or treatment of the infection source, and intensive supportive care.

topics.name: Toxins as Mass-Casualty Weapons
topics.clinical_significance: Toxins used as mass-casualty weapons cause poisoning through the harmful chemicals made by organisms, rather than infection by living microbes. They do not multiply in the body or spread from person to person. Depending on the toxin, illness may cause paralysis, severe vomiting or diarrhea, breathing failure, or shock; suspected exposure needs urgent medical and public health response.

topics.name: Toxocariasis
topics.clinical_significance: Toxocariasis is infection by dog or cat roundworm larvae after a person swallows eggs from soil contaminated with animal feces or eats undercooked infected tissue. Larvae can move through organs and cause fever, cough, rash, or an enlarged liver; if they reach the eye, they can cause inflammation and impaired or lost vision. Mild illness often resolves on its own, but severe or eye disease needs medical care.

topics.name: Toxoplasmosis
topics.clinical_significance: Toxoplasmosis is infection with the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, usually acquired from food, water, or soil contaminated with cat feces or from undercooked infected meat. Most healthy people have no symptoms or only a mild, flu-like illness. In people with weakened immunity, it can cause severe brain or eye disease. A new infection during pregnancy can pass to the fetus and cause serious harm.

topics.name: Trabecular Cell Carcinoma
topics.clinical_significance: Trabecular cell carcinoma, now usually called Merkel cell carcinoma, is a rare, aggressive cancer of the skin. It often appears as a fast-growing, painless, firm nodule that may be flesh-colored or bluish-red, usually on sun-exposed skin. It can spread to nearby lymph nodes and other parts of the body. Risk is higher in older adults and people with weakened immunity or long-term sun exposure.

topics.name: Tracheal Intubation
topics.clinical_significance: Tracheal intubation is placement of a tube through the mouth or nose into the windpipe to keep the airway open. The tube allows oxygen and air to reach the lungs and supports mechanical ventilation. It is used when a person cannot breathe adequately, cannot protect the airway, or needs a secure airway during some procedures. It also helps limit aspiration and allows removal of secretions from the lower airway.

topics.name: Tracheal Tumors
topics.clinical_significance: Tracheal tumors are uncommon growths in or around the windpipe; they may be benign, cancerous, or spread there from another site. Many primary tracheal tumors are cancerous and locally advanced when found. As they narrow the airway, they may cause gradual cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, noisy breathing, or coughing up blood. Severe narrowing can block breathing and become life-threatening.

topics.name: Tracheitis, Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial tracheitis is an uncommon, potentially life-threatening infection of the windpipe that mainly affects young children and often follows a viral respiratory infection. It can cause high fever, a harsh cough, noisy breathing (stridor), and shortness of breath. Swelling and pus can narrow or block the airway, and breathing may worsen quickly.

topics.name: Trachoma
topics.clinical_significance: Trachoma is a chronic infection of the conjunctiva (the lining of the eyelids and the white of the eye) caused by certain strains of \textit{Chlamydia trachomatis}. It spreads through contact with infected eye or nose discharge, contaminated items, or flies. Repeated infections can scar the eyelid, turn it inward, and make the eyelashes rub against the cornea. Corneal scarring can cause lasting vision loss or blindness; trachoma is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide.

topics.name: Traditional Chinese Medicine
topics.clinical_significance: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is a medical system that includes herbal remedies, acupuncture, massage, diet, and movement practices such as qigong. It explains illness using traditional ideas such as qi and balance between yin and yang; these ideas do not match modern biomedical models. Evidence of benefit varies by practice and condition. Herbal products may vary in content and can cause side effects, interact with medicines, or be contaminated.

topics.name: Transdermal and Vaginal Ring Hormonal Contraceptives
topics.clinical_significance: These methods deliver estrogen and progestin through a skin patch or vaginal ring to prevent pregnancy. Because the patch is changed weekly and the ring is used on a monthly cycle, they may be easier to use consistently than daily pills; delayed or missed changes can reduce protection. Their side effects and medical restrictions are similar to those of combined oral contraceptives, including an increased risk of blood clots and interactions with some medicines.

topics.name: Transfusion Medicine
topics.clinical_significance: Transfusion medicine covers the testing, selection, and use of donated blood and its components. Red blood cells, platelets, plasma, and cryoprecipitate are chosen for specific needs such as anemia, low platelet counts, or bleeding. Blood-group testing helps prevent incompatible transfusions. Transfusions can still cause complications, including immune reactions, fluid overload, or lung injury.

topics.name: Transient Global Amnesia
topics.clinical_significance: Transient global amnesia causes a sudden inability to form new memories, sometimes with a gap for recent events. People usually remain alert, know their identity, and may repeatedly ask the same questions. The episode usually resolves within 24 hours, although memory for the episode may remain lost. Stroke, seizure, and other causes of sudden amnesia must be ruled out.

topics.name: Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy
topics.clinical_significance: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy is a temporary delay in antibody production that causes low immunoglobulin levels, especially IgG, after maternal antibodies decline. Most infants have no symptoms, but some develop repeated sinus, lung, or gut infections. Antibody responses to vaccines are usually normal, and immunoglobulin levels typically recover over months to a few years.

topics.name: Transient Ischemic Attack
topics.clinical_significance: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of sudden neurologic symptoms caused by reduced blood flow to a specific part of the brain, spinal cord, or retina, without an area of dead tissue (infarction). Symptoms usually resolve within an hour. A TIA signals a high risk of stroke, especially during the first 24 to 48 hours.

topics.name: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn
topics.clinical_significance: Transient tachypnea is a short-lived breathing problem in newborns caused by delayed absorption of fluid from the lungs after birth. It causes rapid, sometimes labored breathing soon after delivery and is more common after elective cesarean birth or in premature infants. It usually resolves within 2 to 3 days; rarely, it can cause persistent high blood pressure in the lungs or a collapsed lung (pneumothorax).

topics.name: Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies
topics.clinical_significance: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies are rare prion diseases that progressively damage the brain, causing worsening memory, thinking, movement, or other neurologic problems. They result from an abnormal form of a normal protein and can arise spontaneously, be inherited, or, rarely, be acquired through exposure to infected tissue. They are fatal and have no curative treatment, but they do not spread through casual contact.

topics.name: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)
topics.clinical_significance: Transposition of the great arteries is a congenital heart defect. In the common form, dextro-transposition (d-TGA), the aorta leaves the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery leaves the left, creating two separate circuits that do not deliver oxygen-rich blood to the body. Newborns become severely cyanotic unless oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood can mix through a heart opening or a blood vessel that remains open after birth. Without enough mixing, the condition is life-threatening.

topics.name: Transthoracic Needle Biopsy
topics.clinical_significance: Transthoracic needle biopsy uses a needle passed through the chest wall to collect tissue from a lung, pleural, or nearby chest lesion for laboratory examination. Imaging, usually computed tomography, guides the needle. It is used to investigate lung nodules or masses and other chest abnormalities, especially when bronchoscopy cannot provide a diagnosis. Important risks include air leaking around the lung (pneumothorax) and bleeding.

topics.name: Transvestic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: Transvestic disorder is recurrent, intense sexual arousal from cross-dressing that causes significant distress or interferes with daily functioning and lasts at least 6 months. Cross-dressing alone is not a disorder and does not determine a person’s gender identity.

topics.name: Transvestic Fetishism
topics.clinical_significance: Transvestic fetishism is an older term for recurrent, intense sexual arousal from cross-dressing. It may be diagnosed as transvestic disorder only when it causes significant distress or interferes with daily functioning for at least 6 months. Cross-dressing itself is not a mental disorder.

topics.name: Transvestism
topics.clinical_significance: Transvestism is a term for recurrent, intense sexual arousal associated with cross-dressing. Most people who cross-dress do not have a mental disorder; transvestic disorder is diagnosed only when this pattern causes significant distress or impairs functioning for at least 6 months.

topics.name: Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Trauma- and stressor-related disorders are mental health conditions that develop after a traumatic or stressful event. Symptoms vary and may include anxiety, low mood, irritability, intrusive memories, avoidance, feeling disconnected, or sleep problems. The group includes acute stress disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), adjustment disorders, prolonged grief disorder, and certain childhood attachment disorders. The specific diagnosis depends on the symptoms and how long they last.

topics.name: Trauma Patient, Approach
topics.clinical_significance: The approach to a trauma patient is a structured assessment that finds and treats life-threatening injuries first. The primary survey checks airway, breathing, circulation, and neurologic status, and examines the whole body while preventing heat loss. After the patient is stable, a detailed head-to-toe examination and selected imaging look for other injuries.

topics.name: Traumatic Anterior Uveitis
topics.clinical_significance: Traumatic anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and nearby uveal tissue, usually developing within 3 days after a blunt eye injury. It can cause eye redness, aching pain, tearing, sensitivity to light, and blurred vision; the pupil may become enlarged or irregular.

topics.name: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
topics.clinical_significance: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is damage to brain tissue from a blow, jolt, or penetrating injury that temporarily or permanently changes brain function. It can cause confusion, memory loss, headache, loss of consciousness, seizures, or lasting thinking and movement problems. Bleeding or swelling inside the skull can raise pressure and reduce blood flow, causing further injury; severe TBI can be fatal.

topics.name: Traumatic Hemolytic Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Traumatic hemolytic anemia is mechanical destruction of red blood cells from excessive shear or turbulence in the circulation, causing intravascular hemolysis. The blood smear often shows fragmented red cells called schistocytes. Causes include small-vessel disorders, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and abnormal or artificial heart valves.

topics.name: Traumatic Iritis
topics.clinical_significance: Traumatic iritis, also called traumatic anterior uveitis, is inflammation of the iris and nearby uveal tissue after an eye injury, usually blunt trauma. It typically develops within 3 days and can cause eye pain, redness, tearing, sensitivity to light, and blurred vision. The pupil may become enlarged or irregular.

topics.name: Traumatic Perforation of the Tympanic Membrane
topics.clinical_significance: A traumatic tear in the eardrum can cause sudden pain, bleeding, hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo. Most perforations heal on their own, but penetrating injuries may also damage the small middle-ear bones, inner ear, or facial nerve. Infection or lasting hearing loss can occur, and a perforation that does not heal may need surgical repair.

topics.name: Traveler’s Diarrhea
topics.clinical_significance: Traveler’s diarrhea is an intestinal infection acquired during travel, usually from contaminated food or water. It is most often caused by bacteria, but viruses and parasites can also cause it. It causes loose stools, often with cramps, nausea, or vomiting. Most cases are mild and short-lived, but dehydration can occur; blood in the stool, fever, or severe pain can signal more serious illness.

topics.name: Treatment of Acute Asthma Exacerbations
topics.clinical_significance: An acute asthma exacerbation is a sudden worsening of airway narrowing that causes wheezing, cough, chest tightness, or difficulty breathing. Treatment uses inhaled medicines to open the airways and, except in the mildest attacks, corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. Oxygen is used when blood oxygen is low; severe attacks may need additional medicines and hospital care.

topics.name: Treatment of Acute COPD Exacerbation
topics.clinical_significance: An acute COPD exacerbation is a sudden worsening of breathing symptoms, often triggered by an infection or air pollution. It can cause low blood oxygen and, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Treatment aims to open the airways and restore oxygen; it may include inhaled bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics when bacterial infection is suspected, and breathing support for severe illness.

topics.name: Treatment of Anemia
topics.clinical_significance: Treatment of anemia depends on its cause, which is treated when possible. A red blood cell transfusion can quickly improve the blood’s ability to carry oxygen when anemia is dangerously severe, bleeding is uncontrolled, or low oxygen delivery threatens the heart, brain, or other organs. Transfusions are used selectively because they also carry risks.

topics.name: Treatment of Pain
topics.clinical_significance: Pain treatment is matched to its cause and duration. It may include medicines or procedures. Long-term pain often needs coordinated care that also includes physical rehabilitation and psychological support; these approaches can help reduce pain and improve movement, daily activities, and coping.

topics.name: Treatment of Stable COPD
topics.clinical_significance: When COPD is stable, ongoing care aims to ease breathlessness, preserve activity, and prevent flare-ups. It includes inhaled medicines that open the airways, stopping smoking, and pulmonary rehabilitation. Oxygen is used for people with persistently low blood oxygen. Vaccination and good nutrition also help support health; selected patients may benefit from surgery or lung transplantation.

topics.name: Trematodes (Flukes)
topics.clinical_significance: Trematodes, or flukes, are parasitic flatworms that can infect the blood vessels, intestines, lungs, or liver and bile ducts. Most human infections follow ingestion of the parasite; schistosomes enter through skin exposed to contaminated freshwater. Their effects depend on the species and the organ infected.

topics.name: Trematodes (Flukes), Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: Flukes are parasitic flatworms with complex life cycles that usually involve at least two hosts. Different species infect the blood vessels, intestines, lungs, liver, or bile ducts, where they can cause organ-specific disease.

topics.name: Tremor
topics.clinical_significance: A tremor is involuntary, rhythmic shaking, often of the hands, head, voice, or legs. It may occur at rest, while holding a position, or during movement. A slight tremor can be normal and become more noticeable with stress; other tremors may result from medicines or neurologic or metabolic disorders. Its pattern helps identify the cause.

topics.name: Trench Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Trench fever is an infection caused by Bartonella quintana and spread by body lice. It causes sudden bouts of fever, headache, weakness, and often severe pain in the shins and legs; the fever may recur. The bacteria can remain in the blood and sometimes cause endocarditis, an infection of the heart’s inner lining or valves.

topics.name: Trench Mouth
topics.clinical_significance: Trench mouth (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis) is a rapidly developing, painful gum infection. It causes bleeding, foul breath, and crater-like ulcers between the teeth; fever or feeling unwell may also occur. Risk is higher with smoking, poor oral hygiene, poor nutrition, stress, lack of sleep, or weakened immunity.

topics.name: Trichiasis
topics.clinical_significance: In trichiasis, eyelashes turn inward and rub against the eye even though the eyelid itself is in a normal position. This can cause a gritty feeling, redness, and tearing. Ongoing rubbing may scratch the cornea or lead to ulcers and scarring.

topics.name: Trichilemmal Cyst [Wen]
topics.clinical_significance: A trichilemmal (pilar) cyst, sometimes called a wen, is a usually benign, keratin-filled lump that forms from a hair follicle. It most often occurs on the scalp and may run in families. Cancerous change is very rare.

topics.name: Trichinellosis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichinellosis (trichinosis) is an infection caused by Trichinella worms, usually after a person eats undercooked meat containing the larvae. It may begin with stomach or bowel upset, followed by fever, muscle pain, and swelling around the eyes. Severe infection can affect the heart or nervous system.

topics.name: Trichiniasis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichiniasis is another name for trichinellosis (trichinosis), a parasitic infection acquired by eating undercooked meat containing Trichinella larvae. It can cause early digestive upset followed by fever, muscle pain, and swelling around the eyes.

topics.name: Trichinosis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichinosis is another name for trichinellosis, an infection with Trichinella worms acquired by eating undercooked meat, especially pork or wild game. It may begin with digestive upset, followed by fever, muscle pain, and swelling around the eyes. Severe infection can affect the heart or nervous system.

topics.name: Trichocephaliasis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichocephaliasis (trichuriasis) is whipworm infection caused by swallowing infective eggs from feces-contaminated soil, food, or hands. Light infections often cause no symptoms. Heavy infections can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia; rectal prolapse may occur, especially in children.

topics.name: Trichomoniasis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. It infects the vagina or male genital tract and often causes no symptoms, but may cause genital irritation, discharge, or pain with urination. People without symptoms can still pass the infection to sexual partners.

topics.name: Trichotillomania
topics.clinical_significance: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) is repeated pulling out of one’s hair, often from the scalp, eyebrows, or eyelashes. It causes hair loss and distress or problems in daily life, and people repeatedly try but struggle to stop. Swallowing pulled hair can form a mass in the digestive tract and sometimes cause a blockage.

topics.name: Trichuriasis
topics.clinical_significance: Trichuriasis is whipworm infection caused by swallowing infective Trichuris trichiura eggs from feces-contaminated hands, food, or soil. Light infections often cause no symptoms. Heavier infections can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia; rectal prolapse may occur, especially in children.

topics.name: Tricuspid Atresia
topics.clinical_significance: Tricuspid atresia is a congenital heart defect in which the tricuspid valve is absent and the right ventricle is underdeveloped. Blood cannot flow directly from the right atrium to the right ventricle, so it must pass through an opening between the atria and another route to the lungs, often a hole between the ventricles. It can cause bluish skin (cyanosis) or heart failure and usually requires staged surgery.

topics.name: Tricuspid Incompetence
topics.clinical_significance: Tricuspid incompetence (regurgitation) is backward leakage through the valve between the right heart chambers when the right ventricle contracts. It is often caused by enlargement of the right ventricle or atrium, sometimes related to lung or left-heart disease. Mild cases may cause no symptoms; severe leakage can cause swelling, fluid in the abdomen, liver congestion, or right-sided heart failure.

topics.name: Tricuspid Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Tricuspid insufficiency is another name for tricuspid regurgitation: blood leaks backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium when the ventricle contracts. It is often caused by enlargement of the right ventricle or atrium. Mild cases may cause no symptoms; severe leakage can lead to swelling, fluid in the abdomen, liver congestion, or right-sided heart failure.

topics.name: Tricuspid Regurgitation
topics.clinical_significance: Tricuspid regurgitation is leakage through a tricuspid valve that does not close fully, allowing blood to flow backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium when the heart contracts. It is often linked to enlargement of the right heart. Mild cases may cause no symptoms; severe leakage can lead to swelling, abdominal fluid, liver enlargement, or right-sided heart failure.

topics.name: Tricuspid Stenosis
topics.clinical_significance: Tricuspid stenosis is narrowing of the valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, which slows blood flow into the right ventricle. It is usually caused by rheumatic fever and often occurs with other valve disease. It may cause fatigue, neck pulsations, liver congestion, or swelling in the legs.

topics.name: Trigeminal Neuralgia
topics.clinical_significance: Trigeminal neuralgia causes repeated, brief attacks of severe, electric-shock-like pain on one side of the face. Chewing, speaking, brushing the teeth, or light touch can trigger an attack. It is usually due to a blood vessel pressing on the trigeminal nerve; facial numbness may point to another cause, such as multiple sclerosis or a tumor.

topics.name: Trigger Finger (Stenosing Flexor Tenosynovitis)
topics.clinical_significance: Trigger finger occurs when a finger tendon or its sheath thickens and catches as the tendon moves through a narrow tunnel at the finger’s base. The finger may be painful, click, or lock in a bent position, then suddenly straighten with a snap. It is more common in people with diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.name: Trimethoprim and Sulfamethoxazole
topics.clinical_significance: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a combination of two antimicrobial medicines that block consecutive steps in bacterial folate production. It treats selected bacterial infections, including some urinary infections, and is also used for Pneumocystis pneumonia. It is not effective against all bacteria, and resistance limits its use for some infections.

topics.name: Trisomy 13
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) is a serious chromosomal condition, usually caused by an extra copy of chromosome 13. It causes severe intellectual disability and multiple birth defects, often involving the brain, face, and heart. Many affected infants die in the first weeks of life.

topics.name: Trisomy 18
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) is a chromosomal condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 18. It leads to poor growth, severe developmental impairment, and multiple birth defects, often including heart defects and differences in the head, face, and limbs. The condition has a high risk of death in infancy; fewer than 1 in 10 affected infants survive beyond the first year.

topics.name: Trisomy D
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy D is another name for trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), a chromosomal condition caused by an extra chromosome 13. It causes severe developmental disability and multiple birth defects, often affecting the brain, face, eyes, and heart. Most affected infants die in the first weeks of life.

topics.name: Trisomy E
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy E is another name for trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), a chromosomal disorder usually caused by an extra copy of chromosome 18. It causes severe developmental delay, small birth size, and multiple birth defects, often including heart defects. The condition has a high risk of death in infancy; fewer than 1 in 10 affected infants survive beyond the first year.

topics.name: Trisomy G
topics.clinical_significance: Trisomy G is another name for Down syndrome, usually caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. It can cause mild to moderate intellectual disability, low muscle tone, characteristic physical features, and birth defects such as heart problems. People with Down syndrome also have an increased risk of certain health conditions.

topics.name: Tropical Sprue
topics.clinical_significance: Tropical sprue is a rare intestinal disorder, probably related to chronic infection, that prevents the small intestine from absorbing nutrients normally. It occurs mainly in tropical regions and can cause ongoing diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies of folate, vitamin B12, or iron. These deficiencies may lead to megaloblastic anemia.

topics.name: Tropical Typhus
topics.clinical_significance: Tropical typhus is another name for scrub typhus, an infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by bites from infected chigger mites. It usually causes fever and may cause a dark scab at the bite site, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash. Severe illness can affect multiple organs.

topics.name: Tsutsugamushi Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Tsutsugamushi disease is another name for scrub typhus, an infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by bites from infected chigger mites. It usually causes fever and may cause a dark scab at the bite site, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash.

topics.name: Tubal Dysfunction and Pelvic Abnormalities
topics.clinical_significance: Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes can prevent sperm and egg from meeting or keep a fertilized egg from moving to the uterus. Scar tissue, endometriosis, fibroids, or other pelvic or uterine abnormalities may also prevent fertilization or implantation. These problems are important causes of infertility.

topics.name: Tuberculosis, Extrapulmonary
topics.clinical_significance: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis is TB affecting organs outside the lungs, usually after the bacteria spread through the bloodstream. It can affect many body sites, so symptoms depend on the organ involved; fever, tiredness, and weight loss are common. Treatment usually requires several TB medicines taken together for months.

topics.name: Tuberculosis (TB)
topics.clinical_significance: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that most often affects the lungs. It may remain inactive without symptoms (latent TB) or become active, causing cough, fever, weight loss, and tiredness. Active TB of the lungs or throat can spread through the air; TB can also affect organs outside the lungs.

topics.name: Tuberculosis (TB), Perinatal
topics.clinical_significance: Perinatal TB is tuberculosis acquired before or around birth from an infected mother or another close contact. It can pass through the placenta or infected amniotic fluid, or spread through the air after birth. In newborns, it may affect several organs and look like sepsis, with fever, lethargy, breathing problems, or poor growth.

topics.name: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC)
topics.clinical_significance: Tuberous sclerosis complex is a genetic disorder that causes usually benign growths in several organs, often the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and lungs. It can cause seizures, skin changes, learning or developmental problems, and kidney problems. The effects vary widely from person to person.

topics.name: Tubulointerstitial Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Tubulointerstitial diseases are kidney disorders that damage the kidney tubules and the tissue around them. They include tubular necrosis and interstitial nephritis and may result from medicines, toxins, or metabolic problems. Severe or long-lasting damage can impair the whole kidney and lead to kidney failure.

topics.name: Tubulointerstitial Nephritis
topics.clinical_significance: Tubulointerstitial nephritis is injury to the kidney tubules and nearby tissue that reduces kidney function. Acute cases are often caused by a medicine reaction or infection; chronic cases can result from medicines, toxins, urinary blockage, or metabolic or genetic disorders. Long-lasting damage may lead to kidney failure.

topics.name: Tularemia
topics.clinical_significance: Tularemia is a bacterial infection caused by Francisella tularensis, often spread by tick or deer-fly bites or contact with infected animals such as rabbits. It causes sudden fever and may produce a skin ulcer with swollen nearby lymph nodes. Depending on how infection occurs, it can also affect the eyes, throat, lungs, or whole body.

topics.name: Tumor Antigens
topics.clinical_significance: Tumor antigens are molecules made by cancer cells or displayed on their surface that the immune system can recognize. Some are mostly found on tumors, while others are unique to tumor cells. The immune response is often too weak to stop cancer growth, but these antigens can help guide immune recognition and may serve as targets for cancer treatment.

topics.name: Tumor Immunodiagnosis
topics.clinical_significance: Tumor immunodiagnosis uses immune-based tests to detect tumor-associated markers in blood or tissue. These markers can help diagnose some cancers and track treatment response or recurrence, but they may also be raised in noncancer conditions. No single tumor marker is accurate enough to screen the general population for cancer or diagnose it early on its own.

topics.name: Tumor Immunology
topics.clinical_significance: Tumor immunology studies how the immune system recognizes and responds to cancer. T cells, natural killer cells, and other immune cells can recognize and kill tumor cells, but tumors may evade or suppress these defenses. These interactions help explain how cancer grows and provide the basis for treatments that strengthen or redirect immune responses.

topics.name: Tumors, Host Response to
topics.clinical_significance: The host response to tumors is the body’s immune reaction to cancer cells. T cells and natural killer cells can recognize and destroy tumor cells, often after detecting tumor antigens. However, tumors can suppress or evade these defenses, and the immune response may be too weak to stop cancer growth.

topics.name: Tumors of Bones and Joints
topics.clinical_significance: Bone and joint tumors may be benign or cancerous; cancer may start in bone or spread there from another organ. Most bone tumors in children are benign, while in adults, tumors that have spread from another cancer are more common than primary bone cancer. Persistent or worsening bone pain, especially at rest or at night, or a mass can signal a tumor.

topics.name: Tumors of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts
topics.clinical_significance: Gallbladder tumors include common benign polyps and uncommon cancer; most bile duct tumors are malignant. Cancer can block bile flow, causing yellow skin or eyes (jaundice), itching, and other signs of blockage, though early disease may cause no symptoms. These cancers are often diagnosed late and generally have a poor outlook.

topics.name: Tumors of the Gastrointestinal Tract
topics.clinical_significance: Tumors of the gastrointestinal tract are abnormal growths in the digestive organs, from the esophagus to the rectum. They may be benign or cancerous. Symptoms depend on the tumor’s location and may include pain, bleeding, blockage, anemia, or weight loss; some cause few symptoms until they are advanced.

topics.name: Tumors of the Head and Neck
topics.clinical_significance: Head and neck tumors are growths in the mouth, throat, voice box, nose, sinuses, salivary glands, or nearby areas; they may be benign or cancerous. Most cancers in these sites are squamous cell cancers. Symptoms vary by site and may include a persistent sore throat, hoarseness, ear pain, trouble swallowing, or a neck lump. Tobacco, alcohol, and HPV are important risk factors.

topics.name: Tumors of the Lungs
topics.clinical_significance: Lung tumors may start in the lung or spread there from another part of the body. Primary lung tumors can be benign or cancerous; most lung cancers are non-small-cell cancers. Cancer may cause cough, coughing up blood, shortness of breath, or chest pain, but early tumors may cause no symptoms. Smoking is a major risk factor.

topics.name: Tumors of the Orbit
topics.clinical_significance: Orbital tumors are growths in the tissues around the eye. They may be benign or cancerous and can start in the orbit, spread from nearby structures, or metastasize from another part of the body. They may push the eye forward or out of position and cause pain, double vision, or vision loss.

topics.name: Turf Toe
topics.clinical_significance: Turf toe is a sprain of the supporting tissues under the big toe joint, usually caused by bending the toe too far upward during push-off. It causes sudden pain and swelling, and moving the toe hurts. Severe sprains can tear these tissues and may lead to lasting pain or stiffness.

topics.name: Turista
topics.clinical_significance: Turista is another name for traveler’s diarrhea, an intestinal infection usually acquired from contaminated food or water while traveling. It can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites and may cause loose stools, cramps, nausea, or vomiting. Most cases are mild and short-lived, but dehydration can occur.

topics.name: Turner Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal condition, usually in females, in which all or part of one X chromosome is missing. It often causes short stature and poorly functioning ovaries, which can delay puberty and lead to infertility. Heart, kidney, thyroid, or hearing problems may also occur; features vary, especially when only some cells are affected.

topics.name: Tylomas
topics.clinical_significance: Tylomas are areas of thickened skin caused by repeated pressure or friction, often over a bony area. Calluses are usually broader and painless; corns are deeper and often painful. Ongoing pressure can cause irritation or discomfort.

topics.name: Tympanic Membrane Perforation, Traumatic
topics.clinical_significance: A traumatic perforation is a tear in the eardrum caused by injury. It can cause sudden ear pain, bleeding, hearing loss, or ringing; vertigo may signal inner ear injury. Many tears heal on their own, but infection or damage to the small middle-ear bones can affect hearing.

topics.name: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
topics.clinical_significance: Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system destroys insulin-making cells in the pancreas, leaving the body with little or no insulin. Blood sugar rises, and diabetic ketoacidosis can develop if insulin is lacking. Insulin is required; over time, high blood sugar can damage blood vessels, nerves, and kidneys.

topics.name: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and adolescents, type 1 diabetes results from immune damage to the insulin-making cells of the pancreas. High blood sugar can cause frequent urination, thirst, and weight loss. Diabetic ketoacidosis may be the first sign and can be life-threatening, so insulin treatment is essential.

topics.name: Type 2
topics.clinical_significance: This index label refers to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A), an inherited syndrome linked to medullary thyroid cancer and sometimes tumors of the adrenal or parathyroid glands; see that entry.

topics.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: In children and adolescents, type 2 diabetes occurs when the body resists insulin and the pancreas cannot make enough to meet its needs. High blood sugar may cause thirst and frequent urination, but many young people have few symptoms. Ketoacidosis can still occur, and blood vessel, kidney, or nerve complications may begin early.

topics.name: Type 2B
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 2B is a genetic syndrome usually linked to a RET gene change; it can occur without a family history. It causes a high risk of aggressive medullary thyroid cancer, often in early childhood, and may also cause tumors of the adrenal glands, bumps on the lips or tongue, and a tall, slender body shape with skeletal problems.

topics.name: Type 4
topics.clinical_significance: MEN 4 is a rare inherited syndrome caused by a change in the CDKN1B gene. It can cause tumors or overgrowth in the parathyroid glands, pancreas, and pituitary gland; overactive parathyroid glands and high blood calcium are common. It resembles MEN 1 but often begins later and progresses more slowly.

topics.name: Type I
topics.clinical_significance: This is an alternate name for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), an inherited syndrome that can cause tumors in the parathyroid glands, pancreas, and pituitary gland; see that entry.

topics.name: Types of Complementary and Alternative Medicine
topics.clinical_significance: Complementary and alternative medicine includes five broad groups: whole medical systems, mind-body practices, natural products and other biologic treatments, hands-on body practices, and energy-based practices. The groups describe different approaches, but evidence and risks vary by therapy. Cupping, scraping, and moxibustion can leave skin marks that may be mistaken for injuries.

topics.name: Typhoid Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Typhoid fever is a body-wide infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually spread by food or water contaminated with infected stool. It causes prolonged high fever and abdominal symptoms; severe disease can lead to intestinal bleeding or perforation. Some people continue to carry and spread the bacteria after recovery.

topics.name: Tyrosine Metabolism Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These disorders affect the body’s breakdown of tyrosine, an amino acid used to make pigments and other substances. Different enzyme problems can cause liver or kidney disease, nerve or developmental problems, skin and eye damage, or dark urine and joint disease. Some forms respond to diet or medicine, so identifying the specific disorder is important.

topics.name: Ulcerative Colitis
topics.clinical_significance: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammation of the colon lining that usually starts in the rectum and may spread through the colon. It often causes flares of bloody diarrhea, urgency, and abdominal cramps; joint, skin, or eye inflammation can also occur. Severe disease can cause dangerous colon swelling or perforation, and long-standing disease raises the risk of colon cancer.

topics.name: Ulnar and Radial Shaft Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: Fractures through the radius or ulna cause forearm pain, swelling, bruising, and sometimes deformity. A joint may also be dislocated: a proximal ulna fracture can dislocate the radial head (Monteggia fracture), and a distal radius fracture can disrupt the wrist joint (Galeazzi fracture). These associated dislocations can be missed and may require urgent orthopedic care.

topics.name: Ulnar Collateral Ligament Sprains
topics.clinical_significance: This injury is a sprain or tear of the ligament on the inner side of the thumb’s base joint, often after the thumb is forced away from the hand. It causes pain and tenderness and may pull off a small piece of bone. If the ligament heals poorly, the joint can remain weak or unstable.

topics.name: Ulnar Neuropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow occurs when the ulnar nerve is compressed or stretched, often with prolonged elbow bending or pressure on the elbow. It can cause elbow pain and tingling or numbness in the little finger, ring finger, and inner side of the hand. More severe or long-lasting injury can weaken the hand and reduce grip or pinch strength.

topics.name: Ultrasound
topics.clinical_significance: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to make real-time images of organs and soft tissues, assess blood flow, and monitor pregnancy. It uses no ionizing radiation and can guide procedures such as biopsies. Bone or gas can block clear images, and results depend partly on the operator’s skill.

topics.name: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
topics.clinical_significance: Umbilical cord prolapse means the cord lies in front of or beside the baby’s presenting part. It may stay inside the uterus or protrude from the vagina after the waters break. If the cord is compressed during labor, the baby may not get enough oxygen, making this an obstetric emergency.

topics.name: Uncommon Gastritis Syndromes
topics.clinical_significance: This group includes rare stomach conditions such as Ménétrier disease, eosinophilic gastritis, stomach MALT lymphoma, and inflammation linked to other illnesses, injury, or infection. Symptoms and risks differ by cause; some forms can lead to protein loss, stomach outlet blockage, or perforation. Treatment depends on the specific condition, and treating H. pylori can sometimes cure stomach MALT lymphoma.

topics.name: Uncommon Hereditary Coagulation Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: These rare inherited disorders affect clotting factors other than those involved in hemophilia. Most cause excessive bleeding, often after injury or surgery, but the effects vary: some cause abnormal clotting tests without bleeding, factor XIII deficiency can impair wound healing, and some fibrinogen disorders can increase the risk of blood clots.

topics.name: Undernutrition
topics.clinical_significance: Undernutrition occurs when the body does not get or absorb enough calories or nutrients, or when its needs increase. It can cause weight and muscle loss and specific nutrient deficiencies. It is especially harmful during childhood, pregnancy, illness, and older age, when nutrient needs are high or the body is more vulnerable.

topics.name: Undernutrition, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Undernutrition occurs when calorie or nutrient intake, absorption, or use does not meet the body’s needs, or when nutrient loss or increased needs create a shortfall. It may develop slowly or quickly, and can progress from changes in blood and tissue nutrients to muscle loss and visible deficiency symptoms. It is especially harmful during growth, pregnancy, serious illness, and older age.

topics.name: Understanding Medical Tests and Test Results
topics.clinical_significance: Medical tests help diagnose illness in people with symptoms or screen for disease before symptoms appear. Results can be false positive or false negative, so they must be interpreted with the person’s symptoms, baseline risk, and the test’s limits. Testing is most useful when the result can guide care; unnecessary tests can cause harm, stress, or more testing.

topics.name: Undescended Testes
topics.clinical_significance: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) means one or both testes are not in the scrotum; it may be noticed at birth or later in childhood. Some descend on their own during the first year. Persistent undescended testes can reduce fertility and raise the risk of testicular cancer; torsion or an inguinal hernia can also occur. Early surgery may improve fertility potential and reduce cancer risk.

topics.name: Undulant Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Undulant fever is another name for brucellosis, an infection caused by Brucella bacteria. It is usually caught through contact with infected animals or by consuming unpasteurized dairy. Fever may return in waves with sweats, weakness, and muscle or joint aches; less often, the infection affects the heart, nervous system, or bones.

topics.name: Unequal Pupils
topics.clinical_significance: Unequal pupils (anisocoria) means the pupils differ in size. A small difference, usually less than about 1 mm, is common and often harmless. A new or larger difference, especially with a drooping eyelid or trouble moving the eye, may signal an eye or nerve disorder; checking pupil reactions in light and dark helps guide evaluation.

topics.name: Unexplained Infertility
topics.clinical_significance: Unexplained infertility is diagnosed when a couple has not conceived but standard testing finds no clear cause: semen is normal, and ovulation, eggs, fallopian tubes, and uterus appear normal. Pregnancy may still occur, but treatment can help achieve it sooner. Some fertility treatments raise the chance of a multiple pregnancy.

topics.name: Unit of Measure Conversions
topics.clinical_significance: Unit conversions let clinicians compare measurements reported in different systems, including laboratory concentrations, temperature, weight, and volume. Correct conversion supports accurate interpretation of results and measurements. Household spoons vary in size and should not be used when precise liquid volumes are needed.

topics.name: Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome is severe brain dysfunction with periods of eye opening and preserved basic brainstem functions, but no observable awareness of self or surroundings and no purposeful responses. Reflex movements or eye motion can be mistaken for awareness, so repeated careful assessments help distinguish it from a minimally conscious state, where some awareness is present. Care is mainly supportive, and outlook depends on the cause and time since injury.

topics.name: Unstable Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Unstable angina is temporary reduced blood flow to the heart causing prolonged chest pain at rest, new severe angina, or a worsening pattern of angina, without evidence of heart muscle death on troponin testing. It is an acute coronary syndrome that can progress to a heart attack or dangerous heart rhythm and needs emergency assessment.

topics.name: Upper Respiratory Infection
topics.clinical_significance: A common upper respiratory infection, or cold, is an acute viral infection of the nose and throat. It usually causes a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, and cough, and gets better on its own. Colds can worsen asthma or chronic bronchitis; antibiotics do not treat the viral infection.

topics.name: Urban Typhus of Malaya
topics.clinical_significance: Urban typhus of Malaya is another name for murine (endemic) typhus, a flea-borne infection caused by Rickettsia bacteria. Fleas from rodents and other animals can spread it to people. It causes fever, chills, headache, and sometimes a rash. It is usually milder than epidemic typhus; death is rare but more likely in older adults.

topics.name: Urea Cycle Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Urea cycle disorders are inherited problems with removing ammonia, a waste product that can build up to toxic levels. Illness, fasting, or a high-protein load can trigger vomiting, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, confusion, or seizures; severe hyperammonemia can cause brain swelling, coma, permanent brain injury, or death. Early recognition and treatment are important to prevent lasting harm.

topics.name: Ureteral Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Ureteral anomalies are structural differences in the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder; they may occur with kidney anomalies or alone. Depending on the type, they can block urine flow or cause urine to flow backward, leading to kidney swelling, recurrent urinary infections, stones, incontinence, or reduced kidney function. Some cause no symptoms.

topics.name: Ureteral Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Ureteral injury is damage to the tube that carries urine from a kidney to the bladder. Most cases occur during surgery, but penetrating injuries can also cause it. Signs may be vague, and blood in the urine may be absent, so injury can be missed. Urine leakage can lead to infection or fistulas, while scarring can narrow or block the ureter.

topics.name: Urethral Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Urethral anomalies are structural differences in the tube that carries urine out of the body, such as an abnormal opening, narrowing, duplication, or obstructing valve. They may cause an abnormal urine stream, urine leakage, or recurrent urinary infections. Severe blockage can damage the bladder and kidneys and, before birth, interfere with lung development. Treatment depends on the effect on function; surgery is often needed when function is impaired.

topics.name: Urethral Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Urethral cancer is rare but can cause blood in the urine, difficulty passing urine or retention, bloody urethral discharge, or a mass. It may grow into nearby tissues early and spread to groin or pelvic lymph nodes, so these symptoms need prompt evaluation. Outlook depends on the tumor location and depth, and recurrence is common.

topics.name: Urethral Dilation
topics.clinical_significance: Urethral dilation widens a narrowed urethra, usually to treat a stricture or meatal stenosis and improve urine flow. A catheter may be left in briefly afterward, and some people need regular self-dilation to keep the urethra open. It should not be done during an untreated infection or in a person with a bleeding disorder.

topics.name: Urethral Stricture
topics.clinical_significance: A urethral stricture is scar tissue that narrows the urethra and can obstruct urine flow. It may cause a weak or split stream, difficulty starting, incomplete emptying, or repeat urinary infections or prostatitis. Trauma and gonorrhea are common causes, though sometimes no cause is found. Severe cases can cause a urethral pouch and, rarely, an abscess or fistula.

topics.name: Urethral Trauma
topics.clinical_significance: Urethral trauma may occur with pelvic fractures, straddle injuries, or medical procedures. Blood at the urethral opening or difficulty urinating is an important warning sign. In men with suspected injury, imaging of the urethra should be done before inserting a catheter, since catheterization can worsen a tear. Complications include infection, incontinence, erectile dysfunction, and later narrowing of the urethra.

topics.name: Urethroceles
topics.clinical_significance: A urethrocele is descent of the urethra into the front wall of the vagina, often together with bladder prolapse. It may cause vaginal pressure or a bulge, urine leakage, or trouble emptying the bladder; mild prolapse may cause no symptoms. Care depends on symptoms and may include pelvic floor exercises, a vaginal pessary, or surgery.

topics.name: URI
topics.clinical_significance: URI commonly refers here to the common cold: an acute, usually mild viral infection of the upper airways. It causes a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, and cough; symptoms usually settle within about 10 days, and care is supportive. It can worsen asthma or chronic bronchitis. Antibiotics do not treat an uncomplicated viral URI.

topics.name: Urinary Calculi
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary stones may cause severe, wave-like flank pain, nausea or vomiting, and blood in the urine. A stone that blocks urine flow can swell the kidney and temporarily reduce kidney function. Fever or chills may signal infection; infection with blockage needs urgent treatment. Stones can recur, so identifying their type and cause can help guide prevention.

topics.name: Urinary Frequency
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary frequency means needing to urinate often, usually in normal or small amounts; unlike polyuria, it does not mean that total urine output is high. It may be caused by infection, bladder overactivity, stones, or prostate or bladder-outlet problems. Fever with back pain or new leg weakness needs prompt assessment.

topics.name: Urinary Incontinence in Adults
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine. Leakage may follow a sudden urge, coughing or exertion, an overfull bladder, or problems with movement or thinking; more than one cause may be present. It can affect daily life, irritate the skin, and increase fall risk in older adults. Sudden onset with new back pain or leg weakness needs urgent assessment.

topics.name: Urinary Incontinence in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Urine wetting in a child is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Nighttime wetting can persist as bladder control develops, but daytime wetting, continuous leakage, or wetting that starts again after at least 6 months of dryness may point to a cause such as infection, constipation, or a urinary or nerve problem. Assessment and supportive care matter because wetting can affect a child physically and emotionally.

topics.name: Urinary Retention
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary retention is inability to urinate or to empty the bladder fully. Sudden inability to urinate needs urgent treatment, usually with a catheter. Long-lasting retention may cause frequent small voids, a feeling of incomplete emptying, or leakage from an overfull bladder, and can increase the risk of urinary infection and kidney damage. Causes include blockage (often from prostate problems in men), weak bladder muscles, medicines, or nerve disease.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infection in Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: UTIs are more common during pregnancy. Bacteria in the urine can be present without symptoms, so screening with a urine culture and treatment are important because infection may progress to kidney infection. Pyelonephritis can quickly cause severe illness, including sepsis, and urinary infection in pregnancy raises the risk of preterm labor and low birth weight. Fever, chills, or flank pain need prompt assessment.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) in Children
topics.clinical_significance: UTIs in young children may cause fever, poor feeding, vomiting, or poor growth without clear urinary symptoms; serious infection and sepsis can occur, especially in infants. A UTI, particularly a febrile or recurrent one, can signal an underlying urinary tract problem such as blockage or reflux. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are important, and imaging may be needed to look for an abnormality.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infections
topics.clinical_significance: A urinary tract infection usually affects the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis). It may cause burning, urgency, frequent urination, or pain in the lower abdomen or flank; some infections cause no symptoms. Most are bacterial, commonly due to E. coli. Kidney infection can spread to the blood and cause sepsis.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infections, Bacterial
topics.clinical_significance: Bacterial urinary infections usually affect the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis), most often because of E. coli. They may cause burning, urgency, frequent urination, or lower abdominal pain; kidney infection may cause flank pain, fever, and severe illness, including sepsis. Urine testing and culture help confirm infection and guide antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infections, Fungal
topics.clinical_significance: Fungi in urine often reflect colonization, especially in people with urinary catheters, rather than a true infection, and usually do not need treatment. Fungal UTI is more likely with catheters or other urinary procedures, diabetes, blockage, or a weakened immune system. True infection may cause burning, urgency, blood in the urine, or fever; fungal masses can block urine flow. Antifungal treatment is generally reserved for people with symptoms or high risk.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs), Introduction
topics.clinical_significance: UTI usually means infection of the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis). These sites can be hard to distinguish, and either infection can progress to urosepsis. Most UTIs are bacterial, often caused by E. coli; fungal or other unusual infections are more likely with a weakened immune system, urinary blockage, or recent urinary procedures. Urethritis is often caused by a sexually transmitted infection and is considered separately.

topics.name: Urinary Tract Obstruction
topics.clinical_significance: Urinary tract obstruction is partial or complete blockage, or impaired flow, anywhere from the kidney tubules to the urethral opening. It may cause pain or difficulty urinating; slow or long-lasting blockage may have few symptoms. Stones, prostate enlargement, scar tissue, tumors, birth defects, or poor bladder function can cause it. Ongoing blockage can lead to infection and kidney dysfunction, so it should be relieved promptly, especially if infection or inability to pass urine occurs.

topics.name: Urogenital Chlamydial Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Chlamydia is a common sexually transmitted infection and often causes no symptoms, especially in women. If untreated, it can spread to the upper reproductive tract and cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, or ectopic pregnancy; in men it can cause epididymitis. Infection can also pass to a newborn during birth and cause eye or lung disease. Testing is important even when symptoms are mild or absent.

topics.name: Urogenital Mycoplasmal Infections
topics.clinical_significance: Mycoplasma genitalium is a sexually transmitted cause of urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID); infection may cause no symptoms. PID can lead to infertility. Testing is mainly used for recurrent urethritis or cervicitis, or when a partner is infected. Antibiotic resistance affects treatment, so resistance testing is used when available.

topics.name: Urolithiasis
topics.clinical_significance: Urolithiasis means stones in the urinary tract. Stones may cause severe, wave-like flank pain, nausea or vomiting, and blood in the urine, especially when one lodges in a ureter. Blockage can reduce kidney function, and fever or chills may signal infection. Analyzing stones can help identify the cause and guide prevention of recurrence.

topics.name: Urologic Patient, Evaluation
topics.clinical_significance: Evaluating urinary symptoms helps find causes such as infection, stones, or blockage. It uses the symptom history, a focused examination, and usually urinalysis; suspected infection also calls for urine culture and testing for sexually transmitted infections. Blood in the urine needs a full evaluation, including for stones and cancer. Weak urine flow or worsening kidney function may require tests for blockage.

topics.name: Urticaria
topics.clinical_significance: Urticaria (hives) causes itchy, raised welts that move or fade. An episode is acute if it lasts less than 6 weeks and chronic if it continues longer; acute hives may follow medicines, foods, insect stings, or infections, while chronic hives often have no clear cause. Swelling of the tongue or throat, or trouble breathing, may mean dangerous airway swelling and needs emergency care.

topics.name: Uterine Adenomyosis
topics.clinical_significance: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue growing within the uterine muscle, which can enlarge the uterus. It may cause heavy menstrual bleeding, painful periods, and chronic pelvic pain; heavy bleeding can lead to anemia. Hormonal medicines may ease symptoms, while hysterectomy is the most effective treatment.

topics.name: Uterine and Apical Prolapse
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine prolapse is descent of the uterus; apical prolapse is descent of the top of the vagina after hysterectomy. It may cause a vaginal bulge or pressure, sexual problems, difficulty emptying the bladder, urine leakage, or constipation. Severe prolapse can expose and ulcerate vaginal tissue. A pessary can support the organs; surgery is another option when needed.

topics.name: Uterine Bleeding, Abnormal
topics.clinical_significance: Abnormal uterine bleeding is bleeding that is too frequent, irregular, prolonged, or heavy, or occurs between periods. Causes include ovulation or hormone problems, fibroids or polyps, bleeding disorders, and endometrial overgrowth or cancer. Pregnancy-related bleeding must be ruled out. Heavy or prolonged bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia or severe blood loss.

topics.name: Uterine Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine cancer in this topic means cancer of the uterine lining (endometrial cancer). It often causes abnormal bleeding, especially bleeding after menopause, and needs prompt assessment; most cases are confirmed by a uterine lining biopsy. Many cases are found while still confined to the uterus, but aggressive cancers can spread beyond it.

topics.name: Uterine Fibroids
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine fibroids are benign growths in the muscle of the uterus; many cause no symptoms. They can cause heavy bleeding, which may lead to anemia, or pelvic pain and pressure. Large fibroids may press on the bladder or bowel, and some can affect fertility or pregnancy. Care depends on symptoms and pregnancy plans and may include medicines, procedures, or surgery.

topics.name: Uterine Inversion
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine inversion is a rare obstetric emergency in which the top of the uterus turns inside out and may protrude into or beyond the vagina, usually during delivery of the placenta. It can cause severe postpartum bleeding, shock, and death. The uterus must be returned to its normal position immediately, with fluids or blood given if needed.

topics.name: Uterine Rupture
topics.clinical_significance: Uterine rupture is a rare tear through the uterine muscle in late pregnancy, before or during labor. It most often occurs at a scar from a prior cesarean or other uterine surgery, but can happen in an unscarred uterus. It can cause severe maternal bleeding and threaten the baby; constant severe abdominal pain, changes in the baby’s heart rate, or signs of blood loss need emergency action. Immediate surgery is required and may include cesarean delivery and, sometimes, hysterectomy.

topics.name: Uterine Sarcomas
