topics.clinical_significance: Uterine sarcomas are rare, aggressive cancers that arise from muscle or other supporting tissue in the uterus. They often cause abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, or a mass. They can spread, often to the lungs, and the outlook is poor if they have spread beyond the uterus. A biopsy may miss a sarcoma, so it is sometimes found only after surgery.

topics.name: Uterus, Inverted
topics.clinical_significance: An inverted uterus is a rare obstetric emergency in which the top of the uterus turns inside out and may protrude through the vagina, usually during delivery of the placenta. Severe bleeding, low blood pressure, shock, or death can result. The uterus must be manually returned to its normal position at once, with fluids or blood given if needed.

topics.name: UTIs
topics.clinical_significance: UTIs usually affect the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis), and it may be hard to tell which part is infected. Most are bacterial, commonly due to E. coli. Infection can spread and lead to urosepsis. Urethritis is usually a separate, often sexually transmitted infection.

topics.name: Uveitis and Related Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Uveitis can damage vision and may be caused by infection, injury, or a bodywide inflammatory disease. Eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, new floaters, or blurred vision need prompt assessment by an eye specialist. Finding the cause matters because treatment differs, and untreated inflammation can lead to lasting vision loss.

topics.name: Uveitis Caused by Systemic Rheumatic Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Some bodywide inflammatory diseases, such as ankylosing spondylitis, juvenile arthritis, and sarcoidosis, can cause uveitis. Repeated or long-lasting eye inflammation can damage vision. In children with juvenile arthritis, uveitis may cause no clear symptoms, so regular eye checks are important. Finding and treating both the eye inflammation and its underlying cause helps protect sight.

topics.name: Uveitis, Infectious
topics.clinical_significance: Infections such as toxoplasmosis and herpes viruses can inflame the eye and damage sight, especially when the retina or other important visual structures are affected. Prompt assessment by an eye specialist helps identify the germ and guide treatment. Treatment must target the infection; for toxoplasmosis, steroids must not be used without antimicrobial medicine.

topics.name: Uveitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Uveitis can affect different parts of the eye. Symptoms may include pain, redness, light sensitivity, floaters, or reduced vision; inflammation toward the back of the eye may cause little pain while still threatening sight. Untreated or poorly controlled uveitis can cause lasting vision loss, cataracts, glaucoma, or retinal damage. Prompt assessment by an eye specialist is important to find the cause and choose the right treatment.

topics.name: Vaccination in Children, Effectiveness and Safety
topics.clinical_significance: Routine childhood vaccines prevent many serious infections and their complications. Common side effects include fever and soreness, redness, or swelling where the shot was given. Rare problems may only be found after a vaccine is in wider use, so safety monitoring continues after approval. A health problem reported after vaccination does not by itself prove the vaccine caused it. Following current vaccination guidance helps protect children from preventable disease.

topics.name: Vaccine Hesitancy
topics.clinical_significance: When caregivers delay or decline recommended vaccines, children remain at risk for infections that vaccination can prevent. If many people are unvaccinated, these diseases can spread more easily, putting the whole community at risk, including people who cannot receive certain vaccines. Clinicians can help by asking about concerns and explaining vaccine benefits, risks, and evidence in clear, respectful language.

topics.name: Vaginal Anomalies
topics.clinical_significance: Congenital vaginal differences vary in their effects. Vaginal agenesis may be found when periods do not start; an obstruction, such as an imperforate hymen, can trap menstrual blood and cause repeated pelvic pain. Cervical or uterine differences often occur as well, and vaginal agenesis may be linked with a kidney anomaly. Examination and imaging help define the anatomy and guide care, which may include dilation or surgery.

topics.name: Vaginal Bleeding
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding outside the usual menstrual pattern can come from the vagina, cervix, or uterus, and sometimes from the urinary or digestive tract. Causes range from hormonal changes and benign conditions to pregnancy complications or cancer. Heavy or ongoing bleeding can cause anemia or, rarely, shock. Pregnancy should be checked in reproductive-age patients, and any bleeding after menopause needs evaluation to rule out gynecologic cancer.

topics.name: Vaginal Bleeding During Early Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding in early pregnancy does not always mean miscarriage, but it needs prompt medical assessment. Miscarriage is a common cause, and the most dangerous cause is ectopic pregnancy, which can rupture and cause life-threatening internal bleeding. Evaluation checks the pregnant person’s stability and where the pregnancy is located. The risk of miscarriage varies with the amount and pattern of bleeding.

topics.name: Vaginal Bleeding During Late Pregnancy
topics.clinical_significance: Bleeding after 20 weeks may be a small amount of blood-tinged mucus as labor begins, but it can also signal serious problems such as placental abruption, placenta previa, vasa previa, or uterine rupture. These conditions can cause severe blood loss and threaten the pregnant person or fetus. The visible bleeding may be slight even when blood loss is serious, so prompt obstetric assessment and monitoring are important.

topics.name: Vaginal Bleeding in Children
topics.clinical_significance: A small amount of bleeding in the first 1 to 2 weeks after birth can occur as the newborn’s hormone levels fall. At other times before puberty, vaginal bleeding is abnormal and needs prompt medical assessment. Common causes include vaginal infection, a foreign object, or injury; clinicians also assess for possible sexual abuse and rare tumors. Heavy bleeding or severe pain needs urgent care.

topics.name: Vaginal Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Primary vaginal cancer is rare; cancer that has spread to the vagina or grown into it from a nearby site is more common. Most primary cases are squamous cell cancers, often linked to persistent HPV infection. Abnormal bleeding, including bleeding after sex or after menopause, is the most common symptom. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis, and the cancer’s stage guides treatment and helps determine outlook.

topics.name: Vaginal Wall Prolapse, Anterior and Posterior
topics.clinical_significance: In anterior vaginal wall prolapse, the bladder or urethra bulges into the vagina; this may cause urine leakage or difficulty emptying the bladder. In posterior prolapse, the rectum or small bowel may bulge into the vagina, causing pressure or difficulty emptying the bowel. Mild prolapse may cause no symptoms. Treatment depends on how much it bothers the patient and may include pelvic floor exercises, a vaginal support device (pessary), or surgery.

topics.name: Vaginitis, Cervicitis, and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Vaginitis may be infectious or noninfectious and can cause discharge, itching, or burning. Cervicitis may cause discharge or bleeding, but can also have no symptoms; it is often due to a sexually transmitted infection. Infection can spread upward and cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which may lead to an abscess, infertility, pregnancy outside the uterus, or long-term pelvic pain. Because symptoms can be mild or overlap, testing and timely treatment are important.

topics.name: Vaginitis in Children
topics.clinical_significance: Before puberty, vaginitis often causes vulvar itching, burning, redness, or discharge. Common causes include external irritants and infection; a foreign object may cause foul-smelling or bloody discharge. Yeast infection is uncommon in most children. Persistent, bloody, or foul-smelling discharge, or symptoms with fever or pain, need medical assessment to find the cause and check for injury or other serious problems.

topics.name: Vaginitis, Inflammatory
topics.clinical_significance: Desquamative inflammatory vaginitis is an uncommon, often recurrent inflammation without evidence of infection. It occurs most often around or after menopause or in other low-estrogen states. It can cause pus-like discharge, vaginal irritation, and pain with sex or urination. Testing helps distinguish it from infections with similar symptoms; treatment may include vaginal clindamycin or hydrocortisone.

topics.name: Vaginitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Vaginitis is inflammation of the vaginal lining; the vulva may also be inflamed. It can result from infection, such as bacterial vaginosis, yeast, or trichomoniasis, or from noninfectious irritation. It may cause unusual discharge, odor, itching, burning, or pain, but these symptoms can have other causes too. Examination and testing help identify the cause because treatment differs.

topics.name: Valerian
topics.clinical_significance: Valerian is often taken as a sleep aid, but evidence that it helps insomnia is inconsistent, and one review found no benefit on objective sleep measures. It may cause drowsiness and increase the effects of alcohol or sedative medicines, making driving or other alert activities unsafe. It is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

topics.name: Valley Fever
topics.clinical_significance: Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis) follows inhalation of Coccidioides spores, usually from disturbed soil in endemic regions. Most infections cause no symptoms or a mild, self-limited lung illness. Some cause pneumonia or spread beyond the lungs to the skin, bones or joints, or the brain coverings. Severe or spreading disease is more likely in people with weakened immunity, during pregnancy, or with other risk factors.

topics.name: Valvular Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Heart valves can become narrowed (stenosis) or leaky (regurgitation), disrupting blood flow and straining the heart. Valve disease may cause heart changes before symptoms appear; later symptoms can include shortness of breath, fatigue, and leg swelling. Echocardiography shows how severe the problem is. Mild disease may only need monitoring, while more severe disease that causes symptoms or affects heart function may need valve repair or replacement.

topics.name: Vancomycin
topics.clinical_significance: Vancomycin is used for serious infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria, including many MRSA infections. IV vancomycin treats infections throughout the body; oral vancomycin is used for certain intestinal infections, such as C. difficile. IV doses must be adjusted for kidney function and may need blood-level monitoring. Infusing it too quickly can cause flushing and itching. Kidney injury is uncommon but more likely with high doses or other kidney-toxic medicines; hearing problems are uncommon and more likely with other hearing-toxic medicines.

topics.name: Vaping
topics.clinical_significance: Vaping delivers nicotine or other drugs in an inhaled aerosol. Nicotine can cause addiction, even in people who would not otherwise smoke. The aerosol can carry fine particles and harmful chemicals into the lungs. Contaminated products, especially some THC products, have caused severe lung injury (EVALI), which can require breathing support. E-cigarettes may help some adults stop smoking, but nicotine addiction can continue.

topics.name: Variably Protease-Sensitive Prionopathy (VPSPr)
topics.clinical_significance: VPSPr is a very rare prion disease that arises without an inherited PRNP gene mutation. It causes progressive problems with thinking, behavior, and speech; poor coordination and parkinsonism may also develop. Diagnosis is difficult because routine MRI, EEG, and spinal fluid tests are often not helpful. Treatment is supportive.

topics.name: Variant Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Variant (vasospastic) angina is caused by a temporary spasm of a large coronary artery. Chest pain usually occurs at rest, often at night, and an ECG may show temporary changes during an attack. Nitroglycerin usually relieves the pain. Some people also have fixed coronary artery narrowing, which increases risk and worsens outlook when it is extensive.

topics.name: Variant Influenza
topics.clinical_significance: Variant influenza is illness in people caused by influenza A viruses that normally circulate in pigs. Infection usually follows direct or indirect contact with infected pigs; spread between people is rare. Symptoms resemble seasonal flu, and specialized testing may be needed to identify the virus. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus now circulates as a seasonal flu strain and is distinct from current swine-origin variant infections.

topics.name: Varicella
topics.clinical_significance: Varicella (chickenpox) is the highly contagious first infection with varicella-zoster virus. It causes an itchy rash with spots and blisters at different stages. It is usually mild in healthy children but can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation, or other severe illness, especially in adults, newborns, and people with weakened immunity; infection during pregnancy can also be severe. The virus remains dormant in nerves and can later reactivate as shingles.

topics.name: Varicella Vaccine
topics.clinical_significance: The varicella vaccine is a live, weakened-virus vaccine that prevents most cases of chickenpox and is highly effective against severe disease. It is routinely given in childhood and is also used for adolescents and adults without evidence of immunity. Because it is a live vaccine, it is not given during pregnancy or to people with severe immune deficiency.

topics.name: Varicella-Zoster Virus Ophthalmicus
topics.clinical_significance: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is shingles in the nerve area of the forehead that can involve the eye. It causes a one-sided painful blistering rash; eye inflammation may scar the cornea or lead to glaucoma and vision loss. A rash on the tip of the nose signals a higher risk of eye involvement, and early antiviral treatment lowers eye complications. Nerve pain may persist after the rash heals.

topics.name: Varices
topics.clinical_significance: Esophageal and gastric varices are enlarged veins in the lower esophagus or upper stomach, usually caused by high pressure in the portal vein system, often due to cirrhosis. They may cause no symptoms until they bleed; rupture can cause sudden, severe, and sometimes fatal bleeding.

topics.name: Varicose Veins
topics.clinical_significance: Varicose veins are enlarged surface veins, usually in the legs. They may result from faulty vein valves or weak vein walls, though the cause is often unclear. Many cause no symptoms; others cause leg aching, pressure, or fatigue. Skin changes, ulcers, clots within the veins, or bleeding can occur but are less common.

topics.name: Variola
topics.clinical_significance: Variola (smallpox) is a highly contagious disease caused by the variola virus. It causes a severe illness with a widespread pustular rash and has a case fatality rate of about 30%. Natural smallpox was eradicated; the last known case was in 1977, and the World Health Organization declared it eradicated in 1980. Accidental or deliberate release of stored virus remains a concern.

topics.name: Vasa Previa
topics.clinical_significance: Vasa previa occurs when fetal blood vessels run through the membranes over or very near the cervix without the protection of the umbilical cord. If the membranes rupture, the vessels can tear and cause rapid fetal blood loss, distress, or death. Prenatal diagnosis allows delivery by planned cesarean before labor or membrane rupture.

topics.name: Vascular Access
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular access provides a route into a blood vessel to give fluids or medicines, draw blood, monitor pressure, or provide dialysis. It may use a peripheral or central catheter, or a surgically created fistula or graft for dialysis. Catheters can cause infection or blood clots; central catheter placement can also cause bleeding or a collapsed lung.

topics.name: Vascular Bleeding Disorders, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular bleeding disorders are conditions in which abnormal or fragile blood vessels cause bleeding into the skin or mucous membranes. This may appear as tiny red-purple spots or larger areas of bruising. Blood-clotting tests are usually normal, and serious blood loss is uncommon except in some disorders such as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. Repeated bleeding can cause iron-deficiency anemia.

topics.name: Vascular Cognitive Impairment and Dementia
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular cognitive impairment and dementia are declines in thinking caused by reduced blood flow or bleeding in the brain, often from strokes or small-vessel disease. Changes may occur in steps after strokes or progress slowly; planning and thinking speed may be affected, sometimes with weakness or walking problems. It is a common cause of dementia in older adults and may occur together with Alzheimer disease.

topics.name: Vascular Disorders of the Liver
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular disorders of the liver interfere with blood flow into or out of the organ. Reduced blood flow can injure liver cells or bile ducts; blocked drainage can cause liver congestion, enlargement, high pressure in the portal vein, or fluid in the abdomen. Causes include blood clots in liver vessels, cirrhosis, and right-sided heart failure.

topics.name: Vascular Disorders of the Liver, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: The liver receives blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery and drains through the hepatic veins. Low blood flow can injure liver cells or bile ducts; blocked venous drainage can cause congestion, liver enlargement, high pressure in the portal vein, and fluid in the abdomen. Examples include portal or hepatic vein blockage, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.

topics.name: Vascular Gastrointestinal Lesions
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular gastrointestinal lesions are abnormal blood vessels in the digestive tract that can cause painless, repeated bleeding, usually in small or moderate amounts. Angiodysplasia is a common cause of lower intestinal bleeding in older adults; a Dieulafoy lesion can rarely cause major bleeding. Repeated blood loss may lead to iron-deficiency anemia.

topics.name: Vascular Lesions of the Skin
topics.clinical_significance: Vascular skin lesions are abnormal blood vessel growths or malformations. Some develop later, while others are present at birth or appear soon after; infantile hemangiomas are vascular tumors, whereas capillary, venous, arteriovenous, and lymphatic malformations are structural defects present from birth that persist throughout life. Their effects depend on the type and location.

topics.name: Vascular Spider
topics.clinical_significance: A spider angioma is a small red skin lesion with a central blood vessel and thin vessels radiating outward; pressing the center makes it fade temporarily. One or a few are common in healthy people. Many may occur with cirrhosis, and lesions may also appear during pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use.

topics.name: Vasculitis
topics.clinical_significance: Vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessels. It can damage or narrow vessel walls, reduce blood flow, and injure tissues or organs; effects depend on the size and location of the vessels involved. It may affect vessels anywhere in the body and can occur on its own or be triggered by infection, medicines, toxins, another inflammatory disease, or cancer.

topics.name: Vasculitis, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Vasculitis includes many diseases in which blood vessel walls become inflamed. The affected vessel size and organs determine the symptoms, which can include fever, fatigue, weight loss, joint pain, or skin spots and bruises. Vessel damage or clots can block blood flow and injure organs; lung bleeding, kidney inflammation, intestinal ischemia, or vision loss can be life-threatening. Vasculitis may be primary or triggered by infection, medicines, toxins, another inflammatory disease, or cancer.

topics.name: Vasospastic Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina is chest pain caused by a temporary spasm of a large coronary artery. It usually occurs at rest, often at night; an ECG may show temporary ST-segment elevation during an attack, and nitroglycerin usually relieves the pain. Coexisting fixed coronary artery narrowing worsens the outlook.

topics.name: Vegetative State and Minimally Conscious State
topics.clinical_significance: After severe brain injury, a vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness syndrome) causes no awareness or purposeful response, although the eyes may open at times and basic brainstem functions remain. In a minimally conscious state, there are small but definite signs of awareness, such as following a command or tracking an object. Distinguishing the two matters because recovery is more likely from a minimally conscious state, and misdiagnosis can affect prognosis.

topics.name: Velopharyngeal Insufficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Velopharyngeal insufficiency is incomplete closure between the mouth and nose due to a structural problem with the soft palate. Air escapes through the nose during speech, causing a nasal-sounding voice and difficulty making pressure sounds; severe cases can cause food or liquid to pass into the nose. It often occurs with a cleft or short palate.

topics.name: Venereal Warts
topics.clinical_significance: Venereal (genital) warts are soft, usually painless growths caused most often by low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. They spread through sexual skin-to-skin contact and may persist, spread locally, or return after treatment, especially in people with weakened immunity. These HPV types differ from the high-risk types that cause most HPV-related cancers.

topics.name: Veno-Occlusive Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Veno-occlusive disease, now called sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, is injury that blocks blood flow through tiny liver vessels; it is not a clot in the large hepatic veins. It can follow stem-cell transplantation, radiation, or exposure to certain medicines or toxins. It may cause tender liver enlargement, jaundice, and fluid buildup in the abdomen; severe cases can lead to liver failure.

topics.name: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia
topics.clinical_significance: Ventilator-associated pneumonia is pneumonia that begins at least 48 hours after a breathing tube is placed or within 48 hours after it is removed. It may cause fever, increased airway secretions, low oxygen levels, or a new or worsening lung opacity. It often involves antibiotic-resistant hospital bacteria and can be serious, especially in people who are already critically ill.

topics.name: Ventilatory Failure
topics.clinical_significance: Ventilatory failure (hypercapnic respiratory failure) occurs when breathing cannot remove enough carbon dioxide, so it builds up in the blood and makes the blood more acidic. Causes include severe COPD or asthma, medicines that slow breathing, and respiratory muscle weakness. It may cause shortness of breath and confusion; severe cases can be life-threatening.

topics.name: Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)
topics.clinical_significance: Ventricular fibrillation is a chaotic electrical rhythm that makes the lower heart chambers quiver instead of pumping blood. It causes sudden cardiac arrest and loss of consciousness, and is usually fatal within minutes without immediate CPR and defibrillation. It often occurs with underlying heart disease, and survivors may be at risk of recurrence.

topics.name: Ventricular Premature Beats (VPB)
topics.clinical_significance: Ventricular premature beats (VPBs), also called premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), are early heartbeats that start in the ventricles. They are common and often harmless in people without structural heart disease, though they may feel like a skipped beat. Very frequent VPBs can weaken the heart and cause a reversible cardiomyopathy; in people with heart disease, frequent VPBs are linked to greater risk.

topics.name: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
topics.clinical_significance: A ventricular septal defect is an opening between the heart's lower chambers. Blood usually flows from the left ventricle to the right, sending extra blood to the lungs. Small defects may close on their own and cause no symptoms. Larger defects can cause heart failure, breathing difficulty or fatigue during feeding, and poor growth in infancy; if untreated, they can lead to high lung blood pressure and reversal of blood flow (Eisenmenger syndrome).

topics.name: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
topics.clinical_significance: Ventricular tachycardia is a fast heart rhythm that starts in the ventricles. Brief episodes may cause no symptoms, but sustained episodes can make the heart pump poorly, causing palpitations, fainting, shock, or cardiac arrest. It often occurs with underlying heart disease and can progress to ventricular fibrillation.

topics.name: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is recurrent, usually seasonal allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea, most often in children and teenagers. It causes intense itching, redness, sensitivity to light, and thick, stringy mucus. Corneal ulcers or scarring can occur and may reduce vision.

topics.name: Verrucae Vulgaris
topics.clinical_significance: Common warts are benign growths of the outer skin layer caused by human papillomavirus. They can spread to nearby skin and often clear without treatment, though some last for years. They are usually painless but may hurt when they occur on weight-bearing areas such as the soles.

topics.name: Vertebral Compression Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: These fractures are often caused by osteoporosis and can occur after little or no injury. Many cause no symptoms; others cause back pain, and repeated fractures can lead to height loss and a rounded upper back. A vertebral fracture also raises the risk of future fractures.

topics.name: Vesicant Chemical-Warfare Agents
topics.clinical_significance: Vesicant agents such as mustard compounds, lewisite, and phosgene oxime can cause severe skin blisters and injury to the eyes and airways. Symptoms from mustard exposure may be delayed for hours. Severe exposure can suppress bone marrow, and long-term effects can include chronic eye disease and cancers of the skin or airways.

topics.name: Vesicoureteral Reflux and Reflux Nephropathy
topics.clinical_significance: Vesicoureteral reflux lets urine flow backward from the bladder toward the kidneys. If infected urine reaches the kidney, it can cause scarring (reflux nephropathy), especially with severe reflux or repeated urinary infections. Kidney scarring may later lead to high blood pressure or chronic kidney disease, although reflux may cause few symptoms at first.

topics.name: Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR)
topics.clinical_significance: Vesicoureteral reflux is backward flow of urine from the bladder into a ureter and sometimes the kidney. It raises the risk of urinary tract infections; infection reaching the kidney can cause scarring, which may later lead to high blood pressure or reduced kidney function. Mild to moderate reflux in young children often resolves as they grow.

topics.name: Vesicular Rickettsiosis
topics.clinical_significance: Vesicular rickettsiosis (rickettsialpox) is a usually mild, self-limited infection caused by Rickettsia akari and spread by infected mites associated with mice and other rodents. A small sore with a dark scab forms at the bite site, followed about a week later by fever and a widespread blister-like rash.

topics.name: Vestibular Neuronitis
topics.clinical_significance: Vestibular neuronitis causes a sudden, severe attack of spinning vertigo, often with nausea and vomiting, but usually without hearing loss or tinnitus. Symptoms generally improve over days to weeks, although imbalance may persist. Because stroke can also cause sudden vertigo, other causes may need to be ruled out.

topics.name: Vestibular Schwannoma
topics.clinical_significance: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is a usually slow-growing, noncancerous tumor of the vestibular part of cranial nerve VIII. It often causes gradually worsening hearing loss in one ear, sometimes with tinnitus or imbalance. A large tumor can press on nearby nerves or the brainstem.

topics.name: Vincent Infection or Vincent Angina
topics.clinical_significance: Vincent angina (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, or trench mouth) is a rapidly developing gum infection. It causes sudden gum pain and bleeding, ulcers between the teeth, and sometimes foul breath, fever, or feeling ill. It is more likely with poor oral hygiene, smoking, stress, poor nutrition, or weakened immunity, and can destroy gum tissue.

topics.name: Violent Behavior in Children and Adolescents
topics.clinical_significance: Children and adolescents may have occasional fights, but most do not develop a lasting pattern of violence or commit violent crimes. Repeated violence, including bullying, can cause physical injury and emotional or school problems for those targeted. Violence that begins before puberty is linked to a higher risk of later criminal behavior; associated factors include exposure to violence, substance use, developmental problems, poverty, gang involvement, and access to firearms.

topics.name: Vipoma
topics.clinical_significance: A vipoma is a rare tumor, usually of the pancreas, that releases vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). It causes prolonged, large-volume watery diarrhea that can lead to severe dehydration, low blood potassium, and excess acid in the blood. More than half of vipomas are cancerous.

topics.name: Viral Cellular Tropism
topics.clinical_significance: Viral cellular tropism is a virus's ability to infect particular types of cells. It helps explain which tissues and organs an infection affects and what symptoms it causes. Some viruses can affect more than one organ system.

topics.name: Viral Conjunctivitis
topics.clinical_significance: Viral conjunctivitis is a highly contagious infection of the membrane covering the eye, usually caused by adenovirus. It causes redness, irritation, and watery discharge, often starting in one eye and spreading to the other. Most cases clear within 1 to 3 weeks, but severe infection can affect the cornea and blur vision.

topics.name: Viral Disorders, Types
topics.clinical_significance: Viral infections can be grouped by the tissues or organs they mainly affect, such as the respiratory tract, gut, skin, liver, or nervous system. This grouping can help relate an infection to its symptoms, although some viruses affect several organ systems.

topics.name: Viral Infections in Infants and Children, Common
topics.clinical_significance: Common childhood viral infections include measles, mumps, rubella, roseola, and parvovirus B19 infection. Many are mild, but some can cause serious problems such as brain inflammation, severe anemia, or harm to a fetus during pregnancy. Vaccines prevent several of these infections, including measles, mumps, and rubella.

topics.name: Viral Labyrinthitis
topics.clinical_significance: Viral labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear that can cause severe vertigo along with hearing loss, tinnitus, or both. The hearing symptoms help distinguish it from vestibular neuronitis, which causes vertigo without hearing loss or tinnitus. Balance problems may continue after the initial illness improves.

topics.name: Viral Meningitis
topics.clinical_significance: Viral meningitis is inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord caused by a virus. It commonly causes fever, headache, and a stiff neck and is usually milder than bacterial meningitis, often resolving over weeks. Bacterial meningitis can look similar but is much more dangerous, so identifying the cause is important.

topics.name: Viral Pleuritis
topics.clinical_significance: Viral pleuritis is inflammation of the lining around the lungs, most often caused by coxsackie B virus. It causes sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths or coughing; some enterovirus infections also cause fever and chest muscle spasms. The illness usually resolves on its own, but pneumonia and pulmonary embolism can cause similar pain and may need to be ruled out.

topics.name: Viral Respiratory Infections, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Respiratory viruses infect the upper or lower airways and cause illnesses such as the common cold, bronchiolitis, croup, or pneumonia. Severity ranges from mild to severe; infants, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease are more likely to become seriously ill. Infection can also worsen an existing heart or lung condition or be followed by a bacterial infection.

topics.name: Viral Skin Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Viral skin diseases include warts, molluscum contagiosum, and rare infections passed from animals to people. They cause skin growths or other lesions; most stay limited to the skin and are benign, but some can spread by contact, persist, or become widespread in people with weakened immunity.

topics.name: Viral Tissue Tropism
topics.clinical_significance: Viral tissue tropism is a virus's ability to infect particular tissues, such as the respiratory tract, skin, or liver. It helps explain which organs and symptoms are affected, although some viruses spread across several organ systems. Cellular tropism refers to the specific cell types a virus can infect.

topics.name: Viruses
topics.clinical_significance: A virus is an infectious particle with DNA or RNA inside a protein coat; it can reproduce only inside a living cell. Viral infections range from symptom-free to severe, and some viruses remain dormant or cause long-term illness. Vaccines prevent some viral diseases, and antiviral medicines work against selected viruses.

topics.name: Viruses, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Viral infections range from symptom-free to severe. Depending on the virus, they spread through respiratory droplets, contact, body fluids, or insect bites. Some infections clear, while others remain dormant and reactivate or cause long-term illness; certain viruses can also cause or contribute to cancer.

topics.name: Visceral Larva Migrans
topics.clinical_significance: Migration of Toxocara larvae through internal organs can cause fever, poor appetite, an enlarged liver or spleen, rash, and lung inflammation or wheezing. Brain or heart involvement is rare but can be fatal.

topics.name: Vision Loss, Acute
topics.clinical_significance: Rapid vision loss may signal a serious problem in the eye, optic nerve, or brain, including a stroke-related event. Urgent assessment is needed because prompt treatment may preserve vision or prevent further harm.

topics.name: Vitamin A Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Early deficiency can cause poor vision in dim light. If severe or untreated, it can dry and damage the eyes and lead to blindness; it also weakens resistance to infection.

topics.name: Vitamin A Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Taking too much vitamin A can cause headache, vomiting, increased pressure inside the skull, skin changes, and liver injury. High doses during pregnancy can cause birth defects; toxicity usually improves when excess vitamin A is stopped.

topics.name: Vitamin B1 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Thiamine deficiency can damage nerves, strain the heart, or cause Wernicke encephalopathy, with confusion, poor coordination, and abnormal eye movements. Without prompt treatment, brain injury may become permanent or lead to coma and death.

topics.name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause anemia with abnormally large red blood cells, but nerve and brain damage may occur even without anemia. Numbness, weakness, poor balance, or confusion can develop, and lasting nerve damage may result if treatment is delayed.

topics.name: Vitamin B2 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Riboflavin deficiency often occurs with other B vitamin deficiencies. It commonly causes a sore throat, cracks at the corners of the mouth and lips, and inflammation of the tongue or skin; anemia and eye inflammation can also occur.

topics.name: Vitamin B3 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Niacin deficiency (pellagra) can cause a rash on sun-exposed skin, mouth inflammation, diarrhea, and changes in thinking or behavior. Untreated disease can become severe, but niacin treatment usually works.

topics.name: Vitamin B3 Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: High doses of nicotinic acid, a form of vitamin B3, can cause skin flushing and itching. Larger doses can raise blood sugar and uric acid and may damage the liver, especially with some slow-release products.

topics.name: Vitamin B6 Deficiency and Dependency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin B6 deficiency or impaired use can cause nerve problems, skin and mouth inflammation, anemia, confusion, or seizures. Seizures in infants may not respond to usual seizure medicines, so this cause should be considered.

topics.name: Vitamin B6 Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Taking very high doses of vitamin B6 supplements can damage sensory nerves, causing numbness, poor position sense, and difficulty walking. Recovery after stopping the supplements may be slow and sometimes incomplete.

topics.name: Vitamin B9 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and, during pregnancy, raises the risk of fetal neural tube defects. Because it can look like vitamin B12 deficiency, B12 should also be checked; folate alone may improve the anemia while B12-related nerve damage worsens.

topics.name: Vitamin C Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Severe vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) weakens connective tissue, causing swollen or bleeding gums, easy bruising or other bleeding, and poor wound healing. In children, it can impair bone growth; vitamin C treatment usually reverses the symptoms.

topics.name: Vitamin C Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Very high doses of vitamin C can cause nausea, diarrhea, and kidney stones. In people with hemochromatosis or thalassemia, they may worsen iron overload.

topics.name: Vitamin D Deficiency and Dependency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin D deficiency weakens bone mineralization, causing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. It can cause bone pain, muscle weakness, and fractures. Rare inherited problems with vitamin D metabolism can cause dependency and may need specialized treatment.

topics.name: Vitamin D Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Excess vitamin D can raise blood calcium, causing nausea, vomiting, weakness, thirst, and frequent urination. Severe toxicity can damage the kidneys, and this damage may be permanent.

topics.name: Vitamin Deficiency, Dependency, and Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin deficiencies can cause problems such as anemia, nerve or bone disease, or vision loss. Rare inherited defects can prevent normal use of a vitamin, while very high supplement doses may cause toxicity. The specific vitamin and cause guide treatment.

topics.name: Vitamin D–Resistant Rickets
topics.clinical_significance: Low blood phosphate prevents normal bone hardening despite usual vitamin D treatment. The disorder is usually inherited and can cause rickets or osteomalacia, bone pain, bowed legs, short stature, and fractures; treatment must address the phosphate problem.

topics.name: Vitamin E Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin E deficiency can cause anemia by making red blood cells break down and can damage nerves, leading to weakness, poor coordination, or reduced sensation. In adults, it is uncommon and is usually linked to poor absorption of fat.

topics.name: Vitamin E Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: High-dose vitamin E can cause weakness, fatigue, nausea, or diarrhea. The main concern is bleeding, especially at doses over 1000 mg per day or when taken with warfarin.

topics.name: Vitamin K Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Low vitamin K impairs blood clotting and can cause easy bruising or dangerous bleeding, including bleeding in a newborn’s brain. Newborn vitamin K prevents this; in adults, deficiency often occurs with fat malabsorption or certain medicines.

topics.name: Vitamin K Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamin K1 from food is not toxic, even in large amounts. The synthetic form menadione can break down red blood cells and cause jaundice; in newborns, severe jaundice can injure the brain. Menadione should not be used to treat vitamin K deficiency.

topics.name: Vitamins, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Vitamins support essential body functions, so deficiencies can cause problems such as anemia, nerve or bone disease, and vision loss. Rare inherited conditions can impair vitamin use, and megadoses of some supplements can be toxic. The specific vitamin and cause guide treatment.

topics.name: Vitiligo
topics.clinical_significance: Vitiligo causes patches of skin to lose color and is not contagious. It is sometimes linked with autoimmune conditions, especially thyroid disease; treatment may restore some pigment or even out skin tone.

topics.name: Vocal Cord Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: The vocal folds close when they should open during breathing in, causing episodes of noisy breathing, throat tightness, or breathlessness that can be mistaken for asthma. Speech therapy can teach breathing techniques that may ease symptoms.

topics.name: Vocal Fold Dysfunction
topics.clinical_significance: The vocal folds close when they should open during breathing in, causing episodes of noisy breathing, throat tightness, or breathlessness that can be mistaken for asthma. Speech therapy can teach breathing techniques that may ease symptoms.

topics.name: Vocal Fold Paralysis
topics.clinical_significance: Paralysis of one vocal fold often causes a hoarse, breathy voice and can let food or liquid enter the airway. Paralysis of both folds can narrow the airway, causing noisy breathing and breathing difficulty that may be life-threatening.

topics.name: Vocal Fold Polyps, Nodules, and Granulomas
topics.clinical_significance: These usually benign lesions can follow vocal strain or chronic irritation and cause gradual hoarseness and a breathy voice. If hoarseness lasts more than 3 weeks, the vocal folds should be examined and a biopsy may be needed to rule out cancer. Voice therapy and treatment of irritants or reflux can help.

topics.name: Voiding Disorders
topics.clinical_significance: Voiding disorders interfere with storing or passing urine and can cause leakage (incontinence) or difficulty emptying the bladder (retention). They may involve the urinary tract, nerves, muscles, or mobility and thinking; finding the cause guides treatment.

topics.name: Voiding, Overview
topics.clinical_significance: Normal urination depends on coordinated nerve signals, bladder and sphincter muscles, and the ability to recognize the need to urinate and reach a toilet. Problems in any of these can cause urine leakage or retention.

topics.name: Volatile Solvents
topics.clinical_significance: Breathing volatile solvent fumes can quickly impair thinking and coordination and may cause seizures, suffocation, or a fatal abnormal heart rhythm. Repeated exposure can damage the brain, nerves, lungs, or liver.

topics.name: Volume Depletion
topics.clinical_significance: Loss of salt and water, such as from vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, or bleeding, reduces circulating blood volume. It can cause dry mouth, a fast heartbeat, and low blood pressure on standing; severe loss can impair organ blood flow and lead to shock or kidney injury.

topics.name: Von Hippel-Lindau Disease (VHL)
topics.clinical_significance: VHL is an inherited condition that can cause tumors and cysts in several organs. These include blood-vessel tumors in the brain, spinal cord, or retina, and kidney cancer. Regular lifelong screening helps find tumors early, before they cause harm.

topics.name: Von Willebrand Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder caused by too little or faulty von Willebrand factor, which helps platelets stick and form clots. It can cause easy bruising, nose or gum bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, and prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery.

topics.name: Voyeurism
topics.clinical_significance: Voyeurism is sexual arousal from watching an unsuspecting person who is naked, undressing, or having sex. This interest alone is not a mental disorder. Voyeuristic disorder is diagnosed in adults when the urges last at least 6 months and are acted on with a nonconsenting person, or cause significant distress or problems in daily life.

topics.name: Voyeuristic Disorder
topics.clinical_significance: A disorder in adults involving recurrent, intense sexual arousal from watching unsuspecting people who are naked, undressing, or having sex. It is diagnosed when this pattern lasts at least 6 months and the person acts on the urges with someone who has not consented, or the urges cause significant distress or interfere with daily life.

topics.name: Vulvar Cancer
topics.clinical_significance: Vulvar cancer is usually a squamous cell cancer that appears as a visible or palpable lesion, sometimes with itching or an ulcer. A persistent lesion, especially one that does not respond to treatment, needs biopsy. The cancer can spread to groin lymph nodes, so its extent guides treatment.

topics.name: Vulvar Endometriomas
topics.clinical_significance: A rare cyst of endometrial tissue in the vulva, often at the site of an episiotomy or childbirth injury. It may swell and become more painful around menstruation or during sex; rupture can cause severe pain. Pelvic examination and biopsy confirm the diagnosis, and treatment is usually surgical removal.

topics.name: Vulvar Inclusion and Epidermal Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Common benign vulvar cysts: inclusion cysts form when surface skin cells are trapped under the skin, while epidermal cysts form when oil-gland ducts are blocked. They are often small and symptom-free, but can become infected, red, and tender, sometimes making sex painful. Symptomatic cysts may be removed; unusual or concerning lumps may need biopsy.

topics.name: Vulvar Sebaceous Cysts
topics.clinical_significance: Vulvar sebaceous (epidermal) cysts form when oil-gland ducts become blocked, trapping secretions under the skin. They are often small and symptom-free but can become infected, red, and tender, sometimes making sex painful. Symptomatic cysts may be removed; an unusual or concerning lump may need biopsy.

topics.name: Vulvovaginal Pruritus or Vaginal Discharge
topics.clinical_significance: Vulvar itching or vaginal discharge can result from infection (such as bacterial vaginosis, yeast, or trichomoniasis), skin irritation or disease, or hormonal changes; the cause varies with age and life stage. Normal discharge is usually clear or white, odorless, and not irritating. Because treatment depends on the cause, persistent or unusual symptoms need evaluation; pelvic pain or fever may signal a more serious infection.

topics.name: Vulvovaginal Pruritus or Vaginal Discharge in Children
topics.clinical_significance: In prepubertal children, vulvar itching or vaginal discharge is usually due to irritation or vulvovaginitis; infection or a vaginal foreign body may also be the cause. Yeast infection is uncommon. Bloody or foul-smelling discharge needs medical assessment, including for a foreign body. Sexual abuse is a less common possible cause, but symptoms alone do not establish it.

topics.name: Vulvovaginitis
topics.clinical_significance: Inflammation of the vagina and vulva that can cause discharge, itching, burning, redness, or pain during sex. Causes include infections such as yeast or trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, and noninfectious irritation or low estrogen. The cause matters because treatment differs.

topics.name: Vulvovaginitis in Children
topics.clinical_significance: In prepubertal children, vulvovaginitis often causes vulvar redness, itching or soreness, and sometimes discharge or painful urination. It is commonly due to irritation or bacteria; yeast infection is uncommon. Foul-smelling or bloody discharge can signal a vaginal foreign body and needs medical assessment.

topics.name: Waldenström Macroglobulinemia
topics.clinical_significance: A slow-growing lymphoma in which abnormal B cells make large amounts of IgM antibody. Many people have no symptoms at first. The disease can cause anemia, recurrent infections, bleeding, or enlarged lymph nodes, liver, or spleen. In some people, excess IgM thickens the blood and causes blurred vision, headache, or other neurologic symptoms.

topics.name: Warts
topics.clinical_significance: Warts are common, benign skin growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and can spread to nearby skin or by contact. Most clear on their own, though warts on the soles may hurt. Ordinary skin warts rarely become cancerous; some genital HPV types carry cancer risk.

topics.name: Water and Sodium Balance
topics.clinical_significance: The kidneys, thirst, and vasopressin keep water and sodium in balance, helping maintain blood volume and fluid concentration. Total body sodium largely determines the volume of fluid outside cells, while the blood sodium level reflects water relative to sodium. Imbalance can cause dehydration, swelling, or dangerous changes in brain function.

topics.name: Weakness
topics.clinical_significance: Weakness is reduced muscle strength, not just fatigue or low energy, and may affect one area or the whole body. Causes include disorders of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, or muscles, as well as illness or medication effects. Sudden one-sided weakness, or weakness with trouble speaking, swallowing, or breathing, needs emergency care.

topics.name: Weight
topics.clinical_significance: A newborn’s weight is interpreted in relation to gestational age, together with length and head circumference. A weight below the 10th percentile is small for gestational age; above the 90th percentile is large for gestational age. These infants may need closer assessment because of risks such as low blood sugar or birth-related complications.

topics.name: Weight Loss, Involuntary
topics.clinical_significance: Unplanned weight loss is clinically important when it exceeds 5% of body weight or 5 kg (about 11 lb) over 6 months. It can be an early sign of a significant physical or mental health problem, sometimes one not yet diagnosed, and warrants evaluation.

topics.name: Well-Woman Visits
topics.clinical_significance: A preventive health visit that supports health across the lifespan. It may include age- and risk-based screening, vaccines, and counseling about sexual, reproductive, and general health. The timing and services are tailored to the person; the visit does not require the same tests or pelvic examination for everyone each year.

topics.name: Wermer Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Wermer syndrome is another name for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), an inherited condition that can cause tumors or overgrowth in the parathyroid glands, pancreas or duodenum, and pituitary. High parathyroid activity and blood calcium are common. Genetic testing and ongoing screening can help detect tumors early in affected people and their relatives.

topics.name: Werner-Morrison Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: Werner-Morrison syndrome (WDHA syndrome) is usually caused by a rare tumor, often in the pancreas, that releases vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). It causes persistent, large-volume watery diarrhea, low potassium, dehydration, and low stomach acid. More than half of these tumors are malignant.

topics.name: Wernicke Encephalopathy
topics.clinical_significance: An acute brain disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, often linked to severe undernutrition or alcohol use disorder. It can cause confusion, abnormal eye movements, and poor balance or coordination, though not all signs may be present. Prompt thiamine treatment is needed to prevent lasting brain damage or death.

topics.name: Wernicke's Encephalopathy
topics.clinical_significance: Wernicke’s encephalopathy is an acute brain disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, often due to severe undernutrition or alcohol use disorder. Confusion, abnormal eye movements, and poor balance or coordination may occur, but not all signs are always present. Prompt thiamine treatment is needed to prevent lasting brain damage or death.

topics.name: West Nile Virus
topics.clinical_significance: West Nile virus is spread mainly by mosquitoes. Most infections cause no symptoms or a mild fever, but about 1 in 150 lead to severe brain or spinal cord disease, such as encephalitis, meningitis, or sudden flaccid paralysis. Older adults and people with weakened immune systems or certain chronic illnesses are at greater risk; severe neurologic disease can cause lasting disability or death.

topics.name: Wheals
topics.clinical_significance: Wheals are raised, often itchy skin swellings caused by fluid in the upper skin. They may move or change, and each usually fades within 24 hours. They are a feature of urticaria and can be triggered by allergy, infection, medicines, or physical factors such as pressure or heat. Tongue or throat swelling or difficulty breathing may signal dangerous airway swelling and requires emergency care.

topics.name: Wheezing
topics.clinical_significance: Wheezing is a high-pitched whistling sound made as air moves through narrowed small airways, usually when breathing out. Asthma and COPD are common causes, but wheezing can also result from an allergic reaction, infection, heart failure, or an inhaled object; it does not always mean asthma. Labored breathing, signs of exhaustion, reduced alertness, or swelling of the face or tongue need emergency assessment.

topics.name: Wheezing and Asthma in Infants and Young Children
topics.clinical_significance: Wheezing is common in infants and young children and is often triggered by viral respiratory infections. Repeated episodes may be an early sign of asthma, especially in children with allergies, eczema, or a family history of asthma, but many young children who wheeze do not later develop asthma. Sudden or persistent localized wheezing needs assessment for other causes, such as an inhaled object.

topics.name: Whipple Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare infection by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei that usually affects the small intestine and can involve joints, brain, heart, and other organs. Joint pain and fever may come first; diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and poor nutrient absorption can develop later, sometimes years afterward. It requires prolonged antibiotic treatment.

topics.name: Whipple's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Whipple’s disease is a rare infection by Tropheryma whipplei that usually affects the small intestine and may involve the joints, heart, brain, and other organs. Joint pain and fever can appear before diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and poor nutrient absorption, sometimes by years. Without treatment, the disease progresses and can be fatal; prolonged antibiotics are required, and relapse can occur.

topics.name: Whipworm Infection
topics.clinical_significance: Whipworm infection (Trichuris trichiura) spreads when people swallow eggs from contaminated soil or food. Light infections often cause no symptoms; heavy infections can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia, and may lead to rectal prolapse, especially in children. It can be treated with antiparasitic medicine.

topics.name: Whitmore Disease
topics.clinical_significance: Whitmore disease (melioidosis) is a potentially life-threatening infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, usually acquired through contact with contaminated soil or water in tropical regions. It commonly affects the lungs but can cause skin or organ abscesses and sepsis. Diabetes and chronic kidney or lung disease increase the risk of severe illness; prolonged antibiotic treatment is needed.

topics.name: Whooping Cough
topics.clinical_significance: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis. It causes prolonged coughing fits that may end in a high-pitched whoop or vomiting, but infants may have pauses in breathing instead. Infants are at greatest risk of severe complications, including pneumonia and life-threatening breathing problems.

topics.name: Wilms Tumor
topics.clinical_significance: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is a kidney cancer that mainly affects young children, usually those under 5 years. It often appears as a painless lump in the abdomen; blood in the urine or high blood pressure may also occur. Treatment depends on the tumor’s stage and other features, and most children are cured.

topics.name: Wilson Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare autosomal recessive disorder in which copper builds up, especially in the liver, brain, and cornea. It can cause liver disease, movement or mood changes, and golden or greenish rings around the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Lifelong treatment is needed to prevent further copper buildup; outcomes are usually good if treatment starts before severe damage occurs.

topics.name: Wilson's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited disorder in which copper builds up in the liver, brain, eyes, and other organs. It can cause liver disease, movement or mood changes, and colored rings around the cornea. Lifelong treatment is needed; early treatment can prevent serious damage.

topics.name: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder that mainly affects boys. It causes eczema, repeated infections, and low numbers of small, defective platelets, which can lead to bleeding. Autoimmune disease and lymphoma can also occur, so specialist care is needed.

topics.name: Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome (WPW Syndrome)
topics.clinical_significance: An extra electrical connection between the upper and lower chambers of the heart can trigger sudden episodes of a very fast heartbeat. If atrial fibrillation occurs, this pathway can make the lower chambers beat dangerously fast and, rarely, cause sudden death. Catheter ablation can often cure the condition.

topics.name: Wolhynia Fever
topics.clinical_significance: A body-louse-borne infection caused by Bartonella quintana. It causes sudden episodes of fever and often severe pain in the shins; a rash may also occur. The bacteria can remain in the blood and sometimes infect the heart valves. Antibiotics treat the infection.

topics.name: Wolman's Disease
topics.clinical_significance: A rare, severe inherited enzyme deficiency that causes fats to build up in organs, especially the liver and spleen. It usually begins in early infancy with poor feeding, vomiting, and a swollen abdomen. Without treatment, it is often fatal in infancy; enzyme replacement treatment is available.

topics.name: Work-Related Asthma
topics.clinical_significance: Asthma that starts because of workplace exposures or preexisting asthma that worsens at work. Triggers include dust, latex, cleaning products, and chemical fumes. Cough, wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath often improve away from work. Work history and breathing tests help identify it; reducing exposure is important.

topics.name: Wrist Dislocations
topics.clinical_significance: Dislocations of the small wrist bones, usually the lunate or nearby carpal bones, often follow a forceful injury. They cause pain, swelling, and deformity and need prompt reduction and orthopedic care. Delayed treatment can injure the median nerve or damage the wrist joint; surgery is often needed.

topics.name: Wrist Fractures
topics.clinical_significance: A common wrist fracture breaks the radius near the wrist, often after a fall on an outstretched hand. It causes pain and swelling, sometimes with deformity. Swelling or a displaced bone can injure the median nerve and cause finger numbness. Some fractures need the bones realigned or surgery, especially if the joint is involved.

topics.name: X Chromosome Abnormalities, Other
topics.clinical_significance: An extra X chromosome in a girl or woman (47,XXX) often causes no obvious physical changes, though mild learning or school difficulties can occur; periods may be irregular, and infertility is possible. Having four or five X chromosomes raises the risk of intellectual disability and birth defects.

topics.name: Xeroderma
topics.clinical_significance: Ordinary dry skin that is not inherited or caused by a systemic disorder. It may look rough or flaky and can itch or crack; severe dryness, especially on the hands, can become inflamed. Cold, dry weather, aging, frequent bathing, and harsh soaps can contribute.

topics.name: Xerophthalmia
topics.clinical_significance: Eye-surface dryness and damage caused by vitamin A deficiency. It can cause poor night vision, dry or foamy patches on the eye, and, if severe, corneal ulcers or softening that may lead to blindness. Prompt vitamin A treatment can prevent progression.

topics.name: Xerosis
topics.clinical_significance: Dry, rough skin that may itch, flake, or crack. It is common with aging, cold or dry weather, frequent bathing, and atopic dermatitis; severe dryness can inflame the hands. Regular moisturizers and avoiding hot water and harsh soaps help keep the skin moist.

topics.name: Xerostomia
topics.clinical_significance: Dry mouth caused by too little saliva. It may make speaking, chewing, and swallowing difficult and increases the risk of tooth decay and oral yeast infection. Medicines are a common cause; head-and-neck radiation and conditions such as Sjögren syndrome can also reduce saliva.

topics.name: Xerotic Keratitis
topics.clinical_significance: Corneal drying and degeneration caused by vitamin A deficiency, often with undernutrition. The cornea can become hazy and ulcerated, sometimes with infection, and severe damage can cause blindness. Prompt vitamin A treatment is important to protect vision.

topics.name: X-linked Agammaglobulinemia
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited X-linked immune disorder, usually in boys, in which few or no B cells lead to very low antibody levels. Repeated bacterial infections, especially in the ears, sinuses, and lungs, often begin in infancy. Immune globulin replacement and prompt antibiotics help prevent and treat infections.

topics.name: X-linked Lymphoproliferative Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A rare inherited immune disorder that mainly affects boys and makes it hard to control Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The first EBV infection can cause severe, sometimes fatal mononucleosis and liver failure. Survivors may develop lymphoma, bone marrow failure, or low antibody levels. Stem cell transplantation is the main treatment.

topics.name: Yellow Fever
topics.clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne infection caused by yellow fever virus. It often begins with fever, headache, and muscle aches; severe disease can cause jaundice, bleeding, shock, and organ failure and may be fatal. Vaccination is the main prevention, and treatment is supportive.

topics.name: ZAP-70 Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: An inherited immune disorder that disrupts T-cell function, especially CD8 T cells. It causes repeated serious infections in infancy or early childhood, including infections by opportunistic germs. Without a blood-forming stem cell transplant, it is fatal; transplant may cure it.

topics.name: Z-E Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A syndrome caused by a gastrin-producing tumor (gastrinoma), usually in the duodenum or pancreas. Excess stomach acid causes repeated, sometimes hard-to-treat ulcers and may cause diarrhea. The tumor may occur with MEN1 or spread to the liver.

topics.name: Zika Virus (ZV) Infections
topics.clinical_significance: A mosquito-borne viral infection that is often symptom-free or causes a mild fever, rash, joint pain, or red eyes. Infection during pregnancy can harm fetal brain and eye development and cause microcephaly; Guillain-Barré syndrome can rarely follow infection. Prevention focuses on avoiding mosquito bites and sexual transmission.

topics.name: Zinc Deficiency
topics.clinical_significance: Low zinc can result from poor intake or poor absorption. It may impair growth and delay sexual development in children, and can cause hair loss, skin rash, diarrhea, reduced taste, poor wound healing, and weakened immunity. Treatment is zinc replacement and correction of the cause.

topics.name: Zinc Supplements
topics.clinical_significance: Zinc supplements treat zinc deficiency, and zinc acetate can reduce copper absorption in Wilson disease. Lozenges may shorten a cold but can cause nausea, mouth irritation, or bad taste; nasal zinc products can cause loss of smell. High or prolonged doses can cause copper deficiency and interfere with some medicines, including antibiotics.

topics.name: Zinc Toxicity
topics.clinical_significance: Too much zinc can cause loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Long-term high doses can lower copper levels, causing anemia, low white blood cell counts, weakened immunity, or nerve damage. Breathing zinc oxide fumes can cause a temporary flu-like illness (metal fume fever).

topics.name: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome
topics.clinical_significance: A syndrome caused by a gastrin-producing tumor (gastrinoma), usually in the duodenum or pancreas. Excess stomach acid can cause severe, recurring ulcers that are hard to treat and may bleed or perforate; diarrhea is also common. The tumor may be linked to MEN1 or spread to other organs.

topics.name: Zoonotic Skin Diseases
topics.clinical_significance: Rare viral skin infections caught through direct contact with infected sheep, goats, or cattle. Orf and milker’s nodules usually cause a single lesion on a finger or hand and heal on their own. Orf may also cause fever and swollen nearby lymph nodes.

topics.name: Zygomycosis
topics.clinical_significance: Zygomycosis, now commonly called mucormycosis, is a rapidly spreading fungal infection. It mainly affects people with weakened immunity or poorly controlled diabetes and can destroy tissue in the sinuses, eyes, brain, lungs, or skin. It is often life-threatening and needs urgent antifungal treatment, usually with surgery to remove dead tissue.
